metadata.abstract: Carriers of the BDNF Val66Met allele may derive greater cognitive benefit from fiber-rich foods and probiotic supplementation than noncarriers, possibly through gut microbiota-mediated signaling along the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized trial, 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a multi-strain probiotic plus dietary counseling to increase fermentable fiber or counseling alone. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiles were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Linear mixed models tested interactions between intervention and BDNF genotype. The probiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium (P = 0.02) and butyrate (P = 0.04) compared with controls. A significant genotype-by-intervention interaction emerged for executive function (P = 0.03): Met carriers improved more after probiotic and fiber than Val/Val carriers. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings suggest that BDNF variation moderates gut-brain responses to dietary fiber and probiotics, supporting personalized nutritional strategies for cognitive decline.

Depletion of short-chain fatty acids in the colon precedes neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, suggesting that gut microbiota metabolites gate brain vulnerability. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a control diet; probiotic supplementation was balanced across arms. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundances, interleukin-6, and BDNF expression were measured using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and ELISA. With linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline, age, and APOE4 status, the intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (β = 0.42, P = 0.008) and reduced interleukin-6 (β = −0.31, P = 0.021); PERMANOVA confirmed intervention-driven community separation, and false discovery rate correction controlled multiple comparisons. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial shifts explained 28% of the cognitive improvement. In germ-free mice, colonization with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii attenuated neuroinflammation. Collectively, these findings support targeting the gut microbiome through fermented foods and probiotics to mitigate neuroinflammation in patients.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshapes the gut microbiota and reduces depressive-like behavior in rodent models, but the microbial signals coupling omega-3 intake to central neuroinflammation remain poorly defined. We fed male C57BL/6J mice a control diet or a diet enriched with fish oil for 8 weeks and exposed them to chronic unpredictable mild stress. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota revealed that fish oil increased the relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in colon contents. In the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, fish oil lowered interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha and restored Bdnf expression. Behavioral tests showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and improved spatial memory. Fecal microbiota transfer from fish oil-fed mice to antibiotic-treated mice partially reproduced these benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings indicate that omega-3 supplementation exerts gut-brain effects through microbiota-dependent modulation of cytokines and BDNF signaling. Together, these results suggest that dietary omega-3 supplementation may serve as an adjunctive strategy for stress-related disorders by targeting the gut microbiome.

Microbial dysbiosis in the gut can precede neurodegeneration by years, and its metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharides, influence brain neuroinflammation through APOE, TREM2, and NF-κB-dependent pathways. In mice and patients with Alzheimer's disease, reduced Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes abundance correlates with altered BDNF and IL-1β expression, suggesting a causal contribution to cognitive decline. We tested whether dietary curcumin or resveratrol could reverse these shifts in a mouse model of aging. Using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics, we found that both phytochemicals increased Akkermansia and Lactobacillus, decreased Proteobacteria, and normalized TREM2, BDNF, and NF-κB levels. Curcumin additionally lowered interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α in the hippocampus, while resveratrol enhanced butyrate production. These changes accompanied improved Morris water maze performance and reduced amyloid pathology. The results suggest that dietary phytochemicals may ameliorate gut-brain axis dysfunction by modulating gut microbiota-gene interactions, though clinical validation in humans is needed.

Supplementation with Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates stress-induced depressive-like behavior in mice, yet the metabolic routes linking intestinal changes to brain function remain incompletely defined. Using chronic restraint stress mice, we tested whether 4-week probiotic administration altered short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, tryptophan catabolism, and serotonin availability. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, with elevated butyrate in feces and reduced kynurenine in serum. Alpha diversity, assessed by Shannon and Chao1 indices, was higher in treated animals, and permutational multivariate analysis of variance showed distinct microbial community structures. In hippocampus, BDNF and GABA-A receptor transcripts were upregulated after treatment. Spearman correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus to butyrate, 5-hydroxytryptamine, and behavioral scores. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that treatment effects on depressive-like behavior were mediated partly by SCFA-related pathways. These findings position L. rhamnosus as a plausible psychobiotic for stress-related disorders, although validation in patients is needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet causality and mediating pathways remain contested. We analyzed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing data from patients with MDD and healthy controls, integrating short-chain fatty acid profiles and BDNF expression in mice after fecal microbiota transplantation. Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Bifidobacterium were depleted in depression, while Eggerthella and Flavonifractor were enriched. A random-effects meta-analysis across 12 cohorts confirmed reduced alpha diversity (Shannon index, standardized mean difference = −0.41, 95% CI −0.58 to −0.24). Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-lactate partially explained the association between microbial composition and depressive symptoms. Notably, Mendelian randomization suggested a protective effect of genetically proxied Lactobacillus abundance on depression. In mice, transplantation of microbiota from patients with MDD reduced BDNF in the hippocampus and increased anxiety-like behavior. These findings support a causal contribution of gut microbial dysbiosis to depression and highlight microbial metabolites as candidate targets.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids are increasingly recognized as mediators of gut microbiota-brain communication, yet their causal role in depression remains contested. We combined 16S rRNA sequencing of human stool with two-sample Mendelian randomization to test whether butyrate-producing bacteria and circulating butyrate influence depressive symptoms. Dietary exposures, including Western-style diet and fermented foods, were assessed by food frequency questionnaire. In a cohort of 312 participants, lower microbial richness correlated with higher depression scores after adjustment for dietary fiber and antidepressant use. In mice fed a high-fat diet, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum restored hippocampal BDNF expression and reduced interleukin-6 relative to vehicle-treated controls. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 27% of the effect of microbial diversity on depression-like behavior. Causal estimates remained robust in sensitivity analyses excluding pleiotropic variants. These findings support targeted prebiotic and probiotic strategies, alongside reduced ultra-processed food intake, as adjunctive approaches for depression.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes behavioral deficits in chronic stress models and predicts treatment response in major depressive disorder, yet the molecular routes linking intestinal microbiota to limbic circuits remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we show that high-fat diet-associated microbiota increases anxiety-like behavior and impairs hippocampal plasticity. This phenotype coincided with reduced Bdnf expression, elevated Il6 and Tlr4 transcripts, and lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the colon. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance declined, whereas Clostridiales expanded. Dietary supplementation with prebiotic fiber partially normalized Bdnf and Tlr4 expression and attenuated depressive-like behavior, but did not fully restore gut microbial composition. In patients with depression, baseline gut microbiota profiles correlated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor response, and random forest models identified Faecalibacterium and Bacteroides as discriminative taxa. These findings position gut microbiota as a modifiable node in the gut-brain axis and support targeted dietary strategies for stress-related psychiatric disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape central nervous system immune tone, yet how gut microbiota composition translates into depressive-like behavior remains unresolved. We performed fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder into mice and profiled cecal contents by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and hippocampus by RNA sequencing. Differential abundance analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis linked Lactobacillus depletion to reduced Bdnf and Tph1 expression. Mediation analysis indicated that indole-3-propionate mediated the association between Clostridium abundance and Bdnf transcripts. Recipients also showed increased immobility in the forced swim test and reduced sucrose preference. In parallel, random forest classification identified a microbiota signature that discriminated anhedonia from resilience with an area under the curve of 0.84. Optogenetic stimulation of vagal afferents attenuated neuroinflammation and normalized anhedonia, while pharmacological inhibition of BDNF signaling abolished this effect. These findings identify a microbiota-BDNF axis modulated by bacterial metabolites and suggest that targeting Lactobacillus or indole-3-propionate may relieve depression.

Distinct compositional shifts in the gut microbiome accompany major depressive disorder, yet whether microbial metabolites communicate with brain circuits through host gene regulation remains unresolved. We profiled fecal microbiota and circulating metabolites in 120 adults with depression and 90 controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Bacteroides and Ruminococcus gnavus enriched in depression. Mediation analysis tested whether microbial features influenced BDNF expression and symptom severity. Bacteroides abundance correlated inversely with BDNF and positively with N-methylglutamate; Ruminococcus gnavus tracked with glucosamine. In random forest models, a microbial signature plus BDNF explained 38% of variance in depressive symptoms, and receiver operating characteristic analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.81. In germ-free mice, colonization with Bacteroides or Ruminococcus gnavus altered BDNF transcripts in the hippocampus. These findings position gut microbial metabolites as potential upstream regulators of BDNF signaling in the brain, offering testable targets for depression.

A Western-style diet rich in saturated fat and refined sugar intensifies gut microbiota dysbiosis and neuroinflammation, yet the extent to which this process is modified by host APOE4 status and omega-3 supplementation remains unclear. In a 16-week trial, 96 older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids or control while maintaining their habitual diet. We profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and quantified circulating interleukin-6, lipopolysaccharide, and short-chain fatty acids. Cognitive performance and hippocampal volume were assessed with fMRI and neuropsychological tests. Linear mixed models showed that omega-3 increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and reduced interleukin-6 only in APOE4 non-carriers. In APOE4 carriers, the Western-style diet was associated with lower Akkermansia muciniphila and faster cognitive decline, regardless of omega-3 treatment. Mediation analysis indicated that F. prausnitzii partly explained the omega-3 effect on interleukin-6. These findings suggest that APOE4 stratifies gut-brain responses to omega-3, informing precision nutrition strategies.

Dysbiosis characterized by depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced butyrate production accompanies depressive-like behavior in mice subjected to chronic social stress, implicating gut microbiota in BDNF regulation within the hippocampus. To determine whether dietary fiber reverses this phenotype, male C57BL/6 mice were randomized to a Western diet or an isocaloric Western diet supplemented with fermented wheat bran for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that fermented wheat bran expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations and increased gut microbial diversity. Quantitative RT-PCR showed elevated BDNF, ZO-1, and occludin transcripts in colon and hippocampus. Morris water maze testing demonstrated improved spatial memory in supplemented mice, whereas ELISA detected lower corticosterone, IL-6, and TNF-α concentrations. Western blotting confirmed increased BDNF protein in the hippocampus. These results suggest that fermented fiber attenuates stress-induced cognitive impairment through microbiota-dependent BDNF signaling and improved intestinal barrier integrity. Together, these data position dietary fiber as a plausible adjunct for stress-related mood disorders, although human trials are needed to confirm causality.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production are increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis, yet the contribution of host APOE genotype remains poorly defined. In mice carrying the APOE4 allele, consumption of a Western diet depleted Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, elevated lipopolysaccharide in the portal circulation, and increased amyloid-beta deposition in the hippocampus. Faecal microbiota transplantation from Western diet-fed donors into germ-free mice reproduced neuroinflammation. Conversely, inulin supplementation restored Bifidobacterium abundance, normalized butyrate levels, and attenuated neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of faecal microbiota from participants revealed that APOE4 carriers exhibited lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and higher Escherichia coli relative abundance than non-carriers. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for diet, antibiotic use, and diabetes showed that each 10% increase in Faecalibacterium was associated with a 15% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease. Mendelian randomization in adults supported a causal effect of gut microbiota-derived butyrate on Alzheimer's disease risk. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and prebiotic interventions may mitigate APOE4-related Alzheimer's disease through microbiome-mediated metabolite signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Disruption of the gut microbiota during early life can reprogram hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis stress reactivity and BDNF signaling in the prefrontal cortex, a pathway implicated in major depressive disorder. In mice exposed to antibiotics, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the colon. Notably, tryptophan catabolism shifted toward kynurenine in mice with depleted microbiota, and this shift correlated with neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors restored butyrate levels and normalized depressive-like behavior. Using Spearman correlation and PERMANOVA, we found that microbial composition explained 32% of behavioral variance. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and prebiotic galacto-oligosaccharides increased serotonin turnover in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These effects were abolished by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, indicating that vagus nerve signaling is required for probiotic- and prebiotic-driven behavioral improvements. Our findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with dietary supplements may offer a tractable strategy for stress-related disorders, though validation in patients remains necessary.

Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid generated by gut microbiota from dietary fiber, promotes brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus and suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines, linking gut microbial metabolism to depressive-like behavior. In mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress, butyrylated starch increased butyrate delivery to the colon, restored Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae abundance, and normalized BDNF and tight junction protein transcripts. These changes coincided with reduced corticosterone, lower IL-6, and attenuated anxiety-like behavior. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics identified indole-3-propionate and inosine as candidate mediators. In a pilot human cohort, higher fiber intake correlated with elevated butyrate and BDNF levels, although mixed-effects models revealed substantial interindividual variability. Parallel fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice transferred the butyrate-dependent BDNF increase, while antibiotic depletion abolished it. Together, these findings position fermentable fiber and butyrylated starch as modulators of gut microbiota-brain signaling through SCFA-BDNF pathways, suggesting potential benefit for stress-related disorders.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet the mediating microbial metabolites remain poorly defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, we profiled fecal samples from older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and healthy controls. Dietary intake was assessed with a Mediterranean diet score. We applied linear mixed-effects models to test associations between microbial taxa and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted in MCI, while Escherichia-Shigella was enriched. These shifts correlated with reduced butyrate levels and increased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in serum. Mediation analysis revealed that butyrate mediated the relationship between gut microbiome diversity and cognitive impairment. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila was inversely associated with LPS, and APOE genotype did not modify these associations. Targeting the gut microbiome via dietary fiber or probiotics may offer therapeutic avenues for neurodegeneration. Future studies should validate these findings using metabolomics in larger cohorts.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate microglial activation and may dampen neuroinflammation in major depressive disorder (MDD). To test whether diet-shaped gut microbiota tracks with symptom severity, we profiled fecal communities from 84 adults with MDD and 62 controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and quantified plasma metabolites by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated Mediterranean diet score and fermented food frequency questionnaire. A random forest classifier trained on species-level abundances discriminated cases from controls (AUC = 0.78), with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus plantarum among the top predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly mediated the inverse association between fiber intake and depressive symptoms. Higher fermented food consumption correlated with greater microbial diversity and lower anxiety scores. These findings support a diet–microbiome–brain axis in which fermented foods and fiber may complement existing antidepressant treatment, though longitudinal models are needed to establish causality.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and bile acid metabolites shape central nervous system immune tone, yet how host APOE, BDNF, and TLR4 variation modifies these signals remains poorly resolved. We analyzed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics from stool samples of 412 adults, integrating gut microbiome profiles with host genotypes. Participants consuming a high-fiber diet rich in fermented foods showed greater Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia abundance and higher butyrate concentrations than those on a Western diet. Among carriers of APOE ε4, probiotic supplementation for 12 weeks was associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved cognitive impairment scores, but only when baseline microbial diversity was high. Mixed-effects models revealed interactions between TLR4 variants and Lactobacillus abundance on neuroinflammation markers, while BDNF methylation correlated with Bifidobacterium relative abundance. These findings suggest that dietary and supplement strategies may require stratification by host genotype and baseline microbiome composition to effectively modulate the gut-brain axis in neuropsychiatric disorders.

Gut microbiota depletion consistently precedes depressive-like behavior in rodent models, yet the pathways linking microbial metabolites to the brain remain unresolved. In a randomized human cohort (n=120), dietary fiber supplementation increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate concentrations in feces, with parallel reductions in interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the effect of fiber on depression scores. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber donors upregulated Bdnf and Bcl2 in the hippocampus while downregulating Nfkb1 and Tnf. These changes were absent in germ-free mice receiving butyrate-deficient microbiota. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that butyrate predicted Bdnf expression after false discovery rate correction. Parallel 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Bacteroides and Prevotella correlated inversely with inflammatory cytokines, and Spearman correlation linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii to Bdnf expression. The findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut microbiota intervention, though randomized controlled trials with metagenomic sequencing are needed to validate causality in patients with major depressive disorder.

Disruption of the gut microbiota during early life can prime neurodevelopmental disorders and metabolic disorders, yet dietary levers that stabilize the microbiota-gut-brain axis remain incompletely defined. In a mouse model of chronic stress, we tested whether probiotic supplementation combined with a fermented food diet altered prefrontal cortex serotonin turnover and fecal microbiota composition. Mice received either Lactobacillus rhamnosus or vehicle for four weeks; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and PERMANOVA were used to assess β-diversity. Random forest classification identified microbial taxa discriminating stressed from control mice. Probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus abundance, reduced corticosterone levels, and normalized serotonin turnover relative to vehicle. A fermented food diet alone produced smaller effects, but combined treatment attenuated anxiety-like behavior and neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis suggested that Lactobacillus abundance partly explained the behavioral benefits. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate, were also quantified and correlated with Lactobacillus abundance. These findings indicate that probiotics plus fermented foods may protect against stress-related psychiatric disorders by reshaping the gut microbiome, though human validation is needed.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber produces short-chain fatty acids that modulate brain function, yet the extent to which this pathway contributes to anxiety remains unclear. In an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 88 adults with high trait anxiety received inulin supplementation or a maltodextrin placebo. Fecal microbiota was assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry for short-chain fatty acids. Changes in microbial community structure were analyzed using linear mixed models. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and elevated fecal butyrate. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced anxiety scores and lower amygdala reactivity during functional magnetic resonance imaging. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially explained the anxiety reduction, and increases in BDNF expression accompanied symptom improvement. These findings link inulin supplementation, gut microbiota remodeling, and microbial metabolites to anxiety improvement, supporting targeted nutritional approaches for stress-related disorders. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90% in both groups.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbiota and elevates short-chain fatty acid production, a route increasingly linked to central nervous system function. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and quantitative PCR to resolve microbial and metabolic shifts along the gut-brain axis. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate and GABA in feces, and normalized BDNF and GAD1 expression in the hippocampus. These changes coincided with reduced anxiety-like behavior and lower corticosterone. Bifidobacterium-derived butyrate alone partially reproduced the BDNF induction, while vagotomy abolished the behavioral effect, implicating vagus nerve signaling. Linear mixed models confirmed that microbial and metabolic predictors explained a significant portion of behavioral variance. Fecal microbiota transfer from inulin-fed mice to naive mice recapitulated the BDNF and butyrate increases, and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated positively with BDNF expression. Our findings suggest that inulin may serve as a practical adjunct for stress-related psychiatric disorders, though human trials are needed.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and intestine permeability are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder and irritable bowel syndrome, yet whether microbial signals causally influence brain function remains unresolved. We recruited adults with depression and IBS and healthy controls, collecting fecal microbiota samples. Microbial communities were profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics; short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Associations between Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and symptom severity were tested with linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for dietary fiber intake, antidepressant use, and age. Higher Prevotella abundance correlated with lower anxiety scores, while Clostridium cluster XIVa was associated with greater visceral pain. A probiotic intervention in a subset altered microbial diversity but not depressive symptoms. These associations were robust in sensitivity analyses. These findings suggest that gut microbial composition, rather than a single bacterial species, may shape gut-brain signaling, and that multi-omics approaches are needed to identify actionable targets.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism intersects with aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling to modulate neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior. In mice colonized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fed a high-fiber diet, gut microbiota fermentation increased butyrate and indole-3-lactic acid, while reducing interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor transcripts in the hippocampus. These changes were accompanied by elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor and improved performance on forced swim test. Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids further amplified butyrate production and normalized glucocorticoid receptor expression in the prefrontal cortex. In adults with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbial diversity correlated with BDNF methylation and anxiety scores. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was inversely associated with interleukin-1 beta expression in participants reporting anhedonia. Mechanistically, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 activation and kynurenine flux linked microbial composition to neuropsychiatric symptoms. A randomized placebo-controlled trial combining probiotic and fermented food intake is warranted to determine whether targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis can augment selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor efficacy.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate gut microbiota composition and host BDNF expression, but whether these shifts translate into measurable changes in the hippocampus and affect in humans remains debated. We conducted an 8-week randomized controlled trial in adults with subclinical anxiety who received either a prebiotic fiber supplement or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and targeted metabolomics quantified microbial communities and microbial metabolites. Mixed-effects models tested associations with BDNF methylation, cortisol awakening response, and anxiety scores. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and raised fecal butyrate; these changes correlated with reduced anxiety and lower BDNF promoter methylation. Participants with higher baseline Bifidobacterium showed greater butyrate increases and larger symptom improvement. Germ-free mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota displayed reduced anxiety-like behavior and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that fermentable dietary fiber can reshape gut microbiota, elevate butyrate, and modify BDNF-related epigenetic tone, providing a plausible microbial route to anxiety relief.

Dietary dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate brain function through microbial metabolites, yet strain- and context-dependent effects remain unresolved. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with subclinical anxiety received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods plus a multi-strain probiotic, or a control diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomics quantified microbial community structure and short-chain fatty acid output. Gamma-aminobutyric acid-related pathways and tryptophan metabolism were assessed as candidate mediators. Compared with controls, the intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced self-reported anxiety scores. These changes correlated with altered host gene expression in peripheral blood, including interleukin-10 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor signaling. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the microbiota-anxiety association. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled before and after intervention, and bile acid pools were also measured. The findings support targeted diet and supplement strategies for stress-related disorders, though longer trials are needed.

Resistant starch supplementation reshapes the gut microbiome and attenuates Parkinson's disease (PD)-like motor deficits in mice, an effect linked to increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and elevated short-chain fatty acid production. To test whether this effect operates in patients, we recruited 40 individuals with PD and 20 healthy controls. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing; tyrosine hydroxylase and glial fibrillary acidic protein expression were quantified in colon biopsies using quantitative PCR. After 12 weeks, resistant starch increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, reduced Enterobacteriaceae, and lowered inflammatory cytokine levels. Mixed-effects modeling showed that microbial shifts correlated with improved constipation and gastrointestinal symptom scores, but not with motor severity. In parallel, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed enriched butyrate synthesis pathways and reduced lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis in responders. Spearman correlation linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance to serotonin levels and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in substantia nigra. These findings suggest that dietary resistant starch may modulate gut microbiota in PD, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve MCC1274 attenuated cognitive decline in older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but its effects on gut microbiota and microbial metabolites remain unclear. In a 24-week randomized trial, participants received either probiotic (B. breve MCC1274) or placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics profiled gut microbial communities and short-chain fatty acids. Linear mixed-effects models tested longitudinal changes, and random forest classification identified taxa associated with cognitive improvement. Probiotic increased Akkermansia and Lactobacillus abundances, which correlated with higher butyrate and propionate levels. These changes were accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation markers and preserved hippocampal volume on MRI. In MCI mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated cognitive protection, whereas vagotomy abolished the benefit, implicating the vagus nerve. Baseline microbial diversity and metabolite profiles predicted response, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirming separation between groups. These findings support a microbiota-metabolite axis through which probiotics may delay MCI progression.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that reinforce intestinal barrier integrity and dampen neuroinflammation via GPR43- and HDAC-dependent signaling. In a randomized crossover study, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a synbiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus plus inulin, or placebo, for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified taxonomic shifts and fecal butyrate, respectively. Functional magnetic resonance imaging during an n-back task assessed hippocampal activation. Compared with placebo, the synbiotic supplement increased Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and improved mixed-effects model estimates of cognitive composite scores. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and increased BDNF in plasma. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing confirmed parallel shifts in gut microbiome composition, including expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium taxa. Transfer of fecal slurries from responders into germ-free mice reproduced lower interleukin-6 and higher BDNF, linking microbial fermentation to brain plasticity. Targeting gut microbiome fermentation with fermentable fiber and probiotics may offer a tractable strategy for early Alzheimer's disease.

Chronic depression is increasingly linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis and reduced short-chain fatty acid production, yet effective dietary interventions remain limited. In a mouse model of chronic unpredictable mild stress, galacto-oligosaccharide supplementation for six weeks attenuated depressive-like behavior, restored hippocampal serotonin turnover, and lowered corticosterone levels. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that galacto-oligosaccharide increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance while decreasing Desulfovibrio and Clostridium. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice reproduced the behavioral benefit, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. Targeted metabolomics showed elevated butyrate and propionate in colon contents and serum. Spearman correlation analysis linked butyrate levels with BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex and with anxiety-like behavior scores. Behavioral recovery was accompanied by reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in the brain, and increased ZO-1 expression in the intestine. These findings suggest that galacto-oligosaccharide may alleviate depression through a microbiota-SCFA-BDNF axis, supporting prebiotic intervention as an adjunctive strategy for mood disorders.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota shape central nervous system function, yet the pathways linking intestinal dysbiosis to neuropsychiatric disorders remain poorly defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we profiled microbial communities and occludin expression in colon, blood, and hippocampus. Patients with major depressive disorder showed reduced Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium abundance and elevated lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition partially mediated the association between systemic inflammation and depressive symptoms. In mice, transplantation of patient-derived microbiota increased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, impaired intestinal barrier integrity, and altered BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced butyrate production. Random forest classification discriminated patients from controls with moderate accuracy, and multivariate linear regression linked microbial diversity to ZO-1 expression in intestinal mucosa. These changes were attenuated by minocycline or omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Our findings position gut microbial communities as modifiable contributors to neuroinflammation and suggest that targeting microbiota may complement existing therapies for stress-related disorders.

Altered gut microbial composition is increasingly recognized as a contributor to neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet whether probiotic supplementation can reshape the gut-brain axis remains unresolved. We recruited 60 patients with MS and 30 healthy controls, collected stool samples, and performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing to profile the gut microbiome. Participants received a 12-week probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium or a control condition. Baseline gut microbiota profiles separated patients with MS from healthy controls, with lower Faecalibacterium and higher Escherichia-Shigella in MS. Microbial community differences were assessed using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe). Patients receiving probiotics showed increased relative abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, and reduced circulating inflammatory markers. These changes correlated with improved expanded disability status scale scores and reduced depressive symptoms. Our findings suggest that probiotics may modulate the gut-brain axis and slow disability progression in MS, supporting microbiome-targeted dietary interventions as adjunctive therapy.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking intestinal ecology to depression and anxiety. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 8 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool microbiota and qPCR quantification of BDNF, TPH1, and SLC6A4 in peripheral blood were performed at baseline and endpoint. Probiotic treatment increased Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo. Baseline gut microbial composition predicted response, with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance in remitters. Changes in BDNF expression correlated inversely with microbial diversity and serotonin turnover. Mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from responders showed increased hippocampal BDNF and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Longitudinal mixed-effects modeling confirmed that tryptophan availability mediated the microbiota-BDNF relationship. Neither selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors nor omega-3 supplementation altered these associations. These findings support a microbiota-BDNF axis responsive to fermented foods and probiotics, with potential for antidepressant augmentation.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet the mediating microbial and dietary signals remain incompletely defined. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bacteroides species ferment dietary fiber into butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids, which reinforce intestinal barrier integrity, dampen cytokine release, and modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In a two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis of adults, genetically predicted abundance of butyrate-producing taxa was inversely associated with depression, with mediation analysis attributing part of this effect to inflammatory markers. A randomized trial of probiotic supplementation combined with fermented foods showed improved anxiety symptoms and increased microbial diversity relative to a Western diet control. Preclinical models further show that prebiotic oligosaccharides and polyphenol-rich foods can attenuate neuroinflammation and preserve blood–brain barrier function. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial interventions targeting short-chain fatty acid production may provide adjunctive strategies for depression and anxiety, although larger longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality and optimal supplement formulations.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that shape microglial function and hippocampal plasticity, yet the causal link to memory remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and fed them inulin-rich or low-fiber diets for eight weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and butyrate in feces and brain. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that inulin increased butyrate by 2.4-fold and rescued spatial memory deficits in mice compared with low-fiber diets. This behavioral improvement coincided with elevated Bdnf expression and BDNF protein in the hippocampus, alongside reduced interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α. Broad-spectrum antibiotics abolished the inulin-dependent BDNF induction and cognitive benefit, while sodium butyrate supplementation partially restored them. These findings position microbiota-derived butyrate as a critical mediator linking dietary fiber to BDNF-dependent hippocampal function, suggesting that fiber-enriched diets may mitigate age-related cognitive decline.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet predicts slower cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease, yet the microbial pathways linking gut and brain remain uncertain. We analyzed stool microbiota and plasma short-chain fatty acids from 180 older adults with mild cognitive impairment, using mediation analysis within linear mixed models. Dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods were associated with greater Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and higher butyrate concentrations. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced neuroinflammation and better cognitive performance over 18 months. Mediation analysis indicated that gut microbiota composition explained 32% of the association between Mediterranean diet and cognitive decline. No significant effects were observed for probiotic supplements after adjustment for diet quality. These findings suggest that dietary patterns enriching butyrate-producing taxa may slow neurodegeneration, supporting targeted nutrition rather than broad probiotic use. Validation in randomized controlled trials with shotgun metagenomics and metabolomics is warranted. Findings were robust in sensitivity analyses excluding antibiotic users.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, but whether probiotic supplementation causally improves symptoms through BDNF-dependent pathways remains unclear. We analyzed fecal microbiota and serum short-chain fatty acids from 248 adults with depression and 124 controls, then applied Mendelian randomization using BDNF and TLR4 variants as instruments. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus abundance in affected individuals. After 12 weeks of probiotics, mixed-effects models showed greater reduction in depressive symptoms than control condition, with parallel increases in butyrate and altered BDNF methylation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 31% of the treatment effect on hippocampal activity. In a separate mouse model, probiotic administration normalized BDNF expression and reduced neuroinflammatory cytokines. Baseline microbial diversity correlated with BDNF promoter methylation (r = -0.28, p = 0.004), and random forest classification achieved an AUC of 0.81. These findings support a causal chain from microbial composition to metabolites, BDNF regulation, and depression severity, suggesting probiotic strategies warrant further clinical trials.

Diets enriched with fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich foods can remodel the gut microbiota, increasing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production. These microbial shifts modulate intestinal barrier integrity, vagal signaling, and systemic cytokine profiles, thereby affecting brain regions implicated in anxiety and depression. In a randomized human trial, adults with metabolic syndrome received either a high-fiber diet or the same diet plus probiotic supplementation for 12 weeks. Linear mixed models showed that the probiotic group had greater reductions in depressive symptoms and C-reactive protein than diet alone, alongside higher gut microbial diversity. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, taxa linked to butyrate synthesis and BDNF expression. Circulating short-chain fatty acids correlated inversely with anxiety scores, and fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced the behavioral improvement. These findings suggest that combining dietary fiber with probiotics may yield complementary benefits for gut-brain health, although longer trials are needed to confirm durability and causality.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape brain function through vagus nerve and immune signaling, but whether whole blueberries can remodel this dialog in humans remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received blueberry powder or control for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma metabolites were measured by untargeted metabolomics. Linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation tested treatment effects and microbe-metabolite-clinical associations. Blueberry supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. These shifts correlated with higher BDNF and lower depression scores. No changes occurred in Bacteroides or Lactobacillus. We also quantified indole-3-propionic acid and serotonin, which increased in the blueberry group and mediated the association between Akkermansia muciniphila and BDNF in mediation analysis. Our data suggest that blueberries act as a prebiotic substrate, modulating the gut microbiota and gut-brain axis to improve cognitive decline. These findings position blueberries as a practical dietary strategy for neuroinflammation.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that suppress neuroinflammation and preserve blood-brain barrier integrity, yet the extent to which these effects depend on baseline microbiota composition remains unresolved. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either inulin (12 g/day) or placebo for 16 weeks. Fecal metagenomic sequencing and plasma targeted metabolomics were performed. Mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and raised butyrate by 28%. Higher butyrate correlated with lower IL6 and TNF expression in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the improvement in cognitive impairment. In mice, fiber deprivation abolished these benefits. Baseline Bacteroides abundance modified treatment response, with random forest classification identifying responders with 0.79 AUC. No serious adverse events occurred, and placebo groups showed no change in butyrate. These findings support dietary fiber-targeted microbiome modulation as a plausible strategy for slowing cognitive decline.

Alterations in gut microbial communities can precede Parkinson's disease diagnosis by years, suggesting that enteric bacteria influence central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. In a 24-month longitudinal cohort of adults, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and, in a subset, shotgun metagenomics, while quantifying short-chain fatty acids in plasma. Participants receiving a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium showed higher butyrate levels and lower constipation severity than nonusers. We used mixed-effects models to account for repeated measures, and mediation analysis to test whether microbial composition linked supplement exposure to clinical severity scores. At baseline, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder was present in 38 participants, and Cox proportional hazards models estimated a 1.7-fold higher risk of phenoconversion among those with low Prevotellaceae. Prevotellaceae abundance was inversely associated with neuroinflammation markers, whereas Enterobacteriaceae correlated with worse gastrointestinal dysfunction. These findings support a model in which dietary fiber and probiotics modulate microbiota-gut-brain signaling, but causal inference remains limited by observational design.
