metadata.abstract: Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of the gut microbiota–brain axis, yet their contribution to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics, we profiled patients with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls. Reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, together with lower butyrate concentrations, distinguished patients from controls. These microbial shifts correlated with decreased BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and with poorer cognitive performance, even after adjustment for age and sex using linear regression. In APP/PS1 mice, sodium butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf transcription in the hippocampus, lowered amyloid-β burden, and attenuated memory deficits. A parallel pilot in older adults showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and fecal SCFA output, accompanied by improved cognitive scores. Higher baseline fiber intake was likewise associated with greater butyrate-producing microbiota and slower cognitive decline. These findings position butyrate-producing bacteria and BDNF signaling as tractable targets, and support prebiotic or butyrate interventions for AD-related cognitive decline.

Dietary polyphenols can reshape the gut microbiota and attenuate neuroinflammation, yet translation into resilient brain function remains constrained by poor bioavailability and interindividual microbial variability. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we tested whether a polyphenol-rich diet supplemented with probiotics alters microbial community structure and stress-related behavior. The diet increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated short-chain fatty acids, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These changes correlated with higher BDNF expression in the hippocampus and lower interleukin-6 levels. Probiotic co-administration further enhanced butyrate production and reduced stress-induced pathology. In healthy adults, a pilot randomized controlled trial showed similar microbiota shifts after 8 weeks of the same polyphenol-rich diet, although effects on depressive symptoms were modest. These findings suggest that combining dietary fibers and probiotics may provide a tractable strategy for modulating the gut microbiota to promote brain health, but larger trials with metagenomic profiling are needed. Longitudinal sampling is required to distinguish causality from association.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that influence brain function, but whether these microbial products mediate the cognitive effects of fiber-rich diets in older adults is unclear. We randomized 120 participants with mild cognitive impairment to a high-fiber diet or inulin for 12 weeks. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma tryptophan metabolites were quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Linear mixed models tested associations with BDNF levels and hippocampal volume. Both interventions increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate producers, with the high-fiber diet producing broader shifts than inulin. Greater Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with higher indole-3-propionic acid and improved memory scores; changes in BDNF tracked with hippocampal volume only in the high-fiber diet group. These effects were independent of Alzheimer's disease risk genes, although APOE carriers showed weaker responses. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and inulin engage distinct microbiota-dependent pathways along the gut-brain axis, with indole-3-propionic acid as a candidate mediator of cognitive benefit.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes nigrostriatal degeneration in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether microbial signals causally modulate SNCA expression remains unresolved. This deficit is accompanied by increased calprotectin and zonulin, suggesting impaired intestinal barrier integrity. In a cohort of 84 participants, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed depleted Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in patients with PD versus controls. Random forest classification separated groups with an AUC of 0.82, and Spearman correlation linked F. prausnitzii abundance to butyrate concentrations and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. A 12-week randomized intervention with the probiotic VSL#3 plus inulin increased gut microbial diversity, raised butyrate, and reduced IL-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and BMI confirmed that these shifts coincided with improved UPDRS-III scores and TREM2 and GLP1R upregulation in monocytes. Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate accounted for 31% of the association between F. prausnitzii and BDNF expression. Our findings suggest that microbiota-directed supplementation can engage immune-metabolic programs relevant to PD progression.

Disruption of the gut microbiome precedes Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related hippocampal pathology, yet whether microbial metabolites causally modulate microglial inflammatory genes remains contested. We colonized germ-free APP/PS1 mice with Bacteroides fragilis and Lactobacillus rhamnosus and quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in feces and serum using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Cognitive performance was assessed by Morris water maze, while Il1b, Tnf, and Arg1 expression in cortex was measured with RT-qPCR. Associations between butyrate, acetate, and behavioral outcomes were tested using linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Colonized mice showed elevated butyrate, reduced Il1b and Tnf, and improved spatial memory relative to controls; probiotic supplementation replicated these effects, whereas vancomycin abolished them. Butyrate correlated inversely with Tnf and positively with Arg1, suggesting that microbiota-derived SCFAs restrain neuroinflammation in AD. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responder mice into naive recipients reproduced the Arg1 shift, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained part of the cognitive benefit. Parallel validation in human cohorts will determine whether these gut microbial metabolites are tractable targets for AD prevention.

Short-chain fatty acid signaling through the gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a modifier of central nervous system function, yet the pathways linking microbial metabolism to affective behavior remain incompletely defined. In a murine model of chronic stress, dietary fiber deprivation depleted Lachnospiraceae and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, reduced cecal butyrate, and increased hippocampal BDNF promoter methylation. Reintroducing a high-fiber diet or oral sodium butyrate restored BDNF expression, lowered corticosterone, and normalized depressive-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic profiling revealed that fiber availability, not total caloric intake, explained most variance in microbial composition. Fluoxetine attenuated behavioral deficits but did not restore BDNF methylation or butyrate-producing taxa, suggesting partially independent mechanisms. In participants with major depressive disorder, lower butyrate correlated with higher BDNF methylation in blood and lower fiber intake. These findings position dietary fiber and butyrate as tractable microbiome-targeted levers for stress-related psychopathology, while highlighting the need for longitudinal multi-omic studies that distinguish cause from consequence.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are reduced in Parkinson's disease (PD), and this deficit correlates with SNCA hyperexpression in the substantia nigra and impaired intestinal barrier function. In a cohort of 72 patients with PD and 68 matched controls, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside increased Enterobacteriaceae. Random forest modeling separated groups by microbiota composition and propionate levels. A 12-week randomized trial of inulin plus Bifidobacterium breve increased butyrate producers, lowered inflammatory cytokines, and improved constipation scores. These changes were accompanied by reduced TLR4 and NF-κB signaling in colon biopsies. In mice colonized with F. prausnitzii, inulin supplementation attenuated motor deficits and restored BDNF expression in the striatum. Notably, GBA1 variant carriers showed blunted butyrate responses to inulin. The findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate SNCA-linked neuroinflammation, supporting further fecal microbiota transplantation-based and dietary interventions for PD.

Gut microbial dysbiosis contributes to major depressive disorder through vagal and immune signaling, yet dietary strategies that reshape the gut microbiota remain inconsistently effective. We randomized 120 adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) to a 12-week Mediterranean-style diet plus omega-3 fatty acid supplementation or habitual diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal calprotectin assays were performed at baseline and endpoint; mixed-effects models tested associations with serotonin metabolites and symptom severity. At baseline, participants showed lower Coprococcus and Roseburia abundance than healthy controls. The intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, decreased Bacteroides enterotype prevalence, and lowered interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. Greater fiber intake correlated with microbial diversity and reduced depression scores. Mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acids explained 28% of the clinical improvement. In mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota, BDNF expression in the hippocampus increased and corticosterone decreased. These findings suggest that diet and omega-3 supplementation may synergize to modulate the gut-brain axis in depression, warranting larger trials.

Chronic consumption of a fiber-deprived diet remodels the gut microbiome and weakens hippocampal plasticity, yet the molecular links remain unresolved. In mice fed a low-fiber diet for 15 weeks, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Bacteroidetes and expanded Proteobacteria, accompanied by lower fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Hippocampal proteomics and Western blotting identified downregulation of CaMKIId and its synaptic partners, GAP43 and SV2C, alongside microglial synaptic engulfment. These changes preceded deficits in object location and temporal order memory, consistent with early cognitive impairment. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-deficient donors into recipient mice reproduced the behavioral phenotype, whereas oral supplementation with SCFA restored CaMKIId expression and improved behavior. Knockout mice lacking SCFA receptors remained impaired. Spearman correlation linked microbiota shifts to hippocampal molecular loss. These data position SCFA production by the gut microbiota as a key mediator of diet-dependent hippocampal dysfunction. The findings suggest that dietary fiber deficiency drives gut-brain dysfunction through SCFA-dependent CaMKIId signaling, identifying a modifiable target for preserving cognition in humans.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depletion of Firmicutes co-occur with major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether dietary fiber intake or BDNF expression explains this link remains uncertain. We recruited 92 adults, including 46 patients with MDD and 46 healthy controls. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; peripheral BDNF mRNA was quantified by quantitative PCR. Dietary intake was estimated with a food frequency questionnaire. We used PERMANOVA to test community differences and mediation analysis to assess whether short-chain fatty acid producers or BDNF mediated symptom severity. Compared with controls, patients with MDD showed lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio, reduced Faecalibacterium, and lower BDNF expression. Fiber-rich food consumption correlated positively with Faecalibacterium abundance and BDNF expression and negatively with depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium partially mediated the association between fiber intake and BDNF expression. Exploratory random forest modeling identified Faecalibacterium and BDNF as discriminative features. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may support gut microbiota taxa that influence BDNF-related pathways in MDD.

Gut microbiota-derived metabolites from dietary fiber can reshape central nervous system immune tone, yet the extent to which probiotic interventions alter this axis in adults with mild cognitive impairment remains unclear. We randomized 84 participants to a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks, with both groups receiving a standardized fermentable fiber-rich diet. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Cognition and depressive symptoms were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and elevated butyrate compared with placebo. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and improved executive function scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the cognitive benefit. The findings indicate that probiotic supplementation, layered onto a fiber-rich diet, may modulate gut microbiota-brain signaling, though larger trials are needed. These preliminary results support further investigation of microbial therapeutics in neurodegenerative disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acid derivatives act as central mediators of the gut microbiota–brain dialogue, yet their causal contribution to neuropsychiatric disorders remains contested. Using fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) into germ-free mice, we tested whether microbiota remodeling alters depressive-like behavior and hippocampal serotonin (5-HT) signaling. Recipients of MDD-derived microbiota showed reduced 5-HT turnover and increased Htr1a expression in the prefrontal cortex, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG plus fructo-oligosaccharides reversed these changes, restored SCFA levels, and normalized anhedonia in mice. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear discriminant analysis linked the benefits to Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium enrichment. Moreover, metagenomic sequencing revealed that MDD-associated microbiota was depleted in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and enriched in Escherichia-Shigella, shifts correlated with exosomal miR-124-3p and miR-3120-3p in plasma. These findings position probiotic–prebiotic combinations as plausible adjuncts for MDD, though validation in patients is needed.

Supplementation with probiotics reshapes gut microbiota and reduces anxiety-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic stress, an effect linked to restored serotonin signaling and BDNF expression in the hippocampus. To determine whether this benefit is transferable, we performed fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from supplemented donors to naive recipients and tracked microbial composition with 16S rRNA gene sequencing. FMT recapitulated the behavioral and neurochemical improvements, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were enriched in responders and correlated positively with short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the gut lumen. Spearman correlation and mediation analysis suggested that microbial changes partly explained the reduction in neuroinflammation. In patients with major depressive disorder, a pilot open-label trial of omega-3 plus probiotic showed improved depressive symptoms and altered gut microbiota composition. Notably, dietary fiber alone did not reproduce these effects, suggesting that live probiotic administration is critical. These findings support targeting the gut-brain axis with dietary supplements and microbiota-based interventions, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Microbial-derived metabolites are now recognized as key modulators of anxiety and depression, but the specific microbial taxa and host transcriptional programs that mediate these effects remain unclear. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled human study, 12-week probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum decreased anxiety scores and improved depressive symptoms compared with placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed increased microbial diversity and enrichment of Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, with parallel increases in fecal butyrate and propionate. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced reduced anxiety-like behavior, whereas 16S rRNA sequencing of non-responders revealed persistent dysbiosis. Mechanistically, butyrate increased BDNF and GPR43 expression in hippocampus and suppressed NF-κB signaling in colon. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate levels explained 38% of the behavioral improvement, independent of baseline anxiety severity. These data support probiotic-based modulation of the gut microbiota as a strategy to influence BDNF- and GPR43-dependent gut-brain signaling in mood disorders.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes brain amyloid-β deposition in APOE4 knock-in mice and correlates with cognitive decline in older adults, yet APOE-dependent microbial signals remain poorly defined. We recruited 180 human participants along the Alzheimer's disease continuum and profiled the gut microbiome using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE genotype tested associations between microbial taxa, short-chain fatty acids, and cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-β42/p-tau181. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted in APOE4 carriers with mild cognitive impairment, while Escherichia-Shigella expanded. These shifts correlated with lower butyrate and higher lipopolysaccharide levels. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of the association between Faecalibacterium and cognitive impairment. Inulin supplementation in APOE4 mice restored Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings position APOE-stratified microbiome profiling as a tractable approach for early Alzheimer's disease risk stratification and suggest butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium as therapeutic targets.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that signal across the gut-brain axis, yet the extent to which these microbial metabolites mediate cognitive benefits remains debated. In a randomized controlled feeding trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable fiber or a control diet for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool samples and untargeted metabolomics of plasma characterized gut microbiome composition and circulating metabolites. Functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed hippocampal connectivity during a memory task. Using causal mediation analysis, we quantified indirect effects of diet on cognition through butyrate-producing taxa and short-chain fatty acids. The fiber-rich diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and plasma butyrate, and improved hippocampal connectivity relative to control. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the improvement in memory performance. These findings support a causal chain linking dietary fiber, gut microbiota, and brain function, and suggest that microbial metabolites are viable targets for cognitive decline prevention.

Twelve weeks of probiotic supplementation combined with a Mediterranean-style diet reshaped gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid profiles in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, yet cognitive benefits were not uniform. In a randomized, double-blind trial, participants received either a synbiotic containing Bifidobacterium and inulin or placebo while consuming fermented foods and whole grains. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, plasma metabolomics, cognitive testing, and MRI assessed gut, blood, and brain outcomes. Using PERMANOVA and linear mixed-effects models, we found that the synbiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced inflammatory cytokines, but cognitive decline did not differ significantly between groups. Changes in Roseburia correlated with butyrate and hippocampal volume. Baseline microbial diversity and tryptophan metabolites moderated the response, with greater hippocampal volume change among participants harboring higher Akkermansia abundance. Peripheral BDNF and serotonin increased only in the synbiotic arm, suggesting a gut-brain axis signaling route. These results suggest that these interventions can reshape the gut microbiome, but larger trials with longer follow-up are needed to establish clinically meaningful brain benefits.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans can remodel the gut microbiome and alter short-chain fatty acid production, yet its impact on mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remains uncertain. In a randomized trial of older adults with MCI, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and fecal metabolomics to profile microbial communities before and after a 12-week intervention that also encouraged fermented foods and whole grains. Compared with placebo, inulin-type fructans increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced lipopolysaccharide. These shifts correlated with improved hippocampal activation during memory encoding and higher BDNF levels. Random forest modeling identified Faecalibacterium and butyrate as top predictors of cognitive improvement. Baseline microbial diversity and adherence to a Mediterranean diet moderated the response, with greater butyrate increases among participants consuming plant-rich foods. In mice transplanted with post-intervention microbiota, butyrate supplementation reproduced the cognitive benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings position inulin-type fructans as a plausible microbiota-targeted strategy for MCI, with dietary patterns and multi-omics guiding personalized approaches.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that signal via the vagus nerve to modulate brain function and behavior. To test whether this axis is disrupted in major depressive disorder, we profiled fecal microbiota from 84 patients and 79 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Patients showed lower relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside reduced butyrate and elevated lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Random forest models distinguished groups with an AUC of 0.81, and BDNF expression correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance and IL-6. In a subset, a 6-week probiotic intervention plus fermentable fiber increased butyrate and reduced IL-6; antidepressant response was associated with baseline Faecalibacterium. In germ-free mice, transplantation of patient-derived microbiota recapitulated reduced butyrate and increased IL-6, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors normalized these measures. These findings link dietary fiber fermentation, gut microbiota, and short-chain fatty acids to depression and suggest prebiotic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that influence central nervous system immune signaling, but whether this pathway mediates cognitive responses to probiotic supplementation remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized trial, 72 older adults with mild cognitive impairment received a probiotic blend containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo, alongside standardized Mediterranean-style diet counseling. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma metabolomics assessed gut microbiome composition and short-chain fatty acid concentrations. Linear mixed-effects models tested intervention effects on Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, with false discovery rate correction. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels compared with placebo, but cognitive scores did not differ significantly between groups. Among APOE ε4 carriers, however, higher butyrate was associated with slower cognitive decline. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-targeted probiotics may benefit only genetically susceptible individuals, and they support larger trials combining fiber-rich diets with microbial therapeutics. Future trials should stratify by baseline microbial diversity and dietary patterns to identify responders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota calibrate central nervous system immune tone, and disruption of this axis is increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder. In a cohort of 212 adults with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder, we combined shotgun metagenomic sequencing with serum metabolomics to test whether butyrate-producing taxa and their metabolites predict conversion to synucleinopathy. Lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and reduced butyrate coincided with elevated interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Cox proportional hazards models showed that each standard deviation decrease in F. prausnitzii was associated with a 1.8-fold higher hazard of phenoconversion after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate effects on neuroinflammation were partly explained by PPARGC1A expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Sodium butyrate supplementation in mice restored Bdnf transcripts in the hippocampus and attenuated depressive-like behavior. These findings position microbial butyrate signaling through PPARGC1A and BDNF as a tractable gut-brain axis target, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Greater adherence to Mediterranean-style diets tracks with higher gut microbial diversity and lower neuroinflammation, yet the pathways linking dietary polyphenols to BDNF expression remain unresolved. In a human cohort of 184 adults, we combined fecal metagenomics with causal mediation analysis to test whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila mediate diet-associated changes in BDNF levels. Dietary fiber intake was associated with increased Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6 (IL-6). Linear mixed models showed that each 10-g increment in fiber predicted a 4.7% rise in BDNF (95% CI 2.1–7.3; p=0.001), with 31% of this effect mediated by F. prausnitzii. Butyrate, a microbial short-chain fatty acid, correlated inversely with depressive symptoms and positively with BDNF. In mice receiving butyrate in drinking water, 16S rRNA sequencing and permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed distinct microbial communities relative to controls. These findings position butyrate-producing taxa as modifiable transducers of diet-gut-brain signaling, though Mendelian randomization is needed to confirm causality.

Microbial catabolism of dietary fiber in the colon generates short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives that tune brain immune signaling, yet how specific gut microbiota members translate fermented food intake into affective resilience remains unresolved. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with untargeted metabolomics in mice colonized with human donor microbiota and exposed to a fermented food-enriched diet or fiber-depleted chow. Fermented food supplementation expanded Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus reuteri, raised indole-3-propionic acid, and lowered interleukin-6 in the hippocampus. Fecal transfer from fermented food-fed mice into germ-free recipients reproduced these shifts, whereas vancomycin abolished them. Mediation analysis attributed 31% of the Bdnf expression increase to indole-3-propionic acid. In patients with major depressive disorder, gut microbiota composition correlated with dietary fiber intake and plasma indole-3-propionic acid. These data support psychobiotic supplementation as a testable strategy for depression, though causal trials are needed. Longitudinal sampling and fecal metagenomics are required to determine whether these microbial and metabolic signatures precede symptom onset.

Disruption of the gut microbiome during early life is increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, yet whether probiotic supplementation can modify this trajectory remains unresolved. In a double-blind infant cohort, fecal microbiota profiles were characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in plasma. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for gestational age and delivery mode revealed that Bifidobacterium abundance was inversely associated with anxiety-like behavior scores at 12 months. Multi-strain probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance and elevated butyrate concentrations compared with placebo. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced fear reactivity and lower interleukin-6 levels, suggesting a gut-brain immune pathway. However, effects were sex-dependent and not explained by BDNF methylation. The findings indicate that early probiotic exposure may shape microbiota-gut-brain signaling, though mediation analysis did not establish causality. Rodent models are needed to define mechanisms. Additional metagenomic sequencing and Mendelian randomization could clarify whether probiotics act directly on enteric neurons or through microbial metabolites.

Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus casei reduces Alzheimer's disease-like cognitive impairment in APP/PS1 mice by remodeling gut microbiota and suppressing peripheral inflammatory cytokines. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that treated mice had higher Akkermansia and Lactobacillus abundance, which correlated with lower lipopolysaccharide in serum and amyloid-β load in hippocampus. In colon and hippocampus, probiotics upregulated ZO-1, occludin, and BDNF expression while downregulating IL-1β and TNF-α. Behavioral testing revealed that probiotic-treated mice showed improved spatial memory in the Morris water maze and reduced anxiety-like behavior in the open field test. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were elevated in cecal contents and inversely correlated with IL-1β expression in prefrontal cortex. No changes in GFAP or Iba1 were observed in striatum. Fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated mice into germ-free mice reproduced the protection against memory deficits and BDNF induction, confirming a causal microbiota-gut-brain axis mechanism. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial communities with probiotics may delay AD progression.

Microbial production of short-chain fatty acids in the colon can attenuate depressive behavior by modulating vagal afferents and brain immune signaling, yet the dietary signals that sustain this protective circuit remain poorly defined. In mice fed a Western-style diet or a fiber-rich chow, we profiled cecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified tryptophan metabolites using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The fiber-rich chow increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus johnsonii, elevated butyrate, and reduced anxiety-like behavior after chronic restraint stress. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-rich chow-fed donors into antibiotic-treated recipients reproduced these effects, whereas IL-6 and Tnf expression in the hippocampus fell. Butyrate supplementation partially mimicked the protection. In a human cohort, baseline fiber intake correlated with fecal microbial diversity and lower depression scores by Spearman correlation. Mediation analysis indicated that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance explained 34% of the behavioral variance. These findings position dietary fiber as a tractable lever for gut microbiome-directed interventions in stress-related mood disorders.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that cross the blood–brain barrier and dampen neuroinflammation, yet whether baseline butyrate-producing taxa predict cognitive response to prebiotic-rich foods remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed either a high-fiber diet enriched with whole grains and legumes or a habitual diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool and untargeted metabolomics of serum profiled microbial and metabolic shifts. Linear mixed-effects models tested diet-by-time interactions, while mediation analysis examined whether butyrate increases explained cognitive gains. The high-fiber diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, raised butyrate, and improved executive dysfunction relative to the habitual diet. Increases in butyrate coincided with lower interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, supporting a systemic anti-inflammatory route. Cognitive improvement correlated with butyrate and was partially mediated by F. prausnitzii abundance. These results suggest that dietary fiber-driven microbiome remodeling may alleviate cognitive decline through SCFA-dependent gut–brain axis signaling.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids mediate gut microbiota–brain signaling, yet their causal contribution to major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain. We profiled fecal microbiota from 312 adults with MDD and 298 matched controls using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, and measured circulating IL-6, TNF-α, and BDNF by multiplex immunoassay. Fermented food and fiber-rich food intake was estimated with a validated questionnaire. Mediation analysis tested whether Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances linked diet to symptom severity. MDD was associated with lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, and higher Bacteroides; these shifts correlated with IL-6 (rho=0.34, P=0.001) and BDNF (rho=−0.29, P=0.002). Greater fermented food intake was associated with higher Lactobacillus and lower depressive symptoms after adjustment for antidepressant use. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fermented food donors attenuated depression-like behavior. A random-effects meta-analysis across two independent cohorts replicated the Bacteroides–IL-6 association. These results support diet-responsive gut microbiota as a modifiable target in MDD.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the microbial and host factors that drive neuroinflammation remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, we profiled fecal microbial communities from patients with PD and matched controls. Shannon index and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity revealed reduced diversity and altered composition in PD; PERMANOVA linked these shifts to Prevotella, Bacteroides, and Faecalibacterium abundance. Random forest classification separated PD patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.81, driven partly by Lactobacillus and Akkermansia. Metagenomic analysis showed decreased butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase genes, paralleling lower fecal butyrate. Fecal calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide correlated positively with TLR4 expression and negatively with Shannon index. In mice receiving PD patient-derived microbiota, Tlr4 and Nfkb1 expression increased in the substantia nigra, with elevated tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-1β. These findings suggest that gut microbial dysbiosis may promote PD-associated neuroinflammation through TLR4/NF-κB signaling and reduced short-chain fatty acid production, highlighting microbiota-targeted interventions as potential PD therapies.

Microbial metabolism of dietary components shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the mechanisms linking specific fermented foods to BDNF regulation remain incompletely defined. We tested whether a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum alters gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production in mice exposed to chronic stress. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that supplementation increased Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in the colon, and normalized corticosterone levels. In the hippocampus, Bdnf expression and serotonin turnover were restored, paralleling reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-propionate mediated the effects of L. rhamnosus on Bdnf expression via the vagus nerve. In patients with irritable bowel syndrome, a parallel probiotic intervention improved depression scores and increased plasma tryptophan availability. These findings suggest that fermented food-derived microbes and probiotic supplementation can engage a BDNF-dependent gut-brain signaling axis, offering a tractable target for stress-related disorders.

Gut microbiota depletion by antibiotics exacerbates depressive-like behavior in mice maintained on a high-fat, high-sucrose diet, while oral gavage with Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium longum restores butyrate levels in the colon and normalizes affective behavior. We tested whether this effect requires GPR43, HDAC2, and BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that dietary fiber fermentation, rather than total microbial load, tracked with short-chain fatty acid production. Random forest models identified Lactobacillus and Clostridium as predictors of anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responder mice into germ-free recipients transferred the behavioral phenotype, and GPR43 deficiency abolished butyrate-dependent BDNF induction. In adults with major depressive disorder, a parallel cohort showed lower BDNF expression and reduced butyrate-producing bacteria; these differences correlated with processed food intake. Our results position microbiota-derived metabolites as mediators of diet-sensitive mood disorders and suggest that probiotic or prebiotic strategies may complement existing therapies.

Dietary inulin supplementation restores gut microbial composition and reduces depressive-like behavior in chronic stress-exposed mice, but the pathways linking these effects remain unclear. We colonized adult C57BL/6 mice with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy donors, then fed them a 10% inulin diet for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin expanded Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while depleting Bacteroides. In the hippocampus, inulin increased Bdnf expression, lowered interleukin-1β and corticosterone, and normalized NLRP3 inflammasome signaling. Behavioral testing revealed that inulin improved sucrose preference test performance and reduced immobility in the forced swim test. Serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and colon tight-junction gene expression were also normalized. Mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acid production and microbial composition independently mediated the behavioral improvement. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice reproduced these benefits in recipient mice, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings identify inulin as a microbiota-dependent modulator of the gut-brain axis and support its evaluation in patients with stress-related mood disorders.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as key transducers of the gut microbiome–brain axis, yet their causal role in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains contested. We profiled fecal microbiota from patients with PD and matched controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified SCFAs by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. A random forest classifier distinguished cases from controls with moderate accuracy, driven by depletion of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and enrichment of Escherichia/Shigella. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and motor severity. Shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase genes in patients with PD, and Spearman correlation linked butyrate levels to constipation and cognitive impairment. In mice receiving a high-fat, low-fiber diet, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with PD reduced striatal dopamine and increased colonic IL-1β expression. Supplementation with sodium butyrate attenuated these changes and restored tight junction protein expression. These effects were accompanied by decreased Iba1 and GFAP expression in the substantia nigra. These findings position butyrate-producing taxa as modifiable targets and support fiber-rich diets as adjunctive strategies for PD.

Greater consumption of Mediterranean diet patterns, particularly fiber-rich vegetables and legumes, is associated with preserved hippocampal volume and lower risk of Alzheimer's disease, but the microbial and metabolic intermediaries are not fully defined. We enrolled older adults with mild cognitive impairment in a 12-week randomized crossover study comparing a plant-based high-fiber diet with a habitual diet. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in stool samples. Cognitive performance and prefrontal cortex activation were assessed using functional MRI. We used linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to test whether diet-induced shifts in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila explained changes in butyrate and cognition. The high-fiber diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and improved delayed recall relative to the habitual diet. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly mediated the association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and memory improvement. These findings support gut microbiota-targeted dietary strategies for early Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Impaired gut microbiota fermentation and low short-chain fatty acid availability are emerging as upstream drivers of depression, yet the host BDNF and IL-6 pathways linking omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation to hippocampal plasticity remain poorly defined. In a mouse model of chronic stress, omega-3 supplementation restored Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, increased butyrate levels, and normalized BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation showed that these benefits required an intact vagus nerve. We then used causal mediation analysis to estimate the proportion of the omega-3 effect on depressive-like behavior explained by IL-6 suppression and microbial shifts. In adults with major depressive disorder, baseline plasma butyrate correlated inversely with IL-6 and symptom severity. A two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis in independent human cohorts supported a protective effect of genetically proxied microbiota butyrate production on depression. These findings suggest that omega-3 exerts gut-brain effects through BDNF- and IL-6-dependent pathways, with mediation analysis supporting microbiota-mediated mechanisms.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans and Lactobacillus rhamnosus reshaped gut microbiota and attenuated depression-like behaviors in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress, an effect accompanied by restored BDNF and TrkB expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. To test whether this gut-brain signaling depends on microbial short-chain fatty acid production, we compared inulin alone, probiotic alone, and combined treatment in male C57BL/6J mice. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed that combined treatment increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, whereas linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Muribaculaceae as enriched in inulin-treated mice. Butyrate concentrations in feces correlated inversely with anxiety-like behavior and positively with BDNF transcript levels. Fluoxetine produced comparable behavioral improvement but did not elevate butyrate or TrkB expression, suggesting that the synbiotic acts through a distinct microbiota-metabolite-BDNF pathway. Together, these data position inulin-probiotic combinations as candidate adjuncts for stress-related mood disorders, with BDNF and TrkB as mechanistic markers and microbiota-derived butyrate production as a modifiable target.

Disrupted gut microbiota signaling along the gut-brain axis contributes to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the microbial taxa and molecular mediators linking peripheral inflammation to hippocampal plasticity remain poorly resolved. In 84 adults with MDD and 62 healthy controls, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics revealed reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and elevated Bacteroides fragilis. Taxonomic differences were confirmed by PERMANOVA (R2 = 0.07, P = 0.004), and calprotectin correlated negatively with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. These shifts correlated with lower BDNF expression and higher IL6 and TNF in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability indirectly linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance to BDNF levels, while random forest classification distinguished patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.81. In a subset receiving 8-week sertraline, baseline Bacteroides fragilis and butyrate predicted symptom improvement. These findings suggest that microbial short-chain fatty acid production may modulate BDNF-related neuroplasticity and that mediation modeling can identify actionable targets for depression.

Consumption of a high-fat, high-sucrose diet reshapes the gut microbiome and elevates lipopolysaccharide translocation, a sequence increasingly implicated in neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In a mouse model, we tested whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation attenuates these effects and whether benefits depend on Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Mice received either the obesogenic diet or standard chow for 12 weeks, with half of each group receiving omega-3s. 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral testing assessed microbial composition and hippocampal-dependent memory. The obesogenic diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, increased Proteobacteria, and impaired spatial memory. Omega-3 supplementation restored Akkermansia relative abundance, lowered interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and improved memory. These improvements correlated with brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the prefrontal cortex. Mediation analysis suggested that Akkermansia partly mediated the cognitive benefit. Thus, dietary fat and omega-3 interact with the gut microbiota to modulate gut-brain axis dysfunction, supporting targeted nutritional strategies for preserving brain function.

Gut microbial dysbiosis predicts mild cognitive impairment and correlates with hippocampal atrophy in carriers of APOE4, implicating a modifiable gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's disease. We profiled fecal microbiota from 120 participants using shotgun metagenomics and quantified short-chain fatty acids and bile acids with targeted metabolomics. Random forest models separated carriers of APOE4 from non-carriers, yielding an area under the curve of 0.84. Reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were associated with lower butyrate and higher neuroinflammation markers. Taxonomic profiling further revealed elevated Bacteroides and depleted Lachnospiraceae in patients with mild cognitive impairment relative to cognitively normal controls. These microbial shifts correlated with amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau in cerebrospinal fluid and APOE genotype. In transgenic mice carrying APOE4, 16S rRNA sequencing showed that butyrate supplementation restored microbial diversity and reduced amyloid pathology in the cortex. These findings suggest that microbiota-derived metabolites mediate APOE4-dependent risk and that mediation analysis can identify targets for prebiotic interventions.

Dysregulation of the gut microbiota contributes to Parkinson's disease pathology, yet whether early probiotic supplementation can modify nigrostriatal degeneration remains unresolved. We administered Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or vehicle to α-synuclein-overexpressing mice from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Motor function was assessed by rotarod testing, and fecal microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing. Expression of BDNF, GFAP, and ZO-1 in the substantia nigra and colon was measured with quantitative PCR. Mice receiving probiotics showed improved motor latency, reduced α-synuclein aggregation, and lower interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide concentrations relative to vehicle-treated mice. Sequencing revealed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and decreased Proteobacteria in treated animals. Multivariate analysis with linear discriminant analysis effect size confirmed these taxonomic shifts. BDNF was upregulated, whereas GFAP and ZO-1 were normalized in the colon. These findings indicate that probiotic supplementation attenuates Parkinson's disease-related pathology in mice, possibly through microbiota-dependent regulation of BDNF and intestinal barrier genes.

Fermentation by the gut microbiota of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity and hippocampal plasticity, yet clinical responses vary widely. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received inulin or a control for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; associations with depressive symptoms were tested using permutational multivariate analysis of variance and linear mixed-effects models. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium and reduced Prevotella, with corresponding rises in fecal butyrate. Symptom improvement correlated with Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentration, but not with BDNF genotype. Parallel mouse experiments using fecal microbiota transplantation from responders and nonresponders reproduced the behavioral effects and showed reduced neuroinflammation in the prefrontal cortex. Circulating lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 fell only in responders. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through prebiotic fiber may alleviate depression in a subset of patients, and that machine-learning classification could identify responders. However, the durability of these effects and the role of antidepressants remain unclear.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and altered gut microbiota composition has been repeatedly detected in major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. In a 12-week randomized trial, 64 adults with major depressive disorder received a multi-strain probiotic alongside standard care, while a comparison group received standard care alone. Participants also completed a fermented food frequency questionnaire and provided fecal short-chain fatty acid samples. Relative to the comparison group, the probiotic group showed greater reduction in depressive symptoms and higher butyrate concentrations. Linear mixed models revealed that Faecalibacterium abundance mediated the relationship between probiotic intake and symptom improvement. Fermented food consumption correlated with Lactobacillus richness but did not independently predict clinical response. Baseline dietary fiber intake did not modify these associations. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may exert antidepressant effects partly by enriching butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium, while fermented foods may support microbial diversity without replacing targeted probiotic therapy. Larger trials with shotgun metagenomics are needed.

Altered gut microbiota composition precedes Parkinson's disease motor onset and may drive α-synuclein pathology through the gut-brain axis. In patients, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic profiling reveal depletion of Prevotellaceae and enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae, shifts correlated with SNCA risk variants and gastrointestinal dysfunction. These taxa modulate short-chain fatty acid production, bile acid metabolism, and inflammatory cytokines, influencing the enteric nervous system and vagal signaling. Preclinical models using mice demonstrate that fecal microbiota transplantation from affected individuals can transmit motor deficits, whereas probiotic or high-fiber diet interventions attenuate neuroinflammation. Integration with random forest classifiers identifies microbial signatures predictive of PD status. Therapeutically, levodopa response varies with microbial composition, and targeted microbiota editing is being explored to restore eubiosis and slow neurodegeneration. Dietary patterns rich in polyphenols and omega-3 fatty acids may reshape gut microbial ecology, increase Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and reduce intestinal permeability. Such interventions could complement dopaminergic therapy by limiting endotoxin translocation and systemic inflammation. Longitudinal cohorts combining shotgun metagenomics with metabolomics are needed to clarify causality and identify GBA and LRRK2 modifiers.

Consumption of a high-fat diet reshapes the gut microbiota and elevates neuroinflammation, yet whether probiotic supplementation can attenuate cognitive decline remains unresolved. In a mouse model of diet-induced cognitive impairment, C57BL/6J mice received either a high-fat diet or standard chow for 16 weeks, with half of the high-fat diet-fed mice receiving a probiotic formulation containing Bifidobacterium breve daily. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that the high-fat diet reduced Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance, whereas the probiotic restored Akkermansia and lowered lipopolysaccharide concentrations. Behavioral testing showed that supplementation improved spatial memory deficits and reduced hippocampal neuroinflammation. Novel object recognition and Barnes maze tests corroborated these findings. Furthermore, supplementation increased ZO-1 and occludin expression in colon, suggesting improved intestinal barrier integrity. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline body weight and batch effects, together with Spearman correlations, confirmed that Akkermansia abundance correlated negatively with interleukin-6 in hippocampus. These results indicate that probiotic supplementation may buffer high-fat diet-induced cognitive dysfunction through microbiota-gut-brain signaling.

Dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation can reshape gut microbiota and modulate gut-brain axis signaling, yet whether these interventions alter BDNF and IL6 expression in adults with depression remains unclear. In an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 96 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement plus a high-fiber diet or a placebo with usual diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and RNA sequencing were used to profile fecal microbiota and peripheral blood transcriptomes. Linear mixed-effects models tested intervention effects on short-chain fatty acid production, BDNF, IL6, and depression severity. The active intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced IL6 expression relative to placebo. BDNF expression did not differ between groups. Depressive symptoms improved more in the active arm, with changes correlating inversely with IL6 and positively with butyrate. These findings suggest that combining dietary fiber with probiotics may relieve depression through microbial metabolite and inflammatory pathways, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota tune central nervous system immune tone, yet how diet shapes this axis remains mechanistically unresolved. In male C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat, fiber-depleted diet, inulin supplementation restored Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, increased butyrate in the colon, and lowered lipopolysaccharide translocation. These shifts attenuated neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior, with reduced NLRP3, IL-1β, and GFAP expression and increased ZO-1 and occludin expression in the hippocampus. Vagotomy abolished the protective effects, implicating the vagus nerve in microbiota-gut-brain signaling. In parallel, probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus produced similar behavioral benefits, whereas fermented food intake correlated with higher BDNF and lower IL-6 in patients with major depressive disorder. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation confirmed that the microbial community was necessary and sufficient for these effects. Together, these findings position prebiotic fiber and probiotics as modulators of BDNF-dependent and NLRP3-dependent pathways, linking diet to affective disorders through the gut microbiome.

Inulin supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in chronic stress mice, but its effects in patients with major depressive disorder remain uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 68 adults received inulin (10 g/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and PERMANOVA tested community-level differences. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces, and reduced depressive symptoms and anhedonia scores. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed lower IL6, IL1B, and TNF expression, while BDNF expression was higher in responders. Baseline Shannon diversity correlated positively with BDNF expression, whereas Bray-Curtis distances separated responders from nonresponders. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in Faecalibacterium and butyrate partially explained the improvement in depressive symptoms. Responders also showed greater increases in Akkermansia and Roseburia. Serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein decreased in the inulin arm. These findings link inulin-driven microbiota shifts to BDNF and inflammatory gene regulation, supporting gut-brain axis modulation as a therapeutic strategy.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone and neurotransmitter synthesis, yet how specific gut taxa influence host gene expression in the brain remains incompletely resolved. We integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metatranscriptomics, and RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue from mice colonized with microbiota from human donors and fed either a probiotic mixture or a fiber-supplemented diet, with quantitative PCR validation. Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum were enriched after probiotic administration and correlated with reduced Il6 and Tnf expression and increased Bdnf expression. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability partially explained these associations. In parallel, fiber supplementation increased acetate and propionate concentrations and attenuated Nfkb1-dependent inflammatory signaling. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic and prebiotic approaches can reshape gut microbial composition, modify brain gene expression, and potentially stabilize gut-brain axis signaling. Further human trials are needed to determine whether these mouse-derived mechanisms translate into clinical benefit for cognitive decline.

Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid generated by gut microbiota from dietary fiber, shapes brain function and neuroinflammation. Whether probiotic supplementation can enhance this pathway in mild cognitive impairment was tested in 84 adults who consumed either a fermented dairy product containing Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus or a non-fermented dairy product, each with or without inulin. Randomized allocation assigned participants to four groups for 12 weeks. <gene>16S rRNA gene</gene> sequencing revealed higher Bifidobacterium abundance, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed increased fecal butyrate in the synbiotic group. Mixed-effects models linked these shifts to improved verbal memory task performance and greater hippocampal activation. Reductions in lipopolysaccharide and neuroinflammation markers accompanied the microbiota changes. Baseline cognitive assessments and fecal sampling were repeated after 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Spearman correlation linked butyrate increases with hippocampal measures. The combination of fermented foods and prebiotic supplementation may thus support gut microbiota-dependent brain health in cognitive decline.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is increasingly linked to BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet the dietary and microbial determinants of this axis remain unresolved in metabolic syndrome. We recruited 84 adults with obesity and randomized them to a high-fiber diet or Western diet for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and serum BDNF protein and inflammatory cytokine concentrations were quantified. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance increased only in high-fiber participants and correlated inversely with interleukin-6. Using linear mixed-effects models, fiber intake predicted BDNF expression change after adjustment for obesity status. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures by diet. Mediation analysis estimated that F. prausnitzii explained 22% of the fiber–BDNF association. Spearman correlation linked butyrate to BDNF and inversely to interleukin-6. Baseline gut microbial diversity did not differ between groups, but Bacteroides abundance decreased with the Western diet. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may enhance BDNF signaling through gut microbiota modulation, with implications for neuroinflammation and cognitive decline.

Supplementation with probiotics can reshape the gut microbiota and improve cognitive impairment in older adults, yet strain-specific effects and mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We tested whether a probiotic formulation containing Bifidobacterium breve M-16V alters cognition and gut microbial composition in healthy older adults with subjective memory complaints. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 72 participants received the probiotic or placebo daily for 12 weeks. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation. The probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances, decreased Collinsella, and improved delayed memory and attention. Fecal butyrate correlated positively with cognitive scores. These effects were independent of depression. These findings indicate that B. breve M-16V may mitigate cognitive decline by modulating the gut microbiome and short-chain fatty acid production.
