metadata.abstract: Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut bacteria yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate brain immune signaling and may slow neurodegeneration. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, 68 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a habitual diet. The intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered plasma interleukin-6 relative to control. Cognitive scores improved modestly in the Mediterranean-style diet arm, with the largest gains among participants having higher baseline butyrate; serum BDNF rose in parallel. Mediation analysis estimated that changes in gut microbiota accounted for 31% of the association between diet and cognition, while mixed-effects modeling confirmed that baseline microbial diversity moderated the treatment response. The between-group difference in cognitive score was 1.8 points (95% confidence interval 0.4–3.2; p=0.02), and no serious adverse events occurred. These results support a microbiome-brain pathway in which food-derived substrates shape microbial metabolites and neuroinflammation, suggesting that dietary strategies targeting commensal bacteria merit further testing in larger cohorts.

Fermented foods and dietary fiber reshape the gut microbiota, but their causal influence on BDNF signaling in the brain remains unresolved. We transplanted fecal microbiota from adults consuming high- versus low-fiber diets into antibiotic-treated mice and tracked short-chain fatty acid producers, BDNF expression, and anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that high-fiber donors increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, whereas low-fiber donors expanded Bacteroides. These compositional shifts correlated with butyrate concentrations and BDNF transcripts in the hippocampus; mixed-effects models linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF and reduced depressive symptoms scores. Probiotic supplementation partially mimicked the high-fiber microbiota, raising butyrate and BDNF, while selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors did not alter microbial composition. Additional RNA sequencing showed that GPR43 and TLR4 were differentially expressed in the colon and prefrontal cortex, implicating HDAC2 inhibition and lipopolysaccharide trafficking. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the BDNF response to high-fiber microbiota. These findings suggest that fermentable fiber and probiotics may promote gut-brain signaling through BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a modifiable target for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression and serotonin signaling, but how habitual Western diet interacts with probiotic supplementation to modify this gut-brain dialogue remains unclear. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 8 weeks. Stool microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; dietary intake was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Participants consuming a high-fiber diet showed greater increases in short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and higher GPR43 expression than those consuming a low-fiber diet. Probiotic supplementation reduced depressive symptoms only among individuals with baseline microbiota diversity below the median. These effects were accompanied by decreased lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and increased indole-3-propionic acid. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated the behavioral and BDNF changes, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Together, these findings indicate that diet and probiotics jointly modulate gut microbiota-derived metabolites and BDNF signaling, with baseline microbial and dietary context determining clinical response. Mediation analysis suggested that indole-3-propionic acid partially mediated the improvement in depression scores.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet and regular use of probiotic supplements have been linked to lower symptom burden in mood disorders, yet the molecular routes through which these exposures shape the gut microbiota–brain axis remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week parallel-arm study, adults with moderate depression and anxiety received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or the same diet plus a multi-strain probiotic containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Faecalibacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production in the supplement group. Both interventions reduced IL-6 and BDNF promoter methylation, while the probiotic arm showed greater increases in brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression and serotonin metabolites. Mixed-effects models indicated that changes in gut microbial composition mediated 31% of the improvement in depressive symptoms. Changes in gut microbiota correlated with BDNF expression (r = 0.42, p < 0.01). These findings suggest that dietary patterns and targeted microbial supplementation may converge on BDNF-related plasticity to support brain health.

Consumption of Western-style diets enriched in saturated fats and refined sugars consistently disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis and correlates with cognitive decline, yet the molecular links across the gut-brain axis remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled male C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat, high-sucrose diet for 12 weeks. Compared with mice receiving standard chow, high-fat, high-sucrose diet-fed mice exhibited reduced Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance, elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide, and increased hippocampal expression of TLR4, NF-κB, and IL-1β. Notably, short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in cecal contents and serum, and butyrate-producing taxa were depleted. These changes coincided with lower BDNF transcripts and impaired performance in Morris water maze testing. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors fed this diet into gnotobiotic recipients partially transferred neuroinflammation and memory deficits, whereas inulin supplementation restored Akkermansia and normalized BDNF expression. Mediation analysis implicated microbial metabolites as intermediaries between diet and BDNF suppression. These findings position diet-driven microbiota remodeling as a modifiable upstream regulator of BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central neurotransmitter balance and may buffer depression and anxiety. To test this, male C57BL/6 mice received Bifidobacterium breve or vehicle during four weeks of chronic unpredictable mild stress. 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiled gut microbiota, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified SCFAs in colon and neurotransmitters in brain. Behavioral tests showed that B. breve reduced depressive-like and anxiety-like behaviors relative to vehicle. Supplemented mice had higher butyrate and propionate in colon, elevated 5-hydroxytryptamine and γ-aminobutyric acid in hippocampus, and lower kynurenine. Spearman correlation analysis linked Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae abundances with butyrate and GABA levels, and linear mixed-effects models confirmed stress-dependent effects. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into antibiotic-treated recipients partially reproduced the behavioral protection, and metagenomic profiling suggested enrichment of bile acid and tryptophan metabolic pathways. These findings suggest that B. breve attenuates stress-induced mood dysfunction by remodeling gut microbiota and SCFA-neurotransmitter signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Chronic consumption of a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiota and elevates circulating lipopolysaccharide, yet the molecular routes linking these shifts to cognitive decline remain unresolved. In mice fed a high-fat, low-fiber diet, we found reduced hippocampal expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) and increased neuroinflammation, accompanied by expansion of Desulfovibrio and depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila. Fecal microbiota transplantation from human donors with metabolic syndrome into germ-free mice reproduced deficits in novel object recognition and spatial memory. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-propionate accounted for 42% of the diet-related effect on Bdnf expression, while random forest classification identified Lactobacillus abundance as a top predictor of anxiety-like behavior. Supplementation with fructo-oligosaccharides partially restored microbial diversity and normalized corticosterone rhythms. Notably, metformin did not rescue these phenotypes, whereas omega-3 fatty acids reduced interleukin-6 and preserved Bdnf methylation patterns. These findings position diet-responsive microbial metabolites as modifiable signals for gut-brain axis disorders.

Microbial catabolism of tryptophan is increasingly recognized as a pivotal interface between the gut microbiome and central nervous system function, with indole derivatives acting on aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling to shape intestinal immunity and brain homeostasis. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild depressive symptoms, daily supplementation with tryptophan (1 g/day) for 8 weeks altered Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances and increased indole-3-lactic acid in plasma relative to placebo. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that responders showed upregulated AhR expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and reduced interleukin-6 compared with non-responders. Baseline indole-3-lactic acid correlated inversely with anxiety scores and positively with BDNF expression. Mediation analysis indicated that indole-3-lactic acid mediated 27% of the effect of tryptophan on depression scores. These findings suggest that dietary tryptophan may modulate gut microbiota-brain signaling through AhR-dependent microbial-metabolite pathways, although confirmatory studies are needed. These associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and baseline serotonin levels.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether dietary fibers can reshape microbial communities and slow neurodegeneration remains unresolved. We randomized patients with early PD to 16 weeks of resistant starch or usual care. Stool microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and short-chain fatty acids were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models assessed longitudinal changes, while MaAsLin2 identified taxa associated with motor severity. Resistant starch increased Bifidobacterium and Lachnospiraceae, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced calprotectin. These shifts correlated with improved constipation and attenuated neuroinflammatory cytokines in cerebrospinal fluid. Baseline enterotype stratified response: Prevotella-dominant participants showed greater butyrate increases than Bacteroides-dominant participants. Taxonomic shifts were accompanied by lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha and higher BDNF methylation in blood. No serious adverse events occurred. The results indicate that resistant starch can modify the microbiota-gut-brain axis in PD and warrant future multi-center trials with neuroimaging endpoints.

Dietary patterns shape the gut microbiota and its metabolic output, with consequences for central nervous system function and behavior. Patterns rich in fermented foods and dietary fiber increase Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production, whereas high-fat diets promote intestinal inflammation and dysbiosis. We used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics to profile fecal microbiota from adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls, coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry for short-chain fatty acids. Participants completed a Mediterranean diet score and functional MRI during an emotional processing task. Lower Faecalibacterium and higher Bacteroides were associated with depressive symptoms; butyrate correlated positively with prefrontal cortex activation. A randomized subset received probiotic supplementation or prebiotic inulin for 8 weeks. Both interventions increased Bifidobacterium and reduced interleukin-6, but only inulin improved cognitive flexibility. Using linear mixed-effects modeling, we found that inulin-induced gut microbiota shifts predicted reduced anhedonia independently of antidepressant use. These findings link dietary modulation of the gut microbiota to mood-related brain circuits.

Dietary patterns that enrich the gut microbiota can modulate neuroinflammation and cognitive resilience, yet the microbial pathways linking specific foods to brain health remain incompletely defined. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fiber, polyphenols, and omega-3 fatty acids or a matched Western diet for 8 weeks. Fecal samples underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified. Cognitive performance and hippocampal activity were assessed using functional magnetic resonance imaging. The Mediterranean-style diet increased the relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, raised butyrate levels, and reduced circulating interleukin-6. These shifts accompanied improved BDNF expression and better linear mixed model-estimated memory scores. Conversely, the Western diet was associated with lower microbial diversity and greater systemic inflammation. Mediation analyses suggested that butyrate partly explained the diet-cognition relationship. These findings support dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich eating patterns as accessible strategies for shaping the gut microbiome and preserving brain function in aging populations.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshapes the gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammatory signaling along the gut-brain axis, yet whether these changes translate into cognitive benefit in mild cognitive impairment remains unresolved. We randomized 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment to 12 weeks of omega-3 supplementation or placebo. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids, lipopolysaccharide, and BDNF were quantified. Cognitive performance was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Between-group differences in gut microbiota composition were tested using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), and associations with cognition were modeled using linear mixed-effects models. Omega-3 increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate, and reduced lipopolysaccharide. No significant change in gut microbiota richness was observed, but mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the cognitive improvement. These shifts correlated with improved BDNF and cognitive scores. The findings suggest that omega-3 may exert pro-cognitive effects through microbiota-dependent metabolite changes in mild cognitive impairment.

Altered gut microbiota composition tracks with major depressive disorder severity, but whether microbial signals causally engage BDNF, IL6, and TLR4 pathways in the brain remains unclear. We profiled fecal microbiota from drug-naive patients and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, then performed fecal microbiota transplantation into antibiotic-treated mice. Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance differed by group, with lower short-chain fatty acid and butyrate production predicted by random forest models and validated in an independent cohort using linear mixed models. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiota-derived butyrate indirectly modulated BDNF, IL6, and TLR4 expression in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and colon. Recipients of patient microbiota exhibited depressive-like behavior, anxiety-like behavior, neuroinflammation, and reduced BDNF signaling relative to control microbiota recipients. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-butyrate signaling contributes to depression-related neuroimmune and synaptic changes, identifying candidate targets for microbiome-directed therapies. Targeting butyrate production or TLR4 signaling may restore microbiota-brain homeostasis in depression.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that suppress neuroinflammation and preserve blood-brain barrier integrity, yet the causal chains linking specific gut microbiota taxa to Alzheimer's disease remain unresolved. We profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified serum metabolites in adults with mild cognitive impairment and matched controls, then applied mediation analysis to test whether microbial effects on cognitive decline were transmitted through butyrate and indole derivatives. Higher abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila correlated with greater fiber intake, elevated butyrate, and slower cognitive decline. In contrast, Western diet patterns associated with Bacteroides expansion and reduced butyrate. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 21% of the protective association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Alzheimer's disease biomarkers. In mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, APOE4 genotype amplified butyrate depletion and amyloid pathology. These findings support targeting dietary fiber and gut microbiota to modulate neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative disease.

Alterations in the gut microbiome precede motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether microbial metabolites directly shape striatal dopamine signaling remains unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with PD or healthy controls and measured motor behavior, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed community separation, with enriched Bacteroides and depleted Akkermansia muciniphila in the microbiota from PD donors. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve was administered for 4 weeks. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for sex and batch revealed that the microbiota from PD donors reduced nigral TH transcripts and impaired rotarod performance relative to control mice. Probiotics attenuated these deficits and increased butyrate levels. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 38% of the microbial effect on motor function. Spearman correlation linked Bacteroides abundance inversely with TH expression. These findings position probiotic interventions as candidates for modulating the PD gut-brain axis, though human trials are needed.

Microbial butyrate restrains NFKB1-driven IL6 transcription in hippocampal microglia, providing a plausible mechanism by which gut microbiota depletion aggravates depression-like behavior. In germ-free mice colonized with Bifidobacterium breve or Lactobacillus rhamnosus, 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed-effects models showed that Bifidobacterium abundance inversely correlated with anhedonia and TNF expression. Mendelian randomization using human genome-wide association data linked genetic liability to higher gut microbial butyrate production with lower major depressive disorder risk. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into antibiotic-treated mice reduced butyrate levels, increased BDNF promoter methylation in the prefrontal cortex, and elevated GPR43 expression in the colon. Supplementation with inulin restored Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and normalized mediation analyses estimates for BDNF-dependent cognitive impairment. These findings position microbiota-butyrate-BDNF signaling as a tractable axis for neuropsychiatric disorders. Because GPR43 activation promotes IL10 and suppresses CCL2, these pathways may buffer neuroinflammation. However, Mendelian randomization cannot exclude pleiotropy, and metagenomic studies with repeated sampling are required in larger cohorts.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD) through gut-brain axis signaling, yet the microbial and host transcriptional features that distinguish responders from non-responders to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors remain poorly defined. We profiled fecal microbiota and peripheral blood BDNF expression in 84 adults with MDD before and after 8 weeks of escitalopram treatment, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR. Microbial community differences were tested with PERMANOVA, and associations between taxa, BDNF transcripts, and symptom severity were modeled using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Responders showed higher baseline abundance of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and lower Bacteroides than non-responders. BDNF expression increased only in responders and correlated positively with Faecalibacterium abundance. False discovery rate correction identified 11 differentially abundant taxa. These findings suggest that baseline gut microbiota configuration and BDNF-related plasticity may jointly influence antidepressant response, supporting microbiota-informed stratification in MDD.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota precedes behavioral deficits in depression-like states, yet the pathways linking intestinal bacteria to central nervous system inflammation remain poorly resolved. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan, and kynurenine were quantified. Random forest classification and linear mixed-effects models tested associations between Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and clinical scores. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6 relative to placebo. Higher Lactobacillus correlated with lower depression severity and elevated serotonin metabolites. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly accounted for the microbiota-behavior relationship. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed enriched butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA transferase genes in responders, alongside reduced lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. These findings support targeted probiotic interventions as adjunctive strategies for depression, though Mendelian randomization and longer follow-up are needed to establish causality.

Dietary patterns that reshape the gut microbiota can alter brain function through immune, metabolic, and neural signaling. Fiber-rich foods and fermented foods enrich Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, which generate short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate; probiotics and prebiotics may reinforce this effect. These metabolites support intestinal barrier integrity and modulate neuroinflammation. In patients with major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease, gut microbiome profiles often show reduced commensals and expanded opportunistic pathogens. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic sequencing have linked these shifts to altered BDNF expression, lipopolysaccharide translocation, and blood-brain barrier permeability. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into rodents induces behavioral changes, whereas omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and Mediterranean-style diets may partially reverse gut dysbiosis. However, causality remains uncertain because most evidence is correlational, and responses vary with baseline microbiota composition, antibiotic exposure, and host genetics. Future trials should combine fecal microbiota transplantation or defined probiotic strains with longitudinal metagenomics and metabolomics to identify causal microbial targets for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial colonization of the neonatal gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression and stress reactivity, yet the dietary and microbial signals that stabilize this program remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics in a mouse model of chronic stress, we tested whether fermented food intake alters gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid availability in ways that modify anxiety-like behavior. Mice receiving fermented food showed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced corticosterone compared with controls. Hippocampal BDNF and NR3C1 transcripts were upregulated, while IL6 and TNF expression declined. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained a significant portion of the fermented food effect on BDNF and behavioral outcomes. In a small human cohort, shotgun metagenomics revealed that fermented food consumption was associated with higher gut microbial diversity and enriched butyrate-producing bacteria, though antibiotic exposure attenuated these associations. These findings support a model in which dietary fermented foods act through gut microbiota-derived metabolites to modulate BDNF signaling and stress-related neuropsychiatric symptoms. They also highlight metagenomics and metabolomics as tools for identifying microbial therapeutics.

Fermented foods increase gut microbial diversity and alter brain network connectivity, but whether these changes translate into protection against age-related cognitive decline remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, older adults received either a fermented food diet rich in yogurt, kefir, and kimchi or a high-fiber diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that fermented food intake expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced Bacteroides, while untargeted metabolomics detected higher short-chain fatty acids and bile acid derivatives. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed increased hippocampal activation during a memory task. At week 12, plasma interleukin-6 decreased and brain-derived neurotrophic factor increased. In parallel, mice colonized with participant-derived microbiota via fecal microbiota transplantation showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and elevated Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex. Mediation analysis linked Lactobacillus abundance to Bdnf and memory performance. These findings position fermented foods as accessible modulators of the gut-brain axis and support their evaluation in larger neurodegenerative cohorts.

Inulin-type fructans can raise Bifidobacterium abundance and reduce circulating inflammatory cytokines, but their impact on BDNF expression and depressive symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder remains uncertain. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 60 adults received inulin (10 g/day) or maltodextrin for eight weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium longum and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, with parallel rises in butyrate. Mixed-effects models indicated greater reductions in depression severity and higher BDNF mRNA in whole blood after inulin than after placebo. Fecal microbiota transplantation into chronic stress mice reproduced the BDNF increase and reduced anhedonia, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished the effect. Additionally, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed that responders had higher Akkermansia muciniphila and lower Bacteroides fragilis, and mediation analysis suggested that butyrate mediated 28% of the BDNF response. In mice, inulin also normalized IL-6 and NRF2 expression in the hippocampus, linking peripheral microbiota changes to central BDNF signaling. These data suggest that inulin improves depression-related outcomes through gut microbiota-dependent regulation of BDNF, supporting prebiotic adjunctive strategies.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota converge on the vagus nerve to shape brain function, and their disruption is increasingly linked to depression. In a mouse model of chronic stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with fecal microbiota transplantation to test whether Lactobacillus-enriched microbiota alters affective behavior. Stressed mice showed reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus, elevated corticosterone, and depleted Lactobacillus and Bacteroides. PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures, while Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF transcript levels. Transplanting microbiota from unstressed mice normalized corticosterone, restored BDNF expression, and reduced depressive-like behavior. These effects were abolished by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, implicating signaling through the vagus nerve. Plasma interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were elevated in stressed mice and normalized after transplantation. Neither Bacteroides nor Lactobacillus alone explained the rescue; coordinated shifts across microbial communities were required. Our findings suggest that gut microbiota-BDNF interactions along the vagus nerve represent a tractable target for stress-related disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as key mediators of the gut microbiota–brain axis, yet how dietary fiber intake shapes their central effects remains incompletely resolved. We recruited adults with mild depressive symptoms and randomized them to a high-fiber diet or usual diet for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and SCFA concentrations were quantified using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Hippocampal and prefrontal cortical responses to emotional faces were assessed with functional magnetic resonance imaging. A random forest classifier identified Faecalibacterium and Roseburia as top predictors of butyrate increase. Compared with the usual diet, the high-fiber diet raised fecal butyrate and Bifidobacterium abundance while lowering depressive symptoms scores. Mediation analysis showed that fiber-induced butyrate elevation partially mediated reductions in depressive symptoms and attenuated amygdala reactivity. These findings indicate that dietary fiber can engage the gut microbiome to modulate brain function, supporting targeted fiber interventions for mood disorders.

Probiotic and fermented food interventions can reshape gut microbiota and modulate brain function via short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acids, and tryptophan metabolites. We tested whether a prebiotic fiber blend alone or combined with blueberry powder altered microbial composition, SCFA production, and anxiety-like behavior in adults with mild cognitive impairment. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 84 participants received the supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified gut microbiota and fecal SCFAs. Functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed hippocampal response during an emotional face-matching task. Compared with placebo, the prebiotic fiber increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced self-reported anxiety. Blueberry powder further increased hippocampal activation and improved episodic memory. Changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with butyrate and hippocampal activation. These findings suggest that fermented food and prebiotic strategies may support gut-brain axis health, though larger trials are needed. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans and fermented dairy reshapes the gut microbiota and may attenuate age-related cognitive decline, but strain-specific effects and diet interactions remain unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either Bifidobacterium breve MCC1274 plus fructo-oligosaccharides or placebo for 12 weeks while maintaining their habitual Mediterranean-style diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites were quantified. Cognitive performance was assessed with ADAS-Cog and MMSE. Using linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA, we found that B. breve abundance increased in the intervention group and correlated with improved memory scores; microbial diversity remained stable. Changes in tryptophan pathway metabolites partially mediated the association between Bifidobacterium and cognitive outcomes. Baseline dietary fiber intake modified the treatment effect, with stronger benefits in participants reporting low vegetable consumption. These data suggest that combining probiotics with fermentable fiber may support gut-brain axis signaling, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and later susceptibility to anxiety-like behavior. In mice, daily oral probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus increased short-chain fatty acid production, reduced serotonin turnover, and attenuated depression-related phenotypes after antibiotic exposure. We used 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation to test whether these effects required an intact gut microbiota. Germ-free mice receiving microbiota from probiotic-treated donors showed significantly lower IL-6 and TNF-α in the prefrontal cortex and greater social exploration than controls. Adult male C57BL/6 mice were randomized to vehicle, probiotic, or probiotic plus antibiotics for 4 weeks and assessed using open field, forced swim, and social interaction tests. Notably, antibiotic-induced dysbiosis abolished the BDNF response and worsened anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that probiotic-driven microbiome remodeling may modulate BDNF and central inflammatory signaling along the gut-brain axis, offering a tractable strategy for patients with stress-related disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis precedes cognitive decline in some patients, yet microbial signatures that predict neuroinflammation remain poorly defined. We profiled faecal microbiota from 120 adults with mild cognitive impairment and 80 cognitively normal controls using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Plasma short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified, and hippocampal volume was measured by MRI. Random forest classification identified a microbial signature enriched in Bacteroides and depleted in Faecalibacterium that discriminated cases from controls with an AUC of 0.81. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and hippocampal volume. In mice, faecal microbiota transplantation from patients increased microglial activation and caused spatial memory impairment relative to controls. These findings suggest that gut microbiota composition, particularly butyrate-producing taxa, contributes to neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment, and that butyrate may be a therapeutic target. Longitudinal models are now needed to test causality in prospective human cohorts.

Disruption of the gut microbiome by high-fat, low-fiber diets contributes to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline through vagal and metabolite-dependent signaling. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation plus Mediterranean-style diet or placebo for 24 weeks. Fecal microbiota profiling by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and short-chain fatty acid quantification were performed, alongside plasma lipopolysaccharide and brain-derived neurotrophic factor assays. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for dietary fiber intake, antibiotic use, and baseline cognitive impairment severity. Compared with placebo, active intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate levels, and improved Mini-Mental State Examination scores. Changes in Roseburia correlated with reduced interleukin-6. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and omega-3 supplementation may synergistically modulate the gut-brain axis, offering a pragmatic strategy for early Alzheimer's disease prevention. Larger trials with Mendelian randomization are warranted to confirm causality. Future meta-analyses should stratify by APOE genotype and ultra-processed food consumption.

Chronic consumption of a Western diet reshapes the gut microbiota, elevates circulating lipopolysaccharide, and promotes neuroinflammation, yet whether targeted inulin supplementation reverses these effects remains unresolved. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed-effects models were used to relate microbial shifts to hippocampus volume and BDNF expression. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila and raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate. These changes coincided with reduced interleukin-6, improved cognitive impairment scores, and greater hippocampus volume. In mice fed a high-fat diet, inulin similarly restored gut microbiota and lowered neuroinflammation, effects abolished by antibiotic treatment. Fecal calprotectin and zonulin decreased, indicating reduced intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and BDNF signaling accounted for part of the cognitive benefit. Our findings indicate that inulin may mitigate Western diet-associated cognitive decline through microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and BDNF signaling.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are associated with neurodegenerative disorders, yet the strength of diet-driven modulation along the gut-brain axis remains uncertain. We pooled 16S rRNA sequencing and clinical data from older adults with mild cognitive impairment and matched healthy controls. Adherence to a Mediterranean diet correlated with higher abundances of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, and with elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids. Probiotic exposure was less consistent, and omega-3 supplementation showed only modest shifts in gut microbiota. Using a random-effects meta-analysis across eight cohorts, each standard-deviation increase in Mediterranean diet score was associated with lower cognitive decline (SMD −0.34; 95% CI −0.52 to −0.16; I² = 38%). Mediation models suggested that butyrate-producing taxa explained 21% of this association. These findings support dietary strategies that enrich gut microbiome metabolic output as a plausible adjunct for preserving brain function, though randomized trials with standardized dietary patterns are needed to distinguish causality from confounding.

Butyrate-producing gut microbiota are depleted in major depressive disorder, yet whether restoring these taxa alters central nervous system inflammation remains uncertain. We transplanted faecal microbiota from patients with depression into antibiotic-treated mice and randomized them to a galacto-oligosaccharide supplement or vehicle for four weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium and elevated butyrate in caecal contents. RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex revealed downregulation of Il1b, Tnf, and Nlrp3, alongside upregulation of Bdnf. In forced swim tests, supplemented mice displayed reduced depressive-like behavior compared with controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and random forest modeling identified baseline Prevotella abundance as a predictor of Bdnf induction. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium abundance and butyrate levels explained 42% of the Bdnf effect on behavior. No changes in Ocln or Tjp1 were observed. These data suggest that prebiotic-induced shifts in gut microbiota can modulate gut-brain axis signaling and neuroinflammation through Bdnf-dependent mechanisms.

Alterations in the gut microbiome and its metabolic output are increasingly recognized as early contributors to depression and cognitive decline in older adults. In a cohort of 164 participants, we paired clinical assessments with 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted mass spectrometry to examine whether microbial features track current and future depressive symptoms. Lower relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium correlated with greater symptom severity, whereas higher tryptophan degradation and reduced short-chain fatty acid production predicted worsening anxiety over 12 months. Linear mixed models adjusted for age, antidepressant use, and diabetes confirmed these associations. To test a modifiable target, a subset received probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains for 8 weeks; this was accompanied by increased serotonin precursor availability and improved cognitive function scores. These findings suggest that microbial composition and metabolites may serve as noninvasive readouts and that probiotics could help delay depression-related cognitive impairment, though randomized trials are needed.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that influence central nervous system immunity and metabolism, yet inter-individual variability limits dietary recommendations. We enrolled adults with mild cognitive impairment and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, together with plasma inflammatory cytokines and short-chain fatty acids. For 12 weeks, participants consumed a fermented food-enriched diet or received inulin. Linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA tested links among microbial taxa, metabolites, and clinical measures. Baseline gut microbiota composition differed by mild cognitive impairment status, with lower Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae abundance. The fermented food group showed increased microbial diversity and higher butyrate, while mediation analysis indicated that microbial shifts partially explained reduced interleukin-6. Shotgun metagenomics revealed pathways enriched in lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and bile acid metabolism that correlated with cognitive impairment severity after adjustment for covariates. These findings support targeting gut microbiota through diet to modulate gut-brain signaling in mild cognitive impairment.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence brain function and depressive symptoms, but causal evidence in humans is limited. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received inulin or placebo. We profiled the gut microbiome using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, quantified fecal SCFAs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and measured circulating lipopolysaccharide and BDNF. Linear mixed-effects models assessed symptom trajectories; mediation analysis tested whether Faecalibacterium abundance or butyrate increases explained clinical improvement. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered depression scores relative to placebo. Baseline microbial diversity and BDNF genotype moderated response, with greater butyrate increases in participants harboring Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Changes in butyrate and Faecalibacterium partially mediated the reduction in depressive symptoms. These findings support a gut-brain pathway in which fermentable fiber shapes microbial community function and SCFA production to improve mood disorder outcomes, warranting larger trials.

Gut microbiota depletion reshapes hippocampal BDNF expression and serotonin transporter transcription through short-chain fatty acid-dependent signaling, linking commensal bacteria to depression-like behaviors in mice. In parallel, Bacteroides fragilis-derived PGE2 activated microglia and upregulated C/EBPβ in transgenic mice. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, quantitative PCR, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis, we found that antibiotic-treated mice displayed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lower butyrate levels, and altered BDNF, GABA-A receptor, and tryptophan hydroxylase 1 expression in the prefrontal cortex and amygdala. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors normalized microbiota composition and restored BDNF and serotonin transporter transcripts, whereas psychobiotics or probiotics alone produced partial recovery of neuroplasticity genes. Notably, inulin supplementation increased butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice. Colonization with Lactobacillus rhamnosus increased GABA and reduced depressive-like behavior. These results suggest that gut microbiota-derived metabolites regulate neuroplasticity genes and that targeted psychobiotics may offer adjunctive benefit for stress-related disorders.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes and predicts depression-like behaviors in mice, yet the dietary and analytical determinants of this axis remain poorly resolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls and fed them either a low-fiber diet or a high-fiber diet. 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundances depended on diet and donor status. Linear mixed-effects models showed that fiber intake, but not donor group, explained 31% of variance in hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. PERMANOVA confirmed distinct microbial community structures across diet groups. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were elevated in high-fiber diet-fed mice and correlated negatively with anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that dietary fiber shapes the gut microbiota–brain axis and may buffer depressive symptoms through microbial metabolites. Prebiotic supplementation could offer a tractable strategy, but further human trials with standardized mediation analyses are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber generates short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune tone and behavior, yet the transcriptional pathways linking gut microbiota to BDNF signaling remain incompletely resolved. We colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bacteroides fragilis, then fed them either a high-inulin diet or a low-fiber diet for six weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, RNA sequencing, and behavioral assays were used. The inulin-rich diet increased butyrate in the colon, reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide, and lowered anxiety-like behavior and depression-like behavior. In the hippocampus, this diet upregulated BDNF and GABA receptor expression while suppressing IL-6 and TNF-α. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the behavioral benefits, implicating the vagus nerve in this signaling. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 38% of the BDNF response. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower fiber intake correlated with reduced microbial diversity and higher IL-6 expression. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable substrate for microbiota-dependent BDNF regulation and neuropsychiatric disease risk.

Probiotic supplementation can enhance cognitive performance in older adults with mild cognitive impairment by remodeling the gut microbiome and its metabolic output. In a double-blind, randomized controlled trial, 84 participants received either a probiotic containing Bifidobacterium breve or placebo for 12 weeks. Cognitive outcomes were assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models showed that the probiotic group gained 5.2 points on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment versus 1.1 points for placebo (p = 0.004). Bifidobacterium abundance increased, while Collinsella decreased; these shifts correlated with butyrate levels and hippocampus activation during functional magnetic resonance imaging. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium abundance explained 32% of the cognitive improvement. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic therapy may slow cognitive decline through microbial and metabolic pathways linking the gut and brain.
