metadata.abstract: Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber can modulate neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity along the gut-brain axis, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation augments these effects in mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 120 adults with MCI received either Lactobacillus plantarum plus inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. Cognitive outcomes were measured with Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were quantified. Between-group differences were assessed using linear mixed-effects models, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Compared with placebo, the active group showed greater increases in Bifidobacterium abundance and BDNF, alongside reduced IL-6. Analysis of covariance revealed improved delayed recall (p=0.018) and global cognition (p=0.032). These findings further suggest that combining probiotics with prebiotic fiber may slow cognitive decline by reshaping gut microbiota and reducing neuroinflammatory tone.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract tunes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and restrains neuroinflammation via short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and lipopolysaccharide-sensitive TLR4 signaling. In germ-free mice, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics showed that high-fiber diets enriched Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, increased butyrate, and attenuated anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into antibiotic-treated mice restored gut microbial diversity, lowered NLRP3 and IL-1β transcripts, and improved cognitive impairment. Conversely, a Western diet depleted Bifidobacterium, elevated trimethylamine N-oxide, and exacerbated Parkinson's disease-like motor deficits. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial of adults with mild cognitive impairment, probiotic supplementation plus fermented foods changed gut microbiota composition and reduced inflammatory cytokines, although APOE genotype modified responses. Mechanistically, butyrate promoted FOXP3 regulatory T cells and occludin expression, limiting endotoxin translocation across the intestinal barrier. These findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as modifiable mediators of neurodegenerative disease risk and support dietary and microbial strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Microbial metabolites from the gut microbiota influence central nervous system function, and perturbed gut-brain axis signaling is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). We enrolled 84 adults with MDD and 62 healthy controls, profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and measured plasma short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Expression of BDNF, IL6, and TNF was quantified in peripheral blood. Associations were tested with linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use. MDD was associated with lower Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced butyrate concentrations. In a subset, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with MDD into mice induced depressive-like behavior and increased IL6 expression in the hippocampus. A mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium and BDNF expression. Neither selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors nor benzodiazepines explained the observed microbiota differences. These results link specific microbial taxa and metabolites to BDNF and IL6 regulation, supporting the gut microbiome as a therapeutic target in MDD.

Higher intake of fermentable fiber and probiotic supplements predicts slower cognitive decline in older adults, but whether this effect is mediated by gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids remains unresolved. In a 24-week randomized trial, participants with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with whole grains, legumes, and fermented foods plus a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium lactis or standard care. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and fecal butyrate, respectively. Using causal mediation analysis, we found that intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which correlated with higher butyrate and lower interleukin-6. The intervention effect on cognitive decline was partly mediated by butyrate (average causal mediation effect, 18%; p=0.01). Exploratory linear mixed models further showed that baseline microbial diversity modified treatment response, with greater improvement in individuals harboring higher Faecalibacterium abundance. These results suggest that targeting the gut microbiota through diet and probiotics may slow neurodegeneration, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Conversion of tryptophan by the gut microbiota into indole derivatives can modulate serotonin availability in the hippocampus, yet whether dietary fiber intake alters this pathway in depression remains uncertain. We colonized germ-free mice with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then fed them either a low-fiber diet or a high-fiber diet for 4 weeks. Behavioral despair was assessed by forced swim test, and gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. PERMANOVA revealed diet-driven separation of microbial communities, while random forest identified Bacteroides uniformis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii as top discriminators. High-fiber diet increased short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in the colon and prefrontal cortex. Serotonin turnover was elevated in the hippocampus. Circulating corticosterone was lower in high-fiber diet-fed mice, and BDNF expression increased in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiota and attenuate neuroinflammation, offering a modifiable target for depression.

Alterations in the gut microbiota and its metabolic output are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders through the gut-brain axis, yet dietary strategies that target this axis remain poorly defined. We examined whether a probiotic supplement combined with a fiber-rich diet modulates short-chain fatty acid production, intestinal barrier function, and depression-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic stress. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we profiled fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids before and after intervention. Stress increased Lactobacillus depletion, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and reduced ZO-1 expression in the colon. The probiotic plus fiber-rich diet restored Lactobacillus abundance, increased butyrate, normalized ZO-1, and attenuated depressive-like phenotypes. These benefits were abolished by vagotomy, implicating the vagus nerve. Mechanistically, butyrate increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. Our findings suggest that combining probiotics with dietary fiber may provide a tractable gut-brain therapeutic strategy for stress-related disorders, warranting validation in patients with major depressive disorder.

Consuming a Western-style diet depleted in fermentable fiber reshapes the gut microbiota and may impair hippocampal function, yet the causal microbial signals remain poorly defined. We fed mice either a fiber-rich chow or an isocaloric fiber-deprived diet for 12 weeks and assessed anxiety-like behavior and cognition. 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing revealed that fiber deprivation reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while expanding Bacteroides. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed lower butyrate and propionate in cecal contents. In parallel, BDNF expression fell in the prefrontal cortex, and linear mixed models linked butyrate concentrations to anxiety-like behavior. Oral sodium butyrate partially rescued these deficits, whereas inulin supplementation restored Bifidobacterium and normalized BDNF transcripts. In a small human cohort, fecal metagenomics showed similar Bacteroides enrichment among participants reporting low fiber intake. These findings suggest that dietary fiber supports gut microbiota-dependent production of short-chain fatty acids, which in turn tune corticolimbic circuits underlying anxiety. These results position fermentable fiber as a modifiable prebiotic target for stress-related disorders and warrant further randomized controlled trials in patients.

Fermentable dietary fibers and probiotics can remodel the gut microbiota and reduce neuroinflammation, yet the microbial and metabolic signals linking these interventions to brain function remain incompletely defined. In C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet, daily fructo-oligosaccharides plus Bifidobacterium breve increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in cecum, and lowered hippocampal interleukin-6 compared with high-fat diet alone. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry profiled microbial communities and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), while open field, forced swim, and novel object recognition tests assessed anxiety-like behavior, depressive-like behavior, and cognitive impairment. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Lactobacillus and Bacteroides as taxa enriched by the synbiotic treatment. Butyrate correlated inversely with Bdnf expression in prefrontal cortex and positively with Il6 expression in hippocampus. These results indicate that fermentable fiber and probiotic co-supplementation may modulate the gut-brain axis through SCFA-dependent BDNF and inflammatory signaling, supporting clinical testing in patients with mild cognitive impairment.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract influences BDNF expression and serotonin availability in the brain, making the gut microbiome a modifiable contributor to depression and anxiety. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received multi-strain probiotics or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, while liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry detected higher fecal short-chain fatty acids. These microbial shifts coincided with lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha concentrations, reduced depressive symptoms, and elevated BDNF expression in blood. Mixed-effects models linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF expression and symptom improvement. Fecal bile acids also correlated with BDNF changes. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated donors reproduced the behavioral and neurochemical changes, an effect attenuated by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy. Together, these findings indicate that probiotic supplementation can engage the vagus nerve and BDNF-dependent pathways to alleviate depression, although strain-specific mechanisms and durability require further study.

Dietary supplementation with inulin increases Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate production in the gut microbiota, an effect linked to reduced depressive behaviors in rodent models. To determine whether this axis operates in humans, we conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with mild depression. At baseline, lower microbial richness and reduced Faecalibacterium abundance were associated with greater anhedonia. Fecal samples were profiled using 16S ribosomal RNA gene amplicon sequencing, and serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations among microbial diversity, short-chain fatty acids, and symptom severity. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance and elevated fecal butyrate compared with placebo. These changes correlated with reduced anxiety scores and increased serum BDNF, but not with cytokine changes. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the improvement in depression. These findings support prebiotic fiber as a modifiable strategy for microbiota-targeted interventions in mood disorders.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber and polyphenols in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids and other neuroactive metabolites that shape brain function through immune, endocrine, and vagal routes. Disruption of this gut microbiota–brain dialogue has been linked to depression, anxiety, and irritable bowel syndrome, yet causal mediators remain poorly defined. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder and healthy controls into germ-free mice. Recipients of patient microbiota showed increased interleukin-6, reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus, and altered anxiety-like behavior relative to controls. These effects were attenuated by probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, but not by omega-3 fatty acid supplementation alone. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability accounted for part of the behavioral phenotype. The findings position microbial butyrate production as a modifiable node linking diet, gut microbiota, and mood disorders. These results support targeting the gut microbiota with dietary supplements or fermented foods to modulate brain-gut disorders.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids are critical for maintaining microglial homeostasis, and their depletion following chronic stress may drive depressive-like behaviors. We exposed male C57BL/6J mice to chronic unpredictable mild stress for 6 weeks and assessed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Random forest and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Lactobacillus and Bacteroides as depleted, while Desulfovibrio and Akkermansia were enriched. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors into naïve recipients induced microglial priming in the hippocampus and dentate gyrus, evidenced by increased lipopolysaccharide-induced IL-1β and TNF-α expression and hyper-ramified morphology on immunohistochemistry. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF levels and behavioral resilience. Mediation analysis indicated that BDNF downregulation accounted for 32% of the behavioral effect. Minocycline reversed microglial priming and restored stress resilience. These findings suggest that gut microbiota depletion of Lactobacillus and Bacteroides contributes to depression via microglial activation, and that targeting microbiome or microglial function may offer therapeutic strategies for stress-related disorders.

Fermented foods and probiotic supplements can reshape the gut microbiota, yet their capacity to modify BDNF expression and neuroinflammatory cytokines in older adults with mild cognitive impairment remains inconsistent. In a 12-week randomized trial, 96 participants received either a multi-strain probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis or a fermented dairy placebo. Fecal microbiome profiling by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia after supplementation. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, rose in feces and correlated with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression in peripheral blood. Cognitive testing revealed improved hippocampal-dependent memory, and mixed-effects models linked these gains to microbiome shifts rather than baseline diet. Exploratory analyses found that APOE ε4 carriers showed weaker BDNF increases but similar butyrate responses. These changes were accompanied by reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with fermented food intake may modulate BDNF and cytokine pathways, offering a scalable strategy for cognitive decline.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon shapes BDNF expression and serotonin signaling along the vagus nerve, linking gut microbiota composition to major depressive disorder (MDD). This bidirectional gut-brain axis is further modulated by bile acids and tryptophan metabolites. In a cohort of adults with MDD, mediation analysis indicated that microbiome diversity indirectly influenced depressive symptoms through butyrate and BDNF promoter methylation. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet and fermented food intake correlated with higher abundances of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus, whereas dysbiosis was associated with elevated lipopolysaccharide and neuroinflammation. A random-effects meta-analysis of human trials found that probiotic supplementation and prebiotic fiber improved anxiety scores, but effect sizes varied by baseline microbiome profile and FKBP5 genotype. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with depression induced anhedonia and altered TLR4 signaling, an effect attenuated by selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial interventions may modulate BDNF-dependent pathways, though longitudinal sampling and Mendelian randomization are needed to establish causality.

Depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii within the gut microbiota is associated with more severe social-communication deficits in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet whether this dysbiosis drives behavior or reflects dietary and medication confounders remains unresolved. We characterized the gut microbiota of 118 children with ASD and 94 neurotypical controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed diagnosis-related differences in community composition, and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antipsychotic use linked lower butyrate with higher ASD severity scores. Metagenomic functional profiling showed reduced abundance of butyrate synthesis genes, including butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase, and these findings survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Microbial metabolite depletion, rather than a single taxon, may contribute to ASD-related behavioral symptoms. Prebiotic and probiotic interventions targeting butyrate production warrant controlled trials. Longitudinal sampling and metabolomics are needed to determine whether these signatures precede symptom onset and whether they can guide personalized psychobiotic therapy.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly recognized as modifiable contributors to age-related cognitive decline, yet causal evidence from dietary interventions remains sparse. We tested whether a 12-week probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus altered the gut microbiome and hippocampus function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Fecal microbiota were profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Cognitive performance and BDNF methylation were assessed at baseline and week 12. Linear mixed-effects models tested intervention effects, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance and butyrate concentrations compared with the control group. These shifts correlated with improved hippocampus-dependent memory and reduced BDNF promoter methylation. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings suggest that targeted probiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate BDNF epigenetics, offering a plausible gut-brain axis mechanism for preserving cognition in mild cognitive impairment.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract exerts a profound influence on brain function, and disruptions in this dialogue are increasingly linked to depression and anxiety. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics have revealed reduced microbial diversity and altered abundances of Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Faecalibacterium in patients with major depressive disorder. These taxa modulate short-chain fatty acid production, tryptophan metabolism, and immune signaling, thereby affecting central nervous system homeostasis. Dietary interventions may partially restore this balance: fermented foods, whole grains, legumes, and fish supply substrates that promote beneficial gut microbiota. In adults with mild-to-moderate depression, a randomized controlled trial found that a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with these foods improved symptom scores alongside increased diversity. Probiotic supplementation has shown smaller and less consistent effects, perhaps because strain specificity, baseline microbiota composition, and host genetics shape responses. Collectively, the evidence supports targeting the gut microbiome through diet, yet mechanistic studies are needed to identify which microbial metabolites mediate benefit and whether these effects persist.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet how dietary patterns remodel this dialogue remains incompletely defined. We compared adults consuming a high-fiber diet rich in fermentable carbohydrates with those on a Western-style diet for 8 weeks. Dietary intake was recorded using food frequency questionnaires. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and BDNF expression was quantified in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were enriched in the high-fiber group, accompanied by higher butyrate and propionate concentrations. These shifts correlated with increased BDNF and reduced interleukin-6 after adjusting for age and body mass index using linear mixed models. In a subset, 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed gut microbial diversity was inversely associated with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Our findings suggest that fiber-rich foods may support BDNF-linked neuroplasticity via gut microbiota-derived metabolites, offering a modifiable target for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Disruption of gut microbiota by early-life antibiotics predicts elevated BDNF promoter methylation and poorer depression outcomes in adults, yet the microbial signals linking intestinal mucosa to prefrontal cortex remain poorly resolved. In a cohort of patients with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid anxiety, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum abundance, alongside lower fecal short-chain fatty acids and increased plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Using mixed-effects meta-regression, we found that omega-3 supplementation and probiotic supplementation each attenuated IL-6 expression and improved cognitive impairment scores; effects were stronger when baseline microbial diversity was low. Mediation analysis estimated that short-chain fatty acids explained 28% of the association between Bifidobacterium longum and BDNF methylation. Mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from high-BDNF donors showed increased hippocampal serotonin and reduced anxiety-like behavior, whereas vagotomy abolished these effects. These findings position omega-3 and probiotics as modulators of the gut-brain axis and suggest that microbial diversity and BDNF methylation may serve as stratification biomarkers for dietary interventions in depression and anxiety.

Microbial depletion with broad-spectrum antibiotics exacerbates anxiety-like behavior and neuroinflammation in mice, and this phenotype is reversed by butyrate supplementation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we found that gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) reduced Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia abundance in recipient mice, accompanied by increased interleukin-6 in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. RNA sequencing revealed downregulation of BDNF and upregulation of TLR4 in the hippocampus; quantitative PCR confirmed these changes. Spearman correlation linked Roseburia abundance to BDNF expression and butyrate levels. Inulin or probiotic administration restored Roseburia, normalized BDNF and TLR4 expression, and attenuated depressive-like behavior. Notably, subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the protective effects of butyrate, implicating vagal afferents in this gut microbiota-brain axis. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived butyrate modulates BDNF-TLR4 signaling in the brain, offering a tractable target for MDD. Fecal butyrate concentrations were lower in patients with MDD than in healthy controls.

Depletion of Clostridium clusters IV and XIVa within the gut microbiome is repeatedly linked to multiple sclerosis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, yet the molecular relay connecting commensal bacteria to central nervous system autoimmunity remains unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from MS patients and healthy controls, then used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics to map taxonomic and metabolic shifts. Loss of Clostridia correlated with reduced butyrate and lower Foxp3 and Il10 expression in colon and mesenteric lymph nodes. Dietary fiber fermentation was impaired in mice colonized with microbiota from MS patients, while a high-fiber diet or sodium butyrate restored short-chain fatty acid pools, expanded regulatory T cells, and attenuated demyelination and astrocyte reactivity. Notably, butyrate supplementation alone produced only partial protection, indicating that additional Clostridia-derived signals, potentially acting through AhR and IL-22 pathways, are required. These findings position fiber-responsive Clostridia as tractable modulators of the gut-brain axis and suggest that microbiota-informed diet strategies may complement immunomodulatory therapy in MS.

Curcumin supplementation reshapes the gut microbiome and attenuates neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, yet the microbial taxa mediating its neuroprotective effects remain unresolved. Seventy-two patients with early Parkinson's disease received curcumin (1 g/day) or placebo for 16 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic sequencing plus serum short-chain fatty acid profiling were performed at baseline and endpoint. PERMANOVA showed distinct community composition after curcumin (R2 = 0.14, p = 0.002), and linear mixed-effects models linked Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii to lower interleukin-6. Mediation analysis indicated that these taxa explained 31% of the interleukin-6 reduction and 24% of the BDNF increase. Spearman correlation showed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was inversely associated with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (ρ = −0.42, p = 0.008). A random forest classifier identified baseline Prevotella copri abundance as a discriminative feature of responders. The curcumin arm also showed increased fecal butyrate and reduced calprotectin. In mice overexpressing α-synuclein, curcumin reduced dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the substantia nigra. These data support microbiota-targeted curcumin as a potential adjunct to levodopa in Parkinson's disease.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber reshapes the gut microbiota, yet how these dietary signals translate into central BDNF expression and affective behavior remains contested. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with irritable bowel syndrome received either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet for 6 weeks; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics quantified microbial and short-chain fatty acid shifts. High fiber intake increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate in feces, and reduced anxiety scores. Exploratory analyses linked butyrate increases to reduced amygdala reactivity during functional MRI and lower interleukin-6. In parallel, mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota showed elevated BDNF in the hippocampus and lower corticosterone after 4 weeks of fiber supplementation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 38% of the anxiety improvement. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may act as a microbiome-targeted intervention for gut-brain axis disorders, though IBS heterogeneity warrants caution.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans, a fermentable dietary fiber found in chicory root, reshapes the gut microbiome and alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a tractable route to modulate the gut-brain axis. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with mild depressive symptoms received either inulin (12 g/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and elevated butyrate concentrations after inulin versus placebo. Serum BDNF rose by 18%, and depressive symptom scores decreased more in the inulin group. Parallel experiments in mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota reproduced the BDNF increase in the prefrontal cortex and reduced neuroinflammation. No serious adverse events occurred, and compliance exceeded 90%, with short-chain fatty acid producers remaining enriched at follow-up. Mediation analysis using bootstrap resampling indicated that butyrate and BDNF jointly explained 34% of the intervention effect. These findings support prebiotic fiber as a dietary supplement strategy targeting microbial-metabolite-neurotrophic signaling in depression.

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation attenuates depression-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress, yet the contribution of the gut microbiota to this effect remains incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we profiled fecal microbial communities and short-chain fatty acids in male C57BL/6J mice randomized to receive omega-3 supplementation or vehicle for six weeks. Stress increased anxiety-like behavior and corticosterone levels, reduced microbial alpha diversity, and depleted Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus spp. Omega-3 supplementation normalized corticosterone levels, restored microbial diversity, and enriched Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. These microbial shifts correlated with increased butyrate and propionate in the colon and reduced neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice to recipients partially reproduced the behavioral protection, whereas 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed engraftment of Bifidobacterium. The findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation promotes stress resilience through microbiota-dependent short-chain fatty acid signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial production of short-chain fatty acids in the colon is increasingly recognized as a determinant of central nervous system function, yet how habitual dietary fiber intake shapes this axis remains uncertain. We analyzed gut microbiota composition, faecal SCFA concentrations, and inflammatory cytokines in 184 adults who completed 3-day dietary records and standardized neurocognitive testing. Using mediation analysis within linear mixed models, we tested whether butyrate-producing taxa, particularly Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, link fiber-rich foods to depressive symptoms and cognitive impairment. Higher fruit and vegetable intake was associated with greater butyrate availability and lower depression scores. The indirect effect through F. prausnitzii abundance was significant (β = −0.14, 95% CI −0.26 to −0.04), whereas lipopolysaccharide attenuated the association. Probiotic use did not modify these relationships. These findings suggest that dietary patterns rich in fermentable substrates may support gut-brain signaling and mental health, although Mendelian randomization and interventional studies are needed to establish causality.

Alterations in gut microbial communities and their metabolites are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disorders, yet causality and therapeutic leverage remain contested. We profiled older adults with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls, combining shotgun metagenomic sequencing with targeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to quantify short-chain fatty acids and bile acids. Dietary intake was assessed using food frequency questionnaires; omega-3 fatty acid supplementation was recorded as a covariate. Using PERMANOVA and sparse partial least-squares discriminant analysis, we found that Bacteroides and Prevotella abundances explained 11.4% of cognitive impairment variance after adjustment for age, sex, and medication use. Lower butyrate production potential correlated with higher neuroinflammation markers and worse hippocampal volume. In mice, colonization with microbiota from patients recapitulated cognitive deficits, while inulin supplementation restored butyrate levels and improved behavioral testing performance. These findings position microbial metabolites as modifiable mediators of the gut–brain axis and support targeted prebiotic interventions; however, longitudinal trials are needed to establish causality.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate microglia and enteric neurons, linking gut microbial ecology to neurodegeneration. In a human cohort of 120 adults with Parkinson's disease, shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA gene amplicon profiling revealed depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia alongside elevated Escherichia coli. Participants consuming a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermentable fiber showed higher butyrate and propionate in stool, lower calprotectin, and reduced constipation severity. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber diet-fed mice into gnotobiotic mice attenuated α-synuclein aggregation in substantia nigra and preserved dopaminergic neurons. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 were quantified by ELISA; both declined after a 12-week randomized controlled trial of fiber supplementation. Mediation analysis suggested that gut microbiota-derived butyrate production accounted for part of the association between dietary fiber intake and motor dysfunction. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain axis signal and support microbiome-targeted dietary trials in Parkinson's disease.

Microbial catabolism of tryptophan into indole derivatives predicts cognitive decline in older adults, yet whether this relationship is modified by habitual diet remains unresolved. In a cohort of 312 participants, we quantified gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and measured circulating indole-3-propionate, indole-3-acetate, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Mediterranean diet adherence was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, and obesity, higher Clostridium sporogenes abundance was associated with lower neuroinflammation scores and better executive function. This association was strengthened among individuals with high Mediterranean diet adherence and attenuated by high-fat diet patterns. Mediation analysis indicated that indole-3-propionate explained 27% of the protective effect. Notably, short-chain fatty acids did not mediate this effect, suggesting specificity for aromatic amino acid metabolites. In mice fed a Western diet, oral tryptophan supplementation failed to rescue microglial activation, whereas colonization with Clostridium sporogenes reduced interleukin-6 in the hippocampus. These findings position diet-microbe interactions as modifiable determinants of brain health.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that calibrate brain immune activity, yet this gut-brain signaling is disrupted in Alzheimer's disease (AD). In APOE4 knock-in mice and human fecal metagenomics, we tested whether inulin plus Bifidobacterium breve could restore microbial butyrate production and modify APOE-linked neuroinflammation. Supplemented mice showed higher Akkermansia and Lactobacillus abundance, increased butyrate in plasma, and lower TREM2 and IL1B expression in the hippocampus. Parallel 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed these taxonomic shifts, while targeted metabolomics showed reduced lipopolysaccharide and amyloid-beta in cortex. Notably, serotonin and indole-3-lactate correlated with Turicibacter abundance, and CX3CR1 expression tracked with less severe cognitive impairment. Among participants with mild cognitive impairment, random forest modeling linked Prevotella depletion to cognitive decline; butyrate was the strongest protective feature. These findings suggest that fiber-based synbiotic interventions may act through TREM2-dependent microglial pathways to attenuate AD-related neuroinflammation. Future clinical trials should stratify by microbiome composition.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids that calibrate brain immune tone via the gut-brain axis. In mice consuming a high-fat diet, inulin supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, raised butyrate in feces, and reduced neuroinflammation. These changes coincided with lower TNF and higher IL-10 expression in hippocampus, along with improved performance in a Morris water maze and reduced anxiety. Gut microbiota profiling by 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that inulin restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations depleted by the high-fat diet. Mechanistically, butyrate promoted GPR43 and GPR109A signaling in intestinal epithelium, enhancing serotonin synthesis and BDNF expression in the brain. In adults with metabolic syndrome, a fermented food-rich diet increased microbial diversity and decreased interleukin-6, suggesting translational relevance. The findings position inulin and fermented foods as modulators of the gut-brain axis, although BDNF signaling and short-chain fatty acid receptor pathways require further validation in patients.

Altered gut microbiota–derived bile acid and short-chain fatty acid production along the gut-brain axis is increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (PD), but whether these metabolites drive or merely reflect nigrostriatal degeneration remains unresolved. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics of fecal and serum samples from patients with PD and matched controls, then transplanted patient-derived microbiota into germ-free mice to test causality. Bacterial baiCD and butyrate synthesis genes were quantified, and substantia nigra neuronal loss and α-synuclein aggregation were assessed in the brain. Linear mixed-effects models identified microbial taxa and metabolites associated with motor severity, while mediation analysis tested whether gut-derived metabolites statistically linked dysbiosis to neuropathology. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high deoxycholic acid and low butyrate reproduced motor deficits and enhanced α-synucleinopathy in recipient mice, effects attenuated by a bile acid sequestrant. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-mediated bile acid transformation is a modifiable driver of PD-related neurodegeneration and a candidate target for microbiome-directed interventions.

Microbial depletion of butyrate in the colon precedes depressive-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress, suggesting that gut microbiota-derived metabolites gate brain serotonin synthesis. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we found that stress-susceptible mice harbored reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside lower tryptophan and 5-hydroxytryptamine in the hippocampus. Random forest classified mice by depression phenotype with high accuracy, and Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF, TrkB, and TPH1 expression. Transplantation of microbiota from unstressed mice restored butyrate, normalized BDNF and TrkB transcripts, and attenuated neuroinflammation in the prefrontal cortex. In an independent human cohort, low fecal Lactobacillus abundance tracked with higher depression severity and lower butyrate, reinforcing the translational relevance of this microbiome-brain circuit. These data position gut microbiota-butyrate-BDNF signaling as a candidate gut-brain axis pathway for depression, with mediation analysis indicating that butyrate mediates the effect of Lactobacillus on BDNF expression.

Gut microbiota depletion in germ-free mice impairs brain immune maturation and exacerbates Alzheimer's disease-like amyloid-beta pathology, an effect reversed by colonization with microbiota from healthy adults but not from patients with mild cognitive impairment. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and metagenomic sequencing, we identified Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium as major producers of butyrate and propionate. Oral administration of these short-chain fatty acids restored FFAR2 signaling in hippocampus, reduced interleukin-1beta, and improved cognitive performance in APP/PS1 mice. In contrast, FFAR2 deletion abolished the protective effects, while TLR4 deficiency attenuated cytokine release. Fecal microbiota from patients showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced butyrate production, correlating with Mini-Mental State Examination scores. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus were also depleted in patients, and indole-3-propionic acid was lower in gut microbiota cultures. These results position gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and FFAR2 as therapeutic targets for Alzheimer's disease. This signaling may be conserved in humans and amenable to dietary fiber or probiotic intervention.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon shapes central nervous system immune tone, and its disruption is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder. We recruited 78 adults with subthreshold depressive symptoms and randomized them to a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo for 8 weeks. Baseline dietary fiber intake was estimated using a food frequency questionnaire and treated as a covariate. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma inflammatory cytokines and tryptophan metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Probiotic intake increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated inversely with depressive symptom scores, whereas the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio did not differ between groups. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with probiotics may modulate inflammatory pathways relevant to depression, although clinical benefit requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, linking gut microbiota composition to depression and anxiety. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with moderate depressive symptoms received either omega-3 fatty acid supplementation plus probiotic capsules or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance in the intervention arm. Serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor and serotonin concentrations rose, while interleukin-6 declined. Short-chain fatty acids produced by these taxa enhanced intestinal barrier integrity and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline obesity and antibiotic exposure revealed that microbial shifts mediated improvements in depressive symptoms. BDNF rs6265 genotype moderated the effect, with Met carriers showing greater symptom reduction. Clinical response rates were 62% versus 38%, with only mild gastrointestinal symptoms reported. These findings suggest that omega-3 and probiotic co-supplementation may enhance microbiota-gut-brain axis signaling and offer a precision approach for mood disorders.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that signal to the brain through immune, vagal, and endocrine routes, and disruption of this axis is increasingly linked to depression and cognitive decline. To test whether a Mediterranean-style diet reshapes gut microbiota and improves hippocampal function, we conducted an 8-week randomized controlled trial in adults with mild depressive symptoms. Fecal samples were analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma tryptophan metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Dietary adherence was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Using mixed-effects models, we found that the intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lachnospiraceae abundance and reduced Bacteroides relative abundance. These shifts correlated with higher indole-3-propionic acid and lower kynurenine levels, which in turn predicted improved mood scores. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial changes explained 31% of the dietary effect on mood. Our findings support whole-diet approaches, rather than single nutrient supplements, for targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis in clinical populations.

Metabolites produced by the gut microbiome in the colon shape brain function through vagal, immune, and endocrine signaling, and their imbalance is increasingly linked to anxiety, depression, and Alzheimer's disease. In a mouse model of chronic stress, supplementation with triphala polyphenols restored gut microbiota diversity, increased Akkermansia muciniphila, and reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide. These changes coincided with higher Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and lower corticosterone levels. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that triphala polyphenols enriched production of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, which correlated with behavioral resilience. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a randomized pilot trial showed that triphala polyphenols altered fecal microbiome composition and reduced inflammatory cytokines, although effects on APOE-related amyloid pathology remain unclear. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with triphala polyphenols may support brain health, but larger clinical trials with metagenomic and multivariable modeling are needed to define responders and host mechanisms. Longitudinal sampling will be essential to distinguish cause from consequence.

Microbial tryptophan metabolism has emerged as a decisive interface between dietary intake and central nervous system homeostasis. In 184 adults, we profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified tryptophan catabolites alongside aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) expression in peripheral blood. Participants consuming a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermentable fiber showed higher abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and elevated indole-3-lactic acid compared with those on a low-fiber diet. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for false discovery rate, indole-3-lactic acid was inversely associated with depressive symptoms and positively associated with AHR expression. Mediation analysis indicated that AHR signaling explained 27% of the relationship between microbial composition and anxiety scores. Metagenomic data further linked these shifts to enriched tryptophanase and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase genes in gut microbiota. These findings suggest that dietary fiber reshapes gut microbiota toward indole production, engaging AHR-dependent pathways that influence brain function and emotional behavior in humans.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that influence central nervous system function through endocrine, immune, and neural routes. In adults with major depressive disorder, lower fecal abundance of Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus has been linked to reduced quality of life, whereas Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species can attenuate stress-related behaviors in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and random forest classification, we compared gut microbial communities in participants consuming a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermented foods versus a habitual Western diet. The intervention increased gut microbiota diversity, raised butyrate levels, and decreased anxiety scores; these changes correlated with altered expression of BDNF in peripheral blood. Probiotic supplementation alone produced smaller effects, suggesting that whole-diet patterns, rather than single probiotics, more effectively engage the gut microbiota–brain axis. In germ-free mice, colonization with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii restored butyrate production and normalized depressive-like behavior, while fecal microbiota transplantation from responders transferred beneficial metabolic profiles. These findings support dietary intervention as a tractable strategy for depression and anxiety.

Dietary fiber depletion rapidly reshapes gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid production, yet its consequences for depression-like behavior remain incompletely resolved. In a mouse model of chronic social defeat stress, animals fed a low-fiber diet showed increased anhedonia, elevated corticosterone, and reduced hippocampal BDNF expression relative to standard chow-fed mice. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed expansions of Bacteroides and Enterobacteriaceae and depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Fecal microbiota transplantation from low-fiber diet-fed donors into germ-free recipients transferred behavioral deficits, implicating microbiota composition rather than diet alone. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability explained 38% of the effect on depressive-like behavior, while linear mixed-effects models linked microbial metabolites to prefrontal cortex serotonin transporter expression. Butyrate supplementation restored BDNF signaling and normalized stress-induced behavioral abnormalities. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain axis signal and suggest that prebiotic or butyrate-based strategies may mitigate stress-related mood disorders. Together, these data link fiber intake, microbial community structure, and metabolite signaling in a tractable gut-brain circuit.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet the extent to which this pathway buffers Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk remains unclear. We recruited older adults with subjective cognitive decline and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, quantified plasma butyrate by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and measured BDNF and IL6 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Participants completed a Mediterranean diet adherence score and a neuropsychological battery. A linear mixed-effects model tested associations between microbial diversity, butyrate, and BDNF expression, adjusting for age and APOE genotype. Higher fiber intake correlated with increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and elevated butyrate (r = 0.42, P = 0.003). BDNF expression was positively associated with microbial richness and inversely with IL6. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the relationship between F. prausnitzii and BDNF (indirect effect = 0.18, 95% CI 0.05–0.31). These findings suggest that dietary fiber and gut microbiota jointly influence BDNF-related neuroplasticity, offering a modifiable target for AD prevention.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid production predicts age-related cognitive decline more strongly than amyloid burden, yet whether dietary inulin can modify this trajectory remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 84 older adults with subjective cognitive impairment received either inulin (12 g/day) or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; plasma propionate, butyrate, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundances and raised butyrate levels relative to placebo. These shifts correlated with improved cognitive scores, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the cognitive benefit. Random forest classification further linked baseline Bacteroides abundance to treatment response. No changes occurred in lipopolysaccharide-binding protein or depressive symptoms. Compliance exceeded 90%, and no serious adverse events were reported. Baseline microbial diversity did not moderate the effect. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation may support brain function through gut microbiome-derived metabolites, warranting longer trials in prodromal dementia.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate microglial activation and behavior, yet the extent to which whole-food interventions alter this axis remains unclear. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed a walnut-enriched diet or a refined-carbohydrate control for 12 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and plasma untargeted metabolomics were used to profile microbiota and circulating metabolites. Linear mixed-effects models adjusting for age, sex, and baseline values showed that the walnut diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate levels, while decreasing lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. These changes correlated with improved executive function scores. Spearman correlation analyses linked Faecalibacterium with butyrate and cognitive gains. Compared with control, these shifts were accompanied by reduced C-reactive protein. No significant changes were observed in depressive symptoms or intestinal permeability. The findings suggest that walnut consumption may beneficially reshape the gut microbiota–brain axis, though larger trials are needed to confirm causality and durability.

Microbial colonization of the gut microbiota during early life shapes hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity and may predispose to anxiety-like behavior and metabolic dysfunction. In male mice fed a high-fat diet supplemented with inulin, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids in cecal contents. BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex was quantified by quantitative PCR; fluoxetine served as a positive control. Linear mixed-effects models showed that dietary fiber intake interacted with microbial composition to predict depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test. In a parallel cohort of adults with major depressive disorder, baseline fecal microbiota was profiled using shotgun metagenomics. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor and inflammatory cytokines were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; higher Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with lower depression severity after false discovery rate correction. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived metabolites may mediate nutritional effects on BDNF signaling and affective symptoms, offering targets for prebiotic interventions.

Consumption of fermented foods rich in polyphenols can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate brain function, yet the microbial signals linking dietary patterns to cognitive decline remain poorly resolved. We analyzed fecal metabolites and 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and healthy controls after a 12-week randomized Mediterranean-style diet intervention. Using mediation analysis within a linear mixed-effects model, we tested whether Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundances mediated changes in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations and hippocampal volume. Adherence to the diet increased Faecalibacterium and butyrate, and these shifts correlated with improved MCI scores. The indirect effect through butyrate was significant (β = 0.18, 95% CI 0.05–0.31), whereas Bifidobacterium showed no mediation. A random forest classifier further ranked butyrate, propionate, and Faecalibacterium as top features distinguishing responders. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-driven microbial metabolites may support brain health, and that causal mediation models can identify candidate pathways in the gut microbiota-brain system.

Microbial signalling along the gut-brain axis can reshape BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a mechanism increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). In mice exposed to chronic stress, gut microbiota depletion reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lowered BDNF transcripts, whereas probiotic administration restored both. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and faecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into rodents reproduced social withdrawal and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. In a separate cohort, random-effects meta-analysis of shotgun metagenomics confirmed that Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted in MDD, with butyrate synthesis pathways under-represented. To test causality in human populations, we applied two-sample Mendelian randomisation using BDNF and gut microbial taxa as exposures. Genetically predicted Lactobacillaceae abundance was inversely associated with MDD risk, and mediation analysis indicated that BDNF mediated 18% of this effect. These findings position BDNF as a plausible molecular node linking gut microbiota to depression, supporting probiotic and fermented food interventions while cautioning that antidepressant response may depend on baseline microbial composition.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with preserved hippocampal volume and lower risk of mild cognitive impairment, yet the microbial and inflammatory pathways underlying this relationship remain incompletely resolved. In a longitudinal cohort of older adults (n=180), we quantified gut microbiota composition using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, plasma short-chain fatty acids, and inflammatory cytokines, and assessed brain network connectivity with resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Linear mixed-effects models showed that higher dietary fiber intake predicted greater abundance of Butyricicoccus and Faecalibacterium and higher butyrate concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate statistically mediated 31% of the association between fiber-rich food consumption and default-mode network connectivity, with a significant indirect effect after adjustment for APOE4 status. Permutation testing confirmed that these indirect effects were unlikely to arise by chance, and false discovery rate correction preserved significance across butyrate-producing taxa. These findings position microbiota-derived metabolites as plausible transducers of diet on brain function and support targeting fermentable fiber in cognitive decline prevention.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids shape hippocampus BDNF expression and cognitive resilience, yet causal routes linking gut microbiota to Alzheimer's disease remain unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with mild cognitive impairment or from healthy controls, then fed them a high-fat diet or standard chow. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and quantitative PCR, we quantified Akkermansia muciniphila, Bacteroides fragilis, and Lactobacillus abundances. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for cage effects showed that donor status, not diet, predicted Bdnf and Tnf expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Mice receiving mild cognitive impairment-derived microbiota exhibited impaired spatial memory, reduced butyrate, and elevated neuroinflammation. Probiotic supplementation with A. muciniphila restored butyrate, normalized Bdnf, and improved cognitive deficits. Notably, butyrate concentrations correlated positively with Bdnf and negatively with Tnf, suggesting a short-chain fatty acid-dependent mechanism. These findings position gut microbial composition as a modifiable regulator of gut-brain axis signaling and suggest A. muciniphila-directed probiotics for early Alzheimer's disease.

High Western diet intake predicts lower gut microbial diversity and altered short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in APOE4 carriers, suggesting an interaction among diet, APOE4, and gut microbiota relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD). To test this, we recruited 120 older adults (60 carriers of APOE4, 60 non-carriers) and collected stool and serum samples. Microbial communities were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and SCFAs were quantified by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Dietary patterns were assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Using multivariable linear regression, we found that Western diet adherence was inversely associated with Faecalibacterium abundance (β = −0.34, P = 0.006) and butyrate concentrations (β = −0.29, P = 0.012), with stronger effects in APOE4 carriers. Bacteroides was enriched in non-carriers consuming Mediterranean-style diets. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of the association between diet and AD-related amyloid markers. These findings support targeting gut microbiota through diet interventions, particularly in APOE4-positive individuals.

Microbial colonization of the intestine shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and modulates depression-like behavior through immune and metabolic signals. In a cohort of 48 adults with major depressive disorder and 24 healthy controls, we profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Alpha diversity was lower in patients, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was depleted. Plasma interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and tryptophan metabolites were measured by ELISA and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Relative abundance of Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium correlated with BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood, and serum interleukin-6 was negatively correlated with BDNF exon IV methylation. Using Spearman correlation, PERMANOVA, and mediation analysis, we identified microbial taxa and metabolites associated with symptom severity. In mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress, probiotic supplementation or fluoxetine restored butyrate levels, increased BDNF expression, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived butyrate may influence BDNF-dependent brain circuits, offering a target for stress-related disorders.

Fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich foods reshape the gut microbiota and modulate the gut-brain axis, but the neuroactive consequences of specific dietary patterns remain poorly resolved. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet or a control diet for 8 weeks, with or without inulin supplementation. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acids, and tryptophan metabolites. The Mediterranean diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia intestinalis, and Bifidobacterium, while inulin amplified butyrate production and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines. These microbial shifts correlated with improved executive function scores and lower hippocampal neuroinflammation markers. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and indole-3-propionate partly explained the cognitive benefit, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood tracked with microbial diversity. Parallel experiments in germ-free mice colonized with participant-derived microbiota reproduced the butyrate-dependent improvement, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. The findings position dietary fiber and targeted prebiotics as tractable modulators of microbiota-gut-brain signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and vagus nerve signaling, and dietary substrate availability is a key determinant of this signaling. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depression received a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 8 weeks while consuming a fiber-rich diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolite profiling showed increased gut microbiome diversity, enriched butyrate synthesis genes, and higher butyrate in the supplement group. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Plasma serotonin turnover increased, while interleukin-6 decreased, indicating immune-metabolic coupling. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated the improvement. In a parallel mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders attenuated stress-induced social avoidance and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. The findings support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics and fermentable fiber as an adjunctive strategy for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Dietary fiber deprivation reshapes the gut microbiota and elevates risk for cognitive impairment, yet the molecular links across the gut-brain axis remain unresolved. Using a mouse model of long-term fiber deficiency, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with hippocampal proteomics and random forest modeling to identify microbial and host signatures associated with memory decline. Fiber-deficient mice displayed gut microbiota dysbiosis, marked by reduced Bacteroidetes and expanded Proteobacteria, alongside lower short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and impaired intestinal barrier. In the hippocampus, synaptic ultrastructure was disrupted, with downregulation of CaMKIId and GAP43, neuroinflammation, and microglial synaptic engulfment. Mediation analysis linked altered microbial composition to cognitive deficits. Notably, oral SCFA supplementation or SCFA receptor knockout mice experiments confirmed that SCFA signaling is required for the microbiota-hippocampal axis. These findings position adequate intake of fiber-rich foods as a modifiable strategy that protects human brain function by sustaining gut microbial communities and SCFA-dependent hippocampal plasticity, and may reduce risk of neurodegenerative disease.

Altered gut microbial ecology precedes motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD) and may modulate nigrostriatal degeneration through immune and metabolic signaling. We profiled fecal microbiota from 68 PD patients and 62 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, then validated candidates in mice overexpressing SNCA. Random forest classification separated patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82. Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae were depleted, whereas Verrucomicrobiaceae and Enterobacteriaceae were enriched in PD patients; these shifts correlated with colon short-chain fatty acid concentrations and constipation severity. Microbial metabolite profiles also differed by PD duration and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder status. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from PD donors exacerbated motor impairment, reduced dopamine in striatum, and increased α-synuclein aggregation. TLR4 and IL-1β expression rose in midbrain. Levodopa response was unchanged, but probiotic treatment restored Lachnospiraceae abundance and attenuated neuroinflammation. These findings implicate gut microbiome-brain signaling in PD and support multivariable modeling of microbial and clinical features for patient stratification.
