metadata.abstract: Chronic intake of a high-fat, low-fiber diet reshapes the gut microbiota, increasing Firmicutes and depleting Bacteroidetes, and this dysbiosis propagates to the central nervous system through short-chain fatty acid, lipopolysaccharide, and vagus nerve signaling. In mice fed this diet, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced microbial diversity, while fecal microbiota transplantation from dysbiotic donors into germ-free recipients elevated IL-1β and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus and impaired performance on the Morris water maze. These changes coincided with cognitive impairment, anxiety-like behavior, and microglial activation. Supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or inulin partially restored gut microbial balance, lowered circulating cytokines, and improved spatial memory. In adults, similar dietary patterns associate with altered gut microbiota and poorer executive function, though causality remains unresolved. Notably, antibiotic depletion of commensal microbiota abolished these effects, implicating live bacteria rather than metabolites alone. Targeting the gut microbiota through diet and microbial therapeutics may offer a tractable strategy for preventing neurodegenerative disease.

Fermented foods and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation independently modulate the gut microbiota–brain axis, yet their combined influence on chronic stress and intestinal permeability remains unclear. We randomized adults with self-reported anxiety to a high-fiber, fermented food diet plus omega-3 capsules or a control condition for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Linear mixed models tested associations with depressive symptoms, perceived stress, and serum interleukin-6. Compared with control, the intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced interleukin-6. These changes correlated with lower anxiety scores and higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in mice transplanted with post-intervention microbiota. In germ-free mice, this microbiota reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased hippocampal serotonin and TPH1 expression. Our findings suggest that combining fermented foods with omega-3 supplementation may produce additive benefits for stress-related psychopathology through microbiota-dependent metabolite signaling.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence BDNF expression in the hippocampus and dampen neuroinflammation. In mice consuming a high-fiber diet, Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus expanded alongside butyrate production, with reduced depressive-like behavior and lower IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts. These benefits disappeared after gut microbiota depletion, implicating microbial metabolites as mediators. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus reproduced some effects, but only when combined with fermentable fiber, indicating substrate availability is critical. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a randomized controlled trial of omega-3 fatty acids plus prebiotic foods increased serum BDNF and improved cognition. Mechanistically, butyrate promoted HDAC inhibition and GPR43 signaling in intestinal and brain tissues, while fiber supplements alone failed to rescue BDNF when microbial diversity remained low. Together, these findings position dietary fiber, probiotics, and omega-3 fatty acids as modifiable inputs that shape gut microbial ecology and BDNF-dependent brain circuits, offering a tractable strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota can prime neuroinflammation and alter gut-brain axis signaling in multiple sclerosis (MS). Among pediatric-onset MS patients, amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene revealed reduced short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Alloprevotella, with variable increases in Bacteroides and Streptococcus. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance and linear regression associated these shifts with short-chain fatty acid depletion, intestinal permeability, and host factors such as body mass index, but not consistently with disease-modifying therapy. In mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, oral Alloprevotella rava and prebiotic supplementation reduced neuroinflammation and increased propionate, suggesting that microbial metabolites mediate protection. Because probiotic supplementation may expand Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, stabilize short-chain fatty acid pools, and dampen depressive symptoms, microbiota-targeted adjuvants are plausible. Still, heterogeneity across cohorts, small sample sizes, and confounding by immunomodulatory treatment limit causal inference. Future trials should combine metagenomics, metabolomics, and standardized mixed-effects models to determine whether restoring gut microbial communities can slow MS progression.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and bile acids shape brain function through immune, vagal, and endocrine routes, yet causal direction within the gut microbiota–brain axis remains contested. In a randomized controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received a 12-week probiotic formulation or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and neuropsychological testing were performed at baseline and endpoint. Baseline fecal microbiota composition differed by cognitive impairment severity, and Spearman correlation confirmed dose-dependent relationships. We used linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA to test associations between microbial abundance and cognitive scores. Active treatment increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and reduced Ruminococcus. Higher Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with improved Digit Span Backward performance, whereas Ruminococcus was inversely associated with Recognition Trials. Mediation analysis suggested that changes in short-chain fatty acids partly explained cognitive gains. These findings support a bidirectional model in which gut microbial shifts can influence brain networks, and they identify Bifidobacterium and Ruminococcus as candidate targets for early cognitive decline.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the gut yields short-chain fatty acids that signal across the gastrointestinal tract to the brain, yet whether this axis can be therapeutically harnessed in major depressive disorder remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, adults with moderate depressive symptoms received either probiotic supplementation or placebo while consuming a fermented-food-enriched diet. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae abundance, butyrate concentrations, and BDNF expression were measured at baseline and week 12. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that probiotic supplementation increased Lachnospiraceae relative abundance and reduced depressive scores compared with placebo, but only among participants with higher baseline fermented food intake. Butyrate mediated this effect, whereas BDNF expression did not. No significant changes in Bacteroidetes were observed. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with fermented foods may modulate the gut microbiota and improve mood, supporting targeted dietary strategies for depression.

Microbial dysbiosis may precede central symptoms in mild cognitive impairment, yet whether diet can reverse this trajectory remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a multispecies probiotic supplement or placebo alongside standardized fermented food and fiber-rich food guidance. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that the probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance and reduced Prevotella compared with placebo. These shifts coincided with lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha concentrations and higher short-chain fatty acid levels in plasma. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells, BDNF and IL-6 expression changed in opposite directions: BDNF increased while IL-6 decreased. Mixed-effects models indicated that Akkermansia abundance mediated the association between probiotic intake and improved cognitive scores. Parallel fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced the inflammatory profile, while RNA sequencing of hippocampus revealed Nrf2-dependent antioxidant pathway enrichment. These findings support a gut-brain axis in which dietary fiber and probiotic interventions modulate BDNF and inflammatory signaling, offering a tractable strategy for early cognitive decline.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life critically shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet how dietary fiber intake interacts with this axis remains poorly defined. We colonized germ-free C57BL/6 mice with gut microbiota from healthy adults or patients with major depressive disorder and fed them either a high-fiber chow or refined low-fiber diet for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and RNA sequencing quantified microbial composition and hippocampal transcription. Linear mixed models adjusted for cage and batch effects. High-fiber chow increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and normalized BDNF expression relative to low-fiber diet. Mice receiving depression-associated microbiota showed reduced BDNF and increased interleukin-6 regardless of diet, but probiotic supplementation partially rescued these effects. No differences in FKBP5 or NR3C1 were detected, yet high-fiber chow lowered corticosterone. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics may mitigate depression-linked neuroinflammation through BDNF-dependent pathways, though antidepressant exposure and baseline microbiome diversity modified responses.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet reshapes the gut microbiota and dampens vagal signaling, yet whether targeted prebiotic fiber supplementation can reverse associated cognitive decline remains unresolved. In a randomized adult cohort and mice, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and resting-state functional MRI to test inulin against control. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in feces and plasma, and strengthened hippocampal connectivity. These changes correlated with improved verbal memory testing scores and reduced interleukin-6 (IL-6) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels. In germ-free mice colonized with post-supplement microbiota, the behavioral benefit was transferable, whereas vagotomy abolished it, implicating a vagus nerve-dependent gut-brain circuit. Metagenomic analysis identified butyrate kinase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase as enriched pathways in responders. Notably, inulin responders showed greater prefrontal cortex activation during cognitive flexibility testing. These findings indicate that inulin supplementation mitigates diet-induced neuroinflammation and supports resilience against cognitive decline through microbiota-derived SCFAs, offering a pragmatic dietary strategy for metabolic-brain disorders.

Microbial depletion of butyrate in the colon is associated with heightened neuroinflammation and impaired BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, suggesting a tractable axis for depression. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we tested whether gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder transfers behavioral and molecular deficits. Transplanted mice showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated lipopolysaccharide, increased IL-6 and TNF-α, and decreased BDNF expression in the hippocampus relative to controls. Fecal short-chain fatty acids were lower, and untargeted metabolomics identified depleted propionate and acetate. RT-qPCR and Western blot confirmed these changes, while Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF levels. Butyrate supplementation or a dietary fiber-enriched diet restored BDNF expression, reduced neuroinflammation, and normalized behavior; Akkermansia muciniphila administration produced similar benefits. Mediation analysis indicated that BDNF downregulation explained a substantial portion of the behavioral effect. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a mediator of gut-brain signaling and support probiotic interventions for depression.

Consumption of a Western diet enriched in saturated fat and refined sugars reshapes the gut microbiome, increasing Bacteroides and Clostridium while depleting Akkermansia and Lactobacillus. This dysbiosis elevates circulating lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6, promoting neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In male C57BL/6J mice fed the Western diet for 12 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed altered microbial composition, while behavioral testing showed impaired hippocampus-dependent memory. RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex identified downregulation of Bdnf, Pgc-1α, and Tjp1, alongside upregulated Nfkb1. Linear discriminant analysis linked Desulfovibrio abundance to memory deficits. Fecal transfer from Western diet-fed mice to germ-free recipients reproduced microglial activation and synaptic loss. Supplementing inulin or omega-3 fatty acids partially restored Bdnf expression and reduced tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Notably, minocycline attenuated microglial activation and restored Bdnf levels, whereas antibiotic depletion of gut bacteria prevented diet-induced neuroinflammation. These data suggest that diet-driven gut microbial shifts prime central immune cells and suppress neurotrophic signaling, linking processed food intake to depression risk in humans.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet microbial and metabolic mediators remain poorly defined. We profiled fecal microbiota from 120 patients with MDD and 120 matched controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Patients showed reduced alpha diversity and depletion of Faecalibacterium, Lachnospiraceae, and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside enrichment of Bacteroides and Escherichia-Shigella. These shifts correlated with lower fecal short-chain fatty acids and elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Host transcriptomic analysis revealed suppressed BDNF and increased IL6 and TNF expression in peripheral blood, linking dysbiosis to neuroinflammation. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD donors induced depressive-like behavior, reduced BDNF in the hippocampus, and altered serotonin metabolism. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium abundance partially mediated the association between gut microbiota composition and MDD severity. Collectively, these data suggest that targeting gut microbial communities and microbial metabolites may offer therapeutic avenues for MDD.

Microbial dysbiosis along the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to Parkinson's disease (PD) through immune and metabolic signaling, but the relative contribution of specific bacterial taxa and host transcriptional programs remains unresolved. We performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics on fecal samples from 138 patients with PD and 102 healthy controls, paired with RNA sequencing of blood and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry metabolomics. Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae were reduced in PD, while Verrucomicrobiaceae and Bifidobacteriaceae were increased. These alterations correlated with lower short-chain fatty acids and higher lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, as well as elevated fecal calprotectin. Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis suggested that Prevotellaceae depletion influences PD risk partly via LRRK2 and GBA1 expression. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations were inversely correlated with SNCA expression in colon tissue, and linear mixed models confirmed this association after adjustment for age and sex. In mice, transplantation of microbiota from patients with PD exacerbated substantia nigra neuroinflammation and motor deficits. Targeting gut microbial composition may therefore modify PD progression.

Gut microbiota composition shapes central nervous system immune tone and behavior, yet the extent to which probiotic and fermented food interventions translate into clinically meaningful brain effects remains uncertain. In mice fed a high-fat diet, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve increased short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in the colon, restored brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These effects were absent in microbiota-depleted animals and were partially recapitulated by fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated donors. In a parallel human cohort, higher intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber correlated with greater gut microbial diversity and lower circulating inflammatory cytokines, but not with improved cognitive decline scores. Prebiotic supplementation alone showed weaker and more variable effects. Together, these findings suggest that probiotics and fermented foods can modulate the gut-brain axis through SCFA-dependent and immune-mediated pathways, but baseline microbiome composition and host diet may determine whether brain benefits emerge.

Depletion of short-chain fatty acids in the colon can amplify neuroinflammation and weaken hippocampal synaptic plasticity, a mechanism increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We tested whether dietary inulin plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reshapes the gut microbiota and Bdnf-dependent brain signaling in APP/PS1 mice. Mice received control diet, inulin, L. rhamnosus GG, or both for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified fecal microbiota; quantitative PCR measured Bdnf, Nfkb1, and Il6 expression; immunoassay measured IL-6 and TNF-α. Linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction tested group, time, and interaction effects. Combined treatment increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, reduced amyloid-beta deposition, lowered IL-6, and restored Bdnf expression relative to controls. Mediation analysis suggested that gut microbiota shifts partly explained Bdnf recovery and improved cognitive impairment. These findings support inulin and L. rhamnosus GG as modifiable microbiota-targeted interventions, though human trials are needed to confirm causality and optimal long-term dosing.

Dietary plant polysaccharides can reshape gut microbial communities and alter short-chain fatty acid production, offering a plausible route for modulating neuropsychiatric disorders along the gut-brain axis. We examined whether inulin-type fructans supplementation modifies microbiota composition, BDNF and IL-6 expression in the hippocampus, and anxiety-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic stress. After 4 weeks, inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in feces, and reduced stress-induced anxiety-like behavior. Hippocampal BDNF expression was higher, while IL-6 and TNF were lower in supplemented mice. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR linked these changes to gut microbiota shifts. Spearman correlation analysis associated Bifidobacterium with BDNF expression and butyrate with IL-6. In patients with depression, similar fiber interventions remain less conclusive, but current evidence supports targeting the gut microbiome to influence BDNF and inflammatory signaling in the brain. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may serve as an adjunctive strategy for depression and anxiety, although dose, baseline microbiota composition, and host genetics modulate outcomes.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) generated from dietary fiber in the colon modulate depression-related neurocircuitry, yet causal links remain uncertain. We recruited 84 adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and 42 healthy controls, profiled stool gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified serum SCFAs using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA showed distinct community composition in MDD, with lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and higher Eggerthella. Linear regression associated butyrate with reduced anhedonia and elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the link between Faecalibacterium and anhedonia. Baseline severity was measured with Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, and random forest classification separated MDD from controls with moderate accuracy. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD donors induced depressive-like behavior, whereas probiotic plus fermented foods increased Lactobacillus and normalized SCFAs. After an 8-week Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods, participants showed increased gut microbial diversity and lower depression scores. These findings support targeting the gut microbiota with fiber-rich foods and probiotics as adjunctive MDD therapy.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that tune brain circuits implicated in depression and anxiety, yet the microbial taxa and metabolic routes underlying this effect remain poorly resolved. We profiled stool and serum from 142 adults with major depressive disorder and 96 matched controls, using shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics. Random forest classifiers identified Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Lactobacillus as depleted in cases, while linear mixed-effects models linked lower butyrate with higher depressive symptom severity. In mice fed a low-fiber diet, butyrate supplementation reduced hippocampal BDNF deficits and normalized anxiety-like behavior; mediation analysis suggested butyrate mediated the fiber–depression association. Probiotic co-administration enhanced Lactobacillus abundance but did not alter butyrate. Baseline microbial diversity correlated inversely with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and causal mediation models estimated that butyrate accounted for 31% of the protective fiber effect on depression scores. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable substrate for gut microbiota-driven pathways that influence depression.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids act as potent modulators of brain function, with butyrate crossing the blood-brain barrier to inhibit HDAC1 and HDAC3 in hippocampal microglia. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we profiled gut microbiota and fecal short-chain fatty acids in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress. Stressed mice exhibited reduced Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, lower butyrate levels, and increased BDNF promoter methylation in the hippocampus, accompanied by depressive-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from non-stressed mice restored butyrate production, normalized BDNF expression, and reduced immobility in the forced swim test. In a parallel human cohort, stool microbiota from individuals with major depressive disorder showed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and reduced butyrate synthesis potential. Linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation linked Lachnospiraceae abundance to BDNF methylation and behavioral scores, while mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability partially mediated the relationship between Faecalibacterium abundance and BDNF methylation. These results identify a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis that may be targeted by prebiotics or probiotics in depression.

Probiotic supplementation can attenuate anxiety-like behavior in adults with mild psychological distress, but whether these effects depend on baseline gut microbiota composition remains unclear. We conducted an 8-week randomized controlled trial in 96 adults randomized to Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or placebo. Fecal samples were collected at baseline and week 8; 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics were used to profile microbial composition. Anxiety and depression symptoms were measured with validated scales. Linear mixed-effects models showed that probiotic reduced anxiety scores relative to placebo (Cohen's d = -0.42, p = 0.03). Responders had higher baseline relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, and random forest classification separated responders from non-responders with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.78. Gut microbiota shifts included increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced Bacteroides. These findings suggest that probiotic efficacy in anxiety is linked to baseline microbiome features, supporting microbiota-informed selection for gut-brain axis-targeted interventions.

metadata.abstract: short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as key mediators of gut-brain signaling, yet their effects on BDNF expression and affective behavior depend on dietary context. In a randomized, controlled trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms consumed either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet for 8 weeks; fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing, and serum SCFAs were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. The high-fiber diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, elevated butyrate, and upregulated BDNF in peripheral blood. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and lower cortisol levels. In contrast, the Western diet enriched Bacteroides, decreased butyrate, and did not alter BDNF. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 31% of the diet-related improvement in mood. Our findings indicate that dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiome to promote BDNF-dependent brain plasticity, offering an accessible strategy for depression prevention. However, effects were attenuated in participants with low baseline microbial diversity, highlighting the need for personalized nutrition.

Gut microbiota metabolites act as key mediators of the gut-brain axis, influencing brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. Short-chain fatty acids produced by butyrate-producing bacteria modulate BDNF expression and microglial activation, while tryptophan catabolites regulate serotonin synthesis and neuroinflammation. Disruption of this bidirectional communication is implicated in irritable bowel syndrome, major depressive disorder, and Alzheimer's disease. In murine models of Parkinson's disease, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium restored microbial diversity, reduced nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration, and improved motor deficits. Dietary fiber and fermented foods similarly increase short-chain fatty acid availability, but responses vary with baseline microbiome composition. A 12-week randomized trial in adults with mild cognitive impairment found that omega-3 fatty acid combined with inulin altered gut microbiota and improved cognitive scores, although effects on APOE carriers were attenuated. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through diet and supplements may complement levodopa therapy, but longitudinal multi-omics are needed to identify responders.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber suppress neuroinflammation by modulating BDNF expression and histone acetylation in the hippocampus, suggesting a tractable gut-brain axis for depression and anxiety. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received inulin-type fructans or placebo for 8 weeks; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice were used to assess causality. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated fecal butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide concentrations. These changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms and cognitive impairment, alongside increased BDNF and ZO-1 expression in the prefrontal cortex and colon. Linear mixed-effects models showed that gut microbiota composition explained 34% of the variance in symptom improvement. Baseline Bacteroides abundance and GPR43 genotype moderated treatment response. The findings indicate that prebiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate brain function via the vagus nerve, although larger trials in diverse populations are needed.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress, yet the molecular mediators linking these effects remain incompletely defined. We tested whether inulin alters Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and Nlrp3 signaling in the prefrontal cortex. Mice received inulin (10% w/w) or cellulose for 6 weeks, then underwent 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, RT-qPCR, and behavioral testing. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance and reduced anxiety-like behavior. In the hippocampus, Bdnf expression was elevated, whereas in the prefrontal cortex, Nlrp3 and IL-1β were suppressed. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium with Bdnf and anxiety-like behavior. Fecal butyrate and propionate concentrations were higher in inulin-fed mice than in cellulose-fed mice, and mediation analysis indicated that Akkermansia abundance partially mediated the reduction in Nlrp3 expression. No changes were observed in Tnf or Il6 expression. Together, these data position inulin as a potential prebiotic intervention for stress-related disorders through microbiota-Bdnf-Nlrp3 signaling.

Disruption of the gut microbiome can precede Parkinson's disease (PD) motor onset by years, suggesting that intestinal bacteria and their metabolites shape neurodegeneration through the gut-brain axis. Sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and shotgun metagenomics has shown consistent depletion of Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae in patients, alongside altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. These microbial metabolites influence microglial activation and neuroinflammation, potentially amplifying α-synuclein pathology in the substantia nigra. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, prebiotic feeding and probiotic supplementation reduce motor deficits, lower microglial activation, and restore microbial diversity. Levodopa response may also vary with gut microbiota composition, complicating treatment. However, causality remains difficult to establish because PD itself, disease-modifying therapies, and dietary fiber intake alter the gut ecosystem. Larger longitudinal studies combining metagenomic sequencing, metabolomics, and multivariable modeling are needed to define which taxa or metabolites are causal, and whether targeting them can modify PD progression. Clinically, these findings highlight dietary interventions as plausible adjuncts for older adults at risk of PD.

Dietary fiber insufficiency and excess saturated fat intake reshape the gut microbiota in ways that amplify neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet whether targeted probiotic or prebiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. In a randomized adult cohort, we compared a Western-style diet with a fiber-rich plant diet for 12 weeks, with half of each group receiving a probiotic containing Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis plus inulin. Fecal shotgun metagenomics and plasma metabolomics revealed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and reduced lipopolysaccharide binding protein. These microbial shifts correlated with improved hippocampal-dependent memory and lower depressive symptoms, independent of APOE genotype. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and indole-3-propionate partly explained the cognitive benefit. Notably, baseline gut microbial diversity moderated the response, with low-diversity participants showing the largest butyrate increase. The findings indicate that pairing fermentable fiber with live biotherapeutics may buffer diet-induced gut dysbiosis and support brain health, though longer trials are needed to confirm durability.

Fermentable dietary fiber and probiotic supplements can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate the microbiota-gut-brain axis, but their independent and combined effects on anxiety and depressive symptoms in adults with subclinical psychological distress remain unclear. In an 8-week, 2×2 factorial randomized controlled trial, 124 participants with low habitual prebiotic food intake received either a probiotic supplement, a high-prebiotic diet, both, or placebo. Linear mixed-effects modeling of total mood disturbance showed a significant advantage for the high-prebiotic diet versus placebo (Cohen's d = −0.58, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.04; p = 0.035), with secondary improvements in anxiety, perceived stress, and sleep quality. Probiotic supplementation alone did not significantly reduce mood disturbance (d = −0.17, p = 0.54), and the synbiotic arm showed no additive benefit. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium in the high-prebiotic diet group, correlating with reduced anxiety scores. These findings suggest that prebiotic-rich foods may outperform isolated probiotics for mood improvement, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and mechanism.

Disruption of the gut microbiome–brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether microbial metabolites directly modify BDNF and NLRP3 expression in the hippocampus remains unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with MDD received either a multi-strain probiotic (Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Bifidobacterium longum) plus standard care or placebo for 12 weeks. All participants consumed a Mediterranean diet and were counseled to increase fermented foods and dietary fiber. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that probiotic supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and butyrate production. Serum short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites rose, while cortisol and IL-6 declined. RNA sequencing of peripheral blood revealed upregulation of BDNF and downregulation of NLRP3 in responders. Linear mixed models associated these changes with reduced depressive symptoms and improved anxiety scores. These findings suggest that probiotics combined with Mediterranean-style eating may modulate BDNF/NLRP3 signaling via gut microbiota-derived metabolites, offering a tractable adjunctive strategy for MDD.

Microbial butyrate generated through dietary fiber fermentation is a central mediator of gut-brain axis signaling, yet its impact on BDNF expression in the hippocampus remains poorly resolved. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and quantitative PCR, we compared gut microbiota composition and BDNF transcription in mice maintained on either an inulin-enriched diet or a low-fiber diet for six weeks. The inulin-fed mice exhibited greater relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, higher butyrate concentrations in colonic contents, and increased BDNF mRNA in the hippocampus. These shifts were accompanied by reduced depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test and lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α levels. Among patients with major depressive disorder, baseline fiber intake correlated positively with microbial diversity and inversely with inflammatory markers, but not with circulating BDNF. Collectively, these data suggest that dietary fiber shapes gut microbiota metabolism to modulate BDNF-related hippocampal plasticity and depression-associated inflammation, although clinical translation will require additional longitudinal sampling and causal mediation analysis.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced from dietary fiber act on enteroendocrine cells and vagal afferents to modulate central nervous system inflammation and behavior, yet strain-level mediators remain poorly resolved. We profiled gut microbiota and tryptophan metabolites in 184 adults with major depressive disorder and 172 healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics. Mediation analysis tested whether Lactobacillus-derived indole-3-lactate links fermented food intake to symptom severity. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium were depleted in cases, whereas Eggerthella correlated with quinolinic acid. Circulating lipopolysaccharide and IL6 expression were elevated in cases and inversely correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance. Linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use showed that each 10-g/day increase in dietary fiber was associated with higher butyrate and lower depressive symptoms. In a mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber responders reduced neuroinflammation and increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These findings support a microbiota-gut-brain axis in which fermentable fiber and microbial indoles shape depression-related biology.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that act as key mediators of the gut-brain axis. In germ-free mice colonized with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and fed a high-fiber diet, butyrate concentrations rose in the colon, accompanied by increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced depressive-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics revealed that fiber supplementation enriched Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium, while linear mixed-effects models linked these shifts to lower neuroinflammation. In healthy adults, a randomized controlled trial of inulin showed parallel increases in SCFA-producing taxa and improved stress reactivity, although effects varied by baseline microbiome composition. In an independent cohort, greater fruit and vegetable consumption correlated with higher BDNF and GPR41 expression in peripheral blood. Antibiotic treatment abolished the Bdnf response in mice, confirming microbiota dependency. These findings suggest that targeting dietary fiber-microbiota interactions may offer a tractable strategy for promoting brain health, but host genetic and microbiome factors must be integrated to predict individual responses.

Disruption of the gut microbiota during aging amplifies Alzheimer's disease-related neuroinflammation, yet the microbial signals linking intestinal dysbiosis to hippocampal dysfunction remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and metagenomic sequencing in APP/PS1 mice, we found that Akkermansia muciniphila depletion correlated with reduced butyrate production and elevated Nlrp3 expression in the brain. Spearman correlation, PERMANOVA, and linear mixed-effects models linked microbial community shifts to cognitive impairment and decreased Bdnf transcripts. Probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus abundance, lowered amyloid-β load, and normalized Trem2 and Bdnf expression. These improvements were accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation and higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the gut. Fecal lipopolysaccharide and calprotectin were elevated in patients with mild cognitive impairment, and these markers correlated inversely with Bdnf methylation in blood. In mice receiving antibiotics, the protective effects of probiotics were diminished, whereas Lactobacillus recolonization partially rescued cognitive decline. Our data suggest that targeting gut microbial butyrate signaling may modify Alzheimer's disease progression through the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition can precede depressive symptoms and may modulate central serotonin availability through vagal and immune pathways. In a 12-week randomized trial of 84 adults with major depressive disorder, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis supplementation was compared with placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma inflammatory cytokine profiling were performed at baseline and endpoint. Baseline gut microbiota profiles differed by MDD severity, with lower Faecalibacterium and higher Bacteroides in symptomatic patients. We applied mixed-effects regression to test whether changes in microbial diversity mediated symptom reduction. Participants receiving probiotics showed increased Lactobacillus abundance and lower depression scores than placebo (β = -4.2, p = 0.01); mediation analysis indicated that gut microbiota shifts explained 31% of the effect. These findings support targeting the gut-brain axis with probiotics as an adjunctive strategy, though larger trials with longer follow-up are needed. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90% in both arms.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that signal to the central nervous system via the immune system, endocrine system, and nervous system, and disruptions in this dialogue are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders and neurodegeneration. These metabolites modulate BDNF expression, GPR43-dependent signaling, and TLR4-mediated inflammation, while gut microbiota also influence serotonin synthesis and gamma-aminobutyric acid availability. In human cohorts and rodent models, Western-style diets low in fermentable fiber reduce Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, increase intestinal barrier permeability, and exacerbate anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. Conversely, fermented foods and prebiotics can restore butyrate production and improve behavioral outcomes. Probiotic supplementation has shown variable efficacy, likely because strain specificity, baseline microbiome composition, and host COMT variation shape responses. Fecal microbiota transplantation and 16S rRNA sequencing are refining causal inference, yet meta-analyses remain limited by heterogeneous endpoints. Longitudinal metagenomic sequencing paired with mediation analysis is needed to clarify causality. Integrating diet, microbiome, and neuroimmune data may identify actionable targets for gut-brain disorders.

Fermented foods and dietary fiber reshape the gut microbiota and its metabolite output, offering a plausible route by which diet influences central nervous system function. In a 10-week randomized controlled trial, 45 adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed either a high-fiber diet or a fermented-food diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomics were used to profile microbial communities and metabolites; linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction tested longitudinal associations. The fermented-food diet increased microbial diversity and Lactobacillus abundance, whereas the high-fiber diet enriched Bifidobacterium and raised short-chain fatty acid levels, particularly butyrate. Both interventions reduced systemic inflammation and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, but only the fermented-food diet correlated with increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Mediation analyses suggested that microbial metabolites partly explained the diet-cognition link. These data support using fermented foods and fiber to modulate the gut microbiome as a tractable strategy for cognitive decline, though longer trials are needed. Baseline fecal microbiota composition predicted response, suggesting that food-based interventions may require personalization.

Gut microbiota composition predicts Parkinson's disease severity more accurately than single bacterial taxon abundance, yet the pathways linking dietary fiber fermentation to brain function remain incompletely defined. We recruited adults with Parkinson's disease and matched controls, collected fecal and serum samples, and profiled microbial communities using V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Participants also completed a validated diet history, allowing us to estimate fiber intake and probiotic use. Higher fiber consumption correlated with increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance and elevated butyrate in stool. Butyrate levels were inversely associated with constipation and depressive symptoms. In mice colonized with microbiota from high-fiber donors, Bdnf expression in the hippocampus increased and anxiety-like behavior decreased relative to mice receiving low-fiber microbiota. These associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate-sensing GPR43 and vagus nerve signaling partly explained these effects. These findings support probiotic and fiber interventions that target short-chain fatty acid production to modify Parkinson's disease progression.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that act as signaling molecules along the gut microbiota-brain axis, yet how these metabolites translate into durable BDNF regulation remains contested. We combined 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue from mice colonized with human donor microbiota and fed either inulin-rich or low-fiber diets. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundances tracked with butyrate concentrations and BDNF methylation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the diet-related increase in BDNF expression, with GPR41 and HDAC1 as candidate mediators. In chronic stress exposed mice, inulin supplementation restored BDNF transcripts and reduced corticosterone relative to low-fiber diet controls. These findings suggest that dietary fiber shapes gut microbiota metabolism to influence BDNF via SCFA-sensitive epigenetic pathways, nominating prebiotic interventions for stress-related disorders. Parallel shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics in patients with major depressive disorder revealed lower BDNF and Faecalibacterium abundance relative to healthy controls, although random forest classification did not establish causality.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the gut microbiome sustains short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and constrains neuroinflammation, yet the extent to which Western diet drives shifts in the gut microbiome that predict cognitive decline in older adults remains unclear. Rodent and human evidence implicates Lactobacillus and Bacteroides in this axis, but causal biomarkers are lacking. We analyzed fecal metagenomes, serum metabolomics, and hippocampal volume in 184 participants. Mediation analysis tested whether Akkermansia muciniphila and butyrate mediated associations between diet and cognition, adjusting for linear mixed-effects models. Fiber intake correlated with higher butyrate and BDNF expression; Western diet correlated with dysbiosis, lower butyrate, and greater cognitive impairment. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber donors reduced microglial activation and attenuated memory impairment; vancomycin abolished these effects. Prebiotic inulin reproduced butyrate increases and suppressed microglial activation via vagus nerve signaling. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and A. muciniphila-derived butyrate are modifiable gut-brain mediators, and causal mediation modeling can identify targets for age-related cognitive decline.

Gut microbiota-derived butyrate is emerging as a key mediator of hippocampal BDNF expression and depressive symptoms, but whether this axis is causal in humans remains unclear. We examined 1,208 adults from a population-based cohort, combining 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and metabolomics. Habitual dietary fiber and fermented food intake were estimated with a validated food frequency questionnaire. We applied Mendelian randomization to assess causality and multivariable linear regression to test associations, adjusting for age, sex, obesity, and antidepressant use. Higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with greater butyrate production and lower depression scores. BDNF promoter methylation partially mediated the association between microbial diversity and depressive symptoms in mediation analysis. Genetically predicted gut microbiota diversity was inversely associated with major depressive disorder (MDD) risk, with butyrate explaining a modest proportion of the effect. These findings support a microbiota-BDNF pathway modulated by dietary fiber and suggest that fermented foods may offer a pragmatic strategy for depression prevention.

Inulin supplementation in adolescent male rats reshapes the gut microbiome and reduces depressive-like behavior after chronic stress. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling, we found that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate and propionate in the colon, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. PERMANOVA revealed that diet explained 18.7% of microbial community variance, while random forest classification identified Alloprevotella and Roseburia as discriminative taxa. Lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 concentrations were lower in supplemented rats, and corticosterone responses to forced swim stress were attenuated. These effects were abolished by antibiotic depletion of the microbiota, implicating commensal microbes as necessary mediators. In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a parallel randomized controlled trial is warranted to test whether inulin improves cognitive dysfunction through microbial metabolites. Mechanistic work should also examine tight junction proteins and cytokine trafficking across the blood-brain barrier, because microbial metabolites may tune neuroinflammation independently of vagal afferents.

Supplementation with probiotics reshapes the gut microbiota and improves mild cognitive impairment through immune and vagal signaling, yet the microbial taxa and metabolites that mediate this effect remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with metabolic syndrome and subjective cognitive decline received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and plasma metabolomics were integrated with cognitive testing. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that the probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and reduced Bacteroides prevalence. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in short-chain fatty acids and indole-3-propionic acid accounted for 31% of the improvement in cognitive performance. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium with lower interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Shotgun metagenomics further identified Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii as responders, while PERMANOVA confirmed distinct community shifts. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may attenuate neuroinflammation and support brain function via the microbiota-gut-brain axis, offering a tractable adjunct for cognitive decline.

Inulin supplementation restores gut microbiota homeostasis and attenuates neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) by elevating butyrate and Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. In a randomized, placebo-controlled mouse study, APP/PS1 mice received inulin (5% w/w) for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that inulin increased the relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, while decreasing Clostridium. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), showing higher acetate, propionate, and butyrate in the colon and serum. Western blotting showed increased Ocln and Tjp1 expression in the colon, while lipopolysaccharide (LPS) was lower in serum. These changes coincided with reduced amyloid-β plaques, lower IL-1β and TNF-α, and improved cognitive impairment. Correlation analysis linked butyrate levels to Bdnf expression and reduced memory deficits. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice into germ-free mice reproduced the neuroprotective effects. These data position inulin as a candidate prebiotic for early AD intervention. The findings suggest that inulin may prevent AD-related cognitive decline through the microbiota-SCFA-brain axis.

Microbial tryptophan metabolism within the gut microbiota shapes central serotonin availability and major depressive disorder risk, yet whether dietary fiber and fermented foods modify this axis independently of overall diet quality remains unresolved. We profiled fecal microbiota, plasma short-chain fatty acids, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein in 428 adults, then applied linear mixed-effects models and Mendelian randomization to separate association from causation. Higher fiber intake correlated with enriched Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, greater butyrate production, and lower depression severity; fermented food consumption showed weaker, strain-specific links. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed that these associations were partially mediated by butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase and butyrate kinase abundance. In mice receiving probiotics, butyrate increased, blood-brain barrier permeability decreased, and neuroinflammation markers fell in the hippocampus. Vagotomy abolished these effects, implicating the vagus nerve. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and select probiotics may improve depressive symptoms by promoting butyrate-dependent microbiota-brain signaling, though randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm clinical benefit.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with depression severity and anxiety-like behavior, yet causal pathways remain contested. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 120 adults with major depressive disorder received either probiotic supplementation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum) or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by high-throughput sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene; short-chain fatty acids and serotonin metabolites were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline depression scores and dietary fiber intake. Spearman correlation and PERMANOVA tested associations between microbial taxa and depressive symptoms. Probiotic treatment increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced neuroinflammation markers compared with placebo. Changes in Lactobacillus correlated inversely with cortisol and anxiety scores. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial metabolites partially explained the relationship between gut microbiota shifts and depressive symptoms, implicating the vagus nerve and intestinal epithelium in microbiota-gut-brain axis signaling. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics may modulate brain function via microbial metabolites, though murine mechanistic studies and metagenomic validation are needed.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that influence prefrontal cortex and hippocampus circuits underlying emotion regulation, but whether targeted prebiotic supplementation improves cognition during a Western diet remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, 104 adults with habitually low fiber intake received inulin (12 g/day) or microcrystalline cellulose. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, PERMANOVA assessed beta diversity, and mediation analysis examined whether microbial shifts explained changes in BDNF and depressive symptoms. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, elevated butyrate, and improved anxiety scores compared with cellulose. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate increases partially accounted for the inulin-related reduction in anxiety. No significant between-group differences emerged for microbial alpha diversity or depression, and random forest classification separated treatment groups with moderate accuracy. These findings position fermentable fiber as a plausible gut microbiota-targeted strategy for stress-related psychopathology, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Supplementation with galacto-oligosaccharides plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus increased prefrontal cortex gamma-aminobutyric acid receptor expression and reduced anxiety in mice, identifying gut microbiota as a modifiable component of the gut-brain axis. We translated this observation into a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of adults with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid depression. For 8 weeks, participants received either a synbiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve and fructo-oligosaccharides or placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and functional magnetic resonance imaging were performed at baseline and endpoint. Mixed-effects modeling showed that the supplement enriched Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and these increases correlated with lower depressive symptoms and reduced interleukin-6. Control participants exhibited no such changes. Exploratory 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that responders had higher baseline Roseburia abundance, while nonresponders showed elevated Escherichia coli. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic and probiotic combinations can reshape microbial communities and modulate gut-brain signaling, although host genotype and habitual diet may influence response.

Disruption of microbial tryptophan metabolism may lower BDNF expression in the hippocampus and drive anxiety-like behavior, yet the dietary and microbial determinants remain poorly resolved. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed a polyphenol-rich diet or a low-fiber control diet for 8 weeks, with stool sampled before and after each phase. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified gut microbiota and indole-3-lactic acid, respectively. The polyphenol-rich diet increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal indole-3-lactic acid, and normalized BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. These changes correlated with improved cognitive scores in multivariate models. Conversely, the low-fiber control diet enriched Bacteroides and reduced indole-3-lactic acid, without BDNF recovery. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium-derived indole-3-lactic acid accounted for 31% of the diet-related BDNF increase. Baseline microbiota composition explained 18% of the variance in indole-3-lactic acid response. These findings position polyphenol-rich foods as modulators of the gut-brain axis through microbial indole signaling and BDNF-dependent plasticity, warranting longer trials in neurodegenerative disease.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly recognized as a contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) through the gut-brain axis, yet causal pathways remain unresolved. We integrated shotgun metagenomics of fecal microbiota with cerebrospinal fluid biomarker profiling in cognitively unimpaired adults and patients with AD dementia from two independent cohorts. Using two-sample Mendelian randomization, weighted median regression, and mediation analysis, we tested whether microbial taxa influence AD risk via APOE- and TREM2-related pathways. Higher abundance of Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium was associated with lower AD odds, whereas Escherichia correlated with elevated trimethylamine N-oxide and worse hippocampal integrity. Butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids partially mediated protective effects, and BDNF expression modified these associations. APOE ε4 carriers showed attenuated microbial associations. After false discovery rate correction, no significant effects emerged for Prevotella or Lactobacillus. These findings suggest that gut microbial composition may causally modulate AD risk through microbial metabolites and APOE-dependent mechanisms.

Inulin supplementation reversed Alzheimer's disease-like cognitive decline in APP/PS1 mice, an effect accompanied by reduced amyloid-beta plaques and normalized Bdnf, Il-6, and Tnf expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. To test whether gut microbiota mediates this response, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-fed or control mice into antibiotic-treated recipients. Linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, which correlated with lower pro-inflammatory cytokines and improved Morris water maze performance. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition explained 34% of the treatment effect on Bdnf expression. Inulin also elevated short-chain fatty acids in gut and serum and reduced Nfkb1 and Cd68 expression in brain. In germ-free mice, the neuroprotective effect of inulin was abolished, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors restored Bdnf expression and reduced neuroinflammation. These results suggest that inulin mitigates AD-related pathology through gut microbiota-dependent Bdnf signaling, offering a dietary strategy for AD.

The gut microbiota converts dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence brain function, yet how fiber intake interacts with specific commensal taxa to modulate BDNF signaling remains unresolved. We recruited 120 adults and measured fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA sequencing, serum SCFAs, and cytokines. Using multivariable regression, we found that higher fiber consumption correlated with greater abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, elevated butyrate, and increased BDNF expression. These associations were attenuated in participants with low microbial diversity. After adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use, each 10-g increase in fiber intake was associated with 12% higher butyrate and 8% higher BDNF. Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate accounted for 31% of the fiber-BDNF relationship. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with F. prausnitzii plus inulin raised butyrate, restored BDNF transcripts, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Conversely, antibiotic treatment depleted butyrate producers, lowered butyrate, and suppressed BDNF. Butyrate supplementation partially rescued these effects. Our findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable input to the microbiota-gut-brain axis and suggest that Faecalibacterium-butyrate-BDNF signaling may mediate resilience to stress-related disorders.

Dietary patterns rich in fermentable fibers and polyphenols can reshape the gut microbiota and influence brain function through immune, metabolic, and neural routes. In a randomized adult cohort with mild cognitive impairment, twelve weeks of a Mediterranean-style diet supplemented with probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, and lowered lipopolysaccharide compared with a Western diet control. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed parallel enrichment of BDNF expression in hippocampus and reduced interleukin-6 signaling. Random forest classification separated intervention from control participants with 82% accuracy, and shifts in gut microbiota correlated with improved cognitive impairment scores. Mice receiving fecal microbiota from responders showed restored hippocampal BDNF and less neuroinflammation, whereas germ-free mice colonized with non-responder microbiota did not. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotic interventions may act synergistically on the gut-brain axis to delay cognitive decline, though the underlying mechanisms require further study.

Short-chain fatty acids generated by gut microbiota in the colon modulate BDNF signaling and peripheral immune tone, linking microbial composition to Alzheimer's disease progression. In a 24-week randomized trial, older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal calprotectin assays showed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, reduced Prevotella, and lowered trimethylamine N-oxide and IL-1β expression in blood. Parallel experiments in APPswe/PS1dE9 mice confirmed that probiotic administration reduced Escherichia coli and lipopolysaccharide translocation, and improved Morris water maze performance relative to vehicle-treated controls. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance linked these shifts to improved cognitive impairment scores; carriers of the APOE ε4 allele showed weaker responses. Probiotic effects were independent of baseline fecal microbiota diversity but correlated with reduced neuroinflammation markers. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with probiotics may attenuate cognitive decline, although larger trials using metagenomic sequencing are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone and hippocampal plasticity, yet whether inulin supplementation can amplify this signaling in mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. We randomized 48 adults with mild cognitive impairment to 12 weeks of inulin or placebo, with gut microbiota profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated fecal butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. These shifts accompanied improved cognitive impairment severity scores and lower anxiety ratings, but not changes in BDNF or tau. Fecal microbiota transplantation into mice reproduced the butyrate increase and improved memory deficits, whereas vancomycin abolished the benefit. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate production by the microbiota explained 31% of the cognitive effect, and baseline microbial diversity correlated with response. No serious adverse events occurred, and inulin was well tolerated. These findings position inulin as a plausible microbiota-targeted adjunct for mild cognitive impairment, though longer trials are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) traverse the intestinal epithelium and modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, providing a mechanistic link between gut microbiota and affective behavior. To test whether dietary substrates amplify this pathway, we fed germ-free mice either a fermented milk diet or a tryptophan-rich diet and colonized them with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation were used to track microbial composition; ELISA quantified serotonin and BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. In patients with major depressive disorder, we also measured plasma SCFAs and BDNF levels. Compared with controls, colonized mice on the fermented milk diet showed increased Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test. These effects were attenuated by antibiotic treatment and correlated with BDNF expression. Linear mixed models revealed that butyrate predicted BDNF after adjusting for probiotic intake. The findings suggest that fermented foods and tryptophan may shape gut microbiota to influence BDNF-dependent mood regulation.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids modulate plasticity in the hippocampus and depressive symptoms, but whether dietary fiber intake amplifies this effect via BDNF signaling is unclear. We studied 120 adults with major depressive disorder and 80 healthy controls, profiling gut microbiota by 16S rRNA sequencing and measuring butyrate, IL-6, and BDNF expression. Using mixed-effects models, mediation analysis, and random forest classification, higher fiber intake correlated with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and with butyrate levels. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was inversely associated with depression severity; this association was mediated by BDNF and IL-6. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors consuming high fiber increased Bdnf expression in prefrontal cortex, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and improved cognitive impairment on a novel object recognition test. Mediterranean diet adherence and fermented food consumption showed similar microbial and BDNF signatures. No comparable association emerged for COMT. These findings support targeting gut microbiota through dietary fiber and fermented foods to influence BDNF-related neuropsychiatric outcomes.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder, yet the molecular mediators remain poorly defined. In a 12-week randomized trial of adults with mild-to-moderate depression, daily probiotic supplementation combined with a fermented food-rich diet was compared with usual care alone. The active intervention increased abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered plasma lipopolysaccharide. These changes coincided with reduced IL6 and TNF expression in immune cells and increased BDNF concentrations. Participants receiving the probiotic plus fermented food diet showed greater improvement in depressive symptoms than controls, and this improvement correlated with baseline microbial diversity. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and BDNF partially explained the clinical response. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings support a model in which probiotic and fermented food interventions reshape the gut microbiome, modulate IL6, TNF, and BDNF signaling, and alleviate depression. Longer follow-up is needed to confirm durability.

Fermentable dietary fiber intake reshapes gut microbial communities and their production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which act on enteroendocrine cells, vagal afferents, and the central nervous system to influence neuropsychiatric symptoms. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a high-fiber diet or a low-fiber control diet for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal microbiota composition and SCFA concentrations, while functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed hippocampal connectivity. The high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate and propionate, and improved cognitive impairment relative to control. These changes correlated with reduced systemic inflammation and altered BDNF expression. Mixed-effects models indicated that butyrate mediated the association between F. prausnitzii abundance and hippocampal connectivity. Baseline microbiota diversity and propionate levels also predicted individual responses. The findings suggest that dietary fiber may support gut microbiota-targeted strategies for cognitive decline, though longer trials are needed.

Signals from the gut microbiota can shape brain function, yet the dietary and genetic modifiers of this communication remain poorly defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from donors consuming either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet, then measured short-chain fatty acid production, BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fiber increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance, whereas the Western diet expanded Bacteroides. Using fecal microbiota transplantation into recipient mice, we found that microbiota from fiber-fed donors raised butyrate levels and normalized BDNF transcripts. Linear mixed-effects models showed that butyrate mediated the association between Bifidobacterium abundance and BDNF expression. In contrast, microbiota from Western diet-fed donors increased IL-6 and TNF-α expression and exacerbated anxiety-like behavior. These results indicate that dietary fiber promotes gut microbiota taxa that support BDNF-dependent plasticity in the hippocampus, while Western diet-driven microbiota shifts may amplify neuroinflammation. Targeting these microbial and metabolic pathways could offer new strategies for stress-related disorders.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence central nervous system immune tone and synaptic plasticity. In mice colonized with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, inulin supplementation increased butyrate and normalized BDNF and ZO-1 expression in the hippocampus and colon. These changes coincided with reduced neuroinflammation, less anxiety-like behavior, and improved cognitive impairment in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that fiber intake expanded Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium while suppressing Proteobacteria. Fecal calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide decreased, whereas occludin and claudin-1 increased. Mediation analysis linked microbial composition to BDNF levels and behavioral outcomes, suggesting that SCFAs transduce signals from the gut microbiome to the brain. In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a Mediterranean-style diet enriched in fermentable fiber produced parallel shifts in gut microbiome and reduced interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable lever for neurodegenerative disease risk, though randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm causality.

Dietary fiber depletion reshapes gut microbiota and diminishes short-chain fatty acid production, a metabolic axis increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disorders. In mice fed low-fiber diets, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics revealed expansion of mucin-degrading taxa and loss of butyrate-producing Clostridia. These shifts coincided with increased intestinal permeability, elevated lipopolysaccharide in circulation, and microglial activation in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-deprived mice into germ-free recipients reproduced neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment, whereas supplementation with inulin or resistant starch restored butyrate levels and attenuated neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole derivatives accounted for a substantial fraction of the protective effect. Mechanistically, butyrate promotes expression of tight junction genes and limits pro-inflammatory cytokines, while indole derivatives engage aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in intestinal epithelium and central nervous system. In older adults, lower dietary fiber intake correlated with altered gut microbiome composition and worse executive dysfunction, although causality remains unresolved. These findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable prebiotic strategy for sustaining metabolite signaling along the gut-brain axis and reducing risk for neurodegeneration.

Altered gut microbiota composition precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. In a 12-week randomized trial, patients with PD received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or the same diet plus a multi-strain probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified gut microbiota composition, while liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry measured SCFAs in serum and stool. The supplement group showed increased Bifidobacterium abundance, higher butyrate levels, and lower IL-6 compared with diet alone. These changes accompanied improved clinical scores and reduced constipation. In parallel, germ-free mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota from the supplement group displayed less nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss and lower microglial activation than mice receiving baseline microbiota. Polyphenols and fiber alone increased Akkermansia but did not alter butyrate or neuroinflammation. Together, these findings suggest that probiotic supplementation amplifies diet-driven microbiota metabolic shifts, enhancing SCFA availability and dampening inflammation along the gut-brain axis. Larger trials are needed to determine whether such diet and supplement strategies can modify PD progression.

Fermented food and dietary fiber intake associate with distinct gut microbiota profiles and lower systemic inflammation, yet their causal role in depression remains uncertain. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 180 adults, including patients with major depressive disorder and healthy controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate. Patients showed lower relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced butyrate compared with controls. Beta diversity differed by diagnosis (PERMANOVA, p=0.003), and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Faecalibacterium depletion in cases. A random-effects meta-analysis across three independent cohorts confirmed this butyrate signature. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the inverse association between fermented food intake and depressive symptoms. In germ-free mice colonized with human microbiota, dietary fiber supplementation increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and attenuated neuroinflammation. These results link diet, microbial metabolism, and brain function, suggesting that targeting SCFA-producing commensals may complement conventional antidepressants.

Probiotic supplementation alongside fermented foods may reshape gut microbiota and modulate brain function through the gut-brain axis. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks while maintaining their habitual diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples showed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and decreased Proteobacteria in the probiotic group. Concomitantly, serotonin and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels rose in plasma, whereas interleukin-6 and cortisol declined. Plasma short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, increased in the probiotic arm and tracked with Bifidobacterium expansion. Mixed-effects modeling revealed that changes in Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with reduced depressive symptoms scores. Notably, participants reporting higher intake of fiber-rich vegetables showed greater microbial shifts, suggesting that dietary fiber amplifies probiotic efficacy. These findings indicate that targeting the gut-brain axis with probiotic supplementation and fermented food consumption could offer a complementary strategy for mood disorders, though confirmatory metagenomic and metabolomic studies are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate brain immunity and may influence Alzheimer's disease (AD). We profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified fecal metabolites by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry in older adults with mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls. Associations were adjusted for age, sex, medication use, and total energy intake using linear regression. Gut microbiota composition separated groups; Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Faecalibacterium were enriched in controls, while Escherichia and Shigella were more abundant in AD. A random forest classifier discriminated groups with moderate accuracy, and mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and propionate partially mediated the link between microbial diversity and cognitive impairment.
