Findings remained after sensitivity analyses excluding type 2 diabetes. Greater fiber intake correlated with higher butyrate-producing bacteria abundance and better cognitive performance. These results support a microbiota-SCFA axis through which diet may affect AD-related neuroinflammation, warranting trials of prebiotic and fiber-rich foods for dementia prevention.

Supplementation with probiotic Bifidobacterium breve MCC1274 for 16 weeks attenuated mild cognitive impairment in older adults, yet the microbial and molecular mediators remain incompletely defined. We randomized 120 participants with MCI to probiotic or placebo and collected feces and serum at baseline and endpoint. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. BDNF and IL-6 expression were measured in peripheral blood mononuclear cells using quantitative PCR. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that probiotic increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and butyrate concentrations relative to placebo. These changes correlated with improved ADAS-Cog scores and reduced BDNF promoter methylation. Mediation analysis indicated that A. muciniphila-derived butyrate partially accounted for BDNF upregulation and cognitive benefit. Spearman correlation further linked A. muciniphila with BDNF methylation and IL-6 levels. The findings suggest that probiotic targeting the gut microbiota may slow MCI progression via BDNF-dependent pathways. These results warrant larger patient cohorts to confirm causality.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural pathways, and its disruption is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder. In mice exposed to chronic stress, gut microbiota depletion lowered BDNF expression in the hippocampus, raised circulating lipopolysaccharide, and increased neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, while fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors reproduced behavioral deficits in recipients. Dietary probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids attenuated these effects, restored BDNF signaling, and normalized short-chain fatty acid profiles. In patients, a random-effects meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials found that probiotic supplementation modestly improved depressive symptoms, with larger effects in those harboring low baseline Bifidobacterium abundance. Host BDNF Val66Met genotype and baseline microbial diversity may explain heterogeneous responses. These findings position the gut microbiota as a modifiable node linking diet, BDNF regulation, and affective pathology, though mechanistic causality and strain-specific effects require further clarification.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and bile acid metabolites shape central BDNF signaling and hippocampal plasticity, linking gut microbiota composition to anxiety and depression. In a 12-week randomized study of 180 adults with moderate anxiety, participants receiving a Mediterranean-style diet plus probiotic supplementation showed greater reductions in anxiety scores than controls receiving usual care. Fecal Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance increased, while Enterobacteriaceae decreased. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline anxiety, antidepressant use, and dietary fiber intake revealed a significant group-by-time interaction. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in SCFA-producing bacteria explained 31% of the symptom improvement. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing further showed enrichment of butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase genes in responders. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 concentrations fell only in the intervention group. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial interventions targeting the gut microbiota may complement conventional treatment for anxiety, though larger trials with false discovery rate correction and standardized assessments are needed.

Consumption of a Mediterranean-style diet rich in polyphenols and fermentable fiber is associated with greater gut microbial diversity and lower risk of neurodegeneration, yet causal pathways remain unresolved. Baseline fruit and vegetable intake was assessed with a food frequency questionnaire. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics in a cohort of older adults, we found that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila were depleted in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) compared with cognitively normal controls. These taxa correlated inversely with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and IL-6, and positively with butyrate in stool. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with MCI into gnotobiotic mice impaired hippocampal BDNF expression and increased anxiety-like behavior. Conversely, inulin supplementation restored butyrate production and attenuated neuroinflammation in mice. Mediation analysis suggested that microbiota-derived butyrate partly mediates the protective association between fiber intake and cognitive decline risk. These findings position gut microbiota-directed fiber interventions as plausible early interventions for cognitive decline.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism has emerged as a plausible mediator linking intestinal ecology to major depressive disorder, yet causal pathways remain incompletely resolved. In a cohort of 84 adults, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota with plasma tryptophan, kynurenine, and serotonin profiling. Participants with depression showed reduced Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus abundance and elevated IDO1 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium depletion indirectly associated with symptom severity through an increased kynurenine/tryptophan ratio. Spearman correlation further linked Coprococcus with serotonin and BDNF transcripts. Plasma kynurenine levels correlated positively with anxiety scores and negatively with Faecalibacterium. In a murine mouse model, oral Lactobacillus rhamnosus normalized hippocampal BDNF expression and reduced depressive-like behavior; these effects were absent in IDO1-deficient mice. Random forest classification identified Coprococcus and kynurenine as top predictors of group status. These findings support a microbiota-IDO1-kynurenine route to mood symptoms and suggest that targeting microbial tryptophan metabolism may complement existing antidepressant therapies.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber consistently increases gut microbiota diversity and short-chain fatty acid production, which in turn strengthens barrier integrity and dampens neuroinflammation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo for 8 weeks while maintaining habitual plant-rich diets. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota revealed that probiotic supplementation enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced Bacteroides abundance. These microbial shifts correlated with lower interleukin-6 and cortisol levels and higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in serum. Linear mixed-effects models showed that the probiotic group had greater improvement in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores than placebo, with effects partially mediated by changes in gut microbiota composition. In mice, BDNF expression in the hippocampus increased after probiotic exposure. These findings suggest that combining fermented foods with targeted probiotics may offer a practical strategy for depression by engaging the gut microbiota–brain axis.

Higher intake of fiber-rich foods and lower consumption of ultra-processed foods associate with distinct gut microbiota profiles that may protect against major depressive disorder (MDD). We recruited 84 adults with MDD and 42 matched healthy controls, profiled stool microbiota via 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified short-chain fatty acids using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Multivariable linear regression and random forest models tested associations. Relative to controls, patients showed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, higher Eggerthella, and reduced butyrate. Fecal calprotectin was higher in patients than in controls, suggesting low-grade intestinal inflammation. Mediterranean-style diet adherence correlated positively with Faecalibacterium and butyrate and negatively with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Mediation analysis suggested butyrate partly explained the inverse association between fiber-rich foods and depressive symptoms. In mice, fiber supplementation increased Roseburia, lowered hippocampal interleukin-6, and normalized BDNF expression. These findings link diet quality to microbiota-derived metabolites and gut-brain axis function, supporting prebiotic strategies for MDD.

Microbial conversion of dietary polyphenols into 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)propionic acid (3-HPPA) attenuates α-synuclein aggregation and may slow Parkinson's disease progression, yet the dietary and microbial determinants of circulating metabolite levels remain poorly resolved. We profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified targeted polyphenol metabolites in older adults consuming habitual diets enriched in berries, green tea, and whole grains. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antibiotic exposure linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance to higher 3-HPPA and 3,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid (3,4-diHBA) concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial dehydroxylation explained 34% of the association between berry intake and 3-HPPA. Fecal Bacteroides abundance correlated inversely with 3,4-diHBA, suggesting taxon-specific metabolic routes. In α-synuclein A53T mice, dietary 3-HPPA supplementation reduced aggregated α-synuclein in striatum and colon, with parallel decreases in pro-inflammatory cytokines. These findings position gut microbial polyphenol metabolism as a modifiable axis linking diet to synucleinopathy and support prebiotic or probiotic strategies that enhance 3-HPPA production.

Probiotic Bifidobacterium breve supplementation improves Parkinson's disease (PD)-like motor deficits in mice by reshaping gut microbiota and suppressing TLR4/NF-κB signaling. In MPTP-treated mice, 4 weeks of oral B. breve increased Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance, reduced Enterobacteriaceae, and lowered lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in colon and striatum. Behavioral recovery was accompanied by higher tyrosine hydroxylase and BDNF expression, fewer α-synuclein aggregates, and decreased IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in substantia nigra. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and Western blotting confirmed that B. breve reversed microbiota dysbiosis and inhibited TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB activation. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF levels and motor scores. These findings suggest that B. breve may be a therapeutic probiotic for PD, though clinical trials are needed. Furthermore, B. breve-treated mice showed restored intestinal barrier integrity, with increased occludin and ZO-1 in colonic mucosa. Fecal microbiota transplantation from B. breve-recipient mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced the neuroprotective phenotype, while TLR4 knockout abolished the anti-inflammatory effects. In patients with PD, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with BDNF and TNF-α levels, supporting translational relevance.

Disruption of the gut microbiota can precede Parkinson's disease and depression diagnosis, implicating the vagus nerve and neuroendocrine routes in the gut-brain axis. In a cross-sectional study of adults, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus alongside elevated Proteobacteria. Fecal short-chain fatty acids and circulating tryptophan metabolites were lower in cases than in controls. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet rich in fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains correlated with higher microbial diversity and reduced neuroinflammation markers, while a Western diet showed opposite associations. An 8-week randomized trial of probiotics plus prebiotics increased Bifidobacterium and improved depressive symptoms; in mouse models, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders upregulated BDNF in the hippocampus. Multivariate random forest modeling separated cases from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82, and mediation analysis linked serotonin pathway intermediates to BDNF expression. SSRIs use did not abolish these associations. These results support dietary strategies targeting the gut microbiota as adjunctive for gut-brain disorders.

Depletion of gut microbiota diversity and reduced butyrate availability are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety through the gut-brain axis. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 60 adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either inulin-type fructans or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acids. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations with BDNF methylation, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and clinical scores. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo. These changes correlated with decreased BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood, lower IL-6, and higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels. Butyrate-producing taxa at baseline predicted treatment response. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate production by gut microbiota accounted for 32% of the observed clinical improvement. The findings suggest that prebiotic fiber supplementation can modulate gut microbiota-BDNF signaling and may offer a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for depression.

Disrupted gut microbiota composition and reduced short-chain fatty acid production are consistently observed in major depressive disorder and irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting that microbial signals modulate central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. In a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study, adults with depression and IBS received either multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics characterized fecal microbiota, while nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified plasma metabolites. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms and gastrointestinal discomfort relative to placebo. These changes correlated with decreased interleukin-6, cortisol, and lipopolysaccharide, alongside increased BDNF expression and improved intestinal barrier integrity. Exploratory analyses linked microbial composition to dietary fiber intake and omega-3 fatty acid use. The findings support targeted probiotic interventions as adjunctive strategies for gut-brain axis disorders, though larger trials with fecal microbiota transplantation and machine learning are needed to confirm causality.

Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuates stress-induced depressive-like behavior in mice through gut microbiota-dependent modulation of serotonin availability along the gut-brain axis. To translate these findings, adults with irritable bowel syndrome and subclinical anxiety were randomized in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial to consume fermented milk containing the same strain or a placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing profiled fecal microbiota. Linear mixed-effects models showed that probiotic treatment increased microbial diversity and reduced anxiety scores relative to placebo, with parallel decreases in cortisol and inflammatory cytokines. At week 8, probiotic recipients showed a 1.8-point greater reduction on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale than placebo recipients, and Spearman correlation analysis linked microbial shifts to serotonin metabolites. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in gut microbiota composition explained 32% of the probiotic effect on anxiety. These results suggest that fermented dairy enriched with L. rhamnosus may serve as an accessible psychobiotic intervention, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and strain specificity.

Supplementation with probiotics and increased intake of fermented foods can reshape gut microbiota and modify central nervous system immune signaling, yet their combined effects on depression remain unclear. Preclinical work in germ-free mice has shown that microbiota depletion alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus, but translation to humans remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo while consuming a high-fiber diet. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed-effects models assessed microbial composition and symptom trajectories. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures between groups (R2 = 0.08, P = 0.012). Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations, including butyrate. These shifts correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and improved depressive symptoms scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the association between Bifidobacterium and symptom improvement. The findings support adjunctive probiotic plus dietary fiber as a plausible strategy for modulating the gut-brain axis in depression, though larger trials are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by a high-fat diet exacerbates cognitive decline, yet the microbial signals linking intestinal and hippocampal dysfunction remain poorly defined. In male C57BL/6J mice fed either a high-fat diet or a Mediterranean-style diet for 16 weeks, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide in plasma. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that high-fat diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, increased Bdnf promoter methylation, and elevated Il6 and Tnf expression in the hippocampus. These changes coincided with poorer Morris water maze performance and greater anxiety-like behavior. Mediterranean-style diet partially restored Lactobacillus abundance and butyrate levels, effects associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved memory retention. Fecal microbiota transfer from high-fat diet-fed mice into antibiotic-treated recipients recapitulated cognitive deficits, whereas probiotic supplementation attenuated them. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbial shifts influence neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity, offering targets for gut-brain axis disorders.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract during infancy shapes gut microbiota composition and influences central nervous system development through the microbiome-gut-brain axis. Disruption of the microbiome-gut-brain axis has been associated with irritable bowel syndrome, depression, and anxiety, conditions in which patients often exhibit altered Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances. Dietary interventions that supply probiotic supplements and fermented foods can modulate gut microbial communities, increase short-chain fatty acid production, and reduce neuroinflammation in rodent models. However, whether these effects translate to adults remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in 120 adults with mild depressive symptoms, assigning them to a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium in the probiotic group, alongside higher dietary fiber intake. Mixed-effects models showed a significant reduction in depression scores only among participants with baseline microbial diversity above the median. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with fiber-rich foods may support brain health, but baseline gut microbiome composition determines responsiveness.

Supplementation with probiotics can reduce depressive symptoms in some patients, but the microbial and metabolic mediators remain poorly resolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo alongside standard care. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, and serum short-chain fatty acids, cortisol, and interleukin-6 were quantified. Linear mixed models tested group-by-time interactions, with random forest used to identify baseline taxa predictive of response. Relative to placebo, the probiotic group showed greater reductions in depression severity and anxiety scores. These changes coincided with increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, decreased Desulfovibrio, and higher butyrate concentrations. Interleukin-6 fell only in responders, whereas cortisol changes were nonsignificant. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90%. Baseline gut microbiota composition predicted response with 72% accuracy. The findings suggest that probiotic effects on depression may be mediated through microbiota-short-chain fatty acid signaling along the gut-brain axis, though confirmatory mechanistic studies are needed.

Disruption of gut microbial homeostasis can precede Alzheimer's disease (AD) by years, yet whether this reflects causality or reverse causation remains contested. Using two-sample Mendelian randomization with genome-wide association study data, we tested bidirectional relationships between gut microbiota taxa and cognitive decline. Genetic instruments for APOE and 31 microbial features were analyzed; inverse variance weighted estimates, MR-Egger, and weighted median were complemented by Cochran's Q and leave-one-out sensitivity tests. We identified several Bifidobacterium and Ruminococcus taxa with protective or risk effects on AD scores. In parallel, polyphenol and fiber intake modified these associations, likely via microbial conversion to urolithins and short-chain fatty acids. These metabolites may influence brain function through vagus nerve signaling and systemic immune pathways. Our findings support a causal contribution of specific gut microbes to AD and suggest that dietary polyphenols and fermentable fibers could mitigate risk, particularly in individuals carrying APOE risk alleles. Validation in mouse models and fecal microbiota transplantation trials is warranted.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape hippocampal BDNF expression and microglial reactivity, linking gut microbiota composition to depressive-like behavior. We colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or vehicle, then measured BDNF, NLRP3, and IL-6 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Behavioral outcomes were assessed with forced swim test and open field test. Spearman correlation and linear mixed-effects models related microbial abundances to host BDNF and NLRP3 expression. Colonized mice showed elevated butyrate in feces, reduced neuroinflammation, and higher BDNF than controls. Lactobacillus abundance correlated positively with BDNF (ρ = 0.62) and negatively with IL-6 (ρ = −0.48). In parallel, patients with major depressive disorder displayed lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and BDNF expression than healthy controls; 16S rRNA sequencing and random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium as a top discriminant. Probiotic supplementation attenuated anxiety-like behavior and increased butyrate. These findings suggest that targeting microbiota-derived butyrate may normalize BDNF signaling and limit neuroinflammation in stress-related disorders.

Tryptophan catabolites sustain AHR-dependent intestinal immune homeostasis, yet their loss during dysbiosis amplifies neuroinflammation and behavioral deficits. We profiled gut microbiota, tryptophan metabolites, and cytokines in adults with major depressive disorder and mice subjected to chronic stress. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics revealed reduced Bacteroides uniformis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, alongside lower indole-3-propionic acid and butyrate. Fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced the metabolite deficit and increased Tnf, Il6, and Nlrp3 expression in the hippocampus. In mice, antibiotic depletion of microbiota decreased Ahr and Bdnf expression, impaired blood-brain barrier integrity, and elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and random forest classification separated patients from controls with moderate accuracy. Indole-3-propionic acid supplementation restored Ahr signaling, normalized cytokine profiles, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis linked microbial composition to prefrontal cortex serotonin turnover via vagus nerve signaling. These findings identify AHR-indole signaling as a tractable axis for depression.

Diets rich in fermented foods and dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate brain function, but the microbial taxa and metabolic signals responsible for this effect are only partly defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal and plasma samples from adults with mild cognitive impairment who consumed a fermented food-enriched diet for 12 weeks. Compared with baseline, the intervention increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, raised levels of short-chain fatty acids, and reduced markers of systemic inflammation. These changes correlated with improved cognitive scores and higher BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced part of the cognitive benefit, whereas antibiotic depletion of gut bacteria abolished it. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and indole-3-propionate partially mediated the association between microbial composition and cognitive outcomes. These findings support a causal role for diet-responsive gut microbiota in gut-brain signaling and highlight fermented foods as a feasible strategy to attenuate age-related cognitive impairment.

Variants in BDNF and COMT interact with dietary and microbial signals to shape anxiety-like behavior along the gut-brain axis. In mice, a high-fat diet depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while elevating circulating lipopolysaccharide, an effect partially reversed by probiotic supplementation. We profiled the gut microbiota with 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and assessed depressive-like behavior using the forced swim test. Random forest models linked Faecalibacterium abundance to BDNF expression in the hippocampus, while butyrate levels tracked with BDNF exon IV methylation. A separate cohort of healthy adults consuming a Mediterranean diet showed higher Roseburia and Coprococcus relative to those on a Western diet, with parallel reductions in self-reported depressive symptoms. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Mediterranean diet-fed donors into antibiotic-treated mice recapitulated these behavioral and transcriptional changes. These findings suggest that host genotype, diet, and microbial communities converge on neuroimmune pathways, and that targeting this triad may offer tractable strategies for stress-related disorders.

Depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in the gut microbiota tracks with neuroinflammation and amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that microbial restoration could modify cognitive decline. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received multi-strain probiotic supplementation or placebo for 12 weeks while increasing fermented foods, fiber-rich plant foods, and Mediterranean diet adherence. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed higher relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila in the probiotic group. Computerized neuropsychological testing showed improved executive function and memory scores, accompanied by increased serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and reduced interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide. These changes correlated with microbial diversity, short-chain fatty acid production, and ZO-1 expression. Metagenomic sequencing further showed reduced Bacteroides fragilis and enriched Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens in responders. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings indicate that probiotic supplementation combined with fermented food-enriched dietary patterns may slow cognitive decline through gut-brain axis mechanisms, warranting larger trials.

Microbiota-derived tryptamine and short-chain fatty acids modulate central nervous system immune signaling, yet their relationship with APOE genotype and cognitive decline remains unresolved. We profiled gut microbiota from older adults with mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and untargeted mass spectrometry. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models, Spearman correlation, and random forest tested associations among microbial metabolites, BDNF expression in peripheral blood, and cognitive scores after false discovery rate correction. Bacteroides abundance correlated inversely with tryptamine and positively with BDNF expression. Lactobacillus was depleted in mild cognitive impairment and associated with lower indole-3-propionic acid. In mice, tryptamine administration increased hippocampal serotonin turnover, activated TPH1, and impaired Morris water maze performance. These associations remained significant after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-APOE interactions shape metabolite profiles influencing brain function, offering targets for Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Microbial regulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in the hippocampus provides a plausible route through which dietary fiber influences depression-like phenotypes. In mice exposed to chronic corticosterone, six weeks of inulin supplementation (5% w/w) increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate concentrations in feces, and restored BDNF expression and cyclic AMP response element-binding protein (CREB) phosphorylation in the dentate gyrus. These effects were accompanied by fewer anhedonia behaviors in sucrose preference testing and lower neuroinflammation markers. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics linked these outcomes to microbial short-chain fatty acid production. In a parallel human cohort, higher fiber intake correlated with elevated BDNF promoter methylation in blood, although this relationship was attenuated after adjusting for antidepressant use. Our findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable input to the gut-brain axis and suggest that BDNF-related epigenetic tone may mediate its behavioral benefits. Together, these data support a model in which gut microbiota-derived metabolites tune BDNF signaling and behavior.

Disruption of the gut microbiota during early life can persistently alter hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling and increase vulnerability to anxiety-like behavior later in life. In male C57BL/6 mice, maternal separation reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lowered serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. Daily oral galacto-oligosaccharide supplementation from weaning to adulthood restored Bifidobacterium levels, normalized BDNF exon IV mRNA expression, and attenuated depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test. These effects were absent in mice lacking GPR41, a short-chain fatty acid receptor, indicating that microbial metabolites mediate the oligosaccharide response. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that supplementation also increased Lactobacillus and Akkermansia and reduced Clostridiales. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a parallel randomized trial found that inulin improved Mini-Mental State Examination scores and correlated with increased BDNF serum levels. Thus, targeting gut microbiota with prebiotic fibers may modulate BDNF-dependent brain plasticity, though causal mediation analyses in larger cohorts are needed.

Microbial γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthesis in the gut is increasingly linked to depression, but the bacterial glutamate decarboxylase (gadB) variants that govern GABA output remain poorly defined. We analyzed gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder and healthy volunteers using shotgun metagenomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing, then measured GABA, glutamate, and short-chain fatty acids in feces by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium carried gadB more frequently in controls than in patients, and gadB abundance correlated positively with GABA concentrations. In germ-free mice colonized with Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, gadB expression increased GABA in the colon and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These effects were accompanied by higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. Fecal fiber intake and probiotic supplementation were associated with distinct microbial community shifts and GABA levels, suggesting that dietary and microbial factors jointly influence brain function. Our findings suggest that targeting microbial gadB could provide a tractable strategy for modulating gut microbiota and brain function.

Converging evidence implicates gut microbiota-derived metabolites in modulating Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk through immune, metabolic, and neuroendocrine routes. In transgenic mice modeling AD, dietary supplementation with polyphenol-rich pomegranate extract reshaped cecal microbiota, elevated urolithin A, and reduced amyloid-beta deposition in the hippocampus. These changes coincided with lower IL-6 and TNF transcripts and increased BDNF expression. In vitro, butyrate promoted BDNF expression in enteric neurons and reduced NF-κB activation. To test whether microbial signals were necessary, we used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from human donors with mild cognitive impairment into antibiotic-treated mice. Transplantation of microbiota from donors with AD increased lipopolysaccharide translocation and impaired hippocampal plasticity, whereas fiber supplementation increased butyrate and Lactobacillus abundance. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and BDNF partly link diet, microbiota, and cognition. These findings position APOE-dependent lipid metabolism and microbial short-chain fatty acids as tractable targets for slowing AD progression.

Consumption of a western diet depletes Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, altering gut microbiota composition and increasing neuroinflammation susceptibility through vagus nerve and systemic immune routes. In mice exposed to chronic corticosterone, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts. These changes coincided with lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations and reduced microbiome diversity, measured by 16S rRNA sequencing. A randomized controlled trial in patients with major depressive disorder found that probiotics plus omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids improved Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores and increased circulating BDNF compared with placebo. The effect was stronger in participants consuming a Mediterranean diet rich in fiber. Mechanistically, microbial short-chain fatty acids and bile acids modulate BDNF and IL-6 signaling, linking intestinal microbiota to brain function. These findings suggest that probiotic co-administration may augment conventional antidepressant therapy, but longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality and define responder subgroups.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition can precede depressive-like behavior and alter BDNF expression in the hippocampus, suggesting that microbial signals actively shape mood circuits rather than merely reflecting them. In a mouse model of chronic stress, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation increased Lactobacillus abundance and short-chain fatty acid production, while reducing corticosterone and IL-6 transcripts. Fecal microbiota transfer from supplemented mice to germ-free recipients reproduced the behavioral benefit, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium as key taxa. In adults with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota profiles showed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia relative to healthy controls. A linear mixed-effects model adjusted for fiber intake and antidepressant use linked these taxa to BDNF methylation. Using mediation analysis, microbial butyrate availability explained 31% of the effect on prefrontal cortex BDNF expression. However, metagenomic sequencing and Mendelian randomization are needed to distinguish causation from confounding. These findings position omega-3 supplementation as a plausible gut-brain modulator and support randomized controlled trials targeting microbiota-BDNF pathways in stress-related disorders.

Microbial depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium coincides with reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota to depression. To test causality, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder and healthy controls into germ-free mice. Recipients of patient-derived microbiota displayed increased corticosterone, reduced serotonin turnover, and lower BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex compared with controls. Parallel RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue revealed downregulation of BDNF, NR3C1, and FKBP5. These neurochemical shifts were accompanied by anxiety-like behavior and anhedonia. Lactobacillus abundance correlated inversely with corticosterone (rho = -0.62, P = 0.008) and positively with BDNF expression (rho = 0.58, P = 0.007). A mediation model indicated that corticosterone partially mediated the relationship between Lactobacillus abundance and BDNF expression. Probiotic supplementation with L. rhamnosus restored BDNF expression and normalized corticosterone in mice, effects attenuated by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy. These findings position BDNF as a mediator of microbiota-gut-brain signaling and support probiotic or fiber-based strategies for depression.

Microbial depletion precedes SNCA aggregation in Parkinson's disease, suggesting that gut microbiota modulate nigrostriatal degeneration through immune and metabolic signaling. In a patient cohort and mouse model, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and untargeted metabolomics to test whether Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii alter butyrate availability. Patients with low butyrate showed reduced BDNF expression and elevated NLRP3 in colon biopsies. Mice colonized with A. muciniphila had increased short-chain fatty acids, suppressed NLRP3, and less substantia nigra dopamine loss. In germ-free mice, A. muciniphila colonization raised butyrate and BDNF while lowering IL1B and TNF. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 38% of the protective effect. Fecal calprotectin and TLR4 correlated inversely with butyrate, and random forest models separated patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84. Butyrate supplementation restored BDNF and motor function. These findings link specific gut bacteria to NLRP3-dependent neuroinflammation and support microbiota-targeted probiotics as a potential adjunct in Parkinson's disease.

Disruption of the gut microbiome by high-fat diet reduces short-chain fatty acid production and lowers BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, a pathway linked to anxiety and cognitive decline. To test whether dietary countermeasures restore this axis, mice received inulin or omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids elevated eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid in serum. Both interventions normalized BDNF and reduced interleukin-6 in the hippocampus. In participants consuming a Mediterranean diet, baseline microbial diversity correlated with linear mixed models estimates of depression severity, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance mediated this association. These findings suggest that prebiotic and omega-3 supplementation, together with fiber-rich foods, may stabilize gut-brain signaling; however, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors did not alter the microbial effects, indicating distinct mechanisms. Future work should define how host genetic variants modify these responses.

Dietary blueberries combined with probiotic supplementation attenuates chronic stress-induced depression-like behavior in mice, an effect linked to increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and remodeling of the gut microbiota. In this mouse study, animals received a high-fat diet with or without blueberry powder and Lactobacillus rhamnosus for eight weeks. Behavioral testing showed that combined treatment reduced immobility in the forced swim test and increased sucrose preference compared with high-fat diet alone. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate and propionate. Serum IL-6 and TNF-α were lower, and corticosterone normalized. Correlation analysis associated BDNF expression with butyrate levels and microbial composition. In patients with major depressive disorder, similar probiotic and blueberry interventions are being explored as adjuncts to fluoxetine. Fecal microbiota transplantation from treated mice into naive mice partially reproduced the behavioral benefits, supporting a causal role for the gut microbiome. These findings suggest that blueberries and probiotics may act through the gut-brain axis to modulate neuroinflammation and support BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity.

Disruption of gut microbiota–brain signaling precedes amyloid plaque deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the microbial metabolites that drive this axis remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal material from patients with mild cognitive impairment and measured cognitive performance, hippocampal neuroinflammation, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium alongside expanded Bacteroides in donors who later converted to AD. Compared with cognitively stable controls, converters also showed lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and higher trimethylamine N-oxide. Fecal microbiota transplantation from these donors into mice lowered butyrate and propionate in the colon, increased lipopolysaccharide translocation, and elevated NLRP3 and BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Western blotting and immunofluorescence confirmed microglial activation and synaptic loss. Oral prebiotic fiber restored Bifidobacterium abundance, normalized BDNF expression, and reduced amyloid burden, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished these benefits. These findings position microbial short-chain fatty acid depletion as an early modifiable driver of AD-related neuropathology.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone, and their depletion correlates with major depressive disorder (MDD) severity. In a cohort of 48 adults with MDD and 32 healthy controls, fecal microbiota profiles were assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; Shannon diversity was lower in MDD (p=0.004), while PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures (R2=0.11, p=0.001). Relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bacteroides differed between groups. BDNF expression in peripheral blood was reduced and negatively associated with IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts. Fecal calprotectin and IL-1β were elevated in MDD and correlated inversely with BDNF. Probiotic supplementation for 8 weeks increased Shannon diversity and BDNF expression, and decreased IL-6 expression compared with placebo. These findings suggest that gut microbiota remodeling may modulate BDNF-related neuroplasticity and inflammatory signaling in MDD, though causal mediation analyses are needed. Future trials should test whether selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors interact with microbial communities to alter BDNF and IL-6 trajectories.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder tracks with reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus and elevated circulating interleukin-6, implicating microbial control of neuroimmune tone. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, metagenomics, and metatranscriptomics, we profiled stool from 120 adults and found that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus rhamnosus were depleted in cases relative to controls, while Bacteroides uniformis was enriched. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from affected donors increased anxiety-like behavior, reduced BDNF transcripts, and elevated IL6 expression in the prefrontal cortex; these effects were attenuated by probiotics, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, and prebiotics. Mendelian randomization supported a causal link between Lactobacillus abundance and depression risk. Dietary fiber intake and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors showed independent associations with gut microbiota diversity. Short-chain fatty acids correlated with BDNF methylation. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila was inversely correlated with depression severity. These data position gut microbiota as a modifiable contributor to depressive symptoms, with probiotic and omega-3 supplementation as candidate adjuncts.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis promotes neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior, but the molecular mediators remain poorly resolved. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and measured short-chain fatty acids in feces, BDNF and IL6 expression in hippocampus, and anxiety-like behavior after 6 weeks. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline body weight showed that F. prausnitzii increased butyrate (β=0.42, P=0.003) and reduced IL6 (β=-0.31, P=0.014), whereas B. fragilis had no effect. BDNF expression correlated with butyrate (r=0.61, P<0.001) and with reduced anxiety-like behavior. In patients with major depressive disorder (n=48), fecal microbiome 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed lower F. prausnitzii abundance than in healthy controls, and this deficit tracked with lower BDNF and higher IL6 expression. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 38% of the association between F. prausnitzii and BDNF (P=0.008). These findings identify F. prausnitzii-derived butyrate as a potential mediator linking gut microbiota to BDNF/IL6 regulation and depression.

Enrichment of Mediterranean diet components reshapes gut microbiota toward Lactobacillus and Akkermansia expansion, a shift linked to elevated short-chain fatty acids and reduced lipopolysaccharide in portal circulation. In aged mice, this dietary pattern attenuated cognitive decline and lowered amyloid-β burden in the hippocampus, while restoring BDNF expression and suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines in the intestinal epithelium. We profiled fecal communities by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and applied random forest modeling to identify taxa predictive of memory impairment. Lactobacillus abundance and butyrate concentration emerged as top predictors, and their combination classified mice with high accuracy. In a small human cohort, adherence to Mediterranean diet correlated with higher fecal butyrate and better cognitive scores, although causality remains unresolved. Notably, butyrate increased tight junction proteins and reduced endotoxin translocation, suggesting a mechanistic route by which microbial shifts influence brain function. These findings position diet-driven microbial metabolites as modifiable signals along the gut-brain axis and support fecal microbiota transplantation or prebiotic supplementation as candidate strategies to delay neurodegeneration.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and altered Prevotellaceae abundance accompany Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether these shifts reflect cause or consequence remains unresolved. We recruited patients with idiopathic PD and healthy controls, collected fecal and serum samples, and applied shotgun metagenomics plus targeted transcriptomics. SNCA expression was elevated in patients with PD and inversely correlated with Prevotella copri relative abundance. Multivariable regression adjusted for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose showed that each log-unit decrease in P. copri was associated with a 0.42-unit increase in SNCA (P = 0.003). Gut microbiota from patients with PD also produced more lipopolysaccharide in vitro, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in stool. In a mouse model, colonization with microbiota from patients with PD exacerbated motor impairment and neuroinflammation. These findings support a mechanistic link between gut microbial composition, SNCA regulation, and PD progression, suggesting probiotic or prebiotic interventions targeting Prevotella may merit clinical testing.

Accumulating evidence positions the gut microbiota as a key modulator of brain function, with short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shaping hippocampal plasticity and emotional regulation. In older adults, reduced microbial diversity correlates with cognitive decline, depression, and heightened neuroinflammation, suggesting that dietary strategies may preserve central nervous system health. Polyphenol-rich foods such as berries, green tea, and extra virgin olive oil supply bioactive compounds that modulate gut microbial communities, increase Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and promote butyrate production. Similarly, probiotic supplements and prebiotic fibers can reinforce intestinal barrier integrity and attenuate stress-related psychiatric symptoms. Clinical and preclinical studies using 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation indicate that these interventions alter microbiota-gut-brain signaling, although effect sizes vary by baseline microbial composition, dietary pattern, and host genetic variation. Nevertheless, causality remains incompletely resolved, and many trials are limited by short duration, small samples, and inconsistent supplement formulations. Future work should pair multivariable modeling with longitudinal sampling to determine whether whole-diet approaches or targeted nutraceuticals most effectively translate microbiome modulation into durable brain benefits.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as epigenetic modulators of BDNF in the hippocampus, and their depletion during gut microbial dysbiosis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). To test whether probiotic supplementation could reverse this axis, we randomized adults with MDD to 12 weeks of multi-strain probiotics or a control condition. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial composition; qPCR measured BDNF and IL-6 expression in peripheral blood. At baseline, patients showed lower BDNF and higher C-reactive protein than healthy controls. Probiotic-treated participants showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, reduced lipopolysaccharide, and higher BDNF expression relative to control. Changes in BDNF correlated with gut microbiota shifts (Spearman correlation ρ = 0.42, P = 0.003). Clinical response, defined as ≥50% reduction in Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score, occurred in 62% of probiotic-treated adults versus 34% of control-treated adults. These findings suggest that probiotics may ameliorate depressive symptoms by restoring microbial signaling to BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, although FTO and TLR4 variants may moderate response.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease and correlates with constipation, a prodromal feature. In a cohort of patients and healthy controls, fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Random forest classification identified Prevotellaceae depletion and Akkermansia enrichment as discriminative. Short-chain fatty acid producers, including Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, were reduced, while butyrate levels in colon were lower. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum altered gut microbiota and improved constipation scores in a randomized controlled trial. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to reduced inflammatory cytokines. In gnotobiotic mice, prebiotic fiber increased Akkermansia and attenuated neuroinflammation. Levodopa response correlated with microbial composition. PERMANOVA revealed that vitamin D and omega-3 supplementation shifted microbial beta diversity. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors reduced α-synuclein aggregation in substantia nigra and protected dopaminergic neurons. These findings support targeting the gut microbiota to modulate PD in patients.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiome yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that act as histone deacetylase inhibitors and G-protein-coupled receptor ligands in the central nervous system. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a polyphenol-rich whole-grain diet or a refined-grain control for 12 weeks. We used shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry to profile fecal microbiota and metabolites. The intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, elevated fecal butyrate, and upregulated BDNF and IL-10 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. These changes correlated with improved executive function scores and reduced inflammatory markers. Mice transplanted with post-intervention microbiota showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased Bdnf in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that Roseburia intestinalis abundance explained 31% of the variance in BDNF methylation. Our findings suggest that fermentable fiber-rich foods may promote butyrate-dependent BDNF signaling, offering a tractable strategy for age-related cognitive decline.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF signaling and hippocampal plasticity, linking gut microbiome composition to cognitive aging. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet or a low-fiber control diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomics revealed that the Mediterranean-style diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance and raised butyrate concentrations. These shifts coincided with upregulated BDNF and NGF expression in peripheral blood and improved cognitive scores in mixed-effects models. APOE4 carriers exhibited weaker BDNF induction despite similar microbiome changes. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into mice recapitulated butyrate increases and reduced neuroinflammation. However, antibiotic exposure abolished these effects. Baseline gut microbiome diversity and Bacteroides abundance predicted response, whereas proton pump inhibitors blunted it. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber-responsive Faecalibacterium and Roseburia may modulate BDNF via butyrate, but host APOE4 status modifies the gut-brain response. Longitudinal sampling is needed to establish causality.

Supplementing inulin alongside fermented foods reshapes gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid production, with downstream consequences for hippocampal BDNF expression and anxiety-like behavior. In a randomized crossover trial, 48 adults with mild depression received either a fructo-oligosaccharide supplement plus yogurt or a control condition for 8 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics showed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, while linear mixed models linked butyrate enrichment to reduced anxiety scores. Vagal tone and BDNF methylation changed in parallel, and tryptophan availability predicted depressive symptom improvement. In mice, inulin and fermented milk increased hippocampal BDNF and reduced depressive behavior, but effects were abolished by vagotomy. In a separate study of 120 older adults, higher fermented food intake correlated with greater gut microbial diversity and lower depression prevalence; mediation analysis suggested that indole-3-propionic acid and serotonin partially explained this link. These findings suggest that prebiotic and fermented food interventions may modulate the gut-brain axis through gut microbiota-derived metabolites and BDNF-dependent plasticity.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids sit at the interface between diet and neuropsychiatric disorders, yet their causal role in anxiety-like behavior remains contested. We colonized germ-free C57BL/6 mice with microbiota from patients with generalized anxiety disorder or healthy controls, then fed them a high-fat, low-fiber diet or a fermented food-enriched diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that donor microbiota engrafted differently, with Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium dominating the fermented food-enriched diet group. Untargeted metabolomics of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex revealed elevated butyrate and indole-3-lactate after fermented food-enriched diet consumption. Using mediation analysis, we found that butyrate levels explained 38% of the reduction in anxiety-like behavior, measured by open field test and elevated plus maze. This effect was accompanied by increased Bdnf expression in the dentate gyrus and reduced Il6 transcription. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that microbial diversity predicted behavioral resilience independently of donor diagnosis. These findings suggest that fermented food-enriched diet intake may buffer anxiety through microbial metabolites and Bdnf-dependent plasticity, providing a tractable target for stress-related disorders.

Supplementation with probiotics and inulin reshapes the gut microbiota and modifies BDNF, TH, and SNCA expression in the brain, suggesting a tractable route to slow Parkinson's disease progression. In a randomized patient cohort and mice model, daily probiotic exposure increased Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and raised fecal butyrate and propionate concentrations. Baseline gut dysbiosis correlated with motor deficits and elevated lipopolysaccharide; after eight weeks, supplementation restored microbial ecology and lowered C-reactive protein. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed expanded commensal microbiota diversity, while RT-qPCR showed reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in the colon and substantia nigra. ELISA confirmed lower circulating inflammatory cytokines and higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Behavioral testing showed improved latency to fall and travel distance, paralleling increased GDNF and PINK1 expression; LRRK2 remained unchanged. Spearman correlation linked A. muciniphila abundance to TH and BDNF transcripts, whereas butyrate inversely correlated with SNCA expression. These findings indicate that probiotic-prebiotic formulations may modulate the microbiota-gut-brain axis, reduce neuroinflammation, and preserve nigrostriatal function in Parkinson's disease.

Depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and concurrent expansion of Bacteroides in the gut microbiome track with elevated inflammatory cytokines in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether these shifts predict treatment response remains unclear. We profiled feces and serum from 72 patients with MDD and 48 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Random forest classified MDD with an area under the curve of 0.81, driven by Bacteroides abundance and butyrate levels. Linear mixed-effects models showed that lower butyrate correlated with higher IL6 and TNF expression and worse depressive symptoms. Baseline butyrate below 12 μmol/L predicted non-response after 8 weeks of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment. BDNF expression was reduced in patients and inversely associated with Bacteroides relative abundance. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the relationship between F. prausnitzii and BDNF. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a plausible modulator of BDNF and inflammation in MDD, warranting longitudinal validation.

Microbiota-derived butyrate and propionate can accelerate Alzheimer's disease–like amyloid-β pathology in APP/PS1 mice, whereas probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve attenuates amyloid-β deposition in the hippocampus and restores gut microbial composition. In germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from donors with Alzheimer's disease, short-chain fatty acid production rose and amyloid-β plaque load increased relative to mice receiving control microbiota. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and metabolites in patients with mild cognitive impairment and mouse models. Dietary fiber intake correlated inversely with circulating lipopolysaccharide, while omega-3 fatty acid supplementation was associated with lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α. Fecal Bacteroides abundance and trimethylamine N-oxide levels distinguished Alzheimer's disease from cognitively normal controls with an area under the curve of 0.86. These findings position the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target, where diet and probiotics may mitigate inflammatory signaling and amyloid burden. Longitudinal metagenomic and metabolomic studies are needed to confirm causality.

Alterations in gut microbial composition correlate with Parkinson's disease severity and may modulate SNCA-linked neuroinflammation through the gut-brain axis. We profiled fecal microbiota from 48 patients with Parkinson's disease and 32 healthy controls, quantifying Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Prevotellaceae depletion and Enterobacteriaceae enrichment in patients. SNCA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells negatively correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance, whereas probiotic supplementation for 12 weeks increased Bifidobacterium and reduced constipation scores. Random forest classification separated patients from controls with 82% accuracy. Baseline microbial diversity was lower in patients than in controls, and Roseburia abundance tracked inversely with motor scores. Associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose. These findings suggest that SNCA-associated neuroinflammation may be shaped by gut microbiota and that probiotics could serve as an adjunctive strategy, though longitudinal trials are needed to confirm causality and define optimal strains and doses.

Disruption of the gut microbiome by a Western diet can promote neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment, yet whether targeted probiotic or polyphenol supplementation reverses these effects remains uncertain. In aged mice colonized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fed a high-fat, high-sucrose diet, daily curcumin increased microbial diversity, enriched Akkermansia muciniphila, and elevated butyrate in colon. These changes coincided with reduced hippocampal inflammation, lower interleukin-6, and improved performance on Morris water maze testing. RNA sequencing revealed upregulation of Bdnf, Zo-1, and Nrf2 in brain and intestinal tissue. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance partially explained the cognitive benefit. Fecal microbiota transplantation from curcumin-treated donors into naive recipients recapitulated the Bdnf and Zo-1 expression shifts, whereas curcumin alone without microbiota failed to do so. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot randomized controlled trial of curcumin plus fiber showed similar trends, although effects were limited by sample size. These findings support a gut-brain axis in which diet, supplements, and microbiota-derived metabolites converge on BDNF signaling to modulate neurodegeneration.

Microbial colonization of the neonatal gut shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and modulates stress reactivity, implicating the gut microbiota in neuropsychiatric disorders. In mice, dietary fiber deprivation reduces butyrate production by Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium, weakening intestinal barrier integrity and elevating lipopolysaccharide translocation. A randomized trial in adults with mild cognitive impairment tested whether inulin plus a Mediterranean-style diet alters gut microbiota composition and IL-6 expression. After 12 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium; shotgun metagenomics confirmed enriched short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. Linear mixed models showed that inulin responders had lower C-reactive protein and improved BDNF methylation scores. Fecal metabolomics linked inulin intake to elevated propionate and acetate, while selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors attenuated these associations. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii increased BDNF and reduced IL-1β in the prefrontal cortex; these effects were abolished in GPR43-deficient mice, supporting a receptor-dependent mechanism. These findings suggest that fermentable fiber and prebiotic supplementation may stabilize microbiota-gut-brain axis signaling, though APOE genotype modified effects.

Diets enriched with fermented foods and dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate gut-brain axis signaling, yet the microbial mediators linking these foods to depression and anxiety remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized controlled feeding trial, 120 adults with mild depressive symptoms received either a high-fermented food diet, a high-fiber diet, or usual care. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites were quantified. Both interventions increased microbial diversity and the abundance of Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. High-fermented food intake was associated with greater gamma-aminobutyric acid production potential and reduced inflammation, whereas high-fiber intake enriched butyrate-producing taxa and increased butyrate. Linear mixed models showed that changes in gut microbial composition correlated with improved depression scores. Effects persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and baseline microbiome composition. These findings suggest that fermented foods and fiber may alleviate mood symptoms through distinct microbiome-mediated pathways, supporting dietary strategies for gut-brain disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced in the colon can modulate central nervous system immune tone, yet the extent to which dietary fiber supplementation alters this axis in older adults remains contested. We analyzed fecal microbiota, serum metabolites, and cognitive scores from 120 participants enrolled in a 12-week randomized trial of inulin. Linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced neuroinflammation-associated interleukin-6 relative to baseline. These shifts correlated with improved executive function scores, but only among participants with baseline microbial diversity above the median. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that responders harbored higher baseline butyrate-producing taxa, suggesting a microbiome-dependent response. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the cognitive effect. By contrast, trimethylamine N-oxide and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein remained unchanged, indicating that the effect was not driven by generalized endotoxemia. These findings support targeted prebiotic strategies for age-related cognitive decline and argue that baseline gut microbiome profiling should guide future fiber interventions.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis can accelerate Alzheimer's disease pathology, yet whether magnesium-L-threonate corrects microbial and neuronal deficits in tandem remains unclear. We treated APP/PS1 mice with magnesium-L-threonate for 8 weeks and profiled the fecal microbiome by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, serum metabolites by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and hippocampus BDNF expression. Supplemented mice showed improved cognitive impairment and reduced amyloid-β deposition. Magnesium-L-threonate increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, decreased Allobaculum, and elevated short-chain fatty acids. These shifts accompanied lower neuroinflammation, reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α, restored intestinal tight junction proteins, upregulated BDNF, and improved memory retention. Western blotting confirmed increased zona occludens-1 and occludin in colon. Treatment also lowered oxidative stress and increased glutathione in cortex. Spearman correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acids with BDNF levels and amyloid burden. The findings indicate that magnesium-L-threonate may ameliorate Alzheimer's disease through microbiota-gut-brain axis remodeling, supporting magnesium-L-threonate as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by chronic psychosocial stress promotes depressive-like behavior and alters hippocampal plasticity, yet microbial strategies that reverse these effects remain incompletely defined. We administered Bifidobacterium breve M-16V to adult male C57BL/6J mice exposed to 14 days of chronic unpredictable mild stress and compared outcomes with sertraline-treated and vehicle-treated mice. Behavioral responses were assessed using the forced swim test, sucrose preference test, and open field test. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that stress reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance while increasing Bacteroides; supplementation partially normalized these microbial communities. In the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, B. breve M-16V restored serotonin, norepinephrine, and BDNF expression, reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α, and lowered corticosterone, and increased short-chain fatty acids. Correlation analysis linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF levels and anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that B. breve M-16V attenuates stress-induced depressive-like behavior through microbiota-gut-brain signaling and may complement conventional antidepressant therapy.

Gut microbial dysbiosis driven by a high-fat diet (HFD) accelerates Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like pathology through microglia-dependent and independent control of astrocytes. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), we tested whether Lactobacillus and Bacteroides modulate glial reactivity in APPPS1-21 mice fed an HFD. HFD-fed mice exhibited reduced Alloprevotella and elevated Bifidobacteriales, together with increased amyloid beta plaques and neuroinflammation. FMT from untreated donor mice restored microbial diversity and attenuated plaque-associated astrocyte recruitment. Butyrate supplementation mimicked these protective effects, whereas broad-spectrum antibiotics depleted gut microbiota and reduced GFAP+ astrocytes. In germ-free mice, GFAP+ astrocytosis and plaque-associated astrocytes were similarly diminished, and CSF1R inhibitor treatment revealed that microglia were required for astrocyte morphological changes but not for C3 loss. Correlational analysis linked pathogenic bacteria to astrocyte morphology. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbiome shifts regulate glial phenotypes and amyloid pathology, identifying short-chain fatty acids as mediators of gut-brain signaling.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids can reshape hippocampal BDNF expression and dampen neuroinflammation, yet whether these signals translate into measurable relief from major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unresolved. In a cohort of adults with MDD and healthy controls, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified plasma cytokines, cortisol, kynurenine, and BDNF transcript levels in peripheral blood. Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were depleted in patients, whereas Bacteroides were enriched. Associations between bacterial taxa and SLC6A4 methylation were tested with linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use; multiple comparisons were controlled by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate. Lower Faecalibacterium abundance predicted higher anxiety scores and reduced BDNF expression. In mice receiving probiotic supplementation, Faecalibacterium restoration normalized serotonin turnover and BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. These findings position gut microbiota–BDNF signaling as a candidate axis for stratifying patients with MDD and for developing microbiota-informed biomarkers.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression in the central nervous system, yet how dietary fiber supplementation translates into microbiome-mediated neuromodulation remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics in mice fed a high-fat diet, we tested whether inulin alters Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, short-chain fatty acid production, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. Inulin increased butyrate and propionate in cecal contents, restored BDNF transcripts in the hippocampus, and reduced anxiety-like behavior relative to unsupplemented controls. These effects coincided with higher Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and lower lipopolysaccharide translocation. In human participants with mild cognitive impairment, a randomized fiber supplement similarly modulated gut microbiota composition and plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels, although correlation analysis did not establish causality. Mechanistically, BDNF upregulation was accompanied by increased indole-3-propionic acid and decreased trimethylamine N-oxide, suggesting a microbiota-BDNF signaling axis. These findings position prebiotic fiber as a plausible adjunct for neuropsychiatric disorders, with BDNF signaling and microbiome-derived metabolites as candidate mediators.

Microbial metabolites from dietary fiber shape central nervous system immune tone, but whether diet-driven shifts in the gut microbiome alter neuroinflammatory disease activity remains uncertain. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics on stool and serum from adults with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and healthy controls enrolled in a 12-week randomized dietary trial. Participants consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable fiber or a Western diet comparator. Linear mixed models tested changes in Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations. The Mediterranean-style diet increased butyrate and propionate, expanded Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and reduced Bacteroides relative abundance compared with the Western diet. These microbial and metabolic shifts correlated with lower interleukin-17A expression in peripheral blood and improved clinical disability scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced butyrate-dependent reductions in spinal cord IL-17 and IFN-γ expression. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and prebiotic supplementation may provide adjunctive benefit in multiple sclerosis by reinforcing gut microbiota–brain communication.

Prebiotic inulin supplementation reverses Western diet-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis and attenuates neuroinflammation in mice, yet the microbial and metabolic pathways linking these effects remain incompletely defined. We fed C57BL/6 mice a high-fat, high-sucrose diet with or without inulin for 12 weeks and assessed hippocampal BDNF expression, activation of microglia, anxiety-like behavior, and depressive-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and untargeted metabolomics quantified cecal microbiota, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and lipopolysaccharide. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium, Akkermansia, and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate and propionate, and reduced TNF-α, IL-6, and Iba1 in the hippocampus. It also restored ZO-1 and occludin expression in the colon. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donor mice into antibiotic-treated recipient mice recapitulated these benefits. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and propionate partly explained the improvement in anxiety-like behavior. These findings indicate that inulin may protect against Western diet-driven neuropsychiatric disturbances by modulating gut microbiota-derived SCFAs, intestinal barrier integrity, and brain immune signaling.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that influence brain immune homeostasis, yet whether these metabolites mediate age-related cognitive decline remains unresolved. We fed aged C57BL/6 mice either a high-fiber diet or low-fiber diet for 12 weeks and assessed cognitive impairment, microbial composition, and neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that fiber increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while reducing Proteobacteria. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed elevated butyrate and propionate in feces and serum. In hippocampus, fiber intake suppressed Il1b and Tnf expression and increased Bdnf. Behavioral testing demonstrated improved spatial memory in mice receiving fiber. Notably, antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion abolished these benefits, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber donor mice restored them. Parallel analysis of older adults from a longitudinal cohort showed that higher fiber intake correlated with lower depression scores and greater microbial diversity, although mediation analysis indicated partial dependence on butyrate. These findings suggest that dietary fiber shapes the gut microbiome to attenuate neuroinflammation and support hippocampal function, identifying fiber supplementation as a modifiable strategy for cognitive aging.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in mice exposed to chronic stress, yet whether these effects require host BDNF signaling remains unresolved. In a randomized mouse model, inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance in the colon, elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and reduced depressive-like behavior.
