Hippocampal Bdnf expression and brain-derived neurotrophic factor protein were higher after supplementation, whereas Il6 and Tnf transcripts declined. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that inulin did not alter overall microbial richness but shifted community composition toward Bifidobacterium-enriched taxa. Notably, Bdnf knockdown in the hippocampus abolished the behavioral benefit without reversing microbial shifts, suggesting that inulin acts through a microbiota-BDNF axis. Depletion of gut microbiota with an antibiotic cocktail prevented the inulin-induced rise in brain-derived neurotrophic factor and blocked its behavioral effects, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors restored them. These findings position inulin as a potential prebiotic strategy for stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders, though human trials are needed to determine whether this microbiota-BDNF mechanism translates beyond rodents.

Adolescent exposure to a high-fat diet reshapes the gut microbiota and increases susceptibility to depression, but the protective potential of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids remains poorly defined. To test whether omega-3 supplementation reverses high-fat diet-driven depressive-like behavior, male C57BL/6 mice received a high-fat diet with or without omega-3 for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that omega-3 restored gut microbiota diversity and enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed higher short-chain fatty acid levels in feces, and Spearman correlation linked these increases to reduced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. Omega-3-treated mice also expressed more Bdnf and displayed fewer depressive-like behaviors than high-fat diet-fed controls. Fecal microbiota transplantation from omega-3-treated donors partially reproduced these benefits in recipient mice, whereas Lactobacillus depletion abolished them. No comparable shifts occurred in chow-fed mice. These findings indicate that omega-3 supplementation mitigates high-fat diet-induced depressive-like phenotypes through microbiota-short-chain fatty acid-BDNF signaling, identifying a modifiable gut-brain axis target.

Fermentable dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods reshape the gut microbiome, increasing Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production. These metabolites reach the brain, where they modulate BDNF and NF-κB signaling, suppressing neuroinflammation and attenuating cognitive decline. To test this, we analyzed fecal microbiota from 94 community-dwelling older adults using 16S rRNA sequencing, and measured circulating SCFAs, BDNF, and IL-6. Higher Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium correlated with greater BDNF and lower IL-6; Prevotella showed the opposite pattern. A random forest classifier based on microbial features distinguished participants with high versus low BDNF (AUC 0.81). Mediation analysis suggested that SCFAs accounted for 32% of the association between Faecalibacterium and BDNF. In a 12-week randomized sub-study, participants receiving a fiber-enriched diet showed increased Bifidobacterium and BDNF alongside reduced IL-6 compared with controls. These findings position dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods as modifiable microbiota-derived signals that may protect against neuroinflammation-related cognitive decline.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids act on intestinal enterochromaffin cells and vagal afferents to modulate central nervous system immune tone, yet whether this axis alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus during depression remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then measured BDNF, IL6, and TNF transcripts. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundance correlated inversely with BDNF expression. In the hippocampus, BDNF correlated with Lactobacillus abundance and butyrate concentrations, while IL6 and TNF were elevated in depression-associated microbiota. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with depression reduced BDNF and increased IL6 in the prefrontal cortex; fluoxetine partially reversed these changes. Microbiota from healthy donors increased BDNF and reduced interleukin-6 protein. These results suggest that gut microbial composition influences depressive-like behavior through BDNF-dependent and cytokine-mediated pathways, and that 16S rRNA gene sequencing plus fecal microbiota transplantation can identify targets in the microbiome for depression.

Microbial tryptophan catabolites shape central serotonin availability and may contribute to major depressive disorder (MDD). In a cohort of 84 adults, fermented foods and dietary fiber intake correlated with higher abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in the gut microbiome, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing. Using mediation analysis, we found that indole-3-lactate mediated 31% of the inverse association between dietary fiber and depressive symptoms scores. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with Lactobacillus reuteri, fermented food supplementation increased tryptophan metabolites in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex was elevated in colonized mice relative to germ-free controls. Fecal microbiota from patients with MDD transferred into antibiotic-treated mice recapitulated despair-like behavior, whereas fiber supplementation rescued indole-3-propionate levels. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that Lachnospiraceae abundance predicted BDNF methylation in the hippocampus after adjusting for age and antidepressant use. These findings suggest that fermented foods and fiber promote beneficial gut bacteria that modulate neuroactive metabolites, offering a plausible dietary route to improve mood disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) signal through FFAR2 and FFAR3 on enteroendocrine cells, shaping hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis reactivity and depressive behavior. In mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress, gut microbiota depletion increased corticosterone and reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus; these effects were reversed by colonization with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or by dietary inulin. To translate these findings, we analyzed participants with major depressive disorder and healthy controls in a cross-sectional analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics. Lower microbial diversity and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with higher depression severity and lower butyrate. A 12-week randomized controlled trial of omega-3 supplementation plus resistant starch increased butyrate-producing bacteria and reduced interleukin-6. In parallel, lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation was attenuated in mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from responders, an effect accompanied by lower Tlr4 and Nfkb1 expression. These data position FFAR2/FFAR3 signaling and dietary fiber as modifiable nodes in the gut-brain axis, though causal direction requires further gnotobiotic mice and patient validation.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids sustain plasticity in the hippocampus and BDNF signaling, yet their depletion is increasingly implicated in depression and anxiety. To test whether fermentable whole-grain barley and inulin restore this gut-brain circuit, adults with mild depressive symptoms received a dietary fiber supplement combining these substrates or a control for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, accompanied by higher fecal butyrate and propionate. The intervention also reduced systemic inflammation, lowered IL6 and TNF expression in peripheral blood, and upregulated BDNF and GPR43 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. These molecular changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms. In mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from responders, 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic prediction confirmed enrichment of butyrate-producing taxa, while BDNF and GPR43 increased in the prefrontal cortex. Our findings suggest that whole-grain barley plus inulin may alleviate depression by reshaping gut microbiota and SCFA-GPR43-BDNF signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the gut microbiome predicts Alzheimer's disease biomarkers more strongly than taxonomic diversity alone. In 240 older adults, we combined shotgun metagenomics with 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metabolomics to test whether Mediterranean diet adherence and omega-3 supplementation reshape the gut microbiome and hippocampal function. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, APOE ε4 status, and body mass index showed that higher fiber-rich food intake was associated with increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. These taxa correlated with lower neuroinflammation markers and better prefrontal cortex connectivity. Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve further reduced cognitive decline scores over 24 weeks, but only among participants with low baseline butyrate. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial butyrate partly mediated the diet–cognition relationship. Random forest classification achieved 0.78 area under the curve for discriminating individuals with mild cognitive impairment from cognitively unimpaired controls. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics may synergistically support brain health via gut microbiota-derived metabolites.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition can modulate central nervous system function through microbial metabolites, short-chain fatty acids, and bile acids, yet the extent to which dietary patterns shape this dialogue remains incompletely resolved. In a 12-week randomized controlled feeding study, 84 adults with metabolic syndrome received either a high-fiber, plant-rich diet or a Western-style diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing was used to validate taxonomic shifts. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial taxa, plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. The high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised butyrate production, and reduced inflammatory markers compared with the Western-style diet. These changes correlated with improved hippocampal connectivity on functional magnetic resonance imaging. BDNF expression in peripheral blood was higher after the high-fiber diet, and this increase was partially mediated by specific microbial taxa. The findings suggest that diet-driven microbiota remodeling may influence brain function via metabolite-sensitive pathways, offering a plausible target for neuropsychiatric disorders risk reduction.

Fermented foods and dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiota and increase short-chain fatty acid production, a mechanism linking intestinal ecology to central nervous system function. In a randomized adult cohort with mild cognitive impairment, we tested whether a Mediterranean-style diet altered microbial taxa and butyrate availability over 12 weeks. Dietary intake was recorded using food frequency questionnaires. Stool samples underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Associations among microbial features, butyrate, and BDNF were assessed with linear mixed-effects models, PERMANOVA, Spearman correlation, and mediation analysis. The intervention enriched Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila, while Bacteroides declined. Higher butyrate correlated with improved cognitive scores and elevated BDNF, and butyrate partly mediated the gut microbiota-BDNF association. These findings suggest that fermented food and fiber interventions may modulate the gut microbiota-brain axis and support probiotic or dietary strategies for mild cognitive impairment. No serious adverse events occurred; adherence exceeded 85% in both arms.

Gut microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids shape central nervous system immune tone, yet their dietary modifiability in mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, older adults with subjective memory decline received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods and fiber or a habitual diet; half also received omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Shotgun metagenomics and untargeted metabolomics quantified gut microbiome composition and plasma metabolites. Compared with controls, the intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced trimethylamine N-oxide. These shifts correlated with improved executive function scores and lower IL6 expression. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 28% of the cognitive effect, whereas TMAO attenuation was independent of omega-3 intake. Baseline microbial diversity modified the response, with greater butyrate increases in participants consuming higher fiber amounts. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings support dietary strategies targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis in early cognitive impairment, though larger trials are needed to confirm whether these effects persist.

Anthocyanin-rich berry extracts reshape gut microbiota and reduce neuroinflammation, but the microbial and metabolic routes connecting berries to brain function remain poorly defined. We tested whether a 12-week blueberry polyphenol supplement alters gut microbiota, short-chain fatty acid production, and depressive-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic social stress. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we observed that supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in feces, and normalized brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. These changes were accompanied by reduced anhedonia and anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced the behavioral and neurochemical benefits, while mediation analysis implicated butyrate as a key mediator. Our findings suggest that berry polyphenol supplements may support gut-brain signaling and emotional resilience, though clinical trials are needed to confirm efficacy and optimal dosing. Because patients with major depressive disorder often show altered gut microbiota, these preclinical results warrant further randomized controlled trials.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with distinct gut microbiota profiles and lower neuroinflammatory tone, yet the molecular routes linking these shifts to cognitive resilience remain poorly defined. We examined 120 older adults with mild cognitive impairment, measuring 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling, and BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis, we tested whether microbial and metabolic features explained diet-related differences in BDNF methylation and cognition. Greater Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with enriched Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium, higher butyrate, and reduced IL6 expression. BDNF methylation was lower in high-adherence participants and partially mediated the association between microbial composition and executive function. Associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, education, and antidepressant use. No significant interactions were observed with type 2 diabetes status. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbiota remodeling may influence BDNF regulation and cognitive outcomes, offering a plausible gut-brain mechanism for early intervention in mild cognitive impairment.

Consumption of a high-fat, low-fiber diet reshapes the gut microbiota, increases permeability of the intestine, and elevates circulating lipopolysaccharide, thereby promoting neuroinflammation and depressive symptoms. To test whether this cascade is reversible, adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls provided blood and fecal microbiota samples before and after a 12-week intervention combining probiotics with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed lower gut microbial diversity and depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in patients relative to controls. Untargeted metabolomics showed reduced short-chain fatty acids and elevated trimethylamine N-oxide. At baseline, participants with low dietary fiber intake exhibited higher C-reactive protein and greater anhedonia severity. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, lowered interleukin-6, and improved depressive symptoms. After intervention, linear discriminant analysis effect size linked Akkermansia muciniphila abundance to clinical response. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders reduced anxiety-like behavior and restored brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial interventions targeting the gut microbiota may attenuate neuropsychiatric disorders.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) susceptibility is influenced by gut microbiota, but whether probiotic supplementation can reshape central nervous system immunity during neuroinflammation is uncertain. We enrolled MS patients and mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and assigned them to a Mediterranean-style diet alone or combined with a multi-strain probiotic. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics showed that probiotic supplementation expanded Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, increased butyrate, and reduced demyelination. In mice, flow cytometry revealed higher Foxp3 expression and lower interleukin-17, while interleukin-10 rose in spinal cord and brain. Intestinal permeability assays indicated restored occludin and zonula occludens-1 expression, supporting gut barrier integrity. The protective effect required an intact microbiota, because antibiotic depletion abolished probiotic-mediated immune suppression. In patients, ELISA showed reduced C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, and no serious adverse events occurred during the trial. These data suggest that pairing probiotics with dietary fiber may stabilize gut microbial communities and slow MS progression.

Chronic consumption of a Western-style diet disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis and promotes neuroinflammation, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. We fed C57BL/6 mice a high-fat, high-sucrose diet or standard chow for 12 weeks; half of the Western diet-fed animals received a multi-strain probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that the Western diet reduced Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance and increased the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio, while probiotics partially restored α diversity. Behavioral testing revealed that probiotic treatment improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior. In the hippocampus, probiotics lowered Tnf and Il6 expression and increased Bdnf transcripts. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces and serum were higher in probiotic-treated mice than in Western diet controls. Fecal SCFA profiling correlated positively with Bdnf expression and negatively with Tnf. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation mitigates Western diet-induced cognitive decline by modulating gut microbiota and microbial metabolites, supporting a gut-brain axis mechanism.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet the molecular mediators linking microbial signals to BDNF expression remain poorly defined. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids plus a probiotic supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal microbiota showed that active treatment increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations. At baseline, lower BDNF and higher IL-6 correlated with greater anxiety scores and lower microbial diversity. These changes correlated with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression and increased BDNF in peripheral blood. Mixed-effects models revealed that butyrate mediated the association between Bifidobacterium abundance and depressive symptoms improvement. The findings suggest that omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids combined with probiotics may modulate the gut-brain axis through BDNF- and IL-6-related pathways, offering a potential adjunctive strategy for depression.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans reshapes gut microbial communities and modulates brain function along the gut-brain axis, but whether these effects translate into improved depressive symptoms remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either inulin or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and prefrontal cortex activity was assessed with functional magnetic resonance imaging. Circulating short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo. Responder rates were higher in the inulin arm (62% vs 38%), and no serious adverse events occurred. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in Bifidobacterium and butyrate partially mediated the clinical improvement. Baseline microbial diversity moderated treatment response, with lower diversity predicting greater benefit. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation may influence brain function and mood through microbiota-derived metabolites, supporting further investigation of gut-brain therapeutics.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly recognized as a contributor to cognitive decline, yet whether microbial modification can alter brain outcomes remains uncertain. We combined two-sample Mendelian randomization with 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation in aged mice to test causality and mechanism. Instrumental variables for 119 gut microbial taxa were derived from genome-wide association data; inverse variance weighting with MR-Egger sensitivity analyses identified Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus as protective against Alzheimer's disease risk. In parallel, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received a 12-week probiotic supplement or control. The probiotic increased Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered circulating lipopolysaccharide, and improved neuropsychological testing scores relative to control. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced these benefits, accompanied by reduced microglial activation and elevated BDNF in the hippocampus. These findings support a causal role for gut microbiota in cognitive impairment and suggest that probiotic supplementation may complement existing therapies.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiome and dampens stress-related behavior in mice, yet the transcriptional pathways connecting microbial shifts to central BDNF signaling remain poorly defined. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus and randomized them to a prebiotic fiber or control diet. Behavioral assays included the open field test and forced swim test; hippocampus expression of BDNF, GR, IL-6, and TNF was quantified by RT-qPCR. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and reduced corticosterone levels, with parallel upregulation of BDNF in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial short-chain fatty acid production accounted for 38% of the effect on BDNF expression. These findings position inulin as a potential nutritional strategy for supporting stress-related disorders. Collectively, these data suggest that inulin-driven microbial metabolism may modulate central plasticity and affective behavior.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat diet can accelerate cognitive decline through brain-resident immune signaling, yet the molecular links remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into mice, we found that high-fat diet-shaped microbiota increased Lactobacillus and decreased Akkermansia, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These changes correlated with neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and memory impairment. Colonization with high-fat diet microbiota was sufficient to reproduce cognitive impairment in gnotobiotic mice, whereas prebiotic fiber supplementation restored BDNF and attenuated neuroinflammation. Notably, NLRP3 deletion in mice blocked microbiota-induced cognitive deficits, implicating inflammasome activation as a downstream node. Mechanistically, short-chain fatty acids were reduced in cecal content, and metabolomic profiling linked butyrate depletion to BDNF downregulation. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, similar microbial signatures were associated with lower BDNF and higher inflammatory cytokines. These results suggest that diet-driven gut microbial shifts influence brain function via BDNF and NLRP3-dependent pathways, identifying dietary fiber as a potential intervention for gut-brain axis disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids maintain blood-brain barrier integrity and dampen neuroinflammation, yet their contribution to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remains unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with MCI received omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids or placebo for 24 weeks. Fecal gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Cognitive performance was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Linear mixed-effects models tested intervention effects, and mediation analysis examined whether microbial or metabolic shifts explained cognitive change. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and raised plasma docosahexaenoic acid and butyrate; it also reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. The supplement group showed improved cognitive scores versus placebo. Microbial butyrate production mediated 31% of the treatment effect on cognition. These findings suggest that omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids may ameliorate MCI through gut microbiota-brain signaling, supporting larger clinical trials.

Inulin supplementation increases Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production, changes that correlate with reduced depressive-like behavior in mice. In adults, 8 weeks of inulin raised fecal butyrate and improved anxiety scores, but only in participants with low baseline microbial diversity. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium longum. In the prefrontal cortex, BDNF and NR3C1 expression increased after supplementation, while IL6 and TNF decreased. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the effect on BDNF and 24% on depressive symptoms. Additional fecal microbiota transplantation from responders to germ-free mice reproduced the BDNF increase and reduced corticosterone levels, implicating vagus nerve signaling and TLR4-dependent cytokine suppression. These findings position inulin as a prebiotic candidate for microbiota-targeted mood disorders, although effects depend on baseline gut microbiota composition and host genotype. The microbiota–metabolite–host gene axis may guide future clinical precision psychobiotic strategies.

Higher dietary sugar intake independently predicts dementia incidence, but whether gut microbiota-related genetic susceptibility modifies this risk is uncertain. Among 158,408 UK Biobank participants without dementia at baseline, repeated 24-hour dietary recalls assessed free sugar and non-free sugar intake. Polygenic risk scores for triglyceride-glucose metabolism, gut microbiota, and Alzheimer's disease were derived from genome-wide association studies. We applied Cox proportional hazards models with restricted cubic splines and multiplicative interaction terms, adjusting for demographics, lifestyle, and obesity. Over 9.94 years, 1,219 dementia cases occurred. Both free sugar and non-free sugar showed dose-response associations with dementia; the highest versus lowest quartile hazard ratios were 1.43 and 1.26, respectively. Genetic susceptibility amplified risk: lower polygenic risk scores for Ruminococcaceae UCG-014 or higher scores for Oscillospira strengthened the sugar-dementia association. These associations persisted across sensitivity analyses excluding early dementia diagnoses. These findings support personalized nutritional interventions that integrate sugar intake reduction with genetic risk profiling to prevent dementia.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by broad-spectrum antibiotics exacerbates Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice, but whether this effect depends on APOE4 remains unresolved. We treated mice carrying APOE4 or APOE3 with an antibiotic cocktail and then colonized them with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Akkermansia muciniphila. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Morris water maze, and hippocampal amyloid-β burden was quantified by immunofluorescence. Two-way ANOVA revealed that antibiotic exposure increased amyloid-β plaques and impaired spatial memory, with stronger effects in APOE4 carriers. L. rhamnosus colonization reduced plaque load and restored short-chain fatty acid levels, whereas A. muciniphila had no effect. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed successful engraftment and showed that APOE4 shaped microbial composition independently of AD status. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations inversely correlated with plaque burden, and minocycline did not rescue memory deficits. These findings suggest that gut microbiota modulation may attenuate AD-related pathology in a APOE4-dependent manner.

Chronic consumption of a Western diet disrupts gut microbiome ecology, increases intestinal permeability, and amplifies neuroinflammation, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. In a randomized mouse model of diet-induced cognitive decline, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and behavioral testing to examine whether Bifidobacterium breve and galacto-oligosaccharides could restore microbiota-gut-brain axis signaling. Western diet-fed mice showed reduced Lactobacillus and Akkermansia muciniphila, elevated lipopolysaccharide, depleted short-chain fatty acid pools, and impaired spatial memory. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium, normalized butyrate concentrations, and attenuated hippocampal BDNF deficits. These changes were accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation, lower interleukin-6 in the prefrontal cortex, and improved performance in Morris water maze tasks. Notably, the combined supplement also reduced serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and NF-κB expression in the hippocampus, while increasing Akkermansia abundance and propionate production. The findings suggest that probiotic plus prebiotic supplementation can partially counteract Western diet-induced cognitive impairment by remodeling the gut microbiome and strengthening microbial-gut-brain communication.

Dietary fiber intake reshapes the gut-brain axis by expanding short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and dampening neuroinflammatory tone. In a 12-week randomized trial of 120 adults with mild-to-moderate depression, we tested whether a high-fiber Mediterranean-style diet altered gut microbial composition and symptoms. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing, and plasma cytokines and tryptophan metabolites were quantified. Causal pathways were assessed with mediation analysis, adjusting for baseline body mass index, antidepressant use, and energy intake. Compared with habitual diet, the high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundances, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depression scores. Microbial alpha diversity correlated inversely with interleukin-6 and positively with kynurenine. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate-producing taxa explained 28% of the diet-related improvement in depression, whereas changes in interleukin-6 explained 17%. These effects were independent of weight loss. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated reduced anxiety-like behavior and elevated hippocampal BDNF expression. The findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable dietary lever on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, with short-chain fatty acids and immune signaling as candidate mediators. Validation in larger, diverse cohorts and with metagenomic and metabolomic techniques is warranted.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiome influence brain circuits implicated in major depressive disorder, yet dietary strategies to modify this gut-brain axis remain imprecise. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with moderate depression received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a high-fat, low-fiber diet; half of each group also took a multi-strain probiotic supplement or omega-3 fatty acid supplement. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that the Mediterranean-style diet plus probiotic increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations. These shifts correlated with lower depressive symptoms and altered BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the symptom improvement. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders reproduced the behavioral benefit, while antibiotic depletion abolished it. Baseline microbial diversity and FTO genotype moderated response, with stronger effects in participants consuming fewer ultra-processed foods. The findings support diet and targeted supplementation as modulators of microbial communities relevant to depression.

Inulin-type fructans supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation-associated cognitive decline, yet the contribution of habitual fermented foods to this axis remains unclear. In a randomized human trial, 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment received inulin (12 g/day) or yogurt enriched with Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial community composition; ELISA measured short-chain fatty acids, IL-6, and BDNF in plasma. Both interventions increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced IL-6. Inulin produced larger gains in BDNF and mixed-model analyses showed improved cognitive deficits compared with yogurt alone. Changes in Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with BDNF increases, while Faecalibacterium was inversely associated with IL-6. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with fermentable dietary fibers and fermented foods may support brain health, though effects on APOE-related risk and long-term dementia outcomes require further study.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, yet causal mediators remain unclear. We profiled fecal microbiota from adults with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid anxiety after 8 weeks of Bifidobacterium longum supplementation or placebo. Shotgun metagenomics and untargeted metabolomics were integrated, and random forest classification identified taxa discriminating responders from nonresponders. Supplementation enriched Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. Mediation analysis indicated that IL-10 expression and serotonin turnover partially explained symptom improvement. In germ-free mice, transfer of post-supplement microbiota lowered depressive-like behavior and increased hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Parallel mouse experiments showed that probiotic supplementation reshaped gut microbial ecology, elevated short-chain fatty acid production, and modulated BDNF and IL-10 transcription. Mediation models suggested that microbial metabolites partially mediate the diet–microbiota–brain axis. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings support personalized dietary supplementation strategies targeting gut microbial communities to improve mood symptoms.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber is increasingly linked to altered gut microbial ecology and improved neuropsychiatric symptoms, yet the mechanistic routes remain incompletely defined. We recruited adults with mild anxiety and depressive symptoms and assigned them to a high-fiber, fermented-food diet or habitual diet for 8 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool samples quantified microbiota composition and tryptophan metabolic gene abundance, while targeted metabolomics measured indole, kynurenine, and short-chain fatty acids in plasma and feces. The intervention increased Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced Bacteroides abundance. These shifts correlated with lower anxiety scores and higher serotonin metabolites, but not with depression severity. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate jointly accounted for 31% of the anxiety improvement. In a parallel mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders reproduced the behavioral and neuroinflammation changes, whereas microbiota-depleted mice showed no benefit. These findings support fermented food and fiber intake as accessible levers for microbiome-targeted modulation of the gut-brain axis.

Depletion of microbial butyrate precedes nigrostriatal degeneration in Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with reduced BDNF expression in the substantia nigra. To test causality, we performed 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing on fecal samples from 84 patients with PD and 71 controls, then transplanted gut microbiota into gnotobiotic mice overexpressing α-synuclein. Microbiota from patients showed reduced Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and increased Bacteroides, alongside lower fecal butyrate and elevated plasma IL-6 and TNF-α. Recipient mice developed motor deficits, neuroinflammation, and α-synuclein aggregation; these phenotypes were attenuated by butyrate supplementation or a Mediterranean diet rich in fermentable fiber. Metagenomic sequencing further linked TLR4 signaling in microglia to microbiota composition. In a mediation analysis, fecal butyrate explained 31% of the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and PD motor severity. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics targeting butyrate-producing bacteria may delay PD progression, though levodopa treatment did not modify these microbial associations in our cohort.

Altered gut microbiota composition and reduced short-chain fatty acid output are associated with major depressive disorder, but whether diet-driven microbial shifts causally influence symptoms remains unclear. We profiled adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, then applied mediation analysis to test whether gut bacterial genera and microbial metabolites link Mediterranean diet adherence to depressive symptoms. Higher Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with greater abundance of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Bifidobacterium, and with elevated butyrate and indole-3-propionate. These microbial features were inversely associated with depression severity. Mediation models indicated that Faecalibacterium and butyrate explained 18% and 14% of the protective association, respectively. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-adherence donors reduced depressive-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings position diet-responsive gut microbiota and their metabolites as plausible mediators of mood regulation, supporting fiber-rich foods and probiotic interventions in depression.

Metabolism of dietary fiber and fermented foods by the gut microbiome yields short-chain fatty acids that shape central nervous system immune tone and BDNF signaling, providing a mechanistic route by which gut bacteria influence anxiety and depression. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with moderate major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement or an inert control for 8 weeks while maintaining their habitual diet. The probiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, higher fecal butyrate concentrations, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with the control group. Mixed-effects modeling revealed that changes in gut microbiota composition mediated the improvement in depression scores, whereas fermented food intake at baseline predicted greater Bifidobacterium responsiveness. No serious adverse events occurred, and probiotic tolerability was high. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotic supplementation alongside dietary fiber-rich foods as an adjunctive strategy for mood disorders, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and strain specificity.

Dietary fermented foods containing live Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can reshape the gut microbiome and influence brain function via microbial metabolites. In a double-blind crossover trial, older adults with subjective cognitive decline consumed kefir or pasteurized milk daily for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance after kefir intake, alongside elevated fecal butyrate. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging showed enhanced prefrontal cortex–hippocampus connectivity, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay detected lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in serum. Fecal calprotectin and zonulin concentrations also declined, suggesting improved intestinal barrier function. Parallel in vitro assays showed that butyrate suppressed NF-κB signaling following lipopolysaccharide stimulation. Cognitive scores improved modestly, but mixed-effects models indicated that changes in microbial composition explained 28% of variance in cognitive decline severity. These findings suggest that kefir supplementation may mitigate neuroinflammation and support gut-brain axis health in aging populations, though larger trials are needed to confirm clinical benefit.

Disruption of gut microbiota homeostasis during early life can persistently alter brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, promoting anxiety-like behavior and cognitive impairment. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, whose abundance is shaped by dietary fiber and probiotic supplements, produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence microbial-gut-brain signaling through intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability. In male and female mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, alongside lower butyrate and acetate concentrations. Probiotic supplementation restored BDNF expression, normalized SCFA levels, and attenuated depressive-like behavior; these effects were absent in antibiotic-treated mice. Moreover, antibiotic exposure depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, reduced butyrate production, and exacerbated neuroinflammation in mice. Evidence from human trials remains mixed, partly because randomized controlled trials vary in probiotic strain, dose, and duration. These findings position gut microbiota as a modifiable target, but strain-specific mechanisms and host genetic factors require further resolution.

Dysregulated gut microbiota and impaired intestinal barrier function are increasingly recognized as contributors to multiple sclerosis (MS) pathogenesis, yet the mediating molecular pathways remain unresolved. We profiled serum metabolites and stool microbial taxa in patients with relapsing-remitting MS and matched controls, then applied Mendelian randomization to infer causal direction. Reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii correlated with lower butyrate and higher neurofilament light chain; HLA-DRB1*15:01 carriers showed stronger associations. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing further revealed depletion of Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, with enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila. In a subset, daily vitamin D3 supplementation for 12 weeks increased butyrate-producing bacteria and reduced interleukin-17. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 22% of the effect on inflammatory markers. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed these shifts, and germ-free mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota developed more severe experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with dietary fiber or probiotics may complement immunomodulatory therapy in MS.

Converging evidence positions the gut microbiome as a modifiable regulator of BDNF signaling and neuropsychiatric disease risk. In a 12-week randomized trial of adults with major depressive disorder, daily probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum increased short-chain fatty acid production and reduced depressive symptoms. Participants also received fermented foods and dietary fiber to support microbial diversity. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing showed enrichment of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, while serum metabolomics revealed elevated butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid. These changes correlated with increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and decreased interleukin-6. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 31% of the clinical improvement. Mixed-effects models further showed that carriers of a BDNF variant experienced greater symptom reduction than non-carriers, whereas baseline FTO genotype did not modify response. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings indicate that probiotic plus fermented food interventions may engage the microbiota-gut-brain axis through BDNF-dependent and inflammatory pathways, offering a scalable adjunct for depression.

Microbial metabolism of dietary tryptophan-rich foods converges on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) to constrain neuroinflammation along the gut-brain axis. In mice colonized with Lactobacillus reuteri, tryptophan supplementation increased indole-3-lactic acid in the intestinal lumen, expanded mucosa-associated microbiota, and elevated IL-22 transcripts in the colon. These changes were absent in Ahr-deficient mice, indicating a host AHR-dependent mechanism. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that a Western-style diet depleted Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced short-chain fatty acid production, whereas butyrate rescued intestinal barrier integrity and lowered anxiety-like behavior. Notably, inulin supplementation restored Reg3γ expression and attenuated colonic inflammation in mice fed a low-fiber diet. In patients with irritable bowel syndrome, random forest modeling of fecal microbiota predicted visceral hypersensitivity better than FUT2 genotype alone. Fecal microbiota transplantation from butyrate-treated donors partially transferred protection, suggesting that microbial metabolites act as mediators. These findings position dietary fiber and tryptophan as modifiable inputs that interface with host genetic variation to shape brain function.

Inulin supplementation reverses stress-induced cognitive impairment by remodeling gut microbial communities and suppressing interleukin-6 signaling in the hippocampus. In male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance while decreasing Desulfovibrio. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into germ-free mice reproduced the behavioral benefits, whereas vancomycin abolished them. Random forest classification linked Bifidobacterium abundance to Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex and to brain-derived neurotrophic factor concentrations. Transcriptomic profiling of intestinal epithelium showed that inulin upregulated Ocln and Zo-1, reinforcing blood-brain barrier integrity. Optogenetic stimulation of vagal afferents mimicked the protective effects, while capsaicin-induced vagal deafferentation blocked them. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly mediated the effects of inulin on anxiety-like behavior. Mixed-effects modeling confirmed that butyrate and Bifidobacterium independently predicted Bdnf expression. These findings position inulin as a plausible prebiotic intervention for stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders, though human trials are needed.

Microbial dysbiosis driven by a Western diet can precede cognitive decline, but the pathways linking gut microbiota to central nervous system remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with human donor fecal microbiota from older adults with mild cognitive impairment or normal cognition, then fed them either high-fat diet or fiber-rich chow. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified microbial taxa; untargeted metabolomics profiled short-chain fatty acids and bile acids. Mediation analysis tested whether microbiota-derived metabolites explained associations between diet and hippocampal amyloid burden. Dietary fiber increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, elevated butyrate, and reduced neuroinflammation; Western diet enriched Bacteroides and Escherichia coli, increased lipopolysaccharide, and impaired blood-brain barrier integrity. Mendelian randomization in human cohorts supported a causal effect of Roseburia on Alzheimer's disease. These findings position diet-responsive gut microbiota and microbial metabolites as modifiable mediators of cognitive impairment along the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Together, these data suggest that targeting dietary patterns may restore gut microbial ecology and attenuate neurodegeneration.

Butyrate, a microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid, reinforces the gut-brain axis by inducing BDNF in the hippocampus and limiting microglia activation. Among adults with major depressive disorder, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing of stool with plasma metabolomics and applied mediation analysis to determine whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance affects symptom severity through butyrate. Lower F. prausnitzii and butyrate tracked with higher depression scores, and linear mixed models revealed a significant indirect effect via BDNF (β = −0.18, 95% CI −0.31 to −0.07). Baseline serotonin and kynurenine ratios partially explained this association, while TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells moderated the microbial effect. In mice, butyrate supplementation restored BDNF and reduced interleukin-6 in the prefrontal cortex while normalizing vagus nerve tone. These data indicate that gut microbiota-directed butyrate production may alleviate depression-associated neuroinflammation, but Mendelian randomization and gnotobiotic mice are needed to establish causality and identify additional CREB pathways.

Multi-strain probiotics supplementation alters gut microbiota composition and reduces depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder, yet the mechanistic links to brain function remain unclear. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 60 patients, assessing fecal microbiota via 16S rRNA gene sequencing and brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during an emotional face matching task. After 8 weeks, probiotic recipients showed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated serotonin metabolites, and reduced amygdala reactivity compared to placebo (p < 0.05). Linear mixed models revealed that changes in Lactobacillus correlated with serotonin levels and depression scores. Furthermore, metabolomic profiling identified increased indole-3-propionic acid, a tryptophan metabolite, which negatively correlated with anxiety scores. These microbial and neural changes were accompanied by improved depression remission rates at 12 weeks. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may modulate gut microbiota and brain communication through microbial metabolites, offering a potential adjunctive treatment for depression. Larger trials are needed to confirm causality.

Depletion of gut microbiota and altered short-chain fatty acid production precede motor deficits in Parkinson's disease, implicating the gut-brain axis in neurodegeneration. To test whether microbial signals modify SNCA-driven pathology, we colonized germ-free mice expressing SNCA with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium or vehicle, then assessed substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss, colon inflammation, and lipopolysaccharide-induced TLR4 signaling. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing confirmed community engraftment, and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with Parkinson's disease was compared with healthy controls. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for batch and sex revealed that Lactobacillus-dominant communities increased BDNF expression and reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation, whereas Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with interleukin-6 and worse motor impairment. PERMANOVA of metagenomic profiles linked Akkermansia depletion to SNCA pathology. Probiotic supplementation, butyrate, and a fiber-rich diet partially rescued these effects, while levodopa did not alter microbial composition. These findings suggest that early targeting gut microbial communities may slow Parkinson's disease progression and improve outcomes in patients.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD). We hypothesized that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium breve could modulate the gut-brain axis and improve cognitive outcomes. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 60 patients with mild cognitive impairment received either probiotics or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) were measured by ELISA. Short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Cognitive function was evaluated with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-cognitive subscale (ADAS-cog). Results showed that probiotic treatment significantly increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate levels, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels, and improved MMSE and ADAS-cog scores compared to placebo. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with probiotics may offer a therapeutic strategy for AD by modulating neuroinflammatory pathways and microbial metabolites.

Dietary fiber-rich whole grains and fermented foods can reshape gut microbiota and influence central nervous system function through the gut-brain axis. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 68 adults with mild cognitive impairment received a probiotic plus inulin supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia-Shigella in the active group. Linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation linked these shifts to higher fecal butyrate, lower IL-6, and improved delayed recall. Adjusting for age, sex, and baseline microbiota diversity, PERMANOVA confirmed distinct microbial communities between groups. Baseline gut microbiota composition did not differ between groups. The active group also showed increased BDNF expression, and the effect on recall was partially mediated by Bifidobacterium abundance. No serious adverse events occurred. Compliance exceeded 90% in both arms. These findings support targeted dietary fiber and probiotic interventions as modulators of the gut-brain axis and suggest that short-chain fatty acid signaling contributes to their cognitive benefits.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape microglia reactivity and may modify major depressive disorder risk through BDNF signaling. To test whether gut microbiota composition predicts treatment response, we profiled adults with MDD before and after SSRI therapy. Fecal samples underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics; random forest models integrated taxa with host BDNF rs6265 genotype. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 were quantified to estimate microbial translocation and systemic inflammation. Responders harbored higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, and elevated butyrate; non-responders showed expanded Bacteroides and Escherichia-Shigella. At baseline, permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed distinct microbial communities according to depression severity (R2 = 0.08, p = 0.01). Transfer of responder microbiota into mice reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased Bdnf expression in hippocampus. BDNF rs6265 Met carriers showed weaker association between Faecalibacterium abundance and butyrate than Val/Val individuals. These findings link microbiome structure, BDNF variation, and short-chain fatty acid output to depression outcomes, suggesting prebiotic fiber or probiotic interventions may complement antidepressants.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and bile acids modulate central BDNF expression and microglial activity, linking gut microbial ecology to affective and cognitive phenotypes. In adults with major depressive disorder and matched controls, we integrated 16S rRNA sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and fecal metabolomics with dietary records. Baseline gut microbial diversity was lower in cases than controls, and random forest classification separated groups with moderate accuracy. Multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis tested whether fiber-rich foods and fermented foods associate with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, butyrate production, and symptom severity. Higher fiber-rich food intake correlated with increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, elevated butyrate, and lower depression scores; these associations were partially mediated by BDNF expression. Mendelian randomization using host BDNF genotype suggested a causal effect of gut microbiota on depressive symptoms, not reverse causation. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-butyrate donors reduced neuroinflammation and restored BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. These findings support dietary and microbial interventions targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

Chronic consumption of a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiome and suppresses BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, a pathway implicated in depression. We tested whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation could reverse these effects in mice exposed to chronic stress. Mice received either a high-fat diet or standard chow, with or without omega-3, for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF, GR, and IL-6 expression were quantified in the hippocampus. Linear mixed models showed that the high-fat diet reduced microbial diversity and increased the Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio, while decreasing BDNF and increasing IL-6 expression. In the forced swim test, mice fed the high-fat diet displayed longer immobility, whereas omega-3 reduced immobility by 32%. Omega-3 supplementation partially restored microbial diversity, lowered lipopolysaccharide concentrations, and normalized BDNF expression. Correlation analyses linked Lactobacillus abundance with BDNF levels (r = 0.61, P < 0.01). These findings suggest that omega-3 may buffer diet-induced neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior through microbiome-brain signaling.

Altered gut microbiota composition and barrier dysfunction may precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease, suggesting that gut-derived signals contribute to neurodegeneration. In patients carrying LRRK2 or GBA variants, intestinal inflammation and reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance associate with worse cognitive trajectories. We profiled 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and metagenomics in 120 participants, measuring short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and lipopolysaccharide. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium increased butyrate production and improved motor scores in a subset of patients. Linear mixed models showed that response depended on baseline microbiota and LRRK2 carrier status. Compared with controls, patients exhibited lower diversity of the gut microbiota and altered metabolite profiles. Probiotics alone were insufficient; combining them with prebiotics more effectively normalized gut microbiota and reduced neuroinflammation. At 12 weeks, probiotic-treated patients showed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and BDNF expression compared with baseline. These findings support genetically stratified use of probiotics and prebiotics to target the gut–brain axis in Parkinson's disease.

Alterations in gut microbial composition can precede the onset of depressive symptoms, yet the dietary and microbial signals that modulate brain function remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus alongside lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations. Participants reporting high intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber showed higher BDNF expression in peripheral blood and attenuated anxiety-like behavior scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation into mice reproduced the depressive phenotype, with decreased Bdnf transcripts in the hippocampus and altered tryptophan metabolism. Treatment with probiotic supplementation restored serotonin turnover and normalized IL-6 and TNF-α expression. Random forest modeling identified Bacteroides and Prevotella as taxa distinguishing responders from non-responders in this clinical cohort. These findings suggest that diet-microbiome interactions regulate neurotrophic and inflammatory pathways relevant to depression, supporting targeted metagenomic profiling and dietary intervention as complementary strategies.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of gut microbiota–brain signaling, yet their association with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains inconsistently reproduced. In a cohort of 128 adults, we quantified fecal Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Lactobacillus using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and measured circulating interleukin-6 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire, and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation was recorded. Using multivariable linear regression, lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was associated with higher depressive symptom scores (β = −0.31, P = 0.008), independent of age, sex, body mass index, and omega-3 use. Mediation analysis suggested that interleukin-6 explained 18% of this association. Probiotic supplementation did not modify the relationship, whereas higher dietary fiber intake attenuated it. These findings support a pathway in which gut microbial composition, particularly F. prausnitzii depletion, contributes to MDD-related inflammation and highlight fiber- and probiotic-focused interventions as candidate strategies for depression.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide translocate across the intestinal epithelium to shape hippocampal plasticity, anxiety-like behavior, and depression severity in mice and adults. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with metabolic syndrome received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented yogurt or the same diet plus probiotic and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal microbiota revealed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus relative abundance, alongside reduced Bacteroides, only in supplemented participants. Linear mixed models showed that these microbial shifts correlated with lower interleukin-6 and cortisol, improved depressive symptoms, and greater prefrontal cortex N-acetylaspartate concentrations. SSRI use did not modify the associations. At baseline, participants with higher abdominal obesity and insulin resistance harbored lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance; after intervention, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice recapitulated reduced anxiety-like behavior and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that diet and supplement interventions targeting the gut microbiome may complement psychotropic drugs in gut-brain axis disorders.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that signal across the gut microbiome–brain axis, yet the extent to which these metabolites causally influence depression remains uncertain. We profiled fecal SCFAs and gut microbiota composition in adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Mendelian randomization was applied to publicly available genome-wide association summary statistics to test bidirectional associations between SCFA production and depressive symptoms. Lower butyrate and propionate concentrations were associated with higher depression severity, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and depressive symptoms. Mendelian randomization supported a protective effect of genetically proxied Butyricicoccus on depression but not the reverse. These findings position microbial SCFAs as plausible mediators of diet–microbiome–brain communication and suggest that interventions increasing fermentable fiber intake may complement existing antidepressant treatments. Because butyrate production is modifiable through diet, targeting the gut microbiome may offer a tractable strategy for depression prevention.

Microbiota-derived metabolites produced in the gut can influence brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the clinical translation of this gut-brain signaling remains uneven. In patients with major depressive disorder, reduced microbiota diversity and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles have been reported, alongside increased lipopolysaccharide translocation and neuroinflammation. Preclinical models using fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed donors into rodents reproduce anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors, implicating gut microbiota as a causal contributor rather than a passive biomarker. Interventions that target the microbiome—including probiotics, prebiotics, and fermented foods—may modulate tryptophan metabolism, serotonin availability, and gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling. However, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic profiling reveal substantial interindividual variability, and randomized controlled trials of probiotic supplementation in depression have produced mixed results. Stratifying patients by baseline microbiota composition, inflammatory markers, and diet may identify responders to psychobiotic formulations. These findings support a model in which gut microbiota-derived metabolites tune brain circuits, and they argue for mechanism-based biomarker-guided trials rather than broad probiotic use.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) sustain hippocampal BDNF expression and restrain microglial synaptic pruning, yet how dietary fiber insufficiency disrupts this gut-brain axis remains unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with microbiota from humans consuming low- or high-fiber diets and assessed cognitive impairment after 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed that low-fiber microbiota depleted Bacteroidetes and Faecalibacterium while expanding Proteobacteria; PERMANOVA confirmed distinct community structures. Morris water maze testing showed impaired spatial memory, accompanied by reduced butyrate and propionate in feces and serum. RNA sequencing of hippocampus identified downregulation of Bdnf, Arc, and Zif268; weighted gene co-expression network analysis linked these changes to neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate mediated 38% of the cognitive effect. Fecal microbiota transplantation from low-fiber donors reproduced cognitive deficits, whereas butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings position gut microbiota-SCFA signaling as a modifiable determinant of hippocampal function.

Supplementation with the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus during early life reduces anxiety-like behavior in mice and reshapes gut microbiota in a vagal-dependent manner. To test whether these effects require an intact gut-brain axis, we compared male C57BL/6 mice receiving the probiotic or vehicle, with or without subdiaphragmatic vagotomy. Behavioral testing revealed that the probiotic decreased immobility in the forced swim test and increased exploratory behavior in the open field. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that the probiotic increased Lactobacillus abundance and shifted gut microbiota composition. Notably, these microbial shifts were accompanied by higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces and reduced gut barrier dysfunction. In the hippocampus, BDNF expression and serotonin turnover were elevated, whereas corticosterone was lower. These changes were abolished by vagotomy. Data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models, PERMANOVA, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Our findings indicate that early-life probiotic supplementation modulates brain and behavior through vagal and microbial pathways, supporting targeted probiotic strategies for stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone and may modify Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk. In a human cohort of older adults with mild cognitive impairment, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, targeted metabolomics, and cognitive testing. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE genotype showed that higher Faecalibacterium abundance tracked with greater butyrate and slower decline in cognitive impairment. In a randomized subset, inulin or placebo was administered for 12 weeks; inulin expanded Bifidobacterium and butyrate-producing bacteria, lowered inflammatory cytokines, and improved cognitive deficits. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial shifts accounted for part of the cognitive benefit. Mechanistically, butyrate promoted occludin expression and suppressed NF-κB signaling in intestinal epithelium, while microbial lipopolysaccharide translocation fell. In gnotobiotic mice transplanted with post-intervention microbiota, inulin-associated communities reduced amyloid-beta burden and microglial cytokines. These findings position prebiotic fiber as a plausible adjunct for AD prevention, though larger trials are needed.

Inulin supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and increases short-chain fatty acid production, but whether it modifies APOE-linked Alzheimer's disease risk remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 120 older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment received inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified gut microbiota taxa; APOE genotype was determined at baseline. Linear mixed models assessed changes in hippocampal volume, BDNF methylation, and interleukin-6. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and elevated butyrate compared with placebo. Among APOE4 carriers, inulin attenuated cognitive decline and reduced interleukin-6; no effect appeared in non-carriers. BDNF methylation decreased in the treatment arm and correlated with microbiota shifts. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein fell only in carriers, suggesting reduced intestinal permeability. Baseline microbiota diversity predicted response, and Akkermansia abundance correlated with improved cognitive scores. These findings suggest that inulin may exert APOE-dependent neuroprotective effects through gut microbiota-brain signaling, warranting larger trials.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis can precede Parkinson's disease motor symptoms by years, implying that enteric signals reach the central nervous system through vagal and immune pathways. In 148 adults, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and measured short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. APOE4 carriers exhibited lower Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced butyrate than non-carriers (P=0.006, Mann-Whitney U test). Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Bacteroides and Prevotella as discriminators of high versus low SCFA profiles. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium abundance accounted for 18% of the association between APOE4 and cognitive decline. In mice, oral gavage of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii restored butyrate and attenuated neuroinflammation. Random forest classification achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 for separating APOE4 carriers from non-carriers. These findings in humans position microbial metabolites as modifiable contributors to neurodegeneration and motivate fecal microbiota transplantation or prebiotic interventions targeting Faecalibacterium.

metadata.abstract: Consumption of a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiota and promotes neuroinflammation, yet the microbial signals linking diet to anxiety and depression remain poorly defined. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with metabolic syndrome received either a probiotic supplement (Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis) or placebo for 12 weeks while continuing their habitual diet. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA confirmed distinct microbial community structures between groups. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, butyrate, and depressive symptoms. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo. These changes correlated with decreased IL-6 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly accounted for the improvement in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota through probiotic supplementation may attenuate neuroinflammation and improve mood in patients with metabolic syndrome.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract modulates brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and disrupted gut microbiota–brain signaling is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder and anxiety. In mice exposed to chronic corticosterone, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated depressive-like behavior and restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Bacteroides and decreased Bifidobacterium; PERMANOVA confirmed separation by treatment (R2 = 0.18, p = 0.002). Serum interleukin-6 and cortisol correlated with gut microbiota composition according to Spearman correlation analysis, while TLR4 and IL6 expression in the prefrontal cortex was elevated. Baseline microbial diversity and short-chain fatty acid profiles predicted treatment response in a linear mixed-effects model. These findings suggest that targeting the microbiome with prebiotics or probiotics may complement selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and other antidepressants in patients with depression, although randomized controlled trials are needed to establish causality and define optimal strains, doses, and treatment duration.

Short-chain fatty acids generated by gut microbiota serve as key signals along the gut-brain axis, influencing intestinal barrier integrity, brain immune tone, and neurotransmitter synthesis. In rodent models of chronic stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing has linked reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance to depressive-like behavior and lower BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into germ-free mice reproduces anxiety-like phenotypes, whereas probiotic supplementation or prebiotic fiber restores short-chain fatty acid pools and normalizes BDNF and IL-6 transcription. Metagenomic profiling further reveals that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii depletion correlates with elevated kynurenine and lipopolysaccharide translocation, implicating microbial composition in neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial communities through psychobiotics or microbiota-directed therapies may modulate BDNF-dependent plasticity and serotonin signaling, offering a tractable strategy for stress-related psychiatric disorders. However, causality remains difficult to establish because correlation analysis alone cannot disentangle microbial effects from diet, medication, and host genetic variation.

Consumption of ultra-processed foods rich in emulsifiers and non-caloric sweeteners has been linked to cognitive decline, yet the mediating role of the gut microbiota remains unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 180 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a probiotic consortium (n=90) or placebo (n=90) for 12 weeks while maintaining habitual diets. We used linear mixed-effects models to assess changes in Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, fecal microbial composition, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and improved cognitive assessment scores compared with placebo (mean difference, 1.8 points; 95% CI, 0.6–3.0). At baseline and week 12, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that probiotic receipt was associated with higher microbial diversity and reduced Proteobacteria.
