Changes in microbiota correlated with improved cognitive test performance and higher BDNF expression. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through probiotics may attenuate neuroinflammation and slow cognitive decline, though effects of background diet require further study.

Disruption of the gut microbiota, especially reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, tracks with age-related cognitive decline and altered short-chain fatty acid production in older adults. To test whether microbial shifts predict mild cognitive impairment (MCI), we profiled fecal communities from participants with MCI and cognitively intact controls using 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Random forest models and Spearman correlation related microbial taxa to serum lipopolysaccharide, hippocampal BDNF, and cognitive scores. MCI participants showed lower microbial diversity, depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila, and enrichment of Escherichia coli. These shifts correlated with elevated lipopolysaccharide and poorer hippocampal function. Fecal microbiota transplantation from MCI donors into antibiotic-treated mice increased neuroinflammatory cytokines and induced memory impairment, whereas probiotic supplementation partially restored microbial balance. BDNF and JNK signaling in the gut-brain axis may mediate these effects. These findings suggest that trans-kingdom microbiome signatures could aid risk stratification and that targeting gut bacteria may slow cognitive decline.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and bile acid metabolites shape central nervous system function, yet the extent to which host genetic variation modifies these interactions remains unclear. Using Mendelian randomization and weighted gene co-expression network analysis, we integrated human fecal metagenomes with brain imaging and plasma metabolomics. Higher abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was associated with increased butyrate production and altered hippocampal connectivity. This association was strengthened in carriers of APOE ε4 alleles, a known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. In mice fed a high-fiber diet, butyrate supplementation recapitulated the connectivity changes and reduced neuroinflammation. Conversely, antibiotic treatment depleted butyrate-producing taxa and attenuated these effects. Longitudinal sampling showed that butyrate levels predicted depressive-like behavior in mice, and 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed Lachnospiraceae depletion after vancomycin. These effects were absent in BDNF knockout mice, implicating BDNF signaling in microbiota-brain communication. Our results suggest that APOE genotype and microbial metabolites jointly influence brain network organization, providing a mechanistic link between dietary fiber, gut microbiota, and cognitive decline.

Inulin-type fructans supplementation reshapes gut microbial communities and reduces depression-like behaviors in mice, yet whether these benefits extend to patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 60 adults with MDD received either inulin or placebo for 8 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomics profiled microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and raised fecal butyrate concentrations relative to placebo. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and cortisol levels and improved Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate production partly accounted for the clinical improvement. In parallel, inulin increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus of mice exposed to chronic stress. Baseline gut microbiota composition did not predict response, but Faecalibacterium abundance at week 4 correlated with symptom reduction. Our findings indicate that inulin-type fructans may serve as an adjunctive dietary supplement for MDD by targeting the gut-brain axis, though larger trials are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiome along the gut-brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the microbial and metabolic signatures that distinguish patients from healthy controls remain incompletely defined. We analyzed fecal microbiota from participants with mild cognitive impairment and AD using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, complemented by untargeted metabolomics of serum and feces. Multivariate analysis and random forest models identified Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Bifidobacterium as differentially abundant, together with altered bile acids, tryptophan, and short-chain fatty acids. These changes correlated with amyloid-beta burden and inflammatory cytokines. Notably, Bifidobacterium abundance was inversely associated with cognitive decline, while tryptophan metabolites predicted AD status with an AUC of 0.84. APOE4 carriers showed stronger microbial shifts than noncarriers. These signatures were validated in an independent cohort and associated with neuroinflammation. Our findings suggest that gut microbial dysbiosis and metabolite shifts may serve as noninvasive biomarkers and therapeutic targets in AD.

Supplementation with dietary fiber reshapes the gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production engages BDNF signaling remains unclear. In APP/PS1 mice and patients with mild cognitive impairment, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and mediation analysis to test whether inulin increases Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances, elevates butyrate in the colon, and restores BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Baseline gut microbiota composition differed between APP/PS1 mice and wild-type littermates, with lower Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in APP/PS1 mice. Inulin raised butyrate and Bifidobacterium in both mice and participants, and these changes correlated with improved cognitive performance. BDNF and GPR43 transcripts increased in the hippocampus, while IL-6 and TNF-α decreased. These effects were abolished by antibiotic treatment. Mediation models indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium jointly explained 42% of the inulin effect on BDNF. These findings position dietary fiber as a plausible gut-brain modulator in early AD.

Supplementation with probiotics and inulin reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in adults with mild cognitive impairment. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants received a probiotic blend plus inulin or placebo while consuming yogurt daily. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased, and butyrate concentrations rose. Plasma IL-6 and TNF-alpha decreased. Cognitive scores improved, with a standardized mean difference of 0.45 (95% CI, 0.12–0.78). Hippocampus volume and BDNF expression also increased. A mixed-effects model confirmed that changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with reduced neuroinflammation and better memory. In mice fed a high-fat diet, the same probiotic formulation reduced anxiety-like behavior and depressive-like behavior, increased serotonin in the prefrontal cortex, and normalized corticosterone levels. Fecal microbiota transfer from treated donors to mice reproduced the cognitive benefits, implicating Lactobacillus-derived metabolites. These findings suggest that probiotic and prebiotic supplementation, alongside fermented foods, may modulate the gut-brain axis and slow cognitive decline. Larger trials using 16S rRNA sequencing and meta-analysis are needed.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to depression and anxiety, yet the mediating microbial signals remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, we profiled fecal communities from adults with major depressive disorder and matched controls. Reduced Lachnospiraceae and Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with lower short-chain fatty acid production and elevated neuroinflammation. In mice, colonization with depression-associated microbiota increased hippocampal BDNF methylation and despair-like behavior. Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids plus probiotics restored microbial diversity, reduced interleukin-6, and normalized BDNF expression. These effects were accompanied by increased butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid in plasma. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 31% of the behavioral improvement. Baseline gut microbiota composition predicted treatment response with an area under the curve of 0.78. Our findings support a tractable microbiota-gut-brain axis pathway in which omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and probiotics may attenuate depression-related neuroimmune and BDNF alterations. Further randomized trials with shotgun metagenomic sequencing are needed.

Microbial tryptophan catabolites act as key intercellular signals along the gut-brain axis, yet how dietary fiber availability reshapes this dialogue in metabolic syndrome remains poorly defined. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and fed them high-fat, low-fiber diets or fermentable fiber-supplemented diets. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that fiber supplementation increased butyrate and indole-3-propionate in the colon and reduced neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that F. prausnitzii abundance explained 31% of the fiber-associated decrease in IL-1β expression. In participants with mild cognitive impairment, higher dietary fiber intake correlated with greater gut microbial diversity and better executive function, although Mendelian randomization did not support causality. Notably, fiber withdrawal reversed these microbial shifts within one week, and permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed diet-driven separation of microbial communities (R² = 0.24, p = 0.001). These findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable determinant of microbial neuroactive metabolite production and suggest that interventions targeting the gut microbiome warrant testing for cognitive decline.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence brain function through immune, endocrine, and vagal pathways. In adults with major depressive disorder, lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance correlates with reduced butyrate and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a region critical for mood regulation. To test whether this axis is modifiable, 120 participants were randomized to a fermented food-rich diet or usual care for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics and fecal metabolomics quantified microbial community structure and SCFA output; linear mixed models assessed changes in depressive symptoms and BDNF methylation. The intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium diversity, raised butyrate by 28%, and reduced depression scores compared with control. BDNF promoter methylation decreased in the intervention group and correlated inversely with butyrate. These changes were independent of baseline depression severity. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 85%. These findings suggest that fermented food and fiber-driven microbiota changes may modulate BDNF-related plasticity, offering a tractable target for depression.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life calibrates the developing brain, but the molecular relays linking gut microbiota to stress-related disorders remain unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we tested whether Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium-enriched microbiota from healthy donors alters Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Colonized mice showed elevated butyrate and propionate, reduced corticosterone, and lower Tnf and Il6 transcripts. These changes coincided with increased Bdnf exon IV and Gabra1 expression, and with fewer anxiety-like behaviors. Metagenomic sequencing further linked these phenotypes to Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. In patients with major depressive disorder, a parallel cohort showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. Our findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids act as epigenetic and neurotrophic regulators, positioning prebiotic fiber or psychobiotics as candidate interventions for stress-related psychopathology.

Supplementation with prebiotic oligosaccharides can reshape gut microbiota and alter BDNF expression in limbic circuits, linking intestinal ecology to affective behavior. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild depression received either galacto-oligosaccharides plus polydextrose or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances increased in the supplemented group, accompanied by elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations and reduced cortisol awakening response. Quantitative PCR and 16S rRNA sequencing showed that changes in microbial composition correlated with BDNF mRNA and IL-6 mRNA in peripheral blood. Participants receiving prebiotics reported lower anxiety scores and improved depressive symptoms relative to placebo. Mediation analysis suggested that Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate production partially explained the BDNF-related improvement. Stool metabolomics further revealed increased indole-3-propionic acid, a microbial-derived metabolite previously linked to BDNF upregulation in the hippocampus. These findings indicate that targeted prebiotic interventions may modulate microbiota-gut-brain signaling and neurotrophic gene expression, offering a tractable adjunct for mood disorders.

Supplementation with probiotics and fermented foods reshapes gut microbiota composition and may attenuate depression- and anxiety-like behaviors through gut-brain axis signaling. We tested whether a 12-week intervention combining Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and a high-fiber diet enriched with inulin altered short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF expression in mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium abundance, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified butyrate and propionate. Behavioral outcomes were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model, and associations between microbial taxa and cytokine levels were assessed by Spearman correlation with false discovery rate correction. Randomization was stratified by baseline body weight and corticosterone; mice received antibiotics or vehicle to deplete gut microbiota, confirming that microbial colonization was necessary for the behavioral effect. The combination, but not either alone, reduced immobility in the forced swim test and lowered interleukin-6 in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that probiotics plus fermentable fiber may mitigate stress-related disorders by promoting butyrate-producing bacteria and BDNF signaling.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract in early life calibrates hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression, yet how gut microbiota contributes to affective disorders remains unresolved. In germ-free mice, faecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder produced anxiety-like behaviour and altered serotonin turnover, while probiotic treatment lowered interleukin-6 and corticosterone. Amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and shotgun metagenomics show that short-chain fatty acid-producing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium are depleted in depression, whereas Enterobacteriaceae expand. These shifts correlate with reduced butyrate in faeces and increased lipopolysaccharide translocation, suggesting that microbial metabolites modulate vagal afferents and neuroinflammation. In adults, high-fat diets reduce microbial diversity, whereas fermentable fibre increases short-chain fatty acid production and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance; these changes associate with sleep disturbances and low-grade inflammation. Dietary fibre and psychobiotics may restore gut microbial ecology, but randomised controlled trials with 16S rRNA-based endpoints are needed to translate these findings into clinical recommendations.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder is accompanied by reduced bile acid deconjugation and blunted FXR and TGR5 signaling in the colon and hippocampus. This shift correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acids and serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that Bacteroides and Lactobacillus were depleted in patients, whereas Clostridium species were expanded. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into mice increased lipopolysaccharide translocation, activated hippocampal neuroinflammation, and induced depressive-like behavior. Germ-free mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota showed similar behavioral deficits. These effects were reversed by ursodeoxycholic acid or GW4064, but not by SBI-115, a TGR5 antagonist. RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue revealed that BDNF and NR3C1 were downregulated, while IL1B and TNF were upregulated. These changes implicated IL6 and COX2 in the neuroinflammatory response. Western blotting confirmed reduced FXR protein and increased RELA phosphorylation. Collectively, microbiota-dependent bile acid pools regulate FXR-TGR5 balance, linking dysbiosis of the gut microbiota to neuroinflammation and depression. These data position FXR and TGR5 as tractable nodes for microbiota-directed interventions in depression.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate BDNF, GPR41, and GPR43 signaling in the brain, linking gut microbiota to depression and anxiety. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a Mediterranean diet enriched with fermented foods or a high-saturated-fat diet; stool Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, plasma butyrate, and tryptophan metabolites were measured using 16S rRNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. The Mediterranean diet group showed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, reduced lipopolysaccharide, and lower depressive symptoms; mediation analysis attributed 31% of symptom improvement to butyrate and BDNF methylation. Probiotic supplementation further increased butyrate only in participants carrying the FUT2 secretor allele. In germ-free mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated these metabolic and behavioral changes, while antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings suggest that diet-microbiome interactions shape BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity and may inform precision psychobiotic strategies for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbiota fermentation of dietary fiber modulate central nervous system immune signaling and may slow age-related cognitive decline. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with flavonoid-rich foods or a control diet; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled fecal microbiota, while cognitive testing assessed memory and executive function. The intervention increased butyrate-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, and raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations. These shifts correlated with improved cognitive scores and reduced inflammatory cytokines. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial diversity and butyrate partly explained the cognitive benefit. Responders also showed lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, indicating reduced endotoxemia. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders reproduced the short-chain fatty acid increases and behavioral changes, whereas antibiotic depletion attenuated them. These findings support a causal role for gut microbiome-brain signaling in neurodegeneration and suggest that flavonoid-rich diets may complement conventional treatment.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) maintain intestinal barrier integrity and temper neuroinflammation, yet their causal contribution to Parkinson's disease (PD) remains contested. In a mouse model of PD induced by 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), we compared germ-free mice colonized with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii or Akkermansia muciniphila against conventionalized control mice. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified microbial community structure and butyrate in striatum and plasma. Colonization with F. prausnitzii increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, reduced tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) transcripts, and attenuated dopaminergic neuron loss. Linear mixed-effects models adjusting for batch and sex showed that butyrate mediated 42% of the protective effect. Dietary fiber supplementation recapitulated these benefits, whereas vancomycin abolished them. In patients with PD, lower fecal butyrate and F. prausnitzii abundance tracked with worse motor scores. These findings position gut microbiota-SCFA signaling as a modifiable axis in PD and support fiber-rich diets as adjunctive microbiome-targeted intervention.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that engage GPR41 and HDAC signaling to shape hippocampal plasticity and affective behavior. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation in mice, we found that high-fat diet consumption reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate in the gut, and increased depression-like behavior. These changes were accompanied by decreased BDNF expression and elevated IL-6 in the prefrontal cortex. Vagotomy attenuated the behavioral effects, implicating the vagus nerve. In patients, Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher gut microbiota diversity and lower anxiety scores. Probiotic supplementation restored BDNF and SCFA levels in mice, while fluoxetine produced overlapping but distinct transcriptional responses. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated the relationship between microbiota composition and depression-like behavior. These findings position GPR41-dependent SCFA signaling as a mechanistic link between diet, gut microbes, and mood disorders, and support targeting gut microbiota in patients with depression.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet predicts higher circulating short-chain fatty acids and lower depressive symptoms, but whether this relationship is causal remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with subthreshold depression received either a prebiotic inulin supplement plus dietary counseling or counseling alone. We assessed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal butyrate, serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and depression severity. Linear mixed models tested group-by-time interactions. The inulin group showed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated butyrate, and greater reduction in depressive symptoms than controls. Changes in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii correlated with BDNF increases and depression improvement. Effects were independent of body mass index and baseline serotonin, and mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 22% of the intervention effect. These findings suggest that combining Mediterranean-style eating with a prebiotic supplement may engage the gut-brain axis to reduce depression risk, though larger trials with shotgun metagenomics and metabolomics are needed.

Gut microbiota depletion with antibiotics exaggerates neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aged mice, whereas recolonization with Bacteroides fragilis restores short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF expression in the hippocampus. To define the responsible pathways, we used 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 editing of Ffar2 in mice. Ffar2 deletion abolished Bacteroides fragilis-mediated glucagon-like peptide-1 secretion and prevented microglial activation in the brain. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower Bacteroides abundance correlated with reduced BDNF and elevated C-reactive protein, and a random forest classifier distinguished cases from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84. Dietary fiber supplementation increased butyrate and BDNF in a mouse model, but not in Ffar2-deficient mice. Collectively, these data indicate that Ffar2-dependent microbiota sensing couples metabolite availability to brain immune homeostasis, and that early-life microbial colonization may shape brain immune development, suggesting that fiber or probiotic interventions may mitigate depression.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that can attenuate neuroinflammation and preserve blood-brain barrier function, but whether targeted nutritional strategies translate into cognitive benefit in older adults remains unresolved. We conducted a 24-week randomized controlled trial in 140 participants with mild cognitive impairment, comparing a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable fiber plus omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation against a low-fiber control diet. Gut microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and butyrate concentrations were quantified in stool. Linear mixed-effects models assessed changes in cognitive function and systemic inflammation. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced C-reactive protein compared with control. Baseline gut microbiota diversity did not modify these associations. Greater Bifidobacterium enrichment correlated with improved executive function and episodic memory. These findings suggest that combining dietary fiber with omega-3 supplementation may modulate the microbiome-gut-brain axis and support cognitive function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment.

Depletion of Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae in the gut microbiota correlates with reduced butyrate and elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma, a pattern repeatedly observed in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, faecal metagenomics, and targeted metabolomics in patients and mice, we found that LRRK2 and GBA variants modified the association between microbial composition and neuroinflammation. Mendelian randomization supported a protective effect of butyrate on PD risk, whereas mediation analysis indicated that lipopolysaccharide-driven systemic inflammation accounted for part of the substantia nigra vulnerability. In mouse models, probiotic supplementation restored Lachnospiraceae abundance, increased butyrate, reduced TNF-α and IL-6, and limited SNCA aggregation. Random-effects meta-analysis across cohorts confirmed that lower butyrate was associated with worse motor severity. The effect remained after adjusting for antibiotic exposure, dietary fiber intake, and false discovery rate. These findings position the gut microbiota as a modifiable contributor to PD and suggest that probiotics or butyrate-targeted interventions may complement levodopa therapy.

Short-term dietary EPA supplementation reshapes the gut microbiota and lowers microglial inflammatory activation in APP/PS1 mice, implicating the gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's disease pathology. To examine this, 13–14-month-old APP/PS1 and wild-type littermates received control chow or 0.3% EPA for 3 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, while hippocampal and retinal tissues were assessed by flow cytometry, RT-qPCR, and lipid mediator profiling. EPA increased Firmicutes and butyrate-producing bacteria but decreased Bacteroidetes and LPS-producing Gram-negative bacteria. In transgenic mice, MHCII expression and MHCII-positive microglia were reduced in the hippocampus and retina, alongside lower plasma arachidonic acid-derived 5-HETE and AEA. Linear regression associated butyrate-producing bacteria with decreased MHCII and cytokine signals, whereas permutational multivariate analysis of variance showed no genotype effect on overall community structure. These data suggest that EPA may dampen neuroinflammation through microbiome-dependent mechanisms, though longer interventions are needed to test effects on AD progression in this pilot.

Metabolites generated by the gut microbiota from fermentable dietary fiber can influence central BDNF expression and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity, linking the gut microbiome to stress-related psychiatric disorders. To test whether this pathway is modifiable, we colonized gnotobiotic mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum and fed them either a control diet or one enriched with inulin and galacto-oligosaccharides. 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed stable engraftment, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified cecal short-chain fatty acids. Mice receiving the fiber supplement showed higher butyrate and propionate concentrations, reduced hippocampal Il6 mRNA, and increased Bdnf transcripts relative to controls. These changes coincided with lower corticosterone after acute restraint and fewer anxiety-like behaviors in open field and elevated plus maze tests. In healthy adults, a parallel open-label pilot using probiotic supplementation showed similar directional shifts in fecal microbiota composition, though BDNF changes were not significant. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber and probiotics may engage gut-brain signaling through microbial short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF-related pathways, warranting larger randomized trials.

Inulin supplementation restores gut microbial diversity and reduces depressive-like behavior in mice fed a high-fat diet, yet the mechanisms linking these effects to central brain circuits remain unclear. We tested whether inulin alters microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and vagus nerve signaling in mice receiving either a high-fat diet or standard chow. After 8 weeks, 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed elevated butyrate and propionate in feces. Behavioral tests demonstrated reduced anxiety-like behavior and cognitive impairment. Vagotomy abolished these benefits, and RNA sequencing of hippocampus identified Bdnf and Nrf2 as mediators. Correlation analysis linked butyrate levels with Bdnf expression and depressive-like behavior. In a parallel human cohort, baseline fecal butyrate correlated inversely with perceived stress and positively with prefrontal glutamate. These findings indicate that inulin ameliorates high-fat diet-induced neuropsychiatric dysfunction through a gut microbiota-SCFA-vagus nerve axis, supporting targeted prebiotic interventions.

Dietary resistant starch supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and elevates butyrate availability, a metabolic route increasingly linked to hippocampal plasticity and mood regulation. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, eight weeks of resistant starch increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the gut lumen, and normalized depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test and sucrose preference test. Specifically, resistant starch increased butyrate in the colon and acetate in blood, known modulators of enteroendocrine signaling. These changes coincided with restored BDNF and GPR43 expression in the prefrontal cortex and reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha levels. 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed that resistant starch selectively enriched Roseburia and Faecalibacterium, taxa capable of butyrate synthesis. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced the behavioral and BDNF changes, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Together, these findings indicate that resistant starch promotes butyrate-dependent gut-brain signaling and may offer a tractable strategy for stress-related disorders.

Depletion of butyrate-producing bacteria within the gut microbiota is now recognized as an early feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), preceding neuroinflammation and loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons. To test whether microbial butyrate signals through GPR43 to constrain neuroinflammation, we colonized germ-free SNCA-overexpressing mice with Roseburia intestinalis or administered sodium butyrate. Microbial and metabolomic profiling used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics of colon, serum, and striatum. In patients with PD, serum butyrate correlated inversely with GPR43 expression in blood and with motor impairment compared with healthy controls. Correlations were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex. In mice, R. intestinalis and butyrate restored GPR43 signaling, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF), and attenuated dopaminergic neurodegeneration; these effects were abolished in Gpr43-deficient mice. These findings identify a microbiota-GPR43 axis that links butyrate availability to neuroinflammation and suggest that faecal microbiota transplantation or butyrate supplementation warrants evaluation in patients with PD.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet reshapes gut microbiota composition and elevates lipopolysaccharide translocation, a process linked to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In mice fed a high-fat diet, Bacteroides abundance fell while Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium expanded, paralleling reduced butyrate in the colon and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics of caecal contents revealed that secondary bile acids and trimethylamine N-oxide correlated with BDNF methylation. Supplementation with inulin, a fermentable dietary fiber, restored butyrate levels, increased Akkermansia muciniphila, and normalized BDNF expression, effects abolished in GPR43-deficient mice. Faecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-fed donors into germ-free mice reproduced the BDNF increase, whereas antibiotic treatment depleted Akkermansia and reversed the effect. In participants with metabolic syndrome, higher fiber intake was associated with greater microbial diversity and lower circulating interleukin-6; mediation analysis attributed 22% of this association to butyrate. These findings position BDNF and GPR43 as molecular nodes through which diet and gut microbiota jointly influence brain function.

Dietary patterns that enrich gut microbiota with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can attenuate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, but host APOE4 status may modify these benefits. In a randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet or a Western-style diet for 12 weeks, with or without omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified in plasma. The Mediterranean-style diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate levels, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α. Omega-3 supplementation further improved microbial diversity only in APOE4 non-carriers. Mediation analysis indicated that gut microbiota changes accounted for 31% of the diet-related improvement in mild cognitive impairment severity. In parallel, mice colonized with microbiota from responders showed reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation and elevated BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that diet and omega-3 interact with APOE4 to shape gut microbiota-brain signaling, offering a tractable target for Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that shape hippocampal function and emotional behavior, but whether these effects translate to depressive symptoms in humans remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with subthreshold depression received either a high-fermentable-fiber diet or a habitual Western diet; gut microbiota composition, butyrate levels, and depressive symptoms were assessed. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia in the fiber group. Using linear mixed-effects models, the fiber group showed greater reduction in depressive symptoms than controls. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Faecalibacterium abundance partially mediated this improvement. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed increased prefrontal cortex activation to positive stimuli. Changes in microbial diversity correlated with anxiety scores, and bootstrapped confidence intervals confirmed robustness. No significant adverse events were reported, and adherence remained high. These findings suggest that fermentable fiber interventions may improve depressive symptoms through microbiota-SCFA signaling, supporting dietary strategies for depression.

Twelve weeks of inulin-type fructan supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and lowered depressive symptoms in adults with irritable bowel syndrome, according to a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Eighty-four participants completed the trial; baseline depression and microbiota did not differ between inulin and placebo arms. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing; linear mixed-effects models tested time-by-treatment interactions, and mediation analysis quantified indirect effects through short-chain fatty acids. At week 12, inulin increased butyrate and acetate and reduced anxiety scores; PERMANOVA showed distinct microbial community composition between arms. Changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with reduced depression severity (r = −0.38, p = 0.02), but not with BDNF or hippocampal measures. Random forest classification identified Bifidobacterium and butyrate as top predictors of mood response. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with prebiotic fiber may improve mood via microbial metabolites, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Accumulating evidence links gut microbiota dysbiosis to Parkinson's disease (PD) progression, yet causality and metabolic mediators remain unresolved. We profiled fecal microbiota and serum metabolites in patients with PD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Microbial community differences were assessed with PERMANOVA and Random Forest, with false discovery rate correction. PD subjects showed reduced Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia and elevated Enterobacteriaceae. Trimethylamine N-oxide and short-chain fatty acids correlated with motor severity, while lipopolysaccharide was higher in patients. In mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, nigral neuroinflammation, alpha-synucleinopathy, and microglial activation increased relative to controls. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into mice recapitulated motor deficits. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of the association between Roseburia and PD severity. Levodopa response was associated with Prevotella abundance and bile acid profiles. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-derived metabolites contribute to PD pathogenesis and may inform probiotic or microbiota-targeted interventions.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the gut can modulate brain circuits implicated in depression, but whether fermented food intake alters this relationship in adults is unclear. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants with mild depressive symptoms received a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or continued their usual diet. Fecal shotgun metagenomic sequencing and circulating cytokine assays were completed at baseline and endpoint. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations among dietary group, gut microbiota composition, butyrate-producing taxa, and depressive symptoms. The intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced IL-6 and C-reactive protein concentrations. These shifts correlated with lower depression scores and greater microbial diversity; however, associations with IL-6 did not survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Butyrate-producing bacteria remained linked to improved anxiety scores. Baseline dietary fiber intake modified the effect: participants in the highest tertile showed greater increases in Faecalibacterium and butyrate. These findings suggest that fermented food-enriched Mediterranean diet patterns may influence depressive symptoms through microbiota-related pathways, although confirmatory trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) sustain intestinal barrier integrity and tune microglia activity along the vagus nerve, yet whether their depletion causally contributes to major depressive disorder remains unresolved. We tested whether inulin or probiotic supplementation could reverse depressive-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic corticosterone. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances, lower gut microbiome diversity, and diminished butyrate production. Supplementation restored Lactobacillus relative abundance, increased butyrate, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In patients with major depressive disorder (n=42), baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with BDNF serum levels and depression severity; PERMANOVA indicated significant group differences. Plasma interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α were elevated in patients with low butyrate, and linear regression linked these inflammatory markers to BDNF and depression severity. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotic interventions may modulate the gut microbiome–BDNF axis, though fecal microbiota transplantation from responders did not fully transfer benefits. Further randomized controlled trials are needed.

Disruption of gut microbiota–brain signaling is increasingly linked to depressive symptoms, yet whether probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial, adults with major depressive disorder received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and PERMANOVA tested community-level differences. Probiotic-treated participants showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and reduced Escherichia-Shigella. These shifts correlated with higher fecal short-chain fatty acids, lower inflammatory cytokines, and enriched tryptophan metabolism. To test causality, mice underwent fecal microbiota transplantation from patients; the probiotic regimen restored hippocampal BDNF expression and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that changes in Bifidobacterium abundance mediated the improvement in depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics may offer an adjunctive strategy for depression, though larger clinical trials are needed.

Reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and short-chain fatty acid output in the gut accompany major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether this association is causal or confounded by diet remains unresolved. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 428 adults, including 176 with MDD, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, antidepressant use, and Mediterranean diet adherence revealed that F. prausnitzii was inversely associated with depression severity (β = −0.21, P = 0.003). Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of this association. In mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD patients, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression fell in the hippocampus, while interleukin-6 rose. Supplementation with inulin-rich chicory root restored F. prausnitzii, increased butyrate, and normalized BDNF in mice. Notably, Mantel tests linked microbial composition to serum butyrate and BDNF expression in patients. These findings position F. prausnitzii and butyrate as tractable targets in the gut microbiota and support dietary fiber interventions for MDD.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–BDNF signaling axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the dietary and microbial determinants of this interaction remain poorly defined. In a cohort of adults with MDD and healthy controls, we combined shotgun metagenomics, fecal metabolomics, and serum cytokine profiling. Consumption of a Western-style diet was associated with reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower circulating tryptophan metabolites, whereas probiotic supplementation correlated with higher BDNF expression and attenuated interleukin-6 levels. Participants with MDD showed decreased gut microbial diversity and altered FKBP5 methylation in peripheral blood compared with controls. A random forest model integrating microbial taxa and host genes involved in tryptophan metabolism distinguished MDD patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84. Notably, BDNF expression inversely correlated with the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio and with Bacteroides abundance. These findings suggest that diet and probiotics may modulate the microbiota–BDNF axis, offering a tractable target for adjunctive depression treatment.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a modifier of stress-related depression and Alzheimer's disease (AD). In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either Lactobacillus helveticus plus Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum cortisol, interleukin-6, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, while mediation analysis explored whether microbial shifts explained clinical improvement. Probiotic-treated participants showed greater reductions in depressive symptoms and cortisol than placebo, alongside increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, higher BDNF expression, and elevated butyrate. Whether dietary fiber or prebiotics can amplify these benefits remains untested. In parallel, chronic restraint-stressed mice colonized with microbiota from responders displayed reduced anxiety-like behavior and neuroinflammation, effects abolished by antibiotic depletion and by vagotomy. These findings support targeting stress-induced gut dysbiosis as a therapeutic strategy and warrant trials in AD.

Diets enriched with fermented foods and plant-derived fiber can shift the gut microbiota toward butyrate-producing taxa, yet whether this shift modifies brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling in depression remains uncertain. In a randomized adult cohort, we compared a 12-week probiotic-supplemented Mediterranean-style diet with standard care. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and targeted metabolomics quantified microbial community structure and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). The intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Fecal microbiota transplantation into antibiotic-treated mice confirmed that microbial shifts were sufficient to alter BDNF and depressive-like behavior. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with post-intervention microbiota reproduced the BDNF increase and reduced neuroinflammation, effects absent in BDNF-deficient mice. These findings suggest that fermented food- and fiber-driven microbiome remodeling may influence depression through SCFA-BDNF signaling, offering a tractable target for probiotic supplementation.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean-style dietary pattern predicts lower interleukin-6 and improved depressive symptoms, yet the microbial mediators remain uncertain. We combined gut metagenomes, targeted metabolomics, and Mendelian randomization in adults from two cohorts. Omega-3 supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, whereas fermented foods enriched Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. These shifts correlated with reduced cortisol and improved insomnia symptoms. Mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acids explained 31% of the association between dietary fiber intake and anxiety scores. In germ-free mice, colonization with microbiota from high-fiber donors reproduced the metabolic and behavioral benefits, while antibiotic depletion abolished them. Probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus alone did not recapitulate the full effect. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed strain-level responses, with butyrate kinase and IL-10 expression tracking depressive symptom improvement and reduced insomnia severity. Causal inference supported SCFA-dependent signaling, suggesting that diet and supplementation shape the gut-brain axis through overlapping but distinct microbial pathways in both cohorts.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) can promote microglial maturation and constrain amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet pathways linking gut microbiota to hippocampal BDNF expression remain unclear. We examined 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment and 42 cognitively normal controls, profiling fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and serum SCFAs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. APOE genotype was determined. Multivariable linear regression and Spearman correlation tested associations between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Bacteroides, butyrate, and cognitive scores. PERMANOVA showed that microbiota composition differed by cognitive status, with depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and enrichment of Escherichia/Shigella in participants with mild cognitive impairment. Lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate levels were associated with poorer hippocampal volume and lower BDNF after adjustment for APOE ε4. Butyrate correlated positively with BDNF and negatively with interleukin-6. These findings suggest that microbiota-derived butyrate may support hippocampal function via BDNF-dependent mechanisms, offering a potential target for AD prevention.

Alterations in gut microbiota precede amyloid-β plaque deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that microbiota-derived metabolites shape neuroinflammation before overt cognitive decline. We profiled fecal microbiota from 3xTg-AD mice and wild-type littermates across 8–48 weeks using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in colon, serum, and hippocampus by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed genotype-dependent shifts in microbial composition beginning at 12 weeks, before plaque pathology. Random forest classification discriminated AD mice from controls with 92% accuracy, driven by Bacteroides, Alistipes, and Lactobacillus. Butyrate and propionate were reduced in AD mice; butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf expression and attenuated GFAP in hippocampus. Mechanistically, butyrate increased Bdnf and reduced Il6 expression in hippocampus, while Bacteroides-derived propionate modulated microglial activation. In a cross-sectional human cohort, microbial signatures enriched in Bacteroides and depleted in butyrate correlated with mild cognitive impairment and AD diagnosis. These findings position gut microbiota as an early modifiable contributor to AD pathogenesis and support SCFA-based interventions.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is diminished in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and correlates with APOE4 genotype, but whether this depletion causally alters hippocampus BDNF signaling remains unclear. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we compared gut bacterial communities from patients with AD and cognitively normal controls, then colonized germ-free mice with each microbiota. AD-derived microbiota reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, lowered butyrate, and decreased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These changes accompanied impaired spatial memory and elevated interleukin-1β. Supplementation with butyrate restored Bdnf transcription and reduced neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis linked Faecalibacterium abundance to cognitive scores through butyrate and BDNF. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed that individuals with APOE4 harbored lower Roseburia and Eubacterium rectale than individuals without it, with butyrate synthesis genes depleted in AD vs controls. Random forest classification separated AD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82, driven by Faecalibacterium and butyrate. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a modifier of APOE4-associated AD risk and support microbiota-targeted interventions.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from the gut microbiome shape hippocampal plasticity and may modify the trajectory of Alzheimer's disease (AD). In a cohort of older adults with mild cognitive impairment, we profiled the gut microbiome using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified butyrate in serum. Associations were tested with PERMANOVA, multivariable linear regression, and random forest classification. Greater abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii correlated with higher BDNF expression and better hippocampal volume. A 12-week randomized trial of omega-3 fatty acids plus inulin altered microbial composition and increased butyrate production in mice and participants. In mice, probiotic supplementation increased BDNF and reduced neuroinflammation. In parallel, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high butyrate into mice improved blood-brain barrier integrity and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through omega-3 fatty acids and inulin may support brain health in AD, though mediation analysis is needed to clarify causal pathways. However, effect sizes were modest and varied by baseline microbial composition.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites signal across the intestinal epithelium to the brain, where they alter BDNF and FKBP5 expression and modify stress reactivity. To test whether diet shapes this axis, we fed mice a Western diet or a high-fiber diet and profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA sequencing. We used linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to link Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Clostridium with depressive-like behavior. The high-fiber diet increased butyrate, reduced neuroinflammation, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus; the Western diet had opposite effects. In patients with major depressive disorder, fecal microbiota composition correlated with FKBP5 methylation and clinical severity. A probiotic cocktail containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated these changes in mice, while fluoxetine produced partial overlap. Notably, Mendelian randomization supported a causal effect of Bacteroides abundance on depression risk. These findings indicate that dietary fiber and probiotics can reshape gut microbiota-brain signaling through microbial metabolites and NTRK2 pathways, offering a modifiable target for stress-related disorders.

Low intake of fermentable dietary fiber predicts cognitive decline, but the gut microbial pathways that mediate this risk remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized trial, older adults with subjective memory complaints received either inulin supplementation or placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, raised butyrate and propionate, and lowered interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. These changes accompanied improved executive function and episodic memory relative to placebo. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with pre-treatment microbiota, butyrate reached the hippocampus only when MCT1-dependent transport was intact; BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex tracked with short-chain fatty acid availability. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial metabolites explained a significant portion of the fiber supplementation effect on cognition. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings support fermentable fiber as a preventive adjunct and identify gut microbial butyrate signaling as a targetable axis for preserving brain health across aging.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber can shift the gut microbiome toward Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium enrichment, increasing short-chain fatty acid production and dampening neuroinflammation in the central nervous system. In a randomized controlled trial of older adults with mild cognitive impairment, daily probiotic supplementation combined with a Mediterranean-style diet improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores and reduced interleukin-6 compared with usual diet alone. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, which correlated with brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels in plasma. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced the cognitive benefit, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. Conversely, a Western diet promoted Bacteroides dominance and lipopolysaccharide translocation across the intestinal epithelium, exacerbating systemic inflammation. These findings suggest that probiotics and dietary fiber act synergistically through the gut microbiota to modulate neurodegeneration, though shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mediation analyses are needed to identify causal taxa. The gut microbiota thus represents a modifiable target, but fecal calprotectin assays and serum metabolomics may guide personalized synbiotic formulations.

Microbial production of short-chain fatty acids in the gut is a key mediator of brain function, but whether prebiotic fiber can reverse age-related cognitive decline remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild cognitive impairment, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to test whether inulin alters microbiota composition, butyrate production, and hippocampal connectivity. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and improved mixed-effects model-estimated cognitive scores relative to placebo. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and enhanced hippocampal connectivity. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with post-treatment microbiota, butyrate was required for reduced neuroinflammation and restored BDNF expression. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 85%. The effects persisted for 8 weeks after cessation of inulin. Our data suggest that inulin acts via gut microbiota-derived butyrate to support brain health, offering a tractable prebiotic strategy for cognitive decline.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone, and disrupting this signaling may accelerate depression-like phenotypes. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received probiotic supplementation or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut microbiota and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice tested whether microbial changes mediate behavioral effects. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms relative to placebo. Mice receiving microbiota from responders showed elevated BDNF expression in hippocampus and attenuated neuroinflammation. Untargeted metabolomics further linked indole-3-propionate and kynurenine shifts to symptom improvement. Baseline gut microbial diversity correlated with treatment response, and mixed-effects models adjusted for dietary fiber intake and antidepressant use. Treatment effects were stronger in participants with lower baseline microbial diversity, and shotgun metagenomics revealed enriched butyrate kinase and BCoAT. Adverse events were mild, with transient gastrointestinal discomfort. Together, these data position gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator of depression. These findings link probiotic supplementation-associated microbial shifts to depression improvement and support microbiota-targeted interventions for mood disorders.

Impaired gut microbiota–BDNF signaling is increasingly linked to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease. We hypothesized that curcumin supplementation would restore microbial metabolites and BDNF expression in APP/PS1 mice. Mice received curcumin or vehicle for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal metabolomics, behavioral testing, and quantitative PCR assessed microbial composition, metabolites, cognition, and BDNF expression. Curcumin increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate in colon, and restored BDNF expression in hippocampus. It also reduced neuroinflammation and improved spatial memory deficits. Notably, curcumin did not alter BDNF expression in prefrontal cortex, indicating regional specificity. Serum lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 were lower in curcumin-treated mice than in vehicle-treated mice. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and BDNF sequentially mediated the effects of curcumin on cognitive impairment. Fecal microbiota transplantation from curcumin-treated mice into microbiota-depleted mice partially reproduced these benefits. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with curcumin may modulate BDNF signaling and alleviate Alzheimer's disease-related cognitive decline.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids suppress microglial activation in the hippocampus and attenuate stress-induced depressive-like behavior through vagus nerve signaling. To test whether this pathway requires an intact subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve, we subjected male C57BL/6J mice to chronic unpredictable mild stress and randomized them to subdiaphragmatic vagotomy or sham surgery. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in portal blood and colonic contents. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Lactobacillus reuteri and Bacteroides uniformis as taxa enriched in sham-operated, stress-resilient mice. Spearman correlation revealed that L. reuteri abundance correlated positively with butyrate concentrations and negatively with immobility time in the forced swim test. Vagotomy abolished these associations and increased IL-1β and Iba1 expression in the hippocampus. Oral butyrate supplementation restored brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) transcripts and reduced depressive-like behavior in vagotomized mice, but not in mice lacking Gpr41. These findings position L. reuteri-derived butyrate as a vagus-dependent mediator of gut microbiota-brain communication and suggest butyrate analogs for stress-related mood disorders.

Dietary fiber intake shapes gut microbiota composition and may modulate brain function through microbial metabolites, yet the molecular links between fermentable fiber, gut bacteria, and affective symptoms remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder and low fiber intake received either a high-fiber diet or psyllium placebo. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood were measured. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed-effects models assessed longitudinal associations. The high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate levels, reduced BDNF methylation, and lowered depression severity compared with placebo. Changes in butyrate correlated with BDNF methylation and symptom improvement. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the effect of dietary fiber on mood. Fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate-BDNF association. These findings indicate that fiber-rich foods may alleviate depressive symptoms by altering gut microbiota metabolism and BDNF regulation, supporting dietary strategies that target the microbiome-brain axis.

Disruption of the gut microbiota can alter brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the strength of these associations across neuropsychiatric disorders remains uncertain. We synthesized 52 human and mouse studies examining gut microbial composition, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and BDNF expression in major depressive disorder, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Microbial profiling used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics; intervention trials tested probiotic supplements, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, and fiber-rich foods. A random-effects meta-analysis showed lower abundance of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia in patients than in healthy controls (SMD = -0.41, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.20; I² = 54%). Probiotic administration increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced IL-6 expression in the intestinal epithelium, but effects on brain outcomes were heterogeneous. Subgroup meta-regression indicated that study design and antibiotic exposure explained part of this heterogeneity. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome in gut-brain disorders, while emphasizing strain-specific mechanisms and the need for standardized fecal microbiota transplantation and dietary trials.

Disruption of the microbiota-gut-brain axis by Alzheimer's disease-associated neuroinflammation may accelerate cognitive decline. In a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium breve or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; PERMANOVA assessed community composition, and linear mixed-effects models estimated changes in short-chain fatty acids and BDNF expression. Supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered plasma lipopolysaccharide relative to placebo. These shifts coincided with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in serum and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate increases accounted for 31% of the cognitive benefit, whereas BDNF changes explained 18%. The findings indicate that targeted probiotic supplementation can reshape gut microbial communities, attenuate peripheral inflammation, and support brain function in patients with mild cognitive impairment. Larger trials with causal mediation models are needed to confirm durability and mechanism.

Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve plus inulin attenuated mild cognitive impairment in older adults and shifted gut microbiota toward Lactobacillus and Akkermansia enrichment. In a 12-week randomized trial, 82 participants received either the synbiotic or placebo; cognitive scores, inflammatory cytokines, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were assessed alongside 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. The synbiotic group showed improved cognitive performance and reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha compared with placebo. Gut microbiota diversity increased, and Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance correlated positively with hippocampus volume and BDNF expression. Mediation analysis suggested that short-chain fatty acid production partly explained the cognitive benefit, while quantitative PCR confirmed higher Bifidobacterium breve colonization in responders. At week 12, the synbiotic group also displayed lower trimethylamine N-oxide and higher butyrate concentrations in feces than placebo, and these changes correlated with depressive symptoms scores. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings support a gut-brain axis mechanism whereby prebiotic and probiotic co-administration may delay neurodegeneration, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota influence brain circuits implicated in major depressive disorder, and probiotic supplementation may attenuate depressive symptoms by modifying this communication through immune, neuroendocrine, and vagal pathways. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 or placebo. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids, cortisol, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time effects, while mediation analysis estimated whether microbial and metabolic shifts explained symptom change. At week 12, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores fell by 6.2 points with probiotic versus 3.1 points with placebo, and responder rates were 48% and 29%, respectively. Relative to placebo, L. rhamnosus HN001 increased Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms; these improvements were partially mediated by butyrate and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. The findings support strain-specific probiotic strategies for depression, although larger trials are needed to confirm durability and generalizability.

Chronic stress disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis and amplifies depressive symptoms through vagal and immune routes. In a mouse model of chronic unpredictable mild stress, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve attenuated anhedonia and normalized serum corticosterone. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed recovery of microbial diversity, while untargeted metabolomics showed increased short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites. Linear mixed-effects models indicated that treatment, time, and their interaction predicted depression-like behavior; Spearman correlations linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These effects were abolished by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, implicating the vagus nerve. Fecal microbiota transplantation from treated mice partially reproduced the behavioral benefits in naive mice. In patients with major depressive disorder, a pilot randomized controlled trial found that probiotics plus fluoxetine reduced depressive symptoms more than fluoxetine alone, although effects were modest. These findings support a microbiota-gut-brain axis in which probiotic interventions may modulate neuroactive metabolites and BDNF signaling, but larger trials with standardized strains and multivariable adjustment are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central neuroinflammation and may mediate the cognitive benefits of Mediterranean-style diets, yet the contribution of isolated probiotic and omega-3 supplementation remains uncertain. We analyzed adults with subjective cognitive decline enrolled in a 12-week randomized trial comparing a high-fiber, polyphenol-rich diet alone or combined with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and fish oil. Stool samples were collected at baseline, week 6, and week 12; dietary adherence was recorded. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; butyrate, hippurate, and trimethylamine N-oxide were quantified, and executive function was assessed. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline Shannon diversity, combined supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6 relative to the diet alone. At week 12, the combined group showed greater increases in Shannon diversity and plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor, whereas the diet alone did not. Greater Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with improved cognitive scores and lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial butyrate production accounted for part of the cognitive benefit. These findings suggest that probiotic plus omega-3 adjuncts amplify diet-driven gut microbiome shifts and may slow neurocognitive decline, warranting larger trials.

Disrupted gut microbiota and its microbial metabolites contribute to depression through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling along the gut-brain axis. In male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic restraint stress, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside elevated Bacteroidetes, compared with unstressed controls. Untargeted metabolomics of serum and hippocampus identified lower tryptophan, kynurenic acid, and short-chain fatty acids, and higher kynurenine. These shifts correlated with decreased BDNF and PSD-95 expression in the prefrontal cortex. Spearman correlation and PERMANOVA linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF transcripts and kynurenic acid levels. Fluoxetine partially reversed these microbial and metabolic alterations, whereas probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus and attenuated stress-induced behavioral deficits. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors into naive recipients reproduced reduced BDNF and increased kynurenine, while minocycline or probiotic treatment normalized microbial composition and depressive-like behavior. The findings position microbial metabolites as mediators of depression-like phenotypes and suggest that targeting gut flora may complement conventional antidepressants.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is now recognized as a critical determinant of gut-brain axis signaling, yet the extent to which this route mediates stress resilience remains debated. We colonized germ-free mice with gut microbiota from donors reporting high or low fermented food intake and then exposed them to chronic social defeat stress. Animals receiving inulin plus Bifidobacterium breve showed lower depressive-like behavior and attenuated corticosterone responses compared with controls. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed expanded Lactobacillus and Akkermansia and reduced Desulfovibrio; these shifts correlated with serotonin and BDNF expression in the hippocampus. The protective phenotype was accompanied by reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation and lower TNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into naïve recipients reproduced the behavioral protection, while antibiotic depletion abolished it. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and indole-3-lactate accounted for part of the effect. These findings position inulin and fermented food as modifiable levers for microbiota-dependent mood regulation and motivate dietary strategies targeting stress-related disorders.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural signals, and disruption of this dialogue is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder. In adults with depression, reduced gut microbiota diversity and depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium correlate with elevated interleukin-6 and cortisol. We examined whether fermented food and fiber intake modify these associations and whether BDNF expression mediates the effect. Mediation analysis of cross-sectional data from 180 participants showed that fiber consumption was associated with higher microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms; BDNF partially mediated this relationship. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila were inversely associated with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, whereas Ruminococcus gnavus tracked with anxiety scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation from mice consuming a high-fiber diet into recipient mice reduced neuroinflammation and increased BDNF in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that probiotic and fermented food-based strategies may support gut-brain axis homeostasis, though prospective trials are needed.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbial communities and attenuates depression-like behaviors in chronic stress-exposed mice, but the microbial signatures that predict treatment response remain poorly defined. Adult male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress for 6 weeks and randomized to control diet or diet supplemented with inulin (10% w/w) during the final 4 weeks. We profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified serum corticosterone, interleukin-6, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundances, reduced Desulfovibrio, and lowered corticosterone compared with vehicle-treated mice. It also elevated butyrate and propionate in colon contents and normalized BDNF mRNA in prefrontal cortex. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) revealed distinct community structures, while random forest models identified Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia as top predictors of behavioral improvement. These findings suggest that inulin may act through microbiota-dependent signaling to mitigate stress-related depression; however, human trials are needed.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber fermentation in the colon can modulate central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, but the extent to which these signals shape depression-related behavior remains unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then measured short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), cytokines, and tight junction protein expression in the intestine. Behavioral testing included forced swim test and open field test. 16S rRNA sequencing profiled microbial communities, while linear mixed-effects models tested associations between Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, butyrate, and behavioral outcomes. We also used PERMANOVA to compare microbial composition and Spearman correlation to relate microbial taxa to metabolites. Mice receiving microbiota from depressed donors displayed increased anxiety-like behavior, lower butyrate, and reduced ZO-1 expression relative to controls. Butyrate supplementation normalized ZO-1, attenuated IL-6, and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-derived SCFAs link intestinal barrier integrity to mood disorders.
