Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiota and reduces Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in mice, yet the microbial signals that translate into hippocampal plasticity remain unresolved. We fed transgenic mice diets containing inulin or cellulose for 12 weeks, then profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and measured Bdnf, Arc, Tnf, and Pgc1a transcripts in the hippocampus. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and lowered amyloid-beta burden. Behavioral testing showed that treated mice spent more time in the target quadrant of the Morris water maze and had lower anxiety-like behavior in the open field test. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium relative abundance to Bdnf expression and cognitive impairment scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly accounted for the Bdnf increase. Plasma lipopolysaccharide was reduced, while Bdnf and Pgc1a were elevated. These findings indicate that inulin may improve Alzheimer's disease-related memory deficits by promoting gut microbiota-derived butyrate and Bdnf signaling in the brain.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether probiotic supplementation modifies PD risk remains uncertain. We pooled adult cohort and randomized controlled trial data to assess associations between probiotic use, gut microbial composition, and PD-related outcomes. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium among probiotic users, alongside increased short-chain fatty acid production and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels. Using random-effects meta-analysis, probiotic exposure was associated with improved gastrointestinal symptoms and modest motor benefit, but not with reduced PD incidence. Mendelian randomization did not support a causal effect of gut microbiota on PD. In mice overexpressing α-synuclein, probiotic treatment attenuated nigrostriatal degeneration and restored BDNF expression in the striatum. These findings suggest that probiotics may alleviate select PD symptoms through microbiome-mediated gut–brain signaling, but evidence for disease modification in patients remains limited. Longer-term placebo-controlled trials are needed to define strain-specific effects.

Gut microbiota depletion is accompanied by reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and altered γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) signaling, yet whether probiotic supplementation can restore these gut-brain mediators in mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. We randomized 68 adults with mild cognitive impairment to 12 weeks of a multi-strain probiotic formula or a control condition. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; GABA, SCFA, and lipopolysaccharide were quantified using LC-MS and ELISA. Cognitive performance and plasma pTau-181 were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Associations between bacterial genera, neuroactive metabolites, and cognitive scores were evaluated using Spearman correlation and mixed-effects models. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal GABA, and reduced LPS compared with control. These changes correlated with improved ADAS-Cog scores and lower pTau-181. Collectively, these findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with psychobiotic interventions may modulate amyloid-related pathways, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism in the gut acts as a conserved rheostat for central nervous system serotonin availability, yet its causal role in affective disorders remains disputed. We profiled the gut microbiome of 812 adults using shotgun metagenomics and untargeted plasma metabolomics, then applied two-sample Mendelian randomization to separate microbial effects from reverse causation. Higher abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium correlated with increased indole-3-lactate and lower depressive symptoms. In mice, dietary fiber supplementation increased short-chain fatty acid production, upregulated BDNF and GABRA1 expression in the hippocampus, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the association between microbial diversity and anxiety scores. In a random-effects meta-analysis of 14 cohorts, each 1-SD increase in gut microbial diversity was associated with 12% lower odds of major depressive disorder. Fecal Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance mediated this effect through butyrate and propionate signaling to vagal afferents. These findings position fermented foods and prebiotic supplements as plausible adjuncts for stress-related disorders, although host 5-HTTLPR genotype may modify responses.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone, yet whether dietary fiber intake modifies this relationship in humans remains unclear. We analyzed fecal microbiome and plasma metabolites from 120 adults with irritable bowel syndrome and 80 healthy controls. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and fasting blood metabolomics was performed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Participants completed validated food frequency questionnaires, and habitual intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber was estimated. Associations between microbial taxa, metabolites, and anxiety scores were tested using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis. Higher abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia spp. was associated with greater fecal butyrate and lower anxiety severity. Fermented food consumption correlated with increased microbial diversity and reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. The association between gut dysbiosis and anxiety was partially mediated by butyrate. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented foods may support gut-brain communication through microbial metabolite production, offering a modifiable target for intervention.

Gut microbiota-derived metabolites shape central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and disruptions in this axis are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild depressive symptoms, 8-week supplementation with a multi-strain probiotic plus prebiotic fiber altered fecal microbiota composition, increasing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance while reducing Proteobacteria. These shifts coincided with lower circulating lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6, and improved anxiety scores. Transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed downregulation of NFKB1 and IL1B, alongside upregulation of BDNF, suggesting reduced inflammatory signaling and enhanced neurotrophic support. In mice receiving microbiota from responders, fecal microbiota transplantation reproduced the behavioral and Bdnf expression changes, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels partially explained the improvement in depression scores. These findings support synbiotic interventions as modulators of the gut-brain axis, with BDNF and inflammatory pathways as candidate mediators.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with higher gut microbial diversity and reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease, but the microbial mediators remain unclear. We studied 180 older adults with mild cognitive impairment or without dementia. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and plasma short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Dietary intake was assessed using a food frequency questionnaire; hippocampal volume was measured with MRI. Mediation analysis and linear regression tested associations, adjusting for age, sex, and APOE genotype. Higher Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with enrichment of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, increased butyrate, and decreased trimethylamine N-oxide. Butyrate was positively associated with hippocampal volume, whereas trimethylamine N-oxide was inversely associated. In mediation models, butyrate explained 18% of the association between diet and cognitive impairment. Sensitivity analyses excluding antibiotic users and applying false discovery rate correction preserved the main findings. These results support a gut microbiota-metabolite pathway linking diet to Alzheimer's disease risk.

Higher dietary fiber intake is associated with distinct gut microbiome features and lower neuroinflammation in older adults, yet the microbial mediators linking diet to brain health remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of 180 participants, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics with dietary records and cognitive testing. Mediation analysis and linear mixed-effects models tested whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia, and short-chain fatty acids explained associations between fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and cognitive decline. Greater fiber intake correlated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate concentrations. These microbial features were inversely related to IL-6 and C-reactive protein and positively related to BDNF expression. In mediation models, butyrate accounted for 22% of the fiber–cognition association, while Roseburia explained 15%. No significant mediation was observed for probiotic use. These findings suggest that fiber-rich diets may support brain health through gut microbiota-derived metabolites, offering potential targets for neurodegenerative disease prevention in humans.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune tone, yet the transcriptional routes linking gut microbiota to depression-like behavior remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, RNA sequencing, and linear mixed models, we profiled fecal microbiota and hippocampal transcriptomes in mice fed a fiber-depleted diet or an inulin-enriched diet. Fiber depletion reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate concentrations, increased circulating lipopolysaccharide, and elevated anxiety-like behavior. Hippocampal BDNF expression fell, whereas IL6, TNF, and TLR4 transcripts rose. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-depleted mice into germ-free mice reproduced the BDNF reduction and behavioral phenotype; probiotic supplementation partially reversed these changes. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing further linked these shifts to altered tryptophan metabolism. In participants, lower gut microbial diversity correlated with higher IL6 expression in blood and self-reported depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that dietary fiber insufficiency disrupts microbiota-BDNF signaling, and that targeting this axis may offer a therapeutic strategy for stress-related disorders.

Chronic stress disrupts the gut microbiota and elevates proinflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus, contributing to depression-like phenotypes. We tested whether inulin supplementation could reverse these effects in C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress. After four weeks, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances and reduced Proteobacteria. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed elevated short-chain fatty acids in feces and plasma. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus as key taxa enriched by inulin. Parallel fecal metabolomics in healthy adults receiving inulin showed comparable increases in short-chain fatty acids and bile acid derivatives. Inulin-fed mice displayed lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha levels, restored BDNF expression, and reduced anxiety-like behavior compared with controls. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors partially reproduced these benefits in antibiotic-treated recipients, whereas vancomycin abolished them. These findings indicate that inulin shapes the gut microbiome and gut-brain signaling through microbial metabolites, offering a potential adjunct for stress-related disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease and may promote nigrostriatal degeneration via microbial metabolites, inflammatory mediators, and spread along the vagus nerve of α-synuclein. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, we profiled patients with PD and healthy controls, integrating SNCA and LRRK2 genotype data. Compared with controls, patients showed reduced Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae, increased Enterobacteriaceae, and lower fecal short-chain fatty acids. These shifts correlated with colon inflammation, enteric nervous system α-synuclein deposition, and motor severity. Random-effects meta-analysis across cohorts confirmed Enterobacteriaceae enrichment and Prevotellaceae depletion, though effect sizes varied by LRRK2 status and levodopa exposure. Notably, lipopolysaccharide-driven blood-brain barrier disruption and reduced butyrate production may facilitate α-synuclein misfolding. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition explained 18% of the variance in PD motor scores, independent of age and sex. Our findings suggest that gut microbial dysbiosis interacts with host SNCA and LRRK2 variants to influence Parkinson's disease progression, supporting microbiota-targeted strategies and early fecal microbiota transplantation trials.

Microbial metabolites produced in the gut can influence brain function and emotional behavior, yet the dietary levers that translate this cross-talk into clinically meaningful change remain uncertain. In a double-blind trial, 72 adults with mild depression received either probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis or placebo for 8 weeks; all participants also completed fermented food counseling. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of stool samples showed increased Lactobacillus abundance and higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the probiotic arm. Random forest classification separated groups by microbial composition, and mediation analysis indicated that changes in gut microbiota diversity partially explained reductions in depressive symptoms. These effects coincided with elevated BDNF expression and reduced neuroinflammation markers. Baseline Prevotella abundance moderated the microbial response, and participants with higher gut microbiota diversity showed greater symptom improvement. The findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may modulate the gut microbiome and support mental health, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids that dampen neuroinflammation and sustain BDNF signaling in the brain. In germ-free mice colonized with Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, 16S rRNA sequencing showed that gut microbiota composition tracked with cytokine profiles and motor deficits. Spearman correlation linked TREM2 expression in the substantia nigra to butyrate levels, whereas high-fat diet depleted Bifidobacterium and increased lipopolysaccharide translocation. Mechanistically, butyrate promotes FOXP3 expression in intestinal regulatory T cells and limits IL-6 and TNF-α release, while Mediterranean diet patterns rich in polyphenols enhance Akkermansia abundance. The vagus nerve relays these metabolite signals to the brainstem, linking gut microbiota to neurodegeneration. Among patients with Parkinson's disease, lower fiber intake and reduced microbial diversity were associated with worse cognitive scores. Supplementation with probiotics or prebiotics restored butyrate production, attenuated neuroinflammation, and improved levodopa responsiveness in preliminary trials. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal and suggest that targeting TREM2-dependent microglial pathways may complement existing therapies.

Gut microbiota fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that reinforce intestinal barrier function, modulate intestinal mucosa immunity, and dampen neuroinflammation. In rodent models of depression and cognitive impairment, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation have linked reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance to altered serotonin turnover, kynurenine metabolism, and BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Fermented foods and probiotic supplements may restore microbial diversity, yet responses vary with host genetics, baseline microbiota, and antibiotic exposure. Metagenomic profiling combined with untargeted metabolomics has identified bile acids, tryptophan metabolites, and trimethylamine N-oxide as candidate mediators of vagus nerve signaling and gut-brain axis communication. Nevertheless, causality remains difficult to establish because most clinical studies are observational and rely on correlational analysis. Randomized controlled trials using standardized prebiotic or probiotic interventions, paired with shotgun metagenomics and metabolomics, are needed to determine whether targeting gut bacteria can modify neuropsychiatric disease trajectories. Such trials should stratify by diet, medication use, and age to clarify which patients benefit.

Alterations in the gut microbiota often precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease by years, implying that microbial signals actively shape neurodegeneration. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, recent cohorts have linked reduced Prevotella and elevated Akkermansia muciniphila to faster progression in patients. These taxa modulate short-chain fatty acid production, especially butyrate, which influences gut barrier integrity and neuroinflammation. In mouse models, fecal microbiota transplantation from affected donors into gnotobiotic mice exacerbates SNCA-driven pathology in the substantia nigra, while dietary fiber supplementation restores butyrate levels and attenuates motor impairment. A random forest classifier trained on fecal microbiome profiles discriminated cases from controls with moderate accuracy, supporting microbial signatures as early biomarkers. However, causality remains contested because levodopa and constipation independently alter gut microbial composition. Longitudinal prospective studies combining metagenomics with metabolomics and dietary records are needed to determine whether targeting the gut microbiota can modify Parkinson's disease trajectory.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to depression and anxiety, yet interventions that restore microbial metabolites remain incompletely defined. In a double-blind study of adults, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum was compared with placebo over 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled stool microbiota, while short-chain fatty acids and butyrate were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, and Spearman correlation linked microbial taxa to BDNF expression and interleukin-6 levels. Probiotic treatment increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations, reduced interleukin-6, and improved depressive symptoms relative to placebo. These changes were associated with altered BDNF methylation in participants. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated the depressive-like behavior reductions and hippocampal BDNF upregulation. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated the improvement in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that targeted probiotic strategies may modulate the gut microbiome–brain axis, although larger trials are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis precedes mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease, yet the microbial signals that mediate this transition remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of older adults with subjective cognitive decline, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, alongside reduced butyrate synthesis. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability explained 31% of the association between microbial dysbiosis and hippocampal volume. Linear mixed-effects models further linked lower microbial diversity to thinner entorhinal cortex, independent of APOE4 status. In mice colonized with microbiota from donors with low butyrate potential, sodium butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf expression and reduced neuroinflammation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-butyrate donors improved cognitive deficits in mice, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished this effect. These findings position butyrate-producing Clostridia as tractable targets, and they support dietary fiber or prebiotic interventions as early strategies to protect the aging brain. Together, these data suggest that restoring butyrate production may delay cognitive decline by preserving synaptic integrity.

Microbial-derived metabolites shape neuroinflammatory tone in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the taxa driving this gut-brain axis remain poorly resolved. We colonized APP/PS1 transgenic mice with fecal microbiota from cognitively normal donors or donors with mild cognitive impairment using fecal microbiota transplantation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled cecal contents, serum, and hippocampus. Random forest separated donor groups with 0.89 AUC, while linear mixed-effects models linked Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium to short-chain fatty acid production. Mice receiving MCI-associated microbiota showed cognitive decline, amyloid-beta accumulation, and IL-6 elevation; inulin supplementation attenuated these changes. Lactobacillus abundance inversely correlated with neuroinflammation, and PERMANOVA confirmed inulin-driven shifts in gut microbial composition. Behavioral testing with Morris water maze and novel object recognition revealed spatial memory deficits in colonized mice. Lipopolysaccharide and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were elevated in prefrontal cortex. Rifaximin reduced Enterobacteriaceae and improved cognitive outcomes. Collectively, these findings support microbiome-targeted interventions for AD.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as key messengers along the gut microbiota–brain axis, but their cell-type-specific actions remain incompletely defined. Using single-cell RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex and colon from gnotobiotic mice colonized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Bacteroides fragilis, we found that butyrate selectively repressed NF-κB-dependent inflammatory programs in microglia while inducing BDNF and GABA-A receptor subunits in neurons. This transcriptional shift correlated with reduced anxiety-like behavior and lower corticosterone after chronic restraint stress. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into antibiotic-treated mice partially recapitulated these effects, whereas TLR5 or MYD88 deletion abolished them. Mediation analysis suggested that SCFA-driven FFAR2 signaling accounts for a significant fraction of the behavioral benefit. These data position microbial metabolites as tunable regulators of neuroimmune signaling networks and support fiber or probiotic interventions for stress-related disorders. Additional whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in hippocampal slices revealed that butyrate increased inhibitory currents and reduced excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, an effect absent in FFAR2-deficient mice. Together, these findings link microbial metabolites to BDNF- and GABA-A receptor-dependent plasticity and suggest that targeting the gut microbiome may alleviate stress-related disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids can influence BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a mechanism increasingly implicated in depression and anxiety. In mice fed a high-fat diet, reduced gut microbiota diversity corresponded with lower BDNF and TrkB transcripts, while probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus abundance and normalized serotonin turnover. Data from adults are less consistent. A randomized controlled trial in adults with major depressive disorder found that omega-3 fatty acids combined with fiber improved depressive symptoms only in participants harboring specific Faecalibacterium profiles. Similarly, fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi may enhance gut microbiota diversity, but effects on BDNF remain uncertain. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and mediation analysis, recent work suggests that tryptophan metabolites mediate the association between prebiotic intake and prefrontal cortex activity. These effects appear strain-specific and dose-dependent. These findings position dietary patterns and targeted supplements as modifiable inputs to gut microbiota–brain signaling, though causal pathways and optimal dosing require further clinical trials.

Depletion of butyrate-producing gut bacteria, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, tracks with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease and predicts neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. To test causality, APPswe/PS1dE9 mice received sodium butyrate for 8 weeks and were compared with untreated littermates. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. In the hippocampus, IL-1β, TNF-α, and Iba1 expression were measured by quantitative PCR and immunofluorescence. Sodium butyrate restored butyrate levels, reduced amyloid-β deposition, and attenuated microgliosis. Linear discriminant analysis identified Akkermansia and Lactobacillus as taxa enriched in treated mice, while Spearman correlation linked Faecalibacterium abundance to IL-10 and memory deficits. Fecal pellets were collected before and after treatment, and permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed distinct microbial community structures between groups. Morris water maze testing showed improved spatial memory in butyrate-treated mice. In mice, sodium butyrate also lowered lipopolysaccharide and CD68 in serum, suggesting reduced systemic inflammation. These findings suggest that microbiota-derived butyrate is a tractable target for slowing Alzheimer's disease progression.

Altered gut microbiota precedes amyloid deposition in Alzheimer's disease and may accelerate cognitive decline through altered short-chain fatty acid signaling. To test whether host genotype modifies this axis, we colonized germ-free mice carrying APOE3 or APOE4 with fecal microbiota from older adults stratified by APOE4 carrier status. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed that APOE4-associated microbiota was depleted in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, with reduced butyrate production potential. After 12 weeks, mice carrying APOE4 that received APOE4-carrier microbiota showed elevated amyloid-β in the hippocampus, spatial memory impairment, and increased GFAP and CD68 expression. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that butyrate levels inversely correlated with amyloid-β load and neuroinflammation. Butyrate supplementation attenuated cognitive impairment and normalized IL-1β expression in mice carrying APOE4. Notably, female mice carrying APOE4 exhibited stronger memory deficits than male mice, suggesting sex-dependent susceptibility. These findings identify APOE4-dependent microbiota signatures as modifiable drivers of Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis and support butyrate-targeted precision microbiome therapy.

High-fat diet consumption alters gut microbial composition, yet the pathways linking these changes to cognitive impairment remain incompletely defined. We treated adult male mice with a multi-strain probiotic supplement or vehicle while feeding a Western diet for 16 weeks. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we quantified gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acids. Supplemented mice showed restored Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance, reduced IL-1β and TNF-α expression in the prefrontal cortex, and lower amyloid-β accumulation. Behavioral assays revealed improved spatial working memory compared with unsupplemented mice. These effects were associated with decreased neuroinflammation and preserved blood-brain barrier integrity. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into germ-free mice partially reproduced the cognitive benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance with butyrate concentrations and memory scores. The results indicate that probiotic supplementation can mitigate diet-driven gut dysbiosis and protect against Alzheimer's disease-like pathology, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target for early intervention.

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone, yet their causal contribution to major depressive disorder remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls and tracked behavioral, immune, and microbial outcomes. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and SCFA concentrations in feces and serum were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Behavioral data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models, and associations between taxa and depressive-like behavior were tested using Spearman correlation and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Mice receiving depression-associated microbiota showed increased immobility in the forced swim test, elevated interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in the hippocampus, and reduced butyrate compared with control mice. Bacteroides and Clostridium abundances correlated inversely with butyrate and positively with IL-6. Supplementation with sodium butyrate normalized cytokine levels and attenuated behavioral deficits, whereas vancomycin depleted Gram-positive bacteria and abolished the protective effect. These findings position microbial metabolites as modifiable mediators of the gut microbiota–brain axis in depression.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder and anxiety, yet the microbial and metabolic signals that mediate this effect remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with depression or healthy controls and assessed behavioral outcomes using the forced swim test and open field test. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and expansion of Akkermansia in recipient mice receiving depression-associated microbiota. Targeted metabolomics showed lower short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), reduced tryptophan metabolites, and elevated IL-6 and TNF-α in the colon and hippocampus. Untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry further identified bile acids and indole derivatives as differentially abundant between groups. Spearman correlation analysis linked Lactobacillus abundance to serotonin turnover and depressive-like behavior. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors normalized SCFA levels, restored serotonin signaling, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as tractable targets for depression and anxiety.

Microbial colonization of the gut shapes BDNF expression and serotonin synthesis in the brain, linking gut microbiota composition to depression and anxiety. In mice exposed to chronic lipopolysaccharide, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, accompanied by impaired neurogenesis in the hippocampus and elevated interleukin-6. Oral probiotic supplementation restored Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, normalized BDNF and NF-κB transcription, and reduced depressive-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated mice into germ-free mice reproduced these benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Random forest classification identified Prevotella and Bacteroides as discriminative taxa. Targeted metabolomics further linked short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites to BDNF activation. In patients with irritable bowel syndrome, baseline gut microbiota diversity correlated with anxiety scores and BDNF methylation in blood. Clinical responses were stratified by COMT genotype and baseline gut microbiota enterotype. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with probiotics or prebiotics may modulate BDNF-dependent plasticity and serotonin signaling, offering a strategy for stress-related disorders.

Supplementation with probiotics can reshape gut microbiota and modulate central nervous system inflammation, but the pathways linking microbial signals to BDNF expression in the hippocampus remain incompletely defined. In a mouse model of chronic stress, we combined shotgun metagenomic sequencing with fecal microbiota transplantation to test whether Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum alter short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF transcription. Probiotic-treated mice showed higher butyrate in the gut lumen, lower anxiety-like behavior, and increased BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus compared with vehicle-treated controls. These effects were abolished in antibiotic-treated mice and partially restored by fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice that had received probiotics. Linear mixed-effects models identified butyrate and Lactobacillus abundance as independent predictors of BDNF expression. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot randomized placebo-controlled trial of probiotic supplementation is ongoing. These findings position gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids as modulators of BDNF-dependent brain plasticity and support microbiome-targeted probiotic strategies for stress-related disorders.

Consumption of a Western-style diet rich in saturated fatty acids reshapes the gut microbiota and may promote neuroinflammation via the vagus nerve. In male C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet for 12 weeks, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed lower relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, with increased lipopolysaccharide in plasma. Expression in the hippocampus of Bdnf and Tjp1 was reduced, whereas Il6 and Tnf were elevated in diet-fed mice versus controls. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for batch and cage effects linked these microbial shifts to performance in the Morris water maze. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fat-fed donors into germ-free recipients reproduced cognitive deficits. Supplementation with inulin or Bifidobacterium breve partially restored Bdnf transcripts and reduced microglial activation. In adults with obesity, pilot shotgun metagenomic analysis showed similar Akkermansia depletion and higher systemic inflammation. These findings position diet-driven microbiome instability as a modifiable driver of gut-brain axis dysfunction and highlight BDNF as a potential mediator.

Altered gut microbial communities precede motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlate with SNCA risk alleles, implicating a gut-brain axis in α-synucleinopathy. In a case-control cohort of 58 PD patients and 60 age-matched controls, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae but enriched Verrucomicrobiaceae and Enterobacteriaceae. PERMANOVA confirmed community separation by diagnosis (R²=0.08, p=0.001), while random forest classified patients with AUC=0.84. These associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent daily dose. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate and propionate, were lower in PD patients and inversely associated with constipation severity. In mice overexpressing SNCA, colonization with Prevotellaceae-depleted microbiota from PD donors exacerbated substantia nigra dopaminergic loss and colonic inflammation. Levodopa treatment did not restore microbial composition. Probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus and dietary fiber increased butyrate, attenuated neuroinflammation, and normalized BDNF expression in the striatum. These findings link SNCA genotype, gut dysbiosis, and microbial metabolites to PD progression, supporting microbiome-targeted interventions.

Disrupted gut microbiota composition is increasingly tied to BDNF-dependent synaptic plasticity, but whether microbial signatures precede cognitive decline remains uncertain. We characterized fecal microbiota and circulating short-chain fatty acids in 146 older adults, including 84 with mild cognitive impairment and 62 cognitively intact controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics. Random forest classification ranked Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Akkermansia as top discriminators, while PERMANOVA confirmed diagnosis-related community separation (R2 = 0.09, P = 0.001). Lower Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with higher BDNF promoter methylation, reduced circulating butyrate, and worse executive function. In a nested subset, a 12-week fiber supplement increased Roseburia and butyrate, paralleling decreased BDNF methylation and improved processing speed. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially explained the association between Faecalibacterium and BDNF methylation. These results position specific gut microbes as correlates of BDNF epigenetic regulation and support microbiome-directed approaches for early cognitive impairment. Collectively, these findings highlight a potentially modifiable microbiota-BDNF axis relevant to neurodegenerative disease prevention.

Microbial metabolism of dietary substrates in the gut generates neuroactive compounds that modulate brain function, making gut microbiota a tractable target for depression and anxiety. We performed a random-effects meta-analysis of controlled trials in adults, comparing probiotic or prebiotic supplementation and fermented food diets with placebo or habitual diet. Parallel 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics profiled fecal microbiota, short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, and gamma-aminobutyric acid. Across 32 trials, probiotic and fermented food interventions increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced depressive symptoms versus controls (standardized mean difference −0.31; 95% CI −0.48 to −0.14). Effects were stronger when GABA-producing taxa and short-chain fatty acid producers were enriched, whereas prebiotic alone showed smaller, less consistent benefits. These findings support microbiota-directed dietary strategies, particularly fermented foods and probiotics, as adjunctive approaches for mood disorders, though strain-specific and dose-dependent effects require further animal and human validation.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat diet (HFD) exacerbates neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet the microbial signals that communicate with the brain remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we profiled gut microbial communities in mice fed HFD or standard chow. PERMANOVA revealed that diet explained 28% of community variation, with Lactobacillus and Akkermansia depleted and Desulfovibrio enriched after HFD. These shifts correlated with elevated lipopolysaccharide and TLR4 expression in the hippocampus. Probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus abundance, reduced IL6 and TNF transcripts, and improved performance in Morris water maze testing. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, baseline fecal microbiota showed similar Desulfovibrio enrichment, and random forest classification separated cases from controls with moderate accuracy. Our findings position Desulfovibrio and TLR4-dependent signaling as candidate mediators of diet-driven cognitive impairment and suggest that probiotics may warrant testing as adjunctive therapy. Together, these data link specific gut taxa to TLR4-mediated neuroinflammatory signaling and highlight a tractable microbial target for early intervention.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitter precursors are increasingly recognized as modulators of microbiota-gut-brain signaling, yet their therapeutic translation remains constrained by interindividual variation in gut microbiota composition. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum was administered alongside a fermented food-enriched diet for six weeks. Behavioral assays, including the forced swim test and open field test, revealed reduced depressive-like behavior and anxiety-like behavior compared with vehicle-treated controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations, while GC-MS quantified increased butyrate and gamma-aminobutyric acid in cecal contents. In hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, BDNF expression was elevated and interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were suppressed. Spearman correlation linked butyrate levels with BDNF transcripts and behavioral scores. These findings indicate that probiotic supplementation combined with fermented foods may attenuate neuroinflammation and improve stress-related outcomes through microbiota-dependent metabolic signaling, supporting further clinical evaluation.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids derived from dietary fiber fermentation modulate central nervous system immune tone via vagal and endocrine routes, and their depletion is associated with neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In a human cohort, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic functional profiling revealed that APOE ε4 carriers consuming a Western diet had lower gut microbiota diversity and reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance than non-carriers. A randomized intervention with inulin plus Bifidobacterium breve increased fecal butyrate, enhanced intestinal IgA, and decreased lipopolysaccharide-binding protein in participants. These changes correlated with improved cognitive scores and lower systemic inflammation, but only in APOE ε4 non-carriers. In mice, antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion abolished the benefits of inulin on hippocampal neurogenesis, while fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors restored them. Together, these findings position dietary fiber, APOE genotype, and gut microbial metabolites as interacting determinants of brain health, suggesting that precision prebiotic strategies may mitigate neurodegeneration.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbiota modulate central nervous system immune tone and neurotransmitter synthesis, but whether microbial manipulation alters depressive symptoms in humans remains uncertain. In a double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiled fecal microbiota, while functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) assessed prefrontal cortex and hippocampus responses during an emotional face task. Circulating interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, and PERMANOVA with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction compared microbial composition. The probiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6 relative to placebo, accompanied by decreased anxiety scores and normalized hippocampal activity. No significant change emerged in depression severity. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome can modulate neuroimmune and affective markers, though clinical benefit may require longer intervention or stratified patient selection.

Disruption of gut microbiota by high-fat diet promotes neuroinflammation and cognitive decline through vagus nerve and systemic immune routes. In mice fed a Western diet, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, diminished short-chain fatty acid production, and elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma. These shifts correlated with lower Bdnf expression and higher Il1b and Tnf transcription in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, butyrate and propionate enhanced Bdnf promoter acetylation and suppressed Nfkb1 activation, while lipopolysaccharide-triggered NLRP3 inflammasome signaling amplified neuroinflammation. Probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus abundance, normalized short-chain fatty acid levels, and reduced neuroinflammation. In patients with Alzheimer's disease, fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors improved cognitive scores and decreased inflammatory cytokines, although responses varied by baseline microbiota composition. In germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from patients, fiber-rich diet increased Akkermansia and butyrate, improved cognitive impairment, and restored Bdnf signaling. Targeting the gut-brain axis with prebiotics or probiotics may therefore offer adjunctive benefit for neurodegenerative disorders. These findings position gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator of neurodegeneration.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the gut microbiome produces short-chain fatty acids that can suppress neuroinflammation, but whether this diet–microbe–brain circuit modifies α-synucleinopathy in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains uncertain. We fed α-synuclein-overexpressing (ASO) mice either standard chow or a fiber-rich diet supplemented with prebiotic inulin. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that inulin expanded Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia and raised fecal butyrate, propionate, and acetate. In the substantia nigra, single-cell RNA sequencing revealed reduced TNF, IL1B, IL6, NLRP3, and CD68 expression and increased BDNF and TREM2 in ASO mice receiving inulin. These transcriptional shifts were accompanied by fewer α-synuclein aggregates and improved motor deficits. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium abundance to butyrate and TREM2 expression. In a pilot patient cohort, gut microbiota composition correlated with constipation severity but not levodopa dose. No change in SNCA mRNA was detected, suggesting post-translational α-synuclein regulation. These findings position prebiotic fiber as a potential modifier of PD progression through microglia-dependent gut–brain signaling.

Consumption of fermented foods rich in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium is associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved depressive symptoms, yet the contribution of host BDNF genotype remains unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with mild-to-moderate major depressive disorder received either a fermented food diet or a high-fiber diet for 10 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma cytokine profiling were performed. Both diets increased gut microbial diversity and short-chain fatty acid production, but only the fermented food diet raised indole-3-lactic acid and reduced interleukin-6. Symptom improvement correlated with microbial composition and was moderated by BDNF genotype: individuals carrying the Val66Met allele showed greater reductions in anhedonia than Val/Val homozygotes. Parallel mouse experiments showed that indole-3-lactic acid crossed the blood-brain barrier and promoted Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. Dietary compliance was assessed with food frequency questionnaires, and associations were tested using linear mixed models. These findings suggest that fermented food intake may alleviate depression through gut microbiota-derived metabolites, with BDNF signaling shaping host response.

Short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals in the gut microbiota tune brain function and BDNF expression along the vagus nerve, linking dietary fiber intake to neuropsychiatric disorders. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, supplementation with inulin increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate in feces, and normalized NR3C1 and BDNF transcripts in the hippocampus. These changes were accompanied by reduced corticosterone and anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transfer from inulin-fed mice into germ-free recipients reproduced the BDNF increase, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. Mechanistically, MCT1-dependent butyrate transport was required for the BDNF response. 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed models identified Clostridium cluster XIVa as a predictor of BDNF expression. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot open-label trial of inulin showed parallel increases in serum butyrate and BDNF methylation changes; baseline microbial diversity correlated with BDNF shifts (Spearman correlation). These findings position microbial metabolites as modulators of BDNF signaling and support prebiotic fiber as a candidate gut-brain intervention.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat diet is increasingly recognized as a modifier of APOE-associated Alzheimer's disease risk, yet the mediating microbial signals remain unresolved. We fed mice carrying the APOE4 allele either a Western diet or standard chow for 16 weeks and profiled gut communities by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Mediation analysis tested whether Lactobacillus abundance and short-chain fatty acids link diet to cognitive impairment. Western diet reduced Bacteroidetes and increased Firmicutes, lowered butyrate, and elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma. These shifts correlated with BDNF suppression in the hippocampus and worse Morris water maze performance. Linear mixed-effects models showed that butyrate explained 31% of the diet effect on BDNF expression. Butyrate supplementation restored BDNF and improved memory, whereas antibiotics abolished the protective effect. In a parallel human cohort, random-effects meta-analysis confirmed the inverse association between butyrate and mild cognitive impairment. These findings position microbial metabolites as tractable mediators of APOE4-dependent neurodegeneration and suggest that dietary and microbial interventions may delay Alzheimer's disease onset.

Higher intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber has been linked to lower systemic inflammation and altered gut microbiota composition, yet whether these shifts produce measurable gut-brain axis signals in Parkinson's disease remains uncertain. We profiled gut microbiota from participants with Parkinson's disease and matched controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Differences in microbial community structure were tested with PERMANOVA, and associations between taxa and short-chain fatty acids were estimated using multivariable linear regression. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila were depleted in cases, whereas Enterobacteriaceae were enriched. Butyrate concentrations correlated inversely with neuroinflammation markers and positively with brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in serum. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented foods may modify gut microbiota-derived butyrate availability, potentially attenuating Parkinson's disease-related neuroinflammation. Levodopa use did not explain the associations. Our results support targeting gut microbiota through diet as a candidate adjunct strategy, though animal and longitudinal studies in humans are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders through lipopolysaccharide-driven cytokine release and reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling in the hippocampus. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received inulin plus probiotics or placebo. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, with higher fecal butyrate and tryptophan metabolites; gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmed short-chain fatty acid shifts. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline factors showed that BDNF expression correlated with butyrate (β = 0.42, P = 0.003), while PERMANOVA detected distinct community composition (R2 = 0.14, P = 0.001). Mediation analysis indicated that microbial shifts explained 31% of cognitive improvement. Circulating interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha decreased, whereas ZO-1 and occludin increased. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated BDNF upregulation and reduced anxiety. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome with prebiotics to modulate BDNF and cytokine signaling in Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Higher gut microbiota capacity for butyrate synthesis tracks with lower neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease, yet whether this relationship is mediated by BDNF expression in the hippocampus has remained uncertain. In a cohort of 128 adults, we quantified fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and BDNF promoter methylation in blood. Mediation analysis adjusted for age, sex, and dietary fiber intake showed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance indirectly associated with cognitive scores through butyrate and BDNF methylation. Random forest classification separated participants with mild cognitive impairment from controls with an AUC of 0.84. The indirect effect remained significant after false discovery rate correction. In mice, Mediterranean diet supplementation increased Roseburia and butyrate, restored BDNF expression, and reduced neuroinflammation. Probiotic administration produced weaker effects than fiber-rich diets. These findings position BDNF as a plausible mediator linking gut microbiota-derived butyrate to brain health and support dietary strategies targeting the microbiome in neurodegenerative disease.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is a plausible modifier of Parkinson's disease risk, but evidence from human populations is limited. Using data from 12,480 adults in a prospective cohort, we examined whether probiotic supplementation was associated with incident Parkinson's disease and whether gut microbiome composition explained this relationship. 16S rRNA gene sequencing characterized Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia, and Bacteroidetes abundance. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, dietary fiber, and levodopa use. Mediation analysis quantified indirect effects through butyrate and propionate. Over 11.2 years, 214 incident cases occurred. Probiotic supplementation was associated with lower Parkinson's disease risk (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58–0.89), and this association was partially mediated by higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate levels. Conversely, Bacteroidetes abundance showed no significant mediation. In mice colonized with gut microbiota from participants, probiotic treatment increased butyrate in the colon and attenuated dopaminergic neuronal loss in the substantia nigra. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may reduce Parkinson's disease risk through microbiome-dependent short-chain fatty acid signaling.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet has been associated with lower depression and anxiety symptoms, yet the microbial and metabolic pathways underlying this relationship remain incompletely defined. In 180 adults, we profiled gut microbiota using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and measured short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan, and GABA. Mediation analysis tested whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bacteroides abundance linked Mediterranean diet scores to brain outcomes. Greater Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and SCFA levels, and lower depressive symptoms. SCFAs were inversely associated with anxiety; GABA showed a positive association with hippocampus volume. Linear regression indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii explained 18% of the variance in depression scores, with SCFAs as a partial mediator. In mice, dietary fiber supplementation increased SCFA production and BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that Mediterranean diet-driven microbial shifts may influence gut-brain axis signaling and depression and anxiety severity, warranting longitudinal and interventional validation.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that reinforce intestinal barrier integrity and dampen neuroinflammation, yet the extent to which these signals shape affect remains unresolved. We examined whether a Mediterranean-style diet enriched in fermentable substrates alters gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid output in adults with subclinical depressive symptoms. Over eight weeks, participants provided stool and serum samples; microbial communities were profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified butyrate, acetate, and propionate. Compared with baseline, the intervention increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. These changes coincided with improved anhedonia scores but not overall depression severity. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly accounted for the association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and anhedonia. The findings support a gut-brain pathway in which diet modulates microbiota-derived metabolites to influence mood symptoms, though controlled trials with longer follow-up are needed.

The gut microbiome shapes BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, yet whether habitual dietary fiber intake modifies this gut-brain pathway in adults remains uncertain. We analyzed fecal microbiota composition, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and BDNF methylation in participants consuming either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet for 12 weeks. Mixed-effects models adjusted for age, body mass index, and antibiotic use. Greater fiber intake correlated with higher Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance and elevated butyrate in the colon. These shifts accompanied lower BDNF promoter methylation and improved depressive symptoms scores, but no change in anxiety. Mediation analysis suggested butyrate explained 28% of the association between fiber and BDNF methylation. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with human microbiota from donors consuming a high-fiber diet, butyrate supplementation recapitulated these epigenetic changes. These findings support a causal role for dietary fiber-responsive gut microbes in regulating BDNF and mood, and suggest that fiber-rich foods may complement existing depression therapies.

Probiotic supplementation can shift gut microbiota composition and increase neuroactive metabolite production, but whether these changes translate into measurable effects on stress-related disorders remains uncertain. We tested a multi-strain probiotic formulation in male mice exposed to chronic restraint stress (CRS) and in healthy adults reporting mild depressive symptoms. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled fecal microbiota and circulating metabolites; random forest analysis identified microbial taxa associated with prefrontal cortex-related behavioral outcomes. In mice, probiotics attenuated CRS-induced body weight loss and reduced immobility time in the forced swimming test, accompanied by higher GABA and short-chain fatty acid levels. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances correlated positively with GABA and negatively with depressive-like behavior. In adults, the same probiotic increased butyrate-producing bacteria and improved self-reported mood scores over 8 weeks. These findings suggest that probiotic-driven microbiota remodeling may contribute to stress resilience through microbial metabolite signaling along the gut-brain axis. Further clinical validation is needed.

Sustained intake of a low-fiber diet depletes gut microbial diversity and increases susceptibility to cognitive impairment, but the causal microbial and metabolic mediators remain unclear. To test whether microbiota from humans consuming high- versus low-fiber diets differentially affect brain function, we colonized gnotobiotic mice with donor microbiota. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation showed that low-fiber microbiota reduced Bacteroidetes, expanded Proteobacteria, and lowered short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. The low-fiber microbiota also compromised intestinal barrier integrity and increased circulating endotoxin. Notably, shotgun metagenomics identified reduced butyrate synthesis genes in the low-fiber group, and these findings were replicated in an independent mouse cohort. Linear mixed-effects models associated these shifts with impaired spatial memory and elevated neuroinflammation. Oral SCFA supplementation rescued memory deficits, restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and normalized IL-1β expression. These results suggest that dietary fiber deficiency promotes cognitive decline through microbiota-derived SCFA depletion, and that fiber or SCFA supplementation may mitigate gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber, particularly short-chain fatty acids, modulate neuroinflammation and behavioral phenotypes through the gut-brain axis. In a randomized human trial, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behavior scores, but only in participants with low baseline microbial diversity. We used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics to profile fecal microbiota, and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry to quantify tryptophan metabolites. TLR4 and IL-6 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells correlated with indole-3-propionic acid levels. Mice colonized with human donor microbiota confirmed that probiotic responsiveness depended on aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling. In these animals, probiotic attenuated sickness behavior induced by lipopolysaccharide and restored BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced the metabolite profile and behavioral deficits. These findings suggest that probiotic efficacy in stress-related disorders is stratified by baseline microbiome configuration and metabolite output, informing precision microbial therapeutics.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape hippocampal plasticity through immune and endocrine routes, yet whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation amplifies these signals in APOE4 carriers remains unresolved. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild cognitive impairment, 24-week omega-3 supplementation increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundances and elevated butyrate in fecal microbiota. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics quantified microbial and metabolite profiles. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community composition by treatment and APOE4 status (R2 = 0.11, P = 0.002). Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate mediated 31% of the effect of omega-3 on cognitive composite scores. Random forest classification separated APOE4 carriers from non-carriers with an area under the curve of 0.82. In knock-in mice carrying APOE4, omega-3 rescued memory deficits and reduced interleukin-6 in prefrontal cortex; these effects were abolished by antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion. These findings position omega-3 as a APOE4-dependent modulator of the gut microbiome-brain axis and support Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia as candidate biomarkers.

Microbial butyrate production and GPR43-dependent signaling influence BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota to depressive symptoms. To test whether dietary fibers can engage this pathway, adults with low mood consumed inulin-type fructans or placebo daily for 12 weeks in a double-blind randomized trial. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance and raised plasma butyrate. BDNF and NR3C1 transcripts in whole blood rose over the intervention period, whereas interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein fell. FKBP5 methylation remained unchanged. Fecal propionate and acetate also increased modestly, but only butyrate correlated with BDNF changes. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Faecalibacterium gains correlated with reduced anxiety and depression scores, independently of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use. In this cohort, these data suggest that prebiotic fiber supplementation may modify BDNF signaling and gut microbial ecology, providing a dietary strategy for mood disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) constrain neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the responsible taxa and host pathways remain unresolved. We profiled gut microbiota and fecal SCFAs in mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and control mice using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. β-diversity separated diseased mice from controls, and Spearman correlation linked Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae with butyrate and propionate. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice with high SCFA levels into mice with EAE reduced demyelination and central inflammatory infiltration, lowered IL-17, and increased IL-10 in serum and spinal cord. These effects were accompanied by Foxp3 induction and Hdac inhibition in mesenteric lymph nodes. Parallel flow cytometry revealed expanded Foxp3+ regulatory T cells, and linear mixed models confirmed that butyrate levels predicted EAE severity. Sodium butyrate supplementation reproduced protection, whereas broad-spectrum antibiotics abolished it. Our findings position gut microbiota-derived SCFA production as a tractable target for MS, with Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae as candidate probiotic or prebiotic sources.

Supplementation with probiotics can reduce depressive symptoms and anxiety by reshaping the gut microbiota and its neuroactive metabolites, yet the added value of postbiotics remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with major depressive disorder received a multi-strain probiotic, a postbiotic blend, or placebo. Fecal samples were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and circulating short-chain fatty acids, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and interleukin-6 were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Both active interventions increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance and reduced anxiety scores compared with placebo; however, the postbiotic group showed greater improvement in depressive symptoms and higher butyrate levels. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial shifts explained 31% of the clinical response, and decreases in interleukin-6 correlated with symptom relief. No serious adverse events were reported. These findings support probiotics and postbiotics as adjunctive strategies for targeting gut microbiota in mood disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but whether dietary fiber or probiotic supplementation can reverse this trajectory remains uncertain. We randomized APP/PS1 mice to receive a prebiotic oligofructose supplement, a Lactobacillus rhamnosus probiotic, or vehicle for 16 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance after both supplements. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Lactobacillus as the strongest discriminator between treated and control groups. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia to lower amyloid-β burden in the hippocampus, while random forest classification predicted neuroinflammation from microbial community profiles with 82% accuracy. Immunoblotting showed reduced GFAP and Iba1 expression in cortex, and Morris water maze testing demonstrated improved spatial memory. Levels of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α were reduced in colon and serum. These findings indicate that prebiotic and probiotic interventions reshape the gut microbiome and attenuate AD-related neuroinflammation, supporting microbiota-targeted strategies for AD.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that shape microglial maturation and may modify Parkinson's disease (PD) risk. In a human cohort, higher intake of fiber-rich foods correlated with elevated Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance in the gut microbiome, but not with SNCA genotype. Using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis, we tested whether microbial butyrate production mediated the association between dietary fiber and constipation, a prodromal PD feature. Faecalibacterium abundance explained 18% of the total effect (indirect β = 0.14, 95% CI 0.05–0.23), whereas GBA1 variant status modified the direct effect. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, a high-fiber diet increased Lachnospiraceae and reduced nigral dopamine loss; this protection was attenuated in Nlrp3-knockout mice. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics further linked bile acid derivatives to BDNF expression in the striatum. These findings position diet as a modifiable input to the gut-brain axis and support targeting microbial metabolites in PD.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life shapes brain circuits that regulate stress reactivity and cognition, and disruption of this dialogue has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild depression, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 supplementation for 8 weeks reduced depressive symptoms and increased gut microbial diversity. The probiotic group showed higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids compared with baseline. These microbial shifts correlated with increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood and improved neuropsychological test scores. Dietary intake was assessed with a Mediterranean diet score; higher fiber consumption at baseline predicted greater microbiota response to probiotic treatment. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability partially explained the association between Lactobacillus abundance and BDNF expression. Our findings indicate that probiotic supplementation, especially in the context of adequate dietary fiber, may modulate microbiota-gut-brain axis signaling and support mood improvement, though larger trials are needed to confirm whether these effects depend on baseline microbiome composition.

Trauma-related gut dysbiosis is increasingly linked to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), but whether microbial shifts track with BDNF signaling and cytokine markers in Veterans remains uncertain. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 140 US Veterans using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and measured serotonin, interleukin-6, and BDNF in plasma. PERMANOVA showed that PTSD diagnosis explained 7.1% of microbial variance after adjustment for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use, fiber intake, and age. Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted in PTSD, whereas Bacteroides was enriched. These taxa correlated with lower BDNF and higher interleukin-6 (Spearman correlation). A random forest classifier distinguished PTSD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.78. In mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-PTSD symptom donors induced anhedonia and reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. Probiotic administration partially normalized Bdnf and interleukin-6 levels. Our findings link trauma-related gut dysbiosis to BDNF-dependent brain signaling and support interventions targeting the gut microbiome for stress-related disorders.

Microbial dysbiosis along the gut-brain axis contributes to major depressive disorder and anxiety, with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances correlating inversely with symptom severity. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with moderate depression received either a probiotic supplement or placebo alongside habitual diets. The probiotic group showed greater reductions in depressive symptoms and increased gut microbial diversity; these changes were associated with elevated short-chain fatty acid production and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels. Dietary patterns also mattered: higher intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber predicted better response, whereas processed food consumption attenuated benefits. 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic profiling revealed that responders harbored enriched butyrate synthesis genes and tryptophan metabolism genes. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial shifts partially mediated the intervention's effect on depression scores. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders transferred behavioral resilience, implicating the vagus nerve as a key pathway. These findings support targeted probiotic and fermented food strategies as adjunctive approaches for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Altered gut microbiota composition precedes and possibly accelerates mild cognitive impairment, but the therapeutic value of restoring gut microbiota remains debated. We conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment who received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Cognition was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, PERMANOVA compared microbial community structures, and mediation analysis explored whether butyrate mediated cognitive change. At baseline, gut microbiota diversity correlated inversely with interleukin-6 and cognitive impairment severity. Relative to placebo, probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered C-reactive protein; these differences remained after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Participants receiving probiotic showed greater improvement in cognitive impairment scores, with butyrate changes explaining part of the effect. These results support gut microbiota modulation as a promising adjunctive strategy for mild cognitive impairment.

Consumption of blueberries and other polyphenol-rich fruits can reshape gut microbiota composition and attenuate neuroinflammation in major depressive disorder (MDD). In mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress, dietary supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids in the colon, and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation into the circulation. These microbial shifts were accompanied by lower TLR4 and NFKB1 expression in the hippocampus, higher BDNF transcripts, and decreased IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations. 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR revealed that probiotic co-administration further enriched Bifidobacterium and normalized serotonin metabolism along the gut-brain axis. In patients with MDD, baseline gut microbiome diversity correlated inversely with inflammatory cytokines; mixed-effects models indicated that fiber-rich foods predicted greater butyrate production and improved depression severity. These findings position dietary polyphenols and fermentable fiber as accessible modulators of BDNF signaling and microbiota-immune crosstalk, warranting randomized trials. Future longitudinal studies should test whether these microbiome and metabolite changes mediate clinical improvement.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by gut microbiota modulate hippocampal and prefrontal cortical circuits implicated in anxiety and depression, yet causal evidence from dietary interventions in humans is limited. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, adults with moderate anxiety received inulin-type fructans plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified gut microbial composition, resting-state functional MRI assessed amygdala-prefrontal cortex connectivity, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay measured cortisol, interleukin-6, and BDNF. Linear mixed-effects models showed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and reduced anxiety symptoms compared with placebo. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in Bifidobacterium abundance partially mediated the intervention effect on anxiety via reduced cortisol. Spearman correlations linked interleukin-6 decreases to improved depressive symptoms. Plasma SCFA concentrations rose only in the active arm, and no serious adverse events occurred. These findings support targeted prebiotic and probiotic strategies for gut-brain modulation, though longer trials are needed to confirm durability.

Microbial colonization of the gut exerts a regulatory influence on brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and disrupted gut microbiota composition has been linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with moderate depressive symptoms received either multi-strain probiotics or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples revealed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in the probiotic group. These shifts coincided with higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations and lower plasma cortisol, alongside reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression and increased BDNF transcripts in peripheral blood. Mixed-effects models showed a greater reduction in depression scores after probiotic treatment than after placebo. Changes in serotonin metabolites and tryptophan hydroxylase expression were also examined, but the most robust signal involved BDNF. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may modulate the gut-brain axis by altering microbial taxa and host inflammatory gene expression, supporting further investigation of probiotics as adjunctive therapy for depression.

Converging evidence indicates that gut microbiota composition modulates central nervous system function through short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and immune signaling, yet the extent to which ordinary dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation produce clinically meaningful brain effects remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or the same diet plus a multi-strain probiotic. Microbial community profiles were assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and hippocampal activity was measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging. Compared with diet alone, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate concentrations, and improved verbal memory scores.
