Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with reduced amygdala reactivity to negative food cues. Mixed-effects models further linked higher butyrate with lower interleukin-6 and greater BDNF expression. These findings suggest that probiotic co-administration with a plant-rich diet may amplify microbiota-dependent gut-brain signaling in older adults, though larger trials are needed.

Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by gut bacteria exerts far-reaching effects on brain function, yet the dietary and statistical frameworks needed to translate associative findings into causal mechanisms remain unsettled. In rodent models, depletion of the gut microbiota alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, while supplementation with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium attenuates anxiety-like behavior and depressive-like behavior. Human studies report similar associations between gut microbial composition and major depressive disorder, but most rely on cross-sectional designs and 16S rRNA gene sequencing without functional validation. A meta-analysis of adults found no consistent alpha-diversity difference in major depressive disorder, although heterogeneity across cohorts was substantial. Dietary patterns rich in fermented foods and fiber-rich plant foods, such as the Mediterranean diet, may increase short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, and modulate serotonin and tryptophan metabolism. Probiotics and prebiotics show promise as adjunctive strategies, but effect sizes vary and antidepressant interactions remain poorly characterized. Future trials should combine metagenomics with mediation analysis to test whether diet-driven shifts in gut bacteria causally influence psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

Depletion of butyrate-producing taxa in the gut microbiome precedes amyloid-β accumulation in the hippocampus and memory decline, suggesting that diet-driven microbial metabolites buffer early Alzheimer's disease pathology. In a longitudinal cohort of 128 cognitively normal adults, dietary fiber intake was inversely associated with mild cognitive impairment conversion, an effect partially mediated by gut microbiome composition. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted in converters, whereas Escherichia expanded. Fecal butyrate correlated with lower IL-6 and TNF-α and higher BDNF expression in prefrontal cortex biopsies from a nested autopsy subset. In mice fed a high-fat diet, oral butyrate restored Bdnf and suppressed Nlrp3 in the hippocampus, attenuating amyloid-β deposition. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial butyrate synthesis explained 31% of the fiber-cognition association. Parallel fecal metagenomics confirmed reduced butyrate production in converters, and linear mixed-effects models showed that each 5-g increase in dietary fiber predicted slower cognitive decline. These findings position BDNF and NLRP3 as diet-sensitive nodes linking gut microbiota to Alzheimer's disease risk.

Daily intake of fermented milk fortified with inulin reshapes the gut microbiome and dampens neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD). In APP/PS1 mice, this regimen expanded Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, elevated butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid, and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics linked these shifts to suppressed NLRP3 and IL-1β expression in the hippocampus, alongside improved Morris water maze performance. RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex revealed downregulation of TLR4, MYD88, and NF-κB signaling, while Spearman correlation associated Akkermansia abundance with indole-3-propionic acid and amyloid-beta burden. In a pilot human cohort, the same fermented milk plus inulin intervention raised BDNF and lowered inflammatory cytokines in plasma. Fecal microbiota profiles showed enriched Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, which correlated with short-chain fatty acid production and reduced cognitive impairment. These findings suggest that combining fermented milk with inulin may provide a practical strategy for modulating the gut-brain axis and slowing AD progression and amyloid pathology.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition precede motor and cognitive symptoms in Parkinson's disease, suggesting that microbial signals actively shape nigrostriatal pathology rather than merely accompanying it. In mice and human cohorts, depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium correlates with reduced short-chain fatty acid production, impaired BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, and increased lipopolysaccharide-driven TLR4 signaling. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into germ-free mice reproduces motor deficits, while probiotic and prebiotic supplementation restores gut microbiota diversity and lowers IL-6 transcription. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics reveal strain-specific effects, yet causal pathways remain unresolved. Additionally, levodopa response varies with gut microbiome composition, and high-fat diet exacerbates inflammatory cytokines through enteric nervous system signaling. Notably, Mendelian randomization supports a causal link between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and Parkinson's disease risk, independent of LRRK2 mutation status. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable node in the gut-brain axis and support targeted psychobiotics for neurodegenerative disorders.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) sustain intestinal barrier integrity and tune brain immune signaling, yet how dietary fiber availability reshapes this axis in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. We randomized adults with MDD to a high-fiber diet or low-fiber diet for 8 weeks and profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Dietary fiber increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and downregulated NF-κB and IL6 expression. Fecal calprotectin and circulating lipopolysaccharide fell only in the high-fiber diet arm, paralleling GPR43 and occludin induction in colonic mucosa. Mixed-effects models linked these shifts to reduced depressive symptoms and improved anxiety scores. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with responder microbiota from human donors, fecal microbiota transplantation reproduced Bdnf upregulation in hippocampus and serotonin turnover. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable determinant of microbiome-brain signaling and support prebiotic strategies for MDD.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression in the hippocampus and modulates anxiety-like behavior through short-chain fatty acid-dependent signaling. In mice exposed to chronic stress, gut microbiota depletion lowered butyrate and indole derivatives, reduced BDNF and tight junction protein ZO-1 transcripts, and increased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in the prefrontal cortex. Reconstitution with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum restored butyrate production and normalized BDNF expression. Probiotic supplementation and prebiotic fiber were tested in a randomized adult cohort; omega-3 fatty acids served as an active comparator. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed models showed that prebiotic fiber increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance and reduced depressive symptoms scores. Germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder displayed reduced BDNF and altered serotonin and kynurenine turnover. These findings position BDNF and microbial metabolites as mechanistic nodes linking gut microbiota and brain function, supporting probiotic and prebiotic interventions for stress-related disorders.

Gut microbial short-chain fatty acid production is increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk, yet whether dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids modify this relationship through APOE-dependent pathways remains uncertain. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 180 older adults, including 60 with mild cognitive impairment, 60 with AD, and 60 cognitively normal controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and cognitive decline; PERMANOVA assessed community composition, and mediation analysis examined whether butyrate explained these links. Higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with greater butyrate levels and better cognitive performance, and this association was stronger in APOE ε4 non-carriers. Omega-3 supplementation was associated with increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. In mice, omega-3 also attenuated inflammation in the hippocampus and upregulated Bdnf expression. Random forest classification modestly separated AD from controls using microbiome features. These findings suggest that APOE genotype and omega-3 intake jointly shape gut microbiota composition relevant to AD progression.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids influence central nervous system immune homeostasis, yet the dietary and microbial determinants of this axis remain incompletely resolved in Parkinson's disease (PD). We profiled patients with PD and matched controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, then applied mediation analysis to test whether gut bacterial taxa link dietary fiber intake to motor severity. Fiber-rich diets were associated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, elevated butyrate, and lower inflammatory markers. In contrast, processed food consumption correlated with Prevotellaceae expansion and reduced propionate. Mendelian randomization suggested a causal protective effect of Faecalibacterium on PD risk, partially mediated by butyrate. Among levodopa-treated patients, the Faecalibacterium–butyrate axis explained a significant fraction of variance in constipation severity, a common PD comorbidity. These findings implicate modifiable diet-microbiota interactions in PD pathogenesis and support fiber supplementation or probiotic supplementation as adjunctive strategies. Longitudinal validation in larger independent cohorts is warranted.

Disruption of the gut microbiota can precede behavioral deficits in depression, suggesting that microbial signals contribute causally to brain dysfunction rather than merely reflecting it. In mice exposed to chronic stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide and decreased short-chain fatty acids in feces. Supplementation with probiotics or prebiotic fiber restored Lactobacillus levels, lowered corticosterone, and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors into naïve mice reproduced social avoidance, whereas transplantation from supplemented donors did not. PERMANOVA of 16S rRNA profiling confirmed distinct microbial communities across groups (R2 = 0.21, p = 0.001), and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability explained part of the behavioral effect. In humans with major depressive disorder, similar reductions in Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus have been associated with lower quality of life. These findings position probiotics and prebiotics as modifiable inputs to microbiota-gut-brain signaling and support targeting microbial metabolites in stress-related disorders.

Gut microbial composition influences Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk through immune, metabolic, and neural routes, yet the extent to which APOE4 status modifies this relationship remains unresolved. In a cohort of 120 older adults, participants with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD showed lower gut microbiota diversity and enriched Escherichia/Shigella compared with cognitively normal controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures by APOE4 carrier status. Curcumin supplementation for 12 weeks increased Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium, reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores in individuals lacking APOE4 but not in carriers. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate, correlated with cognitive gains. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained part of the cognitive benefit. Plasma lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 were elevated in AD and inversely associated with butyrate. APOE4 carriers exhibited blunted microbial shifts and weaker short-chain fatty acid responses to curcumin. These findings suggest that curcumin may support the microbiota-gut-brain axis in a genotype-dependent manner, with APOE4 shaping responsiveness.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids attenuated lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation and restored Bdnf expression in the hippocampus of adult male C57BL/6J mice, yet the microbial signals coupling this benefit to central immune regulation remain poorly defined. We tested whether a 6-week dietary intervention with omega-3 plus inulin altered cecal microbiota composition, short-chain fatty acid production, and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the gut and brain. Mice received either the supplemented diet or an isocaloric control. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance after supplementation. PERMANOVA confirmed distinct microbial communities, while Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium with reduced Il6 and Tnf expression in the prefrontal cortex. Supplemented mice also showed lower anxiety-like behavior and higher Bdnf expression than controls. Fecal calprotectin and serum interleukin-6 were lower in supplemented mice; linear mixed-effects models showed that Bifidobacterium abundance predicted Bdnf expression after adjusting for baseline body weight. These findings suggest that omega-3 and inulin co-supplementation may improve neuroinflammation-associated behavioral outcomes through microbiota-dependent pathways.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone and synaptic plasticity, yet their contribution to major depressive disorder (MDD) remains poorly defined. We profiled fecal microbiota and SCFAs in 120 adults with MDD and 90 healthy controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted in patients, and lower butyrate correlated with symptom severity. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the association between Roseburia abundance and depression scores. In mice subjected to chronic stress, butyrate supplementation normalized Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced proinflammatory cytokines. Notably, fluoxetine increased Roseburia abundance, whereas microbiota depletion attenuated its behavioral benefit. Dietary fiber-rich foods intake was lower in patients and inversely correlated with MDD severity; fiber supplementation in mice increased Roseburia and butyrate. Transfer of patient microbiota into mice reproduced depressive-like behavior and reduced Bdnf in the prefrontal cortex. These findings link Roseburia-derived butyrate to Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that targeting the gut microbiome may complement antidepressant therapy in MDD.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids generated from dietary fiber by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and other gut microbiota help calibrate central nervous system immune tone, yet how this axis contributes to depression remains uncertain. We integrated shotgun metagenomics with host BDNF genotyping in 312 adults and applied mediation analysis to estimate indirect effects. No significant differences were found in alpha diversity, but beta diversity differed by depression status (PERMANOVA, p=0.01). Higher abundances of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus correlated with elevated fecal butyrate and lower anxiety scores. The BDNF Val66Met polymorphism moderated this relationship: Met carriers showed stronger inverse associations between butyrate and depressive symptoms than Val/Val individuals. In a subset, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high butyrate levels into germ-free mice increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that fermented foods and fiber-rich diets may enhance gut microbial community butyrate production, but host BDNF genotype shapes the neurobehavioral response. Targeting this gut-brain signaling may inform personalized interventions for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone, and their depletion is increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory disorders. In a mouse model of chronic stress, fermented fiber-rich diet supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance in the gut microbiome, elevated butyrate in feces, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus. Behavioral testing showed improved anxiety-like behavior and spatial memory. Taxonomic profiling further revealed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Prevotella copri in treated animals. Serum lipopolysaccharide was lower, while brain-derived neurotrophic factor was higher in the prefrontal cortex. To account for repeated measures and inter-individual variability, linear mixed-effects models were fitted, with false discovery rate correction for taxonomic comparisons. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained part of the diet-related reduction in IL-6. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmed taxonomic and metabolic shifts. These findings support a microbiota-gut-brain axis mechanism in which fermented foods may buffer stress-related neuroinflammation, though validation in humans remains necessary.

Microbial colonization of the neonatal gut shapes hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity, with BDNF expression in the hippocampus serving as a sensitive readout of early-life microbiota status. In mice exposed to maternal separation, dietary supplementation with inulin restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, increased fecal butyrate, and normalized serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that inulin attenuated depression-like behavior and reduced anxiety-like behavior relative to vehicle-treated mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice to germ-free mice recapitulated these behavioral and neurochemical changes, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-propionate mediated the relationship between gut microbiota composition and BDNF expression. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower fecal butyrate correlated with reduced BDNF and altered microbiota composition. Notably, GPR41 and GPR43 expression in enteroendocrine cells increased after inulin treatment, linking short-chain fatty acid signaling to vagal afferents. These findings suggest that inulin may act through a gut-brain axis involving microbial metabolites to modulate stress-related disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production are increasingly linked to anxiety, depression, and cognitive decline, yet interventions that reliably modulate this communication remain limited. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received Bifidobacterium breve plus galacto-oligosaccharides or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing of fecal samples revealed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside reduced Proteobacteria. Functional metagenomic profiling showed enrichment of pathways for butyrate synthesis and tryptophan metabolism. These microbial shifts correlated with lower interleukin-6 and cortisol levels and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) increased in the synbiotic group, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells was upregulated. Fecal calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein also declined, suggesting reduced intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation. The findings indicate that targeted synbiotic supplementation can reshape gut microbial communities and improve cognitive impairment, supporting further fecal microbiota transplantation and metabolomic studies to identify causal mediators.

Gut microbiota composition predicts amyloid-β burden and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the microbial taxa that mediate these effects remain incompletely defined. We colonized APP/PS1 mice with fecal slurries from patients with AD and healthy controls, then treated subsets with probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or vehicle for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and ITS amplicon sequencing profiled the gut microbiome; Morris water maze and immunofluorescence assessed hippocampal function and amyloid plaques. PERMANOVA revealed donor-dependent microbial shifts, and linear mixed-effects models linked Prevotella and Bacteroides abundances to plaque load. Fecal metabolomics further showed that probiotic supplementation restored butyrate levels and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Probiotic treatment also reduced Enterobacteriaceae, increased Lactobacillus, and attenuated memory impairment relative to vehicle. Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids correlated with TREM2 and APOE expression in prefrontal cortex, and mediation analysis suggested that Prevotella effects were partly indirect. These findings indicate that targeting gut microbial communities with probiotics may modify AD progression, though APOE genotype-dependent responses warrant further study.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence gut-brain signaling, but whether direct butyrate supplementation mimics the metabolic and immune effects of fiber-rich foods is uncertain. In an 8-week randomized trial, adults with mild depression received either sodium butyrate or placebo while consuming a high-fiber diet. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and fecal SCFA concentrations were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions. Fecal and blood samples were collected at baseline and week 8. Butyrate supplementation increased butyrate availability and enriched Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, whereas Bacteroidetes abundance fell. Participants receiving butyrate showed greater reductions in depressive symptoms and lower C-reactive protein than controls. These changes correlated with increased SCFA production and microbial diversity. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) increased only in the butyrate group. The findings suggest that butyrate supplementation may complement fiber-rich diets to modulate the gut-brain axis and improve depression-related outcomes, though larger trials are needed.

Gut microbiota-derived metabolites shape central nervous system function, yet the extent to which dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids modify this dialogue in neurodevelopmental disorders remains uncertain. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received omega-3 supplementation or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Cognitive flexibility and depressive symptoms were assessed. Associations were tested using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline values. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures between groups. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated butyrate concentrations. These shifts correlated with improved hippocampal-dependent memory and reduced anxiety scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained the cognitive benefit. No changes occurred in BDNF plasma levels. The findings indicate that omega-3 supplementation can remodel the gut microbiome and may support brain health, although confirmatory studies in animal models are needed.

Gut microbiota depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila tracks with neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in obesity, but whether dietary context modifies this axis remains unresolved. In a cohort of 240 adults, we paired high-fat/high-sugar diet recalls with fecal microbiome sequencing and plasma inflammatory cytokines. Using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis, we found that high-fat/high-sugar diet adherence was associated with lower BDNF and higher interleukin-6; these relationships were partially mediated by Faecalibacterium abundance. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance further linked Mediterranean diet adherence to enriched Roseburia and Eubacterium. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, correlated positively with BDNF and inversely with interleukin-6 in participants. Mice transplanted with human microbiota from high-fat/high-sugar diet donors showed increased anxiety-like behavior and reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Supplementation with inulin restored Akkermansia, lowered lipopolysaccharide, and normalized BDNF. These associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex. These data position gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator linking diet to mood and cognitive dysfunction.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate brain function, yet whether these metabolites causally influence depression remains debated. We integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, mediation analysis, and Mendelian randomization in adults reporting depressive symptoms and in mice fed a low-fiber diet. Lower Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance correlated with reduced butyrate and higher IL-6 expression; BDNF expression was lower in the hippocampus. Mediation models indicated that butyrate explained 22% of the association between gut microbiota composition and depressive symptoms. In mice, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored BDNF and normalized IL-6, but only when fermentable fiber was present; inulin alone had no effect. Neither fluoxetine nor inulin alone altered serotonin turnover, whereas the combination increased tryptophan availability and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mendelian randomization supported a protective role for butyrate-producing microbiota on depression risk. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and gut microbiota-derived metabolites jointly regulate BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, offering a tractable target for depression.

Depletion of the gut microbiota in germ-free mice alters BDNF and serotonin signaling in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, paralleling anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. To test whether restoring the microbiota reverses these effects, adult male C57BL/6 mice were colonized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Bifidobacterium longum and assessed after chronic unpredictable stress. The gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and expression of cfos, BDNF, and 5-HT1A receptor was quantified using quantitative PCR. Linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction showed that L. rhamnosus reduced anxiety-like behavior and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus, whereas B. longum attenuated depressive-like behavior and increased serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with symptom severity by Spearman correlation. Effects were region-specific and independent of body weight, with permutation analysis confirming network-level changes. These findings indicate that specific commensal bacteria modulate brain circuits and may guide probiotic strategies for mood disorders.

Supplementation with resistant starch reshapes gut microbiota and elevates butyrate availability in the colon, yet whether these changes translate into altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus remains uncertain. We colonized germ-free mice with Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, then exposed them to chronic stress. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics quantified microbial composition and short-chain fatty acids. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between butyrate, BDNF, NR3C1, and depressive-like behavior. Mediation analysis assessed whether butyrate mediated the microbiota effects on BDNF. Mice receiving resistant starch showed higher colonic butyrate, reduced neuroinflammation, and increased BDNF and NR3C1 expression in the hippocampus compared with controls. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 38% of the microbiota effect on BDNF. These findings link resistant starch-driven microbiota shifts to BDNF regulation and suggest a tractable dietary route for modulating gut-brain axis signaling in stress-related disorders. Parallel analyses in patients with major depressive disorder revealed lower BDNF and NR3C1 transcripts in prefrontal cortex. Together, these data position butyrate as a mediator of microbiota-BDNF interactions and support resistant starch as a candidate prebiotic intervention.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by early-life microbiota disruption may contribute to autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), yet causal mediators remain uncertain. In a Mendelian randomization analysis of adults and children, we integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing with metagenomics and host BDNF, IL-6, and SHANK3 expression. Greater abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus was associated with higher short-chain fatty acid production and reduced neuroinflammation, whereas Clostridium expansion correlated with tryptophan metabolite shifts and worse behavioral scores. Consumption of fermented foods and fiber-rich foods, but not Western-style diet, predicted beneficial gut microbiome profiles; probiotic supplementation enhanced these effects in mice. In fecal samples from patients with PD, Akkermansia and Enterococcus were enriched, and PERMANOVA revealed compositional differences after adjustment for age and sex. Mediation models indicated that butyrate and BDNF signaling partially explained the association between microbial composition and ASD-related traits. These findings support dietary and microbial interventions targeting the gut-brain axis, but strain-specific and longitudinal clinical validation is needed before clinical translation.

Dietary probiotics and fermented foods can reshape the gut microbiome and attenuate depression and anxiety, yet the microbial functions that mediate these effects remain poorly resolved. We tested whether a 12-week intervention with a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus plantarum and prebiotic fiber altered fecal metagenomes and brain correlates in stressed adults. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and Shannon diversity analysis, we found that recipients of the probiotic maintained microbial diversity, whereas placebo recipients showed a significant decline. Probiotic supplementation enriched Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Bifidobacterium longum, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced Roseburia faecis. It also increased predicted short-chain fatty acids, gamma-aminobutyric acid, and tryptophan metabolites. In parallel, mice receiving ginsenoside Rk3 showed reduced depression-like behavior, lower neuronal apoptosis, and restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. These findings indicate that probiotic and ginseng-derived interventions modulate gut microbiota-neuroactive metabolite axes to promote stress resilience. Our data further suggest that microbial diversity and functional gene shifts, rather than single taxa, may underlie the beneficial effects.

Microbial butyrate is increasingly recognized as a critical mediator of gut microbiota-brain communication, and its depletion correlates with neuroinflammation, mild cognitive impairment, and altered BDNF signaling. Among 312 community-dwelling adults, we profiled fecal microbiota via shotgun metagenomics, quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and measured BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, education, and dietary fiber intake showed that higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance predicted greater butyrate concentrations and lower odds of cognitive impairment (β = 0.24, p = 0.002). Causal mediation analysis estimated that butyrate accounted for 28% of this relationship. In mice consuming a high-fat diet, inulin supplementation enriched butyrate-producing taxa, upregulated Bdnf mRNA in the hippocampus, and attenuated anxiety-like behavior. Notably, carriers of the FTO risk allele exhibited weaker microbiota-cognition associations, suggesting genetic moderation. These data support a model in which diet-driven microbial butyrate production modulates BDNF and cognitive decline risk, offering a tractable target for microbiome-directed therapies.

Consumption of fermentable fiber selectively expands Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, increasing short-chain fatty acid production and strengthening intestinal barrier integrity, but whether this cascade alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus during chronic stress is unclear. In male and female C57BL/6 mice exposed to unpredictable chronic mild stress, a high-fat, low-fiber diet increased anxiety-like behavior and reduced BDNF mRNA, whereas supplementation with inulin plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reversed these deficits. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin enriched Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii; mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 38% of the BDNF increase. Neither inulin nor L. rhamnosus GG altered BDNF in prefrontal cortex, indicating regional specificity. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia abundance to BDNF and anxiety-like behavior. Probiotic alone restored BDNF but did not normalize corticosterone. These preclinical findings position dietary fiber and probiotics as complementary gut-brain modulators and suggest that BDNF is a convergent target for interventions targeting the gut microbiota in stress-related disorders.

Microbial signals from the gastrointestinal tract can shape brain function, and gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety. We tested whether a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods and dietary fiber could alter microbial composition and depressive symptoms in adults with mild-to-moderate depression. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants received either the active diet or a habitual diet control. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing quantified gut microbial taxonomy and functional pathways, while liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry measured short-chain fatty acids in plasma. The active diet increased microbial diversity, raised taxa that produce butyrate, and reduced depression scores compared with control. Changes in butyrate correlated with improved depressive symptoms, suggesting that diet-driven microbiome remodeling may support gut-brain axis signaling. Although the effect size was modest, the coupling between microbial shifts and improved depressive symptoms supports a contributing role for gut microbiota in depression. These findings warrant larger trials combining metagenomics with neuroimaging to confirm causality.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans reshapes gut microbiota and modulates central nervous system signaling along the gut-brain axis. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of adults with major depressive disorder, 8 weeks of inulin (10 g/day) increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance, reduced Proteobacteria, and lowered interleukin-6 and cortisol versus placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed enriched microbial genes for short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. Linear mixed-effects models showed that microbial shifts explained 31% of the variance in depressive symptoms; PERMANOVA confirmed distinct gut microbiota composition between groups. Spearman correlation linked Faecalibacterium abundance to reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and improved anxiety scores. Transfer of post-treatment fecal microbiota into germ-free mice attenuated depressive-like behavior and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus, as assessed by forced swim test and quantitative PCR. These findings position inulin as a potential adjunctive antidepressant strategy that targets gut microbiota-brain communication, though larger trials are needed.

Gut microbiota metabolism of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate intestinal barrier integrity, vagal signaling, and central nervous system inflammation, positioning the microbiome as a tractable target for neuropsychiatric disorders. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 72 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) concentrations, and depressive symptoms were assessed. Between-group differences were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The diet group showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus counts, elevated BDNF, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo. Changes in Lactobacillus correlated with BDNF increases. Circulating interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide decreased in the diet arm, and Spearman correlations linked these reductions to Lactobacillus enrichment. These findings suggest that fermented food-rich dietary patterns may improve depressive symptoms via microbiota-BDNF pathways, though confirmatory studies are needed.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes BDNF expression and serotonin signaling within the central nervous system, linking gut microbiota composition to affective behavior. In a randomized controlled adult trial, daily probiotic supplementation combined with fermented foods increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, reduced interleukin-6, and improved depressive symptoms scores compared with a low-fiber control. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that responders had higher baseline Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium, whereas non-responders showed elevated Bacteroides. These microbial shifts also correlated with decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation and significantly increased short-chain fatty acid production. In mice, prebiotic inulin rescued stress-induced reductions in BDNF and NR3C1 expression in the hippocampus. In parallel, butyrate and propionate suppressed NF-κB activation in brain, and cortisol rhythms normalized only in human participants with increased Faecalibacterium. Together, these findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through probiotics and dietary fiber may modulate BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity and offer adjunctive strategies for stress-related disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat, low-fiber diets is increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, yet the molecular routes remain incompletely defined. In mice fed a Western diet, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide translocation across the intestinal epithelium. This endotoxemia coincided with lower BDNF expression in the hippocampus and increased IL6 and TNF transcripts, changes not observed in mice receiving fermentable fiber. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Western diet-fed donors into germ-free mice partially reproduced these transcriptional shifts and anxiety-like behavior. In adults with major depressive disorder, shotgun metagenomics showed lower buk gene abundance and reduced GPR43 expression in peripheral blood cells. In parallel, mediation analysis estimated that short-chain fatty acids accounted for 28% of the association between microbial composition and BDNF methylation. Notably, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors did not reverse these microbial or BDNF changes in mice. These findings position diet-driven microbial metabolites as modulators of BDNF and inflammatory pathways, suggesting that fiber or probiotic interventions may mitigate gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota can modulate brain circuits underlying mood and cognition, yet the extent to which dietary probiotic supplementation engages these pathways in patients with major depressive disorder remains unresolved. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 120 adults received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples quantified microbial taxa, while functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed amygdala reactivity to emotional faces. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, and mediation analysis examined whether changes in short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria explained clinical improvement. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms; amygdala reactivity decreased only in the probiotic arm. Preclinical work in mice has shown similar BDNF-dependent effects in the hippocampus. These effects were partially mediated by butyrate-related shifts in gut microbial composition. The findings support probiotic strategies targeting the gut microbiota as adjunctive modulation of the gut-brain axis, though larger clinical populations are needed.

Altered gut microbial communities precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating microbial metabolites in nigrostriatal degeneration. In a cohort of patients with PD and matched controls, shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia alongside depleted butyrate, while Akkermansia muciniphila and lipopolysaccharide were enriched. Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher butyrate and lower constipation severity, whereas probiotic use showed no association with motor impairment or levodopa response. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations predicted GBA-associated PD subtype in a multivariable regression model. Parallel 16S rRNA gene sequencing of colon biopsies confirmed that Prevotellaceae depletion tracked with cognitive decline. Longitudinal sampling further linked bile acid dysmetabolism to rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. In mice overexpressing SNCA, fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with PD exacerbated neuroinflammation, an effect attenuated by butyrate supplementation. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial strategies targeting butyrate production may modify PD progression, warranting randomized controlled trials of fiber-rich foods and defined probiotics.
