metadata.abstract: Disruption of the gut-brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder and anxiety, with gut microbiota composition emerging as a modifiable mediator. In adults with depression, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics have revealed reduced Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae, alongside increased Actinobacteria, though findings vary by cohort and fecal sample processing. These taxa influence short-chain fatty acid production, intestinal barrier integrity, and immune signaling, providing plausible routes to neuropsychiatric disorders. Dietary strategies that enrich dietary fiber and omega-3 fatty acids may increase microbial diversity and butyrate availability, while probiotic supplementation has shown modest effects on depressive symptoms in randomized trials. However, causality remains uncertain; Mendelian randomization and rodent studies suggest taxon-specific effects, but human fecal microbiota transplantation trials are limited. Standardizing metagenomic analysis and controlling for antibiotic exposure, diet quality, and host factors will be essential before microbiota-targeted interventions can be translated into clinical care for mental disorders.

Microbial metabolites shape central nervous system immunity, yet the pathways linking gut microbiota to neurodegeneration remain incompletely defined. In mice harboring a humanized gut microbiota, dietary inulin increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated butyrate in the colon. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and metagenomic profiling revealed that inulin suppressed Bacteroides-associated lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. These shifts coincided with reduced IL-1β and TNF-α in the hippocampus, lower NLRP3 expression, and restored BDNF signaling. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, baseline gut microbiome composition correlated with short-chain fatty acid profiles and cognitive scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced the anti-inflammatory brain phenotype and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Spearman correlation linked Bacteroides abundance inversely with butyrate and directly with lipopolysaccharide. Independent cohorts replicated the inverse association between Bacteroides and butyrate, and random forest models prioritized these taxa as predictive biomarkers. Together, these findings position inulin-sensitive microbiota as a modifiable node in communication between the gut microbiota and the brain.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide translocate across the gut barrier to shape brain immune tone, yet host APOE genotype may modify these signals in Alzheimer's disease. We profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified plasma metabolites in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Using mediation analysis within a linear mixed model, we tested whether Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium abundance mediated the association between APOE ε4 and cognitive decline. Higher Akkermansia muciniphila was associated with lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and better cognitive scores, but only among APOE ε4 carriers. Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate explained 18% of this protective effect. In mouse models, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-Akkermansia donors reduced neuroinflammation and rescued hippocampal BDNF expression. Targeted metagenomics further linked Bifidobacterium with bile acid conversion and TLR4 signaling in intestinal tissue. These findings suggest that APOE-stratified microbiome interventions, including probiotics, may delay cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease progression.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to cognitive decline through altered microbial metabolites, but whether curcumin can reverse these changes remains uncertain. We treated APP/PS1 mice and wild-type littermates with curcumin or vehicle for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR were used to profile gut microbiota and BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Curcumin-treated mice showed higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, increased butyrate in feces, and reduced amyloid-beta deposition. These shifts coincided with elevated BDNF transcripts and improved performance on Morris water maze. Linear mixed-effects models linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF expression and memory deficits. Fecal metagenomic sequencing further revealed reduced Escherichia coli and lower lipopolysaccharide translocation, while PERMANOVA confirmed separation of gut communities. In patients with Alzheimer's disease, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with short-chain fatty acid levels and cognitive impairment. These findings suggest that curcumin may modulate the gut microbiota–BDNF axis, offering a potential adjunctive strategy for Alzheimer's disease.

Disruption of the gut microbiota can precede motor onset in Parkinson's disease, implicating the gut–brain axis in α-synucleinopathy. We profiled adults with early Parkinson's disease and matched controls using sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and targeted BDNF expression assays in blood. Relative to controls, patients showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated Enterobacteriaceae, and lower BDNF transcripts. A 12-week randomized intervention with a multi-strain probiotic plus prebiotic fiber restored Lactobacillus abundance, increased short-chain fatty acid production, and upregulated BDNF expression compared with placebo. These changes correlated with improved constipation and depression scores, but not with motor severity. Using linear mixed models, we found that baseline gut microbial dysbiosis predicted BDNF response, and that probiotic supplementation shifted microbial composition toward Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium enrichment. Fecal calprotectin decreased in the probiotic arm, whereas interleukin-6 remained unchanged. Our findings suggest that targeting gut microbial dysbiosis through probiotics may modulate neurotrophic BDNF signaling along the gut–brain axis, supporting further trials in Parkinson's disease.

Consumption of fermented foods rich in polyphenols alongside probiotics may reshape the gut microbiota and modulate brain function via the vagus nerve and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a Mediterranean-style diet plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or a control diet. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundances, SCFA concentrations, and cognitive performance were assessed. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, education, and baseline values showed that the probiotic group exhibited greater increases in Faecalibacterium and butyrate and improved cognitive scores relative to controls. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate changes partially accounted for the cognitive benefit. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor and inflammatory cytokines were also quantified. No serious adverse events occurred. The between-group difference in butyrate remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. These findings indicate that combining fermented food intake with targeted probiotic supplementation may support gut-brain axis health, although larger trials with shotgun metagenomics and fecal metabolomics are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in depression, but whether fermented foods and probiotics can jointly improve depressive symptoms remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fiber plus a multi-strain probiotic supplement or usual care. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Compared with usual care, the intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. Depressive symptom scores declined more in the intervention group, and changes in Bifidobacterium correlated inversely with interleukin-6. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly accounted for the clinical improvement. These findings support combined dietary fiber and probiotic approaches for modulating the gut microbiota–brain axis in depression, although longer trials are needed.

Consuming a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiota, increases Proteobacteria, and depletes Lactobacillus, changes linked to hippocampal neuroinflammation and memory deficits. In mice fed this diet for 16 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced beta diversity, while Morris water maze testing showed impaired spatial learning. Inulin supplementation restored butyrate production, normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and attenuated cognitive impairment. These benefits were abolished in antibiotic-treated mice and in germ-free mice, implicating microbial short-chain fatty acids as mediators. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-fed donors to recipients reproduced the protection, whereas broad-spectrum antibiotics reversed it. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot trial found that inulin plus fermented foods increased Bifidobacterium and improved executive dysfunction. Circulating lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 were elevated in the Western-style diet group but reduced by inulin; fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into recipient mice conferred similar metabolic and cognitive benefits. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through prebiotic supplementation and dietary fiber may delay neurodegenerative disease.

Microbial signals from the gut influence brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural pathways, but the taxa and mediators linking gut microbiome shifts to Parkinson's disease remain poorly resolved. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomic sequencing, and fecal microbiota transplantation in patients and mice. Fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and community differences were tested with PERMANOVA. Compared with healthy controls, patients showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, lower fecal butyrate, and elevated circulating IL-6 and TNF-α. In germ-free mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, striatal dopamine declined and BDNF expression fell. Oral probiotics plus prebiotics restored Lactobacillus abundance, increased butyrate, attenuated IL-6 and TNF-α, and improved open field locomotion. In a mouse model of Parkinson's disease, probiotic treatment reduced motor deficits and constipation. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotic and prebiotic interventions may modify Parkinson's disease progression, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet the molecular relays linking microbial communities to mood remain poorly defined. In chronic restraint-stressed mice, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus abundance and depleted short-chain fatty acid production, paralleled by anxiety-like behavior, anhedonia, and elevated corticosterone. Lactobacillus repletion or fructo-oligosaccharide supplementation restored butyrate levels, normalized Bdnf expression in the hippocampus, and attenuated neuroinflammation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors into germ-free recipients transferred the behavioral phenotype, whereas fluoxetine only partially reversed it. In a separate human cohort, lower Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with reduced BDNF levels and greater depressive symptoms. Machine learning classification of microbial profiles distinguished stressed from control mice with 82% accuracy, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability accounted for a substantial portion of the Bdnf-related effect. These findings position microbial metabolites as modulators of BDNF signaling and suggest that targeting the microbiota may complement conventional antidepressant therapy.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet associates with lower depressive symptoms, but whether this relationship is mediated by gut microbiota and host BDNF variation remains unclear. In 180 adults, we profiled fecal Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes by 16S rRNA sequencing and measured plasma short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Mediation analysis tested whether microbial composition linked diet to depression severity. Greater fiber-rich food intake correlated with higher butyrate and propionate concentrations and expanded Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. BDNF rs6265 moderated this association: among carriers of the Met allele, each standard deviation increase in Mediterranean diet score was associated with a 1.8-point reduction in depressive symptoms, whereas no significant effect appeared in Val/Val homozygotes. Butyrate partially mediated the diet–depression link, and gut barrier integrity markers were higher in responders. These findings suggest that dietary patterns enriched in fermentable fiber may alleviate depression through microbiota-derived SCFAs and BDNF-dependent pathways, supporting personalized nutritional strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Compositional shifts in the gut microbiome are increasingly linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and depression, yet whether microbial signals distinguish comorbid from pure phenotypes remains unclear. We analyzed fecal metagenomic sequencing, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolomics from 84 participants, including patients with IBS, patients with depression, comorbid patients, and healthy controls. Random forest models separated groups with moderate accuracy, driven by Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium, and Escherichia coli. Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus altered short-chain fatty acid profiles and reduced depression-like behavior in mice; these effects were accompanied by increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and lower serotonin turnover. In a separate mouse model, dietary fiber and probiotic co-administration increased acetate and propionate, and correlation analysis linked these metabolites to reduced IBS pain scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly explained the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and symptom severity. Our findings suggest that microbiome-directed probiotics may complement antidepressant treatment, but larger cohorts and mixed-effects models are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial tryptophan catabolites are increasingly recognized as key signals along the gut-brain axis, yet how diet and host genotype shape this communication remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics in 84 adults, we profiled fecal microbiota, tryptophan metabolites, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) expression in peripheral blood. Participants with low Lactobacillus abundance showed reduced indole-3-acetate and higher depressive symptoms; linear mixed-effects models linked these shifts to altered hippocampal connectivity. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed that Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii correlated with indole pathway abundance. In mice fed a tryptophan-rich supplement, Lactobacillus rhamnosus colonization increased indole-3-acetate, enhanced AHR signaling, and normalized anxiety-like behavior. Conversely, antibiotic depletion of gut microbiota lowered serotonin turnover and worsened behavioral deficits, effects reversed by probiotic administration. Mediation analysis indicated that indole-3-acetate explained part of the AHR association with anxiety-like behavior. These data position microbial indole derivatives as modifiable mediators of brain function and suggest that tryptophan or probiotic interventions may complement antidepressant therapy in stress-related disorders.

Depletion of gut microbiota exacerbates Parkinson's disease (PD) pathology in mice, yet the microbial signals that protect dopaminergic neurons remain poorly defined. We colonized germ-free mice with butyrate-producing bacteria from patients with <disease>PD</disease> and healthy controls, then assessed motor deficits, striatal dopamine, and SNCA expression over 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation showed that microbial communities from healthy donors increased butyrate and short-chain fatty acids in the colon, whereas microbiota from patients with <disease>PD</disease> depleted these metabolites. This shift was accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation, preserved blood-brain barrier integrity, and attenuated α-synucleinopathy in recipient mice. In contrast, <disease>PD</disease>-derived microbiota lowered GPR43 and GPR109A expression in the substantia nigra and worsened neuronal loss. Metagenomic sequencing further linked these effects to Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, whose abundance correlated with butyrate levels and motor severity. Our findings suggest that butyrate-yielding prebiotics or defined bacterial consortia may restore gut-brain axis homeostasis and slow PD progression.

Microbiota-derived butyrate and propionate are increasingly recognized as key modulators of hippocampal plasticity and affective behavior, yet the transcriptional programs linking gut microbial metabolism to depression remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids in patients with major depressive disorder and healthy controls. Reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia was accompanied by lower butyrate concentrations and decreased BDNF expression in peripheral blood. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with depression induced anhedonia and reduced GPR43 and HDAC2 expression in the prefrontal cortex. RNA sequencing revealed enrichment of IL-6 and TNF-α signaling pathways. Supplementation with butyrate restored BDNF transcription, normalized serotonin turnover, and attenuated neuroinflammation. Notably, BDNF expression correlated negatively with IL-6 and positively with butyrate levels. These findings suggest that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids influence BDNF and inflammatory signaling networks, offering a mechanistic link between gut microbes and depressive symptoms.

Fermentation of Mediterranean diet-derived fiber by the gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that influence brain function and emotional behavior. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms received either a prebiotic inulin supplement or placebo alongside dietary counseling. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, with parallel rises in fecal butyrate and propionate. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate increases statistically mediated the relationship between Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced depression scores. In germ-free mice colonized with participant fecal microbiota, BDNF expression in the hippocampus and IL-10 expression in the prefrontal cortex were higher after microbiota transfer. Linear mixed models further linked these changes to reduced anxiety symptoms and lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Fecal calprotectin also decreased in the inulin group. These findings suggest that inulin and fermented foods may enhance gut-brain signaling and reduce neuroinflammation, but confirmatory trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and function are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD) via immune, endocrine, and neural signaling along the gut-brain axis. We synthesized data from adult patients with MDD and healthy controls to test whether probiotic supplementation shifts gut microbiota taxa and improves depressive symptoms. A random-effects meta-analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing and clinical outcomes showed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were enriched after probiotic supplementation, whereas Faecalibacterium abundance was reduced in patients relative to controls. Probiotic supplementation was associated with a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms (standardized mean difference = −0.42, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.13), but heterogeneity was high. Gut microbiota-related genes involved in short-chain fatty acid metabolism and tryptophan catabolism correlated with symptom change. These findings support a role for gut microbiota in MDD and suggest that probiotic supplementation may be a useful adjunct, although larger trials with standardized metagenomic sequencing are needed.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota precedes amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease and predicts cognitive decline in older adults, suggesting that intestinal microbiota actively shape brain function rather than merely reflecting it. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with mild cognitive impairment received a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling showed that treatment increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, alongside elevated butyrate and propionate. These shifts correlated with lower serum IL-6 and LPS, and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores. BDNF expression in peripheral blood increased, while NLRP3 and IL1B transcripts decreased. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly accounted for the cognitive benefit. In mice, probiotic treatment reduced hippocampal neuroinflammation and amyloid-beta deposition, an effect absent in BDNF-deficient animals. These findings position gut microbiota-directed probiotics as a plausible adjunct for early Alzheimer's disease, with BDNF and butyrate as candidate mediators. If replicated, these results support early microbiota modulation to delay dementia onset.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiome precedes amyloid plaque deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the pathways linking intestinal microbiota to neuroinflammation remain poorly defined. We profiled fecal microbiota from 84 patients with mild cognitive impairment and 62 age-matched controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic shotgun sequencing. Depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, both butyrate producers, correlated with elevated interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and lipopolysaccharide in serum. In mice colonized with microbiota from AD patients, fecal microbiota transplantation increased TREM2 expression, activated NF-kB signaling, and impaired hippocampal synaptic plasticity. Supplementation with butyrate or a high-fiber diet restored short-chain fatty acid levels, reduced astrogliosis, and attenuated cognitive decline. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial butyrate synthesis explained 31% of the association between gut dysbiosis and cognitive scores. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial communities through dietary fiber and microbiota-based interventions may delay AD progression by dampening peripheral and central chronic inflammation.

Disruption of the gut microbiome–brain axis is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease, yet the signals that modify this trajectory remain incompletely defined. In older adults, adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet enriched in fiber-rich foods and fermented foods correlates with greater gut microbial diversity and lower circulating inflammatory cytokines. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics reveal that Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii are depleted in patients with mild cognitive impairment, alongside reduced short-chain fatty acid production. These butyrate-producing bacteria ferment dietary fiber into butyrate, which strengthens intestinal barrier integrity and attenuates neuroinflammation in the central nervous system. In murine models, probiotic supplementation and fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors restore BDNF expression in the hippocampus and improve spatial memory. Conversely, antibiotic exposure elevates amyloid-beta deposition and proinflammatory cytokine levels. Mediation analysis suggests that microbial composition explains part of the association between diet quality and cognitive decline. Targeting the gut microbiota through diet and prebiotic interventions may therefore offer a tractable strategy to delay Alzheimer's disease onset.

Microbiota-derived butyrate sustains colonic epithelial hypoxia and neuroinflammation control, yet its central benefit requires fermentable dietary fiber and may be amplified by inulin supplementation. In a randomized adult cohort, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and mediation analysis to test whether gut microbiota composition links fermented food intake to BDNF expression and cognitive impairment. Higher fermented food consumption correlated with enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated fecal butyrate, and lower IL-6 and TNF-α. Inulin supplementation increased butyrate producers and reduced neuroinflammation in mice, but effects on hippocampal BDNF depended on baseline microbiota diversity. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the association between fermented food intake and BDNF. In parallel, linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin responders had greater microbial diversity and lower IL-6 than nonresponders. In mice, butyrate also enhanced Foxp3 expression and IL-10 in mesenteric lymph nodes, suggesting a peripheral route for central effects. These findings support targeting gut microbiota with fermentable fiber and inulin to mitigate cognitive decline.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone through vagal and endocrine signaling, and their depletion is repeatedly associated with major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease. To test whether gut microbiota composition predicts circulating SCFAs and BDNF expression, we profiled fecal microbiota and hippocampal transcripts in male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic corticosterone or vehicle. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR quantified Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Akkermansia muciniphila; BDNF, IL-6, and TNF-α were measured in prefrontal cortex. Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for batch and mediation analysis tested direct and indirect effects. Chronic corticosterone reduced Lactobacillus abundance and BDNF expression while increasing IL-6; butyrate supplementation restored BDNF and attenuated neuroinflammation. In an independent human cohort, PERMANOVA of 16S rRNA profiles linked lower Faecalibacterium abundance with reduced BDNF and higher depression scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 38% of the microbiota-BDNF association. These findings support targeting gut microbiota-derived SCFAs to modulate BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity in stress-related disorders.

Tryptophan catabolites crossing the intestinal barrier act as aryl hydrocarbon receptor ligands that tune IL-22 and BDNF expression in the gut and brain, linking microbiota composition to neuroinflammation. In a mouse model of chronic stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and targeted metabolomics to test whether Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bacteroides fragilis modulate this axis. Gut microbiota from stressed donors reduced BDNF transcripts in the hippocampus and elevated NLRP3 and IL-1β in the prefrontal cortex; these changes were accompanied by lower indole-3-propionic acid and butyrate in feces and serum. Colonization with L. rhamnosus restored BDNF and normalized NLRP3, whereas B. fragilis increased IL-10 and improved anxiety-like behavior. Vagotomy abolished the L. rhamnosus-driven BDNF increase, implicating the vagus nerve in this gut-brain signaling. These findings identify a BDNF- and NLRP3-dependent route through which gut microbes and their metabolites influence stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders, suggesting that probiotic or prebiotic interventions could be rationally designed to target this pathway.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiome and attenuates Parkinson's disease-associated motor deficits in mouse models, yet translation to patients remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 62 participants with Parkinson's disease, combining 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples with targeted quantification of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and raised fecal butyrate concentrations relative to placebo. These microbial and metabolic shifts correlated with reduced intestinal permeability and lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, suggesting improved intestinal barrier function. In parallel, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate increase and improved striatal dopamine turnover. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate-producing taxa explained part of the clinical improvement. Notably, baseline Prevotella abundance modified the response, and inulin did not alter trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) levels. Our findings position inulin as a candidate microbiome-targeted adjunct in Parkinson's disease, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and clinically relevant outcomes.

Supplementing a Western-style diet with inulin-type fructans reverses gut microbiota-linked depressive-like behavior in mice, yet the mediators remain unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics in a 12-week randomized controlled feeding trial of adults with mild-to-moderate <disease>depression</disease>, we tested whether inulin alters Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and tryptophan catabolites. Linear mixed-effects modeling adjusted for baseline depression severity and dietary fiber intake showed that inulin increased indole-3-lactic acid and short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces, with parallel reductions in interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. These changes correlated with improved anxiety scores and altered aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis indicated that increases in Bifidobacterium within the gut explained part of the inulin-associated anxiety improvement. No serious adverse events were reported, and effects were independent of antidepressant use. Our findings position inulin as a plausible adjunct for depression, while indicating that microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolism may link diet to brain function.

Supplementation with probiotics and increased intake of fermentable dietary fiber can reshape gut microbiota and alter short-chain fatty acid production, yet their combined influence on depression-related neurobiology remains poorly resolved. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic plus a high-fiber diet or placebo for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified microbial community composition and fecal butyrate. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations with serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and depressive symptoms. Active treatment increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, raised butyrate, and lowered inflammation markers. These changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms and higher BDNF. In gnotobiotic mice, transplantation of post-treatment microbiota reproduced butyrate elevations and reduced anxiety-like behavior, an effect absent after antibiotic depletion. Taxonomic shifts were accompanied by reduced lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and enriched bile acid metabolism. The findings position dietary fiber as a key substrate and probiotics as complementary modulators of gut-brain signaling.

Short-chain fatty acid depletion in the colonic lumen is increasingly linked to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, yet whether dietary substrates can reverse this axis remains unclear. We recruited 48 adults with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder and 32 matched controls, characterized gut microbiota by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and quantified short-chain fatty acids in stool and serum. Dietary fiber intake was estimated from food frequency questionnaires; multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose. Compared with controls, cases showed lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, reduced butyrate concentrations, and higher IL-6 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Dietary fiber correlated positively with butyrate and inversely with IL-6, but only among participants with preserved Lachnospiraceae capacity. A 12-week open-label pilot in 15 patients using resistant starch increased butyrate and improved constipation without worsening motor scores. These findings support a substrate-dependent gut-brain axis and justify randomized trials combining fiber-rich diets with microbial engraftment.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act at the intestinal epithelium and blood-brain barrier to shape BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, linking gut microbial composition to depressive-like behavior. In mice fed a prebiotic inulin supplement, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed expansion of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, accompanied by increased butyrate and propionate in the cecum. Quantitative RT-PCR and immunoblotting showed elevated Bdnf exon IV transcripts and BDNF protein in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, with reduced Nfkb1 and Il6 expression. In the forced swim test and tail suspension test, supplemented mice displayed decreased immobility. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into antibiotic-treated recipients partially reproduced these BDNF-dependent effects, whereas vagotomy attenuated them. Circulating lipopolysaccharide and Tlr4 expression were also lower, and flow cytometry indicated reduced Il1b in brain. In patients with major depressive disorder, similar fecal microbiota shifts and lower butyrate have been reported. These findings suggest that inulin supplementation can engage a microbiota-SCFA-BDNF circuit in the gut-brain axis, offering a plausible adjunct for stress-related disorders.

Modulation of the gut microbiome with probiotics and prebiotic fiber may slow cognitive decline in older adults. In a 16-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with mild cognitive impairment received a synbiotic containing Bifidobacterium longum, Lactobacillus plantarum, and fructooligosaccharides, or a placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, with parallel rises in fecal butyrate and propionate. Shannon index and PERMANOVA confirmed greater microbial diversity in the synbiotic group. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed strengthened hippocampal connectivity, while computerized cognitive testing demonstrated better verbal memory. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate increases explained 31% of the memory improvement. BDNF expression in peripheral blood was higher in the synbiotic group and correlated with Bifidobacterium abundance. No serious adverse events occurred. These data support probiotic-prebiotic combinations as a feasible strategy to modify the gut microbiome and preserve brain function, though confirmation in larger, diverse cohorts is needed before clinical translation.

Microbial gut microbiota composition predicts responsiveness to probiotic interventions in major depressive disorder, yet the dietary context shaping this effect remains poorly defined. In a randomized trial of adults with moderate depression, daily consumption of fermented foods together with a multi-strain probiotic increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced depressive symptoms after 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that responders harbored higher baseline Akkermansia muciniphila and lower Prevotella. Higher dietary fiber intake correlated with butyrate production and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and predicted clinical response in linear mixed models. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in short-chain fatty acids and interleukin-6 partially accounted for symptom improvement, with vagus nerve signaling as a plausible pathway. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders attenuated anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that fermented food-based microbiome remodeling may augment antidepressant effects, though random-effects meta-analysis of existing trials is needed to confirm generalizability.

Depletion of dietary fiber and overconsumption of Western diet remodel the gut microbiota, yet how these shifts translate into major depressive disorder remains contested. In a human cohort (n=180), 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that low butyrate producers, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, were depleted in depression and correlated with serum interleukin-6 and BDNF methylation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into antibiotic-treated mice induced anxiety-like behavior and reduced hippocampal BDNF expression. Supplementation with probiotics or omega-3 fatty acids restored butyrate levels, attenuated neuroinflammation, and normalized behavior. Metagenomic sequencing further linked these effects to microbial butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase pathways. In microglial cultures, butyrate suppressed NF-κB activation and tumor necrosis factor-α release. A random forest classifier based on five genera discriminated depression from controls with 82% accuracy. These findings position fiber-dependent microbial short-chain fatty acids as modifiable mediators of depression and support dietary and probiotic interventions targeting the gut-brain axis.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshapes the gut microbiota and modulates BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet the pathways linking these effects to anxiety-like behavior remain unresolved. We fed male C57BL/6 mice either a control diet or a diet enriched with omega-3s for six weeks and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. BDNF mRNA and protein levels were quantified in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. In the hippocampus, BDNF exon IV promoter methylation was also reduced in supplemented mice. Supplemented mice showed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside reduced Clostridiales. These microbial shifts correlated with elevated BDNF expression and lower corticosterone levels, as assessed by Spearman correlation and linear mixed models. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into naive recipients partially reproduced the BDNF increase, implicating microbiota as a mediator. Our findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation may influence brain plasticity through gut microbiota-dependent pathways, offering a potential adjunct for stress-related disorders.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depletion of butyrate-producing taxa are consistently associated with major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and neurodegenerative disease. In a cohort of older adults, 16S rRNA sequencing and targeted metabolomics revealed that fermented foods and dietary fiber intake correlated with higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, and lower lipopolysaccharide binding protein. Mediation analysis indicated that vagus nerve tone and BDNF expression partially explained the association between microbiota composition and depressive symptoms. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains attenuated neuroinflammation in murine models, an effect dependent on indole derivatives acting at hippocampal receptors. Mixed-effects models showed that each 10-g increase in dietary fiber predicted a 0.18-SD reduction in anxiety scores, while fermented food consumption was associated with greater microbial richness. However, Mendelian randomization did not support a causal effect of gut microbiota on Alzheimer's disease, suggesting confounding by ultra-processed food intake and antidepressant use. These findings argue that dietary interventions targeting microbiome-metabolite signaling, rather than single-strain probiotics, may be required to modify neuropsychiatric disorders.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans alongside a polyphenol-rich diet reshapes the gut microbiome and dampens neuroinflammation in aged mice, but whether these effects translate to older adults with mild cognitive impairment remains unclear. We randomized 68 participants to 12 weeks of omega-3 fatty acids plus inulin or placebo, with both groups receiving counseling to consume fermented foods and fiber-rich vegetables. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial composition; fecal metabolomics measured short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan derivatives. Compared with placebo, the supplement increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced interleukin-6 in plasma. Mixed-effects models showed improved verbal memory scores and lower depressive symptoms, associations mediated by indole-3-propionic acid. In mice, the same regimen increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that combining prebiotic fiber with omega-3s and plant-based foods may support brain health through gut microbiota-derived metabolites.

Supplementation with probiotics and increased dietary fiber intake can reshape gut microbiota and alter brain function, but the extent to which these interventions modulate gut-brain signaling in adults with obesity remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults received probiotic or placebo while consuming a fiber-rich diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance; functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain responses to food cues; gas chromatography-mass spectrometry measured short-chain fatty acids in plasma. Linear mixed models tested associations with BDNF methylation and depressive symptoms. Probiotics increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate, and reduced amygdala reactivity compared with placebo. Greater fiber intake correlated with higher short-chain fatty acids and lower depressive symptoms. Fecal microbiota from responders transferred to germ-free mice reproduced reduced anxiety-like behavior and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These translational data support a causal role for microbiota in gut-brain communication. These findings suggest that probiotic plus fiber may engage microbiota-gut-brain pathways, though effects on BDNF methylation require confirmation.

Altered gut microbiota composition and reduced BDNF signalling are reproducibly observed in major depressive disorder, but whether probiotic supplementation can reverse these changes remains contested. In a 12-week, double-blind randomised controlled trial, 120 adults with moderate depression received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut samples showed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance in the active arm. Linear mixed-effects models detected a significant group-by-time interaction for depressive symptoms (p = 0.021). Peripheral BDNF expression increased, whereas interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein decreased. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium changes partially mediated symptom improvement via BDNF upregulation. Baseline microbiota diversity correlated with response, and Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF expression. No serious adverse events occurred. The effect size was modest. These results support a gut-brain axis mechanism in which probiotic-driven microbiota shifts modulate BDNF and inflammatory signalling, though larger trials using shotgun metagenomics and fecal microbiota transplantation are needed to establish causality.

Microbial metabolism of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF expression and hippocampal plasticity, linking gut microbiome composition to depression and anxiety. Adults consuming a Western diet show reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated lipopolysaccharide translocation, and increased IL-6 and TNF-α transcription in peripheral blood. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with depression into germ-free mice recapitulates anhedonia and alters BDNF and GRM2 expression in prefrontal cortex. Psychobiotics and prebiotics may restore microbial diversity, but antibiotics disrupt this axis. Mendelian randomization supports causal effects of Clostridium taxa on major depressive disorder. In patients with irritable bowel syndrome, 16S rRNA sequencing reveals altered Lactobacillus/Bacteroides ratios that correlate with visceral pain and COMT variants. Serotonin synthesis by spore-forming bacteria modulates enteric nervous system activity, while fermented foods increase Lactobacillus abundance and gamma-aminobutyric acid availability. These findings position diet-microbe-gene interactions as tractable targets for neuropsychiatric disorders, though selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors remain first-line treatments.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans reverses stress-induced cognitive deficits and anxiety-like behavior by remodeling the gut microbiota and dampening neuroinflammation in male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress. After 6 weeks of inulin (10% w/w) or cellulose, mice underwent 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing of cecal contents, Morris water maze testing, novel object recognition, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila as enriched by inulin, while permutational multivariate analysis of variance showed distinct microbial community structures; Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction controlled for multiple comparisons. Inulin-fed mice displayed shorter escape latencies, increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in hippocampus, elevated occludin expression in colon, and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation compared with controls. Plasma corticosterone was quantified by radioimmunoassay, and tight junction protein 1 expression was measured in colon. These findings indicate that inulin may buffer stress-related neurocognitive dysfunction through microbiota-dependent signaling along the gut-brain axis, supporting targeted prebiotic interventions in humans.

Chronic stress disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis and amplifies depression and anxiety through the gut-brain axis. We tested whether resveratrol supplementation restores gut microbiota balance and upregulates BDNF in the hippocampus of mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress. Mice received resveratrol (100 mg/kg) or vehicle for 4 weeks. Behavioral assays showed that resveratrol reduced depression-like behaviors and anxiety-like behaviors. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and decreased Clostridium in resveratrol-treated mice. Short-chain fatty acids and serotonin levels were elevated in the colon and prefrontal cortex, respectively. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Lactobacillus reuteri as a biomarker. BDNF expression and synaptic proteins were increased in the hippocampus, accompanied by lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α in serum. Fecal tryptophan and indole-3-lactic acid concentrations were also higher after resveratrol treatment. In parallel, western blotting confirmed reduced nuclear factor-κB activation in the gut. These findings suggest resveratrol alleviates stress-induced depression by remodeling gut microbiota and enhancing BDNF-dependent plasticity.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as signaling molecules along the gut microbiota–brain axis, where they modulate BDNF expression and neurotransmitter turnover. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, dietary inulin supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and Lactobacillus relative to controls. We profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and quantified BDNF, GSK-3β, and serotonin in the hippocampus. Inulin-fed mice showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and restored BDNF transcripts compared with cellulose-fed mice. Mediation analysis using bootstrapped confidence intervals suggested that Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels partially explained the behavioral effect. Additional behavioral testing, including forced swim and novel object recognition, confirmed the cognitive and affective changes, and BDNF knockdown in the dentate gyrus abolished the inulin benefit. Plasma SCFA concentrations correlated with BDNF methylation in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting an epigenetic route. These findings indicate that inulin can engage the gut microbiome to influence BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, though validation in patients remains needed.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans reshapes the gut microbiome and reduces anxiety-like behavior in adults, an effect partially mediated by BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 participants received either inulin (10 g/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, accompanied by elevated short-chain fatty acids and lower lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased BDNF mRNA and reduced depressive symptoms scores compared with placebo. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium abundance explained 22% of the BDNF increase. In mice fed a high-fat diet, inulin similarly restored BDNF and attenuated neuroinflammation, with lower IL6 and TNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Plasma serotonin and kynurenine were quantified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry; inulin increased serotonin and decreased kynurenine, linking microbiota metabolism to BDNF signaling. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with prebiotic fiber may modulate BDNF-dependent brain plasticity and improve mood disorders.

Microbial-derived metabolites shape brain function and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, yet whether gut microbiota profiles predict motor severity remains unresolved. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 120 PD patients and 90 healthy controls using 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing; qPCR validated selected taxa. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and levodopa dose, while Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate and PERMANOVA controlled multiple testing and community-level effects. Akkermansia muciniphila and Prevotella were enriched in PD patients, whereas Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was depleted. These shifts correlated with reduced short-chain fatty acids and elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma. In germ-free mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, SNCA, TLR4, and GBA expression increased in the substantia nigra, accompanied by nigrostriatal dopamine loss. Probiotic treatment partially normalized gut microbiota and attenuated SNCA upregulation. Mediation analysis estimated that lipopolysaccharide accounted for 28% of the association between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and SNCA expression. Random forest classifiers distinguished PD patients from healthy controls with an area under the curve of 0.81. These findings link gut microbial dysbiosis to transcriptional changes relevant to PD pathogenesis.

Microbial tryptophan metabolism within the gut microbiota shapes central nervous system function, yet its contribution to stress-related disorders remains poorly resolved. We profiled faecal microbiota from 48 adults with generalized anxiety disorder and 52 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified circulating short-chain fatty acids. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated fermented food frequency questionnaire. Participants were randomized to receive either Lactobacillus rhamnosus or no supplementation for 8 weeks. Random forest models classified anxiety status from genus-level abundance with an AUC of 0.84. Bacteroides and Prevotella were enriched in patients, whereas Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were depleted. Higher fermented food intake correlated with increased microbial diversity and lower anxiety severity. Probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus abundance but did not significantly alter anxiety scores. tnaA gene abundance was inversely associated with anxiety severity. These findings suggest that gut microbial composition and dietary fermentation products interact to modulate anxiety-related outcomes, with machine learning offering a promising approach for gut-brain axis biomarker discovery.

Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by gut microbiota exerts profound effects on central nervous system function via short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, and tryptophan metabolites, linking intestinal microbial ecology to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In a double-blind trial of older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, daily probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium breve was combined with fecal microbiota transplantation from metabolically healthy donors. After 12 weeks, the intervention group showed improved global cognition and reduced interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein relative to placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, with decreased Escherichia coli. Linear mixed models associated these shifts with higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor and greater volume in the hippocampus. Among APOE4 carriers, effects on amyloid-beta burden were attenuated, suggesting host genotype modifies microbial benefit. These findings support microbiota-directed probiotic and microbiota transfer strategies as promising adjuncts for preserving brain health, though larger trials with standardized donors and strain-level tracking are needed.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate brain function, yet the microbial and immune pathways linking diet to depression remain poorly resolved. In a 10-week randomized trial, 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received either a fermented-food diet rich in yogurt, kefir, and kimchi or a high-fiber diet. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing; plasma inflammatory cytokines and short-chain fatty acids were quantified, and BDNF expression was measured in peripheral blood. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that the group consuming fermented foods showed greater increases in microbial diversity and Lactobacillus abundance, alongside larger reductions in interleukin-6 than the group consuming high-fiber diet. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in Lactobacillus abundance partially mediated the relationship between fermented food intake and improved depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that dietary fermentation status, not fiber alone, may influence gut-brain signaling through microbiota-immune pathways.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life calibrates central nervous system circuits, and disruption of this dialogue is increasingly implicated in anxiety-like behavior and neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and fecal metagenomics, we compared adults consuming a high-fiber diet with those consuming a Western diet. High fiber intake enriched Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium, raised short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and reduced IL6 and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. In germ-free mice colonized with human donor microbiota, the high-fiber diet increased Akkermansia abundance and normalized corticosterone responses to acute stress. Prebiotic supplementation partially reproduced these effects, whereas vancomycin abolished them. Critically, BDNF expression in the hippocampus correlated inversely with Faecalibacterium abundance and positively with butyrate levels. These findings suggest that dietary fiber shapes the gut microbiota to modulate BDNF and inflammatory signaling along the gut-brain axis, offering a tractable target for stress-related psychopathology. If replicated in longitudinal cohorts, these microbial and BDNF-linked signatures could guide diet or prebiotic interventions.

Reduced intake of dietary fiber consistently reshapes the gut microbiota, yet the molecular routes by which this dietary shift impairs hippocampal function remain unresolved. In a 15-week murine model of fiber deficiency, mice displayed cognitive impairment, synaptic ultrastructural damage, and altered CaMKIId expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed decreased Bacteroidetes and expanded Proteobacteria, shifts that correlated with behavioral deficits. Hippocampal proteomics further linked these changes to synaptic proteins including GAP43 and SV2C, alongside neuroinflammation and microglial synaptic engulfment. The fiber-deficient diet also compromised intestinal barrier integrity and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. Using SCFA receptor knockout mice and oral SCFA supplementation, we confirmed that SCFAs mediate the link between altered gut microbiota and cognitive impairment. Notably, microbiota divergence appeared after only 7 days of fiber deficiency, preceding measurable cognitive decline. These findings position the gut microbiota-hippocampal axis as a modifiable target, suggesting that increasing fiber intake may reduce risk of diet-associated cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease.

Chronic psychosocial stress disrupts gut microbiota composition and increases vulnerability to depression, yet the molecular links between microbial signals and brain remain incompletely defined. In mice exposed to repeated social defeat, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, accompanied by reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6). Dietary polyphenol supplementation with resveratrol restored microbial diversity, normalized Bdnf and Gabra1 transcripts, and attenuated anhedonia-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that gut microbiota composition indirectly linked resveratrol exposure to depressive phenotypes through IL-6 and Bdnf. Fecal microbiota transfer from resveratrol-treated donors to naïve mice conferred resilience to stress-induced behavioral deficits, whereas Lactobacillus depletion abolished these benefits. Parallel RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex showed that resveratrol reversed stress-induced upregulation of Nfkb1 and Il6 and normalized Bdnf promoter methylation. These findings position resveratrol as a microbiota-dependent modulator of Bdnf-related hippocampal plasticity and suggest that targeting microbiota-gut-brain signaling may prevent stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders.

Disturbances in microbial tryptophan metabolism are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether specific taxa drive these changes remains unresolved. We profiled the gut microbiota and tryptophan pathway in MDD patients and healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics. Bacteroidetes were depleted, whereas Actinobacteria and Bifidobacterium were enriched in MDD patients; the latter is often administered as a probiotic. Four microbial tryptophan biosynthesis genes were reduced in MDD patients, and K01626 abundance correlated negatively with symptom severity. Random Forests and the Boruta algorithm identified genus-level gut microbiota features that distinguished MDD patients from controls, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.89. Expression of the BDNF gene in the hippocampus was lower in a mouse model of chronic stress, and fluoxetine partially normalized both BDNF expression and microbial composition. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolites may contribute to MDD pathophysiology and biomarker discovery.
