metadata.abstract: Gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD) through immune, metabolic, and neural routes along the gut-brain axis. In a cohort of adults with MDD and healthy controls, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified plasma cytokines, short-chain fatty acids, and tryptophan metabolites. Random forest classification separated groups with moderate accuracy, while Spearman correlation and mediation analysis tested links among bacterial taxa, metabolites, and depressive symptoms. Relative abundance of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia was lower in MDD patients, whereas Eggerthella and Flavonifractor were enriched. Faecalibacterium correlated positively with butyrate and negatively with IL-6; IL-6 partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium and symptom severity. Functional prediction suggested reduced butyrate synthesis and enriched lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis in MDD patients compared with controls. These associations persisted after adjustment for antidepressant use and fiber intake. Together, these data suggest that targeting gut microbial composition may complement existing antidepressant strategies for MDD.

Dietary curcumin supplementation counteracts Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in mice fed a high-fat diet, an effect coupled to remodeling of the gut microbiome and increased short-chain fatty acid output. To define this gut-brain route, male C57BL/6 mice received a high-fat diet with or without curcumin for 16 weeks, while control mice received standard chow. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that curcumin restored the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia while suppressing Desulfovibrio. Untargeted metabolomics showed elevated butyrate and indole-3-lactic acid in the colon. In the hippocampus, curcumin reduced microglial activation and amyloid-beta deposition, with increased Bdnf expression. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia and butyrate to improved Morris water maze performance. Fecal metagenomic prediction further indicated enriched bile acid metabolism and tryptophan catabolism after curcumin. Parallel reductions in lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 occurred in serum, alongside increased Bdnf and Nrf2 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex. These findings position curcumin as a microbiota-targeted supplement that may mitigate diet-driven cognitive decline.

Microbial dysbiosis in the gut microbiota can alter gut-brain signaling via vagus nerve afferents, short-chain fatty acids, and cytokines, contributing to major depressive disorder (MDD). In mice subjected to chronic social defeat, fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with MDD decreased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, elevated interleukin-6, and increased corticosterone; daily probiotic treatment restored BDNF and normalized these inflammatory markers. 16S rRNA sequencing showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium with lower tryptophan catabolites. Germ-free mice display reduced serotonin in the colon and brain, an effect reversed by probiotic colonization and prebiotic supplementation. In a randomized trial of adults with MDD, omega-3 fatty acids plus prebiotic fiber increased gut microbial diversity and reduced C-reactive protein; response was moderated by BDNF genotype. Collectively, these preclinical and clinical data suggest that probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids may enhance BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity and dampen peripheral and central inflammation, offering a tractable strategy for depression.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that signal across the blood-brain barrier and tune BDNF expression, yet whether inulin supplementation can reproduce these effects when a Western diet is consumed remains unclear. We randomized adult volunteers with metabolic syndrome to 12 weeks of inulin (10 g/day) or placebo while continuing their habitual Western diet. Fecal microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF, IL-6, and TLR4 expression were quantified in peripheral blood mononuclear cells by qPCR. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and elevated butyrate concentrations. These shifts correlated with reduced IL-6 and TLR4 expression and increased BDNF expression. Mixed-effects models confirmed that changes in Bifidobacterium explained 31% of the variance in BDNF. No significant changes in PPARGC1A or COX5B were observed, suggesting selectivity for inflammatory and neurotrophic pathways. Our findings indicate that inulin can partially counteract Western diet-driven neuroinflammation through microbiota-BDNF interactions, supporting targeted prebiotic strategies for gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbiota are increasingly recognized as key mediators of brain function, yet how omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation interacts with dietary fiber to influence this axis remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms received either omega-3 plus a fiber-rich Mediterranean-style diet or a control diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF expression was measured in peripheral blood. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances increased in the intervention group and correlated with reduced depression scores. Mixed-effects models showed that changes in butyrate mediated the association between BDNF expression and symptom improvement. Exploratory analyses revealed that baseline Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance moderated the treatment effect. These findings suggest that combining omega-3 with fiber-rich foods may enhance microbiota-derived butyrate production, support BDNF-related brain plasticity, and reduce depressive symptoms in adults. Further trials should test whether baseline gut microbial composition predicts response to this combined intervention.

Consumption of a Western diet shifts the gut microbiota toward Bacteroides and exacerbates Alzheimer's disease-related cognitive decline, but the mediating molecular routes remain uncertain. Using Mendelian randomization combined with mediation analysis, we tested whether gut microbial taxa influence Alzheimer's disease risk through short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and secondary bile acids. Genetic instruments for 211 microbial taxa were derived from human cohorts; outcomes included late-onset Alzheimer's disease and plasma SCFA levels. In parallel, APP/PS1 mice received a high-fat, high-sucrose diet with or without butyrate supplementation. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled colon contents and hippocampus. Holdemanella and Parabacteroides showed opposing causal effects on Alzheimer's disease, mediated by glutamine and alanine. APOE genotype modified the association between Parabacteroides abundance and hippocampal amyloid β load. Butyrate restored BDNF expression and reduced microglial activation. These findings position diet-driven microbiome remodeling as a modifiable contributor to Alzheimer's disease and identify glutamine, alanine, and APOE-dependent pathways as candidate intervention targets.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the molecular routes by which intestinal microbes influence central nervous system function remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of 84 adults, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed reduced Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus abundance in patients with depression, alongside lower butyrate production capacity. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability partially explained the association between microbial community structure and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Specifically, lower BDNF transcripts correlated with elevated inflammatory cytokines and worse depression severity. In a randomized subset, 12-week probiotic supplementation increased Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus, raised butyrate, and normalized BDNF levels relative to placebo. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed time-by-treatment interactions after adjusting for dietary fiber intake and baseline depression severity. These findings support a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis in depression and suggest that targeting gut microbial ecology through probiotics may complement conventional antidepressant treatment. Future trials should stratify by baseline microbial enterotype and BDNF genotype.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota can precede motor and cognitive decline, implicating microbial metabolites in the gut-brain axis. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from patients with Parkinson's disease and healthy controls, we found reduced Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia and increased Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside lower fecal butyrate and propionate. In mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, expression of SNCA in the striatum and neuroinflammation increased, while short-chain fatty acid supplementation attenuated microglial activation. Vagotomy abolished these effects, linking vagus nerve signaling to brain immune tone. Metabolomic profiling further revealed depleted indole-3-propionic acid and altered bile acid derivatives in patients; these changes correlated with BDNF methylation and motor severity. In vitro, butyrate promoted FOXP3 expression, suggesting a tolerogenic mechanism. Our data indicate that gut microbial composition and metabolites jointly influence SNCA- and BDNF-linked pathways in the central nervous system, supporting targeted prebiotic or probiotic strategies for Parkinson's disease.

Inulin supplementation reshapes the gut microbiome and attenuates neuroinflammation in mice challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), yet whether intact vagus nerve signaling is required remains unclear. We treated C57BL/6 mice with inulin (10% w/w) for 4 weeks before intraperitoneal injection of LPS. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and expanded short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) producers. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmed elevated cecal butyrate and propionate. In the hippocampus, inulin reduced Iba1 and GFAP expression and normalized BDNF and IL-10 transcripts. Hippocampal NF-κB phosphorylation and IL-1β were also lower in inulin-treated mice. Morris water maze testing showed preserved spatial memory, while flow cytometry indicated fewer CD68-positive cells. No differences in LPS clearance were observed. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the cognitive benefit without reversing microbiome shifts, implicating a vagus nerve-dependent route. These findings position inulin as a microbiome-targeted supplement that buffers LPS-induced neuroinflammation through SCFA- and vagus nerve-linked gut-brain signaling.

Disrupted gut microbiota composition accompanies major depressive disorder and cognitive impairment, but microbial predictors of symptom trajectories remain poorly defined. In 180 adults, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota with plasma profiling of BDNF, IL6, and TNF. A random forest classifier separated high versus low depressive symptoms with moderate accuracy, driven by Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium, and Lactobacillus. Lower microbial diversity correlated with higher interleukin-6 and lower BDNF expression. In an 8-week randomized subset, a probiotic supplement increased Lactobacillus abundance and reduced interleukin-6 relative to placebo; these changes were accompanied by improved depressive symptoms but not cognitive scores. Mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acids partially mediated the link between microbial composition and BDNF expression. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that baseline Faecalibacterium abundance predicted 12-week symptom change. These results position gut microbiota as a modifiable correlate of depression and support probiotic interventions, though larger longitudinal trials are required to establish causality.

Gut microbial metabolism of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune signaling and behavior. To test whether probiotic supplementation alters this axis, adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed a fermented food-enriched diet or control condition for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; linear mixed-effects models tested associations with hippocampal volume, and mediation analysis assessed indirect effects through Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Compared with the control condition, probiotic supplementation increased gut microbial diversity and butyrate production, and improved depressive symptoms but not memory. Changes in Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and cortisol. In parallel, germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from responders showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that dietary fermented foods and probiotics can engage the gut microbiome to influence brain function, though effects on cognition may require longer intervention or stratification by baseline microbiota composition.

Microbial tryptophan metabolism shapes central serotonergic tone, and its disruption is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder. In patients with depression and healthy volunteers, gut microbiota composition correlated with serotonin turnover and BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance in patients, alongside lower BDNF and HTR1A transcripts. A high-fat diet exacerbated depressive-like behavior in mice, an effect accompanied by diminished Lactobacillus abundance and reduced 5-HT availability in the hippocampus. Conversely, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated anhedonia, restored BDNF expression, and normalized HTR1A levels. Fecal microbiota transfer from supplemented mice to antibiotic-treated recipients partially reproduced the behavioral and molecular benefits, while permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed distinct microbial profiles between groups. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial interventions targeting the gut microbiome may modulate BDNF-dependent plasticity and serotonin signaling, offering a tractable strategy for depression, particularly when combined with Mediterranean diet patterns.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune tone, yet the extent to which these metabolites mediate diet-driven changes in depression remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in adults with major depressive disorder who received a Mediterranean-style diet or habitual diet for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Associations between microbial taxa, metabolites, and depressive symptoms were tested with linear mixed-effects models, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The diet group showed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate concentrations, and these changes correlated inversely with symptom severity. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 22% of the dietary effect on depression scores. These findings suggest that fiber-rich foods may influence depressive symptoms through gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids, supporting targeted nutritional strategies for mood disorders.

Chronic low intake of fiber remodels the gut microbiota and raises susceptibility to cognitive impairment through the gut-brain axis. In mice fed a fiber-deficient diet for 15 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing showed reduced Bacteroidetes and expanded Proteobacteria, paralleled by impaired hippocampal synaptic plasticity and spatial memory deficits. Hippocampal RNA sequencing identified downregulation of CaMKIId, and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations fell in feces and serum. Oral supplementation with SCFA restored CaMKIId expression, attenuated neuroinflammatory markers, and improved cognitive performance; fiber supplementation produced comparable benefits. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-deficient donors into naive mice transferred memory deficits and lowered SCFA levels, whereas transplants from fiber-replete donors did not. Spearman correlation analysis linked SCFA depletion to CaMKIId loss and memory errors. In humans, lower dietary fiber intake correlated with altered gut microbial composition and poorer executive function. These findings position CaMKIId-dependent hippocampal signaling as a mediator of diet-microbiota-brain interactions and support dietary fiber or SCFA interventions for preserving cognition during aging.

Supplementing a Western diet with fermented foods and prebiotic fibers reshapes gut microbiota and dampens neuroinflammation, yet whether these changes translate into improved brain function remains uncertain. In a randomized controlled trial using 16S rRNA sequencing and functional magnetic resonance imaging, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with polyphenol-rich vegetables or the same diet plus galacto-oligosaccharides and Bifidobacterium for 12 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased, while Clostridiales decreased. Serum IL-6 and lipopolysaccharide fell, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor rose. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed enhanced hippocampal connectivity. Plasma metabolomics further showed reduced trimethylamine N-oxide and increased indole-3-propionic acid, linking microbial metabolism to neural outcomes. Changes in microbial composition correlated with short-chain fatty acid production and cognitive scores. The greatest cognitive benefit occurred in participants with higher baseline Bifidobacterium abundance. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings suggest that combining dietary fiber-rich foods with targeted prebiotics may modulate gut microbiota and brain interactions and slow cognitive decline.

Gut microbiota composition predicts depressive symptoms in patients with metabolic syndrome, yet whether probiotic supplementation can modify this association remains unclear. We recruited 120 adults with major depressive disorder and randomized them to Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal bacterial communities were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for body mass index and antidepressant use. Butyrate concentrations correlated inversely with depression severity (r = -0.34, p = 0.008). Probiotic treatment increased Lactobacillus abundance and reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, but did not alter depressive symptoms overall. In a predefined subgroup with low baseline butyrate, probiotics improved anhedonia scores compared with placebo (p = 0.03), an effect accompanied by increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood. These findings suggest that gut microbial metabolites may link intestinal ecology to brain function and that probiotic responses depend on baseline microbiota state.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that influence brain function and behavior, positioning the gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator of depression and anxiety. In a 12-week randomized trial, 84 adults with mild depressive symptoms received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a usual-care control. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and reduced Proteobacteria; these shifts correlated with lower depressive symptoms and improved gut barrier markers. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and linear mixed-effects models revealed that baseline microbial diversity moderated response. Participants with higher omega-3 fatty acid intake showed greater increases in Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia. In germ-free mice, transferring fecal microbiota from responders reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Baseline ultra-processed food intake attenuated these associations, whereas greater diet quality strengthened them. These findings suggest that dietary patterns, rather than single supplements, shape microbial communities linked to mental disorders and may inform depression prevention.

Shifts in gut microbiota composition can precede motor decline in Parkinson's disease, but whether dietary modulation alters gut-brain axis signaling remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, patients with Parkinson's disease received a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermented foods or a habitual diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics quantified microbial taxa and short-chain fatty acids. Baseline 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed lower Akkermansia muciniphila and Prevotella copri in patients than in healthy controls. Linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction showed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii increased in the intervention group, accompanied by higher butyrate and lower calprotectin. These changes correlated with improved constipation scores and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in enteric nervous system. No significant shifts occurred in Prevotella or Bacteroides abundance. The findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented food intake may reshape the gut microbiome toward a butyrate-producing profile, with potential to modify neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease. Larger trials with fecal microbiota transplantation are warranted to test causality.

Black ginseng-derived oligosaccharides improve memory impairment in mice through gut microbiota-mediated neurochemical changes. OSBG administration reversed scopolamine-induced cognitive deficits, reduced acetylcholinesterase activity, and elevated superoxide dismutase and glutathione in a tissue-dependent manner. Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests confirmed reversal of spatial and recognition memory deficits. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that OSBG enriched Barnesiella, Staphylococcus, and Clostridium_XlVb while depleting Eisenbergiella and Intestinimonas. Spearman correlation linked these microbial taxa to cognitive impairment and oxidative stress markers. Compared with fructo-oligosaccharides and galacto-oligosaccharides, OSBG produced broader microbiota shifts. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Barnesiella as a key biomarker. In the brain, OSBG upregulated Keap-1 and downregulated Nrf2, consistent with activation of the Keap-1/Nrf2 pathway. Gut microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, may mediate the microbiota-gut-brain axis and attenuate neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that black ginseng oligosaccharides could serve as a prebiotic intervention for patients with Alzheimer's disease, though fecal microbiota transplantation and random forest analyses are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota can reshape brain immune tone and amyloid-β pathology, positioning diet-responsive microbial pathways as modifiable contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). In APP/PS1 mice and human cohorts, carriage of APOE4 or TREM2 variants altered the abundance of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, with parallel shifts in short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide. A high-fat diet exacerbated neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, whereas probiotics or fiber supplements restored microbial diversity and reduced amyloid-β plaque load. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation further linked these shifts to AD progression and mild cognitive impairment, although causality remains uncertain. In a subset of patients, multivariable regression associated Mediterranean diet adherence and omega-3 supplementation with lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α levels, but not with APOE genotype. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial communities through probiotic and fiber-rich food interventions may complement APOE-stratified prevention, yet clinical trials are needed to determine whether such approaches delay dementia onset.

Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG attenuates stress-related behaviors in rodents, but the pathways linking gut microbiota to the central nervous system remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene and shotgun metagenomics, we profiled fecal microbiota from adults with subclinical anxiety who received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for eight weeks. The 16S rRNA gene revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance after probiotic treatment, accompanied by reduced interleukin-6 and cortisol levels. Metagenomic functional gene profiles showed enrichment of genes involved in short-chain fatty acid and gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. In a parallel mouse model, high-fat diet disrupted microbial composition, whereas probiotic supplementation restored gut microbial diversity and normalized brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. At week eight, participants reported lower depressive symptoms and reduced insomnia severity. These findings suggest that probiotics may improve mood symptoms through microbiome-dependent gene regulation along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial conversion of dietary fiber and high-fat diets alters circulating short-chain fatty acids and trimethylamine N-oxide, providing a mechanistic route from gut microbial ecology to hippocampal function and Alzheimer's disease risk. In 180 older adults, we profiled fecal gut microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and measured plasma metabolites by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Mediation analysis, adjusted for age, sex, education, and type 2 diabetes, tested whether bacterial taxa and metabolites mediate associations between dietary patterns and cognitive decline. Greater Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with higher butyrate and less severe memory impairment; conversely, Bacteroides-dominant communities showed elevated trimethylamine N-oxide and worse executive dysfunction. Mediation analysis attributed 18% of the protective association between fiber intake and executive dysfunction to butyrate (p=0.004), whereas trimethylamine N-oxide attenuated the benefit of Mediterranean diet adherence (p=0.012). In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-trimethylamine N-oxide donors increased BDNF methylation and impaired hippocampal plasticity. These findings position microbial metabolites as modifiable mediators of diet-related brain health.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by antibiotics or low-fiber diets increases neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet the microbial signals that protect brain circuits remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we found that Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium were depleted in patients with major depressive disorder. Colonization with these bacterial strains restored butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids in the colon, enhanced vagus nerve signaling, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex revealed downregulation of TLR4-dependent inflammatory pathways and reduced IL-6 and TNF transcripts. Random forest and Spearman correlation analyses linked microbial community structure to cytokine profiles, while probiotic supplementation recapitulated key benefits. Notably, lipopolysaccharide-induced systemic inflammation was attenuated in colonized mice, and metagenomic sequencing confirmed engraftment of the transferred microbial consortium. These results suggest that gut bacteria-derived metabolites maintain brain homeostasis through BDNF and TLR4 signaling, identifying candidate targets for depression and other gut-brain disorders.

Microbial-derived butyrate is a key mediator of gut-brain signaling, and its depletion has been linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. In patients with Parkinson's disease, reduced fecal short-chain fatty acids and lower abundance of Roseburia and Prevotella correlate with depressive symptoms and altered BDNF methylation in blood leukocytes. Probiotic formulations containing Ligilactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can restore gut microbiota balance, increase butyrate production, and modulate BDNF and TREM2 expression in the hippocampus. In rodent models, 16S rRNA sequencing and targeted bisulfite sequencing reveal that probiotic administration reduces IL-1β and TNF-α, attenuates oxidative stress, and improves cognitive impairment. These effects are accompanied by increased dopamine turnover and normalized SNCA and LRRK2 expression in the striatum. Dietary fiber and probiotics may therefore synergize to reshape the gut microbiome and epigenetically reprogram neurotrophic genes and immune-related genes, offering a tractable adjunctive strategy for Parkinson's disease and related gut-brain disorders. However, causality remains uncertain, and larger longitudinal cohorts with metagenomic and metabolomic profiling are needed to confirm whether these microbial shifts directly modify disease trajectories.

Diets low in fermentable fiber deplete gut microbial taxa that produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), a metabolic signature repeatedly linked to anxiety and depression. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet rich in legumes, whole grains, and fermented foods or a low-fiber control diet for 8 consecutive weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal microbiota showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium after the Mediterranean-style diet, alongside higher butyrate concentrations. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed reduced amygdala reactivity to negative emotional faces. Self-reported behavioral scores on Hamilton Depression Rating Scale improved modestly. Changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with butyrate and amygdala response. In parallel, germ-free mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented food intake may modulate gut microbiota-gut-brain signaling, though BDNF genotype did not modify the effect.

High-fiber diets rich in fermentable substrates consistently expand gut microbial taxa that produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and this ecological shift correlates with reduced inflammatory pathology in Parkinson's disease (PD) models. We colonized germ-free mice with Prevotella copri and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, then fed them either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet before MPTP exposure. PERMANOVA of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data revealed diet-dependent microbiome clustering, while linear mixed-effects models showed that high-fiber diet attenuated motor deficits and loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. This protection was accompanied by elevated butyrate in the colon, decreased Il6 and Tnf expression, and increased Bdnf in the striatum. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiome composition and butyrate jointly mediated the diet effect on Bdnf. Together, these data position dietary fiber as a modifiable input to the gut microbiome–brain axis. These findings suggest that dietary fiber can engage microbiota-derived metabolites to modulate BDNF-dependent nigrostriatal plasticity and may inform nutritional interventions for PD.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder and anxiety, with reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower fecal butyrate concentrations reported in patients. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum improved depressive symptoms and increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood; changes in BDNF correlated with shifts in gut microbial composition and serotonin metabolites in participants. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed enriched short-chain fatty acid biosynthetic pathways, while linear mixed-effects models showed that treatment effects on BDNF at week 12 were mediated by butyrate-producing taxa. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated behavioral improvements and elevated hippocampal BDNF, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished these effects. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics or prebiotic fiber may modulate BDNF signaling and serotonin availability, offering a tractable adjunctive strategy for stress-related psychiatric disorders.

Supplementation with probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids can reshape gut microbiota and modulate brain function through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Diets rich in fermentable fiber, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains increase short-chain fatty acids production, particularly butyrate, which strengthens intestinal barrier integrity and reduces neuroinflammation. In mice exposed to chronic stress, a Mediterranean diet plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus elevated BDNF expression in the hippocampus and lowered depressive-like behavior. Similarly, older adults consuming high-fiber diets showed greater microbial diversity and less cognitive decline. Mechanistically, Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with BDNF and reduced interleukin-6. Germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from patients with depression exhibit altered tryptophan metabolism and reduced hippocampal neurogenesis. Fecal microbiota transplantation from affected individuals into rodents reproduces anxiety-like phenotypes, implicating Lactobacillus and Bacteroides in γ-aminobutyric acid signaling. Clinical trials using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic analysis show that prebiotics and psychobiotics can reduce cortisol and improve stress-related symptoms. These findings suggest that probiotic and dietary fiber interventions targeting the gut microbiome may offer adjunctive strategies for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Dysregulation of the gut microbiota along the gut-brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet microbial signatures that stratify patients remain poorly defined. In a cohort of adults with MDD and healthy controls, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with targeted metabolomics to profile fecal microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Relative to controls, MDD patients showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations and elevated kynurenine/tryptophan ratios. A random forest classifier trained on genus-level abundances discriminated groups with an area under the curve of 0.84, and partial least squares discriminant analysis linked indole-3-acetate to depressive severity. In mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with MDD, behavioral despair emerged with reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus; these effects were attenuated by a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum. The findings position microbial tryptophan metabolism and probiotic supplementation as tractable targets for MDD, though prospective validation is required.

Inulin supplementation restores gut microbiota homeostasis and reduces Parkinson's disease (PD)-like pathology in mice exposed to rotenone. After four weeks of inulin treatment, rotenone-treated mice showed improved motor coordination, higher dopamine levels in the striatum, and fewer α-synuclein aggregates in the substantia nigra. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia while decreasing Proteobacteria in the gut microbiota. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice into germ-free mice reproduced the neuroprotective phenotype, accompanied by reduced IL-1β and TNF-α in the colon and brain. Western blotting further showed decreased TLR4 and NF-κB p65 expression and increased BDNF in the substantia nigra. In patients with PD, lower fecal Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance correlated with worse motor scores, mirroring the mouse findings. Metagenomic profiling and Spearman correlation linked these shifts to reduced short-chain fatty acid production. These findings suggest that inulin modulates the gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid production, thereby attenuating neuroinflammation and PD-related neurodegeneration through the gut-brain axis.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a modifier of Alzheimer's disease progression, yet interventions that simultaneously target microbial communities and amyloid-β pathology remain scarce. We tested whether magnesium-L-threonate, a compound reported to elevate synaptic magnesium, could reshape the gut microbiome and attenuate cognitive deficits in APP/PS1 transgenic mice. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and serum metabolites after eight weeks of treatment. Magnesium-L-threonate increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing Allobaculum, and restored intestinal tight junction proteins including occludin and zonula occludens-1. These microbial shifts correlated with lower hippurate and higher butyrate levels, alongside reduced neuroinflammation and improved hippocampal oxidative stress. Behavioral testing showed that treated APP/PS1 mice performed better in Morris water maze than vehicle-treated littermates. Our findings position magnesium-L-threonate as a potential gut-brain axis modulator in Alzheimer's disease, though fecal microbiota transplantation and metagenomic sequencing are needed to establish causality.

Supplementation with probiotics and fermented foods may reshape gut microbiota composition and attenuate depression-like behaviors, yet the microbial and neural mediators remain unresolved. In a randomized adult cohort, participants with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or control condition for 8 weeks; dietary fiber intake was estimated from 3-day records. Fecal Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, measured by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, increased in the probiotic arm. Linear mixed-effects models showed that changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with reduced depressive symptoms (β = −0.34, P = 0.012). Spearman correlation linked baseline fiber intake to Faecalibacterium abundance (ρ = 0.29, P = 0.018), a taxon associated with depression severity. In parallel, mice colonized with microbiota from responders exhibited lower serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial shifts indirectly influenced brain function through short-chain fatty acids. These findings support targeted probiotic and fermented food interventions as adjunctive strategies for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Distinct gut microbiota signatures are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), but whether they reflect cause, consequence, or treatment response remains debated. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and random forest models, we profiled adults with MDD before and after eight weeks of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Response at two weeks was predicted by host BDNF genotype and FKBP5 methylation, whereas response at eight weeks tracked with gut microbiota composition, particularly Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance. Production of short-chain fatty acids by gut microbes correlated inversely with IL-6 and anxiety scores. Fecal bile acids and tryptophan metabolites also separated responders from nonresponders, implicating vagal signaling and intestinal permeability. In a nested randomized controlled trial, participants receiving a Mediterranean-style diet plus probiotic showed greater diversity of gut microbiota and lower depression severity than controls. Together, these findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented foods may modulate the gut-brain axis and improve outcomes in patients with MDD.

Alterations in the gut microbiome can drive neuroinflammation through epigenetic repression of BDNF in the hippocampus. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls. After 4 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated Bacteroides and depleted Lactobacillus in the gut microbiome of the depression group. Linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA showed that Bacteroides abundance inversely correlated with BDNF expression (p < 0.001) and explained 32% of beta diversity. Short-chain fatty acid levels, particularly butyrate, were reduced and negatively associated with depressive-like behaviors. Western blot confirmed decreased BDNF protein and increased IL-1β in the prefrontal cortex and amygdala. Notably, BDNF promoter methylation was elevated in the depression group, and this correlated with Bacteroides abundance. Treating mice with butyrate restored BDNF expression and reduced neuroinflammation. Additionally, fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors reversed these deficits. These findings suggest that gut dysbiosis contributes to depression via BDNF downregulation, and that butyrate supplementation may offer therapeutic benefit.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat/high-sucrose diet promotes neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment, but whether fermentable fiber can mitigate these effects through the gut-brain axis is unclear. We fed male C57BL/6 mice a high-fat/high-sucrose diet for 16 weeks, with or without inulin supplementation. Behavioral testing revealed that inulin significantly improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin restored Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila abundances, which correlated with short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels in the colon. In the hippocampus, inulin attenuated IL-6 and TNF-α expression and normalized BDNF transcripts. Inulin also increased microbial diversity and colon occludin and ZO-1 expression, while lowering serum lipopolysaccharide. Mediation analysis indicated that Akkermansia muciniphila and SCFAs statistically mediated the cognitive benefits. No changes in standard chow intake or body weight explained the effects. These findings suggest that fermentable dietary fiber supplementation may counteract obesity-related cognitive decline by remodeling the gut microbiota.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii track with heightened depression severity and blunted BDNF expression in hippocampus, yet whether these associations reflect causality remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then measured butyrate, serotonin, and cytokines in colon and brain. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for batch and cage effects revealed that F. prausnitzii abundance explained 31% of variance in BDNF transcripts and inversely correlated with IL6 expression. Inulin supplementation restored butyrate levels and normalized BDNF expression, an effect abolished by antibiotic cocktail. 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomics identified Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium as secondary contributors, while PERMANOVA confirmed community separation by donor group. These findings suggest that microbiota-derived butyrate modulates BDNF signaling and depressive-like behavior, positioning prebiotic fiber as a candidate adjunctive strategy. Randomized trials with mediation analysis are needed to confirm target engagement. These mechanistic links highlight a tractable gut-brain target for adjunctive depression therapy.

Microbial dysbiosis in Parkinson's disease (PD) disrupts intestinal barrier integrity and promotes neuroinflammation through gut-brain axis signaling. We tested whether a probiotic formulation combined with a fiber-rich diet alters gut microbiota and clinical outcomes in adult patients with PD. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants received either probiotics plus fermented foods or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA assessed taxonomic and functional shifts. Probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced Enterobacteriaceae compared with placebo. These changes correlated with lower calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and improved constipation scores. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial shifts partially explained reductions in systemic inflammation. However, no significant change occurred in motor symptoms or dopamine metabolism. The findings indicate that probiotics and dietary fiber can reshape the gut microbiome and modulate inflammatory pathways relevant to PD, though larger trials are needed to confirm disease-modifying effects.

Gut microbiota composition is increasingly recognized as a modifier of neuropsychiatric disorders, yet the extent to which dietary patterns shift microbial communities and neuroactive metabolites in humans remains incompletely defined. We conducted a randomized crossover trial in adults with mild depression, assigning a Mediterranean-style diet or a Western diet for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed microbiota and brain responses. Linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction tested diet-by-time interactions. The Mediterranean-style diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, raised short-chain fatty acids, and lowered lipopolysaccharide relative to the Western diet. These shifts correlated with reduced hippocampal activation to negative emotional cues and improved depressive symptoms. Butyrate mediated part of this association. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber-rich diets may reshape the gut microbiome to support brain health, and highlight dietary intervention as a potential adjunctive strategy for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids shape brain function, but whether they modify Alzheimer's disease pathology through TREM2 remains unresolved. We treated transgenic mice with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii or its metabolite butyrate and assessed amyloid burden by immunohistochemistry and RNA sequencing of the hippocampus. F. prausnitzii colonization raised butyrate in the colon, reduced amyloid plaques, and increased TREM2 and TYROBP expression. In participants with mild cognitive impairment, shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed lower F. prausnitzii abundance, which correlated with fecal butyrate and cognitive decline. A linear mixed model adjusted for age, sex, and APOE genotype confirmed the association, and Spearman correlation linked F. prausnitzii to TREM2 expression. Fecal calprotectin and zonulin did not differ between groups, excluding overt intestinal inflammation as a confounder. Antibiotic depletion of gut microbiota abolished the protective effect, while oral butyrate supplementation partially restored it. These results identify a F. prausnitzii–butyrate–TREM2 axis linking the gut microbiome to Alzheimer's disease and support microbiota-directed interventions.

Microbial depletion of butyrate-producing taxa exacerbates chronic stress-related neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior, yet whether probiotic supplementation restores gut microbiota-host signaling remains uncertain. We randomized male C57BL/6 mice to unpredictable chronic mild stress (UCMS) or control conditions, with half of the stressed mice receiving Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus for four weeks. Behavioral readouts included the forced swim test, sucrose preference test, and open field test. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction showed that L. rhamnosus attenuated stress-induced anhedonia and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbiota composition after treatment, with increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and elevated butyrate. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in the colon and serum. The findings suggest that L. rhamnosus buffers stress-related depression via microbiome-butyrate-BDNF signaling, supporting probiotic-based adjunctive strategies.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by Western-style diets, antibiotics, and psychosocial stress can shift gut microbiota toward Lactobacillus depletion and Bacteroides expansion, a pattern linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with moderate depression received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo alongside standard care. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced depressive symptoms scores; these changes correlated with decreased inflammation and improved anxiety ratings. Linear mixed models showed that baseline microbial diversity moderated treatment response, with greater benefit in participants consuming fiber-rich foods at least three times weekly. Mechanistic work in mice indicates that BDNF and serotonin signaling may mediate these effects. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may augment conventional antidepressant therapy, but confirmatory trials with longer follow-up and standardized dietary assessment are needed.

Alterations in the gut microbiome can precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating intestinal inflammation and short-chain fatty acid dyshomeostasis in α-synucleinopathy. In murine models, SNCA overexpression and LRRK2 mutations disrupt microbial composition, reducing Lactobacillus and Blautia while expanding Enterobacteriaceae and Akkermansia. These shifts impair dopamine metabolism, increase lipopolysaccharide translocation, and promote neuroinflammation, effects attenuated by probiotic administration and fecal microbiota transplantation. Dietary patterns further modify risk: Mediterranean diet and fiber-rich foods support butyrate-producing taxa, whereas western diet enriches pro-inflammatory Bacteroides and Escherichia. In patients, 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomics reveal GBA-linked dysbiosis associated with worse cognition and elevated inflammatory cytokines; PINK1 and PARK7 variants may similarly shape microbial trajectories. Randomized controlled trials are needed to test whether prebiotics, synbiotics, or levodopa-sparing strategies can restore eubiosis and slow PD progression. Integrating host genetic variants with microbial metagenomics may identify biomarkers for early intervention. Longitudinal sampling is required to distinguish cause from consequence, and to define whether dietary supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids or fermented foods alters PD trajectory.

Microbial conversion of dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids is a central route by which the gut microbiome influences gut-brain axis signaling, but whether these metabolic signals predict depressive symptoms remains unresolved. In a cohort of older adults with varying cognitive impairment, we profiled stool microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, and measured plasma butyrate, tryptophan, and GABA. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, antidepressant use, and fermented food intake showed that greater Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated with lower depression severity and higher BDNF expression. Conversely, Bacteroides-dominated communities exhibited enhanced glutamate degradation and predicted worsening anxiety over 12 months. At baseline, higher histamine synthesis and lower glutamate degradation tracked with future cognitive decline; elastic net regression identified these features as top predictors. In mice, probiotic supplementation increased butyrate availability, reduced neuroinflammation, and normalized hippocampal serotonin turnover. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-dependent microbial metabolites may serve as noninvasive biomarkers and therapeutic targets for psychiatric disorders.

Inulin supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in APP/PS1 mice, an effect coupled to BDNF upregulation in the hippocampus. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, 12 weeks of inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, elevated fecal butyrate, and reduced serum lipopolysaccharide. 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic profiling revealed that responders had higher BDNF expression and lower IL-6 in the brain. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate mediated the association between Akkermansia muciniphila and BDNF, whereas random forest classification identified Bifidobacterium abundance as a top predictor of cognitive improvement. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice into germ-free mice reproduced the BDNF increase and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Moreover, short-chain fatty acids, especially propionate, enhanced BDNF promoter acetylation in cortical neurons. Lactobacillus-derived exopolysaccharides further suppressed microglial activation in mice, suggesting a microbiota-BDNF pathway that links inulin to cognitive decline mitigation. No APOE genotype-dependent differences were observed. These findings support targeted prebiotic interventions for Alzheimer's disease.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) mediate gut microbiota-brain signaling, and their disruption is linked to major depressive disorder (MDD). We profiled fecal microbiota and serum SCFAs in patients with first-episode MDD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Differential abundance was assessed with LEfSe, and associations between microbial taxa, SCFAs, and clinical scores were tested by Spearman correlation. Relative abundance of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Coprococcus was reduced in MDD patients, whereas Parasutterella was enriched. Alpha diversity was lower in MDD patients, and random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium and Roseburia as discriminative features. Fecal butyrate-producing bacteria correlated inversely with IL6 and TNF expression in peripheral blood of patients. Serum butyrate was lower in the MDD group and negatively correlated with depressive symptoms. In a mouse model of chronic stress, sodium butyrate supplementation restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced neuroinflammation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD patients into antibiotic-treated mice induced depressive-like behavior, while fluoxetine partially reversed these effects. These findings suggest that gut microbial depletion of butyrate contributes to MDD pathophysiology and that targeting microbiota-derived SCFAs may offer therapeutic potential.

Distinct gut microbial signatures precede depressive-like behavior in chronic stress models, but whether they persist after stress cessation remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, we profiled fecal microbiota from male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) and non-stressed controls across 8 weeks. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were quantified in feces and serum by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Behavioral outcomes were assessed with forced swim test and sucrose preference test. A random forest classifier identified microbial taxa discriminating stressed from control mice; permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) tested community-level differences. Stressed mice showed reduced Lactobacillus and increased Bacteroides abundance, alongside lower butyrate and hippuric acid concentrations. These changes correlated with Il6 and Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. After stress cessation, microbial composition partially normalized, but Bacteroides enrichment persisted and predicted anhedonia severity. Mediation analysis suggested butyrate partly mediated the microbiota-behavior relationship. These findings implicate sustained gut microbiota shifts and SCFA depletion in stress-related depression and support targeting microbiota function for mood disorders.

Supplementation with wild blueberries for 12 weeks increased gut microbiota diversity and short-chain fatty acid production in adults with mild cognitive impairment, an effect accompanied by improved depressive symptoms and cognitive scores. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we found that Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were enriched, whereas Bacteroides fragilis declined. Fecal microbiota from responders transferred to germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate-dependent increase in BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. In mice, Morris water maze testing confirmed better spatial memory after colonization. Baseline microbiota composition predicted response, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the cognitive benefit. These findings suggest that blueberry-derived polyphenols act as prebiotic substrates that reshape the gut microbiome, elevate butyrate, and modulate gut-brain signaling. A randomized controlled trial is now needed to determine whether dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods can delay cognitive decline in older adults.

Targeting the gut microbiome through dietary fibers may modulate brain function and neuropsychiatric symptoms, yet the mechanistic links remain poorly resolved. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either inulin or placebo for 8 weeks alongside usual care. Fecal samples were profiled using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids were quantified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Inulin supplementation increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, with a concurrent rise in butyrate and propionate. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced depressive symptoms measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, although the between-group difference did not reach significance after correction for baseline severity. Exploratory mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially accounted for the association between Bifidobacterium abundance and symptom improvement. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings support a plausible gut-brain pathway in which fermentable dietary fiber alters microbial community structure and metabolite output, but larger trials with longer follow-up and deeper multi-omics profiling are needed to confirm clinical benefit.

Higher intake of dietary fiber and fermented foods associates with greater gut microbial diversity and lower systemic inflammation, yet whether these exposures causally influence neuropsychiatric symptoms remains contested. In a prospective cohort of adults, we combined shotgun metagenomics of stool with plasma metabolomics and assessed depression, anxiety, and cognitive performance. Mediation analysis tested whether short-chain fatty acids and bile acid metabolites link microbial taxa to brain outcomes. Greater abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila correlated with higher butyrate and better executive function; Bacteroides dominance showed the opposite pattern. Linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use. A subsample received inulin or no supplement for 12 weeks; inulin increased Bifidobacterium and reduced self-reported anxiety, with effects partially mediated by propionate. In gnotobiotic mice, transplantation of human microbiota from responders to high-fiber diets lowered neuroinflammation and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings support fiber-rich diets as a modifiable lever for microbiota-gut-brain signaling health, though Mendelian randomization is needed to clarify causality.

Consumption of a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiome and elevates circulating lipopolysaccharide, a microbial signal that can impair hippocampal plasticity and cognitive function. In male C57BL/6 mice, 12 weeks of high-fat, high-sucrose feeding increased Desulfovibrio and Enterobacteriaceae abundance, reduced Lactobacillus, and raised interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α in plasma and prefrontal cortex. These changes coincided with lower Bdnf and Arc expression and poorer Morris water maze performance. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics linked the behavioral deficit to depleted short-chain fatty acids and accumulation of indole derivatives. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Western diet-fed donors into germ-free recipients reproduced neuroinflammation and memory impairment, whereas inulin supplementation partially reversed these effects. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial composition accounted for 31% of the diet-related variance in Bdnf expression. These findings position the gut microbiota as a modifiable node through which dietary patterns influence brain function and identify microbial metabolites as candidate mediators of the gut-brain axis.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune and endocrine signaling, yet whether psychobiotic supplementation amplifies these effects in depression remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or the same diet plus a multi-strain probiotic for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial metabolites, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels, and depressive symptoms. PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures between groups. Compared with diet alone, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered anxiety scores; mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly mediated the improvement. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 decreased only in the probiotic arm, alongside reduced sleep disturbance. Baseline ultra-processed food intake and omega-3 fatty acid use were covariates. These findings suggest that combining fermented foods and fiber with targeted psychobiotics may strengthen the gut microbiota–brain axis and reduce depression severity.

Twelve weeks of whole-grain barley intake increased gut microbiota diversity and improved executive function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, an effect accompanied by elevated butyrate and BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, we found that responders harbored higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis; beta diversity differed between responders and non-responders by PERMANOVA (R2 = 0.14, P = 0.002). Circulating lipopolysaccharide decreased in responders, suggesting improved gut barrier integrity. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed increased prefrontal cortex connectivity, which correlated with short-chain fatty acid production. Linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate mediated the relationship between F. prausnitzii abundance and cognitive improvement. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate increase and reduced neuroinflammation, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished the benefits. These findings support a causal microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis linking whole-grain barley to brain function and suggest dietary strategies for mild cognitive impairment.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites act as key signals along the gut-brain axis, yet their impact on BDNF expression and neuroinflammation remains incompletely defined. In germ-free mice colonized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, supplementation with fermentable fiber increased colonic microbial diversity and butyrate production. This was accompanied by reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus, elevated BDNF and GABA receptor transcripts, and decreased anxiety-like behavior. In healthy adults, a randomized crossover trial using 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metabolomics showed that a Mediterranean-style diet enriched in polyphenol-rich foods shifted gut microbiota toward butyrate-producing taxa and correlated with lower cortisol and improved cognitive flexibility. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors fed fermentable fiber into germ-free mice partially reproduced the metabolic and behavioral changes, supporting a causal role for the microbiome. These findings suggest that dietary patterns can reshape gut microbial communities, modify host gene expression in brain regions, and influence stress-related disorders. However, causal mechanisms and dose-response relationships require further study.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids can modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota composition to depression-like behaviors. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we compared mice receiving a high-fiber diet, a Western diet, or a Western diet supplemented with inulin. Gut bacterial communities enriched in Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus correlated with increased butyrate and reduced neuroinflammation in the prefrontal cortex. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline fecal microbiota showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance and higher Bacteroides relative to healthy controls; these differences were associated with IL6 and CRP expression. Random forest models classified cases from controls with an AUC of 0.81. Probiotic intervention restored Lactobacillus levels and improved depressive symptoms, but only in individuals with low baseline butyrate. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed Bacteroides uniformis and FXR-linked bile acid pathways as mediators of these effects. These findings position diet-responsive microbiota and BDNF signaling as tractable targets for gut-brain disorders.

Probiotic and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation reshapes the gut microbiota and reduces depressive symptoms in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), yet the microbial and inflammatory mediators remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 96 participants received either the combined supplement or placebo. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled fecal microbiota, and ELISA quantified interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha, short-chain fatty acids, and lipopolysaccharide. Linear mixed-effects models tested symptom trajectories, while PERMANOVA and Spearman correlation assessed community composition and metabolite-clinical relationships, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, decreased Prevotella, and lowered IL-6. These shifts correlated with reduced depression scores and improved anxiety scores. BDNF mRNA in peripheral blood increased, and fecal butyrate mediated the association between Bifidobacterium and depression improvement. Fecal calprotectin also decreased in the active arm. In germ-free mice colonized with post-treatment microbiota, BDNF expression rose in the hippocampus, supporting a causal microbiota-brain pathway.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) maintain intestinal barrier function and brain immune homeostasis, yet causal evidence that probiotic supplementation modifies major depressive disorder (MDD) remains scarce. In a 12-week randomized trial, 120 adults with MDD received multi-strain probiotics or placebo while continuing selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Fecal microbiota was analyzed by shotgun metagenomic sequencing; SCFAs were quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. BDNF promoter methylation was measured in blood. Linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis assessed outcomes. Compared with placebo, probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and lowered depressive symptoms. Butyrate and BDNF methylation mediated 31% of the clinical improvement. Baseline microbial diversity and BDNF methylation predicted response, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.78. In germ-free mice transplanted with responder microbiota, inulin potentiated these effects, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate and BDNF regulation as tractable targets for MDD.
