metadata.abstract: Depletion of microbial butyrate production is accompanied by reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a pattern increasingly linked to depression and impaired gut-brain signaling. To test whether this relationship is causal, we colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy donors and assessed behavior, short-chain fatty acid profiles, and BDNF transcripts. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed lower relative abundance of Butyricicoccus and Fusicatenibacter in microbiota from patients. Recipient mice showed increased anxiety-like behavior, reduced butyrate in feces, and downregulated BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors partially reversed these changes. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability accounted for a significant portion of the BDNF effect. Notably, dietary fiber supplementation increased butyrate and normalized BDNF expression in mice colonized with microbiota from patients, whereas selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment did not alter microbial composition. These findings position butyrate-producing bacteria as modifiable contributors to depressive symptoms and support targeting the gut microbiome to restore BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity.

Disruption of gut microbial tryptophan catabolism is increasingly recognized as a contributor to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the specific microbial K00658 and K00837 and host pathways that mediate this effect remain poorly resolved. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing on fecal samples from 42 MDD patients and 38 healthy controls. Microbial K00658 and K00837, involved in tryptophan biosynthesis, were depleted in MDD patients, whereas host IDO1 expression in peripheral blood was elevated. Using Random Forests and the Boruta algorithm, we identified Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium as discriminative taxa. Faecalibacterium abundance correlated negatively with kynurenine and positively with indole-3-propionic acid. In mice colonized with MDD patient microbiota, tryptophan supplementation restored hippocampal serotonin levels, reduced depressive-like behavior, and lowered IL-6 and TNF-α in the prefrontal cortex. Probiotic Bifidobacterium administration recapitulated these benefits, while butyrate alone did not. These findings suggest that microbial tryptophan pathway K00658 and K00837 and host IDO1 represent tractable targets for MDD interventions. The microbiota-gut-brain axis likely mediates these effects.

Probiotic and prebiotic supplementation can reshape gut microbiota and attenuate depressive symptoms, yet strain-specific effects and optimal delivery remain unresolved. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 96 adults with mild-to-moderate major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic plus prebiotic fiber or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group × time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Participants completed dietary recalls and PROMIS measures at baseline, week 6, and week 12. Relative to placebo, active supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated fecal butyrate, and reduced depression scores (Cohen's d = 0.52). Anxiety and sleep quality improved modestly, and no serious adverse events occurred. Adherence exceeded 85%, and no clinically meaningful changes in body mass index or plasma lipids were observed. These findings support prebiotic-probiotic combinations as adjunctive interventions targeting the gut-brain axis, though confirmatory trials in larger cohorts are needed.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone, yet the pathways linking gut microbial composition to neuroinflammation remain incompletely resolved. In a cohort of adults with mild cognitive impairment, we profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA sequencing and quantified plasma SCFAs using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Mediation analysis tested whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance influenced hippocampal volume indirectly through butyrate. Lower F. prausnitzii correlated with reduced butyrate and poorer hippocampal integrity. The association between F. prausnitzii and hippocampal volume was partially mediated by butyrate (indirect effect β = 0.14, 95% CI 0.05–0.27), and BDNF expression moderated this relationship. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with F. prausnitzii increased butyrate, upregulated Bdnf in prefrontal cortex, and attenuated neuroinflammation induced by lipopolysaccharide. A random forest classifier integrating F. prausnitzii, butyrate, and BDNF distinguished cases from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82. These findings implicate a Faecalibacterium-butyrate-BDNF axis in microbiota-brain signaling and support targeting gut microbiota for cognitive decline.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet reshapes the gut microbiota, increases intestinal permeability, and promotes cognitive impairment via the gut-brain axis. Whether targeted probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. We fed mice a high-fat diet for 16 weeks and randomized them to receive Bifidobacterium breve or vehicle. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that the high-fat diet reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus while increasing the Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio. Bifidobacterium breve restored Akkermansia abundance, lowered lipopolysaccharide in serum, and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-1β concentrations in the hippocampus. In novel object recognition and Barnes maze tests, supplemented mice showed improved spatial memory deficits relative to high-fat diet-fed controls. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced the cognitive benefit, implicating microbiota remodeling. In cecum, metagenomic sequencing and linear discriminant analysis linked these benefits to increased short-chain fatty acid production. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation attenuates high-fat diet-induced cognitive dysfunction by modulating the gut microbiome and gut-brain axis.

Altered gut microbiota composition precedes motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet causal pathways remain disputed. In a longitudinal cohort of PD patients and healthy controls, we profiled fecal microbiota and serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Mediation analysis tested whether Clostridia and Lactobacillus abundances influenced constipation severity through butyrate. Lower Clostridia cluster XIVa correlated with reduced butyrate, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and worse motor symptoms; random forest classification linked these shifts to neuroinflammation along the vagus nerve. A randomized subset received resistant starch or placebo for 12 weeks. Resistant starch increased butyrate-producing taxa and improved gastrointestinal dysfunction, but not motor scores. Mixed-effects models revealed that butyrate mediated 28% of the microbiota-constipation association. Baseline microbial diversity and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance predicted constipation improvement in logistic regression models. These findings support targeting gut bacteria with prebiotic fibers or probiotics to modulate microbial metabolites and gut-brain dysfunction, though motor benefit may require earlier intervention.

Compelling evidence now positions gut microbiota as a critical mediator of depression-like behavior, yet the molecular routes linking microbial metabolites to plasticity in the hippocampus remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then randomized animals to receive a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus plus omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids or vehicle for six weeks. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed that supplementation increased Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium while depleting Prevotella. In prefrontal cortex, BDNF and TLR4 expression correlated with serotonin turnover and interleukin-6 levels. Linear mixed models showed that probiotics and omega-3 independently attenuated neuroinflammation and normalized forced swim test behavior. Parallel shotgun metagenomics linked these shifts to short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis, and Spearman correlation associated Faecalibacterium abundance with BDNF expression. In an independent cohort, omega-3 responders showed higher Faecalibacterium and lower interleukin-6. These findings suggest that targeted dietary supplementation can reshape microbiota-brain signaling through BDNF- and TLR4-dependent pathways.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota composition to depressive-like behavior. To test whether this pathway is disrupted by high-fat diet, male C57BL/6 mice received either standard chow or a Western diet for 12 weeks, with or without inulin supplementation. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF, IL-6, and TNF-α transcripts were quantified in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus using RT-qPCR. Western diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate concentrations, and decreased BDNF expression relative to controls. Inulin partially restored Bifidobacterium, increased butyrate, and normalized BDNF expression, but did not alter IL-6. A random forest classifier identified Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium as top predictors of BDNF status. Notably, BDNF changes occurred independently of body weight gain. These findings suggest that dietary fiber fermentation is a modifiable determinant of BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity and may inform prebiotic strategies for depression.

Microbial dysbiosis within the gut-brain axis is increasingly recognized as a driver of neuropsychiatric disorders. In male C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet versus standard chow, we used 16S rRNA gene sequencing to profile fecal microbiota. The high-fat diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma, and diminished butyrate production. These shifts correlated with decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus and increased anxiety-like behavior. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored BDNF levels and normalized behavior. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Allobaculum as a key taxon associated with diet-induced neuroinflammation. Notably, these findings align with observations in patients with major depressive disorder, where gut microbial composition shifts correlate with BDNF methylation. Furthermore, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fat diet-fed mice into germ-free mice recapitulated these BDNF reductions. Our results suggest that modulation of the gut microbiome through diet may influence BDNF-dependent brain plasticity and serotonin metabolism, offering a target for depression and anxiety. These preclinical findings warrant clinical validation.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that shape central nervous system immunity and synaptic plasticity, yet whether this axis predicts cognitive decline remains unclear. In a cohort of older adults with mild cognitive impairment, we combined shotgun metagenomics of stool with plasma metabolomics and longitudinal cognitive testing. Lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and reduced butyrate production correlated with poorer hippocampal volume and lower BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. A 12-week intervention with a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, alongside increased fermented foods and whole grains, raised butyrate levels and improved delayed memory scores. Baseline trimethylamine N-oxide and lipopolysaccharide levels were higher in participants who progressed, while random forest models identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a protective taxon. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in BDNF methylation partially explained the relationship between butyrate and memory. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through probiotics and diet may modulate BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a plausible strategy to slow cognitive decline.

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters the gut microbiota and reduces neuroinflammation in mice subjected to chronic restraint stress, yet the microbial taxa and metabolites that mediate these benefits remain poorly resolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled faecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids in stress-exposed mice receiving omega-3 or vehicle. Supplemented mice displayed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate and propionate concentrations, and reduced BDNF downregulation in the hippocampus. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Akkermansia and Roseburia as taxa enriched by omega-3. FITC-dextran permeability assay revealed that omega-3 restored occludin and ZO-1 expression in the colon, lowered IL-6 and TNF-α, and reduced anxiety-like behaviour. Behavioural testing showed that omega-3 decreased depressive-like behaviour and normalized corticosterone levels. Spearman correlation linked Roseburia and Akkermansia with butyrate and BDNF. These findings suggest that omega-3 exerts gut-brain effects through microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids, offering a potential adjunctive strategy for stress-related disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids exert neuroactive effects that shape vagus nerve signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity, and BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In a randomized controlled trial of adults with major depressive disorder, probiotic supplementation combined with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation increased fecal microbiota diversity and butyrate production relative to placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed higher Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance in responders. Baseline gut microbial composition explained 22% of variance in anxiety scores, and lower butyrate levels correlated with reduced BDNF expression. Mediation analysis indicated that these microbial shifts partially mediated reductions in depressive symptoms, with the indirect effect on BDNF methylation accounting for 18% of the total effect. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated these behavioral and neurochemical changes, whereas antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion abolished them. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through dietary supplementation may modulate BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity and provide adjunctive benefit in depression.

Supplementing high-fat diet-fed mice with inulin increases Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, short-chain fatty acid production, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a tractable route to modify gut microbiota-brain signaling. To test whether this effect translates to humans, we conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with mild cognitive impairment. Participants consumed a Mediterranean-style diet and received either inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing; BDNF methylation in blood and interleukin-6 concentrations were quantified by ELISA. Compared with placebo, inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, reduced BDNF promoter methylation, and lowered interleukin-6; mixed-effects models showed these changes correlated with improved cognitive impairment scores. Exploratory metagenomic sequencing revealed parallel increases in Bacteroides and Roseburia, alongside reduced trimethylamine N-oxide. These findings link a dietary fiber-derived supplement to BDNF-related epigenetic and inflammatory shifts, supporting microbiota-targeted prebiotic strategies for neurocognitive disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to depression and anxiety, but dietary approaches that restore microbial homeostasis remain incompletely defined. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods, legumes, and dietary fiber or a habitual control diet; half also received probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Compared with control, the diet plus probiotic increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations, lowered depressive symptoms, and reduced neuroinflammation markers. Changes in butyrate correlated with symptom severity in linear mixed models. Transfer of post-intervention fecal microbiota into antibiotic-treated mice via fecal microbiota transplantation reproduced the behavioral benefits and elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. These findings indicate that fermented foods and fiber combined with probiotics remodel the gut microbiota and improve depression-related outcomes through butyrate-dependent gut-brain signaling.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids constrain neuroinflammation and modulate BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, yet the extent to which dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids amplify these effects remains unresolved. In a randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received eicosapentaenoic acid-enriched supplement or control for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and circulating cytokines were quantified by ELISA. A linear mixed-effects model tested treatment-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. These changes correlated with improved prefrontal cortex connectivity and lower depression scores. Omega-3 supplementation also increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. However, these benefits were attenuated after a 4-week washout. The findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation may engage a microbiota-butyrate axis to stabilize mild cognitive impairment.

Microbial butyrate availability in the colon influences BDNF expression in the hippocampus, providing a mechanistic link between gut microbiota composition and major depressive disorder. To test whether this pathway mediates stress resilience, we colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bacteroides fragilis and exposed them to chronic social defeat stress. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metabolomics revealed that colonization increased butyrate production and reduced IL-6 and TLR4 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower fecal butyrate correlated with reduced BDNF methylation and symptom severity. Using linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, we found that inulin supplementation, but not fluoxetine, increased Bifidobacterium abundance and restored BDNF expression. We also quantified serotonin turnover and BDNF promoter methylation in blood and brain samples, and performed mediation analysis to test whether Bifidobacterium abundance explained treatment response. These findings suggest that targeting microbial butyrate production may complement existing depression therapies.

Compositional shifts in the gut microbiota precede symptom exacerbation in a subset of patients with major depressive disorder, yet dietary modifiers of this trajectory remain poorly resolved. In a 12-week observational cohort, adults reporting high adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermented foods, legumes, and omega-3-rich fish showed greater microbial diversity and higher relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus than low-adherence counterparts. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids and plasma tryptophan metabolites, which correlated inversely with depressive symptoms. A random forest classifier incorporating diet, microbiome taxa, and BDNF genotype discriminated treatment response with an AUC of 0.84. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability explained 22% of the diet–mood association. In mice subjected to chronic stress, supplementation with probiotics and prebiotics restored hippocampal serotonin turnover and reduced selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor-resistant immobility. These findings position dietary fiber and fermented foods as modifiable levers on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, though randomized trials are needed to confirm causality.

Disruption of the gut microbiome can alter BDNF and TLR4 signaling along the gut-brain axis, yet the causal mediators linking microbial metabolites to affective and motor symptoms remain poorly defined. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and mediation analysis in mice exposed to vancomycin and in patients with major depressive disorder. Antibiotic-treated mice showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated lipopolysaccharide, lower hippocampal BDNF expression, and increased IL-6 transcription; mediation analysis attributed 34% of the behavioral effect to butyrate. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors restored butyrate production, normalized TLR4, IL-6, and BDNF transcripts, and reduced depressive-like behavior. In patients, microbial diversity correlated inversely with depression severity, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance predicted response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. A Mendelian randomization analysis using BDNF and FTO variants supported a causal effect of Faecalibacterium on depression risk. These findings suggest that butyrate-producing probiotics or prebiotics may provide adjunctive benefit, but randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm durability and safety.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune signaling, but the microbial and metabolic pathways linking gut microbiota to Alzheimer's disease remain unclear. We recruited older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls, assessed Mediterranean diet adherence, and measured serum butyrate and propionate. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples was analyzed with PERMANOVA and Spearman correlation; linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and statin use. Compared with controls, patients showed lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and reduced butyrate levels. Mediterranean diet adherence correlated positively with F. prausnitzii and butyrate, and negatively with IL6 expression. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the association between fiber intake and BDNF expression. In APP/PS1 mice, inulin supplementation increased butyrate and BDNF expression while decreasing IL6. These findings support a model in which dietary fiber promotes F. prausnitzii and butyrate production, dampening IL6-related inflammation and preserving BDNF-dependent hippocampal function in Alzheimer's disease.

metadata.abstract: Disruption of the gut microbiome by Western-style diets can precede neurodegenerative disease by years, yet the molecular links between microbial metabolites and brain immune tone remain poorly resolved. We fed male C57BL/6 mice either a high-fat, high-sucrose diet or a fiber-rich control diet for 16 weeks, then quantified Il6, Tnf, and Nrf2 expression in the hippocampus and colon using RT-qPCR. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene, and short-chain fatty acids were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. A permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed diet-dependent microbial community shifts, with depletion of Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium and enrichment of Desulfovibrionaceae. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Il6 expression correlated negatively with butyrate and positively with community dysbiosis scores. In a parallel human cohort, baseline microbiota features predicted IL6 expression after 12 weeks, and mediation analysis implicated butyrate as a partial mediator. These findings position diet-driven microbiota remodeling as an upstream regulator of Il6-dependent neuroinflammation and suggest that dietary fiber may buffer gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Gut microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber can reshape hippocampal BDNF signaling and influence Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression. In APPswe/PS1ΔE9 mice, a high-fat, high-sucrose diet lowered Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide, and accelerated cognitive decline. Conversely, Mediterranean-style diets enriched in polyphenols and omega-3 fatty acids restored gut microbiota diversity and increased BDNF and Arc expression in the prefrontal cortex. We used 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation to test whether microbial shifts mediate these effects. Mediation analysis showed that short-chain fatty acids explained 31% of the diet-related preservation of memory deficits. Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve partially mimicked the fiber-rich diet, reducing amyloid-beta load and neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that targeting diet-microbiome-BDNF interactions may offer a tractable strategy for AD prevention. Larger human trials with longitudinal metagenomic profiling are now needed to confirm causality, define optimal dietary patterns, and identify which patients respond to microbial or nutritional interventions.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by a Western diet can promote neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior, but the microbial signals that converge on brain circuits remain unclear. We colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Bacteroides fragilis and measured BDNF, IL-6, and TNF expression in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. L. rhamnosus increased butyrate and gamma-aminobutyric acid in colon contents, reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation, and normalized BDNF expression. In contrast, B. fragilis produced polysaccharide A and attenuated IL-6 without altering TNF. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder into mice partially reproduced these microbiota shifts. In an independent group of adults, quantitative PCR revealed lower Lactobacillus abundance and higher IL-6 expression in those with irritable bowel syndrome than in healthy controls. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and BDNF statistically mediated the effect of L. rhamnosus on depression-like behavior. These findings suggest that specific commensal bacteria and their metabolites act along the gut-brain axis to modulate neurotrophic and inflammatory signaling, offering targets for stress-related disorders.

Bacteroides fragilis-derived polysaccharide A suppresses experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis by inducing Foxp3 expression and reinforcing mucosal tolerance. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics, we found that dietary fiber deprivation depletes Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, lowering butyrate in gut microbiota and exacerbating neuroinflammation in gnotobiotic mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into antibiotic-treated mice restored BDNF and TJP1 expression, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α, and improved depressive-like behavior. In contrast, FMT from patients with major depressive disorder failed to rescue these phenotypes. Random forest analysis linked Akkermansia muciniphila abundance to GPR43 activation and short-chain fatty acid production. Notably, PGE2 and 12-HHTrE reproduced these transcriptional changes in mice. Targeted CRISPR interference of GPR43 in mice abolished the protective effects of A. muciniphila, while inulin supplementation increased Foxp3 and IL-10 transcripts in the colon. These findings suggest that microbial metabolites transcriptionally tune tight junction protein and neurotrophic factor programs, offering a tractable target for gut-brain disorders.

A Western-style diet high in saturated fat and refined sugar reshapes gut microbiota, impairs intestinal barrier integrity, and promotes low-grade neuroinflammation, yet the microbial mediators linking diet to depressive-like behavior remain incompletely defined. In male C57BL/6 mice randomized to a high-fat, high-sucrose diet or standard chow for 12 weeks, 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed lower relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and higher Desulfovibrionales. Behavioral assays revealed increased immobility in the forced swim test and reduced exploration. Serum lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were elevated. Mediation analysis estimated that LPS and IL-6 explained 31% and 24% of the diet–behavior association, respectively. Supplementation with inulin or Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored Lactobacillus abundance, reduced IL-6, and normalized depressive-like behavior. These results position diet-driven microbiota disruption and LPS-IL-6 signaling as modifiable contributors to gut-brain axis dysfunction, and they support causal mediation modeling for identifying microbial targets. Future work should test whether these pathways generalize to adults with major depressive disorder and whether fermented foods produce comparable benefits.

Microbiota-derived butyrate attenuates neuroinflammation in the hippocampus, but whether this effect requires host BDNF signaling remains unclear. We colonized antibiotic-treated mice with gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then fed them a low-fiber diet or a high-fiber diet. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia were enriched by the high-fiber diet. Fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and hippocampal BDNF expression was measured by quantitative PCR. Using linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis, we found that high-fiber diet increased butyrate and BDNF expression while reducing IL-6 and TNF. These changes correlated with reduced depressive-like behavior in mice, and BDNF partially mediated the microbiota-behavior association. Random forest classification further linked butyrate and BDNF to patient status. Notably, fluoxetine did not reverse behavioral deficits in mice colonized with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder, suggesting that dietary fiber acts upstream of serotonin signaling. Our results identify a diet-sensitive microbiota-BDNF axis that may inform depression interventions.

Alterations in the gut microbiota–brain axis contribute to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. We tested whether a prebiotic inulin combined with a Mediterranean diet could reverse these effects in aged mice. Mice received either a high-fat, high-sugar diet or the intervention for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that the intervention increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium abundance. Behavioral testing showed reduced anxiety-like behavior and improved memory. Hippocampal IL-6 and TNF-α levels were lower, while BDNF expression was higher. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Lactobacillus as a key responder. Notably, the intervention also reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a marker of metabolic endotoxemia. These findings suggest that inulin plus Mediterranean diet modulates the gut microbiota to attenuate neuroinflammation and improve cognitive function. Fecal microbiota transplantation from intervention mice into germ-free mice recapitulated the benefits, confirming causality. These benefits were observed without changes in body weight. Our results support dietary strategies targeting the gut microbiota for age-related cognitive decline.

Consumption of a high-fat, high-sugar diet reshapes the gut microbiota and promotes neuroinflammation, a process increasingly implicated in cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease. In mice fed this diet, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed expanded Firmicutes and depleted Bacteroidetes, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide in the hippocampus. We hypothesized that microbial metabolites cross the blood-brain barrier and modulate BDNF expression. To test this, participants from a longitudinal cohort completed fecal metagenomic sequencing and cognitive testing. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and education showed that microbial diversity was inversely associated with memory impairment (β = −0.18, p = 0.004). Mediation analysis indicated that trimethylamine N-oxide explained 22% of this relationship. Spearman correlation further linked Bifidobacterium abundance to IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts in patients with mild cognitive impairment. After false discovery rate correction, these associations remained significant. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome may influence neurodegeneration through metabolite-driven pathways, offering targets for probiotic or omega-3 intervention.

Gut microbiota composition predicts central nervous system reactivity through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and dysbiosis is repeatedly linked to anxiety and depression. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of adults with mild depression, daily probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced depressive symptoms; mediation analysis suggested that changes in short-chain fatty acids and BDNF expression partially explained the effect. 16S rRNA sequencing with PERMANOVA showed that baseline microbial diversity moderated treatment response, and linear mixed models confirmed that Bifidobacterium abundance tracked with symptom improvement. In mice, prebiotic fiber and omega-3 fatty acids attenuated lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation, lowering IL6 and TNF while increasing BDNF in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice replicated the behavioral benefit, and plasma cortisol also fell significantly. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with probiotics may complement conventional antidepressants, although Mendelian randomization and larger trials are needed to establish causality.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that dampen neuroinflammation and support blood-brain barrier integrity, yet clinical responses to Mediterranean diet interventions vary widely. To identify sources of heterogeneity, we synthesized 14 randomized controlled trials in adults with major depressive disorder using a random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that adherence to fermented foods, whole grains, and extra-virgin olive oil enriched Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, while increasing fecal butyrate. Higher butyrate correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and elevated BDNF in the hippocampus, as measured by functional magnetic resonance imaging. Mediation analysis indicated that gut microbiota composition explained 31% of the diet–behavior association. In contrast, omega-3 fatty acid supplementation alone did not modify microbial diversity or BDNF levels. These findings suggest that whole-food patterns, rather than isolated nutraceuticals, are more likely to engage the microbiota-gut-brain axis and improve mood disorders, though confirmatory randomized trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Disruption of gut microbiota composition during early life can persistently alter hippocampal BDNF expression and serotonin turnover, providing a plausible route through which microbial signals influence depression-like behavior. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids in mice exposed to chronic corticosterone and in patients with major depressive disorder. Chronic stress reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate, and decreased BDNF expression in prefrontal cortex; these changes correlated with Spearman correlation and were reversed by probiotic supplementation or fluoxetine. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed mice to germ-free mice transferred anxiety-like behavior and reduced BDNF–TrkB signaling. In patients, lower Faecalibacterium and higher Bacteroides correlated with anhedonia severity after adjustment in multivariable regression. Dietary fiber and fermented foods may amplify these effects, whereas broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupted the pathway. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-brain communication modulates BDNF-dependent plasticity and that probiotics may offer adjunctive benefit for stress-related disorders.

Fermentable dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome in ways that attenuate anxiety-like behavior, but the microbial mediators and host pathways remain incompletely defined. We recruited adults with mild-to-moderate <disease>major depressive disorder</disease> and randomized them to a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods plus a multi-strain probiotic or to dietary advice alone for 8 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics and fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila. PERMANOVA and linear mixed-effects models tested community and clinical associations. The intervention increased butyrate and tryptophan metabolites, reduced interleukin-6, and raised BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Random forest classification linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance to reduced depressive symptoms; Spearman correlation showed that butyrate correlated inversely with C-reactive protein. Responders also showed higher Bifidobacterium and lower Bacteroides relative abundance than non-responders. These findings suggest that fiber- and probiotic-rich diets modulate the gut microbiome and short-chain fatty acid signaling to influence brain function in depression.

Alterations in the gut microbiome can precede motor and cognitive symptoms in Parkinson's disease, suggesting that diet-driven microbiome signals shape brain function. We profiled gut microbiota from mice fed either a high-fat, high-sucrose diet or a fiber-rich chow for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that the high-fat, high-sucrose diet reduced Lactobacillus and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, increased Bacteroides, and elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide. Plasma short-chain fatty acids, measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, were lower after the high-fat, high-sucrose diet and correlated positively with Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. In the hippocampus, brain-derived neurotrophic factor and BDNF expression fell, while interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha rose. Linear regression linked Akkermansia muciniphila depletion to anxiety-like behavior and impaired Morris water maze performance. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-rich chow-fed donors into antibiotic-treated mice restored Akkermansia muciniphila and attenuated neuroinflammation. These findings indicate that dietary fiber may protect the gut-brain axis by preserving specific microbial taxa and limiting cytokine signaling. However, causal direction and translation to humans require further study.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, yet the dietary and microbial signals that shape central nervous system function remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder, shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal microbiota revealed reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila alongside elevated Bacteroides species. These shifts correlated with lower short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, and with altered expression of BDNF and GPR43 in peripheral blood. A Mediterranean-style diet rich in fiber and fermented foods was associated with partial restoration of microbial diversity and increased butyrate levels after 8 weeks. Random forest analysis identified Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia as discriminative features. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders improved depressive-like behavior and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and specific commensals interact to modulate neuroactive metabolites and host signaling, offering a tractable target for depression.

Metabolites from gut microbiota can modulate brain function, and their depletion is associated with major depressive disorder. We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with major depressive disorder (n=120). Participants received fermented dairy enriched with Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium breve or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. We used linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to test whether changes in microbial composition mediated symptom improvement. Compared with placebo, the fermented dairy increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate, and lowered interleukin-6. Depressive symptoms decreased more in the intervention group, and mediation analysis attributed 31% of the effect to butyrate increase. Exploratory fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate increase and reduced anxiety-like behavior. We applied Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings support microbiota-targeted fermented foods as adjunctive therapy for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Dietary fiber intake shapes gut microbiota composition and may modify Alzheimer's disease risk through the gut-brain axis, yet the microbial and host pathways linking fiber-rich diets to APOE-stratified cognitive decline remain incompletely resolved. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics on fecal microbiota from older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment, then transplanted patient-derived microbiota into mice fed either a high-fat diet or a fiber-supplemented diet. Prevotella and Bacteroides abundance diverged by APOE genotype and tracked with short-chain fatty acid output. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with low butyrate increased neuroinflammation, elevated BDNF promoter methylation, and impaired function in the hippocampus of recipient mice; these effects were attenuated by dietary fiber. Baseline Akkermansia abundance inversely correlated with lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and predicted less cognitive decline. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial composition explained part of the association between diet and cognitive decline. These findings identify APOE-dependent microbial signatures as potential targets for fiber-based interventions in Alzheimer's disease.

Depletion of butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium and Roseburia in the gut microbiome is a reproducible feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with constipation severity. Baseline butyrate concentrations were lower in PD patients than controls (p = 0.006), and calprotectin was higher. We characterized fecal microbiota from 82 PD patients and 60 controls using full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Random forest and Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia enrichment and Faecalibacterium loss to worse postural instability and motor symptoms. In a 12-week randomized sub-study, 40 patients received a probiotic formulation containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, raised butyrate in colon, and reduced calprotectin; these shifts correlated with improved constipation and motor symptoms. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the probiotic effect on constipation. The probiotic was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome as a modifiable contributor to PD progression.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids shape brain circuits governing anxiety and depression, yet the microbial taxa and metabolic pathways that confer resilience to chronic stress remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and metabolites in mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress and in healthy volunteers before and after a prebiotic fiber intervention. Stress-susceptible mice exhibited depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, reduced butyrate, and elevated interleukin-6 relative to resilient mice. Fecal short-chain fatty acids quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmed lower butyrate and propionate in susceptible mice. Random forest modeling identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate as top predictors of resilience to chronic stress. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii-associated butyrate partially mediated the relationship between microbiota composition and anxiety-like behavior. In participants, inulin increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate, with linear mixed-effects models showing a negative association between butyrate and anxiety scores. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through prebiotic supplementation may promote short-chain fatty acid production and gut-brain signaling, offering a tractable strategy for stress-related disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by a Western diet can precede Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology, but whether targeted omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids can restore microbial and cognitive homeostasis remains unresolved. We fed APP/PS1 mice either a standard chow or high-fat, high-sucrose diet for 16 weeks and treated a subset with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut contents revealed that the Western diet reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus while expanding Bacteroides and Clostridium. These shifts correlated with elevated lipopolysaccharide in plasma, increased IL-1β and TNF-α expression in hippocampus, and impaired Morris water maze performance. Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids partially reversed the gut microbial dysbiosis, lowered lipopolysaccharide, and improved cognitive impairment. Fecal transfer from omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids-treated mice to germ-free mice reproduced the cognitive benefit, whereas transfer from Western diet-fed donors did not. Metagenomic sequencing further linked these effects to butyrate production pathways. These findings suggest that omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids ameliorate AD-related cognitive decline through gut microbiota-dependent mechanisms.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone, and their depletion is linked to neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease. We tested whether probiotic supplementation alters gut microbiota, fecal butyrate, and inflammatory mediators in patients with mild cognitive impairment. Fecal and blood samples were collected before and after 12 weeks of probiotics. Microbiota composition was profiled by sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene. Abundances of butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were quantified. Interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and calprotectin were measured. Linear mixed models and Spearman correlation assessed associations. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6. Higher baseline Roseburia abundance correlated with lower tumor necrosis factor-alpha, while butyrate changes correlated with improved performance on neuropsychological testing. Fecal butyrate increases were greater in participants with higher baseline Roseburia. Adherence exceeded 85%, and no serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that probiotics may modulate gut-brain signaling and support further trials in Alzheimer's disease.

Consumption of a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable dietary fiber increases gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids, which can attenuate neuroinflammation and support hippocampal plasticity. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we tested whether adding a multi-strain probiotic to this diet produced greater cognitive benefit in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Participants received the diet alone or with the probiotic for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing characterized fecal microbiota; liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified short-chain fatty acids; and neuropsychological testing plus functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain function. The probiotic group showed higher abundances of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, lower Bacteroides, and elevated butyrate. These shifts correlated with improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores and reduced interleukin-6, with effects strongest in participants showing baseline microbial dysbiosis. Linear mixed-effects models linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF expression and hippocampal connectivity. Thus, probiotic-supplemented Mediterranean-style diets may slow cognitive decline by reshaping gut microbiota and metabolite signals along the gut-brain axis.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with preserved hippocampal volume and slower cognitive decline, yet whether gut microbiota mediate this relationship remains uncertain. We profiled fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and serum short-chain fatty acids in 172 older adults across normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease. Dietary intake was measured using a food frequency questionnaire. A random forest classifier identified microbial signatures distinguishing diagnostic groups; mediation analysis tested indirect effects. Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia were depleted in mild cognitive impairment, and their abundances correlated positively with dietary fiber intake and butyrate concentrations. The random forest model reached an AUC of 0.81 for mild cognitive impairment versus normal cognition. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiota explained 23% of the association between Mediterranean diet and cognitive decline. Greater consumption of fermented foods and fiber-rich foods was associated with higher Faecalibacterium abundance and elevated BDNF expression in brain tissue from a subset. These findings support dietary modulation of the gut-brain axis through gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acids.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is now recognized as a modifier of major depressive disorder and anxiety, yet the bacterial taxa and molecular pathways that mediate this effect remain incompletely defined. We profiled fecal microbiota from patients and mice using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. 16S rRNA gene data revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in depression cases, while Bacteroides was enriched. Metabolomic profiling identified short-chain fatty acids and kynurenine as candidate mediators. Using random forest and mediation analysis, we found that butyrate availability explained a significant portion of the association between Lactobacillus abundance and depressive-like behavior. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from patients recapitulated both microbial and behavioral phenotypes, and fluoxetine partially reversed these changes. These findings support a model in which gut microbiota-derived metabolites modulate brain function and suggest that targeting Lactobacillus or butyrate signaling may offer therapeutic avenues for depression.

Inulin-type fructans reshape the gut microbiota and improve mild cognitive impairment in older adults, yet whether microbiota shifts mediate hippocampal responses remains unresolved. We randomized adults aged 60–75 years with subjective memory decline to 12 weeks of inulin (10 g/day) or placebo. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were quantified by 16S rRNA sequencing; circulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and fecal short-chain fatty acids, including acetate, propionate, and butyrate, were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Cognition was assessed with the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. Using causal mediation analysis, we found that inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations, which predicted reduced memory impairment. The indirect effect through butyrate was significant (β = 0.18, 95% CI 0.05–0.34), whereas the direct effect was not. Linear mixed models showed no change in BDNF. No serious adverse events were reported. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber benefits episodic memory impairment via microbiota-butyrate signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites can modulate BDNF expression and IL-6 signaling in the hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic route by which gut microbiota shape depression and anxiety. To test this, we profiled fecal microbiota from adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, alongside RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Faecalibacterium and Lactobacillus abundances were lower in patients; these taxa correlated inversely with IL6 and CRP transcripts. Random forest classification distinguished cases from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability partially explained the association between gut microbial diversity and symptom severity. Baseline TLR4 expression and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein concentrations were elevated in patients, and mixed-effects models showed that these markers moderated the relationship between Bacteroides abundance and anhedonia. In a separate cohort, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and reduced depressive symptoms, although antidepressant use confounded some effects. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome to influence BDNF-related and inflammatory pathways in stress-related disorders.

Higher abundance of Bacteroides and reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii track with Alzheimer's disease severity, suggesting that gut microbiota composition modifies brain amyloid-beta pathology through immune and metabolic routes. To test whether dietary exposure causally influences this axis, we applied two-sample Mendelian randomization to summary statistics from human cohorts, using inverse variance-weighted estimates with MR-Egger and weighted median sensitivity analyses. Genetic liability to higher fermented food intake was associated with increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower dementia risk, whereas probiotic supplementation showed a similar but weaker protective pattern. In contrast, high-fat diet adherence correlated with elevated lipopolysaccharide and amyloid-beta levels, and with reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Mediation models indicated that microbiota shifts explained 18% of the diet-AD association. We further performed MR-PRESSO and leave-one-out analysis to exclude pleiotropy and influential variants. In germ-free mice, 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed that probiotic colonization increased Bifidobacterium and decreased amyloid-beta deposition. These findings support targeting gut microbiota via dietary fiber and probiotics as adjunctive strategies for Alzheimer's disease prevention, though Mendelian randomization assumptions warrant cautious interpretation.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber modulate central BDNF signaling and neuroinflammation, providing a mechanistic link between gut microbiota and cognitive decline. In rodent models, short-chain fatty acids generated by Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium stimulate vagal afferents and alter microglial cytokines and serotonin availability. We examined whether probiotic supplementation combined with fermentable prebiotic fiber changes BDNF expression and anxiety-like behavior in adults with metabolic syndrome. Over 12 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii; mixed-effects models associated these shifts with higher butyrate and lower IL-6. Participants receiving probiotics exhibited elevated BDNF and improved cognitive symptoms relative to placebo. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein fell, while microbial richness correlated with depressive symptoms improvement. These results suggest that targeting gut microbiota through fermented foods and psychobiotics may complement conventional antidepressants, although APOE genotype and baseline microbial diversity modified responses. Future trials should stratify by APOE and measure neuroactive metabolites longitudinally.

Higher dietary fiber intake is associated with greater gut microbial diversity and lower systemic inflammation, yet the pathways linking these changes to brain function remain incompletely defined. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild major depressive disorder received a fiber-enriched diet or habitual diet for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Associations between Faecalibacterium abundance, butyrate concentrations, and hippocampal activity were tested using linear mixed-effects models. The fiber-enriched diet increased Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae relative abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and improved self-reported mood. Higher butyrate correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and increased hippocampal BDNF expression in a subset undergoing magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Mediation analysis using bootstrapped confidence intervals suggested that microbial butyrate production partially accounted for the association between diet and mood. These findings support a model in which dietary fiber modifies the gut microbiome, enhancing short-chain fatty acid signaling to brain regions implicated in mood regulation. Targeting fiber intake may offer a scalable adjunctive strategy for depression, though confirmatory trials with longer follow-up and direct brain measures are needed.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber fermentation, particularly short-chain fatty acids, shape central nervous system immunity and behavior, yet the extent to which they mediate diet–brain associations remains uncertain. We examined whether gut microbiota composition and butyrate production link high-fiber diets to BDNF expression and depressive-like behavior in mice and adults. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, quantitative PCR, and causal mediation analysis were applied. In mice, inulin supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated butyrate, and upregulated Bdnf in the hippocampus; these changes were attenuated by antibiotics. In participants, linear mixed models revealed that microbial diversity and butyrate explained part of the inverse association between fiber intake and depressive symptoms, independent of antidepressant use. Mendelian randomization suggested a protective effect of genetically proxied Faecalibacterium on depression. These findings position gut microbiota–butyrate signaling as a modifiable pathway through which diet influences BDNF-dependent brain function. Sensitivity analyses confirmed these results, and random-effects meta-analysis across cohorts strengthened the evidence.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape central BDNF expression and serotonin signaling, linking gut microbiota composition to neuropsychiatric disorders. We tested whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids plus inulin could modify this axis in adults with mild cognitive impairment. Over 12 weeks, participants received either supplement or placebo; fecal microbiome was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and hippocampal activity was assessed by functional magnetic resonance imaging. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and upregulated BDNF in participants' blood. Mixed-effects models revealed that changes in Bifidobacterium explained 18% of variance in BDNF, while lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 remained unchanged. Butyrate can inhibit histone deacetylases and promote BDNF promoter acetylation, suggesting a direct epigenetic route. Baseline microbial diversity and Faecalibacterium abundance predicted responsiveness, whereas Bacteroides-dominated microbial communities showed weaker effects. No serious adverse events were reported. These findings support prebiotic and omega-3 co-supplementation as a strategy to engage gut microbiota-brain signaling in early neurodegeneration.

Gut microbiota metabolism of dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) modulates brain function and visceral pain, but whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation amplifies this axis in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is unclear. We randomized 120 adults with IBS and subclinical anxiety to a high-fiber Mediterranean diet plus placebo or plus omega-3 supplementation for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and SCFA concentrations were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models assessed symptom trajectories, while mediation analysis tested whether Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance explained clinical improvement. Compared with diet alone, omega-3 increased butyrate and reduced anxiety scores; effects were strongest in participants with low baseline Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures by treatment arm, and exploratory random forest classification identified Roseburia and Prevotella as discriminators of response. BDNF expression correlated with butyrate availability. These findings suggest that combining fiber-rich foods with omega-3 supplementation may target gut microbiota-brain signaling in IBS.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the extent to which diet can steer these signals in adults remains uncertain. We analyzed fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acid profiles from 120 participants with mild depressive symptoms who consumed either a high-fiber Mediterranean-style diet or habitual diet for 8 weeks. The intervention group also received a multi-strain probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance after intervention. Linear mixed-effects models showed that changes in Roseburia correlated with reduced depressive symptom scores and higher butyrate concentrations. PICRUSt2 predicted enrichment of tryptophan biosynthesis pathways. The magnitude of microbiota shift was greater in participants with lower baseline Roseburia abundance. These findings suggest that dietary and supplemental microbial strategies can modulate the gut microbiome and may influence brain health, although randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Commensal bacteria in the gastrointestinal tract influence brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and gut microbiota imbalance is increasingly linked to depression and anxiety. We tested whether a 12-week probiotic intervention alters gut microbiota composition, short-chain fatty acid production, and BDNF expression in adults with moderate depressive symptoms. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants were assigned to Lactobacillus rhamnosus plus Bifidobacterium animalis or control. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and associations with depression scores were estimated using linear mixed-effects models. Relative to control, probiotic recipients showed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, higher butyrate concentrations, and elevated BDNF expression. These changes correlated with reduced anxiety and depression severity. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and BDNF partially mediated the probiotic effect on mood. The findings support targeting the gut microbiome as an adjunctive strategy for mood disorders, though larger trials with metagenomic sequencing and causal inference are needed.

Gut microbial signals shape central nervous system function, yet whether prebiotic galacto-oligosaccharides can reverse stress-induced depression-like phenotypes remains unresolved. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder and fed them a control diet or one supplemented with galacto-oligosaccharides for six weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that supplementation expanded Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing Bacteroides. In the hippocampus, serotonin turnover and Bdnf expression increased, paralleling reduced anhedonia in sucrose preference tests. Random forest classification linked these behavioral shifts to microbial taxa and short-chain fatty acid profiles. In the cecum, butyrate and acetate concentrations were elevated in supplemented mice, and mediation analysis suggested that these metabolites partially explained the behavioral protection. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into naive mice conferred similar resilience, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished the effect. These findings position prebiotic galacto-oligosaccharides as a tractable modulator of gut microbiota-brain signaling, though validation in humans is needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiome has been linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the microbial taxa and host pathways that mediate this effect remain unresolved. We profiled stool and serum from 84 adults with MDD and 79 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics. Microbial community structure differed by diagnosis, with reduced Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and elevated Eggerthella in patients. A random forest classifier distinguished groups with an area under the curve of 0.78, and mediation analysis indicated that tryptophan metabolites explained part of the association. Expression of BDNF and IL6 in peripheral blood correlated inversely with Faecalibacterium abundance. In germ-free mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD donors increased anxiety-like behavior and reduced hippocampal Bdnf transcripts relative to mice receiving control microbiota. These findings suggest that gut microbial composition influences depressive symptoms through tryptophan metabolism and BDNF-related plasticity, highlighting targets for probiotic or antidepressant intervention. Together, these cross-sectional and causal findings implicate the gut microbiome in MDD pathophysiology.

Altered gut microbiota composition predicts major depressive disorder severity through immune and metabolic routes, yet whether diet-dependent microbial signals causally affect brain function remains contested. In a cohort of adults, mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acid production from fiber-rich foods indirectly reduced depressive symptoms via BDNF expression and circulating interleukin-6. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium were inversely associated with neuroinflammation markers, whereas Lactobacillus abundance correlated with serotonin metabolites. Random-effects meta-analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing studies confirmed modest but reproducible taxonomic shifts in psychiatric disorders, although heterogeneity across diets, antidepressant exposure, and FTO variants was substantial. Mendelian randomization suggested a protective effect of Bifidobacterium on anxiety, but not on depression. However, small sample sizes and inconsistent dietary assessments limit causal interpretation. These findings suggest that probiotic and fermented food interventions may improve depressive symptoms only when baseline BDNF signaling and microbial butyrate capacity are intact. Prospective trials integrating causal inference with longitudinal microbiome profiling are needed to identify which patients benefit.

Dietary fermentation products can reshape gut microbial ecology and modulate vagal signaling, yet their contribution to interoceptive and affective phenotypes remains poorly quantified. We tested whether habitual intake of fermented foods predicts gut microbiota composition and prefrontal cortex responses to visceral cues in 84 healthy adults. Stool samples underwent 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing; plasma short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were quantified. The protocol included a functional magnetic resonance imaging task during gastric distension and weekly records of yogurt, kefir, and kimchi intake. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Greater fermented food consumption was associated with higher Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance and increased butyrate concentrations. These microbial shifts correlated with attenuated amygdala reactivity to aversive visceral stimuli and stronger insula-prefrontal cortex coupling. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly accounted for the relationship between fermented food intake and insula response. In contrast, no associations emerged for high-fiber plant foods. These findings position dietary fermentation as a modifiable gut-brain signal and support targeting microbiome metabolites in interventions for stress-related disorders.

Gut microbial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids, can modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic route by which the gut microbiota influences mood and cognition. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 120 adults with major depressive disorder received either probiotic supplementation or placebo for 12 weeks; 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiled stool communities, and linear mixed-effects models tested changes in depressive symptoms and BDNF methylation. Probiotic-treated participants showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, higher butyrate levels, and greater reduction in symptom scores than placebo. Stool microbiota composition differed by response status (PERMANOVA, R2=0.08, p=0.012). Mediation analysis indicated that microbial shifts explained 31% of the clinical effect, with BDNF promoter methylation partially mediating this association. These findings link probiotic intake, gut microbial ecology, and BDNF-related epigenetic regulation in depression, though confirmatory trials using shotgun metagenomics and longer follow-up are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that cross the blood-brain barrier and dampen neuroinflammation, yet whether this axis preserves cognition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, 120 older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either blueberry powder or placebo. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that blueberry supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus and elevated fecal butyrate and propionate. These shifts correlated with higher BDNF expression in hippocampus and lower NLRP3 in prefrontal cortex, alongside improved memory scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the cognitive benefit. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated these effects, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Baseline gut microbiota composition predicted response, with Bacteroides abundance inversely associated with butyrate production. These findings suggest that blueberry-enriched diets act through the gut microbiota to regulate BDNF and NLRP3 signaling, offering a tractable strategy for early AD intervention.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids shape hippocampal BDNF expression and vagal tone, linking intestinal dysbiosis to affective disorders. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we tested whether Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance predicts depression-like behavior after lipopolysaccharide challenge. Gut microbiota composition explained 31% of variance in prefrontal cortex IL-6, TPH2, and NLRP3 transcripts; linear mixed models and PERMANOVA revealed that Bifidobacterium was inversely associated with neuroinflammation, while Ruminococcus correlated with indole-3-propionic acid concentrations. Metagenomic sequencing further identified microbial butyrate kinase genes enriched in resilient mice; RNA sequencing of vagus nerve showed reduced TLR4 signaling after colonization. In patients with major depressive disorder, probiotic supplementation increased serotonin metabolites and reduced anxiety scores, with effects moderated by baseline microbiota diversity and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use. These findings, spanning rodent models and clinical cohorts, suggest that targeting Lactobacillus-Akkermansia interactions and BDNF signaling may offer a tractable gut-brain therapeutic strategy.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that suppress neuroinflammation and preserve hippocampal function, yet whether these effects causally modify Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk remains unresolved. We integrated summary-data-based Mendelian randomization with colocalization analysis using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and host APOE genotype data from 12,000 participants. Higher genetically predicted gut microbiota abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Butyricicoccus was associated with lower AD odds (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.94; P=0.004). Butyrate mediated 31% of this protective effect. These associations persisted after adjusting for APOE ε4, Mediterranean diet adherence, and metformin use. Sensitivity analyses using MR-Egger and weighted median excluded pleiotropy. Fecal metagenomic profiling confirmed the predicted taxonomic shifts. In APP/PS1 mice, a high-fiber diet increased butyrate, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the brain, and improved Morris water maze performance. Conversely, a Western-style diet depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, elevated IL-1β, and accelerated cognitive decline. These findings position dietary fiber and SCFAs as modifiable mediators of the gut-brain axis and suggest that causal inference can guide fiber-rich diets for AD.

Gut microbial communities shift before motor onset in Parkinson's disease, yet whether these changes are causal or compensatory remains unresolved. We profiled longitudinal stool samples from 120 participants—80 patients with Parkinson's disease and 40 healthy controls—using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Differential abundance analysis identified depletion of Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia and enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae in Parkinson's disease. A random forest classifier trained on baseline microbiota predicted conversion from prodromal symptoms to motor Parkinson's disease with an AUROC of 0.82. Linear mixed models linked these shifts to constipation severity and vagus nerve-dependent brain connectivity. Functional profiles showed reduced short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis and altered lipopolysaccharide production. Metabolomic profiling further revealed lower butyrate and higher trimethylamine N-oxide in patients. Host SNCA genotype and bile acid profiles modified the association between Enterobacteriaceae and cognitive decline. If validated, gut microbiome markers could stratify patients for neuroprotective trials and support probiotic or dietary fiber interventions targeting the gut-brain axis.

Fermented foods and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements can reshape the gut microbiota and modify brain function, yet their combined impact on stress-related disorders remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild anxiety received either a fermented food-rich diet plus omega-3 supplementation or a habitual diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids. Functional magnetic resonance imaging showed reduced amygdala reactivity to emotional faces, and self-report questionnaires indicated lower perceived stress. These changes correlated with BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. In parallel, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Spearman correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance to short-chain fatty acid levels and anxiety scores. The findings suggest that dietary strategies targeting the gut microbiome may offer accessible adjunctive approaches for mood and anxiety symptoms, though replication in larger cohorts is needed.

Microbial production of short-chain fatty acids in the colon shapes central nervous system immune tone, and disruption of this gut microbiota-derived signal is increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative disease. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, dietary inulin supplementation restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and normalized BDNF and IL-10 expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that inulin shifted microbial butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene carriage and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Behavioral testing showed improved anxiety-like behavior and spatial memory, effects absent in Gpr43-deficient mice. Serum IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha concentrations were lower in supplemented mice, while zonulin and markers of intestinal barrier function decreased. Flow cytometry of mesenteric lymph nodes showed expanded Foxp3-positive regulatory T cells, and mediation analysis linked GPR43 expression to behavioral improvement. These findings suggest that fermentable dietary fiber acts through microbiome-host GPR43 signaling to attenuate neuroinflammation and support cognitive resilience. Targeting this microbiome-gut-brain axis pathway may offer a practical adjunct for stress-related psychiatric disorders.

Gut microbial dysbiosis amplifies peripheral immune signals that traverse the vagus nerve and blood-brain barrier, exacerbating neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD). We tested whether inulin supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates cognitive decline in APP/PS1 mice.
