Mice received inulin (5% w/w) or cellulose for 16 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified microbial composition; Morris water maze and novel object recognition assessed memory impairment. Immunofluorescence quantified amyloid-beta deposition and microglial activation in hippocampus. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations and cytokine profiles were measured in colon, serum, and hippocampus. Linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction tested group, time, and interaction effects. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in hippocampus. Treated mice showed shorter escape latency and improved discrimination index relative to control mice. These findings indicate that inulin may slow AD-related neuroinflammation through microbiota-derived metabolites, supporting dietary prebiotic intervention as a gut-brain axis strategy.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life calibrates immune and neuroendocrine circuits that shape stress-related psychopathology across the lifespan. Gut microbiota ferment dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids, which modulate brain function, neuroinflammation, and neurotransmitter availability. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder, higher intake of fermented foods and Mediterranean diet patterns correlated with increased microbial diversity and lower symptom severity. A mediation analysis suggested that short-chain fatty acid production partially explained this association, whereas random-effects meta-analysis of prior trials confirmed modest benefits of probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids. Prebiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced anxiety scores in rodent models, but effects in humans remain heterogeneous. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics reveal strain-level differences that may determine responsiveness. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome through diet and dietary supplementation, while highlighting the need for standardized longitudinal modeling to distinguish causality from confounding. Prospective trials should integrate these measures to guide therapeutic translation.

Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by commensal microbes during early life shapes immune and neurodevelopmental programs that persist into adulthood. Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat, low-fiber diets increases permeability of the intestinal barrier, allowing lipopolysaccharide to enter circulation and promote neuroinflammation. In mice and humans, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation have linked specific Lactobacillus and Bacteroides taxa to anxiety and depressive-like behavior. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, reinforce colon integrity and modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Interventions using fermented foods, prebiotics, and probiotics can reshape microbial communities and reduce neuropsychiatric symptoms, although responses vary with baseline microbiota composition. Mendelian randomization analyses support causal effects of gut microbiota on depression, but confounding by diet and medication remains difficult to exclude. Notably, probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium longum reduced cortisol reactivity in adults with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid anxiety. Integrating metagenomics with metabolomics and targeted clinical trials is needed to translate these findings into therapies directed at the microbiome for gut-brain disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiota contribute to neuroinflammation and behavioral deficits in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the extent to which probiotic supplementation reshapes the gut microbiota–brain axis remains unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 84 adults with MDD received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, and cytokines and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) were quantified in plasma. Mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA tested intervention effects and community-level shifts. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, reduced interleukin-6 (IL-6), and improved Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores relative to placebo. These changes correlated with decreased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and increased short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Baseline microbial diversity and BDNF predicted response, and random forest classification separated responders from nonresponders with moderate accuracy. The findings suggest that targeted probiotic intervention may attenuate MDD-related immune activation through microbiota-mediated pathways, supporting further mediation analyses in larger cohorts.

Gut microbial metabolism of fermented foods can shape neuroinflammation through vagal pathways, yet the magnitude of these effects varies with baseline microbiota composition. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and a prebiotic fiber attenuated corticosterone elevation and reduced BDNF deficits in the hippocampus. We used mediation analysis to test whether changes in gut microbial community structure explained behavioral outcomes. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, which correlated with reduced anxiety-like behavior. A mixed-effects model showed that fermented food intake interacted with supplementation to predict short-chain fatty acid concentrations. Because dietary fibers and polyphenol supplements can independently alter microbial diversity, we quantified their joint effects using redundancy analysis. Moreover, Mantel tests linked microbial metabolites to BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may produce synergistic gut-brain effects, but clinical trials in humans are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid depletion in the gut microbiome is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet whether it directly alters BDNF signaling in the hippocampus remains unresolved. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex in patients and mice to test this. Relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus was lower in depression, and butyrate levels correlated positively with BDNF expression. Lipopolysaccharide was elevated and associated with TNF and IL6 transcripts. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures between groups, and random forest identified Bacteroides as a top predictor of depression status. Using mediation analysis, we found that butyrate mediated the association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and BDNF expression, while linear mixed-effects models confirmed that anxiety-like behavior in mice was attenuated by fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors. These results implicate microbial butyrate in BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that targeting the gut microbiome may alleviate depression and anxiety.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon modulates BDNF expression and serotonin availability, coupling gut microbiota composition to anxiety and depression. In mice, oral probiotic treatment enriched Lactobacillus rhamnosus and butyrate-producing taxa, lowered corticosterone, and reduced FKBP5 expression in the hippocampus. A randomized controlled trial in adults with irritable bowel syndrome compared a fermented food-rich diet with inulin supplementation. Both interventions shifted the fecal microbiome toward Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, but only the fermented food diet increased indole-3-lactic acid and decreased IL6 expression in peripheral blood. These changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms scores and reduced LBP expression, suggesting that dietary fiber and probiotics act through distinct microbial-metabolite routes. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance mediated the association between fermented food intake and BDNF methylation. Overall, targeting the gut microbiome via fermented foods or prebiotic supplementation may offer accessible adjunctive strategies for stress-related disorders.

Microbial metabolites generated from dietary fiber influence gut-brain axis signaling through epigenetic regulation of BDNF and TLR4-dependent neuroinflammation. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment and healthy volunteers received either a high-fermentable fiber diet or habitual diet. Fecal gut microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and serum short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. The fiber intervention increased Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and butyrate compared with control. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that butyrate was associated with higher BDNF expression and lower IL6 and TNF expression in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance mediated the effect of dietary fiber on BDNF expression. Transfer of gut microbiota from fiber-treated donors into germ-free mice recapitulated the BDNF and IL6 changes, supporting causality. These findings suggest that fermentable dietary fiber may improve neuroinflammation and cognitive decline by promoting gut microbiota butyrate production and modulating host BDNF, IL6, and TNF pathways.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids are central mediators of gut microbiota–brain signaling, and their depletion has been repeatedly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD). Using Mendelian randomization across 18,340 adults, we found that genetically predicted lower Faecalibacterium abundance was associated with higher depression risk (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.06–1.23; p=0.001). To test causality, we performed a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 120 patients with MDD. Participants received either a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo. The probiotic group exhibited increased fecal butyrate and reduced IL6 expression relative to placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing confirmed enrichment of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila in responders. Linear mixed-effects models showed a significant group-by-time interaction for BDNF methylation (p=0.018) and depressive symptoms (p=0.031). Mediation analysis indicated that BDNF methylation partially accounted for the probiotic-related improvement in depression severity. No serious adverse events occurred. These results support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics to modulate neurotrophic and neuroimmune pathways in MDD.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber releases short-chain fatty acids that shape microglial reactivity and α-synuclein aggregation along the gut-brain axis, yet how host genotype modifies this diet-microbiome dialogue remains unclear. Using α-synuclein-overexpressing mice carrying SNCA variants, we compared prebiotic fiber supplementation with standard chow and tracked motor deficits, neuroinflammation, and gut microbial composition. Fiber-fed mice showed improved motor performance, reduced α-synuclein pathology in the substantia nigra, and expanded disease-associated microglial subsets. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased Lachnospiraceae and Bacteroides abundance, paralleling elevated butyrate and propionate in feces. Microglial single-cell RNA sequencing revealed suppressed pro-inflammatory signaling and enriched homeostatic programs. Depletion of microglia with a CSF1R inhibitor abolished these benefits, restoring motor deficits despite continued fiber intake. In patients with Parkinson's disease, baseline gut microbiome profiles differed from healthy controls, with lower predicted short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. These findings position SNCA-dependent microglial states as a critical interface through which dietary fiber and microbial metabolites modulate neurodegeneration.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber produces short-chain fatty acids that sustain gut microbial diversity and tune brain immune signaling, but whether APOE genotype modifies these effects during Alzheimer's disease remains unclear. We treated transgenic APP/PS1 mice and wild-type littermates with a high-fiber diet alone or combined with Bifidobacterium breve for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing showed that the high-fiber diet increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, while Bifidobacterium breve further expanded Bifidobacterium and reduced Escherichia coli. In APOE4 carriers, but not APOE3 carriers, the combined intervention lowered amyloid-beta plaque load, interleukin-6, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. This interaction was accompanied by reduced tumor necrosis factor-alpha and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor in the hippocampus. Linear mixed models linked these changes to improved Morris water maze performance. Notably, probiotic effects were absent in germ-free mice, indicating a requirement for resident microbiota. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and Bifidobacterium breve may mitigate Alzheimer's disease-related pathology in a APOE-dependent manner, defining a tractable microbiota-brain target.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fibers generates short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system function, but whether prebiotic supplementation can reproducibly alter anxiety-related circuits remains uncertain. We colonized germ-free mice with human gut microbiota from donors with high or low butyrate production and fed them either a galacto-oligosaccharide-enriched diet or an unsupplemented diet for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that galacto-oligosaccharides increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance, while untargeted metabolomics showed elevated indole-3-propionate and butyrate in portal blood. In the hippocampus, Bdnf expression and serotonin turnover were higher in supplemented mice, and mixed-effects modeling linked these changes to reduced anxiety-like behavior. Vagotomy abolished the behavioral effect, implicating the vagus nerve in the gut-brain axis. Parallel fecal microbiota transplantation into naive recipients transferred the metabolic and behavioral phenotype, whereas antibiotic depletion prevented it. These findings suggest that prebiotic-driven microbial shifts influence brain function through metabolite-sensing pathways, though human validation is needed.

Distinct gut microbiota profiles can precede Parkinson's disease motor symptoms, suggesting that microbial signals contribute to the brain-gut axis before clinical diagnosis. In a 12-week, double-blind randomized controlled trial, adults with chronic constipation and Parkinson's disease received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified stool microbial composition, while shotgun metagenomics profiled genes for short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. Linear mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time interactions after adjustment for baseline microbiota and fiber intake. The probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced constipation severity compared with placebo. Exploratory Spearman correlation analyses linked Roseburia and Faecalibacterium with butyrate and constipation measures. These microbial shifts correlated with improved motor symptoms scores and striatal connectivity on functional magnetic resonance imaging. The findings support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics to modulate gut-brain signaling in Parkinson's disease, although larger trials with standardized probiotic formulations and longitudinal mediation analyses are needed.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbiota and dampens neuroinflammation in mice exposed to lipopolysaccharide, an effect linked to BDNF expression in the hippocampus. We colonized germ-free mice with Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, then administered inulin for four weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids in the gut lumen. In the prefrontal cortex, BDNF and NRF2 transcripts were upregulated, while IL-1β and TNF-α were suppressed. Behavioral testing using forced swim test and novel object recognition showed reduced depressive-like behavior and improved memory. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into naive mice partially reproduced these benefits, but vagotomy abolished them, implicating the vagus nerve. Circulating cytokines correlated with spleen weight, and flow cytometry confirmed reduced cytokine levels. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot randomized controlled trial is warranted to test whether inulin engages BDNF signaling along the gut-brain axis to mitigate neuroinflammation.

Greater intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber tracks with lower depression prevalence, yet whether this reflects causal gut microbiota mediation or confounding by lifestyle remains uncertain. We analyzed adults from a population cohort (n=1,204) with stool metagenomic sequencing, serum liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and validated depressive symptom scores. Microbial functional potential was summarized by principal coordinate analysis, and associations were tested using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use. Higher fermented food intake correlated with enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species and increased short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-propionate explained 21% of the inverse association between dietary fiber and depression. In a subset, functional magnetic resonance imaging showed that these metabolites correlated with amygdala reactivity to negative faces. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and BDNF expression were also linked to hippocampal serotonin turnover. These findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as plausible mediators linking fermented foods and fiber to brain circuits implicated in depression, though Mendelian randomization is needed to confirm causality.

Microbial depletion of short-chain fatty acid producers in the gut microbiome tracks with reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus and elevated depressive symptoms, suggesting a causal rather than incidental link along the gut-brain axis. In a cohort of 412 adults, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance was inversely associated with anxiety severity after adjustment for antidepressant use and dietary fiber intake. Fecal butyrate concentrations mediated 18.7% of the association between Faecalibacterium and BDNF methylation. Using Mendelian randomization, genetically predicted gut microbiota composition showed a bidirectional relationship with major depressive disorder, while mediation analysis implicated indole-3-propionic acid as a potential messenger. In an independent validation set, linear mixed-effects models confirmed that Roseburia depletion predicted worsening anhedonia over 12 months, with TLR4 expression partially accounting for this effect. In mice, oral Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored butyrate levels, normalized BDNF expression, and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings position microbial metabolites as modifiable signals that may inform microbiota-targeted interventions for mood disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease, yet whether restoring microbial balance improves cognition in older adults remains unresolved. In a double-blind trial, 82 participants with subjective cognitive decline received either Bifidobacterium breve plus inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. Cognitive performance was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Computerized Neuropsychological Test Battery; fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. A linear mixed-effects model revealed a significant group-by-time interaction for global cognition (β = 0.34, p = 0.012), with enriched Bifidobacterium and Lachnospiraceae and reduced Bacteroides in the intervention arm. Increases in butyrate correlated with improved hippocampal-dependent memory. These findings support targeted probiotic and prebiotic supplementation as a plausible strategy to modulate the gut microbiome and slow cognitive aging, though larger trials with neuroimaging endpoints are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the microbial signals that shape antidepressant response remain incompletely defined. In a chronic social defeat stress model, mice exposed to repeated defeat exhibited reduced hippocampal Bdnf expression, elevated serum corticosterone, and distinct fecal microbiota. 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing revealed depletion of Lactobacillus and Akkermansia and enrichment of Bacteroides in stressed mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from stressed mice donors to naive mice reproduced social avoidance and decreased Bdnf, whereas FMT from unstressed mice donors attenuated these deficits. Ketamine treatment reversed stress-induced behavioral abnormalities and partially normalized the microbiota; these effects were accompanied by increased Bdnf and reduced interleukin-6 in the hippocampus. Random forest classification and Spearman correlation identified Akkermansia abundance as negatively correlated with immobility time and positively correlated with Bdnf. These findings suggest that depression-associated microbiota shifts contribute to impaired neuroplasticity and that targeting the gut microbiota may enhance ketamine's antidepressant efficacy.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape hippocampal plasticity, yet whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation amplifies this effect when layered onto a Mediterranean-style diet remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, 96 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either omega-3 capsules or placebo while consuming a high-fiber, polyphenol-rich diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; SCFA concentrations were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Omega-3 supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated butyrate compared with placebo. These shifts correlated with improved verbal memory scores and lower IL6 expression in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 31% of the cognitive benefit. In mice, transferring fecal microbiota from responders recapitulated the cognitive benefit, whereas Bifidobacterium depletion abolished it. The findings indicate that omega-3 combined with a fermented-food-rich diet may promote gut-brain axis resilience in mild cognitive impairment.

Depletion of gut microbial taxa that produce short-chain fatty acids is a reproducible correlate of major depressive disorder (MDD), but whether habitual Mediterranean diet intake modifies this association remains unresolved. We analyzed fecal samples from 180 adults with MDD and 120 healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Random forest models identified 14 microbial genera that discriminated groups with 82% accuracy. Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Lachnospira were depleted in MDD, whereas Bacteroides and Alistipes were enriched. These shifts correlated with lower fecal butyrate and higher lipopolysaccharide levels, and with more severe cognitive impairment. Among Mediterranean diet-adherent participants, Roseburia abundance was 2.1-fold higher and butyrate levels were 38% greater than in non-adherent participants. A fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high Roseburia into mice reduced depressive-like behavior and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that Mediterranean diet-associated microbiota may protect against MDD via butyrate-dependent gut-brain signaling.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and serotonin precursors generated in the gut modulate blood-brain barrier permeability, brain immune tone, and stress-related behavior. In mice colonized with gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder, we observed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and lower BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation reproduced these phenotypes, whereas probiotic supplementation attenuated neuroinflammation and normalized corticosterone levels. 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomic sequencing, and random forest classification identified Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii as protective taxa; PERMANOVA revealed distinct community clusters. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial butyrate production indirectly influenced BDNF through TLR4 signaling. In a cohort of 184 adults, omega-3 supplementation combined with probiotics correlated with lower depression scores, but antibiotic exposure was associated with greater symptom severity. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable mediator of gut-brain axis signaling and support targeted probiotic and prebiotic interventions. Collectively, these data link microbial metabolites to neuropsychiatric symptoms and identify tractable dietary and pharmacological targets.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape central nervous system immune tone and blood-brain barrier integrity, yet their role in cognitive decline remains contested. We fed aged mice a high-fat, low-fiber diet or an isocaloric fiber-rich diet for 12 weeks and profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal SCFAs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and hippocampal BDNF expression. Linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis tested associations among diet, Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium, butyrate, and memory impairment. The fiber-rich diet increased Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate, and reduced memory impairment relative to high-fat, low-fiber diet. To probe causality, we colonized germ-free mice with microbiota from donors fed high- or low-fiber diets and quantified cytokines in colon and plasma. Butyrate mediated 38% of the diet effect on BDNF expression. Faecalibacterium abundance correlated inversely with lipopolysaccharide levels. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a mechanistic link between dietary fiber and protection against age-related cognitive decline, suggesting prebiotic supplementation as a candidate strategy for age-related cognitive decline.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that signal to the brain through vagal, endocrine, and immune pathways, and disrupted fermentation is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD). We asked whether a inulin supplement could restore this communication in adults with MDD and low gut microbiota diversity. In a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 84 participants received inulin or placebo alongside standardized care. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and serum mass spectrometry quantified gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acids. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. Depressive symptoms declined more with inulin than placebo; improvement correlated with butyrate and with increased BDNF expression. Baseline Mediterranean diet adherence modified the treatment effect, and linear mixed models showed that inulin responders had greater diversity of gut microbiota. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation can engage the gut-brain axis and may complement conventional depression treatment.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with richer gut microbiota and slower cognitive decline, yet the microbial mediators linking diet to brain function remain poorly resolved. We profiled fecal microbiota from 184 older adults, including 92 with mild cognitive impairment and 92 cognitively normal controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Circulating short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, and IL-6 were quantified. Mediation analysis tested whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bacteroides abundance explained adherence-related differences in BDNF and hippocampal volume. Greater Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate, lower IL-6, and better hippocampal integrity. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 18% of the adherence-cognition relationship, while IL-6 suppression explained 11%. Bacteroides richness correlated inversely with IL-6 but not with BDNF. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a plausible transducer of Mediterranean diet effects on brain health, suggesting that probiotic or fiber-enriched interventions warrant testing in mild cognitive impairment.

Alterations in the gut microbiota are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the molecular routes through which microbial signals reach the brain remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of patients with MDD and matched controls, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside lower fecal short-chain fatty acids. These microbial shifts correlated with BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood and with hippocampal volume. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, we found that Lactobacillus abundance predicted BDNF methylation independently of antidepressant exposure. In mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress, probiotic supplementation restored Lactobacillus levels, decreased BDNF methylation, and reduced depressive-like behavior; these effects were absent after vagotomy. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the relationship between Lactobacillus and BDNF methylation. The findings position BDNF epigenetic regulation as a plausible node linking gut microbial ecology to depression via the vagus nerve, and suggest that microbial or butyrate-directed interventions warrant further testing in patients.

Altered gut microbial communities and their metabolites are now positioned as upstream regulators of neuropsychiatric disorders, with short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acid derivatives shaping brain immune tone. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder (MDD), shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics revealed reduced Faecalibacterium and Roseburia alongside lower butyrate levels. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability statistically accounted for part of the association between microbial composition and depressive symptom severity. In chronic stress mice, oral butyrate or probiotic supplementation normalized neuroinflammation, restored serotonin turnover, and improved anhedonia; fecal microbiota transplantation from responders partially reproduced these effects. A fermented-food-rich diet increased microbial diversity and reduced inflammatory markers in a pilot randomized trial. In parallel, random-effects meta-analysis of clinical cohorts linked higher dietary fiber intake with lower depression risk, although heterogeneity was substantial. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota through fiber-rich foods and microbial therapeutics may complement conventional antidepressants.

Resistant starch supplementation increases short-chain fatty acid production by gut microbiota and upregulates BDNF in the hippocampus, yet the extent to which these effects depend on baseline microbial composition remains unclear. We randomized 120 adults with mild depressive symptoms to receive resistant starch (n=60) or digestible starch (n=60) for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples and quantitative PCR of peripheral blood BDNF expression were performed. Mixed-effects models tested interactions between intervention and baseline Bifidobacterium abundance. Resistant starch increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance and raised butyrate concentrations compared with digestible starch. BDNF expression increased only in participants with low baseline Bifidobacterium abundance, and this increase correlated with reduced depressive symptoms. In germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from high- versus low-Bifidobacterium donors, resistant starch similarly modulated BDNF and butyrate, confirming a causal microbiota-dependent mechanism. These findings suggest that resistant starch may improve mood through microbiota-dependent BDNF signaling, but baseline microbial ecology determines responsiveness.

Disruption of the gut microbiome increasingly appears to precede and possibly drive cognitive decline, yet the molecular routes linking microbial metabolites to brain function remain poorly defined. In APP/PS1 mice and older adults with mild cognitive impairment, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed reduced Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance alongside elevated trimethylamine N-oxide and depleted short-chain fatty acids. These shifts correlated with lower BDNF expression and altered APOE isoform-related lipid handling in the hippocampus, and with increased amyloid-β deposition. Fecal microbiota transplantation from affected donors into germ-free mice reproduced spatial memory deficits, whereas fiber supplementation partially reversed these effects and restored BDNF signaling. Complementary two-sample Mendelian randomization using genome-wide association summary data supported a causal effect of specific microbial taxa on cognitive performance. Our findings position the gut microbiota as a modifiable contributor to Alzheimer's disease risk and suggest that 16S rRNA sequencing-guided stratification, combined with BDNF and APOE profiling, may identify patients most likely to benefit from microbiome-directed interventions.

Microbial colonization of the gut during early life calibrates BDNF expression and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity, yet how diet-derived substrates shape this dialogue in adulthood remains poorly resolved. We recruited 84 adults with major depressive disorder and 62 healthy controls and profiled gut microbiota via 16S rRNA sequencing, quantified plasma short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide, and measured BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated fermented food and fiber questionnaire; a subset received probiotics for 8 weeks. Compared with controls, patients showed lower Faecalibacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, reduced butyrate, and higher BDNF promoter methylation. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium and depressive symptoms. In a parallel mouse model, probiotic supplementation plus fermented food-derived lactate normalized BDNF expression and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-targeted dietary fiber and probiotics may modulate BDNF-dependent brain plasticity, offering a tractable adjunct for depression.

Twelve weeks of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation reshaped gut microbiota and attenuated major depressive disorder symptoms in adults, but microbial predictors of response remain unclear. We analyzed patients (n=120) randomized to omega-3 (2 g/day) or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; plasma interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. At baseline, patients showed lower relative abundance of Faecalibacterium and Bifidobacterium than healthy controls and higher interleukin-6. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and reduced interleukin-6; these changes correlated with decreased depression severity. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing further identified enrichment of butyrate-producing pathways. In mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from responders, hippocampal BDNF expression increased and anxiety-like behavior decreased. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial changes explained 32% of clinical improvement. These findings suggest that omega-3-induced microbial shifts contribute to symptom improvement, supporting microbiota-targeted nutritional strategies for depression. Additional trials combining omega-3 with probiotics are warranted.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and bile acid metabolites shape central nervous system immune tone, yet their causal contribution to anxiety-like behavior remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Lactobacillus rhamnosus and measured prefrontal cortex BDNF expression, serotonin turnover, and depressive-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation were combined with linear mixed-effects models to test whether gut microbiota composition predicted behavioral outcomes. B. fragilis colonization increased GABA concentrations in the hippocampus and reduced neuroinflammation, whereas L. rhamnosus altered kynurenine pathway activity. Tryptophan availability and IDO1 expression correlated with anhedonia severity. Prebiotic inulin potentiated these effects, while vancomycin depleted commensal bacteria and reversed behavioral protection. Patients with major depressive disorder showed parallel reductions in microbial diversity and fecal short-chain fatty acids. These findings position gut microbiota-derived neuroactive metabolites as modifiable mediators of gut-brain signaling and support psychobiotic strategies, though Mendelian randomization is needed to clarify causality.

Depletion of short-chain fatty acids and other microbial neuroactive metabolites is associated with anxiety and depression, implicating gut microbiota in stress-related disorders. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with moderate stress received probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus plantarum P-8 or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal metagenomes were profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and linear mixed-effects models assessed longitudinal changes in microbial diversity, Aitchison distance, and neuroactive metabolite pathways. 16S rRNA gene sequencing validated taxonomic shifts, while PERMANOVA tested community-level differences. The probiotic group maintained Shannon diversity and showed enriched Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Bifidobacterium longum, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii compared with placebo. Conversely, placebo recipients had lower abundances of Roseburia faecis and Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans. Predicted gamma-aminobutyric acid, arachidonic acid, and sphingomyelin synthesis increased, while perceived stress and anxiety scores declined. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation modulates gut microbiome function and microbial metabolite output to alleviate stress-related symptoms, supporting the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target.

Gut microbial fermentation of fermentable fiber yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that reinforce colonic barrier function and attenuate neuroinflammation, but whether this axis can be therapeutically harnessed in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unresolved. We enrolled patients with PD and healthy controls and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Participants received either probiotic supplementation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis) or no supplement for 12 weeks. Relative to controls, patients with PD showed depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Akkermansia muciniphila, and butyrate, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and serum butyrate, and reduced inflammatory cytokines in plasma. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with PD-associated microbiota impaired nigrostriatal tyrosine hydroxylase expression, an effect reversed by butyrate supplementation. Linear mixed-effects models linked Faecalibacterium depletion to motor severity. Baseline Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance, whereas levodopa dose did not. These findings support fiber- and probiotic-based strategies for modulating the gut microbiome in PD.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate tight junction protein expression and neuroinflammation, positioning the gut microbiota as a key regulator of brain function. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with Bacteroides fragilis and Lactobacillus rhamnosus altered BDNF and GABA receptor transcripts in the hippocampus, while 16S rRNA sequencing revealed diet-dependent shifts in microbial composition. Inulin supplementation increased butyrate availability and reduced anxiety-like behavior; these effects were absent in Gpr43-deficient mice, implicating SCFA–GPR43 signaling in gut–brain communication. Parallel human cohort data showed that fiber intake correlated with microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms, but the association depended on baseline BDNF genotype. In a randomized adult trial, probiotic treatment combined with fermentable fiber increased propionate and acetate concentrations and improved cognitive deficits; mediation analysis suggested that microbial diversity explained part of this effect. These findings suggest that targeting microbiota-derived metabolites through fermentable fiber may offer a tractable strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders, although causal host genetic variants require further study.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis promotes Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression through short-chain fatty acid-dependent and independent routes, yet the transcriptional programs linking colon signals to hippocampal inflammation remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Lactobacillus rhamnosus and measured BDNF, TLR4, and IL-1β expression in prefrontal cortex using quantitative RT-PCR. 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed microbial community composition, while ELISA quantified lipopolysaccharide and IL-6. Spearman correlation and linear mixed-effects modeling associated Bacteroides abundance with BDNF downregulation and TLR4 upregulation. B. fragilis colonization increased IL-1β and IL-6 and impaired cognitive function, whereas L. rhamnosus attenuated these changes and elevated butyrate. Flow cytometry revealed increased CD68 expression in hippocampus, and fecal microbiota transplantation from B. fragilis-colonized donors into naive mice reproduced TLR4 induction and IL-1β elevation. All comparisons survived false discovery rate correction. These data indicate that specific gut bacteria sculpt brain immune tone via TLR4-dependent signaling, identifying candidate microbial targets for AD.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids modulate central nervous system immune signaling, yet whether dietary fiber supplementation can alter this gut-brain communication in adults with mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. We conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 84 participants who received either inulin (12 g/day) or placebo. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF expression was quantified in peripheral blood. Mixed-effects linear models assessed changes in BDNF expression, microbial diversity, and cognitive scores, while mediation analysis tested indirect effects. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations relative to placebo. These shifts coincided with higher BDNF expression and improved verbal memory performance. Mediation analysis suggested that Bifidobacterium-related butyrate production partially explained the BDNF-linked cognitive benefit. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings indicate that targeted prebiotic fiber supplementation may engage gut-brain pathways, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and clinical relevance. These preliminary results support further investigation into personalized microbiome-targeted interventions.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that signal to the brain via vagal afferents, positioning the gut microbiome as a modifier of neuropsychiatric disease. In adults with major depressive disorder, lower fecal Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae abundance has been linked to reduced butyrate production and elevated inflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, tryptophan catabolites and bile acids may relay microbial signals to central nervous system tissue, while Tph1 and IL-10 variants modify responsiveness. A 12-week randomized trial of probiotic Bifidobacterium longum plus fermented foods increased gut microbial diversity, raised indole-3-propionic acid, and decreased depressive symptoms relative to control; effects were partially mediated by BDNF expression and serotonin turnover. Conversely, prebiotic inulin alone altered gut microbiota composition but did not change anxiety scores. These findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may produce more robust gut-brain axis effects than single-component supplement regimens, although metagenomic and mediation analyses in larger cohorts are needed to confirm causality.

Depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced butyrate production consistently accompany major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the molecular route linking gut microbiota to hippocampal dysfunction remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD patients into antibiotic-treated mice, we found that microbial transfer increased depressive-like behavior and reduced BDNF expression in the dentate gyrus. RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue revealed downregulation of Ppargc1a and Nrf2, accompanied by elevated interleukin-1β and reactive oxygen species. Butyrate supplementation restored BDNF levels, normalized cytokine profiles, and improved Morris water maze performance. Fluoxetine produced comparable behavioral effects but did not rescue Ppargc1a expression. In patients, LBP correlated inversely with BDNF and positively with interleukin-1β, supporting a peripheral-to-central inflammatory relay. These results position Akkermansia muciniphila-derived butyrate as a critical mediator of microbiota-brain signaling and suggest that targeting Ppargc1a-Nrf2 pathways may complement antidepressant therapy in MDD. Collectively, these findings provide mechanistic insight into how microbiome dysbiosis may drive MDD.

Disruption of gut microbiota by a high-fat, low-fiber diet promotes depressive-like behavior and neuroinflammation in mice, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation reverses these effects remains unclear. We fed C57BL/6 mice either a Western diet or standard chow for 12 weeks, with half of the Western diet-fed mice receiving probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Behavioral outcomes were assessed by forced swim test and open field test. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in colon and serum. BDNF and interleukin-6 expression were measured in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA. The Western diet reduced microbial diversity, depleted butyrate, elevated interleukin-6, and increased depressive-like behavior relative to control chow. Probiotic supplementation restored butyrate levels, normalized BDNF expression, and attenuated neuroinflammation, but did not fully reverse behavioral deficits. These findings suggest that Western diet-driven microbiota perturbations contribute to depression-associated neuroinflammation, and that probiotics may offer partial protection through short-chain fatty acid-dependent pathways.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis, yet microbial and metabolic signatures that precede cognitive decline remain poorly defined. We characterized fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids in older adults with mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated Mediterranean diet score. PERMANOVA revealed significant community-level differences by diagnosis (R2 = 0.08, p = 0.002), and Shannon diversity was lower in impaired participants. Relative abundance of Bacteroides and Prevotella correlated with butyrate concentrations and BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. Mediation models indicated that butyrate partially mediated the association between Bacteroides abundance and BDNF methylation (β = −0.21, 95% CI −0.38 to −0.05). These associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex, fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure. In mice colonized with microbiota from impaired donors, high-fat diet consumption exacerbated memory deficits and reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that diet–microbiota interactions influence BDNF regulation and may contribute to Alzheimer's disease-related cognitive impairment.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a modifier of Alzheimer's disease risk, yet the microbial and host factors that drive this interaction remain poorly defined. In 120 older adults with mild cognitive impairment, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal microbiota with metabolomic profiling and cognitive testing. The APOE ε4 allele was associated with lower abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, reduced butyrate, and higher interleukin-6. These alterations correlated with poorer Mini-Mental State Examination scores and smaller hippocampal volume. In a nested randomized controlled trial, 24 weeks of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation increased Faecalibacterium abundance and butyrate production, and improved mixed-model estimates of cognitive stability, particularly among APOE ε4 carriers. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 18% of the supplement-related cognitive effect. These findings support a model in which APOE genotype shapes gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid availability, with omega-3 supplementation partially compensating for this risk.

Depletion of microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the colon precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating the gut-brain axis in early pathogenesis. We recruited patients with PD and healthy controls, profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified plasma SCFAs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial communities, while random forest classification identified Prevotellaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Ruminococcaceae as discriminative taxa. Lower butyrate correlated with worse PD severity, reduced substantia nigra integrity, and elevated inflammatory cytokines, after adjustment for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose in linear mixed-effects models. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein was higher in patients with PD and inversely correlated with butyrate. A mediation analysis suggested that butyrate depletion partially mediated the association between gut dysbiosis and PD severity. In a mouse model, resistant starch supplementation increased butyrate production, attenuated neuroinflammation, and preserved dopaminergic neurons. These results support prebiotic fiber as a candidate intervention for modulating gut microbiota and slowing PD progression, though longitudinal human trials are needed.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii cross the blood-brain barrier and regulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbial composition to depression-like behavior. To test whether this pathway mediates stress susceptibility, we colonized germ-free mice with microbiota from depressed patients or healthy controls and subjected them to chronic social defeat stress. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundances diverged by donor group, while fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed donors reduced BDNF transcripts and increased interleukin-6 in the prefrontal cortex. Linear mixed-effects models showed that microbial beta diversity explained 18% of variance in anhedonia (p=0.003). Treatment with fluoxetine or omega-3 fatty acids partially reversed these effects, but only in mice harboring Lactobacillus-rich communities. Shotgun metagenomics further linked these behavioral shifts to FKBP5 methylation in peripheral blood. These findings suggest that BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity is a mechanistic node through which gut bacteria shape mood disorders, and they identify microbial targets for adjunctive treatment.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus and shape depressive-like phenotypes in rodent models. In patients with major depressive disorder, gut microbiota composition often shows reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside altered tryptophan metabolism. We examined whether probiotic supplementation could reverse these signatures. Adults with moderate depression received either multi-strain probiotics or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma tryptophan, kynurenine, and BDNF levels were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial diversity and depression severity. Probiotics increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance and plasma BDNF, but did not significantly change depressive symptoms overall. However, baseline microbial richness moderated the treatment effect: participants with lower richness showed greater symptom reduction. Changes in Lactobacillus correlated with BDNF increases, although the relationship was attenuated after adjusting for age and sex. These findings suggest that probiotic efficacy in depression depends on pre-existing gut microbiome architecture and BDNF-linked pathways, warranting stratified clinical trials.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields butyrate, and GPR43-dependent sensing of this metabolite restrains neuroinflammation in mice. To test whether this axis modifies Parkinson's disease progression, we fed α-synuclein-overexpressing mice either a fiber-rich diet or a control diet for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics and untargeted metabolomics profiled gut microbiota and fecal metabolites; motor function was assessed by rotarod and open-field testing. Feeding the fiber-rich diet expanded Lachnospiraceae and Akkermansia muciniphila, elevated butyrate, and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra. These changes were accompanied by reduced motor deficits and lower neuroinflammation. In GPR43-knockout mice, the protective effects of dietary fiber were abolished, despite comparable microbial shifts. Antibiotic depletion of the microbiota similarly negated benefits, whereas prebiotic supplementation partially restored them. In patients with Parkinson's disease, lower fecal butyrate correlated with worse motor scores. Together, these data link microbial butyrate production to host GPR43 signaling and motor outcomes, identifying a diet-sensitive gut-brain pathway that may modify Parkinson's disease outcomes.

Microbial tryptophan catabolites reinforce intestinal barrier integrity and restrain central inflammatory tone through aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling; disruption of this circuit accelerates Parkinson's disease-like pathology in the enteric nervous system. To test whether gut microbiota composition predicts this axis, we profiled patients with Parkinson's disease and healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and 16S rRNA sequencing, then validated findings in mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota. Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundances correlated with short-chain fatty acids and AHR ligands. Mediation analysis attributed 31% of the microbiota-Parkinson's disease association to butyrate. In mice, dietary butyrate supplementation restored AHR activity, reduced IL-6 expression, and lowered alpha-synuclein aggregates in the colon and substantia nigra. Fecal lipopolysaccharide and S100A8/S100A9 were elevated in patients and inversely associated with AHR target genes (CYP1A1, IL-22) in mucosal biopsies. These results position AHR as a mechanistic node linking gut microbiota to Parkinson's disease and support butyrate-targeted interventions.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans altered gut microbiota composition and reduced depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder, but microbial predictors of response remain uncertain. In a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial, 96 participants received inulin (10 g/day) or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids, inflammatory cytokines, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and ELISA. We used linear mixed-effects models to test treatment-by-time interactions, PERMANOVA for community-level shifts, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and improved microbial diversity; these changes correlated inversely with depression severity and anxiety scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 27% of the clinical improvement. No significant changes occurred in lipopolysaccharide-binding protein or IL-6. These findings suggest that inulin may ameliorate depressive symptoms through microbiota-derived butyrate signaling along the gut-brain axis, supporting further trials in depression.

Inulin-type fructans selectively increase Bifidobacterium and may improve hippocampal function, but their effects on mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and gut microbiota composition remain inconsistent. Eighty-four older adults with MCI completed a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of inulin (10 g/day) versus maltodextrin. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified fecal microbiota, and functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed hippocampal activation during a memory task. Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, short-chain fatty acids, and BDNF were measured. Compared with placebo, inulin increased Bifidobacterium (P = 0.003) and Faecalibacterium (P = 0.018), reduced IL-6 (P = 0.021), and improved MCI composite scores (P = 0.040). Linear mixed-effects models showed that changes in Bifidobacterium correlated inversely with IL-6 and positively with short-chain fatty acids, BDNF, and hippocampal activation. Baseline gut microbiota diversity was similar between groups, yet greater increases in Bifidobacterium tracked with larger cognitive improvement. These findings suggest that inulin supplementation may benefit MCI by remodeling gut microbiota and dampening neuroinflammation, supporting a gut-brain mechanism.

Supplementation with prebiotic fibers reshapes gut microbial communities and attenuates neuroinflammation in mouse models of Parkinson's disease, yet translational relevance for patients remains uncertain. We recruited older adults with mild cognitive impairment and randomized them to inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in plasma and feces. Cognitive performance was assessed with MMSE and ADAS-Cog. Associations between bacterial taxa, metabolites, and cognition were tested using linear mixed-effects models, PERMANOVA, and Spearman correlation. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced IL-6 relative to placebo. Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with improved executive function, while butyrate increases tracked with lower LPS-binding protein. Taxa-specific effects were validated in an independent mouse cohort, where inulin failed to improve cognitive impairment after antibiotic depletion of gut microbiota. These findings support a microbiota-dependent route by which prebiotic supplementation may modulate the gut-brain axis and cognitive decline.

Short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber is a plausible mediator of gut microbiota-brain signaling, yet the extent to which prebiotic supplementation reproduces the effects of fiber-rich foods remains unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either inulin (10 g/day) or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids. Linear mixed models tested changes in serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), inflammation markers, and cognitive scores. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate and propionate, and lowered C-reactive protein relative to placebo. These microbial and metabolic shifts correlated with improved hippocampal-dependent memory, but only in participants whose habitual diet was low in fermentable fiber. Notably, these benefits were absent in participants reporting high fiber intake, suggesting a ceiling effect. The findings suggest that prebiotic supplementation can partially mimic fiber-rich food effects on gut microbiota-brain communication, though baseline dietary patterns modify responses.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) calibrate microglial reactivity and may protect against stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders, yet the dietary levers that sustain this microbiota-gut-brain signaling remain poorly defined. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with fecal microbiota transplantation and quantitative PCR to test whether inulin and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshape the gut microbiota and attenuate hippocampal neuroinflammation. Supplemented mice showed higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, increased butyrate in the gut lumen, and reduced IL-1β and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus. Shannon index and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity revealed distinct community structures, while mixed-effects models linked butyrate availability to depressive-like behavior and anxiety-like behavior. Parallel 16S rRNA sequencing of human fecal microbiota showed that major depressive disorder was associated with lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, alongside reduced predicted SCFA production. These findings suggest that targeted dietary supplementation can stabilize microbiota-gut-brain axis function and may complement antidepressant therapy in humans.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiota and alters hippocampal BDNF expression in APP/PS1 mice, yet whether these changes translate to patients with Alzheimer's disease remains uncertain. We performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics on fecal samples from older adults with mild cognitive impairment enrolled in a randomized prebiotic fiber trial. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between gut bacterial taxa, short-chain fatty acids, and APOE genotype. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and raised fecal butyrate; these shifts correlated with improved cognitive scores. The APOE ε4 allele attenuated the Bifidobacterium-cognition association. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice reproduced butyrate increases and reduced neuroinflammation markers. In mice, selective chemogenetic silencing of vagal afferents abolished the butyrate-associated cognitive benefit, and BDNF knockdown in hippocampus blocked Bifidobacterium-dependent synaptic changes. These findings suggest that inulin may modulate APOE-dependent gut-brain signaling, though causal mediation analysis in larger human cohorts is needed.

Chronic stress disrupts the bidirectional gut-brain axis, and probiotic administration may restore microbial equilibrium and reduce depressive-like behavior. In a mouse model of chronic unpredictable mild stress, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus for four weeks lowered corticosterone and interleukin-6 in serum, while increasing brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that supplementation enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and depleted Clostridium in the gut microbiota. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Lactobacillus as a discriminant taxon, and PERMANOVA confirmed separation of fecal communities between groups. These changes coincided with reduced neuroinflammation, as indicated by lower tumor necrosis factor-α and ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 in the prefrontal cortex. Notably, subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the probiotic effects on BDNF and behavioral despair, implicating the vagus nerve in mediating these benefits. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation can modulate the gut microbiome and neuroactive metabolites to attenuate stress-related neuropsychiatric symptoms, although randomized controlled trials in humans are needed to validate clinical translation.

Depletion of Lachnospiraceae and reduced butyrate production in the gut microbiota are detectable in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) before dopaminergic therapy, implicating intestinal dysbiosis in neuroinflammation. In two independent cohorts of de novo subjects with PD and healthy controls, 16S rRNA sequencing and targeted metabolomics revealed lower short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and altered BDNF expression in serum. A 12-week randomized trial then tested whether resistant starch supplementation could restore butyrate and improve constipation and cognitive impairment. Resistant starch increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and upregulated BDNF and IL10 while reducing TNF. These changes correlated with improved performance on cognitive testing and reduced intestinal permeability. Mechanistically, SCFAs can induce FOXP3 and strengthen epithelial barrier integrity, linking gut microbiota to neuroinflammation. The findings suggest that resistant starch may modulate the gut-brain axis in PD, though larger trials are needed to confirm whether this prebiotic strategy alters disease progression. However, causality remains uncertain because patients with PD often take levodopa, which itself alters gut microbial composition.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly linked to Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the microbial signals that drive neuroinflammation and motor decline remain poorly resolved. In a meta-analysis of human fecal samples, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with shotgun metagenomics to profile taxonomic and functional shifts across PD and controls. Random forest classification separated groups with high accuracy and identified depletion of Roseburia, Faecalibacterium, and Lachnospira, taxa that produce butyrate, alongside enrichment of Akkermansia and Desulfovibrio. These taxa correlated with reduced short-chain fatty acids and elevated lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in patients than in healthy controls, and these metabolic shifts tracked with PD severity. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, a high-fiber prebiotic diet restored butyrate availability, attenuated microglial activation in the substantia nigra, and improved motor deficits. CSF1R inhibitor-mediated microglial depletion abolished these benefits, implicating microglia as required mediators. Together, these findings define a diet-microbiome-immune axis that shapes PD progression and suggest prebiotic fiber as a candidate adjunct for neuroinflammation.

Derived from gut microbiota, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) constrain neuroinflammation via gut-brain signaling, yet host BDNF variation may determine whether these metabolites protect or exacerbate depressive symptoms. In 84 adults with major depressive disorder and 42 healthy controls, we profiled gut microbiota by amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene, quantified fecal SCFAs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and genotyped BDNF rs6265, COMT rs4680, and FKBP5 rs1360780. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community composition by diagnosis and genotype. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Faecalibacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations were inversely associated with depression severity, but only in BDNF rs6265 carriers. Bacteroides abundance correlated positively with propionate and anxiety scores. Mediation analysis suggested butyrate accounted for 18% of the BDNF genotype–depression association. Stratification by COMT rs4680 did not alter these associations, whereas FKBP5 rs1360780 showed an interaction with butyrate for anxiety scores. These findings indicate that BDNF rs6265 moderates microbiota-derived SCFA effects on mood, supporting genotype-informed probiotic or fiber interventions for depression.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by a Western diet can precede Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation reverses this trajectory remains unclear. In APP/PS1 mice fed a high-fat, fiber-depleted diet, we observed reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and downregulation of BDNF and PSEN1 in hippocampus. Daily inulin with Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 8 weeks restored microbial diversity, increased butyrate, and lowered amyloid-beta load in cortex and hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and random forest classified responders by Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundance. Behavioral testing (Morris water maze) showed improved spatial memory, while ELISA revealed reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in serum. In a parallel human cohort, greater Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher Faecalibacterium and lower C-reactive protein. In hippocampus, BDNF expression was negatively correlated with amyloid-beta burden. These findings indicate that prebiotic fiber plus probiotics can offset diet-induced neuroinflammation and cognitive decline through microbiota-gut-brain signaling, with BDNF as a potential mediator.

Tryptophan catabolism by the gut microbiota has emerged as a mechanistic bridge to affective disorders, yet causal direction and mediating pathways remain contested. Using mice colonized with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, we found that Lactobacillus-depleted communities increased kynurenine flux, reduced serotonin availability in the prefrontal cortex, and induced anhedonia-like behavior. Faecal metagenomics and targeted metabolomics linked these phenotypes to IDO1 and KMO expression in the hippocampus, with mediation analysis indicating that indole-3-acetate explained 31% of the microbial effect on depressive behavior. These effects were independent of dietary fiber intake and short-chain fatty acid concentrations. Dietary tryptophan supplementation rescued serotonin turnover and normalized BDNF transcripts, whereas minocycline attenuated neuroinflammation without restoring behavior. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate were independent predictors of vagal tone. These data position microbial tryptophan metabolites as modifiable signals in microbiota-brain communication and support Mendelian randomization as a route to test causality in human cohorts.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract can reshape brain function and behavior, and its disruption is increasingly linked to stress-related depression. We combined 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and mediation analysis in mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress. Transfer of microbiota from stress-susceptible donors increased anhedonia-like behavior in antibiotic-treated recipients, with elevated interleukin-6 and reduced Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex. Faecalibaculum rodentium was enriched in susceptible donors and reproduced these neuroimmune and behavioral changes when administered alone. Mediation analysis indicated that interleukin-6 and Bdnf partially explained the microbiota–behavior association. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy attenuated the effects of F. rodentium, implicating the vagus nerve in this signaling. In patients with major depressive disorder, similar microbial signatures correlated with circulating interleukin-6 and symptom severity. These findings suggest that specific gut bacteria can convert stress resilience into depressive phenotypes through Bdnf-dependent and inflammatory pathways, identifying candidate targets for probiotic or immunomodulatory agents.

Microbial signals from the gut shape brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and disrupted gut microbiota composition is repeatedly linked to neurodegenerative disease. In a 12-week randomized trial of older adults with mild cognitive impairment, we tested whether probiotic supplementation alters cognitive trajectories and whether effects are modified by APOE genotype. Participants received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo; fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and circulating short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models showed that probiotic treatment increased Bifidobacterium abundance and improved delayed recall relative to placebo, with a significant treatment-by-APOE interaction. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate changes partially explained the cognitive benefit. In mice colonized with participant-derived microbiota, the same probiotic reduced neuroinflammation and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Sensitivity analyses confirmed modest but consistent effect sizes. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics in APOE-stratified populations, though larger trials with repeated fecal sampling are needed.

Altered gut microbiota precedes amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the temporal relationship between microbial community shifts and brain immune activation remains unclear. We profiled fecal microbiota from 3xTg-AD mice and wild-type littermates every two weeks from 4 to 52 weeks using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. RNA from hippocampus and colon was quantified by RT-qPCR for GFAP, IL6, and MRC1. A random forest classifier separated AD mice from controls with 90-100% accuracy based on microbial composition as early as 8 weeks. PERMANOVA confirmed genotype-dependent microbiota differences at 8 and 24 weeks. Relative abundance of Bacteroides increased over time in 3xTg-AD mice and correlated with IL-6 expression. Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were lower in AD mice, and SCFA supplementation increased amyloid plaque load in germ-free AD mice. These findings indicate that gut microbiota features predict AD-associated neuroinflammation before plaque deposition, supporting the microbiome-gut-brain axis as a source of early biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate BDNF expression and neuroinflammation, linking the gut microbiota to cognitive decline. In a 12-week randomized trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received inulin or placebo; 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice tested causality. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and enhanced hippocampal BDNF signaling. Plasma lipopolysaccharide fell, while GPR41 expression rose in the prefrontal cortex. Antibiotic treatment abolished the inulin-induced butyrate increase and reversed BDNF upregulation, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from responders restored hippocampal BDNF and reduced neuroinflammation in mice. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate predicted mild cognitive impairment improvement independently of Western diet adherence. Baseline microbiota composition explained response variance. These findings position inulin as a plausible, safe microbiota-targeted intervention, although larger, longer human trials with metagenomic sequencing are needed.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites are increasingly linked to central nervous system function, yet the dietary and gut-derived signals that shape this gut-brain axis remain incompletely defined. We recruited adults with irritable bowel syndrome and subclinical anxiety and randomized them to a fermented food-rich diet or a high-fiber diet for 10 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids and serotonin metabolites were quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Psychological and gastrointestinal outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models, with PERMANOVA used for community-level comparisons. The fermented food arm showed greater increases in Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside higher butyrate and reduced anxiety scores. Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with BDNF expression in peripheral blood. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented foods differentially modulate the gut-brain axis through distinct microbiome and metabolite pathways, supporting targeted nutritional strategies for gut-brain disorders.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber reshapes gut microbial communities, enriching short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, which modulate central nervous system immune signaling. In a 12-week randomized study of adults with mild cognitive impairment, participants receiving a Mediterranean-style diet plus inulin showed higher butyrate concentrations and lower interleukin-6 than controls. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium; plasma metabolomics linked these shifts to tryptophan pathway metabolites. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiota composition explained 32% of the diet-associated change in BDNF expression. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Additional Spearman correlation showed that Bifidobacterium abundance tracked inversely with C-reactive protein. These findings support dietary fiber and fermented food intake as accessible strategies for gut-brain axis modulation, though Mendelian randomization is needed to clarify causality.
