Future trials should stratify by baseline microbial diversity, short-chain fatty acid production, and neuroinflammation to identify responders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced from dietary fiber can attenuate neuroinflammation through vagal and systemic routes, yet the causal contribution of specific gut bacteria remains debated. Germ-free mice colonized with depression-associated microbiota show impaired social interaction and altered tryptophan metabolism, but whether diet can reverse these phenotypes is unclear. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from adults with major depressive disorder or healthy controls, then fed them a Western diet or high-fiber diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation tracked community shifts, while forced swim test and open field test assessed depressive-like behavior and anxiety-like behavior. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for batch and cage effects. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium were depleted in depression-derived communities; Lactobacillus correlated with gamma-aminobutyric acid and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. High-fiber diet increased butyrate and propionate, reduced lipopolysaccharide, and normalized neuroinflammatory markers. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and microbial metabolites interact to modulate brain function, offering a testable target for depression.

Fermentable fibers and polyphenol-rich foods reshape the gut microbiome by expanding Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Akkermansia, whose short-chain fatty acid output strengthens intestinal barrier integrity and dampens neuroinflammation. To test whether this dietary effect translates to cognition, older adults with mild cognitive impairment (n=84) were randomized to a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus plus omega-3 fatty acid or placebo for 16 weeks. Habitual vegetable and legume intake was estimated using a food frequency questionnaire; adherence was monitored by stool sample collection and capsule counts. Shotgun metagenomics and fecal metabolomics profiled microbial composition and metabolites; cognitive testing and plasma cytokine assays measured outcomes. Linear mixed-effects models showed that the supplement group had higher Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. Functional magnetic resonance imaging during a memory task revealed increased hippocampal activation in responders, while whole-blood transcriptomics linked response to lower NFKB1 and IL1B expression. These findings indicate that combining probiotics with omega-3 supplementation and fiber-rich foods may support gut-brain axis homeostasis and slow cognitive decline.

Fermentable dietary fiber reshapes the gut microbiome toward butyrate-producing taxa, a shift that tracks with lower neuroinflammation and higher BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received inulin or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA profiling and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial community structure and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay measured interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) in serum. PERMANOVA and linear mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time effects, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. BDNF concentrations rose, whereas IL-6 and TNF-α fell. Spearman correlation linked butyrate with BDNF and inversely with IL-6. These findings suggest that inulin-driven microbiome remodeling may mitigate mild cognitive impairment through SCFA-dependent BDNF regulation and reduced peripheral inflammation. Parallel experiments in APP/PS1 mice fed inulin showed fewer amyloid-β plaques in the cortex and restored BDNF signaling. Immunofluorescence revealed reduced ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1) intensity in the hippocampus, consistent with attenuated neuroinflammation.

Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by gut microbes shapes central nervous system function through immune, metabolic, and neural signaling, and disruption of this axis is increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. In mice exposed to chronic stress, dietary supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve and galacto-oligosaccharides restored gut microbial diversity, increased short-chain fatty acid production, and reduced hippocampal neuroinflammation. These changes were accompanied by normalized brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression and attenuated depressive-like behavior. To test causality, we used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free recipients. Transplanted microbiota reproduced the supplement-associated increases in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated butyrate, and upregulated BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with BDNF levels and symptom severity. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with prebiotic and probiotic interventions may modulate BDNF-dependent plasticity and provide a tractable strategy for stress-related psychopathology. Collectively, these cross-species findings position the gut-brain axis as a modifiable therapeutic target.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the microbial signals that regulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus remain unclear. In 84 adults, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of stool samples revealed reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus in participants with elevated depressive symptoms. These shifts correlated with lower BDNF and NR3C1 expression in peripheral blood, quantified by RT-qPCR, and with higher interleukin-6 and cortisol levels. Linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use confirmed these associations. Fecal microbiota transplantation from affected donors into antibiotic-treated mice induced anhedonia-like behavior and reduced Bdnf mRNA in the prefrontal cortex. Conversely, probiotic administration containing Bifidobacterium longum restored Bdnf expression and attenuated neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium abundance indirectly influenced depressive symptoms through BDNF and IL-6. These findings support targeting gut microbial communities to modulate BDNF-related brain plasticity, although causal direction requires further study.

Disrupted gut microbiota composition is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet strain-level mechanisms and predictive biomarkers remain poorly defined. We profiled fecal microbiota from adults with depression and healthy controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bacteroides uniformis were depleted in depression, while Eggerthella lenta was enriched. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed distinct β-diversity by diagnosis (R2 = 0.08, p = 0.002), and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified 14 discriminatory taxa. Random forest classification achieved an area under the curve of 0.78. Short-chain fatty acid profiles, especially butyrate, correlated inversely with depressive symptoms. Functional profiling indicated reduced butyrate synthesis pathways and enriched lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. These microbial shifts may influence brain function via neurotransmitter and cytokine signaling. These findings suggest that gut microbial alterations and changed metabolites may contribute to depression pathophysiology through the gut-brain axis, supporting further metagenomic and metabolomic studies.

Short-chain fatty acids generated by Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii within the gut microbiota modulate inflammatory tone in the hippocampus and BDNF expression along the gut-brain axis, linking metabolic syndrome-associated gut dysbiosis to cognitive decline. In a mouse model of high-fat diet-induced obesity, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed depletion of Lactobacillus and Akkermansia muciniphila, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6. Fecal microbiota transplantation from lean donors restored microbial diversity, reduced NF-κB activation in the hippocampus, and improved memory impairment. Positron emission tomography further showed normalized brain glucose metabolism after prebiotic fiber supplementation. Plasma metabolomics and mediation analysis identified butyrate as a partial mediator of the BDNF response. Notably, antibiotic-induced depletion of gut microbiota abolished these benefits, whereas probiotic administration recapitulated them in mice. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids may alter BDNF and NF-κB pathways, offering a tractable strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders. Parallel human cohort analyses are needed to confirm whether fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles predict treatment response and guide personalized microbiota-directed interventions.

Dietary patterns rich in fermentable fibers and plant polyphenols shape the gut microbiota and its metabolic output, influencing brain function and behavior. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms received a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo for 8 weeks while maintaining habitual diets. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics showed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, compared with placebo. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced depressive symptoms scores and lower interleukin-6 levels. In parallel, mice colonized with microbiota from supplemented participants displayed less anhedonia-like behavior after chronic stress, an effect absent in vagotomized mice. Correlation analysis further linked butyrate to increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with polyphenol-rich foods may modulate the gut microbiota and vagus nerve signaling to alleviate depression. However, effects were modest and require validation in larger cohorts.

Altered gut microbiota composition contributes to neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior through the gut-brain axis. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, we examined whether multi-strain probiotic supplementation altered gut microbiota composition and cytokine profiles in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium after 8 weeks of probiotic supplementation, with concurrent reductions in Bacteroidetes. Serum interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha decreased, whereas brain-derived neurotrophic factor increased. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that changes in Bifidobacterium abundance correlated negatively with depressive symptom severity scores in this cohort. Mediation analysis suggested that interleukin-6 partially mediated this relationship. In mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from responders, depressive-like behavior was attenuated, and hippocampus Bdnf expression increased. These findings indicate that multi-strain probiotic supplementation may alleviate depressive symptoms by modulating the gut microbiota and systemic inflammation, supporting the microbiome as a therapeutic target in MDD.

Disruption of the gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a driver of neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. To investigate causal links, we performed two-sample Mendelian randomization using APOE and BDNF as instrumental variables, combined with 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from older adults with mild cognitive impairment. In parallel, APP/PS1 mice received probiotic Bifidobacterium breve or placebo for 16 weeks. Morris water maze testing revealed that B. breve significantly improved spatial memory and reduced amyloid-beta plaques in the hippocampus. Linear mixed-effects models showed that BDNF expression correlated positively with Lactobacillus abundance and negatively with Bacteroides. Fecal metabolomics identified deoxycytidine as a key metabolite linking Clostridium to cognitive impairment. Additionally, mediation analysis revealed that BDNF partially mediated the effect of Bacteroides on brain atrophy. No significant changes in overall microbial diversity were observed, but targeted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium genera increased. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome via probiotics may modulate APOE-related pathways and offer therapeutic potential for Alzheimer's disease.

Altered gut microbiota composition is associated with major depressive disorder and anxiety, yet the molecular routes linking microbial communities to the brain remain incompletely defined. In a human cohort, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into gnotobiotic mice revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with depressive symptoms. Butyrate production was lower in cases, and BDNF and TLR4 expression in the hippocampus differed after colonization. Mediation analysis indicated that short-chain fatty acids explained 31% of the association between microbial composition and symptom severity, while random-effects meta-analysis of prior trials showed probiotics reduced anxiety scores versus placebo. These findings support a microbiota-gut-brain axis model in which BDNF signaling, TLR4-dependent inflammation, and microbial metabolites mediate effects of diet and psychobiotics. Effects were strongest among participants with elevated C-reactive protein, and mixed-effects models adjusted for antidepressant use, fiber intake, and probiotic exposure. Longitudinal Mendelian randomization and metagenomic sequencing are needed to distinguish cause from consequence.

Depletion of butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia in the gut microbiome tracks with major depressive disorder (MDD) severity, yet whether this loss is causal remains unresolved. We profiled stool, plasma, and prefrontal cortex samples from 180 patients with MDD and 120 healthy controls using shotgun metagenomics, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics. Lower butyrate was associated with higher depression scores and reduced BDNF and FFAR2 expression in brain. We also found reduced Bifidobacterium and increased Bacteroides in MDD, and random forest classifiers separated groups with moderate accuracy. We used network modeling to link Roseburia abundance to butyrate and BDNF through FFAR2. In mice, dietary inulin, a fermentable fiber, restored Roseburia abundance, raised butyrate, and normalized BDNF expression, an effect blocked by antibiotics. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 31% of the microbiome-depression association. These findings position butyrate as a mechanistic node in microbiome-brain signaling and support prebiotic strategies for MDD.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by low dietary fiber intake is increasingly implicated in age-related cognitive decline and neuroinflammation, yet the pathways linking dietary patterns to hippocampal function remain incompletely defined. In a mouse model of diet-induced cognitive impairment, 14 weeks of a fiber-depleted diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide, and impaired dentate gyrus-dependent memory. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metabolomics revealed depleted short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), especially butyrate. Supplementation with sodium butyrate or a multi-strain probiotic restored SCFA levels, attenuated microglial activation, and reduced spatial memory deficits. Notably, a whole-food diet enriched with fermentable fibers reproduced these benefits, whereas inulin alone produced weaker effects. In clinical populations, baseline microbiota diversity predicted response to a fiber-rich diet, and mediation analysis linked SCFA increases to reduced executive dysfunction. These findings indicate that microbiota-derived metabolites mediate gut-brain signaling and suggest that fiber-rich foods plus targeted prebiotics may mitigate cognitive decline.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape innate immune maturation and α-synuclein pathology along the gut-brain axis, yet whether dietary fiber intake modifies this relationship in carriers of GBA or APOE4 remains unresolved. In a cohort of older adult participants with mild cognitive impairment, we profiled gut microbiota using 16S rRNA sequencing and quantified dietary fiber, fermented foods, and Mediterranean diet adherence. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted in participants with cognitive decline, while Escherichia/Shigella expanded. Butyrate concentrations correlated with APOE4 status and amyloid burden. Linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis tested whether microbial composition linked fiber intake to neurodegeneration. Higher fiber intake was associated with greater butyrate-producing bacteria abundance and slower cognitive decline, but the effect was attenuated in carriers of GBA. Prebiotic supplementation in mouse models recapitulated these associations. These findings suggest that GBA- and APOE4-stratified diets may modulate gut microbiota and neurodegeneration, though Mendelian randomization is needed to establish causality.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by high-fat diet consumption can alter BDNF expression in the hippocampus and promote depressive-like behaviors, yet the microbial signals linking diet to central BDNF regulation remain unclear. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we tracked microbial community shifts in mice fed a high-fat diet for 12 weeks. High-fat diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate in colon, and decreased BDNF mRNA in the prefrontal cortex. Transplanting microbiota from high-fat diet-fed donors into mice on standard chow reproduced these BDNF changes and increased anxiety-like behavior. Correlation analyses linked Lactobacillus abundance to BDNF and butyrate levels. Notably, qPCR revealed reduced BDNF exon IV promoter methylation in the hippocampus. Supplementation with inulin, a fermentable dietary fiber, restored butyrate levels, normalized BDNF expression, and attenuated anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbiome remodeling influences BDNF-dependent brain plasticity through short-chain fatty acid signaling, identifying prebiotic fiber as a potential gut-brain intervention.

Consumption of a Western diet rich in refined fats and low in fermentable fiber correlates with reduced gut microbial diversity and elevated depression risk, whereas Mediterranean-style diets may protect brain function through microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). To test causality, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder into germ-free mice. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum increased butyrate producers and reduced anxiety-like behavior; these effects were abolished by antibiotic treatment. In mice, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation attenuated neuroinflammation and restored hippocampal function only when gut microbiota was intact. Plasma IL-6 and C-reactive protein concentrations, measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, fell after inulin plus Bifidobacterium breve in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether combining fiber-rich foods with probiotics yields durable benefits for mood disorders. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable target for psychiatric disorders.

Gut microbiota-dependent conversion of tryptophan into indole-3-lactic acid is reduced in patients with major depressive disorder and correlates with hippocampal volume. To test whether this pathway is modifiable, we analyzed fecal and serum samples from 120 adults using metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Participants with low indole-3-lactic acid received either probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium plus a fermented food diet or standard care for 12 weeks. Baseline tryptophan levels did not differ between groups, but the intervention group showed a 32% increase in indole-3-lactic acid. We used linear mixed models to assess changes in AHR activation, IL-10 expression, and symptom severity. Probiotic supplementation increased indole-3-lactic acid and AHR activation, reduced depression and anxiety scores, and raised IL-10 more than standard care. These changes were accompanied by greater microbial diversity and higher abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota with probiotics and fermented foods may improve gut-brain signaling in major depressive disorder.

Microbial signals from the gastrointestinal tract can shape central nervous system function, yet the extent to which dietary interventions alter this dialogue in adults with mild cognitive impairment remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, 96 participants received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a control diet, with half also receiving omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. We used linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to test whether Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance mediated cognitive changes. Compared with control, the intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, raised butyrate, and lowered interleukin-6; these shifts correlated with improved hippocampal connectivity and delayed recall. The cognitive benefit was partially mediated by butyrate and BDNF expression. These findings suggest that diet plus omega-3 supplementation may engage a microbiome-dependent pathway, though larger trials with causal inference methods are needed.

Supplementation with psychobiotic formulations may attenuate stress-related disorders by reshaping the gut microbiota and modulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with subclinical anxiety and insomnia received either a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 and Bifidobacterium longum BB536 or placebo for eight weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing, and peripheral BDNF expression was quantified by quantitative PCR. Serum interleukin-6 and cortisol were measured as inflammatory and neuroendocrine readouts. Compared with placebo, the probiotic group showed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, reduced interleukin-6, and higher BDNF expression. These changes accompanied greater reductions in anxiety scores and improved sleep disturbance scores. Spearman correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance with BDNF expression and anxiety improvement. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may engage the gut-brain axis through BDNF-related pathways, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and mechanism. No serious adverse events were reported.

Alterations in the gut microbiota are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the molecular routes connecting microbial ecology to brain function remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of 84 adults with MDD and 79 healthy controls, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, alongside lower fecal butyrate concentrations. These shifts correlated with decreased BDNF expression in peripheral blood and higher depression severity scores. Dietary patterns modified this relationship: Western diet adherence strengthened the inverse association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and BDNF, whereas Mediterranean-style diets attenuated it. Using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis, we estimated that butyrate explained 18.7% of the microbial association with BDNF. In mice, oral butyrate supplementation restored hippocampal Bdnf transcript levels and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings position gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids as modifiable signals for MDD and support targeting dietary fiber and probiotics in stratified patients.

Disturbances in gut microbiota and microbial short-chain fatty acid production are emerging as modifiable contributors to depression and anxiety, but whether dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation can jointly alter brain-relevant outcomes remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo while continuing their habitual fiber intake. Fecal microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Peripheral brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and inflammatory markers were measured at baseline and week 12. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, raised fecal butyrate concentrations, and reduced anxiety scores. These changes were accompanied by higher BDNF levels and lower C-reactive protein. Notably, participants reporting higher fermented food consumption showed stronger microbiota shifts. The findings suggest that probiotics combined with dietary fiber may modulate the gut-brain axis and improve mood symptoms, supporting further randomized controlled trials.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are now recognized as key modulators of microglial maturation and emotional behavior, yet the transcriptional programs linking microbiota signals to hippocampal circuits remain poorly defined. In germ-free mice and antibiotic-treated mice, we combined 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, targeted metabolomics, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing to map SCFA-dependent expression of BDNF, Fos, Il1b, and Tnf in the ventral hippocampus. Butyrate supplementation restored BDNF and Fos expression and reduced Il1b and Tnf transcripts in microglia. Using mediation analysis, we found that microbiota-derived butyrate production explained 38% of the variance in anxiety-like behavior, while vagotomy abolished this effect. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donor microbiota enriched in butyrate into stressed recipients normalized Bdnf methylation and increased social interaction. Behavioral testing used linear mixed-effects models to control for batch and sex, and whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showed reduced excitability in dentate gyrus granule cells after butyrate treatment. These results position butyrate as a causal mediator of microbiota-host signaling and suggest that targeting microbiota-derived SCFA production may alleviate neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Altered gut microbial composition and barrier permeability precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating the gut microbiota in neuroinflammation and α-synucleinopathy. We profiled fecal microbiota from PD patients and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Host GBA and SNCA genotypes were determined by allelic discrimination assays. Prevotellaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Roseburia were depleted in PD patients, whereas Akkermansia and Enterobacteriaceae were enriched. PERMANOVA revealed significant community separation by diagnosis (R² = 0.14, p = 0.001), and random forest classification discriminated PD patients from controls with an AUC of 0.82. Butyrate correlated inversely with SNCA expression in colon biopsies and with constipation severity. These data support a model in which gut microbial dysbiosis, modified by host GBA status, contributes to PD pathogenesis and warrants longitudinal validation. Stratification by levodopa dose and probiotic use in participants did not attenuate these associations.

Consuming fermented foods rich in probiotics increases Lactobacillus abundance and short-chain fatty acid production in the colon, a shift associated with reduced neuroinflammation and altered BDNF signaling in the prefrontal cortex. In a randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks; fecal microbiome profiling and cognitive testing were performed before and after intervention. Probiotic-treated participants showed higher Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium counts, lower interleukin-6, and improved executive function compared with placebo. These effects were attenuated in participants carrying APOE4, suggesting that APOE4 status moderates the gut microbiota–brain response. Baseline fruit and vegetable intake modified the treatment effect, with the greatest microbial diversity gains observed in participants reporting high fiber consumption. Mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antibiotic use confirmed that dietary fiber and probiotic intake may jointly support BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, though confirmatory longitudinal studies are needed. Together, these data suggest a modifiable microbiome-targeted strategy for early cognitive decline.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota can shape central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet clinical translation of probiotic interventions for mild cognitive impairment remains inconsistent. We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in older adults with subjective cognitive decline, comparing 12 weeks of a multi-strain probiotic formulation with placebo. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and a computerized neuropsychological battery; fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and raised butyrate levels relative to placebo. However, no between-group differences emerged in MoCA scores or composite memory outcomes. Exploratory analyses showed that changes in gut microbial diversity correlated with changes in hippocampal-dependent memory only in participants with higher baseline butyrate. These findings suggest that probiotics can modulate the gut microbiome and microbial metabolites, but cognitive benefits may require targeted stratification by baseline microbiome and metabolic status.

Fermentable dietary fiber and inulin supplementation can reshape gut microbiota and reduce neuroinflammation in mice, yet their effects on human brain function remain incompletely defined. We randomized 40 adults with mild cognitive impairment to 12 weeks of daily inulin or placebo. Stool and blood samples were collected at baseline and week 12. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, plasma short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and BDNF was measured by ELISA. Linear mixed-effects models assessed changes in Bifidobacterium, butyrate, and hippocampal activation during functional MRI memory tasks. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations relative to placebo, and these increases correlated with improved hippocampal activation and higher BDNF levels. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence was high. These findings suggest that fermentable fiber supplementation may support brain function through gut microbiota-derived metabolites, though larger trials are needed to confirm clinical benefit in this population.

Microbial fermentation of inulin-type fructans in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that influence central nervous system function and may reduce depression severity. To test this, adults with major depressive disorder received inulin or placebo for 8 weeks; 16S rRNA sequencing profiled the gut microbiota, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal short-chain fatty acids. Linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced depressive symptoms relative to placebo. Changes in Faecalibacterium correlated inversely with serum interleukin-6 and positively with plasma butyrate; mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated the clinical improvement. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor increased with inulin and tracked Bifidobacterium abundance. No serious adverse events occurred. In a separate mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These findings link dietary fiber supplementation to microbiota-dependent metabolite shifts and depression-related outcomes, supporting gut microbiome targeting as an adjunctive strategy.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production from fermentable fiber is a key pathway linking the gut microbiome to brain function, yet the extent to which this axis is modifiable by probiotic supplementation remains uncertain. We randomized adults with major depressive disorder to receive a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks, with Mediterranean-style diet counseling in both arms. Fecal metagenomics and resting-state functional MRI were used to quantify microbial taxa and limbic connectivity. Using linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis, we found that Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased only in the probiotic arm. This increase correlated with reduced depression severity and enhanced prefrontal–amygdala coupling; butyrate availability partially mediated these effects. BDNF expression and serotonin turnover also differed by arm, whereas gamma-aminobutyric acid did not. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. These results suggest that targeted probiotic and fiber interventions can shift the gut microbiome and brain circuits implicated in depression, though larger trials are needed.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition consistently accompany major depressive disorder, yet whether microbial metabolites causally modulate affective circuits remains unresolved. In a randomized controlled trial of 120 adults with moderate depression, daily probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum increased fecal short-chain fatty acids and reduced inflammatory cytokines compared with placebo. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed expanded Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, taxa linked to butyrate production. Concomitantly, BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells rose, and mixed-effects models associated this increase with improved depressive symptoms. In a parallel mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated behavioral benefits and elevated Bdnf in the hippocampus. These findings position gut microbiota as a modifiable node in the gut-brain axis and suggest that psychobiotic strategies may augment antidepressant treatment, though confirmatory trials with fermented food and fiber interventions are needed. Mechanistic work should test whether GPR43 and HDAC pathways mediate these effects and predict clinical response. Longitudinal sampling is needed to clarify causality.

Bacteria in the gut that produce short-chain fatty acids are increasingly linked to brain function and emotional regulation. In a randomized crossover trial, 48 adults with mild depressive symptoms consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet or a high-fat, low-fiber diet for 8 weeks, with a 6-week washout. The active period included a daily inulin supplement (10 g) and omega-3 fatty acid supplement (1 g). 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of fecal samples showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium, alongside higher Shannon diversity, after the Mediterranean-style diet plus supplements compared with the high-fat, low-fiber diet. These microbial shifts correlated with lower self-reported anxiety scores and reduced interleukin-6 concentrations. Mixed-effects models indicated that microbial composition explained 22% of variance in mood improvement, independent of body mass index. The findings suggest that fermentable fiber and omega-3 fatty acids may act through the gut microbiome to modulate gut-brain signaling, though confirmatory trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Microbial dysbiosis along the gut-brain axis contributes to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the pathways linking gut microbiota to central nervous system function remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of 84 patients with MDD and 60 matched controls, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bacteroides, alongside lower fecal butyrate and total short-chain fatty acids; these deficits correlated with symptom severity. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into antibiotic-treated mice increased IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, and reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. Supplementation with inulin, a fermentable fiber, restored butyrate levels, normalized BDNF expression, and attenuated depressive-like behavior in mice. Notably, fluoxetine increased BDNF expression without correcting microbiota composition, whereas inulin plus fluoxetine produced the largest behavioral improvement in mice. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that butyrate was the strongest mediator of the microbiome-behavior association. These findings indicate that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids modulate BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with prebiotic fiber may offer a tractable adjunct for MDD.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that calibrate microglial maturation and may modify susceptibility to Alzheimer's disease (AD). To test whether this axis is causal, we integrated shotgun metagenomics of gut microbiota, targeted metabolomics, and Mendelian randomization in older adults and validated findings in transgenic mice. Higher abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii correlated with fecal butyrate, which was lower in participants with mild cognitive impairment. APOE ε4 attenuated the association between fiber intake and butyrate, suggesting effect modification. In mice, sodium butyrate restored Bdnf expression in the hippocampus, reduced neuroinflammation, and improved Morris water maze performance. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing further showed that Bacteroides- and Prevotella-dominated enterotypes differed by Mediterranean diet adherence. These results position gut microbial metabolism as a modifiable contributor to AD risk, but they also indicate that host genotype and dietary context shape the response. If replicated, dietary fiber or butyrate-targeted interventions may complement existing AD strategies.

Converging evidence positions the gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator of APOE4-related Alzheimer's disease risk through vagal, immune, and metabolic signaling. We examined whether habitual intake of a Mediterranean-style diet and probiotic supplementation associate with gut microbial composition and short-chain fatty acid production in 118 older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and butyrate. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, APOE4 status, and cholinesterase inhibitor use. Greater Mediterranean-style diet adherence was associated with higher Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio and butyrate concentrations, whereas probiotic supplementation correlated with increased Bifidobacteria. Among APOE4 carriers, each standard deviation increase in butyrate was associated with better hippocampal volume and lower neuroinflammation markers. Fecal calprotectin and zonulin did not differ by probiotic use. These findings suggest that Mediterranean-style diet and probiotic strategies may interact with APOE4 to shape gut-brain axis outcomes in Alzheimer's disease.

Gut microbial composition shifts precede cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet causality and mediating pathways remain contested. We transplanted faecal microbiota from patients with AD or age-matched healthy donors into antibiotic-treated mice and assessed memory impairment after 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Bacteroidetes and reduced Lactobacillus in recipients of microbiota from patients. Morris water maze testing showed prolonged escape latency and fewer platform crossings. Immunofluorescence detected elevated amyloid-β and ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 in the hippocampus. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in caecal contents, while lipopolysaccharide was higher. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline performance confirmed group differences. Vagotomy abolished the cognitive effects, implicating the vagus nerve. Donor age and baseline microbiota diversity showed no association with memory impairment in Spearman correlation analyses. Blood-brain barrier permeability increased, and vagal afferent firing was blunted. These findings suggest that gut microbiota from patients with AD can transmit memory deficits and neuroinflammation in mice, partly through microbial metabolites and vagal signaling, supporting probiotic or prebiotic strategies for AD.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota tune brain circuits that govern mood and stress reactivity. In mice exposed to chronic social defeat, depressive-like behavior was accompanied by reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and elevated corticosterone. Oral probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated these changes, restored Bdnf transcription, and normalized serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium after treatment, alongside decreased Clostridium sensu stricto. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline Shannon index correlated inversely with anhedonia severity, and responders to probiotics showed greater BDNF methylation changes than non-responders. Parallel mouse experiments using vagotomy and fecal microbiota transplantation indicated that intact vagus nerve signaling is required for probiotic-induced Bdnf upregulation and behavioral recovery. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics may modulate BDNF-dependent plasticity and alleviate depressive symptoms, though strain-specific effects and causal mechanisms require further randomized controlled trials.

Supplementing blueberries in a high-fat diet reversed gut dysbiosis and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice, an effect dependent on BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. To identify the mediators from gut microbiota and host signaling, male C57BL/6 mice received a high-fat diet with or without blueberry powder for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that blueberry supplementation increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus while decreasing the Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR and Western blot showed restored Bdnf, Zo-1, and Ocln expression in the colon and brain. Short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate, were elevated in feces and correlated with BDNF levels by Spearman correlation. Fluoxetine produced similar behavioral effects but did not alter microbial composition. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot randomized controlled trial showed that blueberry intake increased BDNF and reduced depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that blueberry-derived polyphenols act through the gut microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis to modulate anxiety and cognitive dysfunction.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate brain function and behavior, yet the molecular mediators linking gut microbiota to depression remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Bifidobacterium longum and fed them a high-fat, low-fiber diet or a fermentable fiber-enriched diet. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and untargeted metabolomics, we quantified microbial community shifts and neuroactive metabolites. Fiber supplementation increased butyrate and indole-3-propionate, reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation, and normalized BDNF and GPR41 expression in the hippocampus. In participants with major depressive disorder, baseline fecal microbiota showed lower butyrate kinase abundance, and linear mixed models associated this deficit with anxiety severity. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-fed donors into mice recapitulated the BDNF increase and reduced depressive-like behavior, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished these effects. These findings position dietary fiber as a tractable gut-brain signal and identify BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity as a candidate mechanism. Our data suggest that dietary fiber intake and GPR41 signaling may serve as biomarkers and therapeutic targets in depression.

Disruption of bidirectional signaling between the gut and brain is increasingly linked to Parkinson's disease (PD), with gut microbiota dysbiosis preceding motor symptoms by years. This communication involves neurotransmitters, bile acids, and microbial metabolites that influence central nervous system function. In a cohort of 120 participants with PD and 80 healthy controls, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed significant community-level separation by diagnosis (R2 = 0.08, p = 0.001), while random forest classification discriminated PD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.79. Depletion of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and enrichment of Escherichia were associated with higher intestinal inflammation and worse cognitive impairment. A 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of probiotic supplementation in 60 patients is ongoing to test whether restoring Faecalibacterium improves constipation and motor disability. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome as a disease-modifying strategy in PD.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and its disruption predicts depression-like phenotypes. To test whether targeted probiotic and prebiotic fiber supplementation can reverse these effects, we used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation in mice exposed to a Western diet. Gut microbiota from patients with irritable bowel syndrome and anxiety showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside lower short-chain fatty acid production. Supplementation increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior, but effects depended on baseline microbial composition. Metagenomic functional profiling linked these changes to tryptophan metabolism and IL-6 signaling. A random-effects meta-analysis of cohorts confirmed that probiotic interventions modestly improved depressive symptoms, with stronger effects when combined with prebiotic fiber. Notably, fluoxetine responses were amplified by probiotic co-administration, whereas Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated with reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable mediator of gut-brain axis signaling and support precision synbiotic strategies for stress-related disorders.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that shape central nervous system immune tone and behavior, yet the extent to which these signals mediate depression-like phenotypes remains contested. We colonized germ-free mice with gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls and fed them either a fiber-rich diet or a low-fiber diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics quantified Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and butyrate in feces and plasma. Behavioral assays assessed anhedonia and anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis tested whether microbial butyrate production explained group differences in BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Dietary fiber increased butyrate and Bifidobacterium abundance only in mice receiving control microbiota, while depression-associated microbiota attenuated these responses. Linear mixed-effects models showed that butyrate was inversely associated with anhedonia, and mediation analysis indicated a significant indirect effect through BDNF. These findings suggest that fiber fermentation is a modifiable gut-brain pathway, but its benefit depends on baseline microbiota composition.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in the colon shapes BDNF and TPH1 expression in the hippocampus and raphe nuclei, linking gut microbiota composition to depressive-like behavior and cognitive impairment. To test whether this pathway is modifiable, male C57BL/6 mice received a prebiotic fiber supplement or vehicle for 6 weeks, with 16S rRNA gene sequencing and RNA sequencing used to profile cecal microbiota and brain transcripts. Prebiotic fiber increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in feces, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Behavioral testing using the forced swim test showed reduced immobility, and linear mixed-effects models identified butyrate as a mediator. Flow cytometry revealed reduced interleukin-6 in the plasma, while immunohistochemistry showed increased DCX in the dentate gyrus. In patients with major depressive disorder, similar microbial signatures were associated with lower BDNF expression. Together, these data position microbiota-derived SCFA as a tractable target. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber may modulate the gut-brain axis through SCFA-dependent BDNF regulation.

Disruption of the gut microbiome by a Western-style diet accelerates Alzheimer's disease-related pathology in APOE4 carriers, with microbial metabolites mediating the effect. In APPswe/PS1dE9 mice humanized for APOE4, a high-fat, high-sucrose diet reduced Bacteroides and Lactobacillus abundance, increased Firmicutes, and elevated lipopolysaccharide in the gut. 16S rRNA sequencing of intestinal samples and mediation analysis linked these shifts to lower butyrate and greater amyloid-beta deposition in the hippocampus. Butyrate supplementation restored microglial homeostasis, reduced IL-1β, and improved cognitive impairment. Circulating trimethylamine N-oxide was elevated in high-fat diet-fed mice, while probiotic treatment normalized microbial composition and reduced neuroinflammation. In human participants with mild cognitive impairment, blueberry intake enriched Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium, and higher short-chain fatty acids correlated with better cognitive performance. Fecal microbiota transplantation from blueberry-fed mice into germ-free mice reproduced the cognitive benefit. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods may modify Alzheimer's disease risk through microbiota-SCFA-brain signaling, particularly in APOE4 carriers.

Probiotic supplementation can attenuate stress-related behavioral deficits by reshaping gut microbiota and vagal signaling, yet the extent to which these effects depend on baseline microbial diversity remains unresolved. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, adults with mild anxiety received either Lactobacillus rhamnosus or a control formulation for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut samples revealed increased Lactobacillus abundance and higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations in responders. Functional magnetic resonance imaging showed reduced amygdala reactivity to negative emotional stimuli in the probiotic group, accompanied by lower cortisol awakening responses. These changes correlated with decreased self-reported anxiety and improved cognitive flexibility. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial composition shifts accounted for 32% of the behavioral effect. However, participants with low baseline microbial diversity showed weaker responses, indicating that probiotic efficacy may require a permissive gut ecosystem. These findings support targeted probiotic interventions for stress-related disorders and highlight the need for stratified clinical trials.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids shape neuroimmune signaling in the hippocampus, yet the pathways linking gut microbiota to major depressive disorder (MDD) remain incompletely defined. We recruited patients with MDD and healthy controls, profiled the 16S rRNA gene and BDNF expression, and performed fecal microbiota transplantation into mice. Relative abundances of Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium were reduced in patients, while Prevotella was enriched; these shifts correlated with lower short-chain fatty acids and higher lipopolysaccharide in stool. Mice receiving patient microbiota exhibited increased prefrontal cortex inflammation and reduced BDNF expression. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Faecalibacterium abundance partially mediated the association between gut microbiota composition and MDD severity. A random forest model based on microbiota and short-chain fatty acid features distinguished patients from controls with 82% accuracy. Neither probiotic supplementation nor selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use accounted for these associations, and linear regression confirmed that Faecalibacterium abundance remained inversely associated with MDD severity after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids may offer a tractable strategy for MDD prevention or adjunctive treatment.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) cross the blood-brain barrier and modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbial composition to anxiety-like behavior and cognitive impairment. In germ-free mice, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with irritable bowel syndrome revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with IL-6 and TLR4 expression in the colon. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 32% of the effect of microbiota on prefrontal cortex activation during a functional MRI emotion task. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors attenuated these associations, whereas probiotic supplementation increased microbial diversity and reduced depressive symptoms in adults. Vagotomy abolished microbiota-dependent c-Fos induction in the vagus nerve, implicating neural signaling. This gut-brain axis also influences hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity and cortisol secretion, with FKBP5 methylation mediating early-life stress effects. These findings suggest that targeting the gut-brain axis through dietary fiber or psychobiotics may offer therapeutic benefit, but causal inference requires Mendelian randomization and longitudinal mixed-effects models.

Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid produced by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and other gut microbiota members, strengthens the intestinal epithelial barrier and dampens neuroinflammatory signaling along the vagus nerve, linking dietary fiber intake to brain health. In mice fed fermented foods or given probiotic supplements, elevated BDNF expression in the hippocampus coincided with reduced depressive-like behavior and lower corticosterone levels. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations, whereas patients with major depressive disorder showed depleted butyrate-producing bacteria and altered gut microbiome diversity. A random-effects meta-analysis of adults found that probiotic supplementation modestly reduced depression scores, although effects varied by strain and baseline microbiota composition. Mechanistic studies indicate that dietary fiber and fermented foods can increase short-chain fatty acid availability, promote BDNF signaling, and limit lipopolysaccharide translocation, but strain-specific actions and long-term outcomes remain unresolved. However, heterogeneity in study design, dose, and duration complicates direct comparisons. These findings position probiotics and fermented foods as accessible adjunctive strategies for gut-brain axis disorders.

Metabolism of dietary fiber and fermented foods yields short-chain fatty acids that shape central nervous system immune tone, yet the transcriptional routes linking gut microbiome composition to hippocampal plasticity remain incompletely resolved. In a randomized crossover trial, 48 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a polyphenol-rich diet or an isocaloric control diet for 12 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased after the intervention, paralleling higher butyrate and indole-3-propionate concentrations. RNA sequencing revealed upregulation of BDNF, NR4A1, and IL10, with reduced NFKB1 expression. Using PERMANOVA and linear mixed-effects models, we found that diet-associated shifts in microbial community structure explained 18% of variance in BDNF expression and predicted improved prefrontal cortex-dependent working memory. These effects were not observed in participants consuming the control diet. The findings suggest that fermented food and fiber intake may modulate neuroinflammation through microbiome-BDNF signaling, offering a tractable target for age-related cognitive decline.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced in the colon shape central nervous system immunity, yet their causal contribution to anxiety-like behavior remains disputed. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, and untargeted metabolomics, we found that gut microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and increased Il6 and Tnf transcripts. This was accompanied by elevated corticosterone, impaired vagus nerve signaling, and lower butyrate and indole-3-propionate. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances correlated inversely with Bdnf and positively with interleukin-6. In a separate cohort, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids partially reversed these effects, whereas fluoxetine normalized behavior without restoring Bdnf. Notably, optogenetic stimulation of vagal afferents reversed the Bdnf deficit, while minocycline suppressed Il6 and Tnf but did not alter behavior. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial butyrate accounted for 31% of the behavioral variance. These data indicate that gut microbial communities modulate Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity through immune and endocrine routes, identifying butyrate as a candidate mediator linking the gut microbiome to depression.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans alters gut microbiota composition and may improve mild cognitive impairment through gut-brain axis signaling. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 92 adults with metabolic syndrome received either prebiotic fiber or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance increased, while Ruminococcus gnavus decreased. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed enriched microbial genes for short-chain fatty acid production. Cognitive flexibility improved modestly, and changes correlated with butyrate concentrations. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that treatment assignment predicted hippocampal connectivity after adjusting for baseline insulin resistance. Mediation analysis suggested that Bifidobacterium abundance accounted for 22% of the effect on executive function. Parallel experiments in gnotobiotic mice colonized with post-treatment participant feces reproduced the microbiota shifts and reduced neuroinflammation; hippocampal Bdnf expression also increased. These findings support targeted fiber supplementation as a plausible strategy for modulating microbiota-gut-brain communication, though confirmatory trials using functional magnetic resonance imaging and longer follow-up are needed.

Supplementation with probiotics or fermented foods can alter gut microbiota composition and may reduce depression-like symptoms, but the pathways linking microbial metabolites to brain function remain incompletely defined. In a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, 84 adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Linear mixed models tested associations with depressive symptoms, serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and interleukin-6. Participants receiving probiotics showed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, higher butyrate, and lower anxiety scores than participants who received placebo. Butyrate correlated positively with BDNF and negatively with interleukin-6. In parallel, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into mice treated with antibiotics reduced depression-like behavior and increased serotonin in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that probiotic and fermented food interventions may support microbiota-gut-brain signaling in MDD, although larger trials are needed.

Gut microbial depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa precedes cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease, yet whether dietary interventions can reverse this trajectory remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a fiber-rich diet plus Bifidobacterium breve or usual diet alone. Fecal microbiome was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Compared with usual diet, the fiber-rich diet plus probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and raised butyrate concentrations. These changes correlated with improved verbal memory and reduced systemic inflammation. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 31% of the cognitive benefit. No serious adverse events occurred. The findings indicate that combining dietary fiber with probiotic supplementation may modulate the gut microbiota-brain axis and slow early cognitive impairment, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and mechanism.

Microbial colonization in infancy shapes brain immune maturation, and its disruption has been linked to Alzheimer's disease and autism spectrum disorder. We transplanted gut microbiota from human infants into gnotobiotic mice and compared them with mice receiving probiotic supplementation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium longum were depleted in animals with elevated lipopolysaccharide and reduced butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids. RNA sequencing of hippocampus revealed increased TREM2, IL6, and NLRP3 expression. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for litter and cage confirmed that A. muciniphila abundance predicted TREM2 expression, while PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis distances linked community composition to behavioral deficits. Quantitative PCR validated BDNF downregulation in the prefrontal cortex, and false discovery rate correction controlled for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that early-life gut microbiota composition, particularly A. muciniphila and B. longum, influences TREM2- and NLRP3-dependent neuroimmune pathways, offering targets for psychobiotic interventions.

Microbial modulation of BDNF expression in the hippocampus may couple gut microbiota composition to depressive-like behavior, yet the pathways linking specific taxa to BDNF transcriptional control remain poorly resolved. In mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances were inversely associated with anhedonia, while Clostridiales expansion tracked with corticosterone elevation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors into naive recipients reduced BDNF mRNA and protein levels in the prefrontal cortex and increased immobility in the forced swim test. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability accounted for 38% of the effect of donor microbiota on BDNF expression; linear mixed models confirmed that butyrate supplementation restored BDNF transcripts and normalized serotonin turnover. Peripheral FKBP5 methylation tracked with central BDNF changes, and Spearman correlation linked these epigenetic marks to anhedonia severity. These findings position BDNF as a convergent node through which microbial metabolites shape stress susceptibility, suggesting that butyrate-targeted interventions merit testing in patients with major depressive disorder.

Curcumin supplementation restores BDNF signaling and remodels gut microbiota in major depressive disorder (MDD), but the extent to which microbial shifts mediate these effects remains unclear. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 60 adults with MDD received curcumin (1 g/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing quantified fecal microbiota, while quantitative PCR measured BDNF mRNA in peripheral blood. A random-effects meta-analysis pooled these data with three prior cohorts. Curcumin increased BDNF expression (standardized mean difference 0.62, 95% CI 0.21–1.03) and reduced depressive symptoms. Relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus rose, whereas Clostridium declined. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium abundance explained 28% of the BDNF increase. Baseline gut microbial diversity correlated with BDNF methylation, and linear mixed models showed that Bifidobacterium abundance predicted improvement independently of baseline severity. In chronic stress mice, curcumin failed to elevate BDNF after antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion, supporting a microbiome-dependent mechanism. These findings position curcumin as a gut-brain modulator, though confirmatory trials using causal mediation models are needed.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes neuropsychiatric disease risk through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling. Gut microbiota ferment dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which stimulate enteroendocrine cells and modulate brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. In germ-free mice, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance correlates with reduced anxiety-like behavior and lower corticosterone levels. A randomized trial in adults with mild cognitive impairment tested a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, alongside omega-3 fatty acids. After 12 weeks, shotgun metagenomics showed increased diversity of the microbiome and BDNF promoter methylation changes; however, cognitive scores improved only modestly. SCFA producers, particularly Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, were depleted in non-responders. These findings suggest that probiotic and omega-3 interventions may influence gut microbiome signaling through BDNF-dependent and SCFA-mediated pathways, but baseline microbiome composition likely determines clinical benefit. Nevertheless, causal inference remains limited: most human evidence is cross-sectional, and metagenomic associations do not establish directionality. Dietary patterns rich in fermentable fiber may amplify SCFA production, whereas antibiotic exposure or low diversity of the microbiome may blunt responses. Future trials should stratify participants by baseline microbiome composition and measure BDNF and inflammatory markers longitudinally.

Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation attenuates neuroinflammation and preserves hippocampal function in aging mice, yet whether these benefits extend to adults consuming Western-style diets remains uncertain. We randomized 96 participants with mild cognitive impairment to 12 weeks of fish oil (1.8 g/day eicosapentaenoic acid plus docosahexaenoic acid) or placebo oil, stratified by habitual fiber intake. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples assessed gut microbiome composition, and functional magnetic resonance imaging measured hippocampal activation during memory encoding. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia relative abundance and reduced interleukin-6 concentrations; changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with improved recall accuracy and BDNF methylation. Among participants with low fiber intake, fish oil produced larger microbiome shifts and greater cognitive gains than among those with high fiber intake. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that baseline Prevotella abundance moderated these effects. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and omega-3 supplementation interact to shape gut microbiota and cognitive decline trajectories.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshapes gut microbial ecology and attenuates neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease models, yet the microbial signals linking peripheral lipid availability to central BDNF expression remain poorly resolved. We treated APP/PS1 transgenic mice with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or vehicle for 12 weeks and profiled caecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and ELISA. DHA increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, elevated butyrate in colon, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in hippocampus. These changes coincided with improved spatial memory deficits and restored BDNF and PSD-95 expression. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the DHA effect on BDNF. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment abolished the cognitive benefit, while faecal microbiota transplantation from DHA-treated donors to antibiotic-treated recipients partially transferred the metabolic and cognitive phenotypes. These findings position DHA as a dietary supplement that engages the microbiota-gut-brain axis through butyrate-BDNF signaling.

Adherence to a Mediterranean diet rich in fermented foods has been associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved gut-brain axis signaling, but the molecular mediators remain incompletely defined. In a randomized adult cohort, we tested whether 8 weeks of probiotic supplementation combined with a high-fiber diet altered gut microbiota composition, short-chain fatty acid production, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Participants provided stool and serum at baseline and endpoint and completed a 3-day dietary recall. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography, and BDNF mRNA was measured by RT-qPCR. Compared with controls, the intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and upregulated BDNF expression. These changes correlated with lower depressive symptoms and anxiety scores (Spearman correlation, r = 0.42, p = 0.008). Linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline microbiota diversity confirmed these associations. The findings suggest that probiotic and dietary fiber interventions may modulate the gut-brain axis through BDNF-related pathways, supporting further clinical trials.

Fermented foods and prebiotic fiber supplementation can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, yet their impact on stress-related disorders remains variable across individuals. In a randomized mouse model of chronic social stress, we compared a fermented food-enriched chow with inulin supplementation and assessed colon microbiota, hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) expression, and anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing coupled with PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures; Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were enriched in both intervention groups, whereas Akkermansia increased only with inulin. Random forest classification identified Prevotella as a discriminative taxon linked to reduced anxiety-like behavior. Both interventions lowered corticosterone and increased butyrate, but fermented food produced stronger effects on Bdnf and tight junction protein expression in the hippocampus. Notably, baseline Bacteroides abundance correlated with IL-6 and Bdnf transcripts, suggesting a modifiable microbial set point. These data suggest that fermented foods and prebiotic fiber engage overlapping but nonidentical gut-brain pathways, with microbiota composition predicting behavioral resilience.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate gut microbiota–brain signaling, yet whether this pathway can be harnessed in mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiled stool microbiota, while resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain connectivity. Dietary patterns were captured with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated fecal butyrate, reduced serum interleukin-6, and strengthened connectivity between the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Linear mixed-effects models showed that these microbial and metabolic shifts correlated with improved memory performance. Changes in Bifidobacterium abundance mediated the relationship between probiotic intake and memory performance. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90%. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with probiotics may offer a tractable strategy for mild cognitive impairment.

Alterations in the gut microbiota and its microbial metabolites are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the mechanisms by which probiotic supplementation modulates this axis remain incompletely defined. We recruited adults with MDD and healthy controls, collected fecal and serum samples, and profiled gut microbial communities using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. After 8 weeks of Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis supplementation, patients showed reduced depressive symptoms and increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. Random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium and butyrate as discriminative features between responders and non-responders. Baseline Faecalibacterium abundance predicted treatment response with an area under the curve of 0.81. Spearman correlation revealed that butyrate was positively associated with BDNF expression in peripheral blood and negatively associated with interleukin-6. In mice receiving probiotic, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders attenuated stress-induced behavioral deficits. These findings suggest that probiotic-driven microbiome shifts, particularly butyrate production, may contribute to MDD improvement via the gut-brain axis.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF expression in the hippocampus, coupling diet to cognitive impairment. To test whether this gut-brain signaling is altered in Alzheimer's disease (AD), we profiled fecal microbiota from patients with AD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and metagenomic sequencing. Participants also completed neuropsychological testing and provided diet records. We further quantified short-chain fatty acid producers and used linear mixed models to adjust for age, sex, and medication use. Compared with controls, patients with AD showed reduced abundance of Butyricicoccus and Faecalibacterium, taxa that ferment fiber into butyrate. Lower Faecalibacterium correlated with higher amyloid-β burden and lower BDNF expression in blood. Random forest models classified AD with moderate accuracy, and mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediates the association between fiber intake and BDNF. These findings support targeting gut microbiota and diet to modulate BDNF-related pathways in AD.

Chronic high-fat diet intake disrupts gut microbiota and increases depression and anxiety risk, yet whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation can reverse these effects remains unclear. In C57BL/6 mice randomized to a high-fat diet with or without omega-3 supplementation for 12 weeks, we assessed depressive-like behavior and anxiety-like behavior using open field test, sucrose preference test, and forced swim test. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples showed that omega-3 restored Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance and increased short-chain fatty acids. ELISA and RT-qPCR revealed lower lipopolysaccharide, IL-6, and TNF-α in serum and hippocampus, with normalized BDNF expression. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia muciniphila to serotonin turnover, while PERMANOVA confirmed diet-driven microbiota separation. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from omega-3-treated mice into antibiotic-treated mice partially reproduced the behavioral benefits, whereas omega-3 in germ-free mice did not. These results suggest omega-3 mitigates neuropsychiatric disturbances induced by high-fat diet via microbiota-gut-brain signaling, warranting human trials.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized in Parkinson's disease, where Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances correlate with motor and non-motor symptoms. Preclinical studies in mice further show that probiotic administration reduces alpha-synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra and restores BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, patients with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease received either multi-strain probiotic supplementation or placebo alongside stable levodopa therapy. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial shifts, butyrate levels, and changes in BDNF expression.
