Probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and was associated with improved constipation and depressive symptoms; no significant change occurred in motor severity. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with probiotics may modulate cytokine and BDNF signaling, warranting larger trials with neuroimaging endpoints.

Inulin supplementation reshapes gut microbiota and elevates BDNF expression in the hippocampus, pointing to a tractable strategy for slowing Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. Using a randomized patient cohort and MPTP-treated mice, we integrated 16S rRNA sequencing, qPCR, and ELISA to quantify microbial composition, BDNF transcripts, and short-chain fatty acids. Compared with controls, patients with PD had lower Lactobacillus and butyrate, and reduced BDNF in serum. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, raised butyrate in feces and serum, and attenuated dopamine loss in the striatum. Spearman correlation linked BDNF upregulation to Lactobacillus abundance and butyrate levels, while BDNF knockdown abolished the protective effect in mice. Inulin also decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation and lowered TNF expression in the midbrain. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice partially reproduced these benefits in recipient mice, confirming a causal role for gut microbes. These findings suggest that inulin acts through a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis to protect nigrostriatal circuits, supporting further trials in patients with PD.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reshapes gut microbial communities and attenuates neuroinflammation in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease, yet whether these benefits translate to patients remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received omega-3 or placebo for 24 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled gut microbiota, while serum inflammatory cytokines and BDNF expression were measured. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial composition between groups, driven by enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium and depletion of Prevotella. Random forest classification identified Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii as predictors of BDNF response. Omega-3 increased short-chain fatty acid producers and reduced IL-6, with changes correlated (Spearman correlation) with hippocampal volume. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for baseline BMI and prior antibiotic exposure confirmed that Clostridium cluster XIVa relative abundance predicted BDNF changes. These findings suggest that omega-3 may improve cognitive decline through gut microbiota-BDNF signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Gut microbiota depletion accelerates Parkinson's disease (PD) pathology, yet whether dietary fiber can reverse this trajectory remains unclear. We treated transgenic mice overexpressing α-synuclein with inulin for eight weeks and assessed striatal dopamine, colon inflammatory markers, and motor behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and restored BDNF expression in the substantia nigra. These changes coincided with reduced neuroinflammation, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor performance. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and BDNF partially mediated the protective effects of inulin. In patients with PD, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with plasma butyrate and motor severity. Notably, inulin-treated mice showed reduced constipation and higher short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces than vehicle-treated mice. These preclinical observations suggest that targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis with prebiotics may slow PD progression. Our findings position inulin as a candidate prebiotic intervention for PD, though fecal microbiota transplantation studies are needed to establish causality.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet tracks with higher gut microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms, yet whether this association depends on BDNF genotype is unclear. We examined 184 adults who completed a food frequency questionnaire and provided stool samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multivariable linear regression tested relationships among dietary fiber, BDNF Val66Met, microbial taxa, and depression scores, adjusting for age, sex, and antidepressant use. Higher fiber intake correlated with increased Faecalibacterium and Bifidobacterium abundance and greater fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations. BDNF Met carriers showed a stronger inverse association between Mediterranean diet adherence and depression severity than BDNF Val/Val homozygotes (interaction p=0.018). Mediation analysis suggested that microbial diversity accounted for 22% of this effect. These findings implicate interactions among diet, BDNF genotype, and microbiota in mood dysregulation and support targeting fermented foods and fiber-rich foods in individuals carrying BDNF Met alleles, although validation in larger cohorts is needed. Future Mendelian randomization and faecal microbiota transplantation studies should test causality.

Supplementation with blueberry-derived polyphenols reshapes the gut microbiota and lowers neuroinflammation in aging, yet the pathways linking intestinal microbiota shifts to brain function remain poorly resolved. In a 12-week randomized trial, 84 older adults with subjective cognitive decline received either freeze-dried blueberry powder or control. Fecal Lactobacillus and Akkermansia abundance increased after intervention, alongside elevated butyrate and propionate. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria ratios. Cognitive scores improved, and BDNF plasma levels rose. Using mediation analysis, we found that butyrate and Akkermansia jointly explained 31% of the intervention effect on BDNF, while hippocampal volume was preserved in the blueberry group. Parallel mouse experiments confirmed that blueberry polyphenols increased Akkermansia and butyrate, reduced microglial activation, and improved performance in Morris water maze. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein decreased, indicating reduced endotoxemia. These findings suggest that blueberry-rich diets may delay cognitive impairment by engaging gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF signaling.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that shape gut microbiota and signal to the brain via immune, vagal, and neuroendocrine routes. How specific dietary patterns alter brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression and behavior remains incompletely resolved. We fed mice either a high-fiber diet or a Western-style diet for 12 weeks and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate in feces, and upregulated Bdnf in the hippocampus. In contrast, the Western-style diet reduced Bdnf expression and raised anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from mice fed a high-fiber diet into germ-free mice partially reproduced the Bdnf increase, suggesting a causal microbiota-brain link. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the diet effect on Bdnf. Neither probiotic supplementation nor antibiotic treatment fully mimicked the fiber effect, although both altered community composition. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable lever for BDNF-dependent brain health and justify human trials targeting gut microbiota.

Microbial communities inhabiting the gastrointestinal tract shape central nervous system immune tone and emotional behavior, yet whether diet can reproducibly shift this axis remains unclear. In an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild depressive symptoms consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods and fiber or continued their habitual diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium in the intervention arm, accompanied by higher fecal butyrate and lower IL6 expression. Validated questionnaires showed greater reductions in depression and anxiety scores, and these changes correlated with microbial diversity. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders transferred the behavioral benefit, while antibiotic-induced dysbiosis abolished it. The findings indicate that dietary patterns can modulate gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid production, influencing signaling between the gut and brain and reducing depressive symptoms. These data support fermented food and fiber interventions as accessible adjuncts, though larger trials incorporating metabolomics and neuroimaging are needed.

Microbial butyrate production predicts mild cognitive impairment more strongly than gut microbiota diversity in obesity, yet whether dietary interventions alter this axis remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized trial, 96 adults with metabolic syndrome received a Mediterranean diet or an isocaloric Western-style diet; half in each arm also received omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (1.5 g/day). We quantified fecal Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, plasma short-chain fatty acids, and hippocampal volume. Mediation analysis tested whether butyrate links diet to cognition. The Mediterranean diet plus omega-3 increased F. prausnitzii abundance and butyrate compared with the Western-style diet alone, while A. muciniphila changed only with omega-3. Linear mixed models showed that higher butyrate correlated with improved cognition and greater hippocampal volume. Mediation analysis attributed 34% of the diet-cognition effect to butyrate, independent of APOE genotype. These findings position butyrate as a modifiable mediator of gut-brain signaling and support omega-3 supplementation with Mediterranean diet for protecting against cognitive decline.

Baseline gut microbiota composition stratifies depressive symptom trajectories after omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). In a 12-week trial, 120 participants received either omega-3 or placebo; stool samples were analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. We applied linear mixed-effects models and random forest to relate microbial taxa, short-chain fatty acid profiles, and BDNF methylation to changes in depression and anxiety scores. Higher baseline relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii predicted greater reductions in depressive symptoms, whereas Bacteroides dominance associated with nonresponse. Omega-3 increased butyrate-producing taxa and reduced lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. Taxa within Clostridium cluster XIVa and Lactobacillus correlated with serotonin metabolites and BDNF expression, and omega-3 responders showed enriched microbial pathways for tryptophan metabolism. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial butyrate production partially explained the omega-3 effect on depression. These findings suggest that gut microbial features could guide omega-3 use for IBS-related mood disorders, though validation in larger cohorts is needed.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids combined with a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermentable fiber raises gut microbial diversity and lowers lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation in adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). In a 12-week randomized trial, participants received omega-3 plus inulin or placebo. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed enrichment of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, whereas liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry showed elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in plasma. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and with better performance on neuropsychological testing. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia abundance to SCFA levels and IL-6 decline. No changes in amyloid-beta or phosphorylated tau were detected by plasma biomarker assays. Compliance was confirmed by plasma fatty acid profiling and stool metabolomics. The findings suggest that omega-3 and fermentable fiber may act through microbiota-gut-brain signaling to modulate neuroinflammation in MCI, though larger trials with metagenomics and metabolomics are needed. These effects were independent of baseline dietary patterns.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber shapes central nervous system homeostasis through the gut-brain axis, yet the molecular mediators linking gut microbiota to affective behavior remain incompletely defined. In a mouse model of chronic stress, fiber deprivation reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate in the colon, and decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. These changes coincided with increased depressive-like behavior and elevated corticosterone. Probiotic supplementation restored BDNF expression, normalized corticosterone, and attenuated depressive-like behavior, but only when combined with fermentable fiber. 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing and multivariate analysis revealed that probiotics alone did not reverse stress-induced microbiota dysbiosis. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila was inversely associated with neuroinflammation markers, while circulating lipopolysaccharide increased after stress. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline fiber intake correlated with BDNF methylation in blood. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotic interventions may synergistically modulate gut-brain signaling, warranting further clinical trials.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans during chronic stress alters gut microbiota composition and reduces depressive-like behavior in mice, yet translation to humans remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 92 adults with mild anxiety received either galactooligosaccharides (GOS) or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and cortisol awakening response, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels, and anxiety scores were assessed. Linear mixed-effects models showed that GOS increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced anxiety scores compared with placebo. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium changes partially mediated the GOS-related anxiety reduction, and these changes correlated with BDNF increases. At week 8, GOS also raised fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations and lowered plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a marker of systemic inflammation. These peripheral shifts were most pronounced in participants with higher baseline anxiety. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with prebiotics may offer a tractable adjunct for stress-related disorders.

Chronic consumption of a Western-style diet depletes gut microbiota diversity and reduces short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) output, a metabolic shift increasingly linked to cognitive decline and blunted BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. To test whether this axis is reversible, aged mice received a high-fat, low-fiber diet with or without fructo-oligosaccharides and Lactobacillus plantarum for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that the supplement restored Lactobacillus abundance, increased butyrate and propionate concentrations, and reduced neuroinflammation. In the prefrontal cortex, BDNF expression and NLRP3 inflammasome markers returned toward control levels. Behavioral testing revealed improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability explained part of the BDNF response. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into germ-free recipients reproduced the increase in butyrate and the reduction in NLRP3 activation, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished these benefits. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber and probiotic co-supplementation may protect the gut-brain axis against diet-induced neurodegeneration, although human clinical trials are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that restrain neuroinflammation and may reduce anxiety-like behavior, yet whether this pathway mediates clinical responses to prebiotic supplementation remains unresolved. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with subclinical anxiety received inulin or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolites were quantified using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline anxiety severity and diet quality showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and raised butyrate levels. These shifts correlated inversely with anxiety scores and with interleukin-6. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the prebiotic effect on anxiety. In mice, inulin reproduced the microbiome and metabolite changes and reduced neuroinflammation in the prefrontal cortex. In the mouse model, inulin also increased Bdnf expression and reduced microglial activation in the hippocampus, supporting a BDNF-dependent mechanism. Together, these findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal, though confirmatory trials in major depressive disorder are needed.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans during a Western-style diet reverses stress-induced anxiety-like behavior and restores hippocampal BDNF expression in male C57BL/6 mice, yet the microbial signals mediating this gut-brain effect remain uncertain. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice, we found that inulin selectively expanded Bifidobacterium pseudolongum and Akkermansia muciniphila, increased short-chain fatty acid production, and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation across the intestinal barrier. These shifts correlated with lower neuroinflammation and reduced cognitive dysfunction in mice exposed to chronic corticosterone. In participants with mild cognitive impairment, a randomized inulin intervention produced parallel increases in gut microbiota diversity and Bifidobacterium abundance, alongside reduced depressive symptoms and lower interleukin-6 concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium-driven short-chain fatty acid shifts accounted for 31% of the improvement in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that dietary fiber acts as a substrate for microbiota-derived metabolites that modulate brain function, positioning prebiotic fiber as a plausible adjunct for stress-related disorders.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depletion of butyrate-producing Firmicutes accompany major depressive disorder (MDD), but whether these shifts reflect causal pathophysiology or downstream immune changes remains unresolved. Fecal samples from 96 participants (48 MDD patients, 48 healthy controls) underwent 16S rRNA sequencing. Random forest classification and differential abundance testing identified Faecalibacterium and Roseburia as the most discriminative taxa, with area under the curve 0.81. Their abundances negatively correlated with IL6 and BDNF expression in peripheral blood (Spearman correlation, P = 0.01). Short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in MDD patients and inversely associated with depression severity scores. Plasma lipopolysaccharide was elevated in MDD patients and correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance. Mediation analysis suggested that BDNF downregulation partially explained the link between Faecalibacterium loss and MDD. These findings position Firmicutes depletion and butyrate deficiency as candidate contributors to MDD, with IL6 and BDNF as potential molecular intermediaries. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone and synaptic plasticity, yet how probiotic supplementation modifies this dialogue in age-related cognitive decline remains incompletely resolved. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve and fed a fiber-rich diet or inulin for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased gut microbiota diversity and enrichment of butyrate-producing taxa. RNA sequencing of hippocampus showed upregulated Bdnf and Zfp36 and downregulated Nfkb1. Butyrate concentrations in feces correlated with Bdnf expression and improved performance in Morris water maze and novel object recognition. Concentrations of acetate and propionate in feces were also elevated in colonized animals. Inulin alone did not alter Bdnf, whereas combined probiotic and inulin reduced neuroinflammation, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha levels. These findings suggest that synbiotic approaches targeting butyrate-producing bacteria may modulate BDNF signaling and cognitive impairment. Future studies should test whether these effects translate to older adults and whether BDNF polymorphisms modify responses.

Dietary fermented foods and probiotic supplements can reshape the gut microbiome, yet their impact on age-related cognitive decline remains uncertain. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks while maintaining habitual diets. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, in the probiotic group. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 declined, whereas brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) increased. Cognitive scores improved modestly, and functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed enhanced hippocampal connectivity. These changes correlated with Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels, suggesting that probiotic supplementation may attenuate neuroinflammation through microbiota-derived metabolites. However, effects were heterogeneous and did not persist after washout. Larger trials are needed to determine whether fermented food and probiotic interventions can delay dementia onset. These findings position gut microbial communities as modifiable contributors to neurodegeneration, with dietary patterns and supplementation as plausible preventive levers.

Consumption of a Western-style diet reshapes the gut microbiota and may promote neuropsychiatric disorders by disrupting intestinal barrier integrity and vagal signaling. In a murine model, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with RNA sequencing of the hippocampus to test whether dietary shifts alter microbial composition and host BDNF expression. Mice received either a high-fat, high-sucrose diet or standard chow for 12 weeks; a subset also received Lactobacillus rhamnosus or vehicle. The high-fat, high-sucrose diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, increased the Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio, and lowered hippocampal BDNF mRNA. These changes correlated with elevated interleukin-6 and corticosterone and impaired performance in novel object recognition. Probiotic supplementation partially restored BDNF expression and normalized microbial diversity. To translate these findings, we analyzed fecal microbiota from adults with mild cognitive impairment using shotgun metagenomics and linear mixed models; lower Bifidobacterium abundance again tracked with reduced BDNF and poorer verbal memory test scores. Our findings link diet-driven microbiota shifts to BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, suggesting that probiotics may mitigate cognitive impairment.

Gut microbiota-derived tryptophan catabolites can reshape central nervous system immune tone, yet their causal contribution to depression remains contested. In 180 adults, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal microbiota with untargeted metabolomics, then applied Mendelian randomization and linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use. Higher microbial diversity correlated with greater dietary fiber intake and elevated indole-3-propionic acid (IPA); both were inversely associated with depressive symptoms. Plasma IPA was lower in patients with major depressive disorder than in controls, and BDNF Val66Met genotype modified this relationship. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high IPA levels into antibiotic-treated mice reduced anhedonia-like behavior and increased hippocampal expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). IPA supplementation reproduced these effects, whereas fluoxetine produced distinct microbial shifts. Mediation analysis estimated that IPA explained 31% of the association between fiber intake and depression severity. These findings position indole-3-propionic acid as a diet-sensitive microbial signal that may influence BDNF-dependent mood regulation, though randomized trials are needed.

Depleted gut microbiota diversity and reduced butyrate-producing bacteria precede Parkinson's disease (PD) motor diagnosis and track with constipation, implicating the gut-brain axis in prodromal PD. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 62 patients with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 16 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila were quantified using 16S rRNA gene sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were measured in plasma. The probiotic increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. These shifts correlated with improved constipation and anxiety scores but not motor symptoms. Linear mixed models showed that baseline microbial diversity and GBA variant status modified treatment response, and Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia muciniphila to butyrate. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90% in both arms. The findings suggest that targeted probiotic supplementation may alter gut microbial ecology and systemic cytokine levels in prodromal PD, supporting further metagenomic and clinical studies.

Fermentable dietary fiber can reshape gut microbial communities and alter short-chain fatty acid signaling along the gut-brain axis, yet whether these shifts translate into measurable changes in BDNF expression remains unclear. We conducted an 8-week randomized parallel-group trial in healthy adult volunteers who consumed inulin (12 g/day) or no supplement. Fecal microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. BDNF mRNA in whole blood and cortisol in saliva were measured before and after intervention. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium relative abundance and raised fecal butyrate compared with no supplement. These microbial and metabolic changes coincided with higher BDNF expression and lower cortisol. Mixed-effects models showed that butyrate increases mediated the relationship between inulin intake and BDNF expression. The findings suggest that targeted fiber supplementation may influence BDNF-related pathways through microbiota-derived metabolites, supporting further investigation in larger and clinically diverse populations.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, suggesting that gut microbiota composition may influence depression severity. In a randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation plus a probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. We profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified BDNF and IL-6 expression in peripheral blood with quantitative PCR. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Faecalibacterium, and clinical outcomes. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance (beta = 0.42, p = 0.01) and reduced depressive symptoms (beta = -0.31, p = 0.03) compared with placebo. Higher Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with lower IL-6 expression (r = -0.28, p = 0.04) and greater BDNF expression (r = 0.33, p = 0.02). Mediation analysis suggested that BDNF partially mediated the relationship between Bifidobacterium and symptom improvement. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome with omega-3 supplementation and probiotics to modulate BDNF-related pathways in depression.

Fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich foods shape the gut microbiota and its metabolic output, offering a plausible route for diet-driven modulation of brain function. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or the same diet supplemented with probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids for 12 weeks. We assessed fecal microbiota composition using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, measured short-chain fatty acids in stool, and evaluated cognition with neuropsychological tests. Compared with diet alone, combined supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and improved composite memory scores (P = 0.01). Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with reduced neuroinflammation markers, including lower IL-6 expression. These findings suggest that probiotic and omega-3 supplementation may enhance the cognitive benefits of a fiber-rich diet by reinforcing gut microbial community homeostasis and butyrate production. No serious adverse events were reported, and adherence exceeded 90% in both groups. Larger trials are needed to confirm durability and mechanism.

Converging evidence positions the gut microbiota as a modifiable mediator of central nervous system function, with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains influencing short-chain fatty acid production, BDNF expression, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity. In a secondary analysis of adults with major depressive disorder, we tested whether a probiotic supplement combined with a Mediterranean-style diet altered fecal microbiome composition and self-reported depressive symptoms over 12 weeks. Participants received either the probiotic supplement plus dietary counseling or counseling alone. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified taxonomic shifts, and linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline depression severity, antidepressant use, and fiber intake. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed a modest but significant separation in microbial community structure between groups. Bifidobacterium relative abundance increased in the probiotic arm and correlated inversely with anxiety scores, whereas no between-group difference emerged for BDNF or interleukin-6. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may amplify shifts in the gut microbiota associated with the Mediterranean-style diet, though confirmatory trials with longer follow-up and standardized metagenomic sequencing are needed.

Consumption of a high-fiber diet combined with omega-3 supplementation produced distinct gut microbiome profiles that correlated with reduced neuroinflammation in aged rats. Using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), we found that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were enriched in responders, while Clostridium was depleted. Short-chain fatty acid levels, particularly butyrate, increased and were negatively associated with depressive-like behavior. In a parallel human cohort (n=85), Spearman correlation revealed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was inversely related to anxiety scores. Baseline microbial diversity was assessed using Shannon index, and lower diversity correlated with higher depression severity. 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing confirmed these taxonomic shifts. To further probe causality, we performed fecal microbiota transplantation from responder donors into germ-free mice, which recapitulated the reduced anxiety-like behavior. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the prefrontal cortex was elevated in supplemented animals. Mediation analysis using bootstrapping indicated that Faecalibacterium abundance explained 30% of the effect on anxiety. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber and omega-3 synergistically modulate the gut-brain axis, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

Disruption of gut microbial ecology can shift short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and alter gut-brain axis signaling, a process implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD). We tested whether resistant starch or inulin supplementation modifies this axis in APP/PS1 mice. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and western blotting, we quantified microbiota composition, SCFA levels, and amyloid-β pathology after eight weeks. Both fibers increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate and propionate concentrations, and reduced amyloid-β plaque load in the hippocampus. Transcriptomic profiling revealed lower Nfkb1 and Tnf expression and higher Bdnf and Arc expression. Behavioral testing with the Morris water maze showed improved spatial memory. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that butyrate mediated the relationship between Bifidobacterium abundance and plaque reduction. In prefrontal cortex, immunofluorescence showed fewer Iba1-positive microglia and lower interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α concentrations. These findings suggest that dietary fiber supplementation reshapes microbiota-gut-brain signaling and may attenuate AD-related pathology.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune signaling, yet whether probiotic supplementation relieves depressive symptoms by remodeling gut microbiota remains uncertain. We randomized 120 adults with major depressive disorder to 8 weeks of multi-strain probiotics or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and cortisol, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were quantified in serum. Linear mixed-effects models, PERMANOVA, and mediation analysis tested treatment effects and microbial mediators. Probiotic-treated participants showed enriched Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, reduced interleukin-6, and greater declines in depression severity than placebo-treated controls. At baseline, lower Faecalibacterium abundance and higher cortisol predicted weaker response. Fecal butyrate increased in responders and correlated with Bifidobacterium. Microbiota composition explained 21% of the probiotic effect on depression, and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with interleukin-6. These findings position probiotics as modulators of the gut-brain axis, though confirmatory trials using shotgun metagenomics and causal mediation models are needed.

Gut microbiota composition predicts BDNF availability and short-chain fatty acid signaling within the gut-brain axis, but the taxa-metabolite networks underlying major depressive disorder remain poorly defined. We recruited 84 adults with major depressive disorder and 40 healthy controls; stool and serum were analyzed by <gene>16S rRNA gene</gene> amplicon sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Community-level differences were tested with PERMANOVA, while associations among taxa, metabolites, and BDNF were modeled using Spearman correlation and linear mixed-effects models. Depression was marked by lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, higher Bacteroides, and reduced butyrate; butyrate correlated positively with BDNF and inversely with interleukin-6. An 8-week probiotic intervention increased Faecalibacterium and butyrate, lowered depressive symptoms, and raised BDNF relative to placebo. Preclinical validation in mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with depression recapitulated reduced BDNF and increased interleukin-6 in the hippocampus, effects attenuated by probiotic supplementation. These data identify gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a candidate mediator of BDNF regulation and support psychobiotic strategies for depression.

Reduced intake of fermentable dietary fiber is associated with a proinflammatory gut microbiota profile that may accelerate Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. We analyzed fecal samples from 120 PD patients and 80 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Associations between fiber intake, gut microbiome composition, and clinical scores were tested with linear mixed-effects models and PERMANOVA. Lower fiber consumption correlated with reduced abundance of Prevotella and Faecalibacterium and enriched Akkermansia in PD patients. These shifts were accompanied by lower fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations and worse constipation. Fecal butyrate was lower in PD patients than in healthy controls. In a mouse model of α-synucleinopathy, a low-fiber diet exacerbated substantia nigra neurodegeneration, whereas fiber supplementation attenuated it. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high fiber intake into recipient mice partially reproduced these benefits. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber intake shapes the gut microbiome in ways relevant to PD, supporting fiber-based interventions along the gut-brain axis.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with lower odds of multiple sclerosis (MS), yet whether this relationship is mirrored by compositional shifts in the gut microbiota remains unclear. In a case-control study of 95 participants from a pediatric demyelinating disease cohort—44 pediatric-onset cases with MS and 51 unaffected controls—each 1-point increase in a Mediterranean diet score was associated with 37% reduced MS odds in multivariable logistic regression. Higher fiber and iron intakes showed similar protective associations. Stool microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing; PERMANOVA and false discovery rate correction revealed that diet, not MS, explained most inter-individual variation. Several gut bacterial taxa were associated with both the Mediterranean diet score and MS, suggesting they may mediate diet-related protection. These findings position the interaction between diet and the gut microbiota as relevant to MS pathogenesis. Because cross-sectional sampling limits causal inference, longitudinal studies with larger samples and confounder adjustment are needed to clarify whether microbiota-targeted probiotic or diet-based strategies could modify MS risk.

Fermented foods and probiotic supplementation can shift gut microbiota composition in ways that attenuate depression-like behavior, but the extent to which these effects depend on baseline microbial diversity remains unresolved. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic plus fermented food diet or usual care. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium, with reduced Enterobacteriaceae. Plasma short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate and propionate, rose, while lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 declined. These changes correlated with improved anxiety scores and increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Mediation models using bootstrapped indirect effects indicated that butyrate accounted for 28% of the clinical improvement. Treatment response was stronger among participants with lower baseline microbial richness, and no serious adverse events were reported. The findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may offer a low-risk strategy for depression, although larger trials are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence BDNF expression and serotonin availability in the brain, providing a mechanistic link between gut microbiota and depression. To test whether this axis is modified by habitual intake, we analyzed fecal microbiota, plasma SCFAs, and plasma serotonin in 120 adults reporting high versus low fermented food consumption. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and targeted metabolomics revealed that high fermented food intake was associated with greater abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated butyrate, and lower depressive symptom scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and serotonin partially mediated the relationship between Bifidobacterium abundance and BDNF methylation. In a subset of participants, functional MRI showed that fermented food intake correlated with hippocampal connectivity, a pattern attenuated in carriers of the BDNF Val66Met allele. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented food may support brain health through microbiota-derived SCFAs and BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a modifiable target for mood disorders.

Supplementation with resistant starch increased gut microbial diversity and reduced depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder, yet the microbiota and metabolic mediators of this effect are unresolved. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, 120 participants received either resistant starch or placebo daily for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and circulating short-chain fatty acids were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed models tested associations between resistant starch intake, microbial taxa, butyrate concentrations, and changes in depression severity. Resistant starch increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium and raised circulating butyrate compared with placebo. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and lower BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 28% of the clinical improvement. The findings suggest that resistant starch may modulate microbiota-derived butyrate signaling, supporting further trials in patients with depression. Compliance exceeded 90%, and no serious adverse events occurred.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids during adolescence alters gut microbiota composition and improves stress coping, but whether these effects depend on host BDNF signaling remains unresolved. We randomized male Sprague-Dawley rats to receive omega-3-enriched or control diets for 8 weeks and assessed fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, and corticosterone responses to restraint stress. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that omega-3 increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance and reduced stress-induced corticosterone compared with controls. These changes coincided with higher BDNF exon IV mRNA and BDNF protein in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that Lactobacillus abundance partially mediated the relationship between diet and BDNF expression. In contrast, BDNF heterozygous rats showed blunted microbial and endocrine responses to omega-3 and exhibited longer immobility in the forced swim test. These findings suggest that omega-3 effects on the gut-brain axis require intact BDNF signaling and identify Lactobacillus as a potential microbial mediator.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans during metabolic syndrome reshapes the gut microbiota and improves hippocampal function, yet the transcriptional intermediaries remain unclear. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with obesity and subjective cognitive decline received inulin (12 g/day) or maltodextrin for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics and RNA sequencing of blood immune cells were coupled with functional magnetic resonance imaging. Mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline body mass index. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and raised fecal butyrate. These shifts correlated with reduced expression of TLR4 and IL6 and increased BDNF in peripheral blood. At baseline, lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance tracked with greater insulin resistance and weaker prefrontal activation. Mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota showed lower neuroinflammation and better hippocampal-dependent memory than mice receiving baseline microbiota. Fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling confirmed the butyrate increase, and mediation analysis attributed 31% of the memory effect to BDNF. The findings suggest that inulin exerts gut-brain effects through microbiome-derived butyrate and BDNF-dependent pathways.

Gut microbiota-derived metabolites shape central nervous system immunity and synaptic function, and their imbalance contributes to cognitive impairment. In aged mice, dietary supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus reduced interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide levels in plasma and hippocampus, while improving Morris water maze performance. Probiotic treatment also increased BDNF and PSD-95 expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that probiotic supplementation expanded Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing Proteobacteria. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations were also higher in treated mice. Using mediation analysis, we found that gut microbiota shifts, including higher Akkermansia and Lactobacillus abundance, indirectly linked probiotic exposure to BDNF upregulation and cognitive improvement. Correlation analysis further associated Akkermansia with short-chain fatty acids and BDNF levels. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, plasma trimethylamine N-oxide was elevated and inversely correlated with BDNF, suggesting a translational link. These results indicate that probiotics may ameliorate cognitive decline by remodeling the gut microbiome and promoting BDNF-dependent synaptic plasticity.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites act as inter-kingdom signals that shape central nervous system immune tone and emotional behavior. In a randomized, double-blind trial of adults with mild depression, we tested whether a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum altered gut microbiota composition, butyrate production, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Participants received either the probiotic or control for 12 weeks; 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR quantified microbial and host markers. Linear mixed models adjusted for baseline depression severity and dietary fiber intake. The probiotic increased Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and upregulated BDNF compared with control. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms. In germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from non-responders, the same probiotic failed to induce BDNF, indicating that baseline microbiome composition gates the response. Our findings support a gut-brain axis mechanism in which probiotic supplementation modifies microbiome metabolism and host BDNF signaling, offering a tractable adjunct for mood disorders.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by a Western-style diet precedes cognitive decline, yet the molecular mediators linking gut microbiota to hippocampal plasticity remain poorly defined. In mice fed a high-fat, low-fiber diet for 16 weeks, we observed reduced Bdnf expression, impaired synaptic density, and elevated lipopolysaccharide translocation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside decreased butyrate production. Supplementation with inulin or Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG restored butyrate levels, normalized Bdnf and Arc expression, and improved memory deficits. Notably, probiotic effects were abolished in GPR43-knockout mice, implicating GPR43 signaling in microbiota-dependent brain function. Our data further showed that inulin increased GPR43 expression in colon. Because processed foods low in fermentable fiber are increasingly common, these results position gut microbiota-directed nutrition as a preventive approach. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics may protect against diet-induced cognitive impairment through short-chain fatty acid-GPR43 pathways, offering a tractable strategy for patients at risk of neurodegenerative disease.

A berry-rich diet supplemented with inulin reshapes the gut-brain axis by expanding Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium in the gut microbiota and raising colonic butyrate. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, we found that propionate and butyrate increased in the colon, while IL-6 and TNF-α declined in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Behavioral testing revealed reduced anxiety-like behavior and improved cognitive flexibility. BDNF expression rose in the dentate gyrus, and fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced these effects. Untargeted metabolomics linked these shifts to bile acids and tryptophan metabolites, and random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium as a top discriminator between responders and nonresponders. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, an ongoing randomized controlled trial is testing whether the same berry-inulin combination modulates gut microbiome composition and cytokine profiles. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-rich foods and targeted prebiotic supplements may act through microbial short-chain fatty acids to influence brain function, offering a plausible adjunctive strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the molecular sensors translating gut microbiota signals into behavioral output remain poorly defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, RNA sequencing, and vagotomy in germ-free mice, we found that Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus repletion increased butyrate production and restored Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. Butyrate suppressed Nfkb1-dependent cytokine transcription in the hippocampus, while interruption of the vagus nerve abolished the anxiolytic effects of colonization. Clostridium-derived tryptophan metabolites acted through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor to limit neuroinflammation. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower fecal Akkermansia abundance correlated with reduced BDNF and elevated C-reactive protein; Spearman correlation linked these changes to anhedonia. Colonization also reduced anxiety-like behavior and normalized corticosterone levels, effects absent in Il10-deficient mice. These findings identify a Akkermansia-butyrate-BDNF axis that may be targeted by probiotics or fermentable fiber to modulate depression-related behavior.

Supplementation with inulin and a polyphenol-rich diet remodels the gut microbiota and reduces neuroinflammation in mice exposed to chronic stress. In an 8-week randomized study, mice receiving inulin plus blueberry powder showed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid in feces, and lower corticosterone than controls. Behavioral testing included open field test and forced swim test. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that microbial composition explained 21% of anxiety-like behavior variance. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia to brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) expression in the hippocampus. Linear mixed models confirmed that inulin and blueberry had additive effects on depressive-like behavior and gut barrier integrity, with interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha reduced in plasma. Serum lipopolysaccharide was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. PERMANOVA and false discovery rate correction confirmed these associations. These data suggest that combining prebiotic fiber with polyphenol-rich foods may target the microbiota-gut-brain axis and mitigate stress-related disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced in the colon can signal to the central nervous system via the vagus nerve, but whether these signals causally modify BDNF expression in the hippocampus remains debated. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and measured butyrate, lipopolysaccharide, and BDNF transcripts after 16S rRNA gene sequencing and RNA sequencing. Using mediation analysis within linear mixed-effects models, we found that F. prausnitzii abundance indirectly reduced neuroinflammation through butyrate, with a significant indirect effect on BDNF (β = 0.34, 95% CI 0.12–0.56). Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with Parkinson's disease into mice reversed these effects, decreasing BDNF and increasing interleukin-6. Dietary inulin partially restored butyrate and BDNF levels. These data suggest that gut microbiota-derived SCFAs modulate BDNF and neuroinflammation through a vagus nerve-dependent pathway, offering a target for neurodegenerative disorders.

Inulin supplementation reshapes the gut microbiome and reduces neuroinflammation after traumatic brain injury (TBI), yet the bacterial taxa and metabolic pathways mediating this effect remain poorly defined. We randomized male C57BL/6 mice to receive inulin or cellulose for four weeks before controlled cortical impact. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of feces revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the colon. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into germ-free mice reproduced the cognitive benefit, whereas inulin alone in antibiotic-treated mice did not. Spearman correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance to brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) expression in the hippocampus and to reduced interleukin-6 (IL-6) in plasma. To test translation, we analyzed adults with mild cognitive impairment from a randomized inulin trial using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium partially explained the association between inulin and Bdnf methylation in blood. These findings identify microbiota-dependent metabolite signaling as a mechanism by which inulin may protect against TBI-associated cognitive decline.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition can modulate central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, and emerging evidence links depression to reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a Mediterranean diet enriched with fermented foods or habitual diet counseling. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing showed that the Mediterranean diet increased Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia and decreased Bacteroides. These shifts correlated with lower IL-6 expression and higher BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Serum short-chain fatty acids increased, while lipopolysaccharide-binding protein declined. Linear mixed models indicated that microbial changes mediated the improvement in depressive symptoms independently of antidepressant use. In a parallel mouse model, fecal transfer from responders recapitulated the BDNF upregulation and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-rich Mediterranean diet patterns may reshape the gut microbiome to support brain health, although larger trials are needed to confirm causality.

Disruption of the gut microbiome during development elevates corticosterone and reduces Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex, yet whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation can reverse these effects remains unclear. We exposed male Sprague-Dawley rats to antibiotics from postnatal day 14 to 21, then assigned them to standard diet or diet enriched with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids for six weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that antibiotics depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and increased Bacteroides. Open field and elevated plus maze tests revealed that omega-3 supplementation normalized anxiety-like behavior. Using mediation analysis, we found that Bdnf expression mediated the relationship between microbial composition and anxiety-like behavior. Omega-3 supplementation also restored BDNF protein levels and reduced neuroinflammatory signaling in the hippocampus. Targeted gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified short-chain fatty acids in feces, and Spearman correlation linked butyrate to Bdnf expression. These findings indicate that dietary omega-3 supplementation buffers antibiotic-induced neuroimmune dysfunction through Bdnf-dependent mechanisms.

Wheat germ fermented with Lactobacillus plantarum produces a functional supplement that can reshape the gut microbiota and attenuate stress-related depression. To test this, mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) received the fermented wheat germ supplement or vehicle for four weeks. Behavioral assays, 16S rRNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics assessed depressive-like behaviors, microbial composition, and short-chain fatty acid profiles. The supplement reduced anxiety-like behavior and anhedonia, increased serotonin and BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and normalized corticosterone levels. It also enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while Spearman correlation analysis linked these taxa to prefrontal cortex dopamine turnover and behavioral recovery. Fecal metagenomic sequencing revealed increased butyrate production and tight junction protein expression in the colon, with reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation and neuroinflammation. The supplement also modulated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and tryptophan metabolism, which are implicated in depression. These findings suggest that fermented wheat germ acts through the gut-brain axis to alleviate stress-induced depression, supporting dietary strategies that target microbial communities.

Alterations in the gut microbiome precede motor onset in Parkinson's disease and may modulate SNCA expression through short-chain fatty acid-mediated enteric nervous system signaling. To test this, we profiled faecal bacteria and neuroactive metabolites in 120 participants, including 60 with idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder and 60 healthy controls. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing quantified microbial composition, while targeted metabolomics measured butyrate, propionate, and p-cresol. We applied causal mediation analysis with bootstrapped confidence intervals to estimate direct and indirect effects of Roseburia and Prevotella on motor severity. Results showed that Roseburia abundance was inversely associated with SNCA expression (β = -0.34, p = 0.008) and that butyrate mediated 28% of this relationship. In contrast, Prevotella correlated with higher LRRK2 expression and worse constipation scores. These findings suggest that gut microbial shifts may influence Parkinson's disease risk via SNCA- and LRRK2-dependent pathways, supporting further Mendelian randomization follow-up in larger, diverse prospective patient cohorts.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids bidirectionally modulate central nervous system function, yet whether this axis drives Parkinson's disease (PD) progression remains contested. Fecal microbiota from PD patients transplanted into α-synuclein-overexpressing mice aggravated motor deficits and neuroinflammation, with reduced BDNF and elevated TLR4 expression in the substantia nigra. We profiled gut microbiota using 16S rRNA sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed significant community separation (R2 = 0.18, P = 0.001), and Spearman correlation linked Prevotellaceae abundance with BDNF transcripts. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were depleted in patients, while probiotic supplementation restored BDNF and attenuated neuroinflammation in mice. Additionally, fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into mice increased GDNF expression and improved motor function. Baseline butyrate concentrations were lower in PD patients than in healthy controls (P = 0.004), and Roseburia abundance inversely correlated with constipation severity. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota–BDNF axis may modify PD trajectories.

Chronic Western diet consumption depletes gut microbiota diversity and exacerbates major depressive disorder through the gut–brain axis. We tested whether a fermented food blend could restore Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and improve depressive-like phenotypes in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress. After 8 weeks, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry showed that the fermented food intervention increased short-chain fatty acids in feces and normalized serotonin and brain-derived neurotrophic factor in the hippocampus. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to reduced neuroinflammation and improved forced swim test performance. PERMANOVA confirmed diet-driven microbiota separation, while linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Bifidobacterium as a biomarker of treatment response. In patients with depression, fermented food intake correlated with higher BDNF expression and lower interleukin-6. These findings suggest that dietary fermented foods may serve as accessible adjuncts for depression by targeting gut microbiota–brain signaling. Body weight and corticosterone levels remained stable throughout the study.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis has emerged as a plausible contributor to neurodevelopmental disorders, yet the microbial signals that shape behavioral symptoms remain poorly defined. In a cohort of children with autism spectrum disorder, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing with untargeted metabolomics to profile fecal microbiota and microbiota-derived metabolites. Reduced Lachnospiraceae and Coprococcus were associated with constipation and total gastrointestinal symptoms, while Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with dietary patterns. A probiotic intervention containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus was then tested in a subset. After 8 weeks, probiotic supplementation increased short-chain fatty acid levels, especially butyrate, and improved GI symptoms scores relative to baseline. Mediation analysis suggested that Coprococcus and butyrate partially explained the association between unbalanced diet and GI symptoms. These findings support a model in which gut microbiota and microbial metabolites mediate gut–brain interactions in ASD. Larger trials with shotgun metagenomic sequencing are needed to confirm whether targeted probiotic strategies can modify ASD symptoms.

Dysregulation of the gut microbiota and its microbiome-derived metabolites is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet the dietary and microbial drivers of this association remain poorly defined. We analyzed adults with depression and healthy controls using shotgun metagenomics and untargeted metabolomics, and assessed habitual intake of fermented foods, Mediterranean diet patterns, and probiotic supplements. Lower microbial diversity and reduced short-chain fatty acid production correlated with higher depressive symptoms. Relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium was lower in patients and inversely associated with inflammatory cytokines in plasma. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial metabolites partially mediated the relationship between fermented food consumption and depression severity, whereas probiotic use was associated with altered gut microbiota composition but not symptom improvement. In mice, dietary tryptophan depletion exacerbated stress-induced behavioral deficits, an effect attenuated by omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation. These findings suggest that diet and microbial supplements modulate gut microbiota signaling through metabolite-dependent pathways, offering targets for depression prevention.

Depletion of gut microbiota by chronic antibiotic exposure exacerbates depressive-like behavior and neuroinflammation, whereas restoration of Lactobacillus reuteri reverses these deficits through tryptophan-derived indole-3-lactic acid signaling. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) exhibited reduced L. reuteri abundance and lower indole-3-lactic acid levels in plasma. In mice, L. reuteri colonization increased indole-3-lactic acid in the colon and hippocampus, attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and normalized BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with MDD into germ-free mice recapitulated these molecular changes, while L. reuteri supplementation rescued them. Notably, AHR deficiency in mice abolished the protective effects of L. reuteri, and chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed reduced AHR binding at the IL-6 promoter. Mediation analysis suggested that indole-3-lactic acid partially mediated the association between L. reuteri and depressive symptoms. These findings position microbial indole metabolites as tractable targets for stress-related disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape central nervous system immune tone, and their depletion correlates with neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. In a randomized trial of adults, daily supplementation with prebiotic inulin and a probiotic increased gut microbiota diversity and butyrate production, while reducing circulating interleukin-6. Participants consuming fermented foods rich in Lactobacillus showed similar shifts, but the effect was attenuated without concurrent fiber supplementation. 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed models linked these changes to improved hippocampal connectivity and lower depression scores. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated the metabolic and behavioral benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion of microbiota abolished them. These findings position dietary fiber and fermented food intake, together with targeted probiotics, as modulators of the gut-brain axis and suggest that microbiome-derived metabolites are promising targets for neuropsychiatric disorders. Additional metagenomic profiling revealed that responders harbored higher butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene abundance, supporting a causal role for microbial butyrate in neuroinflammation attenuation.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids reinforce intestinal barrier function and restrain neuroinflammation via GPR43-dependent signaling in microglia. In mice receiving a probiotic combining Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, gut microbiota composition shifted toward Lactobacillus and Akkermansia enrichment, with increased butyrate in feces and plasma. 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed that probiotic intake elevated BDNF and IL-10 expression while reducing TNF-α and Iba1 in the hippocampus. Behavioral testing showed less anxiety-like behavior and improved memory impairment after probiotic treatment. GPR43 knockout abolished these benefits, indicating that short-chain fatty acids act through GPR43 to modulate microglia and preserve blood-brain barrier integrity. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, a pilot trial of the same probiotic lowered lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and improved cognitive scores. These findings position probiotic supplementation as a tractable strategy for gut-brain axis disorders, although larger trials must confirm whether GPR43 activation is required in humans. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors partially reproduced the GPR43-dependent microglial changes, whereas antibiotic depletion of gut microbiota prevented them.

Depletion of short-chain fatty acids in the colon tracks with nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss and microglial activation in Parkinson's disease (PD), suggesting that gut microbiota remodeling may slow neurodegeneration. To test whether a fermentable fiber alters this axis, male C57BL/6 mice overexpressing A53T α-synuclein received resistant starch (20% w/w) or control chow for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice were combined with behavioral and biochemical assays. Resistant starch increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium, raised butyrate and propionate in the feces, and reduced α-synuclein aggregates in the substantia nigra. Linear mixed models showed that butyrate mediated improvement in striatal dopamine turnover and attenuated motor deficits. Parallel metagenomic sequencing of PD patients and controls revealed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance, supporting translational relevance. These results indicate that resistant starch shapes gut microbiota and microbial metabolites to attenuate PD-like pathology through a gut-brain mechanism.

Microbial colonization status reshapes Bdnf, Gad1, and Grin1 expression in the hippocampus, yet whether these shifts track depression-relevant transcriptional signatures remains unresolved. We compared germ-free mice, germ-free mice colonized with Escherichia coli JM83, specific-pathogen-free mice, and conventionally colonized controls. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and synaptic genes were quantified in the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex using quantitative PCR. Spearman correlation and permutation testing assessed co-expression modules and colonization associations. Germ-free mice showed disrupted synaptic gene networks across all three brain regions; colonization with specific-pathogen-free microbiota normalized 14 of 24 altered transcripts, with hippocampal networks restored. Hippocampal profiles from germ-free mice correlated with post-mortem human depression cohorts (ρ = 0.51), a relationship absent after colonization. These findings indicate that gut microbiota absence disrupts EIB-relevant genes in a region-specific manner, and microbial reconstitution partially reverses transcriptional signatures linked to human depression. Collectively, these data support a causal contribution of the gut microbiome to synaptic gene regulation relevant to depression.

Disruption of gut microbial communities can precede motor and cognitive symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), suggesting that intestinal signals shape brain pathology. Fecal samples from patients with PD and healthy controls were profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium were enriched in patients with PD, whereas Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted. These shifts correlated with reduced butyrate, elevated lipopolysaccharide, and increased calprotectin in plasma; ELISA confirmed zonulin elevation. Expression of SNCA and BDNF in peripheral blood differed by enterotype; SNCA correlated positively with Escherichia-Shigella abundance and negatively with butyrate. A random forest classifier using microbial and host transcriptional features distinguished patients from controls with moderate accuracy. Probiotic supplementation in a subset increased Lactobacillus but did not alter BDNF expression. These findings support a model in which gut dysbiosis promotes PD via short-chain fatty acid depletion and endotoxin exposure, with SNCA and BDNF as potential mediators of the gut-brain axis.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) shape hippocampal function, but whether specific butyrate-producing taxa causally influence cognitive impairment remains uncertain. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from older adults with mild cognitive impairment or cognitively intact controls and assessed memory deficits, neuroinflammation, and gut microbial composition. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae and expanded Bacteroidaceae in impaired mice. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified lower butyrate and propionate in cecal contents. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Agathobacter and Faecalibacterium as discriminative markers, while Spearman correlation linked these taxa to hippocampal BDNF expression. Oral sodium butyrate supplementation restored brain-derived neurotrophic factor signaling, attenuated microglial activation, and improved spatial memory impairment. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice treated with butyrate partially reproduced these benefits in recipient mice. Increased BDNF and ZO-1 transcripts accompanied these changes. These findings position microbial SCFAs as mediators of gut-brain axis signaling and support prebiotic or postbiotic strategies for age-related cognitive decline.

Dysregulation of the gut-brain axis is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the causal contribution of gut microbiota remains contested. We profiled faecal microbiota from patients with MDD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites in serum. Microbial alpha diversity was reduced in MDD, with depletion of Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus and enrichment of Alistipes. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified taxa distinguishing groups. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly mediated the association between Faecalibacterium abundance and BDNF expression. Random forest classification using microbial and metabolic features achieved moderate accuracy. In mice, faecal microbiota transplantation from patients with MDD induced anxiety-like behavior and altered Bdnf and Il6 transcripts in the hippocampus; these changes correlated with C-reactive protein and IL1B. Associations persisted after adjusting for antidepressant use and dietary fiber intake. These findings support a causal role for gut microbiota in depression and suggest butyrate-related pathways as therapeutic targets.

Colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium early in life correlates with reduced stress-related disorders, yet the molecular relays remain incompletely defined. In male C57BL/6 mice, oral Lactobacillus rhamnosus JB-1 for 14 days attenuated chronic restraint stress-induced depressive-like behavior and elevated Bdnf and Gabbr1 expression in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation, we found that the gut microbiota shifted toward Lactobacillus and Akkermansia enrichment, with increased butyrate and serotonin concentrations in the colon and plasma. Quantitative PCR confirmed Fos induction in the vagus nerve, and subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the behavioral benefit. Linear mixed-effects models linked microbial composition to Bdnf transcripts and depression scores. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbial diversity and BDNF methylation predicted response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. These findings position probiotic supplementation as a plausible adjunct for stress-related psychiatric illness, contingent on BDNF-dependent and vagus nerve-mediated gut-brain signaling, and warrant further randomized controlled trials.

Depletion of butyrate-producing Roseburia and Faecalibacterium in the gut microbiome tracks with motor impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating microbial metabolites in nigrostriatal degeneration. To test whether restoring this function modifies disease, Gba1 mutant mice received sodium butyrate in drinking water for eight weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that sodium butyrate increased Lachnospiraceae abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced neuroinflammation in the substantia nigra. Gba1 genotype influenced responses: mutant mice showed lower Tyrosine hydroxylase expression and greater dopaminergic neuron loss than wild-type littermates, but sodium butyrate attenuated these deficits. In patients with PD, lower fecal butyrate correlated with worse constipation and REM sleep behavior disorder clinical severity and longer disease duration. Spearman correlation linked gut microbial composition to motor dysfunction and striatal dopamine turnover. These findings indicate that sodium butyrate can partially rescue PD-relevant pathology through microbiota-dependent and independent routes, supporting gut microbiome modulation as a therapeutic strategy.

Inulin-type fructans combined with fermented dairy can reshape gut microbiota and modulate central nervous system function via the microbiota-gut-brain axis, but their additive effects on mild anxiety remain uncertain. In an 8-week randomized, double-blind trial with placebo control, 72 adults with mild anxiety consumed either inulin (10 g/day) plus kefir or placebo. The kefir contributed live Lactobacillus kefiri. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed models assessed microbial composition and anxiety scores. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids, and reduced anxiety scores compared with placebo (p = 0.01). Fecal propionate correlated inversely with anxiety severity and positively with BDNF plasma levels. Exploratory analysis showed that baseline gut microbial diversity moderated treatment response, with greater anxiety reduction in participants harboring lower Prevotella abundance. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota, propionate administration reproduced the behavioral benefit and increased hippocampal BDNF expression. These findings suggest that combining inulin with kefir may alleviate mild anxiety through microbiota-dependent short-chain fatty acid signalling, supporting dietary approaches for stress-related disorders.

Consumption of fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi may alter gut microbial communities and thereby influence central nervous system signaling. In a randomized crossover trial, healthy adults received either a high-fiber diet enriched with fermented foods or a control diet for six weeks. Fecal samples were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, while short-chain fatty acids and bile acids were quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Brain activity and depressive symptoms were assessed with functional magnetic resonance imaging and validated questionnaires. The fermented food diet increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, and reduced neuroinflammation markers in participants with higher baseline anxiety. These changes correlated with altered amygdala reactivity to emotional faces and improved BDNF expression in peripheral blood. The findings suggest that dietary fermented foods can engage gut microbiota-brain communication through microbial and metabolic pathways, offering a plausible probiotic-independent strategy for mood disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the contribution of microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) to BDNF regulation remains unclear.
