In a randomized, double-blind trial, 60 adults with depression received either a multi-strain probiotic supplement or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and serum SCFAs were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Expression of BDNF and IL6 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells was measured by quantitative PCR. Compared with placebo, the probiotic increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated serum butyrate, and upregulated BDNF expression. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms (Spearman correlation, r = −0.42, p < 0.01). In parallel, mice colonized with microbiota from responders showed increased BDNF in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Our findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may modulate the gut microbiota–BDNF pathway and alleviate depression, supporting further investigation in larger cohorts.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbes can influence central nervous system immune signaling, yet whether these metabolites causally affect Parkinson's disease risk remains contested. We integrated fecal metagenomes from 1,208 participants with plasma metabolomics and transcriptomic profiles from prefrontal cortex. Using Mendelian randomization, we tested bidirectional relationships between Lachnospiraceae abundance, butyrate, and neurodegeneration. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified modules enriched for SNCA, LRRK2, and IL-6. Higher Roseburia was associated with increased butyrate (β = 0.31, p = 4.2 × 10−5) and lower Parkinson's disease odds (OR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.66–0.92). Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate explained 22% of this effect. Sensitivity analyses using inverse-variance weighted regression and MR-Egger yielded consistent estimates, with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy. In mice, butyrate supplementation reduced IL-1β and rescued SNCA-induced motor deficits. These findings support a gut-brain axis pathway in which Roseburia-derived butyrate modulates neuroinflammatory genes, suggesting that targeting microbial communities may lower Parkinson's disease risk.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) derived from gut microbiota fermenting dietary fiber exert causal effects on central nervous system immune tone, and BDNF signaling appears to mediate this axis in depression-like phenotypes. To separate correlation from causation, we applied Mendelian randomization to summary statistics from genome-wide association studies in human populations of gut microbial taxa and major depressive disorder. Genetically predicted abundance of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia was inversely associated with depressive symptoms, whereas Eggerthella showed a positive association. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability and BDNF expression explained 21% and 14% of the total effect, respectively. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with low BDNF levels recapitulated anhedonia and reduced hippocampal neurogenesis; these deficits were attenuated by sodium butyrate supplementation. Additional colocalization and sensitivity analyses supported a unidirectional microbiome-BDNF relationship, although horizontal pleiotropy remained possible. These findings position microbiome-BDNF interactions as tractable targets for neuropsychiatric disorders, though randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm clinical benefit.

Chronic stress-induced disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is associated with reduced hippocampal Bdnf expression and elevated interleukin-6, but whether dietary galacto-oligosaccharide supplementation can reverse these changes remains unclear. We subjected mice to chronic unpredictable mild stress for six weeks and randomized them to receive galacto-oligosaccharides or vehicle. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples, real-time PCR for Bdnf, Gfap, and Il6, gas chromatography–mass spectrometry for short-chain fatty acids, and forced swim test were performed. Supplemented mice showed restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lower corticosterone levels, and increased hippocampal Bdnf transcripts relative to controls. These effects were accompanied by reduced depressive-like behavior, attenuated interleukin-6 signaling, and higher fecal butyrate and propionate. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to Bdnf expression and butyrate concentrations. No changes in body weight or locomotor activity were observed. Together, these data highlight a tractable diet–microbiota–Bdnf pathway. Our findings suggest that galacto-oligosaccharides modulate the gut microbiome and Bdnf-related neuroplasticity, offering a potential nutritional strategy for stress-related mood disorders.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism in the colon shapes central nervous system serotonin availability and may alter anxiety-like behavior. In a randomized mouse study, high-fat diet depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while increasing Clostridiales, changes linked to reduced short-chain fatty acid production. We tested whether inulin supplementation reverses these effects. Gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Using linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis, we found that dietary fiber intake explained 34% of the variance in tryptophan metabolites. Inulin increased Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium, elevated indole-3-propionic acid, and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice. These associations were absent in aryl hydrocarbon receptor-deficient mice, implicating AHR signaling. The findings suggest that fermentable fiber can reshape gut microbiota and neuroactive metabolites, offering a plausible dietary route to modulate gut-brain axis function. However, human trials are needed to confirm causality. Together, these data position microbiome-derived metabolites as mediators of brain function.

Consumption of a Western diet reshapes the gut microbiota and can amplify neuroinflammation, yet the microbial signals that couple dietary fat to cognitive decline remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from adults consuming either a Mediterranean-style diet or a high-fat, high-sucrose diet and assessed hippocampal function after 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that high-fat, high-sucrose diet-associated microbiota was enriched in Bacteroides and depleted in Akkermansia. Morris water maze testing showed longer escape latencies and reduced hippocampal BDNF expression in recipients of the high-fat, high-sucrose diet-associated microbiota. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia abundance inversely with interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in colon. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Mediterranean-style diet-fed donors partially restored microbial diversity and lowered cytokine concentrations, and short-chain fatty acids were reduced in cecum. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbiome remodeling contributes to neuroinflammation and memory impairment, and that dietary fiber or polyphenol interventions may interrupt this gut-brain signaling.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and inulin reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates depressive-like behavior in mice fed a Western diet. In a 12-week randomized human trial, adults with major depressive disorder received omega-3 supplementation plus dietary fiber or a control condition. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, alongside elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition changes explained 31% of the reduction in depression scores, with butyrate showing the strongest indirect effect. Baseline gut microbiota diversity predicted response in linear mixed-effects models. Prefrontal cortex BDNF expression and serotonin turnover increased in the intervention group, while fecal lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 decreased. Fecal calprotectin also fell. These effects were absent in germ-free mice, implicating microbiota-derived metabolites. Collectively, dietary fiber and omega-3 act synergistically through gut microbiota-brain signaling to improve depressive symptoms, offering a tractable target for depression prevention.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with reproducible gut microbiome configurations that precede mild cognitive impairment, but the bacterial taxa and neuroactive metabolites linking diet to brain aging remain unresolved. We recruited 180 older adults and combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and structural MRI. PERMANOVA showed that Mediterranean diet adherence explained 9.4% of microbiota variance. Random forest and multivariable linear regression identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis as enriched in high-adherence participants; both correlated with higher butyrate and thicker entorhinal cortex. Fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling confirmed elevated butyrate, acetate, and propionate, yet only butyrate remained associated after adjustment for dietary fiber. Causal mediation analysis estimated that butyrate mediated 22% of the association between Mediterranean diet and mild cognitive impairment, with APOE ε4 status modifying the indirect effect. Longitudinal cognitive testing over 24 months showed that higher baseline butyrate predicted slower cognitive decline and less hippocampal atrophy. These results position butyrate-producing taxa as plausible targets for diet-based strategies aimed at delaying cognitive decline.

Consumption of dietary fiber reshapes the gut microbiota and may modulate brain function through short-chain fatty acid-dependent signaling. In a randomized crossover trial, 68 adults with mild depression received a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable fiber or a refined-carbohydrate diet as control for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and hippocampal N-acetylaspartate and BDNF methylation were measured. Linear mixed-effects models showed that the fiber-rich diet increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance, elevated circulating butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with control. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate changes accounted for 31% of the improvement in depression scores, with BDNF methylation as a secondary mediator. Baseline microbial diversity moderated the treatment response, with greater butyrate production in high-diversity participants. In mice, fecal transfer from responders recapitulated these behavioral effects, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable mediator of microbiota-brain communication and support causal mediation approaches for dissecting microbial contributions to neuropsychiatric disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) regulate central nervous system immune homeostasis, and their depletion is linked to cognitive decline. In a randomized older adults cohort, daily supplementation with inulin-type fructans plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 12 weeks increased fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and elevated butyrate concentrations versus placebo. Participants consuming a Mediterranean-style diet showed stronger responses, with improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores and reduced interleukin-6 in plasma. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed enrichment of butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase genes in responders, whereas 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing showed no significant between-group differences in overall diversity. Baseline gut microbiota composition stratified participants into responders and non-responders, and linear mixed models confirmed treatment-by-diet interactions. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate availability accounted for 31% of the cognitive improvement. These findings suggest that combining prebiotic fiber with probiotic strains and fermented foods may support gut-brain axis function, although larger trials are needed.

Consumption of a high-fat diet depletes Akkermansia muciniphila and lowers short-chain fatty acid production, changes that correlate with depressive-like behaviors in mice. To determine whether this axis is modifiable, male C57BL/6 mice received a high-fat diet with or without multi-strain probiotic supplementation for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled gut microbiota and serum metabolites, while forced swim test and sucrose preference test assessed depressive-like behaviors. Probiotics restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances, increased butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid, reduced lipopolysaccharide, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Spearman correlation linked butyrate to BDNF, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and BDNF partially mediated the behavioral improvement. Random forest identified A. muciniphila and butyrate as top predictors of treatment response, and probiotic-treated mice showed lower IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the colon. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota composition and fecal butyrate predicted symptom improvement after adjunctive probiotics. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors treated with probiotics reproduced the metabolic and behavioral benefits in recipient mice. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with probiotics may complement dietary fiber–rich interventions for depression.

Fermented foods and dietary fiber reshape the gut microbiota, expanding Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increasing butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids, which attenuate neuroinflammation and support hippocampal plasticity. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo; 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia relative abundance and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Expression of BDNF and APOE in prefrontal cortex was quantified, with BDNF upregulation correlating with improved cognitive scores. Multivariate regression indicated that baseline microbiome composition and APOE genotype explained 42% of the variance in response. In parallel, mice fed a high-fat diet showed depleted Akkermansia and elevated interleukin-6 in hypothalamus, effects reversed by prebiotic oligofructose. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may augment the cognitive benefits of Mediterranean-style diets through microbiota-dependent modulation of BDNF and inflammatory pathways, offering a targeted adjunct for Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Dysregulation of the gut microbiota can precede motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD), but whether microbial shifts drive nigrostriatal degeneration or reflect intestinal inflammation remains unresolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with PD or healthy controls, then used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics to profile colon content and serum metabolites. Random forest classification separated donor groups by Prevotellaceae, Lactobacillaceae, and Akkermansia, while linear mixed models linked short-chain fatty acids to tyrosine hydroxylase expression in the substantia nigra. Recipients of PD microbiota showed reduced butyrate, elevated IL-6, and impaired motor coordination compared with controls. Fecal calprotectin correlated with Enterobacteriaceae abundance and colonic inflammation. Microglial activation was quantified using ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 immunohistochemistry, and permutation testing confirmed group differences. Butyrate supplementation partially rescued neuroinflammation and motor impairment, but did not restore dopamine levels. These findings suggest that gut microbial products modulate PD-like pathology through immune signaling, and that butyrate-targeted postbiotics warrant testing as adjunct therapy.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that shape innate immune maturation and blood-brain barrier integrity, yet whether these microbial signals mediate protection against neurodegeneration conferred by diet remains unresolved. In a randomized controlled trial, 120 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a high-fiber diet or a Western diet for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium and plasma butyrate. Mediation analysis tested whether microbial and metabolite shifts explained changes in BDNF and IL-6. The high-fiber diet increased Akkermansia (log2 fold change 1.8, p=0.003) and butyrate (p=0.011), and reduced IL-6 (p=0.024) relative to the Western diet. Fecal Akkermansia abundance correlated with butyrate (r=0.42, p<0.001) and inversely with IL-6 (r=−0.31, p=0.006). Butyrate mediated 32% of the effect of the high-fiber diet on BDNF (95% CI 14–51%). These findings position SCFAs as tractable mediators linking the gut microbiota to the brain and support fiber-rich diets as adjunctive strategies for cognitive decline.

Dietary inulin supplementation reshapes the gut microbiota and elevates BDNF expression in the hippocampus, an effect that coincides with reduced depression-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress. To test whether this response depends on microbial metabolites, we treated stressed mice with inulin or vehicle for six weeks and profiled fecal communities using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Inulin increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and raised butyrate and propionate concentrations. In the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, inulin suppressed IL-1β, TNF-α, and NLRP3 expression, while restoring BDNF and PSD-95 levels. Fecal <microbiome>microbiota</microbiome> transplantation from inulin-fed donors into naïve mice reproduced the behavioral and molecular changes, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF expression and butyrate to NLRP3 suppression. These findings position inulin as a plausible microbiota-targeted intervention for stress-related mood disorders and implicate BDNF and NLRP3 as mediators of the gut-brain response.

Gut microbiota depletion by chronic high-fat, high-sucrose diet exacerbates neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior, yet whether microbial metabolites directly tune Bdnf transcription in the hippocampus remains unclear. In male C57BL/6 mice, 12 weeks of Western diet reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate and indole-3-propionate, and increased lipopolysaccharide in serum and prefrontal cortex. These changes coincided with elevated Il6, Tnf, and Iba1 transcripts and reduced Bdnf exon IV expression. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Western diet-fed donors into germ-free mice recapitulated working memory deficits and social avoidance. Conversely, galactooligosaccharide plus polydextrose restored Lactobacillus, normalized Bdnf expression, and attenuated stress-induced helplessness. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, baseline fecal microbiome composition correlated with BDNF promoter methylation in blood by Spearman correlation. Mediation analysis linked butyrate availability to Bdnf and behavioral outcomes. These findings position microbiota-derived metabolites as modifiable regulators of Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that fermentable fiber-rich foods may protect against gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Dietary patterns rich in fermentable fiber and polyphenols shape the gut microbiota and may attenuate mild cognitive impairment (MCI) through the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized trial, older adults with MCI received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or combined with probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum. We used 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics to profile microbial communities and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to quantify short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in feces. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbiota composition, SCFA concentrations, and cognitive performance. The combined intervention increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels, with parallel improvements in MCI symptoms. These changes were accompanied by reduced inflammatory cytokines and enriched BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed significantly enriched butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase. Spearman correlations linked butyrate increases to improved delayed recall scores and reduced trimethylamine N-oxide. Our findings suggest that probiotic and fiber-rich dietary strategies may modulate the gut microbiome to support brain health in MCI.

Microbial depletion of dietary fiber reshapes gut microbiota and alters BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a mechanism increasingly implicated in depression and anxiety. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermented foods or fiber supplementation alone. Participants completed 3-day food records; fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor was quantified by ELISA. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and BDNF methylation were measured. Mixed-effects linear regression tested associations between vegetable intake and BDNF methylation. Greater vegetable intake predicted increased butyrate producers and lower BDNF promoter methylation, with mediation analysis indicating that microbial composition explained 31% of the effect on depressive symptoms. Adjustment for age, sex, and baseline BDNF methylation did not attenuate these relationships. These findings suggest that dietary patterns targeting gut microbiota may augment BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity, though Mendelian randomization is needed to confirm causality.

Distinct gut microbiota profiles are associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and emotional dysregulation, yet whether they predict treatment response remains unclear. In a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial, 126 children with ADHD received broad-spectrum multinutrients or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal samples were profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. We used linear mixed-effects models to test associations between microbial diversity, Bifidobacterium, Prevotella, and changes in irritability and attention problems. Higher baseline Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with greater improvement in emotional dysregulation among children receiving multinutrients but not placebo. Taxa within Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcus showed treatment-dependent shifts. Short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa were positively associated with prefrontal cortex-related cognitive symptoms; Prevotella showed an inverse relationship. The observed associations remained after adjustment for baseline symptom severity. These findings suggest that gut microbiome composition may moderate nutritional effects on ADHD symptoms, potentially through microbial metabolites acting along the gut-brain axis. Replication and fecal microbiota transplantation studies are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as key mediators of gut-brain signaling, and their depletion is increasingly linked to neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior. In chronic stress mice, Lactobacillus rhamnosus supplementation restored gut microbiota composition and increased hippocampal expression of BDNF and GABRA1, while reducing IL6 and TNF transcripts. These changes were accompanied by lower corticosterone and higher serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), we found that the behavioral benefits were transmissible to germ-free recipients, but only when donor microbiota was collected after probiotic treatment. Untargeted metabolomics further revealed that Lactobacillus-derived indole-3-lactic acid was enriched and negatively correlated with IL6 expression. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota composition predicted responsiveness to Lactobacillus rhamnosus, and shotgun metagenomics identified Lactobacillus strains whose abundance correlated with BDNF methylation. These findings support a causal gut-brain axis mechanism in which probiotic supplementation and FMT reshape microbiota-derived metabolites to modulate BDNF signaling and affective behavior.

Accumulating evidence positions the gut microbiota as a critical mediator of gut-brain communication, with dietary and microbial interventions capable of modifying depression, anxiety, and neurodegenerative disorders. Adherence to a Mediterranean diet, enriched in fiber, polyphenol-rich vegetables, and olive oil, increases Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production, thereby strengthening intestinal barrier integrity and reducing neuroinflammation. Supplementation with probiotics or omega-3 fatty acids has similarly improved behavioral outcomes in adults and rodent models, although effect sizes vary by strain, dose, and baseline microbial composition. In a randomized controlled trial, multi-strain probiotics combined with a high-fiber diet increased gut microbial diversity and reduced depressive symptoms compared with placebo, an effect associated with elevated BDNF and decreased interleukin-6. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome through dietary patterns and dietary supplements offers a tractable strategy for brain health, yet mechanistic links and long-term safety require further metagenomic and clinical investigation.

Disruption of the gut microbiome contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) through immune and metabolic routes along the gut-brain axis. We compared fecal microbial communities from patients with mild AD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Shannon index and PERMANOVA revealed lower diversity and distinct composition in AD patients. Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium were enriched in cases, whereas Prevotella and Clostridium differed by group. Increased intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation may accelerate neurodegeneration in the hippocampus and other brain regions. Probiotics and prebiotics may modulate these taxa and increase short-chain fatty acids; however, randomized controlled trials in psychiatric disorders remain limited and heterogeneous. One trial reported reduced rehospitalization in patients with acute mania, but no benefit in schizophrenia, while major depressive disorder showed modest improvement. These findings support microbiome-targeted interventions as adjunctive strategies for AD, but larger trials with standardized metagenomic sequencing and validated multivariate models are needed.

Gut microbial depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii tracks with major depressive disorder severity and blunted short-chain fatty acid production, yet whether dietary correction reverses this axis remains unresolved. In a randomized crossover trial, 58 adults with mild-to-moderate depression consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermentable fiber or a Western diet for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metabolomics quantified microbiota and metabolites; RT-qPCR measured BDNF, IL-6, and IL-1β expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The Mediterranean-style diet increased F. prausnitzii abundance, butyrate concentration, and BDNF expression while decreasing IL-6 and IL-1β (all false discovery rate-adjusted p < 0.05). Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the diet-associated reduction in depressive symptoms. Parallel experiments in chronic social defeat mice showed that fiber supplementation restored F. prausnitzii and reduced depressive-like behavior, with effects abolished in IL-6 knockout mice. These findings suggest that dietary fiber reshaping of the gut microbiome may attenuate neuroinflammation through short-chain fatty acid-BDNF signaling.

Higher dietary fiber intake associates with slower cognitive decline, but whether this effect is mediated by specific gut microbiota taxa or by host APOE and BDNF variants is uncertain. In a cohort of older adults, 16S rRNA sequencing and Mendelian randomization were combined with mediation analysis to test causal links among Mediterranean diet adherence, gut microbiota composition, and hippocampal volume. Greater adherence to Mediterranean diet correlated with enrichment of Firmicutes, Akkermansia, and Butyricicoccus, and with higher butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids. These gut microbiota shifts were inversely associated with inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, and positively associated with BDNF expression. Mendelian randomization suggested that Bacteroides abundance and dietary fiber intake exert directional effects on hippocampal integrity, while APOE genotype modified the association. Mediation analysis estimated that Akkermansia and butyrate explained a portion of the protective effect of Mediterranean diet on Alzheimer's disease risk. In mice, fiber supplementation recapitulated these gut microbiota and butyrate changes and improved hippocampal BDNF signaling. These findings position gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids as modifiable mediators linking diet to brain health.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis precedes behavioral symptoms in major depressive disorder, yet the molecular routes linking intestinal microbiota to central nervous system inflammation remain poorly defined. In a chronic stress model, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances fell in parallel with tryptophan depletion and elevated kynurenine in plasma. Probiotic supplementation restored microbial diversity, lowered lipopolysaccharide translocation, and normalized BDNF and IL6 expression in the hippocampus. These changes were accompanied by reduced depressive-like behavior and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor signaling. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, mediated the microbiota-brain relationship; mediation analysis attributed 31% of the behavioral effect to butyrate. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors reproduced the BDNF increase in naive mice, whereas IL6 knockout abolished the effect. In patients, baseline IL6 and BDNF methylation correlated with response to probiotic treatment. These findings position microbial metabolites as modifiable signals and suggest that probiotic interventions may require IL6/BDNF-informed stratification.

Chronic stress-related disorders are accompanied by disrupted gut microbiota and altered hippocampal plasticity, yet dietary strategies that target this axis remain poorly defined. We fed adult male C57BL/6 mice a Western-style high-fat diet or standard chow for 12 weeks and assigned half of each group to a multi-strain probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the high-fat diet reduced Lactobacillus abundance and increased Desulfovibrio, while probiotic treatment restored community composition and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces. In the forced swim test, probiotics decreased depressive-like behavior and normalized BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. These effects were absent in mice receiving the high-fat diet without probiotics, suggesting that microbial correction is required for behavioral benefit. In a parallel cohort, patients with major depressive disorder receiving probiotic alongside selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors showed greater reduction in depression severity than SSRI-only controls. Our findings indicate that probiotic supplementation can buffer diet-induced neuropsychiatric risk through microbiota-brain signaling.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and Lactobacillus abundance are increasingly linked to BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a pathway that may explain how the gut microbiome modulates depression and anxiety. In a randomized mouse model, probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus for six weeks increased serotonin turnover and reduced neuroinflammation. We used 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation to test whether these effects were microbiota-dependent. Linear mixed models showed that probiotics elevated BDNF and TPH1 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex, while Clostridia relative abundance correlated negatively with BDNF. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbial diversity predicted response to omega-3 supplementation, and metagenomic profiling identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a potential mediator. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium with indole-3-lactic acid, and SLC6A4 genotype modified the probiotic response in participants. These findings position probiotics and omega-3 as candidate adjunctive strategies targeting the gut-brain axis, but causal links to BDNF regulation require further validation.

Supplementation with inulin, a fermentable prebiotic fiber, reversed depression-like behaviors in chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mice by reshaping the gut microbiota and elevating short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), we found that inulin enriched Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, increased butyrate in the colon, and normalized BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Mice receiving FMT from inulin-treated donors showed reduced corticosterone and interleukin-6 levels, alongside improved performance in forced swim test and sucrose preference test. Moreover, inulin raised acetic acid and propionic acid concentrations, which correlated with reduced neuroinflammation in the prefrontal cortex. In contrast, inulin did not benefit mice treated with antibiotics, implicating live microbiota as necessary. These results position inulin as a dietary supplement that attenuates depressive symptoms through gut microbiota-brain signaling, and suggest that microbial profiling could guide personalized prebiotic interventions. This effect was abolished in mice that underwent subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, confirming a role for the vagus nerve.

Adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with reduced major depressive disorder risk, yet the microbial and metabolic pathways linking diet to mood remain unresolved. In a randomized, controlled feeding trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fiber, legumes, and olive oil or a habitual Western diet for 12 weeks. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in feces using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Behavioral outcomes were assessed with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and, in parallel, mice colonized with human donor microbiota underwent Morris water maze and tail suspension test. The Mediterranean diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms relative to the Western diet. These changes correlated with BDNF expression in the hippocampus and were partially transferred to mice via fecal microbiota transplantation. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and F. prausnitzii explained a significant fraction of the diet-mood association. Dietary strategies targeting the gut microbiota may complement conventional antidepressant treatment.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism within the gut shapes vagal signaling, microglial activity, and central serotonin synthesis, positioning the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target in stress-related disorders. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 60 adults with major depressive disorder received either multi-strain probiotic supplementation or placebo for 8 weeks while maintaining habitual fermented food intake. Probiotic supplementation increased gut microbial diversity, enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and lowered lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. These shifts correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and altered prefrontal cortex glutamate levels. Mediation analysis indicated that Bifidobacterium abundance partially mediated the effect of probiotics on depression severity. Parallel mouse experiments showed that high-fat diet disrupted microbial composition, while probiotic supplementation restored short-chain fatty acid production and reduced neuroinflammation. Faecal 16S rRNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed that responders had higher baseline Akkermansia abundance and greater bile acid conversion. These effects were independent of antidepressant use. Together, these findings support fermented foods and targeted probiotic supplements as accessible interventions for gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, yet whether dietary probiotics can modify this axis remains unclear. We treated APP/PS1 mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG for 12 weeks and assessed cognition, amyloid-β burden, and cecal microbiota composition. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced Proteobacteria after treatment. PERMANOVA showed distinct community structures between groups, while Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance with lower IL-6 and TNF-α in hippocampus. Probiotic-supplemented mice displayed improved Morris water maze performance and reduced amyloid plaques compared with vehicle-treated controls. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were elevated and inversely associated with IL-1β. Serum lipopolysaccharide was lower in supplemented mice, consistent with improved gut barrier function. Moreover, linear mixed-effects models indicated that treatment effects on amyloid-β were partially mediated by changes in Lactobacillus abundance. These findings suggest that probiotics may attenuate AD-related neuroinflammation through microbiota signaling along the gut-brain axis, supporting further clinical trials in humans.

Microbial colonization of the intestinal tract shapes central nervous system function, and loss of Akkermansia muciniphila has emerged as a reproducible correlate of depressive-like behavior in rodent models. In C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced gut microbiota diversity and depleted Akkermansia muciniphila. Behavioral testing with the open field test, sucrose preference test, and tail suspension test confirmed anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. Cytokine profiling by ELISA showed elevated IL-1β, IL-17A, and MCP-1 in serum and hippocampus. Pearson correlation analysis linked A. muciniphila abundance inversely with 5-HT in hippocampus and with neuroinflammation. RT-qPCR quantified BDNF and HTR2A expression; linear regression adjusted for body weight confirmed these associations. Administration of probiotics or fecal microbiota transplantation restored gut microbial eubiosis, decreased IL-1β, and improved anxiety- and depression-like behaviors. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome to modulate BDNF signaling and serotonin availability in patients with neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate central nervous system immune tone and behavior, yet the taxa and pathways driving these effects remain incompletely resolved. We profiled gut microbiota from adults with mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, complemented by targeted quantification of butyrate and lipopolysaccharide in plasma. Lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance coincided with reduced butyrate and elevated inflammatory cytokines, and these shifts correlated with worse executive function scores. In gnotobiotic mice, colonization with microbiota from patients increased hippocampal Iba1 expression and impaired novel object recognition. Supplementation with butyrate or a fiber-rich diet restored short-chain fatty acid levels, attenuated neuroinflammation, and improved memory. Plasma trimethylamine N-oxide and bile acid profiles did not differ significantly, arguing against a dominant role for these metabolites in this cohort. These findings position microbial butyrate production as a modifiable link between diet and cognitive decline, suggesting that fiber-based or postbiotic strategies merit evaluation in patients.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that signal to the brain via enteroendocrine cells and the vagus nerve. In mice fed a high-fat diet, butyrate supplementation restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced depressive-like behavior, an effect absent in GPR41-knockout mice. Similarly, human subjects consuming fermented milk containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus showed altered fecal microbiome profiles and lower cortisol awakening responses. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic prediction revealed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated inversely with anxiety scores. Mechanistically, SCFAs inhibit histone deacetylases, upregulating GPR43 and GPR41 in intestinal epithelium, which modulates serotonin synthesis and cytokine production. These pathways influence microglia activation and BDNF signaling. Additionally, lipopolysaccharide from gram-negative bacteria triggers inflammatory cytokines that impair BDNF signaling, linking gut dysbiosis to neurodegeneration. Our data suggest that dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome could treat neuropsychiatric disorders. Future work should test fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors to patients in randomized controlled trials, and identify optimal dietary patterns that modulate host gene expression through microbial metabolites.

Higher intake of fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich plant foods is consistently associated with greater gut microbial diversity, enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium taxa, and reduced neuroinflammation; however, the incremental benefit of isolated omega-3 fatty acid supplementation on brain health remains debated. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or a Mediterranean-style diet plus omega-3 capsules. We assessed fecal microbiota via 16S rRNA gene sequencing, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. The combined intervention increased Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate, and improved depressive symptoms and executive dysfunction compared with the Mediterranean-style diet alone. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, suggesting that omega-3 supplementation amplifies diet-induced microbiota shifts and gut–brain signaling. No significant changes in amyloid burden or hippocampal volume were detected, indicating that early benefits may arise from peripheral immune signaling and gut microbiota–brain communication rather than direct neurodegeneration modification. The findings support precision nutrition approaches that pair fiber-rich foods with targeted omega-3 supplementation to modulate gut microbiota–brain communication.

Supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve M-16V and galacto-oligosaccharides altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice, but translation to humans remains uncertain. We tested whether a 12-week synbiotic intervention modulated prefrontal cortex BDNF expression and serum inflammatory cytokines in adults with subclinical depression. Participants received synbiotic or placebo; fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, and linear mixed-effects modeling tested group-by-time interactions. At baseline, lower Faecalibacterium abundance and higher lipopolysaccharide were associated with greater depressive symptom severity. Synbiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6. Changes in Faecalibacterium correlated inversely with BDNF methylation and depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate production and interleukin-6 suppression partly explained the BDNF-related symptom improvement. These findings position synbiotic supplementation as a plausible adjunct for mood disorders, though larger trials are needed. The intervention also increased short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and no serious adverse events occurred. These microbial shifts were independent of fiber intake and antidepressant use. Compliance exceeded 90%.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet predicts lower depression severity, yet the contribution of gut microbiota to this relationship remains unresolved. We randomized 96 adults with major depressive disorder to a 12-week Mediterranean-style diet plus omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation or to a placebo control. At baseline and week 12, participants completed the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and provided stool samples. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing; circulating short-chain fatty acids and BDNF were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations among diet adherence, microbial diversity, and depressive symptoms. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and reduced anhedonia scores compared with placebo. Butyrate concentrations correlated positively with BDNF and inversely with inflammation. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiota composition explained 22% of the clinical improvement. These findings suggest that diet and supplement strategies targeting the gut microbiome may augment antidepressant treatment, though confirmatory trials are needed. The intervention was well tolerated.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone and neurotransmitter synthesis, yet the extent to which dietary fiber intake modifies this relationship through host genetics remains unresolved. In a cohort of adults with irritable bowel syndrome, we integrated fecal microbiota profiles, BDNF rs6265 genotypes, and serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor concentrations. Mediation analysis tested whether Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance linked fiber-rich diet to visceral pain severity. Higher fermentable fiber consumption correlated with greater Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate levels, and lower anxiety scores. The BDNF Met allele attenuated this association, whereas mixed-effects modeling showed that microbial diversity explained 18% of the variance in abdominal pain. Shotgun metagenomics revealed that Roseburia intestinalis and Bacteroides uniformis were depleted in high-symptom participants, while random forest classification separated groups with modest accuracy. In gnotobiotic mice colonized with patient microbiota, inulin supplementation increased serotonin in the hippocampus and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may improve gut-brain axis disorders via BDNF-dependent and microbial pathways, but clinical translation requires randomized controlled trials.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids calibrate signaling within the central nervous system, and their depletion is reproducibly associated with major depressive disorder (MDD). In a 12-week cohort of 184 adults, including 92 patients with MDD, we tested whether a fiber-rich diet modified gut microbiota composition and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed that higher dietary fiber intake correlated with expanded Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, alongside elevated butyrate in feces. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use, each 10-g increase in fiber was associated with a 0.42-unit decrease in depression severity scores and a 12% increase in BDNF mRNA. Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate explained 31% of the diet–mood association. In mice receiving fiber supplementation, butyrate increased Bdnf in the hippocampus and reduced neuroinflammation. Together, these findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal and support targeting microbial butyrate producers in MDD.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans alongside a whole-grain-rich diet reshapes the gut microbiota and improves mild cognitive impairment in older adults. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, 88 participants received a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium breve plus omega-3 fatty acids, with dietary counseling to increase fermented foods and dietary fiber. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundances increased, while Ruminococcus decreased. Plasma short-chain fatty acids and BDNF levels rose, and hippocampal volume loss slowed. Cognitive scores improved by 18% on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Gut microbiome profiling used 16S rRNA gene sequencing; PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures between groups. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that treatment group, baseline microbial diversity, and fiber intake predicted cognitive change. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate increases explained 32% of the cognitive benefit. Plasma lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 decreased, indicating reduced systemic inflammation. Adherence was assessed by food frequency questionnaires. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic and prebiotic supplementation, combined with plant-based foods, may modulate gut microbiota and brain function, slowing age-related cognitive decline.

Dietary fiber intake predicts gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, yet whether this relationship causally influences age-related cognitive decline remains unresolved. We analyzed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics from 184 older adults consuming a Mediterranean-style diet or a low-fiber control diet for 12 weeks. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that dietary fiber increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia abundance, with parallel rises in butyrate and propionate. Higher butyrate correlated with better Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores and lower interleukin-6, while propionate tracked with reduced systemic inflammation. In mice fed a high-fat diet, F. prausnitzii colonization reduced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus, preserved Bdnf expression, and improved Morris water maze performance. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 31% of the fiber-cognition association, whereas PERMANOVA confirmed diet-driven microbiome shifts. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable microbiome substrate that may slow cognitive impairment through SCFA-mediated gut-brain signaling. Together, these data support a causal chain from dietary fiber to F. prausnitzii, butyrate, and protection against cognitive impairment.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota contributes to neuroinflammation and behavioral deficits in depression, yet the causal mediators remain incompletely defined. In a randomized, double-blind trial of 84 adults with major depressive disorder, daily supplementation with a multi-strain probiotic for 8 weeks reduced depressive symptoms, measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, and increased serum short-chain fatty acids compared with placebo. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed enrichment of Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and depletion of Escherichia/Shigella in the gut microbiota of responders. Mediation analysis indicated that BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells partially mediated the relationship between Faecalibacterium abundance and symptom improvement. Spearman correlation further linked butyrate levels to BDNF methylation. Baseline microbial diversity was inversely associated with C-reactive protein, and responders showed lower interleukin-6 than non-responders. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may improve depression through microbiota-BDNF interactions, supporting microbiota-based modulation as a therapeutic strategy. However, larger trials with shotgun metagenomics and longitudinal mixed-effects models are needed to confirm causality and identify responders.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids can shift gut microbiota toward taxa that produce short-chain fatty acids, but whether this shift mediates improvements in major depressive disorder remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either omega-3 or a control condition; fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein was measured in plasma. We applied linear mixed-effects models to test taxon-level changes and mediation analysis to assess whether Bifidobacterium or Lactobacillus abundance explained symptom reduction. Omega-3 increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance (β = 0.42, FDR = 0.03) and decreased Flavonifractor prevalence, while short-chain fatty acid concentrations rose in feces. Depression scores improved more in the omega-3 group, and mediation analysis attributed 18% of the effect to Bifidobacterium change. These findings suggest that omega-3 may act through gut microbiota-derived metabolites to influence brain function, supporting a role for microbiome targets in depression treatment.

Dietary prebiotic fiber intake shapes gut microbiota composition and may modulate central nervous system function through microbial metabolites, yet the extent to which this axis depends on host BDNF signaling remains unclear. In a randomized crossover study of 68 adults with mild depressive symptoms, we compared 6 weeks of a fermentable fiber-enriched diet against a low-fiber control. Shotgun metagenomics profiled the fecal microbiome; plasma short-chain fatty acids, BDNF methylation, and GPR43 expression were quantified using qPCR and mass spectrometry. The fiber intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and reduced depressive symptom severity compared with control. Changes in butyrate correlated with reduced BDNF promoter methylation, increased GPR43 expression, and improved hippocampal connectivity. Mediation analysis suggested that microbiota-derived butyrate partially explained the clinical benefit, with BDNF methylation and GPR43 expression as downstream mediators. These findings support a diet-sensitive gut-brain axis and identify BDNF and GPR43 as candidate mechanistic nodes.

Colonization of the gut by microbes shapes brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet the molecular mediators remain incompletely defined. Gut microbiota ferment dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives that modulate BDNF expression and serotonin availability in the central nervous system. In germ-free mice, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium colonization attenuates anxiety- and depression-like behavior, an effect associated with reduced cortisol and interleukin-6. 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomics in patients with irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder reveal altered microbiota composition and reduced BDNF methylation. Prebiotics, probiotics, and omega-3 supplementation have shown modest symptom improvement in randomized controlled trials, while antibiotics disrupt this equilibrium. A meta-analysis of these trials indicates that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains are most consistently associated with reduced depressive symptoms. These findings position gut microbiota as a tractable target, though mechanistic links between BDNF regulation, short-chain fatty acids, and vagus nerve signaling require further elucidation.

Reduced gut microbiome diversity and depletion of Prevotellaceae precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), but whether these shifts reflect causal gut-brain signaling or secondary neurodegeneration remains contested. We integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and blood RNA sequencing from PD patients, healthy controls, and <gene>α-synuclein</gene>-overexpressing mice. Microbial functional profiles were tested for association with SNCA, BDNF, and TLR4 expression using PERMANOVA and linear mixed-effects models, with correction for age, sex, and levodopa equivalent dose. PD patients showed lower Prevotellaceae and higher Lactobacillus abundance, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and reduced short-chain fatty acids. These microbial shifts correlated with SNCA and TLR4 expression in substantia nigra-enriched pathways and preceded motor deficits in mice. Random forest classification separated PD patients from controls with moderate accuracy. The findings implicate gut microbiota-immune-SNCA interactions in PD pathogenesis and support targeting microbial ecology for early intervention.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans and habitual intake of fermented foods independently alter gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production, yet their interactive effects on age-related cognitive decline are poorly defined. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, older adults with subjective cognitive impairment received inulin (n=42) or maltodextrin (n=40) for 12 weeks while maintaining a fermented food-enriched diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial taxa; gas chromatography-mass spectrometry measured butyrate and propionate. Functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed hippocampal activation during memory encoding, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay quantified plasma interleukin-6 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and elevated butyrate relative to placebo. Fermented food intake correlated with greater microbial diversity and lower interleukin-6. The combined intervention improved hippocampal activation and memory scores compared with placebo, with changes mediated by butyrate and Faecalibacterium. These findings support prebiotic fiber plus fermented foods as a pragmatic strategy for cognitive decline.

Dietary fermented foods and fiber reshape the gut microbiota and its metabolic output, influencing brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and targeted metabolomics, we profiled stool and serum from adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls after a 6-week intervention with fermented milk or a control beverage. Intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, and reduced tryptophan catabolism through the kynurenine pathway. Plasma interleukin-6 and cortisol decreased, while BDNF expression increased. These changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms scores. Baseline gut microbiota composition explained 18% of variance in response, with Faecalibacterium depletion predicting treatment resistance. A random forest classifier distinguished responders from non-responders with an area under the curve of 0.82. These microbial and metabolic shifts were independent of antidepressant use and probiotic supplementation. The findings suggest that fermented foods may act as psychobiotics, but causality and dose-response require further animal and human studies.

Microbial conversion of dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is a central route by which the gut microbiota calibrates brain function, yet the transcriptional mediators that translate this signal into behavioral resilience remain poorly defined. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex in mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress, we found that Lactobacillus-derived indole-3-lactic acid was depleted in susceptible mice and inversely correlated with anhedonia. Butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf expression and normalized Il6 transcripts. A mediation analysis indicated that indole-3-lactic acid accounted for 31% of the protective effect of fermented food intake on depressive-like behavior. Random forest classification identified Akkermansia muciniphila and Tph1 as top predictors of resilience, whereas fluoxetine did not rescue the metabolite deficit. In human cohorts, Mendelian randomization supported a causal link between gut microbiota composition and depression risk. These results position microbial tryptophan metabolites as actionable targets linking diet to BDNF-dependent brain plasticity.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolite production are increasingly linked to central nervous system function and depressive symptoms. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with moderate depression received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a habitual diet control. The intervention also included a multispecies probiotic and omega-3 fatty acid supplement. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial community structure. Mixed-effects models tested changes in Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, while mediation analysis examined whether short-chain fatty acids explained brain-related outcomes. Compared with controls, the active group showed greater reductions in anxiety and depression scores, alongside increased butyrate and BDNF expression. These effects were partially mediated by microbiota shifts. In mice, antibiotic-induced dysbiosis attenuated the behavioral benefits, supporting a causal role for gut microbes. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation may synergize to modulate gut microbiota-brain signaling and improve depressive symptoms.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that modulate brain function, yet the transcriptional routes linking gut microbiota to anxiety remain unclear. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with irritable bowel syndrome or healthy donors and fed them either a high-fiber diet or a low-fiber Western diet. Behavioral testing, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and RNA sequencing of the hippocampus were performed. Dietary fiber increased Bacteroides and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Hippocampal Bdnf and Nrf2 expression was upregulated, whereas Nfkb1 and Tlr4 were suppressed. These effects were absent in mice receiving the Western diet. Fecal butyrate correlated positively with Bdnf and negatively with Tlr4 expression, and mediation analysis attributed 42% of the behavioral variance to butyrate and Lactobacillus. Collectively, these data position microbial butyrate as a tractable mediator of microbiota-brain communication. Our findings indicate that fiber-sensitive gut microbiota signals tune Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity and may inform anxiety interventions.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling. In adults with mild cognitive impairment, baseline gut microbiota composition predicted depressive symptoms and cognitive decline over 12 months. To test whether dietary modulation alters this trajectory, we randomized 120 participants to inulin or a control condition for 12 weeks. Stool 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified microbial taxa and functional pathways. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 were measured as inflammatory markers, while cortisol awakening response indexed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activity. We used linear mixed-effects models to relate microbial features to depression scores and mediation analysis to test indirect effects. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, reduced interleukin-6, and improved depressive symptoms relative to control. Changes in Bifidobacterium partially mediated the effect on depression. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed distinct microbial community structures between arms. These findings support prebiotic fiber as a gut-brain axis intervention, though larger trials are needed.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiota and attenuates stress-induced depressive-like behavior in mice, yet the molecular relay between colon, hippocampus, and behavior remains incompletely defined. We colonized adult C57BL/6 mice with Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fed them a pectin-derived prebiotic or vehicle for six weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed elevated butyrate and propionate in feces. In the hippocampus, RT-qPCR and immunoblotting demonstrated increased Bdnf expression and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations. Forced swim test and sucrose preference test confirmed reduced immobility and increased sucrose preference. Spearman correlation linked Akkermansia abundance to Bdnf transcripts and butyrate levels. Neither Lactobacillus rhamnosus colonization alone nor inulin without microbial colonization reproduced these effects. These findings suggest that dietary prebiotics modulate the gut microbiota and gut-brain axis through microbially derived short-chain fatty acids and Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity, offering a tractable target for stress-related disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) sustain intestinal barrier integrity and modulate brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling in the hippocampus, positioning the gut microbiota as a key regulator of stress-related disorders. In a randomized mouse study, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation were combined with behavioral testing to determine whether inulin supplementation attenuates chronic stress-induced anxiety. Mice receiving inulin showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate levels, and restored BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. In the hippocampus, BDNF and tight junction protein claudin-5 expression were similarly increased, while lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and interleukin-6 were reduced. These changes were accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation and lower corticosterone concentrations. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors partially reproduced the behavioral benefits in recipient mice, whereas antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion abolished them. The findings indicate that inulin promotes resilience to stress through microbiota-dependent SCFA production and BDNF upregulation, supporting dietary fiber as a translational strategy for mood disorders.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii consistently accompany major depressive disorder, suggesting that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) buffer neuroinflammation through BDNF-dependent plasticity in the prefrontal cortex. To test whether this axis is causally modifiable, we conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with subclinical depressive symptoms (n=120), assigning fermentable fiber supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice were used to assess microbial mediation. Mediation analysis tested whether changes in F. prausnitzii abundance and butyrate production explained symptom improvement. Fiber supplementation increased F. prausnitzii (log2FC=1.8, p=0.003) and butyrate (p=0.01), with a 4.2-point reduction in depression scores versus placebo (p=0.02). Mixed-effects models showed that butyrate mediated 31% of the clinical effect. FMT from responders recapitulated behavioral benefits in mice. These findings position dietary fiber as a scalable adjunct for depression, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon shapes BDNF expression and TLR4-dependent neuroinflammation along the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a fermented dairy beverage enriched with Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis or placebo. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and butyrate was quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. BDNF methylation and IL6 expression were measured in peripheral blood by quantitative PCR. Mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial diversity, SCFA levels, and cognitive scores. The fermented dairy beverage increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentration relative to placebo. Higher butyrate correlated with lower IL6 expression and improved executive function scores. No significant change in BDNF methylation emerged. These findings suggest that fermented dairy may modulate gut microbiota-derived butyrate, linking IL6 suppression to cognitive benefits in mild cognitive impairment. Parallel mouse experiments using fecal microbiota transplantation from high-butyrate donors reproduced reduced Tlr4 signaling in the hippocampus.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that shape gut microbiota composition and signal to the brain, yet the microbial taxa linking fiber intake to anxiety-like behavior remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and fecal microbiota transplantation, we profiled mice fed a low-fiber diet or a high-fiber diet for eight weeks. High-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Faecalibacterium abundances, elevated butyrate and propionate in the colon, and reduced corticosterone and interleukin-6 levels. In the hippocampus, high-fiber diet upregulated BDNF and GABRA1 expression and decreased neuroinflammation. Open field and novel object recognition tests revealed fewer anxiety-like behaviors and improved memory. Antibiotic-treated recipient mice receiving high-fiber microbiota showed increased butyrate and reduced anxiety-like behavior, whereas low-fiber microbiota failed to transfer these effects. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium and butyrate partially explained the fiber-associated behavioral changes. These findings suggest that dietary fiber promotes microbiota-gut-brain communication through specific microbial taxa and microbial metabolites, offering a prebiotic strategy for stress-related disorders.

Chronic neuroinflammation in the enteric nervous system and brain can be attenuated by probiotic supplementation, but the responsible microbial signals remain poorly defined. We treated mice with antibiotics to deplete the gut microbiota, then administered Lactobacillus plantarum or inulin for four weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin expanded Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, while L. plantarum colonization correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha expression in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into germ-free mice reproduced lower lipopolysaccharide levels and improved anxiety-like behavior. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed enriched butyrate synthesis genes in the inulin group, and untargeted metabolomics detected elevated short-chain fatty acids in portal blood. In the prefrontal cortex, both interventions increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and decreased ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1) immunoreactivity. Behavioral testing showed that inulin was superior to L. plantarum in reducing depressive-like behavior. These results suggest that prebiotic fiber and Lactobacillus plantarum act through distinct microbiome-dependent pathways to modulate the gut-brain axis.

Microglial responses to gut microbiota-derived metabolites may link dietary fiber intake to Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, a high-fiber diet or inulin supplementation reduced motor deficits and α-synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra, paralleled by altered gut microbiome composition and increased short-chain fatty acid production. Single-cell RNA sequencing of midbrain microglia revealed suppressed pro-inflammatory programs and expanded disease-associated microglial states after prebiotic treatment. These effects required microglia, since CSF1R inhibitor-mediated depletion restored motor impairment despite ongoing prebiotic intake. Notably, SNCA genotype influenced the magnitude of microglial transcriptional remodeling, with transgenic mice showing greater baseline inflammatory signaling than wild-type littermates. Fecal 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing further showed that inulin increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, while decreasing Proteobacteria. Linear discriminant analysis linked these shifts to butyrate and propionate pools. In mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, the protective effects of fiber-rich chow were diminished, suggesting that microbial composition determines responsiveness. These data position microbial short-chain fatty acids as mediators of diet-microglia crosstalk and support prebiotic strategies for PD.

Chronic consumption of a Western diet depletes gut microbiota diversity and impairs plasticity in the hippocampus, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains unclear. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, then fed them either a high-fat diet or a fiber-rich chow for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the probiotic cocktail restored Lactobacillus abundance and increased butyrate production. In the hippocampus, BDNF mRNA expression was 2.3-fold higher in supplemented mice than in controls (P < 0.01, ANOVA). Depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test was reduced by 40%. Additionally, IL-6 and TNF-α levels in serum were lower in the probiotic group, suggesting reduced neuroinflammation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented mice into naive mice recapitulated the BDNF upregulation and behavioral improvements. These findings indicate that probiotic and dietary fiber interventions can modulate the gut-brain axis through BDNF-dependent mechanisms, offering a potential strategy for stress-related disorders.

Alpha-synuclein accumulation in the enteric nervous system can precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), suggesting that gut microbiota-derived signals shape SNCA-linked neuroinflammation. We profiled fecal microbiota from patients with PD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, then transplanted patient-derived microbiota into SNCA-overexpressing mice. PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures, with enriched Lactobacillus and depleted Bacteroides in patients with PD. No between-group differences were detected in GBA or LRRK2 carrier status, and dietary fiber intake did not explain the observed microbiota shifts. Mice receiving PD-associated microbiota showed worsened motor function, reduced dopamine in the striatum, and increased TLR4 expression in the substantia nigra. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations were lower in patients and correlated with SNCA copy number. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors partially restored butyrate levels and attenuated neuroinflammation in mice, but did not reverse levodopa-responsive motor impairment. These findings support a causal role for gut microbiota in SNCA-related PD pathogenesis and suggest that probiotic or prebiotic interventions targeting Lactobacillus and Bacteroides balance warrant clinical testing.

Reduced fecal butyrate and depleted Bifidobacterium abundance accompany visceral hypersensitivity in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), yet whether probiotic supplementation reverses these microbiota-linked gut-brain alterations remains unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with IBS received a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including butyrate, were quantified. Serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were measured. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions after adjustment for baseline microbial diversity and dietary fiber intake. Probiotic treatment increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced abdominal pain severity compared with placebo. These changes coincided with increased BDNF and improved anxiety scores. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly accounted for the probiotic effect on pain. The findings support targeted probiotic strategies for modulating gut microbiota-derived SCFAs and gut-brain signaling in IBS, offering an adjunctive approach.

Dietary fiber fermentation by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids that influence brain function, yet the microbial taxa and circulating mediators linking diet to Alzheimer's disease remain incompletely defined. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics on fecal and serum samples from older adults with mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls. Higher fiber intake was associated with enriched Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, along with increased butyrate and propionate. Participants with MCI showed lower microbial diversity and higher lipopolysaccharide than controls. Butyrate and propionate correlated inversely with interleukin-6 in blood. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the association between F. prausnitzii and cognitive impairment. Random forest classification identified F. prausnitzii as a top predictor of MCI. In mice, fiber supplementation increased butyrate, reduced interleukin-6, and upregulated Bdnf in the hippocampus. These findings indicate that dietary fiber shapes gut microbiota metabolism to produce butyrate, which may protect against cognitive decline through the gut-brain axis.

Disturbances in gut microbial ecology can precede motor and cognitive features of Parkinson's disease, implicating the gut-brain axis in alpha-synucleinopathies. We tested whether a high-fiber diet combined with probiotic supplementation alters fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acid production in patients with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Forty-two participants received either the high-fiber diet plus a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus or the high-fiber diet alone for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and butyrate, respectively. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, levodopa use, and baseline abundance, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons.
