The combined intervention increased Lactobacillus relative abundance and butyrate concentrations compared with the high-fiber diet alone, and these changes correlated inversely with SNCA expression in rectal mucosa. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii shifted modestly. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that dietary fiber plus probiotics may modulate the gut microbiome and microbial metabolite profiles relevant to early Parkinson's disease, supporting larger trials.

Disruption of gut microbial communities by antibiotic exposure predicts anxiety-like behavior in mice, yet the dietary and metabolic mediators remain poorly resolved. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with irritable bowel syndrome or healthy controls and fed them either a low-fiber diet or a high-fiber diet supplemented with inulin. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and short-chain fatty acids. Behavioral testing included open field and marble burying. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for batch and cage effects, while mediation analysis tested whether butyrate linked Lactobacillus abundance to anxiety. The high-fiber diet increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and attenuated Il6 expression in the hippocampus. These effects were abolished by vancomycin. Fecal metabolite profiles distinguished colonized mice by donor status using random forest (AUC = 0.84). The results suggest that dietary fiber shapes gut microbiota-derived metabolites that modulate brain function, offering a tractable target for stress-related disorders.

Microbial conversion of dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is a plausible modifier of neuroinflammation, yet evidence linking gut microbiota, host genetic variation, and cognitive decline remains inconsistent. We analyzed community-dwelling older adults (n=312) using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics. Higher fiber intake was associated with greater Faecalibacterium abundance and higher fecal butyrate. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium explained 23% of the inverse association between fiber and plasma interleukin-6. This effect was modified by BDNF Val66Met and TLR4 rs4986790; carriers of the BDNF Met allele showed weaker butyrate-IL-6 coupling. To test causality, we transplanted fecal microbiota from high responders into germ-free mice; recipient mice showed lower IL-6 in brain and increased Bdnf expression. RNA sequencing of brain tissue revealed enrichment of microglial homeostasis genes, while butyrate supplementation reduced microglial activation and improved memory deficits. These findings support a host genotype-dependent microbiota-SCFA axis that may inform preventive strategies for age-related neurocognitive disorders.

Supplementation with inulin-type fructans reshapes the gut microbiome and raises short-chain fatty acid production, yet whether these changes translate into altered central BDNF signaling remains contested. In a randomized adult cohort, 12 weeks of prebiotic fiber increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, elevated fecal butyrate, and reduced self-reported anxiety scores compared with placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics linked these shifts to microbial genes involved in propionate metabolism. In mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota, hippocampus Bdnf expression and Arc transcripts were higher, while prefrontal cortex interleukin-6 was lower. RNA sequencing revealed enrichment of CREB targets and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant pathways, together with suppressed TLR4 and NF-κB signaling in colon. These findings suggest that prebiotic supplementation may improve stress-related behavior through microbiota-dependent regulation of BDNF, but effects depended on baseline microbial diversity and FTO genotype. Larger longitudinal trials with metagenomic and metabolomic profiling are needed to identify responders.

Gut microbiota composition predicts central serotonin availability and blood-brain barrier permeability, linking dietary fiber intake to depression severity. In a human cohort, shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal microbiota showed that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted in patients with major depressive disorder, whereas Bacteroides species correlated with lipopolysaccharide translocation and higher interleukin-6 levels. Butyrate-producing bacteria were associated with increased butyrate in stool and reduced neuroinflammation. A randomized fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into germ-free mice reproduced the patient metabolic profile and induced anxiety-like behavior, an effect attenuated by probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus. In mice colonized with microbiota from patients, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified tryptophan metabolites in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that fermented foods and prebiotic fiber may modulate the gut-brain axis through short-chain fatty acid-mediated signaling. However, 16S rRNA gene sequencing alone cannot establish causality, and Mendelian randomization is needed to disentangle microbial effects from diet and antidepressant use.

Gut microbiota fermentation of dietary fiber and polyphenols generates short-chain fatty acids and other neuroactive metabolites that shape gut-brain signaling, yet whether probiotic supplementation augments these effects during chronic stress remains uncertain. We randomized 96 adults with subclinical anxiety to a high-fiber diet or the same diet plus a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing showed increased Lactobacillus abundance and microbial diversity only in the supplemented group. qPCR of peripheral blood revealed lower IL6 and higher BDNF expression after supplementation, with parallel reductions in cortisol and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Targeted metabolomics further showed elevated indole-3-propionic acid and serotonin in the supplemented group. Mixed-effects models linked these changes to improved anxiety symptoms, while Spearman correlation associated BDNF expression with microbial diversity. These findings suggest that combining dietary fiber with probiotics may enhance microbiota-gut-brain communication, though confirmatory trials are needed. Further studies in larger cohorts and with longer follow-up are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate BDNF expression and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant defenses, linking gut microbiota composition to depression and cognitive decline. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with metabolic syndrome received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or usual care; 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled fecal microbiota, while qPCR quantified BDNF and Nrf2 transcripts in peripheral blood. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate concentrations, and upregulated BDNF and Nrf2 compared with control (mixed-effects models, p<0.05). These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved cognitive impairment scores. Baseline microbial diversity and plasma SCFA levels moderated the treatment effect, with greater BDNF upregulation in participants harboring higher Bifidobacterium abundance. The findings suggest that fermented foods and fiber act through microbiota-SCFA-BDNF/Nrf2 signaling to support brain health, though fecal metabolomics and animal models are needed to confirm causality and exclude reverse causation.

A four-week course of a multi-strain probiotic increased fecal γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and shifted gut microbial composition in adults with subjective cognitive decline. To determine whether these changes reflected altered microbial neurochemical output, we profiled gut microbiota from 68 participants using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, and quantified GABA, glutamate, and short-chain fatty acids in stool by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed models adjusted for age and sex revealed that probiotic exposure was associated with higher abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, increased GABA production potential, and enrichment of glutamate decarboxylase genes. Butyrate-producing species also expanded, while proinflammatory taxa decreased. Fecal acetylcholine remained unchanged, whereas glutamate concentrations declined. Responders showed greater baseline microbial diversity and higher butyrate levels, and these associations persisted after adjustment for dietary fiber intake. These microbial shifts correlated with better cognitive scores, although the magnitude was modest. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may modulate gut microbiota and GABA metabolism, supporting further trials in larger, diverse populations.

Microbial metabolites generated from dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods act on the brain via immune, endocrine, and vagal routes, but whether host APOE genotype shapes these responses remains poorly defined. We recruited older adults with mild cognitive impairment and profiled gut microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, coupled with fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice. Participants received a probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks; cognition was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and Mediterranean diet adherence was recorded. At baseline and week 12, we collected blood and fecal microbiota samples. Short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate, increased in responders and correlated with Akkermansia abundance. APOE carriers showed weaker microbial shifts but greater improvement in delayed recall. Linear mixed models and PERMANOVA revealed that baseline microbial diversity, fiber intake, and interleukin-6 levels predicted treatment response. These findings suggest that dietary and microbial signals interact with host APOE and BDNF to modulate cognitive decline, supporting precision microbiota-targeted interventions.

Fermentable fiber intake reshapes the gut microbiome toward short-chain fatty acid producers, a shift linked to improved executive function in older adults. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants consuming a Mediterranean-style diet plus inulin supplementation showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila in feces and higher plasma butyrate than controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that responders had enrichment of genes for polysaccharide degradation and reduced systemic lipopolysaccharide. Cognitive testing demonstrated better working memory and faster processing speed; these gains correlated with hippocampal N-acetylaspartate measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into antibiotic-treated mice reproduced the gut microbiota and metabolic shifts and attenuated lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Conversely, germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from non-responders showed no benefit. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and inulin supplementation act through gut microbiota butyrate production to modulate gut-brain immune signaling, offering a plausible strategy for mitigating age-related cognitive decline. Larger trials with metagenomic sequencing and metabolomic profiling are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate BDNF expression and blood-brain barrier integrity, linking gut microbiota composition to depression risk. In adults consuming a Western diet, reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium is accompanied by elevated circulating interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α, whereas fermented foods and prebiotic fiber increase butyrate production and BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics, recent murine and human cohort studies show that probiotic supplementation can attenuate neuroinflammation and improve depressive-like behaviors; however, responses vary with baseline microbial diversity, TRANK1 genotype, and diet adherence. Mechanistically, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila are depleted in major depressive disorder, while a Mediterranean diet enriched in polyphenols and omega-3 fatty acids restores commensal microbiota and lowers lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings suggest that precision nutrition targeting the gut microbiome—particularly fiber- and fermented food-rich patterns—may complement antidepressant therapy, but randomized trials with standardized metagenomic profiling are needed to establish causality.

Microbial butyrate crosses the blood-brain barrier and modulates BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a mechanism linking gut microbiota to major depressive disorder (MDD). To test whether dietary fiber and fermented foods alter this axis, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry on fecal and serum samples from 60 adults with MDD and 30 healthy controls. Baseline gut microbiota composition differed by MDD status, with lower Lachnospiraceae and higher Bacteroides in patients. Participants consuming high fiber showed increased relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, elevated circulating butyrate, and higher BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. Akkermansia muciniphila was inversely associated with depressive symptoms, and serum short-chain fatty acids correlated negatively with depression severity scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber donors into mice reduced anhedonia and restored BDNF signaling. These findings suggest that fermented food and fiber intake may reshape gut microbiota to influence BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, offering a dietary strategy for MDD.

Alterations in gut microbial communities are increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether dietary interventions can reshape brain-gut signaling remains uncertain. We treated chronic restraint stress mice with probiotic supplementation containing Bifidobacterium breve and fructo-oligosaccharides for six weeks and profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the hippocampus. Supplemented mice showed reduced depressive-like behavior, increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, and elevated butyrate and propionate compared with controls. These changes accompanied higher BDNF and lower IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial composition and butyrate partially explained the behavioral effects. Correlation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF transcripts and butyrate levels, while Lactobacillus correlated inversely with IL-6. Our findings indicate that specific synbiotic supplementation may attenuate stress-related depression through microbiota-short-chain fatty acid-brain signaling, supporting further trials in patients.

Microbial colonization of germ-free mice normalizes anxiety-like behavior and BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet the microbiota and host pathways that mediate this effect remain poorly defined. We colonized adult C57BL/6 mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus or complex cecal microbiota and measured serotonin, kynurenine, and cytokine concentrations in the prefrontal cortex and colon. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus abundance correlated with BDNF and GABA receptor transcripts. Quantitative PCR confirmed tight junction protein expression, while fecal microbiota transplantation from colonized donors into antibiotic-treated recipients reproduced the microbiota profile and reduced depressive-like behavior. Using linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation, we found that Lactobacillus relative abundance predicted serotonin turnover (β = 0.42, p = 0.008) and BDNF expression (ρ = 0.51, p = 0.003). Mediation analysis indicated that kynurenine pathway metabolites accounted for 38% of the effect of gut microbiota on anxiety-like behavior. These findings position Lactobacillus and kynurenine as modifiable microbial signals affecting brain function, with implications for stress-related disorders.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether dietary interventions can reverse this circuit remains unclear. In a randomized mouse model of chronic stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, faecal microbiota transplantation, and untargeted metabolomics to track microbial and metabolic shifts along the gut-brain axis. Inulin supplementation, but not high-fat diet, restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances and increased short-chain fatty acids in the colon and hippocampus. These changes coincided with reduced BDNF promoter methylation and lower depressive-like behavior; fluoxetine produced comparable behavioral effects without altering microbial composition. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid mediated the inulin-driven improvement. Notably, baseline gut microbiome profiles from patients with MDD showed similar depletion of Lactobacillus, supporting translational relevance. Our findings indicate that targeted prebiotic supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome and attenuate stress-related neuroinflammation, offering a tractable adjunct for MDD.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids alters gut microbiota composition and reduces depressive-like behavior in mice, yet the bacterial taxa and metabolic pathways that link these effects to brain function remain incompletely resolved. We treated adult mice exposed to chronic corticosterone with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids or vehicle, then profiled communities in feces using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified Akkermansia, Lactobacillus, and Bifidobacterium as enriched after omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, whereas Prevotella and Ruminococcus were depleted. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) confirmed separation of microbial profiles between groups. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, increased in feces and correlated with BDNF expression in the hippocampus. In patients with major depressive disorder, similar microbial shifts have been reported, suggesting that omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids may act through gut microbiota-dependent mechanisms. These findings support targeting gut microbiota as a therapeutic strategy in depression.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to major depressive disorder through immune, endocrine, and neural pathways of the gut-brain axis. To test whether probiotic supplementation modifies this relationship, we conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with depression. Participants received either a multi-strain Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus formulation or placebo. Fecal microbiota profiling was performed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and depressive symptoms were assessed with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Peripheral cytokines and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Baseline microbial diversity and C-reactive protein were also measured. A linear mixed-effects model revealed a significant group-by-time interaction for depressive symptoms (p = 0.014), with greater improvement in the probiotic arm. Mediation analysis indicated that changes in Bifidobacterium abundance partially mediated this effect through reduced interleukin-6. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome as an adjunctive strategy for depression, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of gut-brain signaling, yet their relationship to neuroinflammation in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains poorly defined. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with MDD received omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids plus inulin or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and plasma SCFAs, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) were quantified by ELISA. Linear mixed-effects models tested treatment-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii relative abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced LPS compared with placebo (p < 0.05). These shifts correlated with decreased depressive symptoms and increased BDNF. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 23% of the clinical improvement. Exploratory analyses showed that baseline microbial diversity moderated the treatment effect. The findings support targeting the gut microbiome with dietary supplements to modulate brain function in MDD. These preliminary results warrant larger, adequately powered trials.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet causal mediators remain unresolved. Using two-sample Mendelian randomization combined with 16S rRNA sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and untargeted metabolomics, we examined adults with MDD and matched controls. Higher abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was associated with lower depressive symptoms, and this effect was partly mediated by butyrate. A mediation analysis estimated that butyrate accounted for 31% of this protective association. BDNF expression in prefrontal cortex correlated positively with microbial diversity and butyrate levels, while IL6 and TNF expression showed inverse associations. In mice, dietary supplementation with fermented foods rich in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium increased BDNF, reduced neuroinflammation, and improved depressive-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fermented food-fed mice into antibiotic-treated mice reproduced these benefits, whereas vancomycin abolished them. These findings suggest that fermented food intake may improve MDD-related neuroinflammation through gut microbiota-butyrate-BDNF signaling, offering a tractable target for psychobiotic interventions.

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly linked to microbial dysbiosis along the gut-brain axis, yet whether gut microbiota shifts are causal or consequential remains unresolved. We profiled fecal microbiota from adults with MDD and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in stool. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, antidepressant use, and dietary fiber intake revealed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia abundance and reduced butyrate in patients. These microbial and metabolic differences correlated with depressive symptom severity and inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNF-α). Associations survived Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. In a parallel mouse model of chronic stress, microbiota transplantation from MDD donors induced anhedonia-like behavior and altered BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum partially normalized SCFA profiles and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings support a contributory role for gut microbiota in MDD and suggest that targeted probiotics warrant further randomized controlled trial evaluation.

Higher dietary fiber intake consistently correlates with greater gut microbiota diversity, but whether this relationship causally influences cognitive decline remains contested. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, 120 older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a high-fiber diet (30 g/day from whole grains, legumes, and vegetables) or a calorie-matched control diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that the intervention increased relative abundances of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. Linear mixed models revealed improved hippocampal connectivity on functional MRI and better memory scores in the fiber group. Fiber intake also correlated with elevated butyrate levels in feces. To test causality, we performed fecal microbiota transplantation from human responders into germ-free mice, which recapitulated the cognitive benefits; antibiotic depletion abolished these effects. Furthermore, metagenomic sequencing identified butyrate synthesis genes enriched in responders. These findings suggest that dietary fiber modulates the gut-brain axis via specific bacterial taxa and short-chain fatty acids, offering a potential prebiotic strategy for dementia prevention.

Microbial colonization of the gut during critical developmental windows shapes BDNF signaling in the brain, and disruption of this axis is increasingly linked to depression and anxiety. In a randomized mouse model of chronic unpredictable mild stress, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG supplementation attenuated depressive-like behavior, restored gut microbiota diversity, and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the colon. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, while correlation analysis associated these taxa with BDNF expression and serotonin levels in the hippocampus. To test translational relevance, fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder was transplanted into germ-free mice; recipient mice exhibited reduced BDNF and increased interleukin-6 compared with controls. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reversed these effects and normalized corticosterone levels. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions may modulate the gut microbiome–brain axis through BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a potential adjunctive strategy for stress-related disorders.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) constrain neuroinflammation through vagal and endocrine routes, yet the transcriptional programs linking gut microbiota to central nervous system homeostasis remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and RNA sequencing of hippocampus from germ-free mice colonized with Lactobacillus or Bacteroides, we tested whether microbial butyrate production regulates BDNF and IL-10 expression. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed that Lactobacillus-colonized mice had higher BDNF mRNA and lower TNF expression than Bacteroides-colonized or germ-free controls. Sodium butyrate supplementation recapitulated these effects and increased serotonin turnover in the prefrontal cortex. In participants with major depressive disorder, fecal Faecalibacterium abundance correlated negatively with depressive symptoms and positively with BDNF expression after covariate adjustment. Fecal microbiota transplantation from participants with high Faecalibacterium abundance into antibiotic-treated mice increased BDNF and reduced TNF in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that BDNF expression partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium and depressive symptoms. These effects were abolished by vagotomy, implicating vagal signaling. These findings position butyrate-producing Lactobacillus as modulators of BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that targeting the gut microbiota may attenuate depression-associated neuroinflammation.

Gut microbial community structure predicts emotional behavior through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, yet the taxa and metabolic pathways mediating this influence remain poorly resolved. We recruited 96 adults with major depressive disorder and 96 healthy controls, collecting fecal and serum samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and targeted metabolomics. Bacteroides uniformis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were depleted in patients, whereas short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives correlated with symptom severity. Using random forest, PERMANOVA, and linear mixed-effects models, we found that butyrate availability explained 18% of the association between gut microbiota composition and depression scores, with mediation analysis supporting a causal pathway. These microbial shifts were independent of antidepressant use and dietary fiber intake. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into mice induced anxiety-like behavior and reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus; these effects were attenuated by butyrate supplementation. Our results identify a microbiome-butyrate-BDNF axis that may be targeted for depression.

Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus restores gut microbial diversity and lowers lipopolysaccharide translocation in mice exposed to chronic stress, yet its impact on patients with major depressive disorder is uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind trial, 74 adults received either the probiotic formulation or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was change in depression severity. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified fecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids. Functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain responses to emotional faces, while mixed-effects models tested associations with depressive symptoms and interleukin-6 expression. The probiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. These changes correlated with decreased anhedonia scores and normalized amygdala reactivity. Notably, microbial shifts preceded clinical improvement, suggesting a causal role for microbial metabolites in gut-brain signaling. Our findings indicate that probiotic supplementation may alleviate depression through microbiota-derived butyrate and reduced neuroinflammation.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes motor deficits in Parkinson's disease and tracks with diminished short-chain fatty acid output. We profiled fecal microbiota and metabolites in patients, healthy controls, and α-synuclein-overexpressing mice using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics; dietary fiber intake was recorded. PERMANOVA and Spearman correlation analysis tested community and metabolite-clinical associations. Patients exhibited lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, higher Enterobacteriaceae, and reduced butyrate compared with controls. Lipopolysaccharide was elevated and correlated with intestinal barrier dysfunction and SNCA expression in substantia nigra. Fiber intake correlated positively with butyrate and inversely with neuroinflammation. F. prausnitzii abundance also tracked with trimethylamine N-oxide and GPR109A expression in colon. Baseline constipation severity predicted cognitive decline at 24 months, and bile acid profiles differed by Prevotella abundance. Longitudinal sampling revealed that calprotectin and IL-6 declined after levodopa initiation. These findings position gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids as modifiable mediators of Parkinson's disease progression and support fiber-enriched interventions.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate vagal signaling and microglial reactivity, linking intestinal ecology to affective behavior. In a randomized, double-blind trial of 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, daily supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids plus a multi-strain probiotic for 12 weeks reduced depression severity relative to placebo, an effect accompanied by increased gut microbiota alpha diversity and elevated fecal Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Participants also completed a fermented food frequency questionnaire; higher intake strengthened the intervention's association with reduced neuroinflammation. We used linear mixed-effects modeling and mediation analysis to test whether changes in gut microbiota composition explained clinical improvement. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that responders showed greater abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and enrichment of microbial genes involved in butyrate production. Expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells correlated positively with butyrate levels and inversely with depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that combining omega-3 supplementation with fermented foods may promote gut-brain axis resilience, though confirmatory studies in larger human cohorts are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by antibiotics in mice impairs hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression and exacerbates depressive-like behavior, implicating microbial signals in stress-related disorders. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), we showed that microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder transferred to germ-free mice recapitulated anhedonia and neuroinflammation, whereas microbiota from healthy controls did not. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances correlated inversely with interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. TLR2 and NLRP3 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex were elevated in recipients of depression-associated microbiota, and this was accompanied by reduced BDNF and PSD-95 expression. Dietary probiotic supplementation restored BDNF, normalized IL-6, and reduced depressive-like behavior, an effect dependent on aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable regulator of brain function and suggest that microbial profiling may guide stratified therapies for depression. Collectively, these data reveal a AHR-dependent axis through which commensal microbial communities tune central nervous system immune homeostasis.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain dialogue is increasingly implicated in depression and anxiety, yet the microbial signals that bridge intestinal and central nervous system compartments remain incompletely defined. In mice exposed to chronic corticosterone, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations, and altered tryptophan–kynurenine metabolism. PERMANOVA confirmed diet-dependent shifts in microbial community structure, while Spearman correlation and random forest analyses linked indole derivatives to depressive-like behavior and hippocampal BDNF expression. In parallel, serotonin turnover and gamma-aminobutyric acid levels in the prefrontal cortex correlated with Faecalibacterium abundance, suggesting that multiple microbiota-derived metabolites converge on limbic circuits. Dietary supplementation with probiotics and prebiotics restored short-chain fatty acid production, normalized kynurenine pathway activity, and attenuated neuroinflammation; effects were abolished by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy. These findings position psychobiotics as candidate adjuncts for stress-related disorders, although human trials are needed to confirm causality and dose-response relationships.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids can reshape the gut microbiota and modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet whether these changes mediate mood improvement in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain. We randomized 84 adults with MDD to 12 weeks of omega-3 supplementation or placebo. Stool samples were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF promoter methylation in peripheral blood was quantified using bisulfite pyrosequencing. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations among Bifidobacterium abundance, short-chain fatty acid concentrations, BDNF methylation, and depressive symptoms. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate levels, decreased BDNF promoter methylation, and reduced depressive symptoms relative to placebo. Baseline gut microbiota diversity did not predict response, whereas lower Bifidobacterium abundance was associated with greater BDNF methylation decreases. Mediation analysis suggested that Bifidobacterium-related butyrate production partially accounted for epigenetic BDNF changes and clinical improvement. These findings link omega-3 supplementation, gut microbial composition, and BDNF regulation in MDD, supporting strategies targeting the gut microbiota for mood disorders.

Dietary inulin supplementation increases Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and butyrate production, an effect associated with reduced depressive-like behavior in mice. To test whether this gut microbiota shift causally modulates hippocampus-dependent function, adult mice received inulin or cellulose for six weeks, followed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, RNA sequencing, and behavioral testing. Inulin-fed mice showed higher Bdnf and Gpr43 expression in the prefrontal cortex and lower interleukin-6 concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate levels explained 42% of the effect of inulin on Bdnf expression, while PERMANOVA confirmed diet-driven separation of microbial communities. Parallel fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into antibiotic-treated mice recapitulated the Bdnf increase and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α in the colon. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance correlated inversely with anhedonia severity, and gut microbiome composition predicted depression improvement with an area under the curve of 0.78 using random forest. These findings suggest that inulin may improve depression-related phenotypes through microbiota-butyrate-BDNF signaling, though clinical cohorts are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and tryptophan metabolites are increasingly recognized as mediators of gut microbiota–brain communication, yet their causal contribution to stress-related psychiatric disorders remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation in chronic unpredictable mild stress mice, we tested whether Bifidobacterium breve supplementation could reverse depressive-like behavior and normalize BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Bifidobacterium breve reduced immobility in the forced swim test, restored gut microbial diversity, and elevated butyrate and propionate in feces. These changes coincided with increased BDNF and glucocorticoid receptor transcripts and decreased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in the hippocampus. Untargeted metabolomics further revealed altered microbial tryptophan catabolism, including reduced indole-3-acetate, which negatively correlated with hippocampal BDNF. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate levels explained part of the behavioral effect, while microbiota composition correlated with BDNF expression. These findings suggest that Bifidobacterium breve may buffer stress-induced mood dysfunction through microbiota-SCFA-BDNF signaling, supporting targeted probiotic interventions for depression.

Consumption of a Western-style diet consistently shifts gut microbiota toward Bacteroides-dominant communities and reduces Akkermansia muciniphila, a pattern linked to low-grade inflammation and major depressive disorder (MDD). In patients with MDD, shotgun metagenomics and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging reveal coordinated changes in prefrontal cortex connectivity and fecal microbiome composition. We hypothesized that short-chain fatty acids mediate this axis via BDNF and TLR4 signaling. Using causal mediation analysis in a cohort of 180 participants, we found that Lactobacillus abundance indirectly reduced hippocampal BDNF expression through butyrate (indirect effect β = 0.21, 95% CI 0.08–0.34). Fiber-rich foods attenuated this association, whereas selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors did not. In a validation cohort, random forest classification separated cases from controls with an AUC of 0.84, driven by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and TLR4. Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and lower depression severity. Probiotic supplementation in mice reproduced the BDNF increase and normalized lipopolysaccharide-induced TLR4 activation; these effects were partially reversed by fluoxetine. These findings position diet-responsive microbiota and BDNF-TLR4 signaling as tractable targets for MDD.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the gut shapes hippocampal plasticity and depressive-like behavior, yet whether probiotic supplementation can reverse stress-induced cognitive impairment remains uncertain. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and random forest classification, we profiled gut microbiota in mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress and in adults with major depressive disorder. Stressed mice displayed reduced Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower butyrate levels. Probiotic treatment with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored butyrate, normalized BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, and attenuated anhedonia and spatial memory deficits. Dietary fiber and inulin enriched Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, whereas fluoxetine produced distinct microbiome shifts without altering butyrate. In patients, baseline gut microbiota composition correlated with depression severity, and mediation analysis implicated butyrate as a potential mediator. These findings position probiotic interventions as plausible modulators of the microbiota-gut-brain axis, although studies in patients are needed to confirm causality in stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes and possibly promotes depressive-like behavior through vagal, immune, and endocrine signaling, yet the taxonomic mediators and host BDNF-dependent pathways remain poorly resolved. We profiled fecal microbiota from 142 adults with varying major depressive disorder severity using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. PERMANOVA revealed that overall community composition explained 11.4% of variance in depression scores (p=0.002), independent of age, sex, and antidepressant use. Random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Coprococcus eutactus, and Prevotella copri as top discriminators; F. prausnitzii abundance correlated negatively with anxiety severity (ρ=-0.34) and positively with plasma short-chain fatty acids. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila was depleted in participants reporting childhood trauma and tracked with gamma-aminobutyric acid levels. In a subset, mediation analysis suggested that BDNF methylation in whole blood partially mediated the association between F. prausnitzii and depressive symptoms. These findings position F. prausnitzii as a candidate gut-brain axis modulator and support targeting prebiotic fiber or probiotic strains to alter BDNF-related epigenetic tone, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF expression and serotonin synthesis, a gut-brain pathway implicated in major depressive disorder. We randomized 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depression to probiotic supplementation (Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium) or placebo for 8 weeks. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and fecal butyrate was quantified by gas chromatography. Mixed-effects models showed that probiotics increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations relative to placebo. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and higher BDNF methylation in peripheral blood. Participants reporting higher baseline fiber intake showed stronger butyrate responses. In a parallel mouse model, fecal microbiota transplantation from treated mice reproduced the butyrate increase and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Baseline fruit and vegetable consumption modified the treatment effect. Our findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with adequate fiber intake may engage BDNF-related epigenetic mechanisms to improve depression, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Inulin can shift gut microbial composition toward Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus enrichment, a response linked to reduced neuroinflammation and improved depressive symptoms in rodent models, but evidence in humans remains sparse. We conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with major depressive disorder who received either inulin (n=42) or placebo (n=41). Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and plasma interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Relative to placebo, inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6; linear mixed models revealed that Bifidobacterium change was inversely associated with depressive symptom severity and positively associated with BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Fecal short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate, also increased in the inulin group, and zonulin levels declined, suggesting reduced intestinal permeability. Inulin was well tolerated. These data suggest that inulin may engage the gut microbiota-brain axis through anti-inflammatory and neurotrophic pathways, warranting larger trials in mood disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production shapes gut microbiome–brain communication, but whether dietary inulin can rescue stress-induced BDNF downregulation in the hippocampus is unclear. We randomized adult male C57BL/6 mice to control, chronic corticosterone, or corticosterone plus inulin for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of cecal microbiota showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance. Quantitative RT-PCR revealed that inulin normalized BDNF, TrkB, and IL-6 expression in the hippocampus. Western blot confirmed increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor protein. Untargeted metabolomics linked these effects to elevated butyrate and propionate. Behavioral testing using the forced swim test and novel object recognition showed reduced depressive-like behavior and improved memory. Spearman's rank correlation linked butyrate concentrations with BDNF expression and Bifidobacterium abundance. Finally, fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors to naive mice partially reproduced the BDNF and behavioral changes. These findings suggest that inulin may ameliorate stress-related neuropsychiatric symptoms by modulating gut microbiota and BDNF signaling in the brain.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids during mild cognitive impairment may attenuate neuroinflammation through gut microbiota-dependent pathways, yet whether host APOE genotype modifies this response remains unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind clinical trial, older adults carrying APOE ε4 or APOE ε3 received omega-3 or placebo for 24 weeks. Fecal microbiota profiling by 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma short-chain fatty acid quantification were performed at baseline and endpoint. Omega-3 increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and reduced Escherichia in APOE ε3 carriers, accompanied by less cognitive decline and lower plasma interleukin-6. In APOE ε4 carriers, no significant microbiota shift occurred. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate mediated the association between Bifidobacterium and reduced memory impairment. In APP/PS1 transgenic mice, omega-3 restored Akkermansia abundance and lowered amyloid-beta in the hippocampus, but only in APOE3-targeted mice. These findings indicate that omega-3 benefits depend on APOE genotype and gut microbiota modulation, supporting personalized interventions for Alzheimer's disease prevention.

Microbial colonization of the gut during infancy shapes BDNF expression and stress reactivity, yet whether probiotic supplementation can reverse dysbiosis-associated behavioral deficits remains uncertain. In a double-blind trial, 120 adults with irritable bowel syndrome and subclinical anxiety received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and serum cortisol, interleukin-6, and BDNF methylation were quantified. Stool short-chain fatty acids were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons, and mediation analysis explored whether Bifidobacterium abundance mediated clinical improvement. Probiotic supplementation increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced cortisol awakening responses compared with placebo. These changes coincided with decreased anxiety scores and altered BDNF promoter methylation in participants with high baseline inflammation. No significant shifts occurred in Faecalibacterium or Bacteroides. The findings suggest that probiotic-induced microbial remodeling may modulate BDNF-related plasticity and stress-related symptoms, though effects appear stratified by baseline immune activation.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as signaling molecules at the gut-brain interface, and their depletion has been linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety-like behavior. In mice exposed to chronic stress, high-fat diet reduced gut microbiota diversity, decreased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, and lowered butyrate concentrations. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into mice recapitulated these metabolic shifts and increased neuroinflammation. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline body weight revealed that butyrate levels inversely correlated with BDNF expression in the hippocampus and positively correlated with TLR4 signaling. Probiotic supplementation restored microbial composition, elevated BDNF, and reduced depressive-like behavior. Notably, Mantel tests confirmed that microbial community structure was associated with SCFA profiles independently of TLR4 genotype, while amplicon sequencing revealed depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in patients with depression. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota-derived SCFAs may provide a therapeutic strategy for mood disorders, though antidepressant effects and BDNF polymorphisms require further validation.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition consistently precede or accompany depression, anxiety, and Parkinson's disease, yet the dietary levers that translate microbial signals into brain function remain incompletely defined. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms consumed either a Mediterranean-style diet rich in fermented foods and dietary fiber or a habitual control diet for 8 weeks. We profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, and cortisol. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline microbial diversity showed that the intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate concentrations, and reduced depressive symptoms relative to control. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-lactate explained 31% of the symptom improvement, with parallel decreases in IL-6. In mice receiving microbiota from responders, hippocampal BDNF expression rose and anxiety-like behavior fell. These findings position fermented foods and fiber as accessible modulators of the gut-brain axis and support targeted dietary strategies for mood disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly recognized as a modifier of Alzheimer's disease progression, with APOE4 carriers showing distinct microbial signatures and elevated short-chain fatty acid fermentation deficits. In a cohort of older adults, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed that high-fat, low-fiber diets reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, while fermented foods and probiotics increased butyrate-producing taxa. APP/PS1 mice receiving multi-strain probiotics showed improved Morris water maze performance and reduced amyloid pathology in the hippocampus; these effects were accompanied by normalized AKT/GSK-3β phosphorylation and lower interleukin-6. Mediation analysis suggested that short-chain fatty acids partially link microbial composition to cognitive outcomes. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients into gnotobiotic mice reproduced cognitive impairment and altered BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, strengthening causal inference. These findings support dietary and microbial interventions targeting the gut-brain axis as candidate strategies for neurodegenerative disease, though clinical trials in patients with standardized metagenomic and metabolomic readouts are needed.

Disruption of the gut microbiome during early life alters BDNF signaling in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, a pathway increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. In rodent models of chronic stress, reductions in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium coincide with elevated corticosterone, decreased BDNF expression, and behavioral despair. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors to germ-free recipients reproduces these phenotypes, whereas probiotic supplementation restores microbial diversity and normalizes BDNF transcription. Similarly, omega-3 fatty acids and prebiotic fibers modulate gut microbiota composition and reduce depressive symptoms in patients. These findings suggest that the gut microbiota regulates BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity through short-chain fatty acids, cytokines, and vagal signaling, and that dietary and microbial interventions may complement conventional antidepressants. However, heterogeneity in 16S rRNA sequencing and meta-analysis limits causal inference. Standardized clinical trials are needed to identify which patients benefit from microbiota-targeted supplements. Host BDNF polymorphisms, particularly Val66Met, may moderate clinical response to probiotics.

Enteric EphB6 signaling constrains colorectal cancer progression by limiting GABA release from intestinal neurons, yet whether this pathway is modulated by gut microbiota remains unclear. We colonized EphB6-deficient mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fed them a probiotic formulation for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed-effects modeling were used to assess microbial composition, tumor burden, and EphB6 expression. Probiotic supplementation reduced tumor growth, lowered GABA concentrations in the tumor microenvironment, and restored EphB6-dependent synaptosomal-associated protein 25 expression in the myenteric plexus. Mediation analysis indicated that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids accounted for 42% of the effect. Fecal microbiota transplantation from treated mice into germ-free mice recapitulated the protective phenotype, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. In patients with colorectal cancer, low EphB6 expression correlated with reduced Lactobacillus abundance and worse survival. Collectively, these findings suggest that probiotics may act through EphB6-GABA signaling in the gut-brain axis to suppress colorectal cancer.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, and dietary approaches that restore microbial homeostasis may attenuate these processes. In a mouse model of high-fat diet-induced cognitive impairment, 12-week probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium breve and Lactobacillus rhamnosus reduced hippocampal expression of NLRP3 and interleukin-1β, while increasing brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed higher abundances of Akkermansia and Lactobacillus in treated animals. Spearman correlation analysis linked fecal microbial composition with SCFA levels, lipopolysaccharide concentrations, and behavioral scores. Behavioral testing using the Morris water maze confirmed improved spatial memory in probiotic-treated mice and reduced glial fibrillary acidic protein immunoreactivity in the hippocampus. Probiotic-treated animals also showed reduced intestinal barrier permeability and lower serum lipopolysaccharide. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation modulates the gut microbiota to suppress NLRP3-dependent neuroinflammation, offering a potential dietary intervention for age-related cognitive disorders.

Dietary patterns rich in plant-based foods, fermented foods, and fiber are consistently associated with lower risk of depression and anxiety, whereas ultra-processed foods and saturated fats correlate with heightened neuroinflammation and cognitive decline. These associations persist across adults and older adults. The gut microbiota mediates this relationship through short-chain fatty acid production, tryptophan metabolism, and vagus nerve signaling, influencing BDNF expression and serotonin availability in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with depression induces anxiety-like behavior, while Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium supplementation attenuates stress-related pathology. Random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials shows that probiotic interventions modestly reduce depressive symptoms, though effect sizes vary by baseline microbial diversity. Mediation analysis further indicates that fiber intake explains 18% of the association between Mediterranean-style diet adherence and improved affective symptoms. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial ecology through diet modification offers a tractable strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders, but causality and optimal regimens remain unresolved.

Metabolism of dietary tryptophan by gut microbiota in the gastrointestinal tract yields indole derivatives that act on enterochromaffin cells and the vagus nerve, providing a direct route for gut microbiota to influence brain function. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gnotobiotic colonization in mice, we found that Clostridium sporogenes and Lactobacillus rhamnosus differentially regulate tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) expression in the colon. Colonization with Clostridium sporogenes increased serotonin turnover and 5-hydroxytryptamine availability, while Lactobacillus rhamnosus elevated γ-aminobutyric acid and reduced anxiety behavior. Denervation of the vagus nerve abolished these neurochemical effects, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from high-indole-producing donors restored them. In patients with irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder, gut microbiome composition correlated with symptom severity. Interventions using probiotics or SSRIs altered these pathways, suggesting that targeting TPH1 and AADC may complement existing therapies. These findings position gut microbiota metabolism as a modifiable node linking diet to neuropsychiatric disorders.

Reduced gut microbiome diversity and depletion of butyrate-producing bacteria precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating the gut-brain axis in neurodegeneration. In a human cohort, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and linear mixed-effects models revealed that dietary fiber intake was inversely associated with neuroinflammatory cytokines; this relationship was partially mediated by butyrate. Butyrate promoted BDNF expression and suppressed IL-6 and TNF transcription in mouse striatum. Mendelian randomization supported a causal effect of gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids on PD risk. In germ-free mice, colonization with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii elevated butyrate in the colon and decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation across the intestinal barrier, reducing neuroinflammation in the substantia nigra. Fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with PD into mice recapitulated motor deficits, whereas sodium butyrate attenuated them. In mice overexpressing SNCA, probiotic supplementation and fermented food diets restored Lactobacillus abundance, reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation, and improved motor performance; levodopa-induced dyskinesia was unchanged. These findings suggest that targeting microbial metabolites through fiber-rich foods may complement dopaminergic therapy in PD.

Alterations in the gut microbiome can precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease by years, implicating gut bacteria in alpha-synucleinopathy within the enteric nervous system and brain. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics of fecal samples from patients and healthy controls, we found reduced abundance of Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia and enriched Enterobacteriaceae in Parkinson's disease. These shifts correlated with short-chain fatty acid depletion, increased lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, and altered expression of SNCA and TREM2 in the brain. Multivariable regression linked Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia to worse motor severity and cognitive impairment. Fecal microbiota transplantation into mice overexpressing SNCA exacerbated motor deficits and neuroinflammation, while levodopa response was associated with Bifidobacterium abundance. Longitudinal sampling revealed that microbial instability preceded disease progression, with butyrate producers declining as constipation and REM sleep behavior disorder emerged. Our findings suggest that gut microbial composition and function may serve as a noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target in Parkinson's disease.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber can reshape central nervous system signaling by modulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus. In a randomized adult trial, 12-week supplementation with inulin-type fructans plus Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis increased gut microbiota diversity and fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations relative to placebo. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, alongside reduced Ruminococcus gnavus. These shifts correlated with lower depressive symptom scores and improved cognitive flexibility; linear mixed-effects models showed that changes in Faecalibacterium abundance explained 18% of the variance in BDNF methylation. Butyrate exposure in murine enterochromaffin cells enhanced tryptophan hydroxylase 1 transcription and serotonin release, an effect abolished by vagotomy. The findings position targeted prebiotic and probiotic interventions as plausible modulators of the microbiota-gut-brain axis, though clinical benefit requires confirmation across larger, longer trials. Baseline microbial composition and metabolic syndrome status modified treatment response, with stronger effects in participants carrying lower Prevotella abundance.

Altered gut microbiota composition and diminished short-chain fatty acid output are increasingly linked to Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether dietary substrates can shift this axis remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind trial, patients with PD and constipation received resistant starch (n=32) or placebo (n=30). Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial taxa and butyrate. At baseline, gut microbiota composition did not differ between groups, and random forest classification separated post-treatment samples with moderate accuracy. PERMANOVA revealed distinct community structures after supplementation (R2=0.14, p=0.002), with increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia. Linear mixed-effects models showed that butyrate increases correlated with reduced constipation severity, lower inflammatory cytokine levels, and improved motor symptoms. BDNF expression in peripheral blood also rose, while mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated the effect on constipation. Changes in Roseburia abundance were inversely associated with calprotectin. These findings indicate that resistant starch may modulate gut microbiota-brain communication in PD, supporting larger trials of prebiotic fiber.

Altered gut microbiota precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease and correlates with SNCA expression in colonic mucosa. We profiled fecal microbiota from 96 patients and 80 controls using 16S rRNA sequencing, then quantified short-chain fatty acids and neuroinflammation-related IL-6, TNF, and NLRP3 transcripts. Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae were depleted in cases, whereas Bifidobacterium and Verrucomicrobiaceae were enriched. Lower butyrate concentrations tracked with higher SNCA and NLRP3 expression and worse constipation severity. Multivariate linear regression linked Prevotellaceae depletion to SNCA expression independently of age and sex. In germ-free mice colonized with patient-derived microbiota, SNCA expression and neuroinflammation increased, while butyrate supplementation reversed these changes. In a 12-week open-label extension, probiotic plus prebiotic fiber increased butyrate, reduced IL-6 expression, and improved gastrointestinal symptoms; omega-3 fatty acids showed additive effects on NLRP3 suppression. These findings link microbial composition to SNCA-associated inflammatory pathways and support microbiota-directed supplementation as a candidate adjunct in Parkinson's disease.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with higher gut microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms, but whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation amplifies these effects when added to a whole-food Mediterranean diet remains unclear. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 128 adults with mild-to-moderate depression received either omega-3 supplementation or placebo while all consumed a Mediterranean-style diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; circulating short-chain fatty acids, interleukin-6, and docosahexaenoic acid were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions. Omega-3 supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, raised docosahexaenoic acid, and reduced interleukin-6 relative to placebo. Both groups improved depressive symptoms and anxiety, but the omega-3 arm showed greater reductions in depression severity and higher BDNF expression. Benefits were largest among participants with low baseline microbial diversity and high dietary fiber intake. These findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation plus a whole-food Mediterranean diet may synergistically target gut-brain pathways, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Probiotic supplementation can reverse stress-induced shifts in gut microbiota and BDNF expression, yet the bacterial signals linking these changes to depression remain poorly defined. In adult male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic restraint stress, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (1×10^9 CFU) for 4 weeks reduced anxiety-like behavior and anhedonia relative to vehicle, as assessed by open-field test and sucrose preference test. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that stress depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while enriching Alistipes; probiotic treatment partially restored these taxa. In the hippocampus, L. rhamnosus GG increased Bdnf and Nr3c1 mRNA and decreased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α concentrations. Colonic Tjp1 and Ocln expression also increased, consistent with improved intestinal barrier integrity. Plasma corticosterone was lower in supplemented mice, and Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance with Bdnf expression. These findings suggest that L. rhamnosus GG buffers stress-related neuroinflammation and supports BDNF-dependent plasticity through the gut microbiota-brain axis, highlighting a need for validation in humans.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that shape microglial function and neurogenesis, yet how specific diets and supplements converge on BDNF signaling remains unclear. We fed adult male C57BL/6J mice either a refined high-sucrose diet or an isocaloric control for 12 weeks; a third group received the refined diet plus a probiotic and fructo-oligosaccharides. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that the refined diet reduced gut microbiota diversity, depleted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and lowered butyrate in the colon. These shifts accompanied increased anxiety-like behavior, elevated IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus, and decreased Bdnf and Gfap expression. Supplementation reversed several deficits: it restored microbial community structure, raised butyrate, normalized IL-6, and upregulated Bdnf without altering Gfap. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance to Bdnf transcript levels. These findings suggest that probiotic and prebiotic supplementation can partially buffer diet-driven neuroinflammation and support BDNF-dependent plasticity along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber is increasingly linked to prefrontal cortex and hippocampal function, but whether targeted probiotic supplementation amplifies these effects in adults with mild cognitive impairment remains uncertain. In a double-blind, controlled trial, participants received either a multi-strain probiotic or a control condition for 12 weeks while maintaining their usual diets. Gut microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and tryptophan metabolites were quantified in serum. Cognitive performance and depressive symptoms were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances increased in the probiotic group, accompanied by higher indole-3-lactic acid and lower kynurenine levels. These changes correlated with improved attention scores and reduced depressive symptoms and improved hippocampal-dependent memory using linear mixed models. In germ-free mice colonized with post-intervention microbiota, similar benefits were observed, with increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation interacts with diet to modulate gut-brain signaling. These results support a causal role for gut microbiota in cognitive decline and warrant further trials combining probiotics with fiber-rich foods.

Dietary patterns that shape the gut microbiota can alter brain function and emotional behavior, yet the microbial signals and host pathways that mediate these effects remain incompletely defined. In a randomized trial, adult participants consumed either a fiber-rich Mediterranean-style diet or a Western diet for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; PERMANOVA revealed diet-dependent clustering, and linear mixed-effects models identified microbial taxa associated with depressive symptoms. The fiber-rich diet increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and raised fecal butyrate. Higher butyrate correlated with lower anxiety scores and increased BDNF expression in peripheral blood. In mice, transplantation of microbiota from human donors fed the fiber-rich diet reduced neuroinflammation and enhanced BDNF signaling in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary fiber promotes gut microbiota capable of producing short-chain fatty acids, which may support brain health and reduce mood disorders. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained part of the diet-behavior association.

Dysregulation of the gut microbiome along the gastrointestinal tract is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder through short-chain fatty acid-mediated and tryptophan metabolic routes. Preclinical models indicate that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains can alter gamma-aminobutyric acid and serotonin signaling, but evidence in humans remains limited. In a double-blind trial, 84 adults with depression received either Bifidobacterium breve plus inulin or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium abundance, plasma kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, and BDNF expression were measured before and after intervention. We used linear mixed-effects modeling with false-discovery-rate correction to test group × time interactions, adjusting for baseline serotonin metabolites. Compared with placebo, the synbiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium (log2 fold change 1.42), reduced kynurenine/tryptophan ratio (β = −0.31, P = 0.008), and elevated BDNF mRNA (β = 0.27, P = 0.021). Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated inversely with depressive symptom severity (r = −0.38, P = 0.004). No serious adverse events occurred; adherence exceeded 90%. These findings suggest that probiotic-prebiotic strategies may modulate gut microbiota-brain signaling and warrant larger trials. If replicated, these data support targeting the gut microbiome with dietary supplements as an adjunctive approach in depression.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota along the gut-brain axis can amplify neuroinflammation and impair BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, a mechanism increasingly linked to depression. In male C57BL/6J mice subjected to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS), inulin supplementation attenuated depressive-like behavior and restored gut microbiota composition, including increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that stress reduced microbial diversity, whereas inulin enriched taxa capable of producing short-chain fatty acids. Using quantitative PCR and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, we found that inulin normalized BDNF, TLR4, and IL-6 expression and reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced microglial activation in the dentate gyrus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated mice into naïve recipients partially reproduced these benefits, including lower neuroinflammatory tone and improved stress resilience. Forced swimming test and sucrose preference test confirmed that recipients showed reduced immobility and greater sucrose preference after inulin-associated microbiota transfer. These results suggest that inulin shapes the gut microbiome to modulate BDNF-related plasticity and microglial function, offering a potential adjunct for depression.

Wild blueberry supplementation can reshape gut microbiota and improve age-related cognitive decline, yet the microbial and neurotrophic mediators linking this food to memory remain unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, older adults with mild cognitive impairment consumed wild blueberry powder or placebo daily for 12 weeks. The intervention was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia and decreased Clostridium after wild blueberry. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed enhanced hippocampal activation during memory retrieval. Fecal short-chain fatty acid profiling demonstrated higher butyrate and propionate concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that Akkermansia abundance and hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor partially mediated the relationship between wild blueberry intake and improved verbal memory scores. Exploratory Spearman correlation linked increased Akkermansia with delayed recall scores and reduced interleukin-6 in serum. These findings suggest that wild blueberry exerts neurocognitive benefits through a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF pathway, supporting dietary strategies for dementia prevention.

Microbiota-derived butyrate suppresses neuroinflammation and depression-like behavior through BDNF-dependent signaling in the hippocampus, but whether this axis is sufficient to reverse colitis-associated cognitive impairment remains unclear. Male C57BL/6 mice received inulin or vancomycin for 6 weeks, followed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut microbiota, RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex, and behavioral testing. Linear mixed-effects models with Benjamini-Hochberg correction showed that Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus reuteri were enriched by inulin and negatively correlated with interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in serum. BDNF and NLRP3 expression in the hippocampus tracked with butyrate concentrations. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 38% of the effect of Akkermansia muciniphila on depressive-like behavior. In a parallel cohort of 42 adults with major depressive disorder, fecal Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was lower than in healthy controls and inversely associated with IL6 and TNF expression in whole blood (Spearman correlation). These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a modifiable regulator of BDNF and NLRP3 signaling in the brain, with implications for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Depletion of butyrate-producing gut bacteria, particularly Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Coprococcus, is consistently observed in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), yet whether this loss is causal or compensatory remains unresolved. We profiled gut microbiome composition and fecal short-chain fatty acids in 118 adults, alongside RNA sequencing of peripheral blood and shotgun metagenomics. Using Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis, we found that genetically predicted Roseburia abundance was inversely associated with depression severity, with butyrate mediating 31% of the effect. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index confirmed that lower butyrate correlated with elevated IL6 and TNF expression and reduced BDNF expression. Higher dietary fiber intake was associated with greater butyrate production, independent of antidepressant use. In mice subjected to chronic stress, butyrate supplementation normalized hippocampal Bdnf transcripts and decreased proinflammatory cytokines. These findings position microbial butyrate as a mechanistic link between gut microbiota and MDD, and they support butyrate-yielding interventions as candidate adjunctive strategies for patients with depression.

Gut microbial short-chain fatty acid production and hippocampal plasticity are increasingly linked to depression and anxiety. We tested whether a multi-strain probiotic combined with a fermented food diet would reshape the gut microbiota and reduce stress-related behaviors in mice. Adult male C57BL/6 mice received either Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG plus kefir, or vehicle, for 6 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified taxa enriched by treatment. Probiotic-kefir supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, reduced Desulfovibrio, and elevated butyrate in feces. Treated mice showed lower immobility in the forced swim test and greater BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. These changes were accompanied by reduced interleukin-6, corticosterone, and lipopolysaccharide. Spearman correlation linked Lactobacillus abundance with BDNF and butyrate. No changes in body weight or locomotor activity occurred. Our findings indicate that combining probiotics with fermented foods may buffer stress-induced mood dysfunction through microbiota-immune-brain signaling.
