Dietary fiber and fermented foods reshape the gut microbiome and its short-chain fatty acid output, with downstream effects on hippocampus-dependent plasticity and age-related cognitive decline. To test whether these dietary signals causally influence brain function, we analyzed stool and serum from 120 older adults enrolled in a 12-week randomized trial comparing a high-fiber diet with usual care. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing quantified Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry measured butyrate, acetate, and propionate. Participants receiving the high-fiber diet showed increased butyrate and improved verbal memory; changes correlated with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance. Associations between butyrate and memory were tested using linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for age, sex, education, and baseline cognition. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into gnotobiotic mice reproduced butyrate elevation and reduced neuroinflammation, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished these effects. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal and support microbiota-targeted strategies for cognitive decline.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids or probiotics reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in depression, yet the mediating microbial signals remain poorly resolved. In a randomized mouse model fed a Western diet, we tested whether Bifidobacterium breve and curcumin reverse stress-induced behavioral deficits. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Western diet depleted Lactobacillus and Akkermansia, while supplementation enriched Bifidobacterium and increased short-chain fatty acids in colon. PERMANOVA and random forest identified Bifidobacterium abundance as a top predictor of BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Morris water maze and forced swim test showed improved spatial memory and reduced immobility. Serum IL-6 and TNF-α decreased, whereas serotonin increased. Moreover, mediation analysis suggested that short-chain fatty acids partially mediated the effects of supplementation on BDNF. In patients with major depressive disorder, baseline gut microbiota profiles mirrored those of mice, suggesting translational relevance. These findings indicate that omega-3 and probiotic interventions may correct diet-induced dysbiosis and modulate the gut-brain axis, but clinical validation requires longitudinal sampling.

Chronic stress disrupts the gut microbiota and plasticity in the hippocampus, yet the mechanisms linking microbial metabolites to visceral pain remain unclear. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled male C57BL/6J mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress with or without probiotic supplementation. Stress reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lowered butyrate in the colon, and increased Bdnf promoter methylation in the hippocampus. RNA sequencing of the prefrontal cortex further revealed downregulation of Nrf2 and Bdnf and upregulation of Nfkb1. Mediation analysis showed that butyrate explained 38% of the effect of microbiota on Bdnf expression. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors recapitulated these changes, while minocycline attenuated neuroinflammation and restored Bdnf transcription. These effects were absent in germ-free mice colonized with Bifidobacterium alone. Together, these data position butyrate-producing Lactobacillus as a tractable node for stress-related disorders and support microbiota-targeted interventions. These findings suggest that gut microbial short-chain fatty acid production modulates Bdnf signaling via the vagus nerve.

Gut microbiota composition is increasingly linked to central nervous system function, yet whether specific microbial strains causally influence neuropsychiatric disorders remains contested. We profiled faecal microbiota from adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, then integrated host transcriptomics from peripheral blood. Producers of short-chain fatty acids, including Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, were depleted in cases and correlated inversely with IL6 and TNF expression. A weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified an inflammatory module linked to Bacteroides abundance. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability partially mediated the association between Faecalibacterium and depressive symptoms. In a separate Mendelian randomization framework, genetically predicted Bifidobacterium abundance was associated with lower depression risk, although pleiotropy checks were limited. These findings support a model in which gut microbiota affects brain function through microbial metabolites and regulation of immune genes, but they also highlight the need for longitudinal sampling and causal inference to distinguish biomarkers from mediators.

Greater consumption of fermented foods tracks with higher gut microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms, yet the molecular mediators remain uncertain. In a 12-week randomized crossover trial, 84 adults with mild depression received either a fermented food-rich diet or a high-fiber diet. Stool Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance was quantified by 16S rRNA sequencing; plasma short-chain fatty acids and BDNF promoter methylation were measured at baseline and week 12. The fermented food-rich diet increased microbial diversity and Lactobacillus relative abundance, raised plasma butyrate, and reduced BDNF promoter methylation compared with the high-fiber diet. These shifts correlated with improved depressive symptoms and higher serum BDNF concentrations. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate accounted for 31% of the effect of fermented food intake on BDNF methylation. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings link fermented food consumption, gut microbiota, and BDNF regulation in the gut-brain axis, supporting dietary strategies for mood disorders in this randomized trial.

Consumption of polyphenol-rich foods such as blueberries and dark chocolate has been linked to improved cognitive function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We conducted a 12-week study in participants (n=120) assigned to either a high-polyphenol diet or a control diet. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that the intervention group exhibited a significant increase in Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance (p<0.01) compared to controls. Concurrently, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels in serum were elevated, and cognitive decline was attenuated as measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Mediation analysis indicated that the effect of the high-polyphenol diet on cognition was partially mediated by changes in gut microbiota (p=0.03). The observed microbial shifts also correlated with improved scores on the Mini-Mental State Examination (r=0.42, p=0.008). These findings suggest that dietary polyphenols may modulate the gut microbiota and offer a therapeutic strategy for MCI. However, larger trials are needed to confirm long-term benefits.

Chronic gut dysbiosis precedes cognitive decline, yet the microbial signals that impinge on plasticity in the hippocampus remain poorly defined. In APP/PS1 mice, inulin-type fructans restored gut microbial diversity, increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus reuteri, and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Behavioral testing showed improved spatial memory and reduced amyloid pathology. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics linked these benefits to short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, and to suppressed NF-κB signaling in the colon and brain. BDNF expression increased in the hippocampus, paralleling reduced IL-1β and TNF-α transcripts. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-fed donors into germ-free mice recapitulated the BDNF upregulation and cognitive benefits. In a parallel human cohort, baseline fecal microbiota composition correlated with APOE genotype and mild cognitive impairment after adjustment for age and sex. These findings indicate that inulin-type fructans act through a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis to attenuate neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's disease-related phenotypes. Random forest modeling identified Akkermansia abundance and butyrate as top predictors of cognitive outcomes.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with higher gut microbiota diversity and lower systemic inflammation, yet whether this relationship modifies neurodegenerative disease progression remains unresolved. In a cross-sectional cohort of people with multiple sclerosis, we combined dietary scoring with 16S rRNA gene sequencing of stool samples and measured circulating short-chain fatty acids. Participants reporting regular use of probiotic supplements showed enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium genera, but no significant change in Shannon diversity. Higher Mediterranean diet scores correlated inversely with disability scores and fatigue, independent of age, sex, and disease duration. Fecal butyrate concentrations were lower in patients than in healthy controls and associated with increased neuroinflammation markers. These findings suggest that Mediterranean diet-associated microbial shifts, potentially reinforced by probiotic supplementation, may influence central nervous system outcomes through microbial metabolites. Longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to determine causality and to test whether dietary and prebiotic strategies can be translated into clinical benefit.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and bile acids modulate BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, and their depletion accompanies depression and cognitive decline. To test whether restoring gut microbial communities reverses these effects, adults with mild-to-moderate anxiety received a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis or placebo for 10 weeks in a randomized controlled trial. Fecal microbiomes were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF, NR3C1, and IL1B expression was measured in mice that received participant microbiota via fecal microbiota transplantation. Supplementation increased microbial diversity, elevated butyrate and gamma-aminobutyric acid concentrations, and reduced Enterobacteriaceae abundance. Mice colonized with post-supplement microbiota showed lower anxiety-like behavior, higher hippocampal BDNF expression, and reduced IL1B and NR3C1 expression compared with mice receiving pre-supplement microbiota. Plasma cortisol awakening response decreased in the probiotic arm, and microbial production of secondary bile acids correlated inversely with anxiety scores. These results suggest that probiotic supplementation remodels the gut microbiome and modulates BDNF- and NR3C1-dependent stress pathways, offering a potential adjunct for stress-related mood disorders.

Gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate central nervous system inflammation and behavior, yet the taxa and pathways responsible remain unresolved. Using shotgun metagenomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls, we found that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia were depleted in MDD and correlated inversely with interleukin-6. PERMANOVA revealed diet-driven community separation, with high-fat, low-fiber diets associated with lower butyrate production. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with MDD induced depressive-like behavior, reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus, and altered gut microbiota composition. Butyrate supplementation reversed these effects, while fluoxetine only partially restored Bdnf and did not normalize microbiota. Mediation analysis suggested that microbial butyrate production mediates the relationship between diet quality and depressive symptoms. These results position gut microbial metabolism as a modifiable target and support dietary and microbial interventions for stress-related disorders.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract shapes central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and disruptions in this gut microbiota-brain dialogue are increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). In a randomized adult cohort, daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 supplementation for eight weeks reduced depressive symptoms and altered fecal microbial composition. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR of the 16S rRNA gene revealed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, alongside decreased Proteobacteria. Functional magnetic resonance imaging showed attenuated amygdala reactivity to negative affective stimuli and stronger prefrontal cortex-amygdala connectivity. Serum interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein concentrations declined, while brain-derived neurotrophic factor rose. No significant changes in Akkermansia or Clostridium were observed, and mediation analysis suggested that interleukin-6 reduction partially explained the amygdala response. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions can modulate the gut microbiome and brain circuits relevant to MDD, though larger trials with multivariable modeling are needed to confirm durability and causality.

Daily probiotic supplementation combined with a high-fiber diet reshapes gut microbiota and reduces neuroinflammation in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. We conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 120 participants, comparing a multi-strain probiotic plus fermented foods against placebo. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in feces. Linear mixed models showed that SCFA levels correlated with improved executive function scores (r = 0.42, P = 0.003) and reduced depression ratings. Furthermore, functional magnetic resonance imaging indicated enhanced connectivity in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. BDNF expression in peripheral blood was upregulated, and GDNF expression increased. The supplementation group also showed reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and improved anxiety scores compared to placebo. Our findings suggest that combining probiotics with dietary fiber may serve as a therapeutic strategy for cognitive decline by modulating the gut microbiota in this study.

Consumption of a high-fat, low-fiber diet reshapes the gut microbiota and dampens short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, a metabolic shift linked to anxiety-like behavior and impaired Bdnf signaling in the hippocampus. In mice fed fiber-depleted chow for 8 weeks, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, paralleling lower butyrate levels in feces and serum. These changes coincided with increased depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test and reduced Bdnf expression in the prefrontal cortex. Supplementation with sodium butyrate restored Bdnf expression and normalized behavior, whereas antibiotic depletion of gut bacteria abolished the protective effect of fermentable fiber. In adults with major depressive disorder, lower dietary fiber intake correlated with reduced SCFA producers and altered BDNF methylation in blood. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate availability explained part of the association between fiber intake and BDNF expression. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable substrate for microbiota-BDNF interactions that influence mood disorders.

Higher intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber is associated with lower neuroinflammation and better cognition in older adults, but whether targeted supplementation can reproduce these benefits remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 92 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either inulin plus a probiotic containing Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis or placebo while continuing their usual diets. Gut microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified in stool. The active group showed greater microbial diversity, enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and higher fecal butyrate than placebo. These shifts coincided with reduced circulating interleukin-6 and improved memory and attention. Using linear mixed-effects models, changes in gut microbiota correlated with butyrate increases and cognitive gains. The findings suggest that inulin combined with probiotic supplementation, alongside fermented food consumption, may modulate gut microbial signaling and support cognition in mild cognitive impairment. These results warrant larger trials.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary substrates can modulate brain function and emotional behavior, but whether ordinary fermented foods outperform isolated probiotic supplements for improving depressive symptoms is unclear. We randomized 84 adults with mild-to-moderate depression to a 10-week fermented food-enriched intervention or a daily probiotic supplement. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives were quantified. Both interventions increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, yet only the fermented food group showed greater microbial diversity and higher butyrate levels. Changes in gut microbiota composition were assessed using PERMANOVA, and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified taxa discriminating responders from non-responders. Mixed-effects models revealed that butyrate increases correlated with reduced depressive symptoms and lower IL6 expression. Bifidobacterium abundance mediated the association between fermented food intake and symptom improvement. The fermented food group also reported greater consumption of yogurt, kefir, and kimchi. These findings suggest that dietary fermented foods may provide broader microbiome-targeted benefits than probiotic supplements alone, supporting nutritional approaches for depression management.

Supplementing omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids alongside a fermentable fiber-rich diet reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates neuroinflammation in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. In an 8-week randomized crossover study, 64 participants received either the active diet plus omega-3 supplementation or the diet alone. Adherence exceeded 90%, and no serious adverse events occurred. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia muciniphila relative abundance, raised fecal butyrate and propionate, and lowered lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations mirrored these taxonomic shifts. These microbial shifts correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in plasma, and with improved hippocampal connectivity on functional magnetic resonance imaging. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed upregulated BDNF and PPARGC1A expression and downregulated TLR4 and NFKB1 transcripts. Mixed-effects models indicated that butyrate mediated 28% of the cognitive improvement, independent of baseline microbiota diversity. The findings suggest that combining omega-3 supplementation with a fiber-rich diet may engage microbiota-dependent BDNF signaling to support brain health, though confirmatory human trials are needed.

Depleted gut microbiota diversity and reduced short-chain fatty acid production are increasingly linked to mild cognitive impairment, yet whether dietary co-intervention can modify this axis remains uncertain. We enrolled 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment in a 12-week randomized trial comparing omega-3 fatty acid supplementation plus a fiber-rich diet against control. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal microbiota and quantitative PCR for BDNF expression in peripheral blood were performed at baseline and endpoint. Linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. The active group showed increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, elevated butyrate concentrations, and higher BDNF expression than control. Changes in F. prausnitzii correlated with BDNF increases. Baseline gut microbiota composition moderated the treatment effect, with greater BDNF increases in participants harboring higher F. prausnitzii abundance. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that combining omega-3 fatty acid supplementation with a fiber-rich diet may engage gut microbiota-brain signaling and support BDNF-related plasticity in mild cognitive impairment. Larger trials are warranted.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids has been proposed to reduce major depressive disorder severity through gut microbiota-dependent pathways, yet the microbial mediators remain poorly defined. To test this, we conducted a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial in 84 adults with major depressive disorder. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. After 12 weeks, omega-3 increased the relative abundance of Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae and elevated fecal butyrate compared with placebo. These microbial shifts correlated with lower depressive symptoms and reduced circulating interleukin-6. Effects were independent of baseline antidepressant use. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium partly explained the clinical improvement, whereas baseline gut microbiota diversity did not predict response. No serious adverse events occurred. Our findings support targeting gut microbiota with omega-3 as an adjunctive strategy for major depressive disorder, though confirmatory trials with longer follow-up and direct fecal microbiota transplantation are needed.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG supplementation raises BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduces depressive-like behaviour in chronic stress-exposed mice, yet the microbial and transcriptional intermediaries remain contested. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Escherichia coli, administered the probiotic, and profiled serotonin, GABA, short-chain fatty acids, and cytokines in the colon, plasma, and prefrontal cortex. 16S rRNA sequencing and RNA sequencing revealed that L. rhamnosus GG expanded Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, increased butyrate and indole-3-lactate, and normalized BDNF, GABAA receptor, and serotonin transporter transcripts. Mediation analysis linked butyrate to BDNF and anxiety-like behaviour, whereas indole-3-lactate tracked with aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling. In mice lacking BDNF, the behavioural benefit was abolished despite equivalent gut microbiome remodeling. Parallel fecal microbiota transplantation into naive mice transferred butyrate production and partially reproduced the BDNF increase, but not the full behavioural response. These findings position probiotic-driven gut microbiome shifts as modifiers of BDNF-dependent brain circuits, with implications for stress-related disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan catabolites converge on vagal and systemic immune pathways to modulate brain function, but whether they causally affect neurodegenerative disease is unresolved. In a cohort of older adults, we combined fecal microbiome sequencing, APOE, BDNF, and IL6 genotypes, and dietary intake to test associations with cognitive decline. Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis estimated causal effects and the proportion mediated by microbial taxa and butyrate. Higher probiotic and omega-3 intake correlated with enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, lower lipopolysaccharide load, and reduced NF-kB signaling. Genetically predicted microbiome composition showed bidirectional links with BDNF expression; APOE ε4 carriers exhibited stronger associations between fiber intake and dementia risk. Mediation analysis suggested that short-chain fatty acids explained 18% of the protective effect of probiotics on neuroinflammation. These findings support targeting the gut microbiota with prebiotics and probiotics, stratified by APOE and BDNF genotypes, to preserve brain health. These data highlight a modifiable axis in which dietary fiber, probiotics, and omega-3 interact with host APOE and BDNF variation.

Depletion of butyrate-producing Clostridia within the gut microbiome tracks with Parkinson's disease severity and altered dopamine metabolism in the striatum, implicating microbial metabolites in nigrostriatal degeneration. In a 12-week randomized trial, 48 patients with Parkinson's disease received resistant starch plus Bifidobacterium breve or placebo. Fecal shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics quantified short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and trimethylamine N-oxide. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and levodopa dose showed that resistant starch raised fecal butyrate by 38% and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance by 2.1-fold, paralleled by lower serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and IL-6 expression. Spearman correlation linked Roseburia abundance inversely with depressive symptoms. Motor scores improved modestly, yet permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed no global microbiome shift. Plasma p-cresol sulfate remained unchanged, and no serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that selectively feeding butyrate producers may dampen neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, although confirmatory trials using fecal microbiota transplantation and longer follow-up are needed.

Distinct gut microbiota signatures are increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet their relationship to central nervous system immune signaling remains incompletely defined. We profiled fecal microbiota from 78 adults with MDD and 62 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified plasma lipopolysaccharide, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Lachnospiraceae were depleted in MDD, whereas Eggerthella and Collinsella were enriched. Reduced butyrate-producing taxa correlated with higher interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide concentrations. Using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use, Faecalibacterium abundance remained inversely associated with interleukin-6 (β = −0.31, p = 0.008). A random forest classifier based on microbial and inflammatory features discriminated MDD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.79. These findings support a model in which gut microbiota depletion of butyrate producers contributes to systemic inflammation relevant to MDD, and suggest that fiber or probiotic interventions warrant testing for modulating gut-brain axis signaling.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids regulate central BDNF expression and anxiety-like behavior in rodents, but whether dietary probiotic supplementation alters human mood through similar pathways is unclear. We randomized 84 adults with mild depressive symptoms to 8 weeks of Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo, with counseling to increase fermented foods and fiber-rich vegetables. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and peripheral IL6 and BDNF mRNA were quantified. Mixed-effects models tested associations among microbial diversity, short-chain fatty acid producers, and symptom scores. Probiotic assignment increased Lactobacillus abundance and reduced depressive symptoms relative to placebo, but only among participants reporting higher fermented food intake. Responders showed elevated Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium, higher fecal butyrate, and lower IL6 expression; BDNF changes were nonsignificant. Dietary fiber intake correlated with microbial diversity and butyrate, while baseline BDNF methylation moderated symptom improvement. These findings suggest that probiotic effects on depression depend on habitual diet and host BDNF regulation, implicating a gut-brain axis sensitive to fermented foods and microbiome composition.

Microbial colonization of the gastrointestinal tract during adolescence coincides with synaptic pruning and maturation of the prefrontal cortex, and disruption of this dialogue predicts later depression and anxiety. In a cohort of adolescents (n=180), fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and peripheral BDNF, IL6, and COMT expression was quantified. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, higher abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus was associated with lower internalizing symptoms, whereas Prevotella correlated positively with anxiety scores. PERMANOVA revealed that microbial community structure explained 11.4% of variance in BDNF expression; IL6 and COMT showed weaker associations. Short-chain fatty acid producers, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, were enriched in adolescents with high BDNF and low depression scores. A probiotic intervention (n=40) increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance and reduced negative emotionality over 8 weeks. Mediation analysis suggested that IL6 partially mediated the relationship between Prevotella and anxiety. These findings support a modifiable gut microbiota-BDNF pathway linked to adolescent mood disorders.

Microbial metabolites produced by gut microbiota are increasingly recognized as modulators of central nervous system function, with short-chain fatty acids and bile acid derivatives shaping BDNF expression, SLC6A4 activity, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity. In germ-free mice, colonization with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum reduced anxiety-like behavior and normalized GABRA1 transcripts in the prefrontal cortex, whereas antibiotic-induced dysbiosis increased neuroinflammation and depressive-like phenotypes. Dietary interventions that supply fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich foods promote butyrate-producing taxa, and probiotic or prebiotic supplementation has shown modest benefits in irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder. Mechanistic studies using 16S rRNA sequencing, metagenomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation in patients link specific taxa to IL6 and TLR4 profiles. However, causality remains difficult to establish because diet, host genetic variation, and baseline microbial composition interact. Future trials should stratify by BDNF genotype and enterotype to determine whether targeted psychobiotics can translate microbial signals into durable brain health outcomes.

Disruption of gut microbiota composition during early life can alter hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity and anxiety-like behavior, yet dietary levers that stabilize this axis remain poorly defined. In a mouse model of chronic stress, we tested whether a probiotic consortium combined with fermented food-derived short-chain fatty acids could reshape microbiota-brain signaling. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics revealed that the intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated butyrate in colon, and normalized BDNF expression in hippocampus. Linear mixed-effects models showed reduced depression-like behavior and lower corticosterone after treatment, with effects comparable to fluoxetine. Fecal microbiota transplantation from treated mice into naive mice partially reproduced these benefits, whereas prebiotic alone did not. These findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented food components may provide a tractable strategy for modulating gut microbiota and brain function. Because stress-related disorders remain leading causes of disability, dietary adjuncts that engage microbiota metabolism warrant clinical testing in humans.

Gut microbial dysbiosis precedes and predicts mild cognitive impairment in some older adults, suggesting that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharides modulate brain immune signaling through the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants with metabolic syndrome received a Mediterranean-style diet with or without probiotic supplementation; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal calprotectin assays quantified microbial composition and intestinal inflammation. Probiotics increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, reduced Proteobacteria, and lowered trimethylamine N-oxide compared with diet alone. These shifts correlated with lower executive dysfunction scores and reduced depressive symptoms, but not with changes in brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial diversity explained 23% of the cognitive benefit. In parallel, germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from responders showed reduced neuroinflammation and preserved hippocampal Bdnf expression. The findings support targeting the gut microbiome through diet plus probiotics to attenuate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, though confirmatory trials using metagenomic sequencing and standardized cognitive endpoints are needed.

Greater gut microbial diversity and elevated short-chain fatty acid production consistently track with preserved hippocampal volume and slower cognitive decline, yet whether nutritional interventions can shift this axis remains uncertain. In a 12-month randomized, double-blind trial, 180 older adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermented foods or a control diet; half also received omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma metabolomics quantified microbiota composition and circulating metabolites. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The intervention increased Akkermansia and Lactobacillus abundance, raised butyrate levels, and reduced lipopolysaccharide levels. These microbial changes correlated with improved BDNF signaling and better performance on verbal memory tests. Effects were strongest among participants with low baseline omega-3 index. Thus, a fermented-food-rich diet plus omega-3 supplementation may remodel the gut microbiome and mitigate MCI progression, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone, yet their link to BDNF regulation in major depressive disorder remains poorly defined. We enrolled 78 adults with MDD and 62 healthy controls, profiling faecal microbiota via 16S rRNA gene sequencing and plasma metabolites via untargeted metabolomics. PERMANOVA showed significant microbial community separation by diagnosis (R2=0.08, p=0.001), and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified differential taxa. Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted in MDD, whereas Bacteroides was enriched. These shifts correlated with lower butyrate and higher lipopolysaccharide levels. Mediation models indicated that butyrate indirectly linked microbiota composition to BDNF promoter methylation and symptom severity. Baseline IL6 expression was higher in MDD and negatively associated with butyrate after adjusting for age and sex. A random forest classifier using microbial taxa and metabolites discriminated MDD from controls with an AUC of 0.81. Our findings suggest that gut microbial dysbiosis contributes to depression through metabolite-BDNF interactions, highlighting potential targets for probiotic or antidepressant strategies.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly recognized as a contributor to neurodegenerative disease, yet the mechanisms linking microbial metabolites to central nervous system function remain incompletely defined. In older adults, we combined shotgun metagenomic sequencing with targeted metabolomics to examine associations among microbial composition, short-chain fatty acid production, and mild cognitive impairment. Lower abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia correlated with reduced butyrate levels and poorer executive function. Dietary patterns rich in fermentable fiber and polyphenol-rich foods were associated with higher butyrate and favorable cognitive scores. A 12-week intervention using probiotic supplementation plus prebiotic fiber increased Bifidobacterium abundance, reduced circulating interleukin-6, and improved cognitive impairment scores. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that changes in Bifidobacterium partially mediated cognitive improvement. Notably, recent antibiotic exposure attenuated these associations, suggesting that microbial viability is required for the observed metabolic and cognitive effects. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome through diet and dietary supplements as a potential strategy for neurodegenerative disease prevention.

Microbial production of short-chain fatty acids from fermentable dietary fiber is a central mechanism linking gut microbiota to brain function, yet the strength of this relationship in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain. In a cohort of 112 adults, we profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. PERMANOVA revealed that dietary fiber intake explained 11.4% of microbial community variance, while random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium and Roseburia as depleted in patients with MDD. Mediation models indicated that butyrate accounted for 23% of the association between fiber intake and depressive symptoms. Associations were tested with linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use. In mice receiving microbiota from high-fiber responders, Bdnf expression in the hippocampus increased relative to controls, alongside reduced interleukin-6. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-responsive gut bacteria and their metabolites represent tractable targets for adjunctive prebiotic or probiotic strategies in MDD.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes the gut microbiota and modifies BDNF expression in the hippocampus, yet whether these effects depend on habitual diet remains uncertain. We randomized 84 adults with metabolic syndrome to 12 weeks of inulin or placebo while consuming a Western diet or Mediterranean diet. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia only in Mediterranean diet consumers. These shifts correlated with lower lipopolysaccharide and cortisol levels, and with reduced IL6 and TLR4 expression in peripheral blood. In contrast, Western diet consumers showed no microbiota remodeling and a blunted BDNF response. Mixed-effects models indicated that baseline gut microbiota diversity and fiber intake predicted treatment response. In mice receiving faecal microbiota transplantation from responders, inulin improved anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. Our findings suggest that inulin exerts gut-brain benefits only when embedded in a Mediterranean diet, underscoring the need to consider diet context in prebiotic interventions.

Supplementation with dietary fiber reshapes the gut microbiome and attenuates neuroinflammation in mice fed a high-fat diet. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics, we tracked microbial and metabolic shifts across the gut-brain axis. In male C57BL/6 mice, twelve weeks of dietary fiber intake increased Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate in the colon, and restored Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These changes coincided with lower plasma lipopolysaccharide, reduced Il6 and Tnf transcripts, and improved Morris water maze performance. Fecal microbiota transplantation from fiber-fed donors into naive mice reproduced the Bdnf increase, whereas Spearman correlation linked short-chain fatty acids to reduced cognitive impairment. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus alone failed to replicate these benefits, and the effects were abolished in Bdnf knockout mice, suggesting that dietary fiber acts through a broader microbiota-derived butyrate signal. Collectively, these data indicate that dietary fiber protects against cognitive impairment by modulating gut microbiota and BDNF signaling in the brain.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to major depressive disorder, but whether dietary interventions can reverse microbial and metabolic signatures of depression remains uncertain. We recruited adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls, assessed Mediterranean diet adherence, and applied shotgun metagenomic sequencing plus targeted metabolomics to stool and serum. Lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and reduced butyrate correlated with higher depressive symptoms. BDNF expression in peripheral blood was lower in patients than in controls and positively associated with butyrate. In a randomized subset, a high-fiber diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate, and improved BDNF expression relative to usual diet. A probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum did not alter BDNF but reduced depressive symptoms modestly. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate and BDNF partially mediated the diet–depression association. Together, these data implicate microbial butyrate signaling and BDNF regulation in the diet–depression relationship. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome through dietary fiber as an adjunctive strategy for depression.

Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid generated by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber, is a key mediator of the gut microbiota-brain axis. We examined whether inulin-type fructans, a fermentable fiber from chicory root, could modify gut microbial composition and neuroinflammation in adults with mild cognitive impairment. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants received inulin or placebo while consuming a Mediterranean-style diet. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundances, short-chain fatty acids, and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were quantified. Plasma branched-chain amino acids and BDNF expression were secondary outcomes. Cognitive performance was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and associations were tested using linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlation. Inulin increased butyrate and Bifidobacterium relative to placebo. Higher butyrate correlated with lower interleukin-6 and improved hippocampal connectivity. Exploratory mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly mediated cognitive improvement. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with fermentable dietary fibers may slow cognitive decline, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial colonization of the gut shapes brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and its disruption is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder and anxiety. We tested whether probiotic supplementation could reverse microbiota alterations and behavioral deficits in mice exposed to chronic stress. At baseline, stressed mice displayed lower Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances and elevated interleukin-6 compared with non-stressed controls. Fecal samples underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics; short-chain fatty acids and serotonin were quantified in colon and hippocampus. After four weeks, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundances increased in supplemented mice compared with vehicle-treated controls. Forced swim test showed reduced immobility and increased exploratory behavior. Using mixed-effects modeling, we found that Lactobacillus abundance correlated positively with BDNF expression in the hippocampus and negatively with corticosterone. These data suggest that probiotic-driven microbiota shifts may attenuate stress-related depressive-like behavior via gut-brain axis signaling. Our findings support targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics as a potential adjunct for depression, though human trials are needed.

Distinct shifts in gut microbiota composition, rather than simple loss of diversity, track with symptom severity in major depressive disorder and anxiety. Baseline short-chain fatty acid profiles also differed by diagnosis. We recruited 84 adults and analyzed fecal microbial communities by 16S rRNA sequencing, along with circulating interleukin-6, cortisol, and peripheral blood BDNF and NR3C1 expression. PERMANOVA revealed diagnosis-related beta diversity (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.08, p = 0.002), and linear discriminant analysis effect size identified Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Bacteroides as discriminative taxa. Faecalibacterium abundance correlated inversely with BDNF expression (r = -0.34, p = 0.006) and positively with butyrate; mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partly explained this association. A random forest classifier distinguished cases from controls with an AUC of 0.81. In parallel, mice fed a high-fat diet showed comparable microbiota shifts, lower Bdnf and Nrf2 in prefrontal cortex, and increased interleukin-6. These findings link specific gut bacteria and BDNF-related pathways to depression-anxiety phenotypes, suggesting that microbial or probiotic interventions merit testing in stratified patients.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape central nervous system immune tone and BDNF expression, linking gut microbiota composition to depression-like behavior. In a 12-week randomized trial, adults with mild-to-moderate major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus or a control condition. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, and BDNF, IL6, and CRP were measured at baseline and week 12. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Relative to control, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, reduced IL6 expression, and improved depressive symptom scores. Changes in Bifidobacterium correlated with reduced IL6 and increased BDNF; Spearman correlation indicated these associations were independent of baseline depression severity. Post hoc mediation analysis suggested that Bifidobacterium-driven shifts in short-chain fatty acid production partially mediated BDNF increases. These findings support probiotic as a microbiota-targeted adjunct for depression, though larger clinical cohorts are needed to confirm durability and mechanism.

Short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals in the colon shape central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. In a randomized mouse study, dietary inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate in portal blood, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and RNA sequencing of hippocampus showed that butyrate promoted histone acetylation and upregulated Bdnf and Gabra1 while suppressing Nfkb1. Vagotomy abolished the Bdnf induction, implicating vagus nerve signaling. In participants with irritable bowel syndrome, a fermented food intervention increased gut microbiota diversity and decreased interleukin-6, with BDNF methylation inversely correlating with Shannon diversity. A separate cohort of adults with major depressive disorder showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance and higher kynurenine/tryptophan ratios than controls; linear mixed models linked these shifts to BDNF expression and depressive symptoms. These findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as modulators of BDNF and neuroinflammation, but causal direction and strain specificity remain unresolved. Therapeutic targeting of these pathways warrants further study.

Chronic stress-related disorders are accompanied by reduced gut microbial diversity and elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide, a pattern that predicts blunted neurogenesis in the hippocampus and depressive-like behavior in rodents. We tested whether dietary galacto-oligosaccharide supplementation could reverse these effects in mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress. After 6 weeks, galacto-oligosaccharide-treated mice showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, alongside lower corticosterone and interleukin-6 in serum and colon. Fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors into germ-free recipients reproduced the behavioral improvements, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Forced swim test and open field test confirmed reduced despair and anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition shifts explained 42% of the reduction in anxiety-like behavior, with short-chain fatty acids and BDNF expression as partial mediators. Untargeted metabolomics and PERMANOVA further linked galacto-oligosaccharide intake to tryptophan pathway metabolites. These findings position galacto-oligosaccharide as a plausible microbiota-targeting strategy for stress-related neuropsychiatric conditions, though human trials are needed.

Depletion of gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids is increasingly linked to Parkinson's disease (PD) progression, yet whether inulin supplementation can modify this trajectory remains uncertain. In a randomized mouse model of PD induced by 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), we administered inulin for six weeks and assessed striatal dopamine depletion, nigral neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics characterized microbial communities and circulating metabolites. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lachnospiraceae abundance, elevated butyrate, and attenuated neuroinflammation markers in the midbrain. These changes were accompanied by preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive nigral neurons and improved rotarod performance. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate levels explained 38% of the protective effect on striatal dopamine. In patients with PD, fecal metagenomics revealed reduced butyrate-producing taxa, and Mendelian randomization supported a causal inverse association between gut microbiome butyrate potential and PD risk. These findings position inulin as a candidate prebiotic intervention targeting the gut-brain axis in PD.

Adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the mechanisms linking dietary patterns to nigrostriatal degeneration remain unclear. In a prospective cohort of patients with PD, we examined whether gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid profiles mediate this association. 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed higher abundances of Prevotella and Roseburia among individuals with high adherence, alongside elevated butyrate and propionate. Using mediation analysis, we found that butyrate explained 22% of the inverse association between Mediterranean diet adherence and motor severity (β = −0.18, 95% CI −0.31 to −0.06). Fiber supplementation in mouse models of PD recapitulated these microbial shifts and reduced dopaminergic neuronal loss in the substantia nigra. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbial metabolites may slow PD progression and support prebiotic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis. Notably, levodopa absorption did not differ across adherence tertiles, and adjustment for dopaminergic therapy did not attenuate the mediated effect.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural signaling, and their depletion tracks with cognitive impairment. We tested whether a multi-strain probiotic plus fermented food diet altered gut microbiota composition and neuroinflammation in adults with mild cognitive impairment. Participants consumed either probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks while maintaining habitual fermented food intake. At baseline and endpoint, participants completed food frequency questionnaires and cognitive testing; plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified. Fecal microbiota was profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing; linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, Spearman correlation linked taxa to inflammatory cytokines, and mediation analysis assessed indirect effects. Probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced interleukin-6 compared with placebo. Greater fermented food intake correlated with higher microbial diversity and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may stabilize the gut microbiota–brain axis, though confirmatory trials are needed.

Reduced gut microbiota diversity and altered Lactobacillus/Bacteroides ratios track with symptom severity in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the pathways linking microbiota to BDNF signaling remain unclear. In adults with MDD (n=84) and healthy controls (n=72), 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal microbiota was combined with plasma cytokine profiling and mediation analysis. Depletion of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium was associated with higher interleukin-6 and lower BDNF expression. Mediation models indicated that interleukin-6 explained 31% of the association between Bifidobacterium abundance and BDNF levels. In mice exposed to chronic corticosterone, probiotic administration increased serotonin turnover, normalized IL1B and TNFA transcription in the hippocampus, and reduced depressive-like behavior. Notably, SSRIs did not attenuate the microbiota-associated inflammatory signal, whereas a high-fiber diet correlated with greater Faecalibacterium abundance and lower IL6 expression. These findings underscore the need for longitudinal metagenomics and causal inference to distinguish microbial drivers from consequences of MDD. Therapeutic targeting of the gut microbiome may complement existing psychiatric drugs and improve outcomes in patients with MDD.

Gut microbial dysbiosis and constipation often precede Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis by years, suggesting that the gut microbiome contributes to neuroinflammation. We tested whether prebiotic inulin alters α-synuclein aggregation and microglial states in α-synuclein-overexpressing mice. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while decreasing Akkermansia. Single-cell RNA sequencing of midbrain microglia revealed that inulin suppressed pro-inflammatory signaling and expanded disease-associated macrophage subsets. Fecal butyrate and propionate concentrations correlated with P2RY12 and TMEM119 expression; linear mixed-effects modeling with false discovery rate correction confirmed these associations. In patients with PD, baseline oral microbiome composition differed from healthy controls, and Lactobacillus abundance was inversely associated with motor severity in a permutational multivariate analysis of variance. Depletion of microglia using a CSF1R inhibitor abolished the benefits of inulin, restoring motor deficits. These results support a microglia-dependent gut-brain axis in which fermentable fiber may mitigate PD pathology. Together, these data implicate microbial metabolites as modifiable drivers of PD progression.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by a Western diet is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder through immune, metabolic, and neural pathways. In a cohort of adults with depression and healthy controls, we integrated 16S rRNA sequencing, plasma metabolomics, and host BDNF genotyping. Multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis tested associations among dietary fiber intake, microbial composition, short-chain fatty acids, and BDNF methylation. Depressed participants showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance, reduced butyrate levels, and higher BDNF promoter methylation than controls. Fiber-rich foods were inversely associated with depressive symptoms, and this relationship was partially mediated by Faecalibacterium and butyrate. Random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium, butyrate, and BDNF methylation as discriminative features. Receiver operating characteristic analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.82 for this combined signature. Notably, Mediterranean diet adherence scores correlated with higher Faecalibacterium and lower depression severity, independent of antidepressant use. These findings suggest that diet-driven microbiome shifts may influence depression via epigenetic regulation of BDNF, highlighting targets for nutritional intervention.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet tracks with greater gut microbiota diversity and lower neuroinflammation tone, yet whether targeted dietary supplements amplify these effects remains uncertain. We analyzed adults with mild cognitive impairment who received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or the same diet enriched with omega-3 fatty acids and inulin for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing quantified gut microbiota composition, while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry measured short-chain fatty acids. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and linear mixed models tested associations with BDNF and interleukin-6. The supplemented group showed higher Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, increased butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6 compared with the diet-alone group. Fecal calprotectin and serum lipopolysaccharide decreased only with supplementation. Greater butyrate correlated with improved executive function and lower depressive symptoms. These findings indicate that Mediterranean diet adherence combined with specific dietary supplements may engage the gut-brain axis to modulate neuroinflammation and cognition.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet disrupts gut microbiota composition and promotes depressive- and anxiety-like behaviors in mice, yet the molecular links between microbial shifts and central serotonin signaling remain incompletely defined. We fed C57BL/6J mice either a control diet or a high-fat diet for 12 weeks, with or without daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus supplementation. Behavioral testing revealed increased anxiety and depression-like phenotypes, elevated interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α, and reduced BDNF expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed decreased relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus spp. Spearman correlation analysis linked Akkermansia muciniphila abundance negatively with serotonin turnover and positively with BDNF expression. Notably, HTR1A expression in the prefrontal cortex was also reduced and correlated with Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored gut microbiota diversity, normalized cytokine levels, and attenuated behavioral deficits. These findings suggest that probiotic interventions may buffer high-fat diet-induced neuropsychiatric disturbances through BDNF-dependent and serotonin-related pathways, highlighting a tractable gut-brain target.

Gut microbial dysbiosis and diminished short-chain fatty acid production are increasingly implicated in neuroinflammation and depressive symptoms. To test whether dietary fiber intake modifies this axis, we analyzed stool and serum from 120 adults with major depressive disorder and 90 healthy controls. Microbial composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Shotgun metagenomics further revealed depletion of butyrate-producing bacteria and increased Bifidobacterium abundance in responders after treatment. A random forest classifier identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis as depleted in patients, with butyrate showing the strongest inverse association with interleukin-6. In a subset, a 12-week Mediterranean diet enriched with fermented foods increased gut microbial diversity and reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. These changes correlated with improved depressive symptoms and hippocampal connectivity. Our findings suggest that dietary fiber and fermented foods may reshape the gut microbiome to attenuate neuroinflammation, offering a tractable adjunct for depression.

A high-fat diet reshapes the gut microbiome, increases intestinal permeability, and drives neuroinflammation through lipopolysaccharide (LPS)–TLR4 signaling, linking obesity to cognitive impairment. In C57BL/6 mice randomized to high-fat diet or standard chow, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios and reduced Akkermansia muciniphila. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG supplementation attenuated these microbial shifts, lowered plasma LPS, and decreased Tnf and Il6 expression in the hippocampus. It also restored Bdnf and Nrf2 levels, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and improved spatial memory in open field and Morris water maze tests. The protection was absent in mice lacking TLR4, confirming pathway dependence. Fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated mice into germ-free mice partially reproduced this protection, implicating microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids. In patients with metabolic syndrome, lower Akkermansia abundance correlated with worse cognitive decline and higher inflammatory markers. These findings position probiotic interventions as potential adjuncts for gut-brain axis disorders, though randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced from fiber-rich foods cross the intestinal epithelium and modulate brain immune signaling, yet the extent to which this pathway explains diet-related changes in BDNF expression remains unclear. In a human cohort (n=184) and mice, Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with higher gut microbiota diversity and increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of butyrate biosynthesis pathways. Fecal butyrate was quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and Mendelian randomization supported a causal effect of gut microbiota-derived butyrate on BDNF promoter methylation. Using mediation analysis, we found that butyrate explained 31% of the association between Mediterranean diet and BDNF methylation, while linear mixed models showed that BDNF expression correlated with hippocampal volume. Depression scores declined in participants with high microbial diversity. In mice fed a Western diet, inulin supplementation restored microbial diversity and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that fiber-rich foods may influence brain plasticity via gut microbiota-derived butyrate and BDNF-dependent pathways, providing a rationale for targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis in stress-related disorders.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and depleted butyrate-producing bacteria track with Alzheimer's disease (AD) severity, yet whether dietary fiber can reverse this microbiota–brain axis remains unclear. We recruited adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment and cognitively normal controls, collected fecal microbiota and plasma metabolites, and assessed habitual fiber intake. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry revealed lower Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in cases, alongside reduced butyrate and indole-3-propionate. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partially explained the association between Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and hippocampus volume. Fecal calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide were elevated in cases, and Spearman correlation associated these markers with Bacteroides depletion. In mice carrying the APOE4 allele, a high-fat, low-fiber diet exacerbated cognitive decline and neuroinflammation, whereas inulin supplementation restored Bifidobacterium abundance and short-chain fatty acid production. Random forest modeling further linked indole-3-propionate to AD status with 78% accuracy. These findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as modifiable mediators of AD risk and support dietary intervention trials.

Adherence to a Mediterranean diet rich in fermented foods and fiber is associated with lower depressive symptoms, but the microbial and metabolic mediators remain unclear. We tested whether a probiotic plus prebiotic fiber intervention alters gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid output in mice colonized with human donor microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we observed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate, and reduced trimethylamine N-oxide in plasma. Fecal metabolite profiling further revealed higher indole-3-propionate and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, which correlated with increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These shifts coincided with lower BDNF methylation in the prefrontal cortex and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Mediation analysis attributed 32% of the behavioral effect to butyrate. The findings suggest that Mediterranean diet-derived fermented food and probiotic strategies may modulate microbiome-brain signaling through microbial metabolites, offering a testable approach for depression prevention.

Prebiotic inulin and fermented foods can reshape the gut microbiome, yet their combined impact on Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. We recruited 45 PD patients and 30 healthy controls and randomized patients to 12 weeks of inulin plus a Mediterranean-style diet or standard care. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified taxonomic and functional shifts. Linear mixed models tested associations with motor severity and constipation. At baseline, PD patients showed lower Faecalibacterium and Roseburia and higher Akkermansia than controls. Intervention increased Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, and Akkermansia and raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate. These changes correlated with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha and improved gastrointestinal symptoms. SNCA expression in blood did not change, but gut-derived lipopolysaccharide-binding protein decreased. Adherence to high-fiber foods and omega-3 supplementation was associated with greater microbial diversity. Our findings suggest that prebiotic supplementation combined with fermented food intake may modulate the gut-brain axis in PD, supporting larger trials.

Supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids combined with a Mediterranean-style diet reshapes the gut microbiota and reduces neuroinflammation in mild cognitive impairment, but the microbial mediators remain poorly defined. We enrolled 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment and randomized them to 12 weeks of omega-3 supplementation plus dietary counseling or counseling alone. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and plasma interleukin-6 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were measured at baseline and endpoint. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, and PERMANOVA assessed community-level differences. Supplementation increased Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia abundance and decreased Escherichia-Shigella; these shifts correlated with lower interleukin-6 and better hippocampal connectivity. Baseline fiber intake modified the response, with greater Faecalibacterium increases among participants reporting higher legume consumption. Mediation analysis suggested that Faecalibacterium partly explained cognitive improvement. No serious adverse events occurred, and adherence exceeded 90%. The findings indicate that omega-3 and Mediterranean diet components may act through the gut microbiome to modulate neuroinflammation in mild cognitive impairment, supporting microbiome-targeted dietary strategies.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF expression and hippocampal neurogenesis, offering a mechanistic bridge between intestinal bacteria and depression. In a cross-sectional study, adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and healthy controls provided stool samples; 16S rRNA sequencing and linear discriminant analysis effect size were used to profile microbial communities. Participants with MDD showed lower relative abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lachnospiraceae, alongside reduced Mediterranean diet adherence and lower fermented food intake. A subset received probiotics plus a high-fiber diet for 8 weeks; this group exhibited increased BDNF and decreased IL6 expression, with Shannon index and Chao1 richness gains. Antidepressant use did not explain these associations in this cohort. Fecal calprotectin and lipopolysaccharide correlated inversely with BDNF and positively with depressive symptoms. These preliminary findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through fiber-rich foods and fermented foods may complement conventional MDD treatment, though rodent studies are needed to establish causality.

Microbial conversion of pomegranate ellagitannins into urolithin A (UA) depends on gut microbiota composition, and this metabolite may protect against Alzheimer's disease (AD). To test this, APP/PS1 mice received oral UA for eight weeks. Spatial memory improved in the Morris water maze, and immunofluorescence showed reduced amyloid β (Aβ) deposition in the hippocampus. Western blotting of cortical tissue revealed that UA downregulated VDAC1, inhibited PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, and activated AMPK, thereby promoting autophagy. These changes were reversed by VDAC1 overexpression. In Aβ1-42-injured N2a and PC12 cells, UA increased viability and autophagy-related proteins. Parallel in vitro experiments with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium showed that microbiota from healthy donors produced more UA than that from AD patients. Plasma targeted metabolomics further linked higher UA levels to lower VDAC1 expression and better performance. The findings suggest that microbiota-dependent UA production links dietary ellagitannins to VDAC1-mediated neuroprotection, offering a rationale for urolithin A supplementation in AD.

Reduced fecal abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus tracks with faster cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that gut microbiota composition contributes to neuroinflammation and hippocampal dysfunction. To test this, we profiled stool and serum from older adults with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. Lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations correlated with worse cognitive composite scores in multivariable regression. Fecal microbiota transplantation from low-SCFA donors into mice increased neuroinflammation and impaired hippocampus-dependent memory. Conversely, probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus restored butyrate levels, reduced neuroinflammation, and improved hippocampus-dependent memory in mice. In patients carrying APOE4, baseline gut microbiota diversity predicted response to probiotic supplementation. These findings position microbiome-targeted probiotic interventions as a promising adjunct for Alzheimer's disease, though prospective trials in patients are needed to confirm causality. Microbial lipopolysaccharide translocation and altered vagus nerve signaling may mediate these effects, while dietary fiber intake modified the association between gut microbiota and cognition.

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation reshaped the gut microbiota and improved cognition in adults with mild cognitive impairment, yet the microbial and molecular mediators remain uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, 84 participants received either omega-3 or control. We profiled the gut microbiome by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, measured short-chain fatty acids and IL-6 in serum, and quantified BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Linear mixed-effects models tested treatment-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Omega-3 increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance and reduced Escherichia. Higher Lactobacillus abundance correlated with lower IL-6 and greater BDNF expression. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially explained the cognitive benefit. Cognitive scores improved by 2.1 points on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and no serious adverse events occurred. In mice fed a probiotic mixture, similar shifts were accompanied by reduced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. These findings link omega-3-driven microbiota changes to BDNF-related pathways and support nutrition targeting the microbiome for early cognitive decline.

Higher dietary fiber intake and lower processed meat consumption track with distinct gut microbiota profiles that may modify Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk through the gut-brain axis. In a cohort of 4,212 older adults, shotgun metagenomic sequencing quantified Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii; liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry measured short-chain fatty acids and trimethylamine N-oxide. We applied Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis to separate genetic liability from dietary effects. Each standard-deviation increase in dietary fiber corresponded to higher butyrate (β = 0.18, 95% CI 0.11–0.25) and lower AD incidence (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.94). F. prausnitzii abundance mediated 17% of this association. Conversely, processed meat intake associated with elevated TMAO and cognitive decline, with APOE4 carriage exacerbating risk. Fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice reproduced the butyrate-dependent protection, whereas antibiotic exposure abolished it. Longitudinal metabolomics further linked these microbial shifts to bile acid remodeling and neuroinflammation. These findings support fiber-rich diets and targeted probiotic interventions as modifiable strategies against AD.

Depletion of gut microbial diversity and loss of butyrate-producing taxa precede motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), implicating intestinal microbiota in nigrostriatal pathology. In a longitudinal cohort, we profiled fecal microbiota from 112 PD patients and 94 controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics, then quantified short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Patients exhibited reduced Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, lower butyrate, elevated calprotectin, and depleted butyrate kinase genes. Dietary fiber intake correlated positively with Roseburia abundance and butyrate concentrations, whereas processed foods correlated with Enterobacteriaceae expansion. Fecal microbiota from patients induced motor deficits in mice, while antibiotic exposure was associated with lower Roseburia abundance. In mice colonized with fecal microbiota from PD patients, butyrate supplementation restored striatal dopamine and attenuated neuroinflammation. Random forest classification separated PD patients from controls with an AUC of 0.81. These findings link diet-responsive gut bacteria to PD and support fiber supplementation as a candidate disease-modifying strategy.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders via immune, endocrine, and neural signaling. We tested whether gut microbial features associate with BDNF expression and symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder. Fecal samples underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics; short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. BDNF mRNA in whole blood was measured by quantitative PCR. Using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use, we found that Faecalibacterium abundance was inversely associated with depressive symptoms (β = -0.34, p = 0.008) and positively associated with BDNF expression (β = 0.29, p = 0.014). Bacteroides abundance showed the opposite pattern. No significant associations emerged for Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium after false discovery rate correction. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 21% of the association between Faecalibacterium and BDNF. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome to modulate BDNF-related pathways in depression, though randomized controlled trials are needed.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production in the colon is increasingly recognized as a determinant of central nervous system homeostasis, yet strain-level mechanisms linking gut microbiota to depression remain poorly resolved. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received either a probiotic consortium containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and BDNF expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells were quantified at baseline and endpoint. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline severity revealed a significant group-by-time interaction for depressive symptoms (β = −3.1, false discovery rate-adjusted P = 0.02). Lactobacillus abundance correlated inversely with interleukin-6 and positively with BDNF expression. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate producers explained 22% of the clinical effect. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein decreased in the probiotic arm, suggesting reduced microbial translocation. These findings support targeted microbiome modulation as a plausible adjunct for depression, although confirmatory trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Fermented foods and dietary fibers exert distinct effects on the gut microbiota and the brain through metabolite-driven signaling. In a randomized crossover trial, adults with mild metabolic syndrome received either a probiotic blend or inulin for 8 weeks, with polyphenol-rich foods controlled across periods. 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and short-chain fatty acids. Both interventions increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, but only inulin raised fecal butyrate and reduced lipopolysaccharide binding protein. Butyrate elevation correlated with improved executive function and lower interleukin-6. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed increased resting-state connectivity between the prefrontal cortex and amygdala. Fecal propionate and acetate remained unchanged, whereas Akkermansia muciniphila abundance increased only after inulin. Shotgun metagenomics identified enrichment of butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase in responders. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber may produce broader gut-brain axis benefits than probiotics alone, particularly when fermented foods are excluded.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) generated from dietary fiber fermentation in the colon shape central nervous system immune tone and behavior, yet the pathways connecting gut microbiota composition to neurodegenerative disease remain incompletely defined.
