We recruited 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment and 62 matched controls, profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and quantified plasma SCFAs using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Participants completed a Mediterranean diet screener and a 12-week open-label trial of a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG plus inulin. Lower baseline Faecalibacterium abundance and higher Escherichia/Shigella correlated with worse cognitive impairment and higher interleukin-6. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate, and improved executive dysfunction relative to controls after linear mixed-effects modeling adjusted for age and sex. Baseline microbial diversity was lower in participants with mild cognitive impairment than in controls. These findings suggest that probiotic and prebiotic fiber interventions can reshape the gut-brain axis and may slow cognitive decline. No serious adverse events were reported.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to neurodegenerative disorders through immune and metabolic pathways, but the mediating host factors are unclear. In a cohort of 450 adults, we quantified fecal microbiome using 16S rRNA sequencing and measured BDNF, IL-6, and TREM2 expression in peripheral blood. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance negatively correlated with IL-6 (r = -0.38, p < 0.01) and positively with BDNF (r = 0.41, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis revealed that butyrate production explained 32% of the association between F. prausnitzii and BDNF. In a randomized controlled trial, 120 participants received either probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum) or placebo for 12 weeks. The probiotics group showed increased BDNF methylation and reduced depressive symptoms compared to placebo (p = 0.03). Mixed-effects models confirmed that changes in BDNF mediated the behavioral improvement. These data suggest that probiotic supplementation may modulate the gut-brain axis via BDNF and butyrate, offering a potential adjunctive strategy for neuropsychiatric conditions.

Inulin fermentation by gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids that influence hippocampal plasticity and affect, yet the mechanistic link to major depressive disorder in patients remains poorly defined. Preclinical studies in mice link inulin to reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF in the prefrontal cortex. We randomized 48 adults with depressive symptoms to 8 weeks of inulin or maltodextrin and measured fecal microbiota composition by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, serum butyrate by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood by quantitative PCR, with baseline microbial diversity as a covariate. Compared with maltodextrin, inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate, and upregulated BDNF expression. Depression severity scores declined more in the inulin group, and changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with both butyrate and BDNF according to Spearman correlation. These data suggest that inulin may alleviate depressive symptoms through microbiota-dependent butyrate production and BDNF-related pathways, supporting further trials targeting the gut-brain axis.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids tune hypothalamic BDNF signaling, and loss of this axis associates with major depressive disorder. To test causality, we integrated gut metagenomes from 1,248 adults with two-sample Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance was inversely linked to depressive symptoms (β = -0.18, P = 2.1×10−4). Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-F. prausnitzii donors into antibiotic-treated mice increased butyrate in the colon, restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and reduced anhedonia. Sodium butyrate reproduced these effects, whereas BDNF knockdown blocked them. Mediation analysis estimated that butyrate explained 31% of the protective association. Sensitivity analyses using MR-Egger and weighted median yielded consistent estimates, with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that F. prausnitzii engraftment persisted after transplantation. These findings position F. prausnitzii-derived butyrate as a modifiable signal upstream of BDNF in the gut-brain axis, suggesting dietary fiber or probiotic interventions may merit testing in depression.

Disruption of the gut microbiome during early life can alter hippocampal development and stress reactivity, suggesting that microbial signals shape brain circuits long before adulthood. In mice exposed to maternal separation, 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and increased Bacteroides, alongside elevated corticosterone and increased anxiety. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus JB-1 restored microbial diversity, normalized corticosterone, and reduced anxiety in mice. These effects were absent in vagotomized mice, implicating the vagus nerve in microbiota-gut-brain signaling. In humans, randomized controlled trials of probiotics have yielded mixed results for depression and anxiety, possibly reflecting strain specificity, baseline microbiota composition, and short follow-up. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into rodents induces depressive-like behavior, supporting causality. However, translating these findings requires multivariable modeling that accounts for diet, antibiotic exposure, and host genetics. Targeting the gut microbiota with prebiotics or probiotics may complement conventional antidepressants, but biomarker-guided trials are needed to identify who will benefit.

Supplementation with a multi-strain probiotic altered gut microbiota composition and increased γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) production in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, yet the magnitude of benefit varied with baseline microbial diversity. In a 12-week randomized trial, 84 participants received the probiotic or placebo; gut microbiome and serum samples were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects modeling showed that Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased only in the probiotic arm, correlating with lower interleukin-6 and improved cognitive scores. Mediation analysis indicated that the GABA rise partially mediated the association between Bifidobacterium enrichment and cognitive improvement. Random forest classification separated responders from non-responders with 78% accuracy, driven by baseline Faecalibacterium and butyrate levels. Permutation testing confirmed that these microbial features were not due to chance. The probiotic also raised short-chain fatty acids and reduced lipopolysaccharide in plasma, suggesting improved intestinal barrier function. These findings indicate that probiotic efficacy in gut-brain axis disorders depends on individualized microbiome features, supporting precision psychobiotic strategies.

Higher gut microbiota diversity and enrichment of butyrate-producing taxa, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, track with better cognitive function in older adults, yet causality and intervention targets remain uncertain. We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in adults with subjective cognitive decline who received a probiotic supplement or placebo for 12 weeks while all participants consumed a Mediterranean-style diet. Gut and blood samples were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Cognitive performance was assessed with computerized neuropsychological testing. Associations between microbial features, short-chain fatty acids, and cognitive change were tested using multivariable linear regression with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The probiotic group showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and greater improvement in executive function than placebo. Butyrate concentrations mediated this effect, and baseline microbiome composition modified response. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation combined with Mediterranean diet may support cognitive health through gut-brain axis pathways, although larger, longer trials in humans are needed.

Fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that shape central nervous system immune homeostasis and blood-brain barrier integrity. To test whether a high-fiber diet enriched with whole grains and legumes reshapes this axis, we randomized 48 healthy adults to the intervention or a low-fiber control for 6 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, accompanied by elevated fecal butyrate. Host transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed upregulation of CLDN5, OCLN, and BDNF, while mixed-effects models linked these changes to reduced lipopolysaccharide-binding protein. Serum BDNF concentrations, measured by ELISA, increased in the intervention group. Fecal calprotectin decreased, and NFKB1 expression fell, without changes in baseline microbiota diversity. Adherence exceeded 90%, confirmed by food frequency questionnaires and plasma alkylresorcinols. These findings suggest that dietary fiber intake may strengthen gut barrier and neurotrophic signaling via microbiota-derived SCFAs, with potential implications for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Short-chain fatty acid depletion in the colon precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with neuroinflammation in the substantia nigra. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled the gut microbiota and fecal metabolites of patients with PD and healthy controls. Depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia was associated with reduced butyrate and propionate, alongside elevated lipopolysaccharide translocation. In a mouse model of PD, sodium butyrate restored intestinal barrier integrity and attenuated microglial activation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors into mice recapitulated these protective effects, whereas probiotic supplementation with Akkermansia muciniphila failed to rescue dopaminergic neuron loss. A random-effects meta-analysis of three independent cohorts confirmed that lower fecal butyrate was significantly associated with worse motor function. These findings strongly suggest that gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids are critical modulators of the gut-brain axis in PD, and that butyrate-producing probiotics may offer a therapeutic strategy.

The gut microbiota shapes brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling in the hippocampus and modulates stress-related disorders, but whether high-fat diet disrupts this axis through specific Lactobacillus depletion remains unclear. We transplanted fecal microbiota from depressed donors and healthy donors into germ-free mice using fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), then fed the animals either high-fat diet or standard chow for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics profiled microbial communities and short-chain fatty acids. Forced swim test and open field test assessed depressive-like and anxiety-like behaviors. Behavioral deficits were accompanied by reduced intestinal barrier integrity and elevated interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Compared with chow-fed controls, high-fat diet-fed mice showed elevated corticosterone, reduced BDNF expression, and lower Lactobacillus abundance. Mice receiving microbiota from depressed donors recapitulated these deficits, whereas probiotic supplementation restored short-chain fatty acid levels and normalized BDNF expression. These findings indicate that dietary fat and microbial composition interact to regulate depressive-like behavior through BDNF-dependent mechanisms.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis by gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet microbial taxa that influence prefrontal cortex activity and depressive behavior remain poorly resolved. We recruited 84 patients with MDD and 52 healthy controls, profiled fecal communities using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing, and quantified serum cortisol, interleukin-6, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Bacteroides uniformis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were depleted in MDD, whereas Eggerthella lenta was enriched. Using PERMANOVA and random forest classification, microbial composition distinguished patients from controls (AUC = 0.79). Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance indirectly associated with depression severity through interleukin-6 (indirect effect = −0.18, 95% CI −0.31 to −0.07). Taxa depleted in MDD correlated negatively with interleukin-6 and positively with brain-derived neurotrophic factor after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from MDD patients increased anxiety-like behavior and reduced Bdnf expression in the hippocampus. These findings support microbiota-targeted strategies for MDD.

Altered gut microbiota composition and BDNF signaling are increasingly linked to irritable bowel syndrome with comorbid anxiety, yet the pathways connecting probiotic supplementation to central amygdala reactivity remain poorly defined. We recruited 84 adults with IBS and moderate anxiety, randomizing them to 8 weeks of multi-strain probiotics or placebo in a double-blind design. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; serum lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, interleukin-6, and BDNF methylation were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models tested interactions between treatment, baseline BDNF methylation, and microbial diversity. Mediation analysis assessed whether changes in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance explained symptom improvement. Compared with placebo, probiotics increased fecal microbial diversity and reduced anxiety scores; effects were strongest in participants with lower baseline BDNF methylation. Symptom reduction was partially mediated by Bifidobacterium abundance and decreased interleukin-6. These findings suggest that probiotic-induced shifts in gut microbiota may modulate BDNF-related brain circuits, offering a tractable target for IBS and anxiety.

Supplementation with inulin reshapes gut microbiota and attenuates depression-like behavior in mice exposed to chronic stress, yet the mediating BDNF and inflammatory pathways remain incompletely defined. We colonized adult male C57BL/6 mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium adolescentis and fed them a resistant starch diet for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and ELISA quantified microbial composition and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between butyrate, BDNF expression in the hippocampus, and anxiety-like behavior. Resistant starch increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, elevated butyrate, and upregulated BDNF in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. These changes coincided with reduced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α and lower depressive-like behavior. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and BDNF explained 42% of the behavioral effect. Our findings suggest that resistant starch may mitigate stress-related mood disorders by promoting gut microbiota-derived SCFA production and BDNF-dependent brain plasticity. These results highlight a microbiota-dependent mechanism by which resistant starch influences stress-related psychopathology. Future human trials are warranted.

Disruption of the gut microbiome precedes motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether microbial signals directly modify SNCA-driven pathology remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal and serum samples from patients with PD and age-matched controls. Akkermansia and Lactobacillus were enriched in PD, whereas Faecalibacterium and Roseburia were depleted; these shifts correlated with reduced butyrate and altered bile acid pools. A random forest classifier based on microbial and metabolic features discriminated PD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.82. In mice overexpressing SNCA, colonization with PD-associated microbiota exacerbated nigrostriatal degeneration and increased microglial interleukin-1β; butyrate supplementation attenuated these effects. Vagotomy abolished the exacerbation, implicating the vagus nerve. Notably, these responses were absent in germ-free mice colonized with control microbiota. These findings suggest that microbiome composition modifies SNCA-linked neurodegeneration through short-chain fatty acid-dependent neuroinflammation, supporting microbiota-directed strategies for PD.

Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alone rarely normalizes gut microbiota-brain signaling in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its efficacy may depend on concurrent fermented food intake and baseline microbial composition. In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, adults with MDD received either omega-3 plus fermented foods (yogurt, kefir, kimchi) or omega-3 alone. Fecal shotgun metagenomic sequencing and plasma liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry quantified microbial community structure and short-chain fatty acid levels. Combined intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus relative abundance, raised butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms more than omega-3 alone. BDNF expression in peripheral blood correlated with butyrate and Lactobacillus abundance. In mice, fecal transfer from responders recapitulated behavioral improvements and elevated hippocampal BDNF, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished the effect. These findings position fermented foods as a scalable adjunct to omega-3 supplementation and suggest that gut microbiome metabolic output, not supplement dose alone, gates MDD improvement. Baseline Faecalibacterium abundance predicted response, and bile acid profiles differed by treatment arm.

Microbial butyrate signaling through FFAR2 constrains microglial activation in the substantia nigra, yet whether dietary inulin can engage this gut-brain circuit in Parkinson's disease (PD) is unclear. We colonized gnotobiotic mice with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila, then fed them inulin-enriched or control diets before MPTP challenge. 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics profiled the gut microbiome; untargeted metabolomics quantified short-chain fatty acids in feces and serum. In patients with PD, we similarly measured microbial taxa and butyrate alongside FFAR2 expression in blood. Inulin increased F. prausnitzii abundance, raised butyrate, and attenuated dopaminergic loss and microglial reactivity in mice; these effects were abolished in mice lacking Ffar2. Linear mixed-effects models linked microbiome composition to motor scores and inflammatory markers. Notably, baseline microbiome diversity and FFAR2 expression predicted responsiveness, whereas levodopa exposure was associated with lower F. prausnitzii abundance. These findings suggest that inulin may act through FFAR2-dependent butyrate signaling to modulate PD progression.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbial fermentation of dietary fiber act as signaling molecules along the gut-brain axis, modulating neuroinflammation and depressive-like behavior. In rodent models, high-fiber diets increase Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevate butyrate in the colon, and upregulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These changes coincide with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and improved cognitive performance. However, whether these effects translate to humans remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in adults with mild depression, assigning participants to a fiber supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing, and serum short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Linear mixed models assessed changes in BDNF, interleukin-6, and symptom scores. The fiber group showed increased Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, higher butyrate, and greater BDNF levels compared with placebo, alongside reduced interleukin-6. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through dietary fiber may support brain health, though larger trials are needed.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) can suppress neuroinflammation and support hippocampal plasticity, but the dietary and microbial determinants of this gut-brain signaling remain incompletely defined. In a cohort of adults with mild cognitive impairment, we combined 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics with random forest and linear mixed models to identify taxa and metabolites associated with cognitive scores. Higher intake of fermented foods and dietary fiber, together with probiotic supplementation, was associated with enriched Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia and increased fecal butyrate. These shifts correlated with lower circulating IL-6 and higher BDNF expression, and with improved brain network efficiency. Gut microbiome composition explained 18% of variance in cognitive change, while dietary variables explained an additional 9%. In mice, transplantation of post-intervention microbiota recapitulated the metabolic and behavioral benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. These findings position dietary fiber and probiotic strategies as modifiable levers for cognitive decline through SCFA-mediated gut-brain signaling.

Microbial-derived butyrate is increasingly recognized as a key mediator of gut microbiota–brain signaling, yet its effects on BDNF expression and depression-like behavior remain incompletely defined. In mice fed a low-fiber diet, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, lower fecal butyrate, and increased lipopolysaccharide translocation. These changes coincided with elevated IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus, decreased BDNF, and impaired performance in a forced swim test. Supplementation with probiotics or fermented foods restored butyrate levels, normalized IL-6 and BDNF expression, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. In participants, baseline gut microbiome composition predicted response to a Mediterranean-style diet enriched in dietary fiber, with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance associated with greater improvement in depressive symptoms. In parallel, mediation analyses indicated that butyrate availability explained a significant proportion of the BDNF response. These findings suggest that targeting microbial short-chain fatty acid production through dietary fiber and probiotic intake may modulate BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity and neuroinflammation, offering a tractable strategy for stress-related disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is depleted in major depressive disorder, and this deficit tracks with increased interleukin-6 and reduced BDNF signaling along the gut-brain axis. To test whether this axis is modifiable, we conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of probiotic supplementation in 120 adults with major depressive disorder. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of gut microbiota and fecal calprotectin assays were performed at baseline and week 12. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions. Relative to placebo, the probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6. Depression scores decreased by 4.2 points more in the probiotic arm (95% CI −7.1 to −1.3; p=0.005). In germ-free mice colonized with patient microbiota, the same probiotic normalized anxiety-like behavior and hippocampal BDNF expression. These findings position targeted probiotic intervention as a plausible adjunct for depression, though larger, adequately powered trials and deeper mechanistic studies of the gut microbiome are needed.

Microbial metabolites generated from dietary fiber influence brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression and neuroinflammation, linking the gut microbiome to depressive symptoms. To test whether probiotics augment this axis, adults with major depressive disorder received either Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo alongside a Mediterranean diet for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; PERMANOVA, linear mixed-effects models, and mediation analysis tested compositional shifts and whether short-chain fatty acids explained clinical improvement. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, reduced anxiety scores, and lowered plasma interleukin-6 and kynurenine; butyrate correlated inversely with depression severity. Higher baseline ultra-processed food intake attenuated these effects, whereas fiber-rich foods strengthened the association between Faecalibacterium and symptom improvement. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that probiotics combined with fiber-rich foods may shift the gut microbial ecosystem toward a profile associated with improved mood in patients with major depressive disorder.

Microbial signals from the gut microbiota modulate gut-brain axis communication, yet whether probiotic supplementation can alter depressive symptoms through short-chain fatty acid-dependent routes is unresolved. In a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis or a control for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. We used linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to test associations between microbial taxa, metabolites, and symptom scores. The probiotic supplement increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and reduced depressive symptoms compared with control. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate changes explained 31% of the symptom improvement. In mice, the same probiotic supplementation attenuated stress-induced anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may improve depression by remodeling gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid signaling along the gut-brain axis.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is a plausible mediator of gut microbiota-brain signaling, yet evidence from human interventions remains inconsistent. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild depression received inulin-type fructans or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium abundance, serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor, interleukin-6, and depressive symptoms were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Using linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis with bootstrap confidence intervals, we found that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and reduced depressive symptoms relative to placebo. The symptom improvement was partially mediated by changes in Bifidobacterium and short-chain fatty acids. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor did not differ between groups, whereas interleukin-6 decreased modestly with inulin. These results suggest that prebiotic fiber may improve depressive symptoms through microbial and metabolic pathways, supporting targeted microbiome modulation in depression and potentially complementing existing therapies.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain signaling axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet microbial mediators and tractable interventions remain poorly defined. In a randomized, double-blind adult cohort, 120 participants with moderate depressive symptoms received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by shotgun metagenomics, and circulating short-chain fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines were quantified. Linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis tested treatment effects and whether microbial shifts explained symptom change. Probiotic recipients showed greater increases in butyrate-producing taxa, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and higher butyrate concentrations than placebo recipients. These changes correlated with reduced depressive symptoms; mediation analysis attributed 28% of the clinical improvement to butyrate elevation. Baseline microbial diversity moderated response, with lower diversity predicting weaker benefit. These findings support a mechanistic role for gut microbiota-derived metabolites in depression and suggest that probiotic supplementation may complement conventional therapy, though larger trials are needed.

Higher adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet is associated with slower cognitive decline, but the mediating role of the gut microbiota remains unresolved. We profiled older adults (n=180) with shotgun metagenomic sequencing, targeted fecal metabolomics, and food frequency questionnaires. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations among dietary fiber intake, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, butyrate, and mild cognitive impairment over 24 months. Mediation analysis tested indirect effects. Greater Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate concentrations, and with lower odds of mild cognitive impairment (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58–0.89). Butyrate accounted for 21% of this association in mediation models. Type 2 diabetes and metformin use weakened the relationship in this cohort. No significant effects appeared for Bacteroides or secondary bile acids. These results suggest that fiber-rich diets shape gut microbial communities and microbial metabolites, which relate to cognitive decline. Randomized dietary intervention trials with repeated metagenomic and metabolomic sampling are needed to establish causality.

Butyrate, a gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid, regulates hippocampal BDNF expression, but whether inulin supplementation can reproduce these effects in age-related cognitive decline remains unknown. We fed 12-month-old mice a high-fat diet with or without inulin for 12 weeks. Gut microbiota composition was assessed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF expression in the hippocampus was measured by quantitative PCR. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, elevated butyrate in the colon, and restored BDNF expression. These changes were accompanied by improved spatial memory in Morris water maze, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in serum, and lower TLR4 signaling in the colon. Spatial memory was tested before and after intervention, and intestinal permeability was assessed by FITC-dextran. Microbial functional pathways were predicted using PICRUSt. Inulin-fed mice showed higher Occludin and ZO-1 expression in the colon. Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium abundance with BDNF levels. Our data suggest that inulin may ameliorate cognitive decline by modulating the gut microbiome-BDNF axis.

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters gut microbiota composition and increases BDNF expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a tractable route to modulate the gut-brain axis in depression. To test this, 120 adults with major depressive disorder received either omega-3 or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid concentrations were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Peripheral BDNF mRNA was measured at baseline and endpoint. Compared with placebo, omega-3 increased Lachnospiraceae and Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced Proteobacteria. These shifts correlated with higher butyrate and BDNF levels. Mixed-effects models showed that BDNF change mediated the association between Bifidobacterium and improved depressive symptoms. At week 12, analysis of covariance revealed significant group-by-time interactions for BDNF (p = 0.008) and butyrate (p = 0.021). Baseline microbiota diversity predicted omega-3 response, whereas Bacteroides abundance was associated with nonresponse. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders reproduced BDNF upregulation and reduced anxiety-like behavior. These findings link omega-3 to microbiota-BDNF signaling and support further trials combining omega-3 with microbiota-directed therapies.

Consumption of a high-fat, low-fiber diet reshapes the gut microbiota and dampens BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, providing a plausible route to depressive-like behavior. In male C57BL/6J mice, 8 weeks of Western diet increased Desulfovibrio and Enterobacteriaceae while depleting Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free recipients transferred anxiety-like phenotypes and reduced Bdnf expression in the dentate gyrus. Metabolomic profiling revealed lower butyrate and indole-3-propionate in colon contents. Shotgun metagenomics further linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii depletion to reduced butyrate production and BDNF promoter methylation. Supplementation with inulin or Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored short-chain fatty acid levels, normalized BDNF transcripts, and attenuated stress-induced immobility. In patients with major depressive disorder, lower fecal microbial diversity correlated with reduced BDNF expression, while Mediterranean diet adherence associated with higher BDNF and fewer depressive symptoms in linear mixed models. These findings position diet-responsive microbiota and BDNF as coupled targets for mood disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids produced in the colon influence brain function via vagus nerve signaling and systemic immune pathways, but whether diet-driven gut microbiota remodeling alters depressive symptoms through BDNF regulation is uncertain. We analyzed adults with major depressive disorder and healthy controls, integrating 16S rRNA gene sequencing with plasma metabolomics and behavioral scores. Participants consuming fermented foods daily showed higher abundances of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated butyrate, and lower anxiety severity than those on a low-fermentation diet. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate partly explained the association between Bifidobacterium and reduced depression scores, while BDNF methylation moderated this effect. In a murine model, mice receiving microbiota from high-fermentation donors exhibited increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings suggest that fermented food intake may support gut-brain axis homeostasis through microbial metabolites and BDNF-related plasticity, offering a plausible dietary target for mood disorders. Additional untargeted metabolomics and 16S rRNA data revealed that Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium correlated with gamma-aminobutyric acid levels, reinforcing a link between microbial composition and emotional regulation.

Short-chain fatty acid signaling from the gut microbiome to the central nervous system is now recognized as a modifier of neuroinflammation, yet host genetic variation and diet-derived substrates jointly shape this axis. We examined whether FTO and BDNF variants alter responses to a high-fiber diet and omega-3 supplementation in adults with mild cognitive impairment. Over 12 weeks, participants received either a Mediterranean-style diet alone or combined with inulin and docosahexaenoic acid. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and circulating short-chain fatty acids were quantified. Mixed-effects models showed that APOE ε4 carriers exhibited greater microbial diversity increases and lower interleukin-6 after combined intervention. Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with improved hippocampal connectivity. Notably, baseline microbial composition explained 18% of the variance in cognitive response, independent of APOE genotype. These findings suggest that prebiotic and omega-3 co-supplementation may benefit individuals carrying specific APOE alleles, but the effects depend on baseline dietary patterns. This interaction among APOE, diet, and microbiome warrants confirmation in larger trials.

Microbial metabolites derived from gut microbiota shape central nervous system function, and their disruption is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD). In 84 adults with MDD and 42 healthy controls, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and random forest modeling to test whether probiotic supplementation alters the gut microbiota and tryptophan pathway metabolites. Baseline Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundance correlated inversely with depressive symptoms, whereas kynurenine, quinolinic acid, and short-chain fatty acids were altered. After 8 weeks, probiotics increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and reduced kynurenine; these shifts accompanied improved anxiety scores. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into mice reproduced the behavioral benefit, while antibiotic depletion abolished it. A classifier using microbial and metabolic features separated MDD patients from controls with an AUC of 0.81. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with probiotics may complement standard care in MDD, though larger trials with shotgun metagenomics are needed.

Maternal consumption of a high-fat diet during gestation reshapes the offspring gut microbiota and may alter brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR, we compared mice born to dams fed either standard chow or high-fat diet. High-fat diet offspring exhibited increased Firmicutes and reduced Bacteroidetes, elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and lower hippocampal BDNF expression relative to controls. These changes coincided with impaired blood-brain barrier integrity, increased interleukin-1β (IL-1β) in the brain, and poorer performance in the Morris water maze. Faecal short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate, were reduced and inversely correlated with Firmicutes. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored BDNF and normalized LPS, but did not fully reverse microbiota dysbiosis. Correlation analysis using Spearman correlation linked Firmicutes abundance to BDNF and IL-1β. These findings suggest that maternal high-fat diet-induced gut microbiota perturbations influence BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity, identifying a modifiable gut-brain axis pathway relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites shape brain function through immune, vagal, and endocrine routes, and their disruption has been linked to major depressive disorder and irritable bowel syndrome. To test whether probiotic supplementation can modify this axis, we randomized 84 adults with depression to a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and BDNF, IL6, and IDO1 expression was quantified in peripheral blood. Mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time interactions. Relative to placebo, probiotic-treated participants showed increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, higher butyrate levels, and reduced IL6 expression (p=0.02); BDNF and IDO1 did not differ. Depressive symptoms improved modestly, but the change was not statistically significant after correction. These findings suggest that probiotics can shift gut microbial composition and butyrate production, with limited downstream effects on BDNF and IDO1 in this cohort. Larger trials with metagenomics and metabolite profiling are needed to clarify strain-specific mechanisms.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the microbial and metabolic signals that link dietary fiber intake to BDNF expression in the hippocampus remain incompletely defined. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled fecal microbiota and butyrate levels in adults with MDD and healthy controls consuming either a high-fiber diet or a low-fiber diet. MDD was associated with reduced abundances of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium longum, lower butyrate concentrations, and decreased BDNF mRNA in peripheral blood. Dietary fiber intake correlated positively with Faecalibacterium abundance and butyrate levels, and butyrate was inversely associated with depressive symptoms. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber diet-fed donors increased Bdnf expression and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Machine-learning integration of microbial and clinical variables identified Faecalibacterium as a top predictor of BDNF expression. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-responsive gut bacteria may influence BDNF signaling and depressive symptoms through butyrate-dependent pathways.

Microbial metabolites produced by gut microbiota influence brain function, yet the specific bacterial taxa and host pathways linking microbial signals to mood regulation remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls and assessed depressive-like behavior after chronic stress using the forced swim test and sucrose preference test. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene revealed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in mice receiving depression-associated microbiota. These mice also showed lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces and decreased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Treating mice with fluoxetine normalized BDNF expression and reduced anxiety-like behavior, whereas probiotic supplementation only partially restored gut microbiota composition. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors reversed short-chain fatty acid deficits and attenuated depression-like phenotypes. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived metabolites regulate BDNF-dependent hippocampal plasticity and that microbial restoration may complement antidepressant therapy.

Consumption of fermentable fiber is associated with reduced age-related cognitive decline, yet the underlying microbiome and FFAR2-dependent mechanisms remain unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we profiled gut microbiome and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in older adults and mice colonized with human donor microbiota. Low fiber intake correlated with reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, lower butyrate, and worse cognitive impairment. In gnotobiotic mice, inulin supplementation restored butyrate levels, increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus, and reduced microglial activation; these effects required FFAR2 and were absent in FFAR2-deficient mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors with high fiber intake into mice partially recapitulated the Bdnf and neuroinflammation changes, whereas antibiotic treatment abolished them. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 38% of the association between fiber intake and cognitive decline. These findings position dietary fiber as a modifiable determinant of microbiome composition and gut-brain signaling, and identify FFAR2 as a candidate target for cognitive impairment.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet signatures that distinguish depressive symptoms from sleep disturbance remain unclear. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 68 adults, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to profile Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria. PERMANOVA and LEfSe tested associations between gut microbial composition and depressive symptoms, measured by PROMIS T-scores, and sleep disturbance, measured by PSQI. Lower Shannon diversity correlated with greater depressive symptoms (r = -0.34, p = 0.02), while β-diversity separated participants by sleep disturbance (weighted UniFrac, p = 0.04). Bacteroidetes were enriched in individuals without depressive symptoms, whereas Actinobacteria and Firmicutes were more abundant in those with depressive symptoms. No taxon reached significance for sleep disturbance after correction. These findings suggest that gut microbial diversity and specific taxa track with depressive symptoms more strongly than with sleep disturbance in adults, supporting further metagenomic and metabolomic studies to clarify mechanisms along the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate intestinal barrier integrity, vagal signaling, and central nervous system inflammation, positioning gut microbiota as a therapeutic target in neuropsychiatric disorders. This axis is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, anxiety, and Parkinson's disease, where microbial dysbiosis often precedes clinical diagnosis. In a randomized, double-blind trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received either probiotic supplementation plus fermented food or placebo for 12 weeks. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics quantified Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and tryptophan metabolites. Fecal calprotectin, zonulin, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified as secondary endpoints. Compared with placebo, the intervention increased microbial diversity, elevated butyrate, and reduced interleukin-6; mixed-effects modeling showed improved cognitive scores correlated with indole-3-propionic acid. Circulating lipopolysaccharide and tumor necrosis factor-alpha were also lower after the intervention. These findings suggest that combining probiotics with fermented foods may engage the microbiota-gut-brain axis to attenuate neuroinflammation and mitigate cognitive decline.

Gut microbiome dysbiosis and impaired intestinal permeability are emerging as early contributors to Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease, with microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide modulating neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier integrity. In older adults, higher intake of fermented foods and fiber-rich foods associates with greater Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower neuroinflammation markers, whereas ultra-processed foods correlate with Proteobacteria expansion and cognitive decline. We combined shotgun metagenomics with Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis to test whether APOE and TREM2 variants modify these diet-microbe-brain relationships. Data from prospective large-scale cohorts showed that dietary fiber was inversely associated with dementia risk, an effect partly mediated by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and butyrate; processed meats showed opposite trends. Mice colonized with microbiota from high-fiber donors displayed reduced amyloid-β deposition in the hippocampus. These findings support targeting dietary patterns and prebiotics to modulate the gut-brain axis, though randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm causality.

Microbial butyrate production is reduced in Parkinson's disease and correlates with BDNF expression in the brain, suggesting a tractable target for prebiotic intervention. We randomized 84 participants with Parkinson's disease to inulin or placebo for 12 weeks and profiled stool microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomics. Mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and levodopa dose. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and upregulated BDNF and IL-10 expression in peripheral blood. Shannon diversity was unchanged. To test causality, germ-free mice colonized with participant-derived microbiota received inulin or butyrate supplementation. Flow cytometry quantified Foxp3-positive T cells in the colon and spleen, while RNA-seq assessed BDNF, IL-10, and TNF in the striatum. Both interventions decreased TNF and increased IL-10, with false discovery rate correction controlling for multiple comparisons. Fecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations correlated inversely with motor impairment scores. These data support a microbiota-butyrate-BDNF axis that can be engaged by inulin.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids can reshape hippocampal BDNF expression and NLRP3 signaling, linking gut microbiota imbalance to cognitive decline. To test this, APP/PS1 mice received inulin or vehicle for 12 weeks, with fecal microbiota profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolites quantified via untargeted metabolomics. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and batch revealed that inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, elevated butyrate, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts in cortex. These changes correlated with improved Morris water maze performance and lower amyloid-β burden. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate explained 31% of the effect of Akkermansia on BDNF expression, while NLRP3 suppression partially mediated neuroinflammation. In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, baseline gut microbiota composition showed similar Bifidobacterium depletion and butyrate reduction, and random forest classifiers discriminated affected individuals from controls with moderate accuracy. Together, these findings position gut microbiota-derived metabolites as modulators of BDNF and NLRP3 pathways, suggesting that inulin and related prebiotics may help preserve brain function through the gut-brain axis.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are emerging as essential mediators of gut-brain axis signaling, but their causal contribution to stress-related psychiatric disorders remains unclear. We combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal microbiota transplantation, and targeted metabolomics in germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder and healthy controls. Inulin-type fructans selectively expanded Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, raised butyrate concentrations in the colon, and attenuated depressive-like behavior in the forced swim test. These changes coincided with reduced IL-6 and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium explained a substantial portion of the behavioral effect. In a pilot human cohort, inulin supplementation for 8 weeks improved depression scores and altered gut microbiota composition, though not all responders showed parallel BDNF changes. These findings support a causal, diet-modifiable route by which gut microbes influence brain function and suggest that prebiotic fibers may complement existing therapies for depression.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to Parkinson's disease progression, yet interventions targeting microbial short-chain fatty acid production remain limited. In a 12-week, double-blind trial, patients with Parkinson's disease received either a galacto-oligosaccharide supplement or placebo. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, and butyrate, propionate, and acetate were quantified in plasma. Motor severity was assessed with the MDS-UPDRS. Compared with placebo, supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate levels, and improved constipation and motor symptoms. Baseline microbial diversity did not differ between groups, but responders showed greater butyrate production after four weeks. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that changes in Faecalibacterium correlated with butyrate increases and motor improvement. PERMANOVA confirmed distinct microbial communities between groups, while Spearman correlation linked Bifidobacterium enrichment to reduced inflammatory cytokines. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that galacto-oligosaccharide supplementation may modulate the gut microbiota–brain axis and alleviate Parkinson's disease-related symptoms, warranting larger trials.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut bacteria yields short-chain fatty acids that shape microglial function and may modify Parkinson's disease progression. In a mouse model of α-synucleinopathy, a prebiotic high-fiber diet attenuated motor deficits and reduced α-synuclein aggregation within the substantia nigra. The gut microbiome shifted toward health-associated taxa, with Ruminococcus and Lactobacillus abundances correlating with improved outcomes. Single-cell RNA sequencing of midbrain microglia revealed suppressed pro-inflammatory programs and expanded disease-associated macrophage subsets in prebiotic-fed mice relative to standard-diet controls. Depleting microglia with a CSF1R inhibitor abolished these benefits, restoring motor impairment despite continued prebiotic intake. Parallel human cohort analyses showed that dietary fiber intake associates with distinct gut microbial composition and lower neuroinflammation markers, although causality remains unresolved. These findings position diet-microbiome-microglia signaling as a tractable axis for Parkinson's disease modification and support further randomized controlled trials of microbiota-directed nutrition. Mechanistically, butyrate and propionate enhanced Gpr109a-dependent signaling in brain myeloid cells, and Snca genotype influenced treatment response.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids shape central nervous system immune tone, yet the pathways linking gut microbiota composition to neuropsychiatric disease remain incompletely resolved. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder and mouse models, we integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and mediation analysis to test whether Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundance influences BDNF expression via butyrate. Probiotic supplementation increased butyrate and BDNF transcripts in hippocampus, while fluoxetine had no effect on Bacteroides. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Lactobacillus was associated with lower IL6 expression (β = -0.42, p = 0.003) and that BDNF mediated 31% of the association between microbial diversity and depressive symptoms. In mice fed high-fat diet, Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated inversely with TNF and anxiety-like behavior; PERMANOVA confirmed separation by microbial community. These findings position Lactobacillus-derived butyrate as a candidate signal in the gut-brain axis and support targeting gut microbiota to modulate BDNF and IL6.

Gut microbial tryptophan catabolites act as endocrine signals that shape hippocampal plasticity and affective behavior, yet the pathways linking dietary fat, microbiota, and BDNF expression remain incompletely resolved. Using male C57BL/6 mice randomized to high-fat diet or control chow, we performed fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice into antibiotic-depleted recipients. Novel object recognition and forced swim test revealed selective memory deficits and increased depressive-like behavior after high-fat diet microbiota colonization. 16S rRNA sequencing coupled with PERMANOVA and Spearman correlation identified Akkermansia muciniphila depletion and Romboutsia enrichment as taxa associated with serum lipopolysaccharide and hippocampal serotonin levels. In prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, IL-6, TNF-α, and BDNF transcripts showed coordinated changes, while western blot confirmed altered AKT/GSK-3β phosphorylation. Supplementation with probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially reversed these signatures and reduced neuroinflammation in mice. These data position gut microbiota as a modifiable node in the gut-brain axis, suggesting that microbial tryptophan metabolism may mediate obesity-related cognitive impairment and depression.

Diets enriched in fermented foods and fiber-rich plant foods can reshape gut microbiota and reduce depression-like behavior, yet the pathways linking microbial metabolites to central nervous system function remain incompletely resolved. In a randomized parallel-group study, adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received either a Mediterranean-style diet plus fermented food supplement or habitual diet for 10 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified fecal microbiota; plasma short-chain fatty acids, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, and inflammatory cytokines were measured. Mediation analysis tested whether microbial shifts explained symptom improvement. The intervention increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised butyrate and propionate, and lowered interleukin-6. Symptom scores decreased more in the intervention group, and mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium partially mediated this effect. These findings support dietary manipulation of the gut microbiome as a tractable strategy for stress-related psychiatric disorders, although confirmatory trials in animal models and diverse clinical populations are needed.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by the gut microbiota influence central nervous system immunity, and their depletion has been linked to major depressive disorder (MDD). Preclinical work in germ-free mice associates microbial colonization with BDNF and serotonin signaling, yet clinical evidence remains inconsistent. We examined whether inulin supplementation alters gut microbiota composition and BDNF expression in adults with MDD. In a double-blind crossover trial, 48 participants received inulin (12 g/day) or maltodextrin for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR quantified Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, and Akkermansia. Blood samples were analyzed for BDNF, IL6, and NLRP3 transcripts. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline severity, age, and antidepressant use. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance (log2 fold change 1.8; p=0.004) and reduced interleukin-6 concentrations (p=0.018), but did not alter BDNF expression. Changes in Faecalibacterium showed an inverse Spearman correlation with NLRP3 expression (rho=-0.42; p=0.012). These findings suggest that inulin engages microbiota-immune pathways without robust neurotrophic effects in MDD.

Dietary fiber fermentation in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that signal to the brain through vagal and endocrine routes, yet the microbial taxa and host genes mediating these effects remain incompletely resolved. We fed mice low- or high-fiber diets for 8 weeks and profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and hippocampal expression of BDNF, GR, and IL-6. Behavioral testing included open field, elevated plus maze, and fear conditioning. High-fiber feeding increased Akkermansia and Lactobacillus, elevated butyrate, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Microbial composition differed by fiber intake (PERMANOVA, R2=0.18, p=0.001). Using linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis, we found that butyrate explained 34% of the fiber effect on BDNF expression. Serum interleukin-6 and corticosterone were lower in high-fiber mice. No significant changes occurred in prefrontal cortex. These results position dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal and identify butyrate as a candidate mediator, warranting human trials.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) maintain intestinal barrier integrity and limit neuroinflammation, yet their causal role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains debated. We colonized germ-free APP/PS1 mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum and fed a high-fiber diet or Western diet for 16 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and butyrate in feces. Morris water maze assessed spatial memory, while immunofluorescence measured amyloid-β plaques in hippocampus. High-fiber feeding increased butyrate, enriched Lactobacillus, and upregulated tight junction protein ZO-1 and occludin in colon. It also reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression in brain and lowered amyloid-β burden. In contrast, Western diet expanded Bacteroides, depleted butyrate, and worsened memory. Random forest modeling linked Lactobacillus abundance to plaque load. Fecal microbiota from high-fiber mice transferred into antibiotic-treated recipients partially reproduced ZO-1 induction and reduced neuroinflammation, supporting a causal microbiota-gut-brain axis. These findings suggest that dietary fiber shapes gut microbiota metabolism to protect brain health, offering a plausible strategy for AD.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that shape microbiota-gut-brain signaling and may modify neurodegenerative disease risk. Using faecal metagenomics and targeted metabolomics in older adults, we found that low fiber intake was associated with reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, lower circulating butyrate, and mild cognitive impairment. In mice, butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and attenuated lipopolysaccharide-induced microglial activation. Mechanistically, butyrate promoted BDNF transcription via HDAC inhibition, whereas gram-negative taxa enriched in microbiota from low-fiber diets correlated with elevated endotoxin and TLR4 signaling in brain. In an independent cohort, higher fiber intake predicted slower cognitive decline over 6 years, and mediation analysis attributed part of this effect to butyrate. Faecal microbiota transplantation from donors consuming high-fiber diets into antibiotic-treated mice recapitulated these benefits, whereas broad-spectrum antibiotics abolished them. These results position microbial SCFAs as mediators linking diet to Bdnf-dependent hippocampal plasticity and suggest that fiber or SCFA-based interventions could complement existing therapies for cognitive decline.

The gut-brain axis integrates intestinal microbiota signals with central nervous system function, and disruptions in this dialogue are increasingly linked to anxiety, depression, and neurodevelopmental disorders. Gut microbes convert dietary fiber and fermented food components into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acids, and tryptophan metabolites that modulate vagal afferents, intestinal barrier integrity, and neuroinflammation. In gnotobiotic mice, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal metabolomics reveal that high-fat diet consumption reshapes microbial community structure, depletes Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, and reduces SCFA production. These shifts correlate with increased IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, alongside heightened depressive-like behavior. Conversely, prebiotic or probiotic supplementation, or fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors, can restore microbiota diversity and attenuate neurobehavioral deficits. However, meta-analysis of human trials shows heterogeneous effects, reflecting baseline microbiome composition, diet, and antibiotic exposure. Sex, age, and early-life antibiotic exposure further modify these trajectories, complicating translation from mice to patients. Integrating metagenomics with functional neuroimaging may identify actionable microbiome targets, but causal mechanisms require rodent models and longitudinal human cohorts.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber-rich foods yields short-chain fatty acids that modulate blood-brain barrier integrity and neuroinflammation, yet whether targeted probiotic supplementation augments these effects remains uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with mild cognitive impairment received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo while consuming a Mediterranean-style diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomics showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated butyrate in supplemented participants. These changes correlated with improved verbal learning test scores and reduced interleukin-6 levels. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid explained 31% of the cognitive benefit. Plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor increased only in the probiotic arm, and fecal microbiota transplantation into germ-free mice recapitulated the cognitive improvement. At baseline, lower fruit and vegetable intake and higher ultra-processed food consumption were associated with reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and propionate. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation, layered onto fiber-rich foods, may reshape the gut microbiome to support brain health.

Fermentable fiber supplementation reshapes the gut microbiota and reduces depressive symptoms, but the transcriptional pathways linking microbial butyrate production to BDNF signaling remain poorly defined. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 72 adults with mild-to-moderate major depressive disorder received inulin (12 g/day) or maltodextrin for 8 weeks. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; peripheral blood BDNF, IL-6, and IDO1 expression was quantified by quantitative PCR. Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-time interactions, with false discovery rate adjustment, and PERMANOVA assessed community composition. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and elevated fecal butyrate. Compared with placebo, inulin reduced IL-6 expression and increased BDNF expression; these changes correlated with decreased anhedonia scores. Plasma lipopolysaccharide and interleukin-6 concentrations decreased in the inulin arm, whereas IDO1 expression remained unchanged. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate increases partially mediated the BDNF response. These findings support targeted fiber supplementation as a tractable strategy to modulate gut-brain immune signaling in depression.

Dietary fiber and probiotic supplementation reshape gut microbiota and may influence neuropsychiatric disorders via the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized trial of adults with mild cognitive impairment, we tested whether a Mediterranean-style diet enriched with fermentable carbohydrates plus a multi-strain probiotic altered microbial taxa and short-chain fatty acid production. At baseline, participants showed low microbial diversity and elevated C-reactive protein. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, with reduced Prevotella. Linear mixed models linked these shifts to lower interleukin-6 and better cognitive scores. Butyrate concentrations correlated inversely with neuroinflammation markers. Fecal bile acid profiles also differed, with higher deoxycholic acid in responders. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii increased only in the probiotic arm, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood was higher, while IL1B expression decreased. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics may synergistically support microbiome homeostasis and brain health, though larger, adequately powered randomized trials are needed.

Fermented food intake and inulin supplementation can reshape the gut microbiome and improve cognitive flexibility in adults with mild cognitive impairment, yet the mediating microbial taxa remain uncertain. In a 12-week randomized trial, participants received either inulin plus fermented vegetables or placebo. Cognitive performance was assessed with a computerized neuropsychological battery, and fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Microbial community composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, PERMANOVA, and linear mixed-effects models. The intervention increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance and elevated butyrate, with parallel improvements in prefrontal cortex-dependent tasks. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate and Bifidobacterium explained part of the cognitive benefit, while APOE genotype did not modify the response. Fecal calprotectin decreased in the active arm, suggesting reduced intestinal inflammation. These findings support a microbiota-targeted dietary strategy, though larger trials are needed to confirm durability and long-term safety. No serious adverse events occurred during the trial.

Microbial-derived butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids influence BDNF signaling in the hippocampus, providing a mechanistic link between the gut microbiome and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To test whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation modifies this axis, we performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing and plasma metabolomics in 120 participants, including patients with AD and healthy controls. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial communities by group, and random forest classification identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila as discriminative taxa. Omega-3 supplementation was associated with higher butyrate levels and reduced APOE expression in patients, while mice receiving inulin showed increased Bifidobacterium and acetate, and reduced amyloid-beta deposition. Fecal lipopolysaccharide was lower in participants reporting dietary fiber intake, and linear mixed-effects models linked these changes to BDNF and TREM2 expression. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiota with omega-3 may modulate short-chain fatty acid production and BDNF signaling, offering a promising potential adjunct for AD. Future metagenomic studies should validate these interactions in larger cohorts.

Microbial metabolites generated from dietary fiber are increasingly recognized as modulators of hippocampal plasticity, yet how they engage brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling during chronic stress remains unclear. In male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress, we tested whether probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or a prebiotic fiber blend could attenuate depressive-like behavior. After four weeks, both interventions reduced immobility in the forced swim test and increased hippocampal BDNF expression relative to stressed controls. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed expanded Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus populations, accompanied by elevated short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate, in feces. Neither intervention altered body weight, but cecal acetate and propionate concentrations increased, and gut microbiota composition shifted toward putative butyrate-producing taxa. Spearman correlation linked butyrate concentrations with BDNF expression and anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that probiotics and fermentable fibers converge on microbiota-BDNF signaling to promote stress resilience, supporting psychobiotic strategies for mood disorders.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon yields short-chain fatty acids that influence BDNF expression and immune signaling, but whether these actions slow cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment is uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, adults aged 60–85 with metabolic syndrome and subjective memory complaints received either a high-fiber diet enriched with fermented foods or usual care. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundances were quantified. Cognitive performance was assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and a computerized memory battery. Between-group changes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The intervention increased butyrate-producing taxa and BDNF mRNA in peripheral blood, and improved delayed recall compared with control. Changes in F. prausnitzii correlated with BDNF expression and memory scores. These findings suggest that fiber- and fermentation-rich diets may modulate gut microbiota and gut-brain signaling and support cognition in at-risk older adults, though larger trials are needed.

Western diet consumption disrupts gut microbiota and impairs hippocampal plasticity, yet whether inulin supplementation can reverse these effects remains unclear. In male C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet for 16 weeks, inulin (10% w/w) restored gut microbiota diversity, increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundance, and elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces. Behavioral testing using Morris water maze and novel object recognition revealed that inulin improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior. 16S rRNA sequencing coupled with PERMANOVA and Shannon diversity analyses confirmed diet-dependent microbiota restructuring. Inulin also lowered interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in serum and hippocampus, and upregulated BDNF expression. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into germ-free mice partially reproduced these benefits, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished them. Untargeted metabolomics further linked butyrate and propionate to improved hippocampal BDNF signaling. These findings indicate that inulin mitigates high-fat diet-induced cognitive impairment through gut microbiota-brain signaling, supporting prebiotic fiber as a therapeutic strategy for metabolic encephalopathy.

Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) sustain BDNF expression in the hippocampus and restrain neuroinflammation, providing a mechanistic bridge between dietary fiber intake and depressive symptoms. To test whether this axis is disrupted in major depressive disorder (MDD), we profiled gut microbiota and fecal metabolites in 120 adults with MDD and 120 healthy controls using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila were depleted in MDD and correlated with lower butyrate and indole-3-propionate. Mediation models showed that butyrate explained 18% of the association between fiber-rich food consumption and BDNF expression in peripheral blood; linear mixed models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use. In a subset, inulin supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced IL6 expression, but did not alter depressive symptoms. These findings position gut microbiota and microbial SCFAs as modifiable mediators of diet-microbiome interactions in MDD, though clinical benefit may require longer or combined interventions.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber is a plausible mediator of gut microbiota-brain signaling, but its association with BDNF regulation in depression remains unclear. Although faecal metagenomics has implicated several microbial taxa, few studies have linked dietary substrates to BDNF in the same patients. In a cross-sectional cohort of 184 adults, we used 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to quantify faecal microbiota and short-chain fatty acids. Participants with major depressive disorder showed lower Faecalibacterium abundance, reduced butyrate concentrations, and decreased BDNF serum levels relative to controls. Fiber intake correlated positively with Faecalibacterium and butyrate only in controls. Using random forest models, butyrate and Faecalibacterium explained 31% of the variance in BDNF after adjustment for age, sex, and antidepressant use. In mice receiving patient-derived microbiota, butyrate supplementation restored BDNF expression in the hippocampus and reduced depressive-like behavior. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-dependent microbial butyrate production may influence BDNF-related brain plasticity, identifying a modifiable axis for depression.

Altered gut microbiota composition in major depressive disorder is accompanied by reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Lactobacillus abundance, suggesting that microbial pathways contribute to depression rather than merely reflecting it. In a random-effects meta-analysis of adults with depression, probiotic supplementation reduced symptom severity compared with control, although heterogeneity was high and strain-specific effects were evident. Mechanistic studies in mice show that probiotics can increase short-chain fatty acid production, strengthen intestinal barrier function, and modulate brain regions involved in mood regulation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and machine learning classifiers have identified microbial signatures that distinguish responders from nonresponders, but these findings require validation in larger cohorts. Prebiotics and synbiotics may offer complementary strategies by selectively promoting beneficial bacteria, particularly when combined with fermented foods and dietary fiber. These effects are not uniform; dietary patterns and antibiotic exposure modify outcomes. Because diet, antidepressants, and baseline microbiota diversity interact, clinical translation will depend on stratified designs, standardized probiotic formulations, and longitudinal sampling of the gut-brain axis.

Administration of probiotic formulations enriched with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium has been associated with reduced depression and anxiety symptoms in adults, an effect partially mediated by shifts in gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production. To test this, patients with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo for 8 weeks; fecal microbiota was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Compared with placebo, probiotic supplementation increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, elevated butyrate levels, and lowered depression severity scores. These changes correlated with reduced inflammatory cytokines and improved intestinal barrier markers. Because gut microbiota communicates with the central nervous system via vagus nerve signaling and microbial metabolites, these results reinforce the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target. The findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through probiotics may offer an adjunctive strategy for depression, though larger trials with shotgun metagenomics, metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation in rodent models are needed to identify causal taxa and microbial genes.

Fermented foods and probiotic supplements can shift gut microbiota composition and alter short-chain fatty acid production, yet whether these changes causally reduce anxiety and depression remains uncertain. Using a randomized mouse model of chronic unpredictable stress, we combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation to track microbial and metabolic responses to a fermented milk diet supplemented with Bifidobacterium breve. B. breve colonization increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance, elevated butyrate and indole-3-propionate in the colon, and lowered corticosterone and interleukin-6 in serum. These peripheral shifts accompanied reduced depressive-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Dietary fiber alone did not reproduce these effects, whereas co-administration with inulin enhanced butyrate and BDNF responses. Mediation analysis linked Bifidobacterium abundance to BDNF through butyrate, suggesting that fermented food plus probiotic strategies may engage the gut-brain axis. These findings support dietary modulation of the microbiome as a potential adjunct for stress-related disorders, though human trials are needed to confirm causality.
