Microbial metabolites generated from dietary fibre, especially butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids, influence central nervous system function through vagal afferents, the enteric nervous system, and systemic immune signalling. In patients with Parkinson's disease, gut microbiota composition shifts, including reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, correlate with motor severity and SNCA expression. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and faecal microbiota transplantation have begun to clarify whether these associations are causal. A Mendelian randomization analysis using large-scale genetic data found that genetically predicted gut microbiome features were linked to Alzheimer's disease risk, while a random-effects meta-analysis of mouse models showed that probiotic administration reduced amyloid-beta burden and cytokine levels. Butyrate-producing taxa, such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, are often depleted in irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder, and faecal metabolomics has linked these losses to altered tryptophan metabolism. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with fermented foods or dietary supplements may complement levodopa and support brain health, although human trial heterogeneity remains a major challenge.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence brain function and depression-like behavior. Whether high-fat diet reverses this protective signaling through gut microbiota remains unclear. Male C57BL/6 mice were fed either a high-fat diet or standard chow for 12 weeks, with or without prebiotic inulin. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that high-fat diet reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus abundance, while increasing Bacteroides. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fat diet-fed mice into antibiotic-treated mice increased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha in the hippocampus, reduced Bdnf expression, and produced anhedonia. Behavioral testing confirmed increased anxiety-like behavior. In contrast, inulin restored butyrate and propionate levels, attenuated neuroinflammation, and normalized depressive phenotypes. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished these benefits, implicating the vagus nerve. Spearman correlation linked A. muciniphila abundance to butyrate concentrations and depression scores. These findings indicate that dietary fiber and prebiotics counteract high-fat diet-induced mood disorders via microbiota-derived SCFAs and gut-brain signaling.

Microbial tryptophan catabolism along the gut-brain axis has emerged as a modifier of depression-like behavior, yet whether gut microbiota composition predicts BDNF expression in the hippocampus remains unresolved. In male C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress, 16S rRNA gene sequencing of feces revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative to non-stressed controls. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) linked these shifts to interleukin-6 and kynurenine levels. Linear mixed-effects models showed that Lactobacillus abundance predicted BDNF mRNA in the hippocampus (β = 0.42, P = 0.008) and IDO1 expression (β = -0.37, P = 0.014), while Bifidobacterium correlated with 5-hydroxytryptamine turnover. Random forest classification identified Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium as top discriminators of stress exposure. Behavioral assessment using the forced swim test confirmed increased immobility in stressed mice. Supplementation with fructo-oligosaccharides restored Lactobacillus, increased BDNF, and reduced corticosterone, but not IDO1. Mediation analysis estimated that Lactobacillus explained 31% of the stress-induced BDNF decrease. These findings suggest that microbiota-dependent BDNF regulation may mediate stress resilience and identify prebiotic targets for depression.

Gut microbiome composition diverges between patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and healthy controls, yet host genetic mediators remain poorly defined. In a Chinese cohort with paired stool metagenomes and host genomics, linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) and genome-wide association analysis identified microbial taxa and loci associated with depression. Actinobacteria and Pseudomonades were enriched in MDD patients; alpha diversity differed significantly, whereas beta diversity did not. Host–microbial associations emerged, including beta diversity with rs6108 and Actinobacteria with rs77379751. A Romboutsia species co-associated with Ruminococcus gnavus through METTL8, ITGB2, OTULIN, and PROSER3. These findings suggest that gut microbiome diversity may affect expression of SERPINA5 and spatially proximal genes in the brain. The work links depression with the gut microbiome in Asian, Chinese people, potentially through host genes and regulatory pathways. This integrative analysis underscores the value of combining microbial and host genomic data to dissect psychiatric disorders and may guide future microbiome-targeted interventions.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber traverse the intestinal barrier, modulate central nervous system immune signaling, and position the gut microbiota as a modifiable node in the gut-brain axis. In a two-year longitudinal cohort of older adults (n=184), adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet correlated with higher fecal abundance of Lachnospiraceae and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and with circulating butyrate. Using causal mediation analysis, we estimated that short-chain fatty acids explained 31% of the inverse association between plant-rich food intake and mild cognitive impairment. Shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of butyrate kinase and butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase pathways in participants with stable cognition, whereas 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing alone did not separate cognitive trajectories. A randomized crossover trial of inulin and polyphenol supplementation is now testing whether these microbial shifts alter neuroimaging markers of Alzheimer's disease progression. These findings support a model in which interactions between diet and the microbiome, rather than single bacterial taxa, influence neurodegeneration and suggest that longitudinal mediation models can guide precision nutrition trials.

Dietary patterns enriched in fermented foods and dietary fiber can reshape gut microbiota and modulate central nervous system function through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. In a randomized human cohort, increased consumption of polyphenol-rich berries elevated short-chain fatty acid producers and reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide, paralleling improved mild cognitive impairment scores. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, taxa linked to intestinal barrier integrity. These microbial shifts were associated with upregulated BDNF expression and reduced IL6 transcription in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Functional magnetic resonance imaging showed altered hippocampal connectivity, while vagotomy in mice abolished the cognitive benefit, implicating vagal signaling. Probiotic supplementation with Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus replicated part of the effect, but only when combined with fermentable fiber. These findings suggest that diet can act as a gut-brain axis modulator, with BDNF and inflammatory pathways as candidate mediators. However, causality and dose-response remain unresolved, and larger human trials with standardized dietary interventions are needed.

Consumption of fermented foods and dietary fiber is associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved hippocampal function in rodent models, but the mechanisms linking gut microbiota to BDNF expression remain incompletely resolved. We colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, then fed them a high-fiber diet or Western diet for 8 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and RNA sequencing showed that fiber increased short-chain fatty acid producers and upregulated Bdnf and Gabbr1 in the prefrontal cortex. Linear mixed models revealed that butyrate mediated the association between Clostridium butyricum abundance and Bdnf expression. In patients with mild cognitive impairment, a fiber supplement increased gut microbial diversity and reduced IL-6. In APOE4 carriers, fiber supplementation produced weaker BDNF induction and greater IL-1β reduction. Notably, fecal microbiota transplantation from donor mice fed a high-fiber diet into recipient mice partially recapitulated the Bdnf increase and reversed cognitive impairment, supporting a causal microbiota-dependent route. These findings position fermentable fiber as a plausible gut-brain intervention, with BDNF signaling as a candidate mediator.

Altered gut microbiota composition is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, yet the taxonomic and functional signatures that distinguish patients from healthy controls remain inconsistent across cohorts. We recruited 120 adults and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, with shotgun metagenomics in a subset. Plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, interleukin-6, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified alongside PERMANOVA and random forest classification. Compared with controls, patients showed reduced Faecalibacterium and Coprococcus and enriched Bacteroides. Linear mixed-effects models linked Faecalibacterium abundance to lower interleukin-6 and higher brain-derived neurotrophic factor. A random forest model distinguished groups with an area under the curve of 0.78. Bacteroides-derived propionate was inversely associated with depression severity. Mediation analysis indicated that interleukin-6 accounted for 22% of the association between Faecalibacterium and depression severity. These findings suggest that gut microbiome composition, rather than a single taxon, contributes to inflammatory and neurotrophic pathways in major depressive disorder, and support targeting microbial communities in future gut-brain axis interventions.

Alterations in the gut microbiota can precede Alzheimer's disease (AD) and may amplify neuroinflammation through short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and lipopolysaccharide signaling along the vagus nerve. In APPswe/PS1dE9 mice, depletion of gut microbiota altered Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and increased amyloid-beta deposition, whereas colonization with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium reduced cognitive impairment. Human cohorts show that APOE ε4 carriers exhibit distinct fecal microbiome profiles and elevated trimethylamine N-oxide, linking gut microbiota metabolism to AD risk. Dietary interventions that restore butyrate-producing bacteria may therefore modify AD trajectory. We tested whether a multispecies probiotic supplement combined with omega-3 fatty acids could modulate APOE-related microbiome composition and cognitive decline in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and fecal metagenomics, we found that supplementation increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and butyrate production, with mixed-effects models showing improved memory scores in carriers of APOE ε4. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic and omega-3 supplementation may act through microbiome-derived signals to attenuate AD-associated neuroinflammation.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota precedes and accompanies major depressive disorder (MDD), yet causal evidence from patients remains scarce. In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, adults with MDD received either fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) or placebo enema for four consecutive days. Gut microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were quantified in feces. Depressive symptoms were measured with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale at baseline and week 8. Compared with placebo, FMT increased microbial diversity and SCFA producers, including Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, and reduced depression severity. Linear mixed-effects models showed a significant group-by-time interaction (p=0.01). False discovery rate correction was applied to differential abundance testing. Clinical response, defined as ≥50% reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score, occurred in 6 of 10 recipients of FMT versus 1 of 5 placebo recipients. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings support the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target and justify larger trials of FMT in MDD.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the dietary and microbial signals that shape this gut-brain axis remain incompletely defined. We profiled stool samples from 120 adults, including 60 with major depressive disorder and 60 healthy controls, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. Dietary intake was assessed with a validated Mediterranean diet score and fermented food frequency questionnaire. Relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium was lower in depression, while Bacteroides was enriched. These taxa correlated with short-chain fatty acid concentrations and BDNF expression. Fecal butyrate was lower in depression and inversely correlated with anxiety scores. Using PERMANOVA and linear mixed models, Mediterranean diet adherence explained 12% of microbiome variance, and higher fermented food intake was associated with increased Lactobacillus and reduced depressive symptoms. Random forest classification distinguished cases from controls with an area under the curve of 0.78. In mice, fecal microbiota transplantation from high fermented food consumers increased Lactobacillus and normalized serotonin levels. These findings suggest that diet interventions targeting gut microbiota may modulate depression through gut-brain signaling pathways.

Dietary fiber fermentation by gut microbiota yields short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate central nervous system immune tone and intestinal barrier integrity, yet the extent to which prebiotic supplementation reproduces these effects in adults with mild cognitive impairment remains unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 80 participants received either inulin (10 g/day) or placebo for 12 weeks while maintaining habitual diets. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial community structure and fecal SCFAs; functional magnetic resonance imaging assessed brain network connectivity. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance, raised butyrate and propionate concentrations, and linear mixed-effects models revealed improved executive function relative to placebo. Changes in butyrate correlated with reduced IL-6 expression and altered default-mode network connectivity. These findings suggest that prebiotic fibers can shift the gut microbiome toward a SCFA-enriched profile linked to brain function, supporting dietary fiber as a modifiable gut-brain axis target. No serious adverse events were reported, and compliance exceeded 90%.

Greater consumption of fermentable dietary fiber is associated with lower circulating inflammatory markers and fewer depressive symptoms, yet the microbial pathways linking diet to mood remain incompletely resolved. In a cross-sectional cohort of 180 adults, diet was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire, and we profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified fecal short-chain fatty acids. Using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and antidepressant use, each 10-g increase in fiber intake corresponded to higher Faecalibacterium abundance and greater butyrate concentrations. A mediation analysis suggested that butyrate explained 22% of the inverse association between fiber and depression scores. Faecalibacterium abundance also correlated inversely with interleukin-6, while no independent relationship was observed for Bacteroides. Fecal propionate and acetate showed weaker, non-significant trends. These findings support prebiotic or fiber-rich diets as candidate strategies for modulating the gut microbiota and reducing depressive symptoms, though randomized controlled trials are needed to establish causality.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat, low-fiber diet depletes Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus within the gut microbiota, driving neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment through gut-brain axis dysfunction. To test whether this trajectory is reversible, male C57BL/6 mice received a high-fat diet with or without inulin for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that inulin restored Bifidobacterium abundance and increased short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces and serum. In the Morris water maze, inulin-supplemented mice showed shorter escape latencies and more platform crossings than high-fat diet-fed controls. Hippocampal transcriptomics linked these gains to reduced expression of Il1b and Tnf and increased Bdnf. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-fed donors into germ-free recipients partially reproduced the cognitive benefit, whereas antibiotic depletion abolished it. Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed that these microbial and behavioral shifts were independent of body weight. These findings suggest that inulin reshapes the gut microbiome to attenuate diet-induced cognitive decline, warranting validation in patients with mild cognitive impairment.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations influence central nervous system signaling, yet whether dietary inulin plus probiotic supplementation alters major depressive disorder (MDD) outcomes through gut microbiota shifts is uncertain. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, 84 adults with MDD received either inulin plus a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus or a control condition. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial composition and SCFAs. Depression severity was assessed with the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. We used linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction and mediation analysis. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations, and reduced depressive symptoms versus control. These clinical effects were accompanied by increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and propionate concentrations. Changes in butyrate mediated 31% of the clinical improvement. These findings suggest that targeting the gut microbiome with inulin and probiotics may offer adjunctive benefit in MDD, though larger trials are needed.

Alterations in the gut microbiota are increasingly linked to neuropsychiatric disorders and neurodegeneration, yet diet-derived strategies that engage the gut-brain axis remain poorly defined. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild cognitive impairment received a Mediterranean-style diet alone or combined with a multi-strain probiotic supplement for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and plasma short-chain fatty acids and brain-derived neurotrophic factor were quantified. The supplemented group showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, higher butyrate concentrations, and reduced systemic inflammation compared with diet alone. These shifts correlated with improved cognitive performance and lower depressive symptoms, although mixed-effects models revealed that baseline microbial diversity moderated the response. Elevated interleukin-6 and lipopolysaccharide at baseline were associated with weaker responses, suggesting that low-grade inflammation may blunt diet–microbiota interactions. The findings suggest that combining Mediterranean-style diet with probiotics may amplify gut-brain benefits, but larger trials with shotgun metagenomics and longer follow-up are needed to confirm causality.

Dietary fiber-derived short-chain fatty acids shape brain function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes, yet how diet recalibrates this dialogue remains incompletely defined. In a randomized adult cohort, we tested whether a prebiotic fiber supplement alters gut microbiota composition, butyrate production, and BDNF expression in peripheral blood. Participants receiving the supplement showed increased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, elevated butyrate concentrations, and higher BDNF transcript levels compared with controls. These changes coincided with reduced neuroinflammation markers and improved cognitive scores. A parallel mouse model confirmed that butyrate administration recapitulated the BDNF response, whereas vagotomy attenuated it, implicating vagus nerve signaling. Notably, fermented foods and fiber-rich foods produced overlapping microbial shifts, but the isolated prebiotic was sufficient to alter BDNF expression. These findings position gut microbiota-derived butyrate as a key mediator linking prebiotic intake to BDNF-dependent brain plasticity, suggesting that targeted supplementation may complement dietary strategies for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Microbial short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites act as key transducers of gut microbiota–brain signaling, yet their causal contribution to stress-related psychiatric disorders remains contested. We colonized germ-free C57BL/6 mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or from healthy controls and supplemented half of each group with the prebiotic inulin. After 6 weeks, mice underwent 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, behavioral testing, and hippocampal transcriptomics. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures by donor and diet, while random forest identified Bacteroides and Lactobacillus as top discriminators. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium, raised butyrate in the colon, and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice receiving patient microbiota. These effects coincided with normalized BDNF and IL-6 expression in the hippocampus and lower corticosterone. No significant changes in body weight or colitis severity were observed. Linear mixed-effects models linked butyrate availability to BDNF expression and anxiety-like behavior, suggesting that inulin may buffer depression-associated dysbiosis through microbiota-derived butyrate, offering a testable strategy for patients.

Disruption of the gut microbiota–brain axis contributes to depression and cognitive impairment, yet whether probiotic supplementation can reverse these effects remains uncertain. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, adults with major depressive disorder received either a multi-strain probiotic containing Lactobacillus helveticus and Bifidobacterium longum or placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that treatment increased gut microbial diversity and relative abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Linear mixed-effects models revealed greater reductions in depressive symptoms and inflammatory cytokines in the probiotic group, and mediation analysis attributed 31% of the clinical improvement to changes in microbial composition. Fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated participants into mice reduced anxiety-like behavior and increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These mechanistic results suggest that probiotics can modulate the gut microbiome to improve depression-related outcomes, but confirmatory randomized trials using shotgun metagenomics and standardized causal mediation analyses are needed.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production is a key determinant of BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota composition to depression-related behavior. In a randomized controlled trial, adults with low dietary fiber intake received a probiotic consortium or placebo for 8 weeks; 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics quantified Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, while qPCR measured BDNF, IL6, and TLR4 transcripts in peripheral blood. Mixed-effects models showed that probiotic supplementation increased butyrate producers and reduced lipopolysaccharide binding protein; these shifts correlated with lower depressive symptoms scores and higher BDNF expression. Fermented foods and fiber may therefore enhance microbiota-derived signaling along this axis, but effects depend on baseline microbiome diversity and COMT genotype. In mice fed a high-fat diet, fecal microbiota transplantation from responders recapitulated the butyrate-dependent increase in BDNF and reduced activation of microglia. These findings support targeting BDNF-related pathways through diet and probiotics in patients with metabolic and mood disorders.

Gut microbial metabolism of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids that shape central nervous system function through immune, endocrine, and neural routes. In germ-free mice colonized with Akkermansia muciniphila, butyrate increased Bdnf expression in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Notably, subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the behavioral benefits, implicating vagus nerve signaling in microbiota-gut-brain communication. 16S rRNA gene sequencing combined with fecal microbiota transplantation revealed that whole-grain oats enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while gut microbiota from healthy donors improved intestinal permeability in mice. Sodium butyrate supplementation upregulated Tjp1 and Ocln, strengthening tight junctions, and lowered circulating lipopolysaccharide. In a randomized controlled trial, adults consuming fermented barley showed increased microbial diversity and decreased interleukin-6 compared with controls. These findings position microbial metabolites as mediators linking diet, gut ecology, and brain health, suggesting that targeting Bdnf-related pathways via prebiotic fiber may complement existing antidepressant therapies. However, causal direction and dose-response relationships require further metagenomic and metabolomic analyses.

Microbial short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber is increasingly linked to prefrontal cortex function and anxiety-like behavior. We colonized germ-free mice with Bacteroides fragilis or Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fed them a low-fiber diet or inulin for 6 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed-effects models showed that inulin increased gut microbial diversity and butyrate concentrations. Fecal short-chain fatty acid ratios and GPR43 expression in colon differed between mice receiving inulin and low-fiber diet. In healthy adults, a parallel cohort received inulin or placebo; functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed altered amygdala reactivity. Expression of BDNF and GABA receptor subunits in hippocampus correlated with butyrate levels. Mediation analysis suggested that microbiota-derived butyrate partially mediated the association between inulin and anxiety symptoms. Spearman correlation linked microbial composition to amygdala response, while BDNF methylation moderated the effect. These findings position fermentable fiber as a modifiable gut-brain signal, although effects varied by baseline microbiome composition and BDNF genotype.

Microbial conversion of dietary choline and L-carnitine to trimethylamine, followed by hepatic FMO3-mediated oxidation to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), links gut microbial composition to cerebrovascular injury and cognitive decline. Whether this pathway explains variation in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remains uncertain. We profiled fecal microbiota and plasma TMAO in 240 older adults (120 with MCI, 120 cognitively normal controls) using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, education, and cardiometabolic covariates; mediation analysis tested indirect effects through TMAO. Bacteroides and Clostridium genera were enriched in participants with MCI, whereas Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was depleted. Higher TMAO associated with greater odds of MCI (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.15–1.76 per SD) and lower hippocampal volume. Microbial choline utilization explained 18% of the TMAO–MCI association. These findings position TMAO as a modifiable microbiota-dependent mediator and suggest that targeting dietary choline intake or FMO3 activity may reduce cognitive decline.

Alterations in gut microbial communities can precede depressive-like behavior, suggesting that microbial signals converge on brain circuits through immune and metabolic routes. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal slurries from adults reporting high or low dietary fiber intake and supplemented half of each group with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that Lactobacillus and Bacteroides abundances tracked with short-chain fatty acid production, while omega-3 increased docosahexaenoic acid in plasma. Mice receiving low-fiber microbiota showed elevated interleukin-6 and reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in hippocampus; these effects were attenuated by omega-3 supplementation. Linear mixed-effects models linked Faecalibacterium prausnitzii to lower anxiety scores and higher serotonin turnover. In a separate human cohort, shotgun metagenomics confirmed that Bacteroides and Lactobacillus were associated with fiber-rich diets. Collectively, these findings indicate that diet-driven microbiome remodeling, modified by omega-3, influences gut-brain signaling and may offer a target for stress-related disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to depression, yet the microbial signals that impinge on brain reward circuits remain poorly defined. We colonized germ-free mice with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder or healthy controls and assessed depressive-like behavior, tryptophan metabolites, and BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex. Microbiota composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Mice receiving patient-derived microbiota showed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, elevated kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, and lower BDNF and NR2A transcripts. These changes were accompanied by increased anhedonia and despair-like behavior. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy attenuated the behavioral and BDNF changes, implicating the vagus nerve. Treatment with fluoxetine or the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially normalized BDNF expression and behavior. Mediation analysis using bootstrap resampling indicated that kynurenine pathway activity mediated the microbiota-behavior association. These findings identify a BDNF-dependent, microbiota-vagus circuit underlying depression-like phenotypes and support targeting gut microbiota in humans.

Microbial metabolites derived from dietary fiber and polyphenol-rich foods can reshape gut microbiota composition and influence central nervous system function through the gut-brain axis. In a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received either a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus or control, alongside standardized fermented food and fiber-rich diet counseling. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry quantified microbial diversity and short-chain fatty acids in stool and serum at baseline and endpoint. Compared with control, active supplementation increased gut microbial alpha diversity and butyrate levels, and reduced anhedonia scores. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 31% of the improvement in depressive symptoms. Changes in microbial composition correlated with butyrate availability and anhedonia improvement. No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that combining probiotic supplementation with fermentable fiber may modulate gut microbiota and gut-brain signaling, alleviating mood symptoms, though larger trials are needed.

Reduced gut microbial diversity and altered Prevotella/Bacteroides ratios have been linked to major depressive disorder, but whether these associations are causal or reflect confounding by chronic inflammation remains debated. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and Mendelian randomization, we examined BDNF expression, short-chain fatty acid profiles, and depressive symptoms in adults. Participants with low butyrate producers showed higher anxiety scores and lower BDNF transcription in prefrontal cortex-derived induced pluripotent stem cell models. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum was administered for 8 weeks. Compared with placebo, the probiotic group exhibited increased microbial diversity, elevated butyrate, and reduced depression severity. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate partially mediated the effect of Bifidobacterium on BDNF expression. In mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress, the same probiotic attenuated depressive-like behavior and restored BDNF in the hippocampus. These findings support a microbiota-gut-brain mechanism in which probiotics modulate BDNF via short-chain fatty acids, though larger trials with shotgun metagenomics are needed.

Microbial tryptophan catabolites act as signaling intermediaries that couple gut microbiota metabolism to central nervous system function, yet the transcriptional programs translating these cues in the brain remain incompletely defined. We colonized germ-free mice with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bacteroides fragilis, then performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and RNA sequencing of the hippocampus. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis linked a microbial indole-3-lactic acid signature to a module enriched for Bdnf, Arc, and Fos; Bdnf expression was reduced in colonized mice relative to gnotobiotic controls. In parallel, adults with major depressive disorder showed lower fecal indole-3-lactic acid and higher BDNF methylation in blood than healthy volunteers. Fecal short-chain fatty acids were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; these associations were independent of antibiotic use and probiotic intake. Morris water maze testing revealed impaired spatial memory after L. rhamnosus monocolonization, an effect attenuated by fluoxetine. These findings identify a Bdnf-centered hippocampal program through which gut microbes and their metabolites may influence depression-relevant behavior.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking gut microbiota composition to affective behavior. In a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder and matched controls, we profiled fecal microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantified plasma inflammatory cytokines. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and antidepressant use revealed that Faecalibacterium abundance was inversely associated with depression severity and positively correlated with BDNF transcript levels. Bacteroides and Alistipes were enriched in cases, whereas Roseburia and Coprococcus were depleted. Random forest classification discriminated patients from controls with moderate accuracy, implicating microbial TLR4 signaling and tryptophan metabolism. In mice, transplantation of patient microbiota reduced BDNF and increased anxiety-like behavior, effects attenuated by omega-3 supplementation. Mediation analysis suggested that butyrate production partially explained the association between Roseburia and BDNF. No significant differences were observed for COMT or 5-HTTLPR genotypes. These findings support a causal axis in which dietary fiber and psychobiotic taxa may stabilize the gut microbiota.

Disruption of the gut microbiota by antibiotics during a critical developmental window exacerbates Alzheimer's disease-like amyloid pathology in APP/PS1 mice, whereas dietary inulin restores microbial short-chain fatty acid production and mitigates cognitive decline. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, we found that inulin enriched Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, increased butyrate, and suppressed IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus. Morris water maze testing revealed improved spatial memory, and flow cytometry showed reduced neuroinflammation. Mediation analysis linked butyrate levels to BDNF upregulation and plaque burden. Fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into germ-free mice transferred the protective phenotype, with increased Bifidobacterium and butyrate in cecal microbiota. In human fecal samples, baseline butyrate correlated inversely with neuroinflammation markers. Notably, the APOE4 allele attenuated the butyrate-mediated suppression of IL-1β in cortical tissues. These findings position microbiota-derived metabolites as modifiable mediators of neuroinflammation in AD, suggesting that prebiotic fiber supplementation may complement cholinesterase inhibitors.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) act as central relays between the gut microbiota and central nervous system, yet their causal contribution to neuropsychiatric disorders remains unresolved. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and fecal microbiota transplantation into gnotobiotic mice, we examined whether dietary fiber and fermented foods reshape gut microbial communities and alter BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Mice colonized with microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder displayed reduced butyrate production, increased lipopolysaccharide translocation, and impaired blood-brain barrier integrity. Supplementation with probiotics or fiber-rich diets restored Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, elevated SCFAs, and normalized depressive-like behavior. RNA sequencing of prefrontal cortex revealed that these interventions reversed IL-6 and NF-κB signaling. In parallel, metagenomic sequencing coupled with PERMANOVA showed that baseline microbial composition explained 34% of the variance in depressive-like behavior. This effect was abolished in mice depleted of microbiota with antibiotics and restored by butyrate supplementation. These findings position dietary substrates and gut microbes as tractable modulators of brain function, with implications for gut-brain axis disorders.

Disruption of the gut microbiome is increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), with short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan catabolites, and lipopolysaccharide acting as candidate mediators of gut-brain signaling. In a cohort of 312 adults, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed reduced Faecalibacterium and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower butyrate levels in depression compared with healthy controls. Mediation analysis indicated that butyrate accounted for 18% of the association between Faecalibacterium and depressive symptoms. In a parallel mouse model, multi-strain probiotic supplementation restored butyrate production, normalized lipopolysaccharide translocation, and reduced anxiety-like behavior. Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed donors into germ-free mice recapitulated social avoidance, whereas probiotic treatment attenuated this phenotype. Mendelian randomization using GWAS data supported a protective causal effect of genetically predicted butyrate on MDD. These findings position microbial butyrate as a mechanistic link in the gut-brain axis and suggest that probiotics may complement existing antidepressant therapies, though larger randomized controlled trials are needed.

Consumption of dietary fiber and fermented foods reshapes the gut microbiome and may buffer neurodegenerative disease through immune, metabolic, and neural routes. In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a 12-week randomized trial of high-fiber diet increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, raised fecal short-chain fatty acids, and improved Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores. We used shotgun metagenomic sequencing and RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells to identify mediators. Dietary response correlated with BDNF expression and IL-6 suppression; APOE genotype modified the effect, with APOE4 carriers showing weaker microbiota shifts. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders into germ-free mice improved hippocampal Bdnf expression and reduced neuroinflammation. Metabolomic profiling further linked bile acids and tryptophan derivatives to microbial changes. Baseline gut microbiota diversity predicted response, while LBP expression decreased in responders. These findings suggest that fiber-rich diets act on the gut-brain axis in a APOE-dependent manner, and that microbial signatures could guide precision nutrition for cognitive decline.

Consumption of a Western-style diet rapidly reshapes the gut microbiota and disrupts gut-brain signaling, yet the microbial metabolites linking dietary patterns to affective behavior remain poorly resolved. In mice fed either high-fat, high-sucrose chow or standard chow for 12 weeks, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed broad microbial community shifts, including depletion of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and expansion of Clostridiales. Fecal short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline body weight showed that butyrate and indole-3-propionate were inversely associated with anxiety-like behavior, whereas kynurenine tracked positively with neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Mediation analysis indicated that microbial composition accounted for 31% of the variance in BDNF expression linked to diet. These findings position microbial metabolites as candidate mediators through which diet modifies gut-brain function and suggest that prebiotic or probiotic interventions may buffer diet-induced affective dysfunction.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiome may precede and accelerate Alzheimer's disease (AD) through immune, metabolic, and neural signaling along the gut-brain axis. We analyzed fecal microbiota from 212 participants, including cognitively unimpaired individuals and patients with mild cognitive impairment or AD dementia, using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics. We measured cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta, tau, and short-chain fatty acids, then applied linear mixed-effects models and mediation analysis to relate microbial taxa to biomarkers and APOE genotype. Bacteroides and Prevotella differed by AD status. Lower Faecalibacterium abundance correlated with higher amyloid-beta burden and neuroinflammation. In individuals carrying APOE ε4, these associations were stronger. Mediation analysis suggested short-chain fatty acids partly explained the link between microbial composition and AD-related biomarkers. Pathways enriched in AD included lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and branched-chain amino acid metabolism, which correlated with hippocampal atrophy and cognitive decline in a subset. These findings support targeting the gut microbiome for early risk stratification and therapy.

Disruption of gut microbiota by Western diet is increasingly linked to depression and anxiety, yet the molecular mediators remain poorly defined. In mice fed a high-fat, low-fiber diet, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and lower short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces. These shifts coincided with increased lipopolysaccharide translocation, hippocampal BDNF downregulation, and elevated IL-6 and IL-1β expression. Supplementation with prebiotic oligofructose and probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored BDNF transcripts and normalized IL-6 levels, while fecal microbiota transplantation from supplemented donors partially reproduced these effects in germ-free recipients. Parallel shotgun metagenomics identified Akkermansia muciniphila as inversely correlated with IL-1β and neuroinflammation. These microbial and inflammatory signatures were partially reversed by synbiotic treatment. In humans, Mendelian randomization supported a causal association between gut microbiota composition and depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that dietary fiber and probiotics may modulate microbiota-brain signaling through BDNF and inflammatory pathways, offering accessible strategies for stress-related disorders.

Microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon generates short-chain fatty acids that signal to the brain and influence BDNF expression, a mechanism increasingly implicated in depression. We tested whether 12 weeks of inulin supplementation alters gut microbiota composition, butyrate production, and depressive symptoms in adults with overweight and subclinical low mood. Participants received inulin (n=48) or maltodextrin (n=46). Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were quantified by 16S rRNA sequencing; butyrate was measured by gas chromatography. BDNF methylation in blood and serotonin metabolites were assessed at baseline and endpoint. Inulin increased Bifidobacterium abundance and butyrate concentrations relative to maltodextrin (both p<0.05; linear mixed-effects models). Greater butyrate increases correlated with reduced BDNF methylation and lower depression scores. In exploratory functional MRI analyses, inulin was associated with altered prefrontal cortex responses to emotional faces, and these changes correlated with BDNF methylation (Spearman correlation). These findings support a microbiota-BDNF axis in which inulin may reduce depressive symptoms through butyrate-mediated epigenetic regulation.

Disruption of gut microbial communities can precede motor and cognitive symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), suggesting that gut-brain axis signaling contributes to neurodegeneration. In a cohort of patients with PD and healthy controls, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and increased Enterobacteriaceae. Metagenomic profiling further linked these shifts to diminished short-chain fatty acid production and altered GPR43 and BDNF expression in colonic mucosa. Fecal microbiota transplantation from PD donors into mice overexpressing α-synuclein aggravated motor deficits and neuroinflammation, whereas probiotic supplementation or butyrate restored BDNF signaling and reduced inflammatory cytokines. Increased intestinal permeability and lipopolysaccharide translocation correlated with NLRP3 inflammasome activation in substantia nigra, and vagotomy attenuated these effects in rodent models. These findings position the gut microbiome as a modifiable contributor to PD and support fecal microbiota transplantation and probiotics as candidate interventions, although causal mediation analyses in larger populations are needed. Together, these data suggest that targeting microbial composition may delay PD progression.

Gut microbial dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a modifier of neurodegenerative disease progression, yet whether microbiota-derived metabolites causally influence cognitive decline remains uncertain. We recruited 84 adults with mild cognitive impairment and profiled fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between microbial taxa, short-chain fatty acids, and longitudinal cognitive assessments over 12 months. Bacteroides abundance correlated negatively with trimethylamine N-oxide, while Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia were depleted in participants who progressed to dementia. Higher butyrate levels were associated with slower cognitive decline (false discovery rate-adjusted p = 0.012). Random forest classification using baseline gut microbiota and metabolite profiles discriminated progressors from stable individuals with an area under the curve of 0.81. In an exploratory subset, probiotic supplementation enriched Bifidobacterium and reduced trimethylamine N-oxide, but did not alter cognitive decline. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities and their metabolic products may serve as early biomarkers and therapeutic targets in cognitive impairment along the gut-brain axis.

Chronic intake of a high-fat, high-sugar diet destabilizes the gut microbiota and elevates circulating interleukin-6, a pattern linked to major depressive disorder. Whether probiotic supplementation can interrupt this axis was tested in a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial of adults with moderate depression. Participants continued their habitual Western diet and received either a multi-strain probiotic or placebo. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and plasma enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay quantified microbial composition and inflammatory markers. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline depression severity, body mass index, and antidepressant use. Relative to placebo, probiotic increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, reduced interleukin-6 and cortisol, and improved depressive symptoms. These changes correlated with decreased hippocampal activation during emotional processing. Mediation analysis estimated that microbial shifts explained 28% of the interleukin-6 reduction. The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may mitigate neuroinflammation in depressed adults consuming a Western diet, though confirmatory trials with longer follow-up are needed.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and function are increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the mechanisms linking intestinal dysbiosis to nigrostriatal degeneration remain unclear. We performed 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenomics on fecal samples from patients with PD and healthy controls, complemented by fecal microbiota transplantation into gnotobiotic mice overexpressing SNCA. Patients with PD exhibited reduced Prevotellaceae and Lachnospiraceae, depleted short-chain fatty acid producers, and elevated lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. Mice receiving microbiota from patients with PD developed motor deficits, striatal dopamine loss, and microglial activation compared with mice receiving control microbiota. RNA sequencing of midbrain revealed downregulation of Pink1, Park7, and Bdnf, alongside upregulated Il1b and Tnf. Targeted metabolomics further showed decreased butyrate and propionate in colon contents and serum. Random forest modeling discriminated patients with PD from controls with an area under the curve of 0.86 using microbial genera and metabolites. Notably, probiotic administration or levodopa partially rescued behavioral and transcriptomic phenotypes, but only in colonized mice. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities modulate SNCA-related neuroinflammation and dopaminergic injury, identifying candidate microbial targets for PD therapy.

Reduced gut microbiota production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is associated with Parkinson's disease (PD) severity, implicating microbial metabolites in gut-brain axis dysfunction. In a 12-week randomized trial, 52 patients with PD received probiotic supplementation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG plus Bifidobacterium animalis) or placebo. Fecal microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and butyrate, propionate, and acetate were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Linear mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time interactions, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Probiotics increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, raised fecal butyrate, and lowered interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha compared with placebo. These microbial and cytokine shifts correlated with reduced constipation and improved motor symptoms. Baseline Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was higher in responders than in non-responders. Fecal butyrate increases correlated with motor symptom improvement using Spearman correlation. The data support probiotic supplementation as an adjunctive approach for modulating gut microbiota in PD, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and lipopolysaccharide translocate across the intestinal barrier to modulate central immune signaling and BDNF expression in the brain, linking gut microbiota composition to Parkinson's disease progression. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, patients with Parkinson's disease received inulin (12 g/day) or placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, measured by 16S rRNA sequencing, increased with inulin and correlated with elevated fecal butyrate and reduced circulating lipopolysaccharide. Motor severity improved in the inulin group, accompanied by increased BDNF and decreased NLRP3 expression in peripheral blood. Shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics profiled the microbiome and metabolites; no serious adverse events occurred. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and baseline microbiome diversity showed a significant group-by-time interaction for butyrate and motor scores. Mediation analysis indicated that Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance indirectly influenced motor improvement through butyrate. Changes in BDNF correlated with butyrate (r = 0.42, P = 0.008). These findings suggest that inulin supplementation may modulate gut microbiota-brain signaling and warrant larger trials.

Depletion of dietary fiber and excess Western-style diet consumption drive gut microbiota dysbiosis, impairing bidirectional gut–brain signaling that regulates mood. In mice, fiber deprivation reduced microbial short-chain fatty acid output, especially butyrate, and lowered hippocampal serotonin and Bdnf expression. 16S rRNA sequencing and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry showed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances tracked with depressive-like behavior. Spearman correlation linked butyrate concentrations inversely with anxiety scores. Butyrate supplementation restored Bdnf and normalized behavior. In patients with major depressive disorder, gut microbiota from low-fiber diets produced less butyrate ex vivo. A randomized controlled trial of Mediterranean diet enriched with fermentable fiber increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced depression severity. Germ-free mice colonized with microbiota from patients with depression exhibited anhedonia, elevated interleukin-6, and altered tryptophan–kynurenine metabolism. Untargeted metabolomics with linear mixed-effects models identified indole derivatives as mediators. These findings position dietary fiber and microbial metabolites as promising modifiable targets for depression prevention and treatment.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiome precedes motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with reduced butyrate production and elevated lipopolysaccharide translocation. In a cohort of 120 patients with PD and 80 healthy controls, shotgun metagenomic sequencing of the gut microbiome revealed depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia, alongside enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila. These shifts were associated with constipation severity and SNCA expression in blood (false discovery rate q < 0.05). Dietary interventions may modify this axis: higher adherence to a Mediterranean diet predicted greater gut microbiome diversity, while probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium animalis reduced calprotectin and improved anxiety scores in a mouse model. In patients receiving levodopa, omega-3 fatty acid co-supplementation was linked to lower inflammatory cytokine levels, but effects on motor progression remain uncertain. Greater intake of dietary fiber correlated with higher butyrate and lower cognitive impairment, suggesting that fermented foods and targeted synbiotics warrant controlled trials as adjunctive strategies for PD.

Diets enriched with blueberries improve Alzheimer's disease-related cognitive deficits in APP/PS1 mice, yet the microbial signals linking anthocyanins to hippocampal plasticity remain unclear. We treated APP/PS1 mice with anthocyanin extract from blueberries for 16 weeks and profiled gut microbiota by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Morris water maze and fear conditioning revealed restored spatial and associative memory. Supplementation increased Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, elevated butyrate and propionate, and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus. BDNF and PSD-95 expression was upregulated, while neuroinflammation and amyloid-β deposition were attenuated. Plasma lipopolysaccharide was lower, and ZO-1 and occludin in the colon were increased, suggesting improved gut barrier function. Spearman correlation analysis linked butyrate levels with Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and memory scores. Fecal transfer from supplemented mice to antibiotic-treated mice partially reproduced these benefits, implicating a microbiota-gut-brain axis. In adults, baseline gut microbiota composition predicts responses to blueberry supplementation, but causal links require further fecal microbiota transplantation trials. These findings support blueberry-derived anthocyanins as a preventive strategy against Alzheimer's disease.
